problems.title: Chronological relation scoring depends on sample-list order
problems.source_location: Section 2.3.3, Eqs.(6)–(7), PDF p.5; interface_searcher.py, compute_frame_relation_scores and sample_frames
claim: Temporal and causal bonuses depend on the objects’ frame times. The release enumerates only list positions \(j\geq i\), although later weighted samples are unsorted.
analysis: Let object A occur at time \(1\), B at \(4\), with base scores \(0.4,0.6\), relation increment \(0.15\) and temporal window \(5\). List order \((4,2,1,0)\) places B before A. The upper-triangular loop never tests the required A–B orientation, returning \((0.4,0.6)\) at the two endpoints rather than \((0.55,0.75)\). Their actual times satisfy \(1<4\) and \(4-1<5\).
result: The release has an order-dependent scoring omission. Sorting would avoid this particular case; video-answer accuracy is not determined by it.
assumptions: A fresh unsatisfied relation; aligned records remain paired when reordered.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Sort all aligned frame records by time, or enumerate endpoint pairs and apply explicit time predicates.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: A global relation latch suppresses later distinct evidence
problems.source_location: Eq.(4), PDF p.5; Algorithm 2, PDF p.20; compute_frame_relation_scores
claim: The paper awards a spatial bonus to each qualifying frame; the release skips a relation after its persistent Boolean has been set.
analysis: Two batches contain A and B together at distinct times \(1\) and \(8\), with base scores \(0.4\) and \(0.5\). A \(0.15\) bonus produces \(0.55\) in the first call and sets the latch. The next call returns \(0.5\), although the per-frame formula gives \(0.65\). An unrelated remaining target can keep search active. Multiple matches within the first call can still receive bonuses.
result: The intentional one-shot release policy differs from the unqualified per-frame scoring description; its aggregate search effect is unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Track distinct frame/relation evidence and reconstruct scores from base confidence plus valid bonuses, rather than disabling the whole relation.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Single-frame verification changes scores and borrows another target’s confidence
problems.source_location: Eqs.(2)–(4), PDF pp.4–5; verify_and_remove_target, lines 667–713
claim: Individual verification overwrites a relation-integrated registry entry with the maximum base detection score and uses that frame maximum to certify a named target.
analysis: A frame with base \(0.8\) and a valid \(0.15\) relation bonus outranks a competitor at \(0.9\). Verification writes \(0.8\), reversing the ranking although the relation persists. Separately, present objects A and B with confidences \(0.4\) and \(0.95\), unit weights and threshold \(0.7\) yield frame maximum \(0.95\). The target loop can remove A because A is present and that maximum exceeds the threshold, although A’s own confidence does not. Both confidences exceed the detector filter \(0.2\).
result: Both local effects follow from the inspected assignments. Membership prevents certifying an absent object, but does not make a frame maximum target-specific.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Preserve score components and reconstruct valid relation evidence after re-detection. Compare the target’s own detections with the confirmation threshold.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The printed first iteration has linear work
problems.source_location: Algorithms 1–2, PDF pp.4,20; Appendix F.1 and F.3, PDF pp.19,21
claim: The algorithms initialize \(B=N=|V|\), set \(k=\lfloor\sqrt B\rfloor\), and sample \(k^2\) frames; Appendix F.3 claims total time \(O(\sqrt N)\).
analysis: For \(N=m^2\), the first round samples exactly \(N\) entries. In general, \[M_1=\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor^2>N-2\sqrt N+1.\] Thus \(M_1=\Theta(N)\) and \(M_1/N\to1\). Materializing or processing each sampled frame costs at least constant work, giving a first-round \(\Omega(N)\) lower bound. The released constructor instead uses a capped practical budget; that different procedure is not refuted by this literal-pseudocode argument.
result: The ordinary-cost square-root claim is incompatible with the printed algorithm. This does not invalidate measured frame fractions for the differently budgeted release.
assumptions: The first loop executes and per-frame materialization or processing has positive constant cost.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify actual candidate/budget units and account for initialization, sampled entries, relation checks, detector work and dense updates. The printed algorithm’s linear first-round lower bound must be retained.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The alternative Beta sampler needs bounded reward semantics
problems.source_location: Appendix F.4, Eq.(18), PDF pp.21–22
claim: The second Beta shape is \(\beta_t+n-\sum_i S_i(t)\), without an explicit connection between \(S_i\) and bounded rewards.
analysis: If \(S_i\) are the integrated scores, base \(1\) plus two bonuses \(0.15\) gives \(1.3\). With \(n=4\) and unit priors, the shapes are \(6.2\) and \(-0.2\), which cannot define a Beta law. If instead \(S_i\in[0,1]\) are separately normalized rewards, the second shape is at least \(\beta_t>0\). The inspected release does not use this alternative sampler.
result: A conditional specification gap remains; an actual release failure or the intended reward interpretation is not established.

problems.title: Independent axis maxima can cancel in the combined warp
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Eqs.(1)–(2), PDF p.5; utils.py, max_warp_latents
claim: The displayed target maximizes joint latent distance. The release maximizes \(L(d_x,0)\) and \(L(0,d_y)\) separately and combines their offsets.
analysis: For the accepted four-channel \(64\times64\) latent \(z_{c,i,j}=(-1)^{i+j}\), the released \(512\)-pixel flow grid induces latent source coordinate \(j+d_x/8-1/16\), with nearest-neighbor reflection. Offset \(-27\) flips parity at \(61\) of \(64\) positions per axis. Hence \(L(-27,0)=L(0,-27)=1.90625\), but the selected combination gives \[L(-27,-27)=4(61/64)(3/64)=0.1787109375.\] Offset \(20\) flips only \(2\) positions, so \[L(-27,20)=2\{(61\cdot62+3\cdot2)/4096\}=1.849609375.\] Both pairs lie within the source’s own candidate product and \([-40,40]^2\).
result: The accepted-input heuristic need not solve the joint surrogate objective. Reachability of this checkerboard by natural-image inversion, and any resulting attack-quality effect, remain unestablished.
assumptions: The exact source warp and its reflection/rounding convention are retained; the input is a programmatic latent, without an asserted natural-image preimage.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Joint finite enumeration returns a maximizer over its declared candidate product. It does not solve unrestricted continuous flow optimization or prove better watermark removal.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: One low-FPR operating point does not imply indistinguishability
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, PDF p.7; Section 4.2 RQ1, Table 1 and Figure 3, PDF p.8
claim: The discussion infers indistinguishability from shifted detector distances and low \(\mathrm{TPR}\) at \(1\%\) false-positive rate.
analysis: Let lower distance indicate a watermark. Take negative scores \(0,1,\ldots,99\) and positive scores consisting of seven copies of \(-0.5\) and ninety-three copies of \(7.5\). Threshold \(0.5\) gives \(\mathrm{FPR}=0.01\) and \(\mathrm{TPR}=0.07\). Yet the pairwise AUC is \[(7\cdot100+93\cdot92)/10000=0.9256.\] These are explicitly constructed scores, not the paper’s unpublished image scores. Repository issue 2, opened by XiaoxiKong on 27 December 2025, independently raised the high-AUC concern; its empirical measurements were not reproduced here.
result: The operating-point result remains meaningful, but does not establish equality of score distributions or absence of all watermark information.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State that the evaluated detector’s sensitivity falls at the threshold calibrated to \(1\%\) false-positive rate; retain the distinction from distributional indistinguishability.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Distributional image-quality scores do not certify each image
problems.source_location: Image-quality evaluation, PDF pp.8–9 and Appendix quality tables
claim: FID and aggregate CLIP scores assess distributional quality and prompt alignment.
analysis: Permuting generated images within a prompt-compatible collection preserves distributional FID and aggregate semantic scores while changing which source image receives which output. Thus those summaries alone cannot certify instance-wise preservation. The paper’s reported scores themselves are not contradicted.
result: This is a metric-scope clarification; no separate image-level defect is established.

problems.title: The source-to-energy formula can be negative
problems.source_location: Lemma 5.3, Eqs.(10)–(11), PDF p.6; Appendix B.5, Eqs.(65)–(71), PDF pp.28–29
claim: The lemma prescribes \(B_i(0)=0\) and \(B_i^{\prime}=(1-\alpha_i+\lambda_i(\beta_i+t))(\beta_i+t)^{-\alpha_i}\), then identifies a displayed series with Dirichlet energy.
analysis: On the unit circle, one normalized eigenmode of eigenvalue \(1\), with \(\alpha=3\), \(\beta=1/2\) and zero initial state, has \(B=(t+1/2)^{-2}-(t+1/2)^{-1}-2\). Its exact amplitude is \(a=-(t+1/2)^{-1}-2+4e^{-t}\), so the true energy \(a^2/2\) is zero initially while the printed summand is \(-4\).

The infinite-series concern is also avoidable. For both sine/cosine modes of frequency \(k\), take \(\alpha_k=3\), \(\beta_1=1/2\) and \(\beta_k=k^4\) for \(k\ge2\), with \(B_k=-k^2/(\beta_k+t)+(\beta_k+t)^{-2}+k^2/\beta_k-\beta_k^{-2}\). These sources obey the derivative and zero-initial conditions and converge uniformly on compact time intervals, since \(|B_k(t)|\le T(k^{-6}+2k^{-12})\). The printed initial energy is \[-8+2\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}(k^{-2}-k^{-4}-k^{-8})<-6,\] whereas zero initial data has zero true gradient energy. The high-frequency parameters satisfy the main lemma’s \(\beta_k>0\), rather than the appendix’s extra \(\beta_k<1\).
result: The displayed identity and modal derivation fail. This does not refute the weaker existence of specially designed forcing with polynomial energy decay.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The correct modal identities are \[a_i(t)=c_i e^{-\lambda_i t}+\int_0^t e^{-\lambda_i(t-s)}B_i(s)\,ds,\qquad E(t)=\tfrac12\sum_i\lambda_i a_i(t)^2.\] Boundary quadratic forms require their own boundary terms.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Boundary lifting alone does not prevent energy decay
problems.source_location: Theorem 5.4, Eq.(12), PDF p.7; Appendix B.6, PDF pp.29–30
claim: The lift \(v=u-w\), with source \(\Delta w-w_t\), is asserted to satisfy Lemma 5.3 and yield simultaneous mitigation.
analysis: On \([0,\pi]\), boundary values \(u(t,0)=u(t,\pi)=1\) and initial state \(1+\sin x\) have exact solution \(u=1+e^{-t}\sin x\). Its energy is \(E=\pi e^{-2t}/4\to0\). The constant lift \(w=1\) has zero source. Another lift cannot change the physical solution or its energy; cross terms can cancel when reconstructing \(u=v+w\).
result: Ordinary lifting is valid, but neither its algebra nor nonzero boundary data establishes the universal anti-oversmoothing consequence.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the lifting identity and impose separate source and energy hypotheses before drawing an energy-decay conclusion.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The Robin block system and indicator split are inequivalent
problems.source_location: Eqs.(13)–(17), PDF p.7; Appendix B.7, Eqs.(78)–(84), PDF pp.30–31
claim: The scalar Robin sum \(\alpha_i x_i+\beta_i\sum_{j\in S,j\sim i}(x_i-x_j)=\gamma_i\) is converted to the printed block system and indicator-based Jacobi update.
analysis: With one interior node and one boundary node joined by an edge, unit \(\alpha,\beta\), boundary right side zero and interior right side one, the scalar equations are \(x_0-x_1=1\), \(2x_1-x_0=0\), yielding \((2,1)\). The printed block instead requires \(x_1-x_0=0\), an inconsistent system. It loses \(\beta_i d_{iS}x_i\). On the same graph, the printed indicator degree is zero at both nodes, causing division by zero. On an all-interior triangle it avoids zero denominators but counts each normalized off-diagonal contribution twice, producing \(A\) instead of \(A/2\).
result: The claimed scalar-to-block-to-Jacobi equivalence fails even on elementary graphs. A separately defined learned architecture can remain useful.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The raw-difference boundary row is \[(\alpha_i+\beta_i d_{iS})x_i-\beta_i\sum_{j\in S}A_{ij}x_j=\gamma_i.\] Use a genuine disjoint upper/lower splitting; this repairs the linear identity without proving nonlinear convergence.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Variable-width geometry and the Neumann scale are inconsistent
problems.source_location: Theorem 5.1, PDF p.6; Appendix B.3, Eqs.(47)–(57), PDF pp.25–27
claim: The variable-radius tube uses a separated Laplacian and a Neumann-gap scale proportional to \([\varepsilon_0\cosh(aL/2)]^{-2}\).
analysis: For metric \(ds^2+\varepsilon(s)^2g_B\) with fiber dimension \(m\), the Laplacian is \[\partial_{ss}+m(\varepsilon^{\prime}/\varepsilon)\partial_s+\varepsilon^{-2}\Delta_B.\] The omitted drift already changes its value on \(v=s\). Independently, on the Euclidean tube \(0<s<1\), \(|y|<\varepsilon_0\cosh(s-1/2)\), the zero-mean Neumann trial function \(v=s-1/2\) gives Rayleigh quotient \[\frac{\int_0^1\cosh(s-1/2)\,ds}{\int_0^1(s-1/2)^2\cosh(s-1/2)\,ds}\approx11.62161154.\] Thus the first positive gap is uniformly bounded above as \(\varepsilon_0\to0\), contradicting a fixed positive multiple of \(\varepsilon_0^{-2}\).
result: The variable-tube derivation and asserted scale fail. Constant-cross-section separation remains valid; the Neumann zero mode must also be retained.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify the metric and boundary realization and use its actual operator and variational spectrum; no replacement general asymptotic is established.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Local tube dimensions do not order the ambient spectral gap
problems.source_location: Corollary 5.2, PDF p.6; Appendix B.4, PDF p.28
claim: For a constant thin tube, the corollary asserts \(\lambda_D\ge\lambda\ge\lambda_N\), with \(\lambda\) the closed ambient gap.
analysis: Embed \([0,L]\times[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\) in a flat torus of circumferences \(4L,4\varepsilon\). Take \(L=10\), \(\varepsilon=0.1<\xi=0.2\). The ambient gap is \(\lambda=\pi^2/(4L^2)\), while the Neumann rectangle gap is \(\lambda_N=\pi^2/L^2=4\lambda\). The torus is closed and has zero Ricci curvature. Local dimensions alone do not identify a minimizing global bottleneck.
result: The asserted middle inequality is false under the given geometric conditions.

problems.title: The Neumann Bessel condition loses the radial prefactor derivative
problems.source_location: Appendix B.3, Eqs.(43)–(46), PDF p.26
claim: For \(R(r)=r^{-(n-2)/2}J_\nu(kr)\), the source replaces \(R^{\prime}(1)=0\) by \(J_\nu^{\prime}(k)=0\).
analysis: Direct differentiation gives \(R^{\prime}(1)=kJ_\nu^{\prime}(k)-(n-2)J_\nu(k)/2\). In the three-dimensional degree-zero branch, \(R\) is proportional to \(\sin(kr)/r\): the true condition is \(\tan k=k\), while the derivative-Bessel condition gives \(\tan k=2k\). Its first positive root near \(1.16556\) leaves nonzero boundary derivative \(-k\cos k\). The true degree-zero positive root is near \(4.49340946\); this is not the first positive root across all angular branches.
result: The root identity is invalid outside the constant-prefactor special case, including the stated three-dimensional example. Fixed-domain inverse-square scaling survives.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(kJ_\nu^{\prime}(k)-(n-2)J_\nu(k)/2=0\), retaining the Neumann constant mode.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: A convergent upper bound does not establish distance independence
problems.source_location: Theorem 6.3, PDF p.8; Appendix B.8, Eqs.(86)–(95), PDF pp.31–32
claim: The source turns a Jacobian upper bound involving \(\sum_{k=0}^K T^k\) into equality with a resolvent and concludes distance independence.
analysis: Grant fixed stable \[T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/2&1/2\\1/2&0&1/2\\1/8&1/8&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad \rho(T)\approx0.683013.\] Constant boundary coefficients \(\alpha=4,\beta=1\), identity maps and constant source make the printed recurrence \(x^{k+1}=Tx^k+b\). Its initial-state derivative is \(T^K\to0\), whereas the resolvent’s \((1,3)\) entry is \(4/3\). If initial features are instead reinjected each round, a power sum can arise; even then, a nonnegative local matrix with row sums at most \(q<1\) obeys \([(I-T)^{-1}]_{ij}\le q^d/(1-q)\) at distance \(d\).
result: The appendix’s depth-limit equality and the distance-independence inference are not proved. The fixed-graph example is not mislabeled as a growing-distance graph family.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify injection dependence, fixed versus state-dependent operators and uniform derivative bounds; the special linear formulas alone do not prove a general anti-oversquashing theorem.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The transfer score admits a purely local perfect predictor
problems.source_location: Section 7, Figure 5, PDF p.10; Appendix E.1, PDF p.36; data_utils.py generators and graph_transfer.py masks
claim: Endpoint-only loss is interpreted as a test of long-range information transfer.
analysis: The scored source has input/label \((1,0)\) and target \((0,1)\). The node-local predictor \(\widehat y_v=1-x_v\) has exactly zero scored error for every graph and all intermediate features. It uses no edge or remote payload. Under the main text’s alternative signed endpoint convention, \(\widehat y=-x\) supplies the same shortcut.
result: This task cannot distinguish remote transport from a local transformation. It does not establish which shortcut a trained model used or falsify its reported MSE.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use an independently random distant source bit with a fixed target input; a target-only predictor then has expected squared error at least \(1/4\) for a balanced bit.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Fresh validation and test generation reuse one random stream
problems.source_location: Appendix E.1, PDF p.36; GraphTransferDataset.process, lines 220–238; graph_transfer.py split construction
claim: The release declares separate validation and test graphs but uses a seed expression keyed to valid, while callers pass val.
analysis: The expression selects \(1234\) for train, \(2345\) for valid, and \(3456\) otherwise. Both accepted caller names val and test therefore select \(3456\), generate \(100\) graphs and invoke the same topology/features/random sequence after resetting generators. Their fresh-generated content is identical; filenames do not supply independence. Pre-existing caches or unreleased data could alter what published runs consumed.
result: This is a concrete conference-release split defect. Its occurrence and numerical impact in the published runs remain unestablished.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use consistent canonical split names and distinct random streams, regenerate affected splits, and repeat selection/evaluation before quantifying impact.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: TCGA tables do not support the headline magnitude or uniform improvement
problems.source_location: Abstract, PDF p.1; Table 1, PDF p.8; supplementary Section 2.3 and Table S2, PDF pp.23–24
claim: The text describes a two-to-threefold FD improvement including TCGA and broadly superior quality under crop conditioning.
analysis: For the eight shared TCGA encoders, only five FD values decrease and the baseline/new ratios lie between \(0.8268824771\) and \(1.1109190807\). PathDino changes \(4306.7\to3876.7\), a factor \(1.110919\); DINOv2 changes \(117.5\to142.1\), a \(20.94\%\) increase. Any nonnegative consistently weighted ratio of sums is a convex combination of those ratios and cannot reach \(2\). All eleven supplementary recalls and F1 scores decline; for example Lunit recall changes \(0.017\to0.010\), RN50-BT \(0.212\to0.149\), and UNI \(0.016\to0.014\). PANDA improves across the main encoders, and rounding-compatible F1 values are not arithmetic errors.
result: TCGA supports a metric tradeoff and encoder-dependent changes. The displayed measurements, positive PANDA evidence and downstream segmentation results are not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Qualify the headline by dataset: TCGA’s displayed FD improvement factor is at most \(1.111\), with lower recall/F1 across all eleven encoders.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Absolute FLD does not calibrate patient-identification risk
problems.source_location: Supplementary Section 2.1 and Table S1, PDF pp.22–23; cited FLD paper, Eqs.(3),(5)
claim: Values below \(10\) are interpreted as effective protection against patient reconstruction or identification.
analysis: FLD is an adjusted feature-space negative log-likelihood, not an identification probability. Let records be \((z,s)\), with confidential identifier \(s\), and evaluated feature map \(\phi(z,s)=z\). Two generators can return the same four feature vectors \((0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)\), while one repeats confidential identifiers and the other supplies unrelated identifiers. All fitted feature-metric inputs and FLD values are equal, yet direct identifier matching succeeds on \(4/4\) versus \(0/4\). This is a mathematical information-loss witness, not an asserted pathology-encoder collision.
result: An absolute feature score alone cannot supply the claimed general privacy conclusion. The model’s actual leakage risk was not measured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Relabel FLD as a sample-quality/generalization diagnostic and remove the universal privacy-threshold interpretation; no numerical privacy bound is established.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Vertical-flip flag binds to the flow argument
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, PDF p.6; stereosr_image_dataset.py, lines 65–70; BasicSR 1.3.5 transforms.py, augment
claim: The caller expects four augmented images and passes its vertical-flip Boolean as the fourth positional argument.
analysis: The pinned signature is augment(imgs, hflip, rotation, flows, return_status). The flags bind flows to True. With rotation disabled and a sampled false horizontal flip, the dependency returns the pair consisting of the four-image list and that flow value. The caller unpacks two outer values into four variables and must fail. Valid scale-four image pairs of spatial sizes \(256\times256\) and \(64\times64\) do not alter this contract. Other random branches may fail earlier while manipulating the Boolean as flow.
result: The released caller/dependency combination has a sufficient loader failure. It does not establish that no privately patched training environment existed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a shared explicit horizontal/vertical image transformation returning four images. Moving the vertical flag into the dependency’s rotation argument would also enable transpose behavior and is not equivalent.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Standalone export selects the left channels twice
problems.source_location: inference_swinfirssr.py, lines 62–77; SwinFIRSSRModel validation, lines 45–46
claim: Both standalone output branches spatially crop the same six-channel tensor and select the same first three channels.
analysis: For stereo RGB levels \((0.1,0.2,0.3)\) and \((0.7,0.8,0.9)\), both branches export BGR \((0.3,0.2,0.1)\), whereas the right branch should export \((0.9,0.8,0.7)\). The indexing discards channels \(3\)–\(5\). The script also references a local image variable before assignment, so this is a latent defect after that earlier blocker. The separate model-validation path correctly splits at channel \(3\).
result: This export path loses the right view when views differ. The correct validation path prevents inferring that published stereo averages necessarily used duplicate left images.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Split the six-channel output into channels \(0\)–\(2\) and \(3\)–\(5\) before spatial cropping and color conversion.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The release does not identify the narrated training protocol
problems.source_location: Sections 4.1 and 4.3.1, PDF pp.6,9; training YAML lines 78–83; diffssr_arch.py, line 256
claim: The paper describes \(500{,}000\) iterations with cosine decay and selects window \(3\); the release uses \(800{,}000\) iterations, MultiStepLR and window \(5\).
analysis: The first released milestone is \(600{,}000\), so it has not fired by the paper’s endpoint \(500{,}000\), where the stated cosine decay would be complete. The main stereo scores agree with the window-\(5\) ablation row, which supports an alternative run interpretation but does not identify every checkpoint. The paper also studies test-time window changes. Per-GPU batch size and global batch size are not silently equated.
result: The artifact mismatch is established, but the exact historical experiment recipe remains unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Associate each checkpoint/table row with its actual configuration, dependencies, seed, duration and training/test window. Do not replace these with a guessed recipe.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Rejected alternatives mutate the selected continuation
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1, lines 6–9, PDF p.5; DPOAgent.step, lines 180–381
claim: Candidates should execute from the same pre-step history and continue only the selected branch.
analysis: Start with counter \(0\) and empty trail. Candidate A adds \(1\) and appends selected; B adds \(100\) and appends rejected; C prints the counter. The inspected sequential shared-state calls yield observations \(1,101,101\). If A is chosen, its recorded observation is \(1\), but the environment remains at \(101\) with B’s rejected trail entry. Independent branches give \(1,100,0\) and commit counter \(1\). Reordering to C,B,A makes the selected A observe \(101\), showing context contamination rather than merely a stale display. Redefining a helper in B similarly changes the shared custom-tool namespace. Adding two read-only candidates preserves the defect at the paper’s count \(5\).
result: The release violates common-context comparison and selected-state continuation for admissible stateful actions. Pure independent actions can avoid it. Published evaluation disables this sampling path; training-data prevalence and benchmark effect are unestablished.
assumptions: Ordinary assignment/list mutation is permitted. The verifier deliberately selects A, removing verifier-error uncertainty.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Fork the entire relevant execution environment for each candidate and commit only the selected branch. Deep-copying value state repairs the counter/list witness, but does not automatically isolate tool objects, closures, files or external effects.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The public constructor ignores an explicit candidate-count override
problems.source_location: create_agent sampling_size construction; Section 4.5 experimental candidate count
claim: The constructor exposes a formal candidate-count argument but reads the effective value from extra keyword arguments with a default.
analysis: A bound formal argument is removed from the extra-keyword dictionary, so looking it up there uses the default \(5\) even after an explicit different request. The paper itself uses \(5\), so this does not challenge its reported setting.
result: This is a minor API observation; no distinct scientific failure is established.

problems.title: Local nonnegativity does not imply the small-loss bound
problems.source_location: Theorem 4, Eq.(22), PDF p.9; Assumptions 1,4, PDF pp.2,9; Eq.(5), PDF p.4
claim: For nonnegative convex \(M\)-smooth losses on a closed decision set of diameter \(D\), Eq.(22) bounds regret by \(4D\sqrt{M\sum_t l_t(u)}+4D^2M\).
analysis: Take \(\mathcal X=[0,1]\), \(D=T=x_1=1\), comparator \(u=0\), and \(l(x)=x/2+x^2/200\). On the stated domain, \(0\le l\le0.505<1\), while \(l^{\prime\prime}=M=0.01\) exactly. The comparator loss is zero, so the claimed right side is \(0.04\), but the first-round regret is \(0.505\). The nonzero gradient \(0.51\) avoids step-size singularity; no update can undo an already incurred first loss. Setting the ordinary cost to zero and constraint penalty to this loss gives the same violation of the explicit constraint-only illustration. The polynomial is globally smooth but is not globally nonnegative.
result: The local-domain theorem and explicit constant fail. This does not directly refute the expert/covering route or establish a contrary asymptotic rate for every smooth extension.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Add \(\|\nabla l_t(x)\|^2\le2Ml_t(x)\), for example through a globally nonnegative smooth extension. Adaptive projection then gives \(R\le2D\sqrt{M(R+L)}\), whence \(R\le4D^2M+2D\sqrt{ML}\), restoring the more conservative printed constants. Weighted Cauchyâ€“Schwarz supplies the corresponding self-bound for nonnegative surrogates.
This domain omission is inherited from the cited older monograph wording; its later edition explicitly assumes self-boundedness. No paper-specific author adoption is established.

problems.title: The printed covariance conditions permit a negative class gradient
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.2, Eqs.(3)–(5), PDF p.5; Appendix B.4, PDF pp.26–27
claim: The theorem gives nonnegative class-weight gradient when \(\sigma^2\ge\|b\|^2/(4d_{\rm irr})\) and \(\sigma^2\ge\|c\|^2/(4d_{\rm noise})\), where \(c=\operatorname{Cov}(v^{\rm noise},\hat y)\) already includes noise severity.
analysis: Let \(Y,R_0,R_1,R_2,R_3\) be independent uniform signs, \(y=(Y+1)/2\), \[v=(Y,R_0,0,R_1/2,R_2/2,R_3/2)\], \(\mu=1\), \(s=1/2\), and all weights \(1\). Use opposite unit text embeddings in direction \((11/10,0,0,8,4,2)\). Then \(\hat y=\mathbf1\{(11/10)Y+4R_1+2R_2+R_3>0\}\), with strict margin \(0.1\). All \(32\) atoms have norm squared \(11/4\). Their exact moments are \(p=1/2\), \(C=8\), \(\sigma=1/16\), \(b=0\), and \(c=(3/16,1/16,1/16)\). Both printed conditions hold because \(1/256\ge11/3072\). Varying only the class weight \(x\), the retained variance identity gives \[V(x)=\frac{4x^2+11}{64x^2+112},\qquad V^{\prime}(1)=-\frac2{121}.\] The printed derivative instead gives \(5/242>0\).
result: The sign conclusion fails under the stated model. At \(s=1\) the missing factor disappears, and for \(s\ge1\) the printed condition can still suffice. The paper does not impose that restriction on its latent severity. A full update’s accuracy and the autodifferentiated release objective are separate questions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The noise bracket must be \(4\sigma^2s^2d_{\rm noise}-\|c\|^2\), giving sufficient condition \(\sigma^2\ge\|c\|^2/(4s^2d_{\rm noise})\) for positive severity/dimension. Quotient differentiation also gives shift derivative \(-2V(\mathbf1)s^2\delta^2/D_0\); its nonpositive sign survives the coefficient correction. Zero severity or absent components need separate omission rather than division by zero.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Strict magnitude ascent can stop at a plateau
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.3 and proof, PDF p.4; option.take_option_action
claim: For \(L=I+\operatorname{diag}(N)-P\), starting at \(N_i>\operatorname{Re}\lambda\), the theorem promises a strictly increasing magnitude path ending below that threshold.
analysis: Use the directed cycle \(0\to1\to2\to0\), \(N=(1/4,1/8,11/28)\), \(f=(1,1,7/8)\), and \(\lambda=1/4\). Direct substitution gives \(Lf=\lambda f\), and the positive eigenvector is the principal mode after a nonnegative irreducible shift. Starting at \(2\), magnitude rises to \(1\) at node \(0\), but \(N_0=\lambda\). The only next step reaches node \(1\) at equal magnitude, violating strict ascent; only that plateau traversal reaches \(N_1<\lambda\). A connected undirected tree with edges \(01,12,23,14,45\), \(N=(1/2,1/2,0,0,0,0)\), \[f=(0,0,1/\sqrt2,1,-1/\sqrt2,-1)\], and \(\lambda=1-1/\sqrt2\) gives a second exact eigenpair: node \(0\) has only the zero-magnitude successor \(1\), so no first strict step exists.
result: Both positive plateaus and zero plateaus defeat the universal strict claim and the corresponding stop-on-ties interpretation. The more restricted source-maximum theorem and reported reward curves are not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: With nonzero starting entry, strict ascent guarantees only an endpoint \(N\le\operatorname{Re}\lambda\). Allowing nondecreasing steps can restore the strict novelty threshold under strong connectivity, but requires plateau traversal with a visited set and changes the existing termination policy.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: An undirected random walk is not Euclidean Hermitian
problems.source_location: Section 3, PDF pp.3–4; Appendix D, PDF p.22
claim: The operator \(I+\Gamma-D^{-1}A\) is called Hermitian on undirected graphs and assigned an unweighted Euclidean edge-energy formula.
analysis: For the three-vertex undirected path, degrees are \((1,2,1)\), so \(P_{01}=1\ne P_{10}=1/2\). With zero potential and \(x=(0,1,0)\), \(x^\top(I-P)x=1\), but the printed edge sum \(\tfrac12\sum_{ij}P_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2=3/2\). Right eigenvectors \((1,1,1)\) and \((1,-1,1)\) have distinct eigenvalues \(0,2\) yet Euclidean inner product \(1\).
result: Euclidean symmetry and orthogonality fail on irregular graphs. Real eigenvalues survive by similarity to a symmetric matrix; regular graphs remain a valid special case.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the degree-weighted inner product and quotient \[\frac{\tfrac12\sum_{ij}A_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2+\sum_i d_iN_ix_i^2}{\sum_i d_ix_i^2},\] or the symmetric operator \(D^{1/2}LD^{-1/2}\). This does not itself prove orthogonality of nonlinear magnitude-based policies.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Random-option selection occurs outside the epsilon event
problems.source_location: Section 5, PDF p.7; all_functions.py, AgentQ2.option_action, lines 487–514
claim: The paper chooses a random option with probability initP conditional on an epsilon exploration step. The release makes a new option draw after the epsilon-greedy action.
analysis: With one eligible option, no active option, a greedy primitive action and independent draws \(u,v\), let \(\epsilon=\mathrm{initP}=0.1\). At \(u=0.5,v=0.05\), the release overrides a greedy action with an option; the described conditional procedure does not. The eligible-decision branch probability is \(0.1\), versus \(0.1\cdot0.1=0.01\). These are branch probabilities, not fractions of all environment transitions. An outer false exploration flag suppresses this direct branch, but recursive termination calls need not preserve that flag.
result: The released selector and described protocol differ. Published-run correspondence and reward-curve effects remain unestablished.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either condition option sampling on the single epsilon event or document the independent override, according to the actual run protocol. No fully integrated selector repair is claimed.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Unnormalized module rewards do not dominate layer rewards
problems.source_location: arXiv v3, Proposition 2, PDF p.6; conference Eqs.(2),(5), PDF pp.4–5
claim: The comparison maximizes expected squared module/layer gradient gain minus \(\eta^{-1}\) KL to its respective uniform distribution and asserts module-wise objective superiority.
analysis: Take two layers, each containing two scalar modules with gradient \(1\), and \(\eta=1\). Each layer gain is \(2\); each module gain is \(1\). Uniform distributions make the KL penalties zero, so the optimized values are \(V_{\rm layer}=2\), \(V_{\rm module}=1\). More generally the log-sum-exp variational identity and \(a_{ij}\le S_i=\sum_j a_{ij}\) imply \(V_{\rm module}(\eta)\le V_{\rm layer}(\eta)\), reversing the claimed weak ordering. These gradients are realizable in the globally smooth lower-bounded objective \(\sum_{\ell=1}^4(1-\cos\theta_\ell)\) at \(\theta_\ell=\pi/2\).
result: The unnormalized superiority argument is false; it compares different amounts of updated work. The softmax optimizer itself remains valid.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For equal module-count cost, use layer gain \(S_i/K\). Mapping \(q_{ij}=p_i/K\) preserves both this normalized gain and the KL, proving \(K^{-1}V_{\rm layer}(\eta/K)\le V_{\rm module}(\eta)\le V_{\rm layer}(\eta)\). This does not normalize unequal FLOPs or memory.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Positive sampling weights need not give positive inclusion
problems.source_location: arXiv v3, Algorithm 1, PDF p.7; analytical algorithm and convergence appendix; weighted_sample_without_replacement
claim: The practical method rejects selections above a parameter budget, while the analytical method samples a module directly and uses different inherited/maximal second moments.
analysis: Use modules with \(3\) and \(1\) parameters out of \(4\), budget fraction \(\delta=1/2\), and objective \(f=1-\cos\theta_1\), initialized at \(\theta_1=\pi/2\) in the larger module. That module’s ratio \(3/4>1/2\) never fits; the smaller module has zero gradient. All updates leave \(\|\nabla f\|^2=1\), despite global smoothness, bounded deterministic unbiased gradient and zero noise variance. Positive nominal probabilities and least-recently-used preferences cannot overcome a hard size exclusion.
result: An unrestricted convergence transfer to the practical budgeted sampler fails. This example does not contradict the analytical algorithm under its own direct-sampling assumptions or identify an excluded block in the reported LLM runs.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Every optimized block must fit, with suitable actual inclusion bounds and optimizer hypotheses, or the target must be restricted to movable parameters. No sufficient replacement practical convergence theorem is established.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Repeated bias correction distorts the historical score
problems.source_location: block_coordinate_optimizer.py, lines 195–220 and 283–294; gradient-indicator equation
claim: The stored recurrence divides its already corrected EMA by \(1-\beta^t\) again at each observation.
analysis: For unit observations and \(\beta=0.8\), the source recurrence gives \(G_1=1\), \(G_2=1/(1-0.8^2)=25/9\), rather than the constant readout \(1\). Two equally strong modules with one and two observations then receive capped squared logits \(1\) and \(5\), hence probabilities approximately \(0.0179862\) and \(0.9820138\). Raw norm smoothing followed by squaring also differs from smoothing squared size-normalized gradients; modules with \(1\) and \(4\) unit-gradient parameters have raw norms \(1,2\) but equal size-normalized norms.
result: The inspected release’s indicator depends on observation count and an unmatched statistic. Its training effect and historical run correspondence remain unestablished.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Store raw \(M_t=\beta M_{t-1}+(1-\beta)x_t\) and compute separate readout \(M_t/(1-\beta^t)\). For constant \(x_t=x\), induction gives readout exactly \(x\). Reconcile the chosen score statistic separately.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Backward FLOPs omit input-gradient products
problems.source_location: arXiv v3, Appendix F, PDF pp.42–45; conference Appendix G, PDF pp.41–43
claim: The dense-product convention yields printed quadratic coefficients \(34\) for full backward and \(10\) for frozen backward, in units \(bsh^2\).
analysis: For FFN input width \(h\) and hidden width \(4h\), propagating through the first projection requires \(\nabla Z=(\nabla Z_1\odot{\bf1})W_1^\top\), costing \(8bsh^2\). Q/K/V input gradients contribute another \(6bsh^2\). These products remain necessary in frozen layers above trainable parameters. Adding the missing \(14\) gives full/frozen coefficients \(48\) and \(24\), retaining the source’s other operation conventions. Input gradients may legitimately be pruned below the earliest active layer.
result: Absolute dense-backward counts are incomplete. The qualitative budget threshold can survive the same simplified comparison model; hardware runtime and all graph-pruning cases were not measured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Include the explicit missing dense products; the resulting counts are \(48bsh^2+8bs^2h+2bas^2+14bsh\) and \(24bsh^2+8bs^2h+2bas^2+14bsh\) under the stated model.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Fixed exploration need not satisfy the conditional slot-regret premise
problems.source_location: Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 4.2, PDF p.6; Table 4, PDF p.15
claim: The theorem assumes slot regret and proves \(R(K)\le J^{-1}\sum_jR_j(K)+2K\varepsilon\); its sublinear corollary requires a further sublinear slot bound.
analysis: The decomposition follows directly by subtracting the additive rewards and bounding the two interaction terms by \(2\varepsilon\). With one slot, rewards \(1,0\), exact reward estimates and uniform exploration probability \(0.1\), even an oracle selector chooses the bad arm with probability \(0.05\), giving expected regret \(0.05K\). Thus that implementation need not satisfy the added sublinear premise. Positive fixed interaction bound also permits a linear term.
result: The conditional theorem is valid; practical application requires a separate feedback/exploration analysis. This is a scope clarification rather than a refutation.

problems.title: Observed noisy MAE is not a uniform interaction bound
problems.source_location: Section 5.3, PDF pp.9–10; regret_experiment.py, synthetic_reward and compute_interaction_term
claim: Figure 4’s interaction diagnostic is used to support \(\sup_\rho|h(\rho)|\le\varepsilon\).
analysis: The source computes mean absolute error of final slot models on observed noisy rewards. With two binary slots, target \((1,1)\), additive mean rewards \((1,1/2,1/2,0)\) and zero models, a record containing only \((2,2)\) has residual \(0\) while the maximum over all four actions is \(1\). A near-zero Gaussian noise observation gives an approximate version with positive probability. Conversely perfect additive models with \(h=0\) still have expected absolute residual \(0.05\sqrt{2/\pi}\approx0.0398942\).
result: The statistic mixes model error, noise and visited actions; it does not estimate the stated uniform structural quantity.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe it as observed mean absolute prediction residual. Keep noiseless additivity, noise and held-out/uniform residual checks distinct.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Aliased reset snapshots and a differentiable anchor defeat their intended operations
problems.source_location: bandits.py, snapshot creation/reset and UCB initial-anchor construction, especially lines 292–304,404,416–418
claim: Reset dictionaries are saved without cloning, and the purported fixed initialization anchor retains an autograd path to the same parameter leaves.
analysis: A state dictionary’s tensors share parameter storage, so changing a parameter by \(0.25\) also changes its saved reset tensor; reloading that alias cannot restore initialization. Separately, let \(c(\theta)\) concatenate parameters and store its initial numerical vector without detaching. For \(\lambda\|c(\theta)-c(\theta_{\rm initial})\|^2\), backward differentiates both paths to the same leaves, yielding factor \(I-I=0\), even when its numerical value is positive. These are storage and chain-rule consequences; no model execution is required here.
result: The inspected auxiliary classes do not implement their stated reset/constant-anchor semantics. The effect on published rankings and other environment implementations remains unmeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Deep-copy the reset state and detach/clone the anchor; define optimizer-state reset separately. These restore the local operations, not a complete UCB theorem.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Entity-major prompts are consumed as class-major prompts
problems.source_location: Eq.(7), PDF p.6; model.py, lines 58–78,479–490
claim: Prompt construction uses flattened index \(eC+c\), while the reshape/permutation reads \(cE+e\) for entity \(e\), class \(c\).
analysis: For \(E=8,C=2\), only the first and final semantic slots retain their indices, leaving \(14\) of \(16\) mismatched; \(C=3\) gives \(22\) of \(24\). With unit zero-mean vector \(u\in\mathbb R^{512}\), visual features all \(u\), class prompts \(-u,u\), and unit logit scale, proper pairing gives mean logits \((-1,1)\), probabilities approximately \((0.119203,0.880797)\). The release groups alternating prompt rows into both class columns, whose means are \((0,0)\), probabilities \((0.5,0.5)\).
result: The feature-space computation loses semantic pairing and can change predictions. Actual-slide embedding realizability, adaptation to old wiring and benchmark effect remain separate.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Reshape the entity-major array directly to entity, class, embedding dimensions, without the class-major reshape/permutation. This restores the index identity under the stated construction.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Stop-gradient and zero-fusion loss change the stated objective
claim: The paper applies cross entropy to fused entity/slide logits; the release detaches visual entity features for positive fusion weight and changes the loss at zero weight.
analysis: After holding semantic indexing equal, take entity logits \((-\sin\theta,\sin\theta)\), constant zero slide logits, target class \(1\), and \(\lambda=0.3\). The displayed loss derivative at \(\theta=0\) is \(-(1-\lambda)=-0.7\), while the detached path gives \(0\). Attributes and the separate slide branch can still learn. At \(\lambda=0\), half the entities with logits \((1,-1)\), half with \((-1,1)\), give fused CE \(\log2\approx0.693147\), but average individual CE \(\log(2\cosh1)\approx1.126928\). The latter may be a deliberate stronger supervision choice, but is a different objective.
result: The release does not differentiate the literal stated loss in those branches. Neither choice is proved inferior or a cause of the reported scores.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either document the stop operator and separate endpoint loss, or follow ordinary fused-logit cross entropy throughout. No accuracy recovery is claimed.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The released graph is text-fixed rather than slide-dependent
problems.source_location: Eq.(8), PDF p.6; Figure 2, PDF p.4; model.py, lines 102–128,495–523,572
claim: The equation builds neighbors from slide visual entity features, while the release saves generic-text adjacency once.
analysis: Take \(16\) nodes, first eight generic-text vectors \(u\), remaining eight orthogonal vector \(v\), with seven nonself neighbors plus a self-loop. Both text groups have an unambiguous similarity boundary. A slide initially matching text has the same adjacency. Swapping visual vectors of nodes \(0\) and \(8\) makes the visual-neighbor set for node \(0\) equal to \(\{0,9,\ldots,15\}\), but the release still uses \(\{0,\ldots,7\}\). Its current visual inputs set node features, not edges. Figure 2 partly supports a text-graph interpretation, so author intent is ambiguous.
result: The graph specification and release differ; fixed text relations may still be useful, and graph attention is present.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify a fixed semantic-text graph with explicit conventions, or rebuild the declared visual graph per slide. The evidence does not select the better empirical variant.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Expert regularization is not the stated data reweighting
problems.source_location: Proposition 1, Eqs.(4)–(5), PDF p.5; Appendix A.4, PDF pp.26–27
claim: The fixed-variance Gaussian proposition equates full-data NLL plus \(\alpha\) expert-subset reverse KL with data weights \(1+\alpha{\bf1}_{D_e}\).
analysis: Four equal one-step observations share learner inputs and actions \(0,0,0,1\); select the final observation as expert, \(q=1/4\), with learner \(N(\mu,1)\), exact expert fit \(N(1,1)\), \(\alpha=1\). The true loss is \([3\mu^2+(\mu-1)^2]/8+(\mu-1)^2/2\), minimized at \(5/8\). The claimed weighted loss is \([3\mu^2+2(\mu-1)^2]/8\), minimized at \(2/5\). Beyond normalization, use same-state action/return pairs \((-1,10),(1,11),(0,0)\), with the first two experts. Their exact state-only expert mean is \(0\). Independent return-conditioned learner means minimize the actual objective at \((-2/5,2/5,0)\), whereas any positive data-only weights retain minimizers \((-1,1,0)\). A deterministic reward \(10.5a^2+0.5a\) realizes those returns.
result: Both examples satisfy fixed Gaussian variance. Missing expert fraction and mismatched teacher conditioning invalidate the general equivalence, without making the KL regularizer itself illegitimate.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: If the teacher mean equals \(E_{D_e}[a\mid x]\) for all learner inputs and shares fixed covariance, variance decomposition gives weight \(1+\alpha{\bf1}_{D_e}/q\), up to a parameter-independent constant. A state-only teacher needs that extra conditional-mean equality.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Likelihood direction and reverse-KL pooling are changed incorrectly
problems.source_location: Appendix A.5, Eqs.(24)–(29), PDF pp.27–28
claim: The proof identifies behavior NLL with learner-to-behavior KL and then replaces a sum of reverse KL terms by KL to an arithmetic mixture.
analysis: The exact likelihood identity is \(E_p[-\log\pi]=H(p)+D_{\rm KL}(p\Vert\pi)\). For \(p=N(0,1)\), \(\pi=N(0,4)\), forward and reverse KL are approximately \(0.318147\) and \(0.806853\), so no common policy-independent correction makes them identical over that family. Even granting reverse KL, its sum uses normalized geometric pool \(p_{\rm geo}\propto p^{1/(1+\alpha)}q^{\alpha/(1+\alpha)}\). With \(p=N(-4,1)\), \(q=N(4,1)\), \(\alpha=1\), learner \(N(\mu,1)\), the reverse-KL sum is \(\mu^2+16\), minimized at \(0\). For the arithmetic mixture, KL at \(\mu=4\) is at most \(\log2\), while at \(0\) it is at least \(8-4\sqrt{2/\pi}>4.8\). Thus the optimizing behavior changes.
result: These substitutions do not prove the claimed transfer to actual training. The existential auxiliary weak value chains can still hold at \(\alpha=0\), using a feasible baseline and consistent attained global optimizers; no blanket refutation of every auxiliary proposition is claimed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the forward likelihood KL and actual expert reverse KL under their respective measures; use geometric pooling only for a separately defined reverse-KL sum. No complete new policy-improvement proof is supplied.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: State-only occupancy does not control action-dependent return
problems.source_location: Lemma 2 and Eq.(12), PDF pp.23–24; Lemma 3 and empirical-risk step, PDF pp.25–26
claim: The proof uses \(|J(\pi)-J(\pi_\beta)|\le H\|d^\pi-d^{\pi_\beta}\|_1\) with state-only marginals and a claimed constant in \((0,1)\).
analysis: In a one-step MDP with sole initial state \(0\), actions in \([0,1]\), reward \(r(s,a)=a\), policies choosing \(0\) and \(1\) share identical state marginals but returns differ by \(1\). This refutes the intermediate inequality, not every final coverage hypothesis. The proof’s constant \(E_{d_\beta}\int\pi_\beta(a\mid s)\,da\) equals \(1\) by normalization. Under bounded rewards, however, the final numerical form is trivially recovered with \(C=1/2\), since its coverage term is at least \(H^2\ge H\). Statewise coverage and empirical-cross-entropy minimization are additional premises used later beyond initial-state coverage or an arbitrary estimator.
result: The proof requires corrected occupancy reasoning and explicit reward/estimator conditions. The bounded-reward final bound can remain true but vacuous; decreasing an upper bound does not prove monotone return improvement.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use state-action occupancies or maximal action coupling. For rewards in \([0,1]\), coupling gives \(|J(\pi)-J(\pi_\beta)|\le H^2E_{d_\beta}\operatorname{TV}(\pi,\pi_\beta)\). This local identity does not restore every downstream theorem.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Geographic degrees and normalized coordinates are conflated
problems.source_location: Section 3.4 and Algorithm 1, PDF pp.5–6; Appendix J, PDF pp.33–34; MixData.py and Haversine layer methods
claim: The paper defines physical Haversine distances and geographic nearest neighbors; the release feeds min–max-normalized coordinates into a degree-based Haversine formula.
analysis: Points \((100^\circ,30^\circ)\) and \((100.125^\circ,30^\circ)\) are about \(12.0372\) km apart with Earth radius \(6371\) km. After longitude bounds \(70\)–\(140\) and latitude bounds \(15\)–\(55\), the same formula on normalized values gives about \(0.198558\) km, reversing the predicate at threshold \(0.5\). Coordinate-Euclidean ranking also differs: from \((100^\circ,50^\circ)\), candidates \((101.4^\circ,50^\circ)\) and \((100^\circ,51^\circ)\) have coordinate distances \(1.4,1\), but Haversine distances approximately \(100.063,111.195\) km, reversing the nearest neighbor.
result: The physical graph operations differ from the description. Coordinate normalization for learned embeddings remains legitimate; benchmark consequences are unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep raw coordinates for physical distances and normalized coordinates for embeddings; rank the intended neighbors using the declared physical metric.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Multiplying a logit by zero does not remove its edge
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, PDF p.5; GNN_Layer_External.message, lines 87–99; internal counterpart
claim: The paper multiplies normalized attention by gate and decay; the release applies softmax after multiplying the raw logits.
analysis: For logits \((-1,8)\), decays \((0.5,0.2)\), gates \((1,0)\), the source normalizes logits \((-0.5,0)\), yielding weights approximately \((0.377541,0.622459)\). The closed edge receives positive, larger mass, while the paper’s factorized expression has second coefficient exactly \(0\). All-closed groups become uniform. A hard threshold comparison converted to floating point also supplies no ordinary gradient to the threshold, despite its parameter declaration.
result: Closed edges survive aggregation and the hard threshold does not implement the described learned gate path.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Apply the declared gate/decay after normalized attention with explicit neighborhood and empty-group conventions. A masked-softmax alternative requires its own specified normalization and gate-gradient rule.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The consensus score is constant and aggregation crosses examples
problems.source_location: Section 3.6, PDF pp.6–7; selector.py, forward and score reductions
claim: The selector is described as attention across candidates, assigning a candidate-specific consensus score.
analysis: Its input \((N,M,d)\) is permuted to \((M,N,d)\) for default sequence-first attention, so stations are the sequence and candidates are batches. Averaging both station dimensions of a row-stochastic attention matrix gives \(M^{-2}\sum_{u,v}A_{nuv}=1/M\) for every candidate in evaluation mode. Thus candidates \((0,1,3)\) and \((4,2,1)\) both score \(1/3\). Other selector branches remain active. Their unsegmented averaging can also make one example depend on batch mates: candidate scores \((0,2)\) give softmax \((0.119203,0.880797)\), but adding another example with \((10,-10)\) makes the pooled logits \((5,-4)\), reversing the first example’s mixture.
result: The claimed consensus branch cannot distinguish candidates at evaluation, and global pooling can couple separate forecast examples.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the intended candidate/station attention layout and a nonconstant, explicitly defined consensus reduction; segment independent example-level score aggregation.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The grid branch discards every earlier timestep
problems.source_location: Figure 2, PDF p.4; GNN_Layer_External.forward, line 66
claim: The described grid encoder attends over temporal input, while its active forward path selects only the final column.
analysis: Two grid nodes with histories \((1,2,3,4)\), \((5,6,7,8)\) and alternatives \((1001,1002,1003,4)\), \((1005,1006,1007,8)\) both map to \((4,8)\). Holding other inputs and randomness fixed, all downstream values in this branch agree; derivatives with respect to discarded times are zero. A temporal-attention module is constructed but unused in the active path. The separate station-history encoder remains active.
result: The release cannot use the claimed grid temporal history. This does not mean the entire model has no temporal information.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either implement/document the intended temporal encoder or state that only the final gridded field is used. No replacement architecture is established as restoring results.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: One configured submodule exceeds the reported full-model count
problems.source_location: Table 2, PDF p.7; DiffLiG_Launcher.py, line 31; SimpleGraphDiffusion constructor
claim: Table 2 reports \(49{,}361\) full-model parameters, while the launcher uses hidden width \(h=128\).
analysis: The active diffusion constructor contains three \(h\to h\) graph convolutions, two \(2h\to h\) convolutions, a \(2\to h\) position projection, an \(h\to h\) output projection and an \(h\to1\) auxiliary head. Their standard total is \(8h^2+10h+1=132{,}353\). Even the five graph-convolution matrix weights alone contain \(7h^2=114{,}688\), independent of bias or auxiliary-head conventions. Ensemble reuse does not multiply this count.
result: The released configuration cannot be the reported parameter-count configuration. The exact table-producing configuration is unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Identify the actual experiment configuration/checkpoint and count its instantiated parameters; no guessed replacement full-model count is supplied.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The interpolation metric is L1 rather than the described L2
problems.source_location: Eqs.(6)–(7), PDF p.8; approximation Appendix/Table A.4; _compute_anchor_weight_entry
claim: Placeholder distances use mean absolute tensor differences, while the method and norm ablation identify Euclidean weighting.
analysis: Use two identical layers, one token, query \((0,0)\), anchors A=\((0,20)\), B=\((11,11)\), temperature \(1\). Full Euclidean distances are \(\sqrt{800}\approx28.2843\) and \(22\), giving weights approximately \((0.001862,0.998138)\), entropy \(0.01957\) bits below the default \(0.3\) threshold. Reuse is admitted. Placeholder mean absolute distances are instead \(10,11\), giving \((0.731059,0.268941)\) and reversing anchor preference. For offset values \(0,10\), the interpolated coordinate changes from about \(9.98138\) to \(2.68941\). Positive-temperature rescaling cannot repair a reversed ordering.
result: The accepted-input release is a hybrid metric, not the stated L2 interpolation. Actual cache prevalence, performance and table-producing commit are unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either use an explicitly defined Euclidean reduction or describe the hybrid admission/prefix/placeholder metrics and match the ablation configuration.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Activation cutoff differs from conventional top-p selection
problems.source_location: Section 3.3 and cache-maintenance Algorithm 1; predict_as_anchor, lines 1041–1055
claim: The source uses the last cumulative sum below \(p\), and selects all anchors when no cumulative sum is below \(p\).
analysis: At \(p=0.9\), weights \((0.95,0.05)\) select both anchors, while \((0.60,0.35,0.05)\) select only the first with mass \(0.60\). Conventional nucleus selection would select one and two respectively. The first case can pass the entropy admission gate. These counts affect future eviction, not current interpolation weights. The paper does not define activation as conventional nucleus selection.
result: The threshold discontinuity is established, but classification as an unintended defect requires the missing activation contract.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: If standard nucleus selection is intended, retain the smallest prefix reaching mass \(p\), including its crossing element. This conditional correction is not an accuracy guarantee.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Low relative entropy does not bound absolute distance
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, entropy admission Eq.(5); conditional Lipschitz propositions
claim: Low entropy is used as a reuse-confidence heuristic; its mathematical information is relative anchor preference.
analysis: For anchors \(0,10\) and every scalar query \(q>10\), distances are \((q,q-10)\). Their softmax weights and entropy remain fixed, with entropy about \(0.00072045\) bits, while nearest distance grows without bound. For the \(1\)-Lipschitz offset \(F(q)=q\), interpolation remains near \(9.999546\); queries \(20,100,1000\) have errors about \[10.000454,90.000454,990.000454\]. This is a function-class witness, not an asserted unbounded ray in an actual finite-vocabulary model.
result: The heuristic does not supply an absolute-radius guarantee. The paper’s conditional distance bounds are not contradicted.

problems.title: First-token latency is already included in the current table
problems.source_location: Section 4.3 correction footnote and Table 2, PDF p.9
claim: The authors disclose an earlier omission and report updated latency components.
analysis: Agent \(5\) has \(17.5+21.1+16.2=54.8\) ms, and \(428.6/54.8\approx7.82117\), matching \(7.82\). The five rounded speedups agree with component sums. These are TTFT/prefill results; ordinary decoding is not accelerated and full-response speedup is not inferred.
result: No current-table arithmetic error is established; the earlier omission was already corrected by the authors.

problems.title: Universal quality preservation exceeds the reported results
problems.source_location: Abstract and Section 3.1; Table 1, PDF p.8; Table A.2 and AIME discussion
claim: The paper describes operation without quality degradation across its workload results.
analysis: HumanEval with two Qwen-Coder agents changes \(86.3\%\to81.4\%\), a decrease of \(4.9\) percentage points. Other reported configurations decline, including AIME by \(9.2\) points, while some improve or tie. The appendix acknowledges a resource/decoding-length explanation for AIME; it does not erase the observed loss. Rounded point estimates alone do not establish statistical significance or isolate the cache approximation’s causal effect.
result: The supported evidence is heterogeneous performance, not universal preservation. No benchmark result is remeasured or declared fabricated.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Qualify preservation by configuration and acknowledge reported accuracy/resource tradeoffs. Matched output-budget evidence is needed for a causal explanation.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Finite tail batches preclude the claimed uniform curvature premise
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.1, Eq.(32), PDF p.8; Appendix E, PDF pp.19–22
claim: The convergence theorem assumes some deterministic \(\lambda>0\) lower-bounds every empirical Hessian almost surely.
analysis: Take one expert \(q_a(z)\propto(1+z^2)^{-a}\), initial \(a=1\), target \(q_2\), and batch size \(1\). The initial proposal is Cauchy, the unique Fisher-divergence minimizer is \(a=2\), and the score residual there is identically zero. Expert score \(Q=-2z/(1+z^2)\) gives actual Hessian \(8z^2/(1+z^2)^2\). For every \(\lambda>0\), choosing \(R>\max(1,\sqrt{8/\lambda})\) makes the Hessian below \(\lambda\) on \(|Z|>R\), which has positive probability \(2\arctan(1/R)/\pi\). Any finite independent batch can fall entirely in that tail. Larger batches reduce that probability, not to zero. Separately rank is at most \(BD\), so \(K>BD\) forces singularity.
result: The theorem remains conditional, but its stated sampling procedure does not generally meet the fixed almost-sure floor. Finite observed positive eigenvalues cannot establish that deterministic assumption; convergence failure is not proved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A conditional mean-contraction premise \(E[(1+\eta m_t)^{-1}\mid\mathcal F_t]\le\rho<1\), with \(m_t=\lambda_{\min}(M_t)\), yields \(E\|e_t\|\le\rho^t\|e_0\|+\eta\delta(1-\rho^t)/(1-\rho)\) from the quadratic variational inequality. This is a different assumption; its multivariate applicability is unestablished.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Singular experts need the separately acknowledged integrability check
problems.source_location: Section 2.1, PDF p.3; Eq.(30), PDF p.7; Appendix F.4, PDF p.26
claim: Total expert weight above \(D/2\) alone is not sufficient when singular precisions are allowed; the paper explicitly notes and checks this limitation.
analysis: In dimension \(2\), use precisions \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\), \(\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\), \(I\), initial weights \((1,1,6/5)\), target \(N(0,\operatorname{diag}(10,1/2))\), sample \((1,1)\), and proximal coefficient \(1/10\). The unique constrained quadratic minimizer is \((0,319/193,408/965)\), certified by residual \((79/965,0,0)\) and inactive sum constraint. Its total weight exceeds \(1\), but on \(|y|\le1\) the density lower-bounds a positive multiple of \((x^2+2)^{-408/965}\), whose \(x\)-integral diverges because \(816/965<1\). Strict margins persist near that sample. The authors’ full-rank-weight condition or a valid separate certificate excludes this update.
result: This explains the necessity of the extra verification the authors already report. It does not establish any improper plotted model or omitted author check.

problems.title: Bilinear stencil sampling does not implement the patch-wide rule
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, PDF p.6; unproject.py, interpolate_depth, lines 54–67
claim: The paper computes patch-mean depth and skips the \(3\)-D feature when over \(90\%\) of the patch is masked; the release downsamples depth and mask bilinearly.
analysis: At a \(14\)-to-\(1\) reduction with align_corners false, a patch output samples only its four central pixels, each weight \(1/4\). One valid central depth \(2\) among \(196\) pixels gives interpolated mask \(1/4>0.1\), so the release retains it despite \(195/196>0.9\) missingness. If only the four central pixels are invalid and the other \(192\) have depth \(2\), it rejects a mostly valid patch. With every pixel valid, central depth \(2\) and other depths \(4\), the patch mean is \(776/196\approx3.959184\), but the release gives \(2\). Both mask examples avoid ambiguity over averaging zero placeholders; the full-valid example avoids missing data entirely.
result: The stated complete-patch mean/missingness operation and active release differ. Constant/full-invalid controls agree, and no action failure or dataset prevalence is inferred.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For aligned patches compute \(n_P=\sum M_p\) and \(u_P=\sum M_pD_p\). Retain when \(n_P>0\) and \(10n_P\ge A\), and use \(u_P/n_P\). This restores the declared local rule for the stated partition; changed checkpoints/performance require separate evaluation.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Self-counterfactual invariance does not control policy optimality
problems.source_location: Theorem B.4, Eqs.(27)–(32), arXiv v2 PDF p.31
claim: The proof turns a performance-difference identity into a bound involving direct task error and the difference of two policies’ own factual/counterfactual KL values.
analysis: In a one-state self-loop MDP, actions A,B have rewards \(1,0\), discount \(0.9\), and an irrelevant cue changed by the counterfactual prompt. A policy choosing A with probability \(0.1\), and the optimal policy always choosing A, both ignore the cue and have self-counterfactual KL \(0\). Their returns are \(1\) and \(10\). Thus equality of those statistics does not control their return gap. The undefined task-error residual is not silently set to zero: it could absorb the gap, but no calibrated relation establishing that is given. An optimum with divergence merely at most \(\delta\) also leaves residual \(C\delta\) in the limiting argument.
result: The claimed performance step needs an additional operational link to advantage or inter-policy distance. This is an established proof gap, not a numerical refutation made by assigning an undefined residual.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For a fixed intervener and bounded rewards, the ordinary performance-difference identity yields \[J(\pi^*)-J(\pi)\le2R_{\max}E_{d^{\pi^*}}\operatorname{TV}(\pi^*,\pi)/(1-\gamma)^2\]. This compares two policies, not each policy with its own counterfactual, and does not establish that the proposed regularizer controls it.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Strict suboptimality needs a positive expected-advantage condition
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.2, PDF p.4; Theorem B.3, PDF pp.29–31
claim: The strict-loss statement exempts trivial or reward-captured intervention influence but does not define those exceptions or establish a positive total expected advantage.
analysis: A generic one-step action-flip kernel with probability \(p=0.1\), reward A=\(1\), B=\(0\), maps intended A probability \(q\) to return \(0.1+0.8q\). It is nonidentity but retains the same optimum \(q=1\), so strict loss is not implied by nonidentity alone. This illustration has an unobserved flip and is not established to match every detail of the paper’s intervention-observed dialogue protocol. A positive term at one state also does not prove a positive occupancy-weighted expectation if negative contributions remain.
result: The quantifiers/exceptions and strict-advantage premise need specification. A full-assumption dialogue counterexample is not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The weaker statement that an underlying-MDP optimum can become suboptimal is supported. A strict theorem needs an explicit positive discounted expected-advantage condition.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Token aggregation changes the discounted objective
problems.source_location: Lemma B.2, Eqs.(13)–(16), arXiv v2 PDF pp.28–29
claim: Both token and macro MDPs are defined using discount \(\gamma\), but the aggregated response reward uses \(\gamma^{(j-1)/L}\).
analysis: Use two two-token responses with forced suffix and termination. Set \(\gamma=1/4\), temperature \(\beta=0.1\); A rewards are \((0,1)\), B rewards \((0.3,0)\). The true token values are \(0.25,0.3\), so the soft policy gives A probability \(0.377541\). The printed fractional-power reward instead gives \(0.5,0.3\), giving A probability \(0.880797\). A tabular function class is Bellman complete and all suffix actions are forced, so representability or suffix entropy cannot explain this reversal.
result: The stated token/macro objectives are inequivalent. This does not show that experimental training used the printed fractional exponent.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: With token discount \(\gamma_t\), aggregate reward is \(\sum_{j=1}^L\gamma_t^{j-1}r_j\) and continuation discount is \(\gamma_t^L\). For fixed lengths one may define \(\gamma_i=\gamma_t^L\); variable lengths require duration-aware continuation and consistent entropy/reference terms.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Padded-row tails are not response-token positions
problems.source_location: Eq.(4) and response comparison, PDF pp.6–7; ICR_trainer.py, lines 726–787
claim: The release counts response tokens and takes that many values from the end of right-padded factual/counterfactual rows.
analysis: For a short example in a two-row batch, use factual mask \((0,1,1,0,0,0)\) and counterfactual mask \((0,0,0,1,1,0,0,0)\). The same two response tokens have log probabilities \((-0.1,-0.2)\) and \((-1.1,-1.2)\), so their sampled log ratios are \(1,1\), summing to \(2\). Equal final padding values \((-0.4,-0.5)\) make tail subtraction zero instead, with reward scattered to padding positions. An unpadded longer row can agree. Negative sampled log ratios are not themselves an error; their expectation, rather than every sample, is a KL.
result: The supplied path can omit or misplace the intended signal on variable-length right-padded batches. Published-run dependency/import correspondence remains unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Gather values using both valid response masks, verify identical ordered token IDs, compute paired differences and scatter them to factual response positions. Do not truncate unmatched responses.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The supplied task proxy directly rewards participant agreement
problems.source_location: Appendix D.2, PDF pp.42–43; reward_functions.py, calculate_ppo_deli_proxy_reward
claim: The text withholds agreement/common-ground reward during training, but the proxy combines \(0.7\) correctness, \(0.2\) agreement and \(0.1\) format.
analysis: For cards A,7,B,6, let both participants support A and 7. In the aligned output, both oppose B and are unsure about 6. In the mixed output, participant two swaps its oppose/unsure choices on B and 6. Each retains identical task utility, supplied correctness \(0.416667\), and format \(1\); agreement changes \(1\to0.75\). The source’s scaling then changes reward \(0.83125\to0.68875\), difference \(2.85\cdot0.2\cdot0.25=0.1425\). A single-participant path may make this component inactive, and an imported module is absent from the release.
result: The supplied multi-participant proxy contradicts the stated exclusion. Actual agreement leakage into the published training run is not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
