paragraphs: Either remove agreement from the declared task-only reward and evaluate it separately, or disclose explicit agreement training with a matched ablation. No guessed reward rescaling recovers the tables.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Hard-coded A/7 scoring penalizes the paper’s U/9 answer
problems.source_location: Main Example 1, PDF p.4; Appendix D.2, PDF p.43; calculate_deli_correctness, lines 791–879
claim: The rule requires inspecting a vowel and an odd-number card, while the valid-JSON scorer uses the literal key set A,7.
analysis: For the paper’s U,S,8,9 example, correct stances support U and 9, oppose S and 8. The source treats U/9 as non-key and scores correctness \(-1\), proxy \(-2.332\) with full agreement/format. The wrong all-oppose response gets correctness about \(-0.166667\), proxy \(-0.3895\), hence higher reward. Equivalent correct cards A,K,2,7 get a different positive score. The malformed-JSON category fallback does not repair this valid-JSON path.
result: The supplied helper violates logical-category invariance on an in-paper instance. Canonicalized experimental inputs could avoid it, but no trace establishes that preprocessing; final evaluation’s separate category mapping is not accused of the same bug.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Condition on the actual card set/rule and classify vowels or odd numbers as necessary checks. The proposed category-based control restores logical equivalence without establishing a new training reward scale.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Solution-diversity gain does not establish agreement
problems.source_location: Section 6, PDF p.8; Table 1, PDF p.9; evaluator solution-set collection
claim: DeliData common-ground gain is defined through the number of explored solution types relative to initial types.
analysis: If three participants initially all propose V and later propose O,E,C respectively, explored diversity rises from \(1\) to \(4\), giving gain \(3\), while final participants disagree and none selects the correct OV solution. The operational metric remains meaningful for exploration. If the discussion set excludes initial proposals, \(|U|-|I|=|U\setminus I|-|I\setminus U|\) can be negative; it is not the number of newly explored types.
result: This is a metric-scope clarification, not a contradiction in the reported diversity score or an independent measurement of consensus.

problems.title: The two KL directions can reverse the approximation ranking
problems.source_location: arXiv v4 Section 3.2, PDF p.7; compute_kl and intervention-evaluation call
claim: The paper defines \(D_{\rm KL}(Q_S\Vert P)\), where \(P\) is original chat and \(Q_S\) is modified output. The codeâ€™s log-target operation computes \(D_{\rm KL}(P\Vert Q_S)\).
analysis: Let \(P=(0.8,0.2)\), \(Q_A=(0.5,0.5)\), \(Q_B=(0.99,0.01)\). The specified divergences are about \(0.2231435513\) and \(0.1810049606\), preferring B; the released direction gives \(0.1927447570\) and \(0.4286718823\), preferring A. Every entry is positive and finite logits realize them. Adding identical positive tail mass to a larger vocabulary scales all divergences by the same positive factor and retains the reversal.
result: The metric correspondence is wrong in general. Both directions are legitimate choices; the example does not identify an actual Figure 4 reversal or show that codeâ€™s intended metric was intrinsically inappropriate.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either swap the evaluation arguments to follow the manuscript or revise the manuscriptâ€™s direction and associated interpretation to follow the code. Scalar averages cannot recover the opposite KL without underlying distributions.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Variance depends on how the same observations are batched
problems.source_location: RunningMeanStd.update/update_from_moments, lines 347â€“439; Figure 4 uncertainty pipeline
claim: Batch variance uses default sample denominator \(n_b-1\), then merge code multiplies it by \(n_b\) as if it were population variance.
analysis: For observations \((0,2,4,6)\), the mean is \(3\), centered sum of squares \(20\), population variance \(5\), sample variance \(20/3\). One batch stores \(20/3\). Splitting into \((0,2)\), \((4,6)\) gives batch means \(1,5\), sample variances \(2,2\); the source merge returns \((2\cdot2+2\cdot2+16)/4=6\), neither correct convention. Singleton calls also create undefined batch sample variance although the pooled sample becomes defined.
result: The variance arithmetic is not partition-invariant and can change plotted uncertainty. Token dependence and interval coverage remain separate statistical questions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Store centered sum of squares \(M_2\). Merge using \(M_{2,A}+M_{2,B}+(\mu_B-\mu_A)^2n_An_B/(n_A+n_B)\), and divide only at readout by the chosen total denominator.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The public entry point omits object-specific latent blending
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1, PDF p.7; app.py generate_image; pipeline_scenedesigner.py denoising loop
claim: The paper sets \(z_0=x_t+\Delta t\,v_g\), forms each \(u_i=x_t+\Delta t\,v_i\), and replaces masked regions by \(z_i=(1-M_i)\odot z_{i-1}+M_i\odot u_i\).
analysis: The application passes only global condition/prompt data and the denoising path advances a single global prediction; renderer-created individual object files are not consumed by that call. With a \(2\times2\) zero latent, \(\Delta t=1/2\), global velocity \(1\), object velocity \(2\), and a mask selecting one pixel, global-only output is \(0.5\) everywhere, while Algorithm 1 gives \(1\) at the selected pixel. Their difference is exactly \(M_1\Delta t(v_1-v_g)\); empty masks or equal velocities are agreement cases.
result: The released entry point does not reproduce DOS. This does not prove the historical experiments omitted it or that DOS cannot improve outputs.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The published ordered mask recurrence is the verified local update. An integrated implementation additionally needs object prompts, maps, latent masks and matching scheduler/overlap conventions; no complete pipeline repair is claimed.
The public report in repository issue 3, dated 28 February 2026, had already raised this release gap. No accepted integrated correction is established.

problems.title: A singleton prompt truncates parallel image batches
problems.source_location: train.py, lines 146â€“156,188; PyTorch 1.12 scatter_map
claim: Training passes images shaped \((4,1,256,256)\), a degradation prompt \((1,128,128)\), and scenario prompts \((4,64)\) into DataParallel.
analysis: Dimension-zero scattering yields four image/scenario chunks but one degradation chunk. The recursive zip stops at one input, leaving a one-image prediction. For scalar predictor \(f_w(x)=wx\), \(w=1\), four constant images/targets \(0.1,0.2,0.7,0.8\) should have zero loss. Broadcasting the surviving first prediction gives mean absolute loss \(0.35\) and gradient \(-0.075\). Validation passes a scenario vector \((64,)\), which is split into length \(16\) on four destinations, incompatible with the released \(64\)-input linear layer. Single-device operation can avoid this scattering defect.
result: The released multi-device call layout fails its per-example contract. This is a static source/shape finding; no claim of four-physical-GPU execution or false published scores is made.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Before scattering, give every tensor a matching batch axis: degradation \((B,128,128)\), scenario \((B,64)\). Assert equal prediction/target shapes. This restores the identified correspondence, not end-to-end trained performance.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The corruptionâ€™s brightness offset differs from the printed formula
problems.source_location: Appendix A.1.1 Eq.(8), PDF p.22; ranges, PDF p.23; dataset.py/create_corrupt.py and Albumentations 1.4.1
claim: The paper specifies \(C(I)=\alpha(I+\beta M)\); the pinned brightness-by-max transform implements \(\alpha I+\beta M\).
analysis: Use valid uint8 intensities \(0,100,200,255\), \(M=255\), and interior hard-range values \(\alpha=0.5,\beta=0.3\). The printed real outputs are \[(38.25,88.25,138.25,165.75)\]; the dependency gives \((76.5,126.5,176.5,204)\). No value saturates, and the real offset difference is \((1-\alpha)\beta M=38.25\). Quantization cannot explain it. Renaming brightness would require correlated parameter changes; at these values the implied paper brightness \(0.6\) exceeds the hard range.
result: The release and printed parameters define different corrupted inputs. Which produced the historical benchmark images is unestablished.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either document the multiply-then-add generator and ranges, or implement the printed correlated offset. Matching one formula locally does not establish improved restoration or recover historical data.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Mean squared rank can select a different teacher
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, PDF p.5; Appendix C.1; tune_print.py and gen_config_pet.py rank branches
claim: The paper minimizes average validator rank; the default and teacher-generation branches square ranks first.
analysis: Across seven tie-free validators, let A ranks be \(1,1,1,1,1,3,3\), B ranks \(2,2,2,2,2,1,1\), C ranks \(3,3,3,3,3,2,2\). Ordinary means are \(11/7,12/7,19/7\), uniquely choosing A. Squared means are \(23/7,22/7,53/7\), choosing B. Each validator is a valid strict permutation. This is an operator-input example, without asserting the exact joint scores arise in the reported images. Squared mean equals squared mean rank plus across-validator variance, adding a different preference.
result: The two selection rules are inequivalent. A non-squared reporting option exists, but does not change the separately squared teacher-generation branches; actual published choices remain unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Follow the stated mean-rank operation in every relevant branch, or explicitly define and attribute squared-rank selection with its dispersion sensitivity.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Softmax of counts is not a mean one-hot label
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1, PDF p.7; PETHook.init_pl voting branch and distillation target path
claim: The stated target is \(v/K\), whereas the release passes \(\operatorname{softmax}(v)\) into the soft distillation loss.
analysis: Four teachers voting for classes \(0,0,1,2\) give counts \((2,1,1,0)\). Mean labels are \((0.5,0.25,0.25,0)\); the release gives approximately \[(0.534447,0.196612,0.196612,0.072329)\]. At zero student logits, the KL gradient is student probability minus target: the written target gives \((-0.25,0,0,0.25)\), while the release gives \[(-0.284447,0.053388,0.053388,0.177671)\]. Argmax labels agree, but soft training differs. Duplicating every teacher preserves vote proportions while sharpening the released distribution.
result: The release retains scale-insensitive teacher argmax voting but uses a different soft target and optimization path. No actual accuracy change is established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(v/K\) to restore Mean Label, or explicitly specify the count-dependent softmax target and distinguish that design from average labels.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Classical CCA is invariant to invertible feature transformations
problems.source_location: Appendix G.1â€“G.2, PDF pp.28â€“30; comparison Table Appendix 8
claim: The argument claims CCA correlations change under anisotropic diagonal scaling and uses that to justify a scaling advantage of CKA.
analysis: For invertible feature maps \(T,U\), every original projection pair \(Xa,Yb\) is retained by choosing \(a^\prime=T^{-1}a\), \(b^\prime=U^{-1}b\), since \((XT)a^\prime=Xa\), \((YU)b^\prime=Yb\). The inverse mapping preserves the full feasible correlation sets, including subsequent decorrelation constraints. Thus every defined classical canonical correlation is unchanged. Conversely, take centered rows \[A=((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1))^\top\] and \(B=A\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\). CCA is perfect on their shared full-rank column space, but linear CKA equals \(5/\sqrt{34}\approx0.857493\), versus \(1\) for A with itself.
result: The comparative proof is mathematically wrong. CKA retains orthogonal/isotropic invariance and may remain empirically suitable; stronger CCA invariance is not automatically desirable.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State classical CCAâ€™s invertible-feature invariance. SVCCA can lose general anisotropic invariance when truncation changes its retained subspace, rather than because CCA lacks scale invariance. Linear CKA equal to one requires proportional nonzero centered Gram matrices, not identical activations.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: All-clean/all-backdoored endpoints lack the stated metric denominators
problems.source_location: Appendix B.2, PDF p.24; Table Appendix 5 and client composition, PDF p.27
claim: DSR is backdoor sensitivity and FPR is clean-model false-positive rate, but the all-clean endpoint reports DSR \(100\%\) and all-backdoored endpoints report positive FPR.
analysis: Under those definitions, \(\mathrm{DSR}=\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN})\) has denominator zero when all four clients are clean; FPR has denominator zero when all four are backdoored. problems.title: Leaf-first SCOUT incurs a cost excluded by its finite bound
problems.source_location: Algorithm 4 and Theorem 5.2, arXiv v3 PDF p.7; Appendix A.3

Printed SCOUT first pays two reads testing the first child, then one read in its improving re-search, then rereads that leaf at window \([0,0]\), and finally tests the other root child once: total \(5>4\). A full-support uniform distribution on \(\{-1,0,1\}\), conditional root \(0\), likewise gives expected SCOUT \(11/2\) versus summed TEST \(115/24\); the point-mass case is not essential.

Alternatively, for nonempty full windows \(n\ge1\), every extra read can be charged to a preceding TEST read, giving printed cost at most twice corrected cost. problems.title: Optimizing Gaussian candidates does not preserve centering
problems.source_location: Theorem 4.3 and Remark 4.4, PDF pp.5â€“6; Appendix D, PDF pp.19â€“21

problems.title: Lower curvature does not control explicit-step stability
problems.source_location: Proposition 1, Eqs.(3)â€“(4), PDF pp.6â€“7; Appendix B, p.22
claim: The proposition assumes \(-U\) is \(m\)-strongly convex and claims stability when \(\epsilon<[(1+2k_d)m]^{-1}\), then a unique stationary law with Gaussian noise.
analysis: On \(\mathbb R^2\), take \(-U=(x_1^2+10x_2^2)/2,m=1,k_d=1,\epsilon=1/10<1/3\). The second coordinate obeys \(z_{t+1}=-z_t+z_{t-1}\), with root \((-1-\sqrt5)/2\) of magnitude greater than one. Initial values \(z_{-1}=z_0=1\) yield \(1,1,0,1,-1,2,-3,\ldots\), and arbitrarily small scaled initial values still diverge. Gaussian forcing projects nontrivially onto the unstable mode. Any invariant characteristic function would satisfy \[|\phi(u)|\le\exp[-qu^2\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}r^{2j}/2]\to0\] for \(u\ne0\), contradicting continuity at zero.

problems.title: Cycle edges are not independent partition-rank steps
problems.source_location: Appendix B.2, Eq.(B.5), PDF p.25; main Eq.(4), PDF p.4
claim: The derivation identifies top rank with the internal edge count, \(r(\top)=|E|\), to motivate inverse-volume degrees of freedom.
analysis: A connected four-neighbor \(2\times2\) grid has \(4\) vertices and \(4\) edges. A connected-partition chain merges four singleton blocks into one in exactly \(3\) cover steps. In general every cover merges two adjacent connected blocks: merging more would allow an intermediate adjacent-pair merge. Thus \(r(\pi)=|V|-|\pi|\) and \(r(\top)=|V|-1\), not \(|E|\) on cyclic grids. Counting all atoms counts dependencies. Even the corrected reciprocal rank is not automatically statistical degrees of freedom: fixed scalar region-mean fitting has projection trace \(|\pi|\).
result: The formal lattice step supporting the central complexity surrogate is false. A shape-sensitive penalty may still be useful as a heuristic; its hierarchy and reported scores are not numerically refuted.

problems.title: The joint pass rate violates the marginal event bound
problems.source_location: Table 2, Gemini2.5-pro/environmental learning, PDF p.8; caption and Sections 3.2,4.4
claim: Four no-error marginals are \[100\%,90.74\%,92.57\%,84.27\%\], but compilation pass rate is \(65.89\%\).

The displayed joint rate is below the lower bound by \(1.69\) percentage points. Even allowing the first entry to mean \(99.5\%\) and generous remaining rounding gives lower bound \(67.065\%\), above \(65.895\%\). Common-weight averaging preserves the inequality; no independence is needed.

Conditional stages, unequal denominators, extra failure types, different intermediate/final populations or a transcription error remain possible and require explicit protocol clarification; no raw outputs are declared impossible.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Publish output-level flags, denominators, unavailable-test handling and final success. State conditional metrics or additional failure categories explicitly. The consistency interval is not a corrected measurement.

problems.title: Scaling a negative logit increases its attention probability
claim: CGW/RAS multiply selected raw scores by \(w\in[0.7,1]\) before softmax, with a suppression interpretation.
analysis: For legal causal logits \((-2,0)\), scaling the first by \(0.7\) changes its probability from \(e^{-2}/(1+e^{-2})=0.1192029220\) to \(e^{-1.4}/(1+e^{-1.4})=0.1978161114\). Relative odds grow by \(e^{0.6}\). Arbitrary finite scores admit a query/key factorization, so positivity is not a hidden dot-product restriction. Positive logits can instead be suppressed, and empirical average improvement remains possible.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: If probability gating is intended, additive log gates \(z_j+\log w_j\) give odds scaled by \(w_j/w_k\). A common gate below one reduces a selected group’s total mass against its unchanged complement. Arbitrary heterogeneous gates need more careful coordinate claims, and this changed intervention requires experiments.

problems.title: The stopping heuristic is not a signed trajectory increment
problems.source_location: Section 3.3–3.4, PDF p.5; verifier.py, lines 69–97; inference.py, lines 962–1005
claim: The paper sums observed planning/action log-probability ratios and stops when their signed increment is below a positive threshold; source uses a change norm of next-token vocabulary log-ratio vectors.

For three observed ratios \(9\) and an equal final distribution, the required sum is \(3\log9\), but the retained vector is zero.

problems.title: Directional convergence does not preserve tied argmax sets
problems.source_location: Lemma C.6, PDF pp.31–34, especially p.32; Lemma C.5, p.29; Eqs.(10)–(12)
claim: The proof infers finite-time selection equivalence to the limiting direction and applies fixed-gap derivative bounds.
analysis: With embeddings \(e_1,e_2,e_3\), let \(p_R=(R+\sqrt R,R,0)\). Its normalized direction tends to \((1,1,0)/\sqrt2\), but every finite argmax is \(\{1\}\), while the limiting argmax is \(\{1,2\}\). The normalized first/second gap is \[\sqrt R/\sqrt{(R+\sqrt R)^2+R^2}\to0\], so no fixed positive gap follows. Separation between distinct limiting groups does not separate members tied within one group. Relevant-token membership or distinct finite-time scores likewise does not exclude limiting ties.
result: The tied-limit proof step for the central max-margin characterization is unsupported. This algebraic curve is not an actual gradient-flow trajectory or a counterexample satisfying the theorem’s random event; the theorem itself remains unrefuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Unique limiting maximizers with gap \(m>0\) and embedding-difference bound \(D\) preserve selection whenever \(\|u_t-u\|<m/(2D)\). That adds a hypothesis; the full flow needs a proof of strictness or an argument handling tied faces and shrinking gaps.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Multiclass overlaps depend on the classifier Gram matrix
problems.source_location: Section 4.3, Eq.(14), PDF p.7; Appendix E, p.39
claim: The printed leading overlap retains only class coefficient \(c_{sk}\), without a stated orthogonality condition on output classifiers.
analysis: At uniform initial probabilities, \(E_s^1=E_s^0+\eta_0\sum_\ell c_{s\ell}v_\ell\), so \((E_s^1)^\top v_k=(E_s^0)^\top v_k+\eta_0\sum_\ell c_{s\ell}v_\ell^\top v_k\). Take two one-token examples \(a,b\) with labels \(1,2\), and equal unit classifiers \(v_1=v_2=e_3\). Both logits always agree, the loss is identically \(\log2\), and every embedding gradient is zero. The printed class-one term for token \(a\) is instead \(\eta_0/4>0\). Gaussian initial overlap vanishes with dimension, while this omitted leading discrepancy does not.
result: The general multiclass extension lacks a necessary Gram condition. This does not refute the separately formulated binary theorem or empirical correlations for the actual learned classifiers.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the full Gram expression. If \(G=I+\Delta\), the omitted contribution is bounded by \(\eta_0\|c_s\|_1\max_\ell|\Delta_{\ell k}|\); an explicit asymptotic Gram control and initial-remainder analysis can justify the simpler leading formula.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The all-constraints-tight formula is already superseded
problems.source_location: Current Lemma 4.2 and Appendix C.2, PDF pp.5,26; historical arXiv v1 and separate older supplement
claim: The old version gave \(\widehat p=M^\dagger\mathbf1\), assuming every margin inequality is tight. The current main paper asserts uniqueness only.
analysis: For differences \(e_1-e_2,e_2-e_3,e_1-e_3\), the third row is the sum of the first two. Requiring all three margins \(1\) is impossible, while \(p=(1,0,-1)\) is optimal with margins \((1,1,2)\) and KKT multipliers \((1,1,0)\). The old pseudoinverse gives \((2/3,0,-2/3)\), violating the first two inequalities. Current proceedings and later arXiv revisions remove the pseudoinverse assertion. A separately distributed older supplement still contains it, so its derivation must be read as superseded.
result: Known historical correction, not a current-main-paper error; only the material-version discrepancy remains.

problems.title: The moment inequality needs a mixed-term condition
problems.source_location: Lemma B.1, PDF p.15; actual use in Lemma B.2, pp.15–16
claim: The statement claims \(\|X+Y\|_p^2\le\|X\|_p^2+(p-1)\|Y\|_p^2\) for arbitrary finite-moment random vectors.
analysis: At \(p=2\), deterministic \(X=Y=1\) requires \(4\le2\). Even centered equal Rademacher variables give the same failure. The mixed inner product need not vanish. A sufficient condition is \(\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G]=0\) with \(X\) measurable to \(\mathcal G\); the usual martingale smoothness inequality then applies. In Lemma B.2, the past iterate/drift is measurable and iid unbiased gradient noise is conditionally centered, exactly as the proof states.
result: The auxiliary statement is false, but its repaired actual application preserves the one-step recursion and Theorem 2.1 under the paper’s original assumptions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Add conditional centering to the lemma. For its SGD application, identify the past sigma-algebra explicitly; no change to the main recursion is required.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Vanishing steps alone need not remove accumulated noise
problems.source_location: Remark 2.2, PDF p.5; Theorem 2.1, Eq.(2.2)
claim: The isolated remark says the exploration sum is \(o(1)\) when \(\eta_n\to0\).
analysis: For \(f(\theta,\xi)=(\theta-\xi)^2/2\), independent Rademacher \(\xi\), start at optimum \(0\), use \(p=2,\mu=L_2=M_2=1,c_0=1,\eta_t=0.1\,2^{-t}\). The theorem’s step restrictions hold, but the first summand alone gives \(S_n\ge0.0025e^{-0.05}>0\). Actual variance also obeys \(v_n\ge0.0025\prod_{k=2}^n(1-\eta_k)^2\ge0.00225625\). Thus initialization removal does not cure the isolated criterion. Remark 2.1 separately discusses divergent accumulated steps, which may be the intended joint premise.
result: The isolated sufficiency statement needs qualification; the finite bound and separately analyzed Linear-D2Z result are not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For a fixed infinite schedule, require both \(\eta_t\to0\) and \(\sum_t\eta_t=\infty\) with fixed \(c_0>0\). Splitting off finitely many early terms and bounding the tail by \( \delta e^{c_0M}/c_0\), \(M=\sup\eta_t\), proves convergence. Finite-horizon triangular arrays need their own uniform conditions.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.
