problems.title: The actual-tail-product concentration upper bound fails
problems.source_location: Lemma 12, PDF pp.41–42; Eq.(24)
claim: The lemma upper-bounds the tail by \(f(-\log M)\), where \(M\) is the supremum of products of actual upper tails and \(f(u)=(u+3-\log2)e^{-u}\).
analysis: Take one observation \(Z\sim\mathrm{Ber}(0.01)\), independent \(S\sim\mathrm{Lap}(1)\), \(x=0.01,\epsilon=1\). Over \(z\in(0.01,0.02)\), \(\Pr(Z\ge z)=0.01\), so \(M=0.005\). The proposed bound is \(0.005(3-\log2-\log0.005)=0.03802585093\). Direct conditioning gives \(\Pr(Z+S\ge0.02)=0.99e^{-0.02}/2+0.01(1-e^{-0.98}/2)=0.49332178779\). A large below-mean Bernoulli endpoint term is not dominated by the interior upper-tail product used in the proof.
result: The lemma is false under its own assumptions. This is not a counterexample to the different modified-divergence bound or the private mechanism.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Independence yields a direct Chernoff exponent \(I(\lambda)=\sup_{0<s<\epsilon}[s\lambda-\log(1-\mu+\mu e^s)+(n/t)\log(1-s^2/\epsilon^2)]\). Bernoulli/Laplace convex conjugacy identifies it with the stated modified divergence, giving the stronger bound \(e^{-tI(\lambda)}\). This restores the concentration statements and a stopping-rule proof input without relying on the false actual-tail lemma; it is not a full algorithm reproof.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The claimed uniform envelope is smaller than Bernoulli fluctuations
problems.source_location: Lemma 55 and proof, PDF pp.78–79; later expected-time arguments
claim: The lemma claims \(\widetilde N|\widetilde\mu-\mu|\le W_\mu\log(e+\widetilde N)\) with a finite sub-exponential random constant for all geometric releases.
analysis: For \(\mu=1/2,\epsilon=1,\eta=1\), let \(N_k=2^{k-1}\), \(C_k=Z_{N_k}-N_k/2+S_k\), with \(k\) independent Laplace noises. The claimed finite envelope forces \(C_k/\sqrt{N_k}\to0\) almost surely. Yet its characteristic function is \([\cos(t/(2\sqrt{N_k}))]^{N_k}(1+t^2/N_k)^{-k}\to e^{-t^2/8}\), a nondegenerate Gaussian limit. Bounded convergence under the claimed almost-sure limit would instead give \(1\). This rules out the proposed supremum, without any finite-simulation inference.
result: The logarithmic-over-sample rate used in the expected-time proof is invalid. A finite realized stopping horizon does not justify the claimed uniform bound over all potential arm releases; final expected-time conclusions remain unrefuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A valid weaker form is \(\sqrt{\widetilde N}|\widetilde\mu-\mu|\le W^\prime_\mu\log(e+\widetilde N)\). Normalized Bernoulli/Laplace sums have uniformly bounded local moment-generating functions on the geometric grid; a union bound over tails weighted by growing log counts gives a sub-exponential supremum. Polynomial sample thresholds, for example \((6W^\prime_\mu/r_0)^4\), still have finite moments. All downstream uses and leading constants must be updated consistently.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: A single positive weight need not give a unique global minimizer
problems.source_location: Lemma 35 third bullet, PDF p.59; Eq.(3)
claim: For nonnegative weights with positive maximum, the lemma claims the minimizer over \([0,1]\) is unique.
analysis: At \(\lambda=0.8,\mu=0.2,\epsilon=1,w=(1,0)\), the objective is \(d_\epsilon^-(0.8,u)\), equal to zero for every \(u\in[0.8,1]\). Thus \(0.8\) and \(0.9\) are distinct global minimizers. A tie-breaking convention can select one but cannot prove uniqueness.
result: The boundary-domain claim fails. The minimum value and interior optimal-allocation result are not refuted, because both weights are positive at the relevant interior optimum.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Require both weights positive for uniqueness on \([0,1]\), or define the canonical minimizer on \([\mu,\lambda]\). Strict convexity on that restricted interval and compactness yield uniqueness and continuity away from the zero-weight vector.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Signed integer tree noise has a forbidden suffix-shift parity
problems.source_location: Lemma 3.1 Eq.(2), latest PDF p.5; current k_ary_tree_noise.py, prefix_noise_terms
claim: The proof interface requires positive output probability to survive every unit suffix shift; the experimental implementation combines integer geometric-difference noise with signs.
analysis: At supported \(m=k=2\), height \(1\), independent integer nodes \(Z_0,Z_1,Z_2\) give \(N_1=Z_0+Z_1-Z_2\), \(N_2=Z_0+Z_1+Z_2\). Thus \(N_2-N_1=2Z_2\) is even. At ranks \((10000,20000)\), output equal to the ranks has positive probability because all nodes can be zero, while shifting the second output by \(1\) has zero probability. No finite exponential ratio can bound positive by zero. The same adjacent-difference parity appears in the height-one \(m=10\) experimental choice. Increased variance or widely separated ranks cannot repair support.
result: The current discrete module does not instantiate the required counting law. The continuous construction and existence lemma are not disproved; later randomized slice/quantile release may lose the internal parity information, so final-output nonprivacy is not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: An ordinary dyadic-prefix mechanism with independently noised interval counts can satisfy the contract: a unit suffix shift changes one stream increment and at most \(T=\lceil\log_2m\rceil+1\) interval queries. Node mass proportional to \(e^{-\epsilon|z|/T}\) bounds the joint likelihood ratio by \(e^\epsilon\). This conservative alternative changes noise constants and needs full-pipeline integration/review.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The historical node-alias/prefix defect is already fixed
problems.source_location: Conference supplement k_ary_tree_noise.py; author commits of 10 September 2026; current prefix_noise_terms
claim: The conference source reused sibling-index cache keys across parents and stopped at the first rather than last leaf boundary.
analysis: At \(m=8,k=2\), its coefficients force \(-N_1+2N_3-2N_4-N_5+2N_6=0\), whereas suffix shift \((0,1,1,1,1,1,1,1)\) changes that expression by \(1\). Current code uses parent-dependent absolute node keys and stops at rem equal to block size minus one, removing this rational support identity. These local fixes do not remove the separate integer parity above.
result: Known historical defect, cleared in the current source. Neither a historical benchmark change nor complete current privacy is inferred.

problems.title: Nominal repetitions condition on one counting-noise draw
problems.source_location: Section 6/Figure 1, latest PDF pp.9–10; current real_data_eps1.ipynb, cell 19; persistent tree cache
claim: One SliceQuantile object is constructed outside the \(200\)-repetition loop and its tree is not reset between queries.
analysis: Let \(Z\) be shared counting noise, \(Q_i\) random queries and \(E_i\) fresh single-quantile noise. Even if draws are conditionally independent, for loss \(Y_i=f(Q_i,Z,E_i)\), variance of the mean is \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid Z)]/R+\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb E[Y_i\mid Z])\). Bootstrapping observations from one fixed \(Z\) cannot estimate the between-counting-noise term. New outer seeds do not clear an existing cache. Final exponential-mechanism outputs can still differ, so this is not a cached-final-answer claim.
result: The replication scheme supports conditional rather than fully randomized uncertainty unless the between-noise term vanishes. Numeric undercoverage or a ranking reversal is not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For independent complete-mechanism repetitions, create/reset the tree with a continuing nonreplayed RNG stream, while optionally pairing query seeds separately. State which sources of randomness the uncertainty covers.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Substitute delta is loosened instead of tightened
problems.source_location: Theorem 4.2, latest PDF p.7; current slice_quantile.py, is_delta_approximate_DP
claim: The theorem gives final failure bound \(F\delta_{\rm int}\), \(F=1+e^{\epsilon_{\rm CC}+2\epsilon_{\rm EM}}\); source multiplies the requested delta by \(F\) before the internal bound.
analysis: At total epsilon \(1\), split \(0.5\), substitute adjacency, the correctly calibrated epsilon components are \(1/4,1/6\). Thus \(F=1+e^{7/12}=2.7920018257\). Requested \(10^{-16}\) needs internal \(10^{-16}/F=3.5816595491\times10^{-17}\), but source forwards \(F10^{-16}\), yielding only the conditional theorem bound \(F^2\,10^{-16}=7.7952741945\times10^{-16}\). No outer division in the inspected path cancels it.
result: The certification argument does not establish the requested substitute parameter. This is not a lower bound on actual final-output privacy loss, and the separate counting-contract issue remains.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Divide the requested final delta by the theorem’s factor once, keeping internal and target names distinct. This fixes accounting direction without proving privacy of the complete implementation.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Directional maps are assigned by head rather than query group
problems.source_location: Section 3.2/Figure 3, PDF pp.4–5; SD15/ip_adapter/resampler.py, lines 209–227
claim: The paper defines four query-token groups, but reshaped attention is \((B,H,Q,K)\) and the source chunks dimension \(1\), the head axis.
analysis: For production \(H=12,Q=16,K=273\), each directional chunk contains three heads and all sixteen queries. At the first spatial key, head \(0\), query \(4\) receives left coefficient \(1\), though query \(4\) belongs to the right group and needs \(0\). Head \(3\), query \(0\) receives right coefficient \(0\), though the left group needs \(1\). Every query within a head shares the same map. Downstream injection treats the resulting token groups as directional keys; no inspected deterministic head-to-token map supplies the missing query grouping.
result: The source mask does not implement the declared query-group routing. Learned queries may still specialize and relighting may improve; no same-defect claim is made for FLUX.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For the documented design, broadcast \(G_{bhqk}=m_{\lfloor4q/Q\rfloor}(k)\), with \(Q\) divisible by \(4\), along the query axis. This changes the architecture and requires checkpoint/quality evaluation.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: A zero spatial coefficient can favor a negative logit
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF p.5; resampler.py, lines 215–224
claim: The release multiplies raw dot-product scores by maps in \([0,1]\), then softmaxes them.
analysis: Two keys with equal logits \(-2\) and left/right coefficients \((1,0)\) become \((-2,0)\); conditional pair shares are \[0.1192029220,0.8807970780\], rather than equal shares before masking. The supposedly removed right key has odds \(e^2\) times the left. These are valid dot products, for example \(q=(1,0,0,0)\), both keys \((-4,0,0,0)\), head width \(4\). The pair odds hold inside the full \(273\)-key row and are not claimed as full-row probabilities. Positive logits can favor the intended side and zero logits are unaffected.
result: The unconditional attenuation interpretation fails on legal signed scores. No actual PSNR/FID or trained-token counterexample is established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For an unnormalized probability gate, compute \(A=\operatorname{softmax}(L)\), then \(\widetilde A=A\odot G\), with no second softmax. This gives \(0\le\widetilde A\le A\) and preserves coefficient-one special keys. A separately normalized gate equals softmax of \(L+\log G\), but changes absolute special-key weights and must be described as a different choice.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The Jacobi bound needs fixed position-specific randomness
problems.source_location: Section 3, PDF p.4; cited Song et al. Proposition 1
claim: The paragraph writes sampled parallel updates and an at-most-\(N\) iteration bound without specifying coupling between iterations.
analysis: At \(N=1\), a uniform binary token with fresh independent draws has path \(0\to1\to0\) with probability \(1/4\), changing beyond one update. Path \(0\to0\to1\) also has probability \(1/4\), so a coincidental equality is not an absorbing fixed point. In contrast, draw one \(U_1\) once and use the same inverse-CDF map each time: the first update settles the token. In general, fixed \(U_i\) and causal maps \(G_i(x_{<i},U_i)\) settle the first \(j\) positions after \(j\) updates by induction; after \(N\) updates the vector equals the sequential ancestral sample and remains fixed.
result: The unconditional fresh-sampling interpretation is false, but the notation does not establish that the authors implement it. The separate speculative acceptance/progress rule and model quality are not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify reuse of the same random variate for each global token position, or a deterministic map/tie rule. An initially fixed seed that advances on every update is insufficient; an additional equality-check evaluation may be needed unless the known iteration bound is used directly.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: DARE overwrites the cached task cores
problems.source_location: task_merger.py, MatrixPerLayerMerger.get_core_matrices/get_dare_delta_w; released validation-search loop
claim: The cached M_list is returned and its entries are replaced by masked/rescaled tensors during each trial.
analysis: For retained entry \(x\), pruning probability \(p=1/2\), and binary mask \(z\), the first call gives \(2zx\). Resetting the seed repeats \(z\), but the mutated cache makes the second output \(2z(2zx)=4zx\), twice the first. A fresh object gives \(2zx\) again. In general \(j\) repeated same-mask calls give \(zx/(1-p)^j\); removed entries cannot be recovered by a later lower-pruning trial. First isolated calls, \(p=0\), fresh merger objects and non-mutating/full-space paths are countercontrols.
result: Repeated cached hyperparameter trials or final reconstruction can depend on earlier trials. The exact reported cells affected and changed accuracy remain unestablished.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep cached cores unchanged and build a local masked/rescaled list, retaining the first-call arithmetic and random stream. Re-run affected searches before replacing benchmark results.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: A lossless common coordinate map preserves matched SAR
problems.source_location: Section 5.2/Figure 5, latest PDF p.10; common-basis construction, pp.4–5
claim: The text attributes higher core-space SAR to the shared basis filtering task-specific noise.
analysis: For exact \(X=UM_XV^\top,Y=UM_YV^\top\), \(U^\top U=V^\top V=I\), and corresponding positive-singular-value subspaces, a compact SVD gives \(P_{Y,k}=U\widetilde U_k\widetilde U_k^\top U^\top\). Isometry preserves Frobenius numerator and denominator, hence \(\|P_{Y,k}X\|_F/\|X\|_F=\|\widetilde U_k\widetilde U_k^\top M_X\|_F/\|M_X\|_F\). Tied blocks require consistent transport. If \(k\) exceeds rank, arbitrary null completion changes SAR: \(X=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,0)\), \(Y=\operatorname{diag}(1,0,0)\), \(k=2\) gives \(1\) with completion \((e_1,e_2)\), but \(0\) with \((e_1,e_3)\).
result: The lossless coordinate change cannot itself remove represented task components or increase matched intrinsic alignment. Different rank budgets/null completions can explain changed diagnostics; the plotted numbers are not declared false, and nonlinear core merging can still change performance.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State exact rank/tie/null-space conventions and distinguish coordinate isometry from subsequent nonlinear merging. A changed diagnostic requires an explicit extra operation or selection rule.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Token normalization does not sample the general sequence-level target
problems.source_location: Eq.(8), PDF p.5; Algorithm 1 lines 9–11 and target interpretation, p.6
claim: The paper defines \(p_T(x)\propto p_D(x)^R q(x)^{1-R}\), but normalizes mixed logits separately at each token.
analysis: Take two binary positions, uniform factorized \(p_D=1/4\), \(R=1/2\), and verifier joint \(q=(0.49,0.01,0.25,0.25)\) over \(00,01,10,11\). Global normalization gives \(p_T=(7/18,1/18,5/18,5/18)\), first-token probability \(4/9\). Local normalization keeps first token uniform and yields joint \((7/16,1/16,1/4,1/4)\), with total variation \(1/18\). All probabilities are positive. Here identical first-token shared-randomness draws make the draft and sampled target prefix agree, avoiding a separate draft-prefix approximation. In general local denominators depend on the path; one global partition function cannot replace their product.
result: The general target-draw identification is false. Endpoint \(R=0,1\), history-independent conditionals or constant normalizer products are special controls. Eq.(8) is a valid distribution definition, and the final adaptive output was not established to be promised equal to it.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Explicitly define the local verifier distributions and scope the acceptance rule accordingly. Exact global-target conditionals would require suffix partition sums, for which no efficient implementation is established.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The positive-temperature helper effectively squares temperature
problems.source_location: Appendix C, PDF p.14; generation_utils.py, lines 97–123
claim: The sampler divides logits by \(T\), then divides exponentiated scores by \(E^T\), with \(E=-\log U\).
analysis: The maximizing score is equivalent to \(\ell/T^2-\log E\), hence its retained-support law is softmax at \(T^2\). Filtering first uses \(T\), so with active cutoffs the whole sampler is not simply a conventional \(T^2\) sampler. For logits \((0,0.2)\), \(T=0.2\), top-p \(0.95\), both tokens survive filtering. Nominal second-token probability is \(e/(1+e)=0.7310585786\), versus implemented \(e^5/(1+e^5)=0.9933071491\). At \(T=1\) the discrepancy disappears; the zero-temperature greedy branch is separate.
result: The supported positive-temperature path uses a different law from its nominal setting and the repository’s ordinary categorical baseline. Benchmark direction/magnitude and historical use remain unestablished.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Apply temperature once, filter the intended logits, then add standard Gumbel noise: \(X=\arg\max[\operatorname{filter}(\ell/T)+G]\). Preserve a common explicit filtering/sampling convention when comparing methods.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The target call ignores the supplied shared randomness
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1 and one-shot endpoint, PDF p.6; generation_utils.py, apd_accept_criterion lines 126–138
claim: The target sampler call passes noise but omits temperature; its zero default returns raw logits and ignores noise.
analysis: Use two positions with logits \((0,0.2)\), \(T=0.2,R=1\), top-p \(0.95\), positive noise factors \((0.3,0.9)\). Proposal scores are \(1/0.3=3.3333\) and \(e/0.9=3.0203\), choosing token \(0\) at both positions. These factors have an open admissible neighborhood under the source noise transform. The target default chooses greedy token \(1\), and forced first acceptance yields mask \((1,0)\). Identical distributions evaluated with the same sampling map/noise must instead produce \((1,1)\).
result: The helper fails the stated shared-noise endpoint for supported stochastic proposals. Coincidental greedy agreement and zero-temperature proposals are countercontrols; no natural-prompt failure frequency is established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use one canonical noise tensor and identical explicit temperature/filtering/tie conventions for both sampling paths. At the identical-distribution endpoint, equality then follows directly. This does not repair the separate global-target interpretation.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Full positional reconstruction retains omitted quadratic work
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF p.6; Table 1/Figure 3, p.7; vtu_atten_kernal lines 89–132
claim: The text concludes \(O(NUD)\) attention after unique-token contractions, while the exact kernel reconstructs all positional pairs.
analysis: At \(D=2,U=1\), mapping every full token to unique vector \((1,0)\) yields valid scores \(A_{mn}=\cos(\theta_m-\theta_n)\). Explicit output has \(N^2\) entries versus claimed scale \(2N\), an unbounded ratio. In general the code gathers dot/cross tensors of shape \((B,H,N,N,D/2)\), multiplies full positional weights and reduces them, costing \(\Theta(BHN^2D)\). Even the printed \(O(U^2D+NUD+N^2)\) expression cannot simplify as claimed for fixed \(U,D\). At \(B=1,H=32,N=576,D=128\), the two reconstruction products alone require \(BHN^2D=1{,}358{,}954{,}496\) scalar multiplies, omitted by totals matching only two unique-token contractions. Different MAC conventions cannot remove those multiplies.
result: The uniform unique-token complexity and interpretation of listed full attention savings fail for this explicit kernel. This is not a universal lower bound for future implicit/fused algorithms, nor evidence of wrong scores, false benchmark accuracy or absent savings in rowwise/MLP work.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For the supplied exact kernel state \(O(BH(U^2D+N^2D))\), with present materialized intermediate storage \(\Theta(BHN^2D)\). Separate contractions, full reconstruction, softmax/value work and end-to-end execution. Relabel restricted operator counts or recount consistently; the partial omitted count is not a complete replacement FLOP total.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The finite-horizon lower bound can exceed normalized regret
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.8, Eq.(3), PDF pp.5–6; proof Step 2/Step 5, pp.6–7
claim: The theorem gives \[c(C_0)\min\{s^{2/3}n^{2/3}q^{1/3},s\sqrt{pn}\}\], \(c(C_0)=\min\{C_0,e^{-4}/8\}/3\), without a horizon restriction.
analysis: Set \(n=1,s=100,k=1,C_0=1,p=1000,q=10^{12},d=99001\). Use atoms \(\{\pm e_j\}\), so \(Q=\|\cdot\|_\infty,R=\|\cdot\|_1\), baseline \(\theta_0=-e_1\), and \(99\) disjoint groups of \(1000\) remaining basis vectors. Let \(H\) contain all vectors with first coordinate \(1\) and remaining coordinates \(\pm10^{-6}\). Then \(Q(H)=1\), baseline reward \(-1\), each group’s average squared inner product on \(H\) is \(10^{-12}=1/q\), on its atoms \(1/1000=1/p\), and every group tuple plus baseline is a support. All displayed domain requirements hold, including \(s\ge3k+3\). The bound is \(e^{-4}100\sqrt{1000}/24=2.4132973204\). Yet every normalized expected one-step regret is at most \(2\). Gaussian realized rewards are not bounded; their zero-mean noise leaves this expected-regret ceiling intact.
result: The literal all-horizon theorem is false, independently of policy or chosen normalized hard instance. Its proof itself requires \(s\epsilon\le C_0/3\), with branch conditions \(9s^2p\le C_0^2n\) or \(27s^2q\le C_0^3n\). Fixed-parameter eventual rates are not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State the appropriate horizon regime, or clip the construction scale to \[\epsilon_*=\min\{\sqrt{p/n},(q/(sn))^{1/3},C_0/(3s)\}\]. The same testing/gap split then yields the conservative extra term \[c(C_0)\min\{s\sqrt{pn},s^{2/3}n^{2/3}q^{1/3},C_0n/3\}\]. Clipping the instance first is essential; merely clipping a final unsupported bound at \(2n\) is not a proof.
Both concerns were previously documented by the third-party BanditRLlib audit. No paper-author adoption of the stated repair is established.

problems.title: The dual atomic quantity need not be finite on the ambient space
problems.source_location: Axiom 3.1 and Definition 3.2, PDF p.5
claim: Nonempty sign-symmetric unit atoms are allowed without spanning, but \(R(X)=\sup_{Q(Y)\le1}\langle X,Y\rangle\) is called a finite seminorm on all \(V\).
analysis: In \(\mathbb R^2\), atoms \(\{\pm e_1\}\) satisfy the axiom and give \(Q(Y)=|y_1|\). For \(X=e_2\), every \(Y_t=(0,t)\) is feasible and \(\langle X,Y_t\rangle=t\), so \(R(e_2)=+\infty\). Finitely atom-supported \(X=\sum a_iE_i\) instead satisfy \(R(X)\le\sum|a_i|\), and the concrete finite-dimensional application atom systems span their spaces.
result: The global finite-valued definition needs a domain qualification. Constructed succinct parameters and the intended spanning application norms are not disproved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Require \(\operatorname{span}(U)=V\), restrict the ambient space to the atom span, or explicitly use an extended-real support function and state finite-domain operations. These are distinct scope choices.
Previously documented in the third-party BanditRLlib audit; author correction/adoption remains unestablished.

problems.title: Textual print deletion corrupts valid final-answer programs
problems.source_location: code_utils.py, remove_intermediate_prints lines 467–480; exec_python.py call; workflow, PDF pp.4–5
claim: The helper deletes every line containing the substring print( except the last matching line before execution.
analysis: A valid CSV program loads values \(3,5\), then if their sum exceeds \(7\) prints “yes”, else prints “no”. It emits exactly one final answer at runtime. Deleting the first branch’s print leaves an empty if suite, causing a parse error, independently of which branch the data select. Values \(1,2\) give the same structural failure. A second program assigns the six-character string “print(” to label, sets answer to its length, then prints answer; deleting the assignment instead creates an undefined name. One actual final-print control is unaffected.
result: The component can turn correct admissible programs into failures, potentially changing successful-memory inclusion or inference observations. Original generated-program frequency and numerical benchmark effects are unestablished; SQL evaluation is separate.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Remove source-line deletion and handle output according to an explicit runtime contract. Replacing removed statements with pass can still erase the correct final output; no general line-deletion substitute is supplied.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The example planning path ignores per-query meta-instructions
problems.source_location: Eqs.(4)–(5), PDF p.6; run_phi-3_python.sh; rag_final_python_cot_gpu.py active planning loader
claim: The active wrapper inserts shared prompt_sug and never reads each record’s generated rag_mg; the example also points planning at the raw rather than enriched input.
analysis: Hold question, data, template and shared guidance fixed, and change rag_mg from “sum the numeric column” to “count distinct identifiers”. The active wrapper’s prompt is identical because the changed field is absent from its dependencies. The existing mg wrapper does read the field and yields distinct prompts. Thus query-specific generation cannot affect this shown path, although a global-guidance variant can intentionally use it.
result: Confirmed example/configuration mismatch for reproducing the MI variant. The paper discusses multiple variants and the correct wrapper exists; no claim is made that the authors never implemented MI or that published MI results used this bypass.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For the MI variant, pass the enriched instruction output file and select the existing per-query wrapper. Missing prompts/models/configurations still prevent a complete reproduction claim.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The released weighted shrinkage is not the proximal map
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Eq.(4), PDF p.5; Algorithm 1, line 16, PDF p.21; models/clstm.py, lines 342–360
claim: For fixed positive normalized weights, the compression step should minimize \(J(U)=\tfrac12\|U-W\|_F^2+\sum_jt_j\|U_j\|_2\). The release instead divides a column by \(\max(\|W_j\|_2,\lambda\eta)\), even when its weighted threshold is smaller.
analysis: Take two columns \(W=(1/2,2)\), \(\lambda\eta=1\), and \(\alpha=(1/10,9/10)\), embedded in the allowed hidden dimension by zero padding. Grant the release’s threshold convention \(t=2\alpha=(1/5,9/5)\). It returns \((0.15,0.20)\), whereas columnwise soft thresholding gives \((0.30,0.20)\). The objective values are respectively \(2.07125\) and \(2.06\); the first-coordinate derivative at the release output is \(0.15-0.5+0.2=-0.15\), so the return is not the unique minimizer. Uniform weights are a passing special case.
result: The public nonuniform-weight operator differs from the correct printed formula. Its later optimization and benchmark effects are unmeasured.
assumptions: The two learned weights are positive and sum to one; the inspected default-threshold branch is used.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \((1-t/r)_+w\) for \(r=\|w\|_2>0\), with zero output for a zero column. Cauchy–Schwarz reduces the objective to \(\tfrac12(s-r)^2+ts\), uniquely minimized by \(s=(r-t)_+\). Match the threshold scaling to the stated objective.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Cross-station normalization changes the channel histories
problems.source_location: Appendix C, Moléne description, PDF p.22; prepare_data.py, lines 66–84
claim: The released Moléne loader normalizes across stations at each time: \(Y_{j,t}=(X_{j,t}-\min_\ell X_{\ell,t})/(\max_\ell X_{\ell,t}-\min_\ell X_{\ell,t})\). A graph of these channels need not describe raw-station history relations.
analysis: Use independent stationary channels \(X_t=(0,U_t,1,M_t)\), with \(U_t\) iid uniform on \([1,2]\) and \(M_t=3+M_{t-1}/2+\eta_t\), where \(\eta_t\) is iid uniform on \([-1,1]\). Its stationary solution lies in \([4,8]\). No raw channel causes another. Normalization gives \(Y_t=(0,B_t,C_t,1)\), with \(B_t=U_t/M_t\) and \(C_t=1/M_t\). The marker history reveals the previous autoregressive state, and the conditional prediction is \[\mathbb E[B_t\mid M_{t-1}=m]=\frac34\log\frac{4+m/2}{2+m/2}.\] It is strictly decreasing, taking approximately \(0.275794\) at \(m=5\) and \(0.232616\) at \(m=7\).

Even given \(M_{t-2}=m_0\) and the complete earlier target history, observing \(B_{t-1}=b\) leaves the fresh state on the nontrivial interval \((a-1,a+1)\cap(1/b,2/b)\), where \(a=3+m_0/2\). Its conditional density is proportional to \(m\). Thus the strictly varying conditional prediction is not recoverable from the target’s entire history, while the marker reveals it. This establishes a newly created predictive relation, not merely one-step correlation.
result: The normalization is legitimate for a graph of relative temperatures. Inferring raw physical station relations requires a separate justification; no actual weather edge is disproved here.
assumptions: Independent stationary innovations and a nonzero normalization denominator hold throughout the construction.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For raw-channel history preservation, fixed invertible channelwise affine transforms \(Y_{j,t}=a_jX_{j,t}+b_j\), \(a_j\ne0\), preserve each history sigma-field. Otherwise identify the target as the transformed-variable graph.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The public Lorenz generator uses a different observation protocol
problems.source_location: Appendix C, Lorenz-96, PDF p.22; synthetic.py, lines 60–79; prepare_data.py, lines 93–97
claim: The paper specifies output spacing \(0.05\) and noise added at each simulation step. The loader retains the generator’s default \(\delta=0.1\), and the source adds noise after deterministic integration.
analysis: With \(N=T+B\) inclusive grid points from zero to \(N\delta\), actual output spacing is \(N\delta/(N-1)\). At \(T=500\) and \(B=1000\), this is \(150/1499\approx0.100067\). The separate post-integration addition makes observational noise: unlike \(z_{k+1}=az_k+\epsilon_k\), an earlier observation perturbation cannot propagate into a later deterministic state. If “each step” meant observational noise, that portion is descriptive ambiguity rather than a stochastic-model error.
result: The inspected generator does not match the reported spacing; noise placement is explicit in the source. Which version generated the published scores remains unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Pin the historical generator and choose output times \(t_k=k\Delta\) for the intended spacing. Specify observational versus process noise before any experiment revision; an arbitrary stochastic-solver substitution is not justified.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The release does not honor the described batch and optimizer settings
problems.source_location: Section 4, Training and Evaluation Details, PDF p.7; models/clstm.py, lines 497–568; F40T500.yaml
claim: The paper describes full-batch Adam, weight decay \(0.1\), learning-rate warmup \(2000\) and coefficient warmup \(1500\). The public path uses replacement minibatches and constructs AdamW without forwarding the declared decay.
analysis: The sampler requests \(256\,\mathrm{max\_iter}\) replacement draws and the loader hardcodes batch size \(256\), regardless of the exposed argument. With \(T=500\), context \(10\) and stride \(1\), there are \(490\) windows, so such an update is not full batch. The optimizer call forwards only learning rate; logging a decay value in extra keyword arguments does not apply it. The released configuration uses warmup \(2200\) and coefficient start \(2000\). Generic minibatch pseudocode does not resolve the explicit full-batch experimental description.
result: These are distinct reproducibility settings. Neither stochastic optimization nor AdamW is intrinsically invalid, and published-result correspondence is not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Expose and forward the selected optimizer parameters, honor an explicit full-batch or minibatch mode, and retain the resolved experiment configuration. No replacement training run is validated.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Convex angle averaging does not preserve the product-group law
problems.source_location: Appendix A.5.1, PDF pp.17–18; Proposition A.4 and proof, PDF pp.20–21
claim: The proposed map sends component rotations to \(\phi(R(\theta_1),\ldots,R(\theta_n))=R(\sum_iw_i\theta_i\bmod2\pi)\) and is asserted to be a homomorphism for fixed or learned convex weights.
analysis: Take \(G_1=G_2=\{I,-I\}\), weights \(w_1=w_2=1/2\), and \(g=h=(-I,I)\), using angles \(0,\pi\). Then \(gh=(I,I)\), so \(\phi(gh)=I\); but \(\phi(g)=\phi(h)=R(\pi/2)\), giving \(\phi(g)\phi(h)=-I\). A coordinatewise angular carry of \(2\pi\) becomes only \(\pi\) after half weighting. Without a fixed branch, even the representatives \(0\) and \(2\pi\) for the identity give different outputs. A branch makes a function but does not fix the exhibited group-law failure.
result: The claimed product-group homomorphism is false. This does not refute circular-mean equivariance under one common rotation or the empirical prediction results.
assumptions: The group domain includes the two-element rotation subgroup and positive half weights.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Integer angle coefficients give well-defined torus homomorphisms. Alternatively, the paper’s circular mean \(s/|s|\), \(s=\sum_iw_iz_i\), is equivariant under a common rotation when weights are invariant and \(s\ne0\); it has a different guarantee. Keeping the unnormalized sum handles zero resultants globally.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The projected Stiefel operator is not an ambient rotation
problems.source_location: Section 2.3, PDF p.4; Section 2.5, PDF pp.5–6; Proposition A.3 and proof, PDF pp.19–20
claim: Proposition A.3 asserts \(VRV^\top\in SO(d)\) and identity action on the orthogonal complement when \(V^\top V=I_2\).
analysis: For \(d=3\), \(V=(e_1,e_2)\) and \(R=R(\pi/2)\), the operator sends \(e_3\) to zero and has determinant zero. Generally \((VRV^\top)^\top(VRV^\top)=VV^\top\), a rank-two projector rather than the ambient identity. However, Sections 2.3 and 2.5 already give the correct full lift, and an aligned base vector in the plane makes the embedding values coincide. The projected-circle conclusion survives.
result: The appendix’s ambient operator assertion is false, while its restricted-plane interpretation and earlier corrected construction survive. An implementation failure is not established.
assumptions: The ambient dimension exceeds \(2\); the base vector is unrestricted in the appendix statement.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the existing full lift \(Q=I-VV^\top+VRV^\top\). Orthogonal plane/complement blocks give \(Q^\top Q=I\) and determinant \(1\). If projection is intended, restrict the rotation assertion to the plane.
The correct complement-preserving formula already appears in Sections 2.3 and 2.5; reconciliation of the appendix is not established.

problems.title: The reported regression pairs need a matched-evaluation definition
problems.source_location: Tables 15–16, PDF pp.31–32; Appendix A.9.2 and A.10, PDF pp.25–26
claim: The mRFP columns pair Pearson correlation and coefficient of determination for the same named variants. If they use one common nonconstant target/prediction vector and standard definitions, they must satisfy \(R^2\le r^2\).
analysis: Writing \(t=\sqrt{S_{pp}/S_{yy}}\) and \(d^2=N(\bar p-\bar y)^2/S_{yy}\), residual expansion gives \(R^2=r^2-(t-r)^2-d^2\le r^2\). The vanilla row has \(r=0.6875\) and \(R^2=0.8028\), while \(r^2=0.47265625\). The same conditional comparison fails in all thirteen printed mRFP rows, with the smallest gap over \(0.223\), beyond four-decimal rounding. However, separate checkpoints, subsets, target scales or fold/run aggregation can invalidate a direct shared-vector comparison; averaged correlations need not obey the squared-mean bound.
result: The table values are incompatible under a common-vector standard-metric interpretation. The paper does not supply enough evaluation records to establish that interpretation or identify a wrong column.
assumptions: Standard Pearson and test-set coefficient of determination on identical nonconstant paired vectors are required for the inequality.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Identify sample IDs, prediction vectors, target scale, checkpoint, metric implementation and aggregation for both columns. Recompute matched metrics if that was intended; no replacement score is determined by correlation alone.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: A normalized minimum does not encode the raw obstacle threshold
problems.source_location: Section 3.1.3, Calculation of Affordance Map and Eq.(3), PDF p.7; Section 4.1 threshold, p.7
claim: For threshold-admissible navigable points the obstacle preference is min–max normalized, but Eq.(3) uses its zero value as the final exclusion mask. Target-distance normalization also divides by its range without a stated tie rule.
analysis: Let the already processed obstacle cloud be \(O=\{(0,0)\}\), target \(T=(1,0)\), candidates \(n_1=(1/2,0)\), \(n_2=(3/4,0)\), and threshold \(\tau_o=1/4\). Both are safe under the stated raw-distance threshold. Their obstacle distances are \((1/2,3/4)\), hence normalized preferences \((0,1)\); their inverse target preferences are \((0,1)\). Eq.(3) returns \((0,1)\), whereas a raw-distance mask followed by the stated clipping returns \((0.1,1)\). Every safe minimum is similarly excluded when \(d_{\max}>d_{\min}\ge\tau_o\).

Valid geometry also gives undefined ranges. Candidates \((\pm1/2,0)\) around the same obstacle have constant safe obstacle distance and yield \(0/0\). Alternatively, the original candidates with target \((5/8,0)\) have equal target distances \(1/8\), so semantic normalization yields \(0/0\).
result: The literal formulas need a normalization and tie convention. If excluding safe minima is intentional, it is an additional preference rule; normalization over a larger set containing obstacles could remove the first example. No route or success-rate change is established.
assumptions: Distances are finite, candidates nonempty, and extrema are over the navigable points being scored.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Separate the mask \(s(n)=\mathbf1\{d_o(n)\ge\tau_o\}\) from preference. Let \(q\) be inverse target normalization with an explicit common value when distances tie, and set \(\widehat a_f=s\,\operatorname{clip}(q,0.1,1)\). The positive clipped factor makes zero equivalent to raw threshold exclusion. This restores only that property, not collision-free planning.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: One fixed prompt does not cover the calibration set within a training call
problems.source_location: Sections 4.1–4.3, PDF pp.4–7; train-scripts/train-ccrt.py, lines 127–133 and 192–199
claim: The calibration-set procedure is implemented by choosing one random entity before the training loop and repeatedly reusing it.
analysis: For two non-target prompts with student responses \((\theta_1,\theta_2)\) and zero teacher responses, set removal loss \(\mu|\theta_2-1|\), \(\mu=1/200\), and preservation weight \(\lambda=1/100\). Fixing the first prompt minimizes \(\mu|\theta_2-1|+\lambda\theta_1^2\) at \((0,1)\). Uniform full-set preservation instead adds \(\lambda(\theta_1^2+\theta_2^2)/2\), whose minimizer is \((0,1/2)\). Randomizing a single anchor across calls is not the same adaptive trajectory as resampling within a call.
result: The release provides single-anchor training, not within-call set coverage. An external anchor schedule could be intentional; Eq.(4) alone does not specify a sampling law.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: If empirical-set preservation is intended, resample the calibration prompt each step or use a minibatch average. Otherwise document single-anchor training and its schedule. The usual conditional expectation of a sampled fixed-state gradient then equals the empirical-set gradient.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Common starting noise does not give a common latent argument
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, Eq.(4), PDF p.4; train-scripts/train-ccrt.py, lines 214–225; ldm/models/diffusion/ddim.py, lines 239–259
claim: Eq.(4) compares teacher and student at one \(x_t\). The release independently samples their latent states before comparing predictions.
analysis: A valid zero-noise DDIM step with cumulative coefficients \(\alpha=1/5\), \(\alpha_{\rm next}=4/5\) has form \(z_{\rm next}=2z-b\epsilon(z)\), \(b=3/\sqrt5\). Start both at \(z=1\), use teacher \(\epsilon_*(z)=z\), and student \(\epsilon_\theta(z)=kz\), \(k=2/b-1\). Their states become \(z_*=2-b\) and \(z_\theta=b\). The cross-state residual is \(kb-(2-b)=0\), but the common-teacher-state squared residual is \((k-1)^2(2-b)^2\approx0.112422373>0\).
result: The implemented zero discrepancy need not mean zero common-input discrepancy. A trajectory-level objective may still be useful but is a different objective.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Choose and disclose one latent-sampling rule, then evaluate both denoisers on exactly the same latent, time and prompt. Freeze the teacher and treat sampling consistently with the intended gradients.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: One checkpoint path cannot specify both later-stage initializations
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, PDF pp.4–5; Section 4.3, p.7; train-scripts/train-ccrt.py, get_models, lines 99–106
claim: A later stage requires original teacher \(\theta_0\) and student initialized at \(\theta_{i-1}\). Both public loader calls instead receive the same checkpoint path.
analysis: For \(\theta_{i-1}\ne\theta_0\), no single supplied path realizes the required ordered pair. Loading the previous model moves the teacher; loading the original restarts the student. The objectives differ concretely: retained responses \(f_i=i\delta\), \(\delta=0.1\), have previous-stage discrepancy \(0.01\), but original-reference discrepancy \(0.25\) at stage \(5\). This is an exact reference distinction, not a claimed observed model trajectory.
result: The release cannot independently express the described continuous original-teacher procedure. An unpublished wrapper or different generating revision could resolve historical correspondence.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Expose separate original-teacher and student-initialization checkpoint arguments and retain their identities in each stage record. They may coincide at the first stage.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released squared removal loss differs from the stated absolute norm
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, Eq.(3), PDF p.4; train-scripts/train-ccrt.py, lines 185 and 225–229
claim: The paper explicitly uses the residual \(\ell_1\) norm; the public routine instantiates MSELoss for both removal and alignment.
analysis: For a scalar removal target \(1\), retained target zero and \(\lambda=1/100\), the paper-form objective is \(J_1(x)=|x-1|+x^2/100\), uniquely minimized at \(1\). The squared version \(J_2(x)=(x-1)^2+x^2/100\) is minimized at \(100/101\). At that point \(J_1=201/10201>1/100=J_1(1)\). Scalar dimension removes any mean-versus-sum explanation.
result: The two losses can optimize different solutions. Which loss produced each original experiment is unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the stated absolute norm with an explicit reduction convention, or document the squared objective and identify its generating runs. Changing the norm also changes relative weighting in higher dimensions.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The returned genetic population need not be a scored elitist union
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, Algorithm 1, PDF p.6, lines 11–13; eval-scripts/generate-entity.py, lines 233–299
claim: The paper selects the best members of the parent/offspring union. The release scores and truncates before variation, then may terminate after unscored replacements.
analysis: Let \(k=2\) and fitnesses \(F(a)=3\), \(F(b)=2\), \(F(c)=1\), \(F(d)=0\). In an allowed no-crossover realization, initial scoring retains \((a,b)\); mutation removes \(a\) and creates \(d\). Population size is still \(2\), so the loop exits and returns \((b,d)\) without evaluating \(d\). Elitist union selection from unchanged parents and that offspring instead returns \((a,b)\). This traces an allowed control-flow realization, not its frequency in default runs.
result: The public finalization does not enforce the declared selection property. It does not establish global genetic-search failure or quantify generated-prompt quality.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep unchanged parent records, score every new genotype, and apply \(\operatorname{Top}_k(E_j\cup O_j;F)\) after variation on every return path. Its finite union-selection property follows directly from ordering the compared scores.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Single-component flags do not mask the optimized supervised loss
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Eq.(3), PDF p.5; Table 3, p.9; rebind/scripts/sdxl/rebind_lora_sdxl.py, lines 1489–1507
claim: In the ordinary no-SNR branch, active/passive selection flags zero the corresponding logging variables but do not affect the weighted loss returned for optimization.
analysis: Use one active and one passive residual \(r_A=1\), \(r_P=3\), with weights \(5\) and \(1\). The returned mean is \((5+9)/2=7\) under active-only, passive-only and combined flags. The derivative with respect to the allegedly disabled passive residual is \(r_P=3\), whereas a genuine active-only loss has derivative zero. Both source groups are loaded; the combined method itself legitimately uses both.
result: The advertised public flag cannot by itself reproduce a single-component ablation. The code revision or external data selection used for Table 3 is not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Apply component masks to the optimized loss itself, for example \(A\lambda n_A^{-1}\sum r_{A,i}^2+P n_P^{-1}\sum r_{P,i}^2\), omitting disabled terms and their loader requirements. Log the same included terms.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Relative role preference is not an absolute alignment threshold
problems.source_location: Section 4, Bias paragraph, PDF p.6; Table 3 and interpretation, p.9; load_triplet_data, lines 859–928
claim: The paper defines \(\beta=U-M\) and interprets \(\beta\le0\) as an unbiased, well-aligned image. The public pruning path tests relative ordering and does not use its absolute-threshold argument.
analysis: The criterion is exactly \(M\ge U\), satisfied by \((M,U)=(0.01,0)\) or \((0,0)\); it gives no positive lower bound on matching score. At combined weight \(1\), Table 3 gives matching/reversed scores \(63.4,75.5\); at weight \(5\), they are \(57.9,65.8\). The reported direction score improves by \(4.1\) percentage points while matching score falls by \(5.5\). Thus reduced reverse preference is supported, but the stated absolute-matching interpretation does not follow from that statistic. The public filter retains zero and low-score ties because only the sign of \(M-U\) is tested.
result: The relative statistic remains useful within its definition. No real image is assigned the synthetic scores, and human or fine-grained evaluation evidence is not rejected.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe \(\beta\le0\) as intended-over-reversed score ordering and report both scores. If absolute quality is intended, separately calibrate an explicit condition such as \(M\ge\tau\) together with \(M-U\ge\delta\); no numerical threshold is validated here.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: A finite intermediate limit is applied inconsistently across two passes
problems.source_location: create_intermediate_dpo_dataset, rebind/scripts/sdxl/rebind_lora_sdxl.py, lines 1017–1027 and 1083–1094
claim: The first pass slices each relation-type list to the requested finite limit, but the construction pass iterates through the unsliced list and indexes the partially populated dictionary.
analysis: With active relations \((a_1,a_2)\), passive relations \((p_1,p_2)\) and limit \(1\), loading creates only the first relation of each type and its reverse. Construction nevertheless reaches \(a_2\) and accesses its absent dictionary entry. The full-selection default loads all those keys and is a passing control; an image-count ablation is a different parameter.
result: The nondefault finite-relation configuration has a direct missing-key path. This does not show that a default experiment crashed or that Table 10’s image-count experiment is invalid.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Compute the selected relation lists once and reuse them during loading and construction. This prevents requests for unselected relation keys, without guaranteeing that all unrelated dataset errors are resolved.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The response-level rejection rule does not give the required prompt partition
problems.source_location: Definition 2 and Definition 4; Algorithm 2; Appendix A.1 and Lemma 10; current arXiv:2502.08924v2, PDF pp.5–7 and 19–20
claim: Definition 2 rejects a prompt when an individual response fails, while Lemma 10 assumes rejection only after all \(k\) independent trials fail. Appendix A.1 also uses ordinary sets of response pairs.
analysis: Use four prompts \((a,b,c,d)\), binary correctness, \(\alpha=1\), \(\beta=1/2\), a perfect filter and an initially wrong model. On every nonempty prompt subset, let the weak labeler correctly label the first \(\lceil|U|/2\rceil\) prompts. The first weak round correctly labels \(a,b\); the next labels \(c\) correctly with weight \(1/2\), after its earlier wrong weight \(1/4\), giving \(Q_2(c)=2/3\). At the third round, mixed correct/incorrect responses occur with probability \(1-(2/3)^k-(1/3)^k>0\). The written filter then places \(c\) in both accepted and rejected prompt sets.

For an exact Lemma 10 probability violation, use two prompts and \(\beta=\gamma=1/2\), \(T=3\), \(k=12\). The required lower bound on \(k\) is about \(11.5615\). After the first weak round, one prompt is always correct. Ordinary-set deduplication leaves one pair, accepted with probability \(1/2\), so the lemma’s event fails with probability at least \(1/2>1/T\). Keeping occurrences but retaining the any-failure rule instead gives rejection probability \(1-2^{-12}\), also inconsistent with an all-failure estimate.
result: The partition and probability proof do not follow from the literal specification. This is not a direct counterexample to every parameter condition of the final quality theorem; its intended all-trials-fail interpretation is coherent.
assumptions: The weak labeler obeys the required guarantee on every nonempty subset, not merely on the original full prompt distribution.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep independent trial identities until filtering, reject a prompt only when no trial is accepted, and retain exactly one accepted response per prompt per round. Then conditional rejection probability is at most \((1-\beta\gamma)^k\), and a union bound gives \(nT e^{-\beta\gamma k}\).
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The induction needs the first correct weak-label round
problems.source_location: Lemma 11(d) and induction for part (a); current arXiv:2502.08924v2, PDF pp.20–23
claim: The proof invokes a positive-quality lower bound stated for \(r<t\) when a prompt can first receive its correct weak label at \(r=t\).
analysis: Under the explicitly repaired trial-level routing, a newly correct prompt has \(Q_t(x)=\lambda_t/\sum_{s\le t}\lambda_s\). Prior shrinkage gives \(\lambda_s\le(1-\beta)^{t-s}\lambda_t\), so \[Q_t(x)\ge\frac{1}{\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}(1-\beta)^j}=\frac{\beta}{1-(1-\beta)^t}\ge\beta.\] This supplies the omitted first-success case without applying the earlier premise beyond its domain. Previously correct prompts only receive correct accepted responses, so their quality cannot decrease.
result: The written induction omits a necessary boundary invariant. Its repair, together with the explicit filtering repair, supports the intended convergence rate; empirical training is not reproduced.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Track the first correct weak-label round, retain the displayed boundary bound, and then propagate monotone correctness. With \(R=\lceil\log(2/\epsilon)/\beta\rceil\), enough later accepted rounds leave at most \(\epsilon/2\) residual error on the already corrected prompts and at most \(\epsilon/2\) uncorrected mass.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Stationary canonical paths need the missing optimal-control conditions
problems.source_location: Section 2.1, Eqs.(4)–(9), PDF p.3; Section 2.3, pp.4–5; Appendix D.1, pp.24–25; current arXiv:2404.15617v4
claim: Action stationarity and canonical dynamics alone do not select the optimal initial costate or impose terminal transversality. The reward described as penalizing control effort also has a positive quadratic action term under maximization.
analysis: Use \(\dot s=a\), \(s(0)=1\), horizon \(1\), free terminal state and reward \(-\tfrac12\int_0^1(s^2+a^2)dt\). The paper-sign Hamiltonian is \(pa+(s^2+a^2)/2\); stationarity gives \(a=-p\). Initial costate zero yields \(s=\cosh t\), \(p=-\sinh t\), satisfying the displayed equations but giving reward \(-\sinh2/4\approx-0.906715\), below the admissible zero-action reward \(-1/2\). Correct transversality instead gives \(p(1)=0\) and initial costate \(\tanh1\). Separately, maximizing \(a^2/2-1\) prefers \(a=2\) over zero, so that term alone is not an effort penalty.
result: The stationary-to-optimal bridge needs conditions. Appendix D’s value-gradient discussion and an abstract assumption of the optimal operator are valid restricted alternatives; neither is contradicted by the example.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State the canonical equations as necessary conditions along an appropriately selected optimal trajectory. Specify terminal conditions and the initial costate/value gradient, or explicitly assume the optimal operator; reconcile reward maximization and effort cost consistently.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The finite derivative-learning rate needs capacity, local mass and anchor control
problems.source_location: Definition 3.1, PDF p.5; Lemma B.3, pp.17–18; Definition B.5 and Lemma B.7, pp.18–20; current arXiv:2404.15617v4
claim: The stated smooth bounded-parameter conditions alone imply a finite derivative-learning sample count \(O(\epsilon^{-(2d+4)})\); the restricted proof further drops an anchor residual using its linearly bounded condition.
analysis: Take \(d=1\), uniform input on \([0,1]\), target \(g(x)=x\), and the permitted bounded smooth class \(\mathcal H=\{0\}\). Every derivative residual is \(1\), so for \(\epsilon=1/2\) no finite sample count succeeds. A conditional optimization statement when the target belongs to the class does not supply the absent realizability premise.

The cone step also needs sampling geometry: at \(Y=1-\epsilon_1/4\), an outward annular interval \((Y+\epsilon_1/2,Y+\epsilon_1)\) lies outside \([0,1]\) and has zero probability, contradicting a uniform positive local-mass assertion. Finally, linear boundedness controls a difference, not an anchored value: \(h_1(x)=1+x\), \(Y=1/2\), \(X=51/100\) satisfies the difference condition with constant \(1\), yet \(|h_1(X)|=1.51>0.01\). The missing term is \(|h_1(Y)|\).
result: The literal capacity claim is false and the proposed sample-rate proofs lack independent geometric/residual conditions. This does not refute every strengthened realizable learning theorem.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Require quantified approximation capacity, optimization tolerance and suitable local sampling mass. Retain \(|h_1(X)|\le|h_1(Y)|+C\|\nabla h_1(Y)\|\|X-Y\|\), or impose the exact interpolation needed to remove its anchor. No repaired original exponent is established.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The staged proof changes probability and rollout-distribution guarantees
problems.source_location: Definition 3.1 and Theorem 3.2, PDF pp.5–6; Appendix B, Eqs.(31)–(37), pp.15–16; Corollary 3.5; current arXiv:2404.15617v4
claim: The staged argument requires a confidence statement about mean error, retained fit after a new hypothesis is trained, and guarantees on adaptive rollout distributions; its definition and sample budgets do not supply all three.
analysis: A pointwise tail event does not yield the same mean threshold. For uniform \(X\in[0,1]\), set \(w=1/40\) and \(e(x)=(1-((x-1/2)/w)^2)^3\) inside the width-\(2w\) interval and zero outside. Then \(\Pr(e>0.01)<0.1\), but \(\mathbb E e=4/175>0.01\). Taking \(h(x)=\int_0^x e(u)du\) realizes a smooth derivative residual.

The base sample count uses failure probability \(\delta\), but the strengthened induction starts at \(\delta/3^{H-1}\). Reusing samples does not itself retain a population error guarantee for a newly fitted hypothesis. Nor does a continuous initial density imply the same property after rollout: locally, the allowed Euler–Hamiltonian form with \(g(s,p)=-sp/\Delta_t\) maps \((s,p)\) to \((0,2p)\), collapsing a smooth density to a line. A smooth cutoff makes the construction bounded on a compact domain. The small-step limit also requires uniform derivative and confidence/sample-budget control as \(H\) grows.
result: These are substantive unmet proof obligations; the supplied examples isolate invalid transitions rather than claiming to satisfy every hypothesis of a single full staged counterexample.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A sufficient operator statement explicitly assumes simultaneous bounds \(\mathbb E\|F(G^{(i)}X)-G(G^{(i)}X)\|\le\epsilon_{\rm op}\) on every relevant rollout law, with \(F\) Lipschitz. Then \(e_j\le L e_{j-1}+\epsilon_{\rm op}\) gives \(e_j\le\epsilon_{\rm op}\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}L^i\). This does not prove that the proposed sample budgets achieve those stronger assumptions.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Post-fit accuracy cannot bound earlier collection regret
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1, lines 2,4,6–7, PDF p.5; Eq.(20), Corollary 3.6 and Eq.(21), p.7; current arXiv:2404.15617v4
claim: The online training-regret proof assigns the fitted stage-\(k\) error to episodes actually collected using the previous policy, yielding the advertised \(O(K^{5/6})\) special case.
analysis: At permitted fixed horizon \(H=2\), there is one training stage. If the random initial policy has allowed expected episode gap \(c>0\), all \(K=N_1\) collection episodes use it, so expected collection regret is \(cK\), even if learning becomes exact immediately afterward. For \(c=1/4\), its ratio to \(K^{5/6}\) is \(K^{1/6}/4\), unbounded. This is a schedule-level conditional obstruction for any admitted nonzero initialization gap, not a newly simulated Hamiltonian benchmark.
result: The stated post-training accuracy does not establish the claimed online training regret. The loss incurred before fitting cannot be reduced retroactively.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a separate deployment statement or prove accuracy for the policies actually collecting each batch. Under extra exploration and deployment assumptions, an explore-then-deploy comparison has \(C_1\epsilon^{-\mu}+C_2K\epsilon\), giving order \(K^{\mu/(\mu+1)}\); this comparison is not a repaired dfPO theorem.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The replay path pairs a successor score with its predecessor state
problems.source_location: Definition 2.1 and Eq.(12), PDF p.4; query_system.py, get_zero_order_info; memory.py, ReplayMemory._query_samples
claim: The oracle is defined to return a state and its own score; the public query appends a successor and its post-step value, while replay pairs values with the state list excluding its last entry.
analysis: For \(s_{t+1}=s_t+a_t\), \(\mathcal F(s)=s^2\), \(s_0=1\) and \(a_0=1\), the successor is \(2\) with value \(4\). Pairing that value with states[:-1] gives \((1,4)\), although \(\mathcal F(1)=1\). Correct successor pairing is \((2,4)\). Zero action is a passing special case. A next-state value target could be defined, but it is policy-dependent and differs from the paper’s same-state score.
result: The current public replay path has a direct label-alignment discrepancy. No effect on original trained policies is quantified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Pair post-step values with states[1:], or query the intended current-state score before advancing. Reconcile the full stage/oracle semantics before treating a local slice change as a complete repair.

problems.title: Reward decay and baseline constructor settings differ from the description
problems.source_location: Section 4.2 and Appendix C.1/Table 3, PDF pp.8 and 21; envs/bbo.py; benchmarks/sb3_utils.py
claim: The written reward multiplier at step \(m\) is \(\gamma^{-m}\); the release divides by a squared accumulated discount, giving \(\gamma^{-2m}\). DDPG and TQC also omit supplied learning-rate and return-discount constructor arguments.
analysis: At \(\gamma=0.81\), first step, zero action and functional cost \(1\), the written reward is \(-1/0.81\), but the release gives \(-1/0.81^2\). For molecular \(\gamma=0.0067\), the first-step magnitude ratio is about \(149.254\). The inverse get_val uses the same squared convention and remains internally consistent, so terminal reported functional values are not thereby shown wrong. Direct constructor inspection shows four other baseline branches forward the supplied scalars, while DDPG/TQC do not.
result: The public baseline objective/configuration differs from the declared setup. Historical checkpoints and package versions are needed to establish original settings and ranking effects.

problems.title: The significance notebook tests simulated observations
problems.source_location: Appendix C.2 and Table 4, PDF p.21; analysis.ipynb, cell 4; prior public AuditOwl entry 1867
claim: The paper describes tests on seed-level observations, but the released notebook draws new Gaussian samples from table summaries and tests those simulated samples.
analysis: The cell sets sample size \(10\), calls np.random.normal separately for each method and then Welch’s ttest_ind, without reading observed seed means. For the surface comparison, its input summaries are \(6.296\pm0.048\) and \(6.365\pm0.030\). If these were independent sample means/standard deviations of size \(10\), their direct summary-statistic t value would be approximately \(-3.854809\), whereas the recorded simulated-data t value is approximately \(-1.8138\). A paired analysis would additionally require actual covariance; neither value is certified as the correct paper reanalysis here.
result: That cell cannot establish the stated observed-data significance test. The issue was already publicly reported; the notebook alone does not establish exclusive historical use or invented benchmark means.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Recover actual seed-level observations and apply the design-appropriate prespecified test, effect-size and uncertainty calculation. Do not replace observations by new random draws.
Previously reported in public AuditOwl entry 1867; author adoption or a corrected observed-data analysis is not established.

problems.title: The molecular bands are enlarged and capped display intervals
problems.source_location: Figure 1(c), PDF p.8; benchmarks_run.py, molecular std_scale; utils.py, _bootstrap and _tsplot
claim: The current molecular plotting branch uses scale \(3000\); the helper multiplies bootstrap percentile half-widths and caps each at one fifth of the median magnitude.
analysis: If raw percentile deviations from median \(m\) are \(d_-,d_+\), the returned endpoints are \(m-\min(3000d_-,|m|/5)\) and \(m+\min(3000d_+,|m|/5)\). Small uncapped intervals are thus widened by \(3000\); once capped around median \(100\), the interval can be \([80,120]\). Means are not changed. These bands cannot be interpreted as unscaled bootstrap intervals, although intentional visual enlargement is legitimate when labeled.
result: The released plotting transform requires disclosure for inferential interpretation. The exact published-figure generating revision is unresolved, and table standard deviations are not shown to use this transform.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For inferential uncertainty use the untransformed interval and state its unit/level; label any enlarged visualization with its exact factor and cap. Recover original trajectory/plotting provenance before revising published figures.

problems.title: The best-checkpoint option selects current rather than best state
problems.source_location: finetuning.py, lines 12–37 and 155–161; utils.py, get_finetuning_state_dict; current author commit 9b83bf208a124eb9d33f7a680d7924f1f1700953
claim: Both final-save branches serialize the current model. The best-validation state is also captured without an immutable copy.
analysis: Take consecutive parameter states \((1,2,3)\) with validation scores \((1,0,0)\), and enable best-state saving. The highest score is at state \(1\), but the shared final expression serializes state \(3\). Reference-based capture can also change while training storage is updated; the ignored best-state object already establishes failure independently of aliasing. Final-best and final-state-only settings are passing cases.

paragraphs: Capture an immutable selected state, metric and step when validation improves; serialize that snapshot when requested, with explicit no-validation and tie handling.
