problems.title: Validation does not restore the subsequent training mode
problems.source_location: finetuning.py, train_epoch, lines 12–37, and eval_dataset, lines 40–62; current author commit 9b83bf208a124eb9d33f7a680d7924f1f1700953
claim: The epoch sets training mode once; periodic validation sets evaluation mode and never restores it before later optimization batches.
analysis: With three training batches and validation every two, the control flow gives forward modes \((\mathrm{train},\mathrm{train},\mathrm{eval})\). Mode changes do not disable backpropagation. For scalar prediction \(dw\) with inverted dropout \(d=M/(1-p)\), squared loss has expected training gradient \(w/(1-p)-y\), whereas evaluation mode gives \(w-y\). At \(p=1/2\), \(w=1\), \(y=0\), these are \(2\) and \(1\). Zero dropout or validation only after the final batch removes this particular effect.
result: The current source changes the optimization distribution after validation. The direction or size of any LoRA/full-tuning performance effect is not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Save the caller’s mode, evaluate without gradient tracking, and restore that mode on every return or exception. Intentionally mixed child-module modes require corresponding per-module restoration.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Asymmetric reference rounding can create a zero-update intruder
problems.source_location: Definition 3.1 and Algorithm 1, PDF p.4; find_intruder_dimensions.py, lines 12–17 and 34–40; utils.py, get_model_to_train
claim: The public entry point first loads the reference in float16 while the tuned-model helper defaults to float32. Casting both to float32 immediately before SVD cannot recover the lost reference entries.
analysis: Take identical original matrices \(W=(1-c)I_{16}+c\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top\), with stored diagonal \(1\) and off-diagonal \(c\approx2\times10^{-8}\). The leading vector is \(q=\mathbf1/4\), with simple spectral gap \(16c\). Since \(0<c<2^{-25}\), half-precision round-to-nearest erases each off-diagonal entry, yielding identity. A valid identity SVD uses coordinate vectors, giving \(\max_i|q^\top e_i|=1/4<1/2\): one top-vector intruder despite zero actual tuning update. Equal original inputs instead give cosine \(1\) and count zero. The rounded repeated spectrum makes the outcome basis-dependent; no universal backend result or frequency in real model layers is claimed.
result: The current measurement path admits a precision-history false positive. It does not establish that the observed original intruders or behavioral interventions are all numerical artifacts.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Load both original matrices from the same model revision at equal original analysis precision, retain dtype/hash/gap diagnostics, and include a zero-update control. Equalizing dtype after one-sided rounding is insufficient; repeated-spectrum subspace interpretation remains a separate question.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Timing normalization counts channels rather than states
problems.source_location: Table 1, p.7; experiments/eval.py, lines 258–266 and 361; lola/emulation.py, decode_traj, lines 44–70
claim: Table 1 describes inference time per state, including generation and decoding. The evaluator divides elapsed time by the first two dimensions of a decoded trajectory whose layout is \((B,C,L,\ldots)\).
analysis: The denominator is therefore \(BC\), while the number of output states is \(BL\). For elapsed time \(1\) second and shape \((2,3,5,4,4)\), the release reports \(1/6\) second; the per-output-state value is \(1/10\), or \(1/8\) per newly generated state if each trajectory has one context state. Doubling channels alone changes the exported field to \(1/12\) without changing the number of states. The decoder’s explicit rearrangement establishes the axis identity independently of timing execution.
result: The exported unit is not per temporal state. Whether the published table used this field, and the corrected benchmark values, remain unestablished. A per-channel-per-trajectory interpretation would require a different label.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For total output states divide by \(BL\); for newly generated states divide by \(B(L-c)\) with an explicit context count \(c\). State the selected unit and timing synchronization/warmup protocol.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The context sampler uses wrapping rather than Poisson truncation
problems.source_location: Appendix B, p.17, before Eq.(15); lola/emulation.py, random_context_mask, lines 184–221; experiments/configs/train_diffusion.yaml, lines 12–18
claim: The paper describes a Poisson count with parameter \(2\), truncated to allowable positive context lengths. The released configuration samples \(N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(1)\) and sets \(c=1+(N\bmod4)\) for a window of length \(5\).
analysis: Wrapping sends every count in the same residue class to one length. Its probabilities for \(c=1,2,3,4\) are approximately \[(0.383216876,0.370946117,0.184450766,0.061386241)\]. In contrast, conditioning \(\operatorname{Pois}(2)\) on \(1\le c\le4\) gives \((1/3,1/3,2/9,1/9)\). Clipping would also produce a different distribution. Adding a minimum-count offset changes the mean but does not make a wrapped law into the stated conditional law.
result: The source’s training mask distribution differs from the written distribution. This does not determine whether its empirical performance is better or worse.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Document the wrapped law if it is intended, or sample the finite conditional categorical probabilities. Rejection from \(\operatorname{Pois}(2)\) until \(1\le c\le4\) has acceptance probability \(6e^{-2}\).
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The printed second difference drops a sign-relevant remainder
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.6, Claim 3.7 and Proposition 3.8, p.6; Appendix A.3, p.14
claim: Theorem 3.6 prints \(\Delta^2E_t=p_t[\Delta V_{t+1}-\Delta V_t+V_t(\epsilon_t-\epsilon_{t+1})]\). Its proof discards products of small terms without retaining a remainder or a quantitative condition controlling their effect on curvature.
analysis: Use an absorbing incorrect state, horizon \(3\), correct-proposal error \(q=0.01\), beam width \(1\) and two independent expansions. Correct proposals score \(0.5\); an incorrect proposal scores \(1\) with probability \(a_t\), otherwise \(0\). Then \(\epsilon_t=q^2+2q(1-q)a_t\), \(V_t=(1-q)^{3-t}\), \(p_{t+1}=p_t(1-\epsilon_t)\), and \(E_t=p_tV_t\). For \[\epsilon=(0.002,0.00208,0.00216)\], all ranking error rates are below random-selection error \(q\) and increase over time. Yet \[E=(0.970299,0.9781398,0.9859649184)\] has \(\Delta^2E_0=-0.0000156816\), whereas the printed right side is \(+0.00002137608\). The omitted remainder \(-0.00003705768\) reverses the sign.

Increasing errors \((0.002,0.00201,0.00202)\) instead give positive actual curvature \(0.0000534798\); increasing ranking error alone does not imply concavity. The paper’s additional dominance expectation is qualitative, so this does not refute a separately imposed numerical dominance inequality. Claim 3.7 says “we expect,” Proposition 3.8 says “typically,” the footnote calls the shapes conjectural, and Section 4 calls the stopping rule heuristic.
result: The finite equality is false and cannot alone certify curvature. The affine z-score observation and elementary concave-sequence lemma are unaffected; no new beam-search benchmark result is asserted.
assumptions: The example uses independent proposals and an absorbing incorrect state; scores implement the declared selection error probabilities.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: In this absorbing submodel the exact identity is \[\Delta^2E_t=p_t[(1-\epsilon_t)(1-\epsilon_{t+1})V_{t+2}-2(1-\epsilon_t)V_{t+1}+V_t].\] Retain the omitted remainder and require the negative leading contribution to exceed its magnitude before concluding strict concavity. A model with recovery from incorrect states needs additional terms; the absorbing formula is not a universal replacement.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: An unconditional fallback can defeat goal validation
problems.source_location: Section 4.3, Eq.(8), p.5; Appendix A.2, Algorithm 2; Appendix A.3, Figure 8; lazySI.py, forward, lines 1111–1154
claim: When the proposed skill fails goal validation, the printed rule ranks state proximity over \(A(g)\cup\{z_h\}\), where \(A(g)\) contains goal-valid skills. The following prose says the rejected proposal \(z_h\) is only a fallback when no valid candidate exists.
analysis: Take two skills, proposal \(z_h=1\), state \(s=0\), and goal \(g=10\). Give the state prototypes means \(0,1\), the goal prototypes means \(0,10\), and every Gaussian variance \(1\). With threshold \(\sqrt{\chi^2_{1,0.99}}\approx2.575829\), skill \(1\) fails goal validation and skill \(2\) passes. The unconditional union nevertheless ranks skill \(1\) first because its state distance is \(0\), versus \(1\). Four duplicate prototypes satisfy the stated prototype count; small perturbations preserve the strict inequalities. The same construction embeds in \(60\) dimensions with identity covariance, whose threshold is approximately \(9.401<10\). In contrast, the author implementation collects valid candidates and introduces its nearest-goal fallback only when that collection is empty, so it avoids this example.
result: The current printed candidate formula does not enforce its own stated fallback semantics. This is a paper/implementation specification inconsistency, with no demonstrated current-code failure or reward reduction.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Make the rule conditional: retain \(z_h\) if it is valid; otherwise rank over \(A(g)\) when nonempty; use an explicitly chosen fallback only when \(A(g)=\varnothing\). Align the empty-set fallback with the implementation, which uses nearest goal proximity rather than necessarily returning \(z_h\).
The official supplemental implementation and current public implementation already avoid the demonstrated failure. The latest paper formula still contains the unconditional union.

problems.title: A dead branch prematurely terminates depth-first decoding
problems.source_location: Section 4.3, pp.6–7; exp/1/exp_utils.py, constrained_decoding, lines 225–299; exp/1/6-gen.py, lines 95–123
claim: The paper describes backtracking to alternative branches. During the full-candidate pass, the author function returns termination whenever the current prefix has no children, without checking whether its depth-first stack still contains siblings.
analysis: Use vocabulary \(\{0,1,2,3\}\) in that order. The empty prefix admits incomplete prefixes \([0]\) and \([1]\); no extension of \([0]\) is valid; \([1,2]\) is complete; all other extensions are invalid. Set maximum length \(3\), first-pass candidate ratio \(0.01\), and no timeout or requested end token. The restricted pass follows \([0]\) and exhausts. The full pass stacks both siblings, explores \([0]\), then returns termination with \([1]\) still pending. Its returned \([0,3]\) is merely the last rejected candidate. Thus a valid complete branch is missed by control flow, independently of model logits or native mesh code.

The reported mesh strengthening uses planar vertices \[(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(1/2,1,0),(-1/2,1,0),(-1,0,0)\] and faces \((0,1,2),(0,2,3),(0,3,4)\). Operation length is \(10+f_v+e_v\): central vertex \(0\) requires \(17\) tokens, boundary vertex \(1\) requires \(13\). A cap of \(13\) can kill the preferred central branch while a boundary branch remains. This supports the mechanism’s relevance, but the original native validator and reported adapted execution were not rerun here; the complete generic finite-grammar witness already establishes the search defect.
result: The current function can report search exhaustion prematurely; its generation caller then stops further splits. Intentional end-token termination, an actually empty search and timeout are separate cases. No claim about typical model orderings or published mesh metrics follows.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Continue the depth-first loop after a dead branch. Declare exhaustion only after each pass has exhausted its stack; pending prefixes preserve the ordinary finite-search invariant. No complete patched model-generation run is certified.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Inverse-quality weighting can reinforce a bad pseudo-label
problems.source_location: Sections 3.3–3.4, pp.5–6, Eqs.(4)–(8); Appendix B.1
claim: The paper calls both directions supervised fine-tuning and uses model-generated code as the text-to-code supervision target. Equation (8) weights its loss by \(1-S_i\), assigning non-executable code score \(S_i=0.1\). Under ordinary detached-target negative log-likelihood, this fits a low-quality target more strongly.
analysis: Let the two outputs be faithful code and code using an undefined year variable, with scores \(1\) and \(0.1\). Let faithful-code probability be \(q=\sigma(a)\). A bad target contributes \(-0.9\log(1-q)\), whose derivative is \(0.9q\). At \(a=0\), a unit descent step sends \(a\) to \(-0.45\) and \(q\) to approximately \(0.3893607661\); a good target has zero weight and produces no update. Sampling once from the initial model gives expected post-step faithful probability approximately \(0.444680383<0.5\).

For finite outputs with fixed quality scores and targets sampled from the same current policy, the expected detached-target gradient obeys \[\mathbb E[(1-S)\nabla(-\log p_\theta)]=\nabla\sum_c p_\theta(c)S(c).\] Gradient descent therefore moves against the local expected-quality gradient. This establishes the conditional mechanism, not an observed full-training result. Equation (8) does not expand the underlying loss; an unreported target repair, separate frozen sampling policy or rejection stage could change this interpretation, and the alternating reconstruction update can offset it.
result: The written inverse-quality rationale is not justified by ordinary supervised pseudo-label likelihood. Actual checkpoint behavior requires the precise target/loss pipeline; no end-to-end degradation is claimed.
assumptions: Targets and quality scores are detached; loss is ordinary supervised negative log-likelihood; sampled targets are not silently corrected.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For the same restricted setup, confidence weighting \(S[-\log p_\theta]\) reverses the expected gradient sign and improves expected proxy quality to first order. Rejecting or repairing non-executable targets is another proposed condition; neither is established as a validated replacement for the complete method.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The stratified filter audit estimates predictive values
problems.source_location: Section 4.3, p.9, Fact Filtering analysis; Section 4.1, retained/non-factual/invalid fractions
claim: The audit samples \(100\) texts from each predicted factual/non-factual group, yet labels agreement rates \(93\%\) and \(92\%\) as true-positive and true-negative rates.
analysis: Conditioning on predicted group estimates positive and negative predictive values, rather than conditioning on true class. In the displayed balanced sample the counts are \(TP=93,FP=7,FN=8,TN=92\): sample sensitivity is \(93/101\), specificity \(92/99\), while predictive values are \(0.93\) and \(0.92\). If the sampled strata are representative and invalid cases are excluded, weighting by population predicted fractions \(a=0.5374,b=0.2785\) yields sensitivity \(a(0.93)/(a(0.93)+b(0.08))\approx0.957323\) and specificity \(b(0.92)/(b(0.92)+a(0.07))\approx0.871977\). These are conditional plug-in estimates, not validated population performance; the invalid fraction \(0.1841\) needs its own handling.
result: The stated sampling scheme does not directly estimate the named sensitivity/specificity. Individual annotations and uncertainty intervals are unavailable, so no exact population error rate is asserted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Rename the observed stratum agreements as predictive values. To estimate sensitivity and specificity, specify reference labels, sampling weights, uncertainty and the treatment of invalid/abstained cases.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: One SQuAD metric pair needs evaluation provenance
problems.source_location: Table 2, p.9, LLaMA/SymbCoT row
claim: The row reports SQuAD F1 \(82.14\) and exact match \(86.20\).
analysis: For the standard same-example, same-prediction SQuAD metrics, exact match implies token F1 \(1\), and other F1 values are nonnegative. Hence aggregate F1 cannot be below exact match when aggregation weights and examples agree. The printed ordering violates that condition. A transposed cell, transcription error or different evaluation protocol is not distinguishable from the table alone.

problems.title: An ordinary-loss prefix has incompatible shapes and indices
problems.source_location: src/utils/train_utils.py, get_scfm_timesteps, lines 24–70; trainer/flux_scfm.py, shortcut target around lines 1523–1610; trainer/sd3_scfm.py, corresponding target
claim: For batch size \(N\), prefix fraction \(r\), prefix size \(m=\lceil Nr\rceil\) and skip \(s\), teacher durations have shape \((N,s)\). The source assigns row zero of their prefix into a length-\(m\) student slice, then returns full-batch teacher/self indices to a closure receiving only the suffix.
analysis: Take \(N=4,r=0.6,s=2\), teacher steps \(32\), teacher ratio \(1\). The assignment attempts a length-\(2\) row into a length-\(3\) slice. With \(r=0.5\), the dimensions happen to agree, isolating the next defect: indices \([0,1,2,3]\) address a suffix of length \(2\). Generally, for \(0<m<N\), index \(N-1\) belongs to one returned branch but exceeds suffix limit \(N-m-1\). No random selection can avoid that union-of-indices contradiction. The paper’s teacher/self mixture is a separate setting and must not be confused with this ordinary-loss prefix.

paragraphs: Assign the first duration column \(d_{0:m}=D_{0:m,0}\), and return suffix-relative lists \(I_T^{\prime}=\{i-m:i\in I_T,i\ge m\}\), with the analogous self list. These disjoint lists cover exactly the suffix; a complete native training repair remains unverified.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The minimum-step default leaves no self-teaching choice
problems.source_location: src/utils/train_utils.py, lines 35–43; trainer/flux_scfm.py, teacher_min_timesteps parser default; scripts/train_flux_scfm.sh
claim: The self branch samples \(2^j\) with \(1\le j<\lfloor\log_2 n_{\min}\rfloor\). The exposed minimum teacher-step value \(2\) gives an empty range.

With the parser’s teacher ratio \(1/2\), the branch merely becomes stochastic; its conditional occurrence probability over \(N\) independent draws is \(1-2^{-N}\). The supplied launchers instead use \(32\) minimum steps and the nonempty set \(\{2,4,8,16\}\).

problems.title: A later Flux EMA setting needs experiment correspondence
problems.source_location: Section 5.4, p.9; Appendix E; trainer/flux_scfm.py, fast EMA update
claim: The paper describes fast/slow EMA coefficients \(0.99\) and \(0.999\); the current Flux source sets the fast coefficient to zero.
analysis: The current head is the later commit titled “flux param fix,” while the SD3 branch retains the described coefficients. A zero fast coefficient copies current parameters; it is a different setting, but a later deliberate change does not prove the historical experiments used a wrong coefficient.

problems.title: Identical incoming directions survive signature normalization
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, p.5, Eqs.(6)–(8)
claim: Under identical incoming parameters \(a=b\), the paper says the mixed contribution prevents recovery of the normalized incoming signature.
analysis: Provided \((c_1+c_2)a_1\epsilon\ne0\), the displayed ratio is \[(c_1a_2\epsilon+c_2b_2\epsilon)/(c_1a_1\epsilon+c_2b_1\epsilon)=a_2/a_1.\] For \(a=b=(1,2),c_1=1,c_2=3\), the network is \(4\max(0,x_1+2x_2)\). At the common boundary \(0\), positive/negative coordinate perturbations yield changes \(4\epsilon\) and \(8\epsilon\), recovering signature \((1,2)\) exactly. The individual outgoing split remains nonidentifiable; a zero summed coefficient or zero pivot is excluded by the stated nondegeneracy.
result: The paper’s exact-duplication example does not corrupt the shared normalized direction. This does not remove practical finite-precision or nearby-boundary difficulties for approximately equal neurons.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State that identical neurons with nonzero summed outgoing coefficient expose their common normalized direction, while the split of outgoing coefficients is not identifiable from function values.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Exact duplicate merging preserves rank and later activations
problems.source_location: Section 5.2, reduced-representation discussion, pp.9–10
claim: The discussion attributes loss of rank and corrupted deeper representations to merging exactly duplicate neurons.
analysis: For any activation columns, \(H=[h,h,h_3,\ldots]\) and \(H^{\prime}=[h,h_3,\ldots]\) have identical spans and hence identical rank. Replacing outgoing rows \(v_1,v_2\) by \(v_1+v_2\) preserves each subsequent preactivation because \(hv_1^{\top}+hv_2^{\top}=h(v_1+v_2)^{\top}\). Biases and all later deterministic layers are unchanged, so functional preservation holds for every input. For example, with \(h=\max(0,x_1+2x_2)\), preactivations \(h+3h-1\) and \(2h-h+1/2\) become exactly \(4h-1\) and \(h+1/2\).
result: Removing a duplicate reduces width, not rank. Parameter nonuniqueness already exists before merging. Approximate merging and efficient identification require separate error/algorithm analyses.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Distinguish recovery of the exact redundant parameter split from recovery of an equivalent function. Attribute any practical difficulty to approximate estimates, conditioning or search costs rather than rank loss from exact duplicate removal.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The disagreement probability needs clipping and pivot orientation
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Theorem 1 and Eqs.(14),(17), pp.6–7
claim: The bounded-input calculation treats an unbounded strip as its portion inside the box and uses the angle between complete normals to decide whether to complement the probability.
analysis: Let inputs be uniform on \([-1,1]^2\). Normals \(a=(2,1),b=(3,1)\) give printed probability \(1/4\), but actual disagreement area divided by box area is \[\frac12\left[\int_0^{1/3}x\,dx+\int_{1/3}^{1/2}(1-2x)\,dx\right]=\frac1{24}.\] The strip exits the box, so equality fails although an upper-bound interpretation survives this case.

For \(a=(2,1),b=(-2,1)\), the printed strip expression is \(1\), and the negative dot product selects complement \(0\). Actual disagreement is \(y^2<4x^2\), with probability \(\frac12[\int_0^{1/2}4x\,dx+\int_{1/2}^12\,dx]=3/4\). Complementing even the correctly clipped strip would give \(1/4\), still wrong. The sign governing inside/outside thresholds is \(a_2b_2\), not \(a^{\top}b\).
result: The stated equality and general complement rule are invalid. A uniform-input disagreement volume is also not, by itself, parameter-recovery probability or running time; adaptive attack queries require a specified separate model.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: With nonzero pivots, integrate the threshold interval intersected with the box. Use that clipped strip when \(a_2b_2>0\), and its complement when \(a_2b_2<0\). In higher dimensions, the triangle-inequality expression remains a same-pivot upper bound under uniform box input; complementing such an upper bound yields a lower bound.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The stated reflected-resolvent block can expand
problems.source_location: Section 3.1.2, Eq.(2), p.6; Appendix B, p.22
claim: The paper calls \(f=((I+G)/2)^{-1}-I\) a contraction whenever \(G\) is invertible with \(\operatorname{Lip}(G)<1\).
analysis: On \(\mathbb R\), choose \(G(u)=-u/2\), an invertible map with Lipschitz constant \(1/2\). Then \((I+G)/2=u/4\), so \(f(x)=3x\) and \(f^{\circ k}(1)=3^k\). More generally, writing \(d=u-v,e=G(u)-G(v)\) gives \(\|f(x)-f(y)\|^2-\|x-y\|^2=-\langle d,e\rangle\); a norm bound does not impose its required sign. Invertibility and monotonicity remain compatible with this expansion.
result: The architecture’s stated hypothesis does not supply the contraction assumed in its reconstruction theory. This does not imply every learned instance expands or that every benchmark fails.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A new strong-monotonicity hypothesis \(\langle d,e\rangle\ge m\|d\|^2\), \(m>0\), gives squared contraction factor at most \(1-4m/(1+\eta)^2\). Alternatively scale the block by \(0<c<(1-\eta)/(1+\eta)\), using \(\operatorname{Lip}(f)\le(1+\eta)/(1-\eta)\). These are new assumptions/architecture changes, not properties established for current trained models.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Scalar LipSwish does not preserve global invertibility
problems.source_location: Appendix B, p.22; Appendix F.2, p.25
claim: The described post-block activation \(s_\beta(x)=x/[1.1(1+e^{-\beta x})]\) is said to be invertible.
analysis: For \(\beta=1\), put \(r=1+\sqrt2\), \(x_1=-\log r\), \(x_2=-2\log r\). Since \(1+r^2=2(1+r)\), both distinct inputs have output \(-\log r/[1.1(1+r)]\). Thus the scalar activation is noninjective; composing it after a bijection preserves the collision. The active tabular code instead puts LeakyLSwish inside \(G\), which need not itself be injective for \(I\pm G\) to be invertible. That code placement is counterevidence against alleging this exact collision in the released complete flow.
result: The paper’s scalar-invertibility justification and described post-block architecture are false. The witness alone does not prove that the differently structured current full implementation is noninvertible.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Align the description with internal Lipschitz activations and justify the block inverse through the bijectivity of the identity-plus/minus contraction. A true post-block activation would require a separate proof of bijectivity.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Cross-depth convergence does not follow from a product bound
problems.source_location: Proposition 2 and its proof, p.5
claim: The proposition allows independently parameterized contraction layers yet infers that increasing depth moves abnormal outputs closer to a fixed point and a normal target.
analysis: For a fixed composition, \(\|\varphi_K(t)-x_K^*\|\le(\prod_j\eta_j)\|t-x_K^*\|\) is valid, but the fixed point varies with \(K\). Let \(e>0\), \(f_1(t)=t/2+e\), \(f_2(t)=t/2+e/2\). Their nested compositions are \(\varphi_1=t/2+e\), \(\varphi_2=t/4+e\); both reconstruct normal point \(0\) with error \(e\). At \(t=2e\), distance to the respective fixed point increases from \(0\) to \(e/6\), despite a smaller Lipschitz constant.

Global optimization of the stated unsquared loss also does not repair the quantifier. On normal points \(\{-e,e\}\), mean reconstruction loss for any \(L\)-Lipschitz map is at least \((1-L)e\), by the triangle inequality between the two endpoints. Nested maps \(\psi_1=t/2+e/2\), \(\psi_2=t/4-3e/4\) attain that bound for caps \(1/2,1/4\), with fixed points \(e,-e\). At abnormal input \(11e/10\), distances to those fixed points, and to the normal set, increase from \(e/20\) to \(21e/40\). These are global optima for the declared loss classes, not for the released joint MSE/density objective.
result: The per-network bound survives, but neither small training loss nor the product Lipschitz constant establishes monotone actual proximity across independently parameterized depths.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the fixed-composition bound. A common fixed point \(x^*\) for every layer supplies \(\|\varphi_{K+1}(t)-x^*\|\le\eta_{K+1}\|\varphi_K(t)-x^*\|\); normal-set membership still needs its own condition.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The active inverse-density chain drops states and reverses its sign
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Eqs.(4),(6), pp.6–7; flow_net/denet.py, prob_predictor, lines 106–109; flow_net/layers/iMonotoneBlock.py, inverse, lines 67–80 and power-series coefficients around line 141
claim: The inverse-density loop passes the same final latent and original prior to every module, discards inverse states and overwrites density. The component inverse also subtracts a determinant series representing the forward block.
analysis: Even granting correct module inverses, take \(F_0(x)=x/2,F_1(x)=x/4,F_2(x)=x/5\). At \(x=1,z=1/40\), correct inversion visits \(1/40,1/8,1/2,1\) and adds \(\log(1/40)\) to the latent log density. The outer loop instead returns only module zero’s \(\log(1/2)\) correction at the unchanged latent, an error \(\log20\).

The odd-power coefficients \(-2/k\) yield \(\log\det(I-A)-\log\det(I+A)\), the forward determinant. For \(G(w)=w/3\), the block is \(f(x)=x/2\). Subtracting that forward determinant gives \(2\pi(x/2)\), whose integral is \(4\), whereas input density is \(\pi(x/2)/2\), with mass \(1\). The active prior returns an ordinary log density, so a negative-log convention does not explain the sign.
result: The released active tabular path is not the stated change-of-variables density evaluator. A constant affine offset can preserve rankings, and historical checkpoint/benchmark correspondence is unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Carry inverse state and density through every reversed module and add each forward log determinant, or subtract an explicitly inverse determinant. The chain rule proves the sum; both outer propagation and component sign must agree. Native solvers, gradients and benchmark reruns remain unverified.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Validity masks do not protect the full grounding path
problems.source_location: model/vision/basic_modules.py, AP, lines 69–122; model/vision/transformers.py, encoder forward, lines 197–215; pipeline/pipeline_mixin_old.py, lines 563–569
claim: One aggregation branch normalizes over padding; the encoder adapter discards its supplied padding mask; evaluation bypasses the grounding head’s object mask.
analysis: For valid feature \(u=(1,0)\), let \(X_A=(u,u,0,0)\), \(X_B=(u,u,10u,10u)\), both with length \(2\). Admissible zero projection/balance parameters give a masked first branch \(u\), unmasked second branches \(u/2,11u/2\), and final outputs \(3u/4,13u/4\). Only padding values changed, so pooling is not padding-invariant.

The encoder receives a key-padding argument but calls self attention without it. With identity projections, four valid \(u=(1,0)\) and four invalid values changing from zero to \(v=(0,1)\), active attention returns \(cu\) versus \(cu+(1-c)v\), where \(c\approx0.9012299943\); valid-key masking returns \(u\) in both cases. Finally logits \((0.6,0.4,1.2,0.1)\) with validity \((1,1,0,0)\) select padded index \(2\) unmasked versus real index \(0\) masked. These are admissible component examples, not measured checkpoint outputs.
result: Padding can change valid features and permit prediction of no real object along the active release path. Its frequency and effect on published accuracy remain unmeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For each nonempty valid set \(S\), normalize both pooling branches only over \(S\). Propagate and apply key-column validity before retention/softmax, and restrict final argmax to valid objects. Explicitly handle empty valid sets; a final mask alone does not undo earlier feature contamination.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The active retention levels differ from equal quantiles
problems.source_location: Section 4.3, p.6, Eqs.(4)–(5); model/vision/transformers.py, Attention, lines 70–122
claim: The paper describes \(L=6\) equal quantile segments with progressive retention. The six active code branches mix half/full counts with fractions based on eighths.
analysis: At \(n=24\), the paper’s retained counts are \((4,8,12,16,20,24)\); current active counts are \((12,24,9,12,15,18)\). Divisibility removes rounding as an explanation. Branches one and four are equal under strict ranking, so their contribution is \((\mu_1+\mu_4)A_1V\), leaving only five distinct levels. Two additional computed branches do not enter the output and cannot restore the stated family.
result: The release is not an exact implementation of the equal-six-quantile construction. Which schedule generated historical results and which is intended require clarification.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either document the actual fractions and duplicate level or implement the intended \(k_j=\lfloor jn/L\rfloor\), \(j=1,\ldots,L\), with positive-count and valid-key rules. Changing the schedule requires empirical re-evaluation.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Grounding evaluation omits the last incomplete batch
problems.source_location: pipeline/pipeline_mixin_old.py, grounding evaluation, batch_size and num_batches around lines 518–536
claim: The grounding loop uses batch size \(3\) and floor division \(\lfloor N/3\rfloor\), although every query has already been encoded and no divisibility precondition is stated.
analysis: For \(N=5\), only indices \(0,1,2\) are processed. Outcomes \((1,1,1,0,0)\) give retained accuracy \(1\) versus complete accuracy \(3/5\); reversed outcomes give \(0\) versus \(2/5\). Thus the omitted tail can bias either way. For \(N<3\), no query is grounded and the later division has zero denominator. This is exact loop arithmetic, not a fresh neural evaluation.
result: The evaluator visits only \(N-(N\bmod3)\) queries. The actual omitted annotation list and its correctness require checkpoint-specific re-evaluation.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Iterate starting indices \(0,3,6,\ldots<N\) and clamp each end to \(N\). Those disjoint intervals cover every index exactly once. Guard empty sets and absent subgroups before division.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The control-error floor fails even in a scalar linear plant
problems.source_location: Assumption 4.1 and Theorem 4.2, p.5; Appendix F, Theorem F.1 and Eqs.(9)–(16), p.16
claim: The static feedback \(a_t^c=-\eta J_t^{\top}e_t\) is claimed to give floor \(\sqrt{\epsilon^2+P^2/\alpha^2}\), in addition to a decaying initial term.
analysis: Use identity encoding, \(F(z,a)=f(z,a)=2a\), nominal action zero, \(z_0=e_0=0\), additive disturbance \(P=1/10\), \(L=\alpha=2\), \(\epsilon=0\), and \(\eta=1/10<1/4\). All declared Jacobian, mismatch and authority conditions hold. With observed-minus-nominal discrepancy indexed at the next step, \(a_t^c=-e_t/5\) and \(e_{t+1}=-2e_t/5+1/10\). Therefore \(e_1=1/10\) and \(e_t=[1-(-2/5)^t]/14\), whose limit is \(1/14\). Both exceed the claimed floor \(1/20\), while the initial term is zero. Simultaneous steady-state feedback gives the same \(1/14\); changing the printed contraction factor cannot resolve the floor contradiction.
result: The bound is false under the additive perturbation channel used in the appendix. The recurrence is stable, so this is not a claim of universal controller instability or a simulation failure.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For the explicitly defined delayed static recurrence, action-Lipschitz continuity and \(\kappa=\eta L^2<1\) imply \(\|e_{t+1}\|\le\kappa\|e_t\|+\epsilon+P\), hence \[\|e_t\|\le\kappa^t\|e_0\|+(\epsilon+P)\frac{1-\kappa^t}{1-\kappa}.\] This restricted bound does not certify Algorithm 1’s learned-controller updates.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: One-step error does not imply the stated value guarantee
problems.source_location: Theorem 4.3, p.5; Appendix F, Theorem F.2 and Eqs.(17)–(19), p.16
claim: The value loss is bounded by \(H_M(\epsilon^2+P^2/\alpha^2)/2\), using a pure quadratic Taylor expansion and identifying trajectory deviation with one-step prediction discrepancy.
analysis: Let states be real, actions in \([-1,1]\), discount \(1/2\), nominal dynamics \(F(z,a)=z+a\), and \(V(z)=-z^2\). Define reward \(R(z,a)=V(z)-V(z+a)/2-a^2\). Telescoping the discounted return gives \(V(z_0)-\sum_{t\ge0}2^{-t}a_t^2\), since bounded actions imply \(2^{-T}z_T^2\to0\). Thus nominal policy zero is optimal everywhere and \(V\) is its exact optimal value, with Hessian \(-2\).

Perturb to \(f(z,a)=z+a+\delta\), with arbitrarily small \(\delta>0\), \(P=0,\epsilon=\delta,L=\alpha=1,\eta=1/2\), and zero initialization. Then \(e_{t+1}=\delta-e_t/2\), \(z_{t+1}=z_t+e_{t+1}\); controls remain feasible and \(|e_t|\le\delta\). At time \(2\), \(z_2=3\delta/2\), so the value gap from the nominal trajectory is \(9\delta^2/4>\delta^2\). For a one-step reference \(z^*=\delta\), the gap is still \(5\delta^2/4>\delta^2\), because \(V^{\prime}(\delta)=-2\delta\ne0\). The quadratic expansion is exact, so no higher-order remainder explains either violation.
result: The claimed implication fails even when the one-step error bound is independently true and the optimal value is globally quadratic. Neither a stable reference trajectory nor a stationary state-value reference follows from action-Jacobian bounds or policy optimality.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: With an independently \(\rho\)-contractive nominal state map, tracking obeys \(d_t\le\rho^td_0+b(1-\rho^t)/(1-\rho)\). A Hessian bound on the connecting segment gives \(|V(z)-V(z^*)|\le\|\nabla V(z^*)\|d+Hd^2/2\). Removing the linear term requires an additional stationary-reference assumption; neither condition is implied by the original theorem.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Empirical transition targets can be undefined or overflow
problems.source_location: carmania/tokenization_carmania.py, encode_with_bigram; training dataset row normalization; Section 4.1, p.6
claim: The tokenizer counts bigrams in signed \(16\)-bit integers; the dataset then divides each row by its sum without an unobserved-row policy.
analysis: For valid sequence \(A^{114}\), the only nonzero count is \(C_{AA}=113\); the other three rows each divide zero by zero, producing \(12\) undefined entries. Independently, sequence \(A^{40000}TCGA\), with maximum length \(40004\), observes every conditioning base but has \(39999\) repeated \(AA\) transitions. The counter wraps to \(-25537\); its row sum becomes \(-25536\), giving probabilities \(25537/25536>1\) and \(-1/25536<0\). Later addition of \(10^{-6}\) cannot repair either NaNs or the negative logarithm argument. This long-input example does not occur under the default short training-length setting.
result: The released conditional targets are not valid probability rows on these accepted inputs. Neither example estimates their prevalence in historical genomic data.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use sufficiently wide counts and declare either an unobserved-row mask or positive pseudocount \(\alpha\): \(P_{ij}=(C_{ij}+\alpha)/(C_i+4\alpha)\). Positivity and unit row mass follow directly; the pseudocount is a statistical convention that changes the estimator.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Clamping the predicted row denominator does not normalize it
problems.source_location: carmania/loss.py, TMLoss.forward, lines 15–26; Appendix B conditional-row description
claim: The loss forms predicted bigram scores \(S_{ij}\), removes padding, then divides row \(i\) by \(\max(\sum_jS_{ij},1)\). A row sum below one remains deficient.
analysis: On valid sequence \(ATCGAT\), the aligned input has \(5\) predicted positions and \(5\) token categories. All-zero finite logits give probability \(1/5\) per category, hence \(S_{ij}=4/25\) and each retained row sum \(16/25=0.64\). Clamping leaves every entry \(0.16\); conditional normalization instead gives \(1/4\). With concentrated empirical successor rows, the unsmoothed loss becomes \(4\log(25/4)\) rather than \(4\log4\). The extra penalty is row-mass deficit, not merely conditional-pattern mismatch.
result: The released quantity is not generally the stated sum of conditional KL divergences. When every score row sums to at least one, the clamp is inactive; no universal per-example failure is alleged.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For finite nonnegative scores, normalize \(Q_{ij}=(S_{ij}+\varepsilon)/(\sum_kS_{ik}+4\varepsilon)\), \(\varepsilon>0\). Together with an explicit valid-target convention this gives positive normalized rows and a finite conditional divergence.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Long arrays do not imply arbitrary long-range single-output memory
problems.source_location: Figure 4 and Section 4 long-context discussion; carmania/configuration_carmania.py; carmania/model.py, causal local-attention dispatch
claim: The reported long-context interpretation must distinguish processing an array of \(160\) kbp from one output depending on a remote token. The inspected network has \(5\) local layers with previous-position window \(128\).
analysis: For fixed weights, each position in layer \(\ell\) depends only on indices \([\max(0,t-128\ell),t]\), by induction over the union of its local predecessors. Position \(1000\) therefore depends only on input positions \(360\) through \(1000\), at most \(641\) tokens. Two sequences agreeing on that suffix but differing only at position zero have identical logits there under the declared hard local mask. Whole-sequence transition training changes weights, not inference-time edges. Pooling all positions, local motif gains and autoregressive relaying through changed intermediate tokens remain possible.
result: A claim of arbitrary fixed-suffix dependency across the entire input is not supplied by this architecture. The exact Figure 4 rollout/conditioning protocol is unavailable, so its plotted values and long-array task gains are not declared false.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe local contextual representations plus whole-sequence statistical regularization. Any stronger remote-token memory claim requires an identified mechanism and a fixed-suffix intervention whose correct answer changes with the remote prefix.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Finite entropy does not establish strict positivity
problems.source_location: Appendix A, Lemma A.4, proof of the Gibbs optimizer; Theorem A.5
claim: The proof states that an optimizer must have positive density because otherwise its entropy objective is infinite, then uses multiplicative variations to derive an Euler equation over the domain.
analysis: On \([0,1]\), density \(p=2\) on the first half and zero elsewhere has finite entropy \(\int p\log p=\log2\), using \(0\log0=0\). It is not the optimizer; it disproves the finiteness rationale rather than the optimizer formula. Multiplicative variations preserve its zero set, so a separate full-support argument is needed. If “positive density” means only absolute continuity, the existence-of-density statement is reasonable but still does not justify strict positivity in the later variation step.
result: The lemma’s conclusion remains valid under its stated bounded-continuous residual and positive-temperature assumptions; the proof needs completion, not a reversed theorem verdict.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For bounded continuous \(f_0\), let \(Z=\int e^{f_0/\beta}\), \(q=e^{f_0/\beta}/Z\). Then \(E(p)=\beta D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)-\beta\log Z\), proving the unique optimizer \(q\), including full support. At unit domain volume and residual sup norm \(a_n\to0\), \(0\le\beta\log Z_n\le a_n\) and \(p_n\to1\) uniformly.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The boundary penalty changes with shared ball geometry
problems.source_location: Eqs.(8)–(10),(13), main algorithm; boundary-term independence statement near the geometry update
claim: The same centers/radii parameterize normalized expert gates and the adaptive density. Fixed boundary coordinates do not make predictions at those coordinates independent of geometry.
analysis: On \([0,1]\), use constant experts \(U_1=0,U_2=1\), centers \(0,1\), radii \(2,2\), endpoint boundary targets zero and the printed quartic gates. Every endpoint lies strictly inside both balls. Predictions are \(u(0)=9/25,u(1)=16/25\), hence mean boundary loss \(B=0.2696\). Differentiating only the second radius gives \(\partial_{s_2}u(0)=96/625\), \(\partial_{s_2}u(1)=0\), and \(\partial_{s_2}B=864/15625=0.055296\ne0\). Thus dropping the term is not the full tied-geometry gradient. Freezing the ansatz during a density-only surrogate update, exact boundary enforcement or zero residual can legitimately remove it, but fixed sample coordinates alone cannot.
result: The written omission needs a declared detachment/surrogate policy or the missing derivative. Without author implementation, historical computational-graph behavior and numerical impact remain unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For the full tied geometry, include \(\nabla_\varphi B\) and both the direct residual derivative and density derivative in the interior term. A frozen-proposal importance estimator must hold its samples/denominator fixed while differentiating the numerator. Alternatively explicitly define a density-only frozen-ansatz surrogate and analyze that method separately.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Different objective scales confound raw convergence curves
problems.source_location: Section 5.2, p.9, Figure 4; pcl/continual_clip/loss.py, lines 32–43; models_TaPCL.py, lines 109–121; models_CiPCL.py, lines 109–120
claim: The current weighted TaPCL loss has an overall factor \(0.8\); CiPCL has factor \(0.5\) after its symmetric contrastive average. Lower raw objectives need not mean better or faster-learned retrieval representations.
analysis: Give source, target and prompted inputs identical similarity matrix \(S=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Its common symmetric cross-entropy is \(a=\log(1+e^{-1})\approx0.3132616875\). The release returns \(0.8a\approx0.2506093500\) versus \(0.5a\approx0.1566308438\), ratio \(5/8\), despite identical retrieval scores/orderings. Positive scaling is a valid optimization choice, but also scales plotted levels and slopes. Different sampling and negative sets add further comparison limits. Historical Figure 4 plot-code lineage is not established, so its actual gap is not identified with this synthetic ratio.
result: The release supplies a concrete loss-scale confound for cross-method convergence inference. Recall metrics may still support effective retrieval at smaller budgets.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Report each objective under its own weights. Compare checkpoints using the same held-out retrieval measure or a fixed unscaled validation objective, and record time/examples needed to reach a shared quality threshold.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Batch units and imposed budgets do not identify convergence
problems.source_location: Section 5.1, p.8; MSCOCO36_TaPCL.yaml and MSCOCO36_CiPCL.yaml; Sampler.py; both training loops
claim: The paper states batch size \(128\) and compares required iterations. Public defaults use TaPCL loader batch \(64\) with two separate forwards, CiPCL batch \(128\) with one; their samplers retain fractions \(0.7\) and \(1\), and loops run fixed epoch-derived lengths.
analysis: For \(900\) records across nine equal nonempty classes, the sampler allocations are \(630\) and \(900\) per epoch. Ten epochs with final partial batches yield \(10\lceil630/64\rceil=100\) versus \(10\lceil900/128\rceil=80\) optimizer steps. These are imposed budgets, not measured stopping times. Two forwards of \(64\) can approximately match encoder invocation count of one \(128\) forward, a valid favorable interpretation; they still use separate contrastive matrices with \(63\) rather than \(127\) off-diagonal negatives per row. Fixed budgets can reach a plateau, so absent early stopping does not prove nonconvergence.
result: The current defaults need explicit batch/compute accounting and a common convergence criterion before iteration counts can measure required optimization work. No corrected speedup is inferred.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Declare loader size, forwards, matrix dimensions, sampled/unique records, epochs and steps separately. For convergence speed, use a common validation threshold with sustained attainment and report wall time and examples; the proposed comparison has not been run.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Static residuals do not fit the returned conditional model
problems.source_location: models.py, m_step, lines 657–735; paper Eq.(6)
claim: The code estimates noise covariance from a static coefficient, then returns different condition-dependent GP coefficients. In the active emission-GP branch its static coefficient is discarded.
analysis: Use two scalar times, independent standard-normal states, conditions \(0,1\), basis \(\phi(u)=\cos(\pi u)\), current emission coefficient \(w=1\), noise \(q=0.01\), observations \((1,-1)\). Exact Gaussian conditioning gives both posterior means \(m=100/101\), variance \(v=1/101\), and \(s=m^2+v\). The covariance-aware update is \(w_+=2m/(2s+q)\approx0.9948773666\). Static cross-statistics cancel, so the code returns variance \(1\). The actual returned coefficient’s expected residual is \(e=1-2w_+m+w_+^2s\approx0.01002399949\). For fixed coefficient, objective \(\log R+e/R\) has derivative \((R-e)/R^2\), nonzero at the returned \(R=1\), and unique minimizer \(R=e\). These are realizable E-step moments, not arbitrary statistics.
result: The returned emission block is not an exact conditional noise maximizer. The code’s explicit TODO already acknowledges static dynamics statistics; no priority claim or universal full-iteration failure is made.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Compute each new covariance from the expected residual of the actually selected conditional coefficients, including posterior variance/cross-covariance. With positive definite residual sum \(S\), minimizing \(n\log\det\Sigma+\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}S)\) gives \(\Sigma=S/n\). Coupled coefficient updates still need a coherent common-objective schedule.
The current repository explicitly flags static dynamics covariance statistics as a TODO. No completed author correction is established for the broader returned-model residual mismatch.

problems.title: The GP bias/mean normal equation omits noise covariance
problems.source_location: models.py, fit_gplinear_regression, lines 663–670; bias/initial-mean calls, lines 690 and 715; Eq.(6)
claim: With a unit Gaussian weight prior and general noise covariance, the correct normal equation is \(GW+W\Sigma=B\). The helper instead solves \((G+I)W=B\).
analysis: Use scalar dynamics \(A=0\), one constant bias basis, current bias zero, initial variance \(1\), dynamics variance \(Q=4\), observation variance \(1\), emissions \(1\), observations \((0,1.25)\). Exact posterior means are \((0,1)\) and variances \((1/2,0.8)\). Holding dynamics fixed gives bias statistics \(G=B=1\). The helper returns \(0.5\); the covariance-aware update is \(1/(1+4)=0.2\). Its expected objective \(J(b)=[(1-b)^2+0.8]/8+b^2/2\) has derivative \((b-1)/4+b\), equal to \(0.375\) at \(0.5\) and zero uniquely at \(0.2\). No whitening or changed prior is supplied in that call.
result: The helper is correct for identity covariance, but does not generally implement the paper’s MAP update. The initial-mean branch has the same omission; its coupled covariance update is not certified by this local fix.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Solve \(GW+W\Sigma=B\), using the relevant dynamics or initial covariance. For \(G\succeq0,\Sigma\succ0\), the Kronecker-sum eigenvalues are positive, proving a unique conditional minimizer. Preserve actual residuals and coupled-block ordering.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Common-prediction accuracy cannot exceed purity
problems.source_location: Tables 1–2; released ClusteringMetrics.calculate_acc and calculate_purity
claim: The proposed method reports ACC/PUR \((99.67,99.64)\) on BDGP and \((98.66,98.43)\) on Handwritten; numerous baseline pairs also have ACC above purity.
analysis: For contingency counts \(C_{kj}\ge0\), each matching term \(C_{k,\pi(k)}\le\max_jC_{kj}\). Summing and maximizing proves \(\mathrm{ACC}\le\mathrm{PUR}\), including unequal class/cluster counts via zero padding. The inequality survives matched nonnegative-weight averaging and separate maxima over the same run collection. Ordinary common rounding preserves it; even independent \(0.005\)-percentage-point errors cannot explain gaps \(0.03\) and \(0.23\). The current metric functions implement these definitions. Different sample/run collections or nonstandard aggregation could explain coexistence only with an explicit different protocol; transcription remains possible.
result: The table cannot currently be read as mutually consistent metrics from common predictions under its stated definitions. The wrong cell or underlying cause is not identified, and no fabrication or corrected true accuracy is inferred.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Recover sample IDs, true/predicted labels, run IDs and aggregation weights; compute both metrics on each common prediction vector and regenerate affected tables. The ordering is necessary, not sufficient, for experimental validity.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Zeroing rejected scores does not exclude their agents
problems.source_location: Section 3.5, Eqs.(15)–(17); EnhancedAggregator.aggregate, lines 446–489
claim: A failed confidence threshold sets an agent’s raw score to zero before softmax. Its resulting numerator is \(e^0=1\), so it remains in the mixture.
analysis: With \(2\) views, \(2\) samples, \(2\) clusters and threshold \(0.7\), let the only accepted agent predict rows \((0.71,0.29),(0.29,0.71)\); each of three rejected agents predicts \((0.31,0.69),(0.69,0.31)\). Feature norms \(0.01\) give raw scores \((0.0071,0,0,0)\). Softmax assigns total rejected mass approximately \(0.7486663884\); the first fused row is approximately \[(0.4105334446,0.5894665554)\], reversing the accepted decision, with the second reversed symmetrically. All rows are valid positive probabilities. This refutes strict exclusion, while a deliberate softer downweighting interpretation remains legitimate.
result: The printed rule does not implement strict rejection and can let rejected agents determine the result. This is a formula-level witness conditional on a valid routing threshold, without any LLM call or benchmark claim.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For nonempty accepted set \(A\), normalize \(w_a=\mathbf1_{a\in A}e^{r_a-r_*}/\sum_{b\in A}e^{r_b-r_*}\). This gives zero rejected weight and unit mass. If all agents fail, explicitly abstain or declare a relaxed-threshold fallback.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The core detaches both contrastive encoder losses
problems.source_location: LLM_damvc_core.py, get_features, lines 185–190; compute_loss, lines 813–866
claim: The trainer obtains all view features through an accessor using no-gradient recording, then constructs feature and frequency contrastive terms exclusively from those returned features.
analysis: No recorded derivative connects these features back to encoder parameters. The frequency module’s FFT/amplitude/distance operations have no trainable parameter that recreates that missing edge, so adding either loss to another differentiable term cannot supply its intended encoder derivative. Other direct encoder calls remain differentiable, so this does not disable all training. The historical CPU witness reports finite contrastive losses and restored nonzero gradients under a connected-accessor control; those author-method executions were not rerun in this pass.
result: The archived official core cannot realize the stated encoder optimization from these two terms along the inspected path. Full experiment implementation identity and benchmark effects remain unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a training accessor with gradient recording enabled for these losses, keeping inference-only suppression separate. Verify optimizer membership and the connected derivative; no full retrained replacement is certified.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Rank correlations were computed on identifiers
problems.source_location: Table 3 and ranking interpretation, p.9; Tables 4 and 7
claim: Table 3 lists the same \(15\) individual IDs in descending order, but reports Pearson/Spearman \(0.2143\) and Kendall \(0.1429\) as nearly uncorrelated rankings.
analysis: The orderings are \[a=(4,15,5,7,1,8,13,10,11,2,14,6,12,3,9)\] and \[b=(4,15,5,7,8,13,2,11,1,10,12,6,14,9,3)\]. Inverting them to ranks keyed by common ID gives squared displacement sum \(42\). Spearman is \(1-6(42)/(15(15^2-1))=0.925\), also Pearson of rank vectors. The \(11\) discordant and \(94\) concordant pairs give Kendall \(83/105\approx0.790476\), retaining the reported reversal count. Correlating the arbitrary ID arrays directly reproduces \(3/14,3/14,1/7\). Their numerical distances have no ranking meaning.
result: The rankings have substantial agreement. Real reversals remain, and this calculation does not establish which ordering is closer to independently optimal performance.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Invert both orderings to common-ID ranks and report approximately \(0.9250,0.9250,0.7905\). Retain reversals and revise the near-zero-correlation interpretation.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: HSIC transport can favor teacher disagreement
problems.source_location: Section 3, Eqs.(1)–(5); code/HSIC/HSIC.py; code/new_loss.py
claim: The loss minimizes transport cost using HSIC inner-product similarity directly, charging greater association more.
analysis: Use three teacher groups with logit columns \(x_1=(5,2\log0.9,2\log0.1)\), \(x_2=(-1,2,-1)/\sqrt2\), \(x_3=\sqrt{3/2}(-1,0,1)\). Unique argmax coordinates give the required class groups. The latter vectors are centered orthogonal with squared norm \(3\), so their HSIC submatrix is \(I_2\). At temperature \(2\), teacher non-target distribution is \(p=(0.9,0.1)\). Matching it requires diagonal coupling mass at least \(0.8\), hence cost \(0.8\); swapped student \((0.1,0.9)\) admits zero-cost off-diagonal coupling. Swapping those logits preserves target probability and target-category loss, so the distillation component prefers disagreement by \(0.8\beta\), \(\beta>0\).
result: This contradicts the intended guidance component, not the full fusion objective. Appendix datasets using KL instead of HSIC are excluded.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For \(F_i=HK_iH/C\), use \(d_{ij}=\|F_i-F_j\|_F=\sqrt{M_{ii}+M_{jj}-2M_{ij}}\), a metric on distinct representations and a pseudometric when they coincide. Matching then costs zero and swapping \(0.8\sqrt2\). Full retraining remains unvalidated.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Teacher alignment can fail by view and sample
problems.source_location: code/train_tree_youtube.py, loss loop around lines 65–78; code/new_loss.py, separated-loss entry
claim: Stored lambdas share a late-bound view index; each batch also gathers a prefix of the full teacher array from batch size alone.
analysis: After constructing views \(0,1\), both lambdas can use final index \(1\). Independently, a batch with sample IDs \((2,3)\) gathers teacher rows \((0,1)\), despite compatible shapes. A single view and full-batch original-order training are passing special cases; the released minibatch path has neither guarantee.
result: The current path need not distill from the same view/sample. Historical checkpoint and table effects remain unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Bind each view/teacher/cost at construction. Carry stable sample IDs or aligned teacher batches through joint shuffling; do not gather a global prefix again.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: YouTubeFace test labels enter selection
problems.source_location: Section 4 evaluation protocol; code/train_tree_youtube.py, lines 34–37 and 91–107; code/gen_offspring_tree.py
claim: Test labels are passed as validation labels; maximum validation accuracy selects checkpoints and evolutionary fitness.
analysis: The dependency reaches the returned architecture even without test gradients. Two independent one-example test scores with success probability \(1/2\) each have expected score \(1/2\), but their selected maximum has expectation \(3/4\). This illustrates selection optimism, not its size here. Outer test folds do not remove within-fold selection dependence. Other datasets explicitly have validation splits and are not automatically implicated.
result: The released selected-test score is not untouched evaluation. An unpublished independent final test could alter the historical conclusion.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use inner validation for teachers, checkpoints and evolutionary fitness within each outer training split. Freeze selection before outer-test evaluation; corrected scores require re-evaluation.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The flat-price threshold excludes valid purchases
problems.source_location: Eq.(9), Lemma 2, repeated Eq.(36); Algorithm 1
claim: The formula uses budget remaining after the old optimum and excludes old negative-surplus bundles, although replacement frees spending and complementarity can rescue such bundles.
analysis: With budget \(1\), old price \(p_A=1\) and utilities \((0,2,3,3)\) for \((\varnothing,A,B,AB)\), old optimum \(A\) exhausts budget, giving printed new threshold zero. Yet at \(p_B=1\), \(B\) uniquely wins with surplus \(2\). Separately, budget \(4\), \(p_A=2\), utilities \((0,1,1/2,5)\) exclude old \(A\), giving threshold \(1/2\), while \(AB\) uniquely wins at \(p_B=2\). A second buyer with budget \(2\), utilities \((0,3,0,3)\), makes old price \(2\) revenue-optimal. Creation costs \(1/4\) allow positive profits, so nonoptimal old sellers do not explain the examples.
result: The closed-form demand threshold and price-candidate set fail in the permitted nonadditive model; empirical prices are not recomputed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For all affordable old bundles \(\mathcal A\), let \(G_0=\max_{S\in\mathcal A}[u(S)-c(S)]\) and \[\tau=\max\{0,\max_{S\in\mathcal A}\min[b-c(S),u(S\cup\{j\})-c(S)-G_0]\}.\] A positive price qualifies exactly up to this threshold when a new-containing maximizing bundle is accepted at ties. Seller endpoint attainment needs explicit tie handling.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Unconditional surplus does not bound conditional continuation
problems.source_location: Assumption 2, Eq.(7); Bellman Eq.(8); argument around Eq.(29)
claim: A state-conditional continuation value is bounded using an unconditional surplus mean without temporal independence or uniform conditional assumptions.
analysis: Draw persistent observed states \(H,L\) equally. Set budget/fair price \(1\), utilities \(2,11/10\), participation \(\pi(p,1)=p\), sensitivity \(1\) and discount \(3/4\). Unconditional fair surplus \(11/20\) gives required discount \(20/31\), satisfied strictly. In low state fair value is \(2/5\), while half-price value is \((3/5)/(1-3/8)=24/25\). The contingent policy improves ex-ante value from \(11/5\) to \(62/25\). All offered prices exceed creation cost \(1/4\).
result: Fair payment need not be optimal under the displayed stochastic assumptions. Independence or uniform conditional continuation control would be substantive additions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Require every reachable fair continuation value to be at least \(m/(1-\delta)\), with payment-independent exogenous transitions. Then \(\delta Lm/(1-\delta)\ge1\) makes fair payment a Bellman maximizer. The low state requires \(\delta\ge10/11\), excluding this example.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: A uniform finite crossover does not follow
problems.source_location: Lemmas 3–4 and strict eventual-inferiority/uniform-threshold proof
claim: The weak discount condition is used to infer strict eventual loss for underpayment and one finite horizon covering every underpaying schedule.
analysis: With utility \(2\), fair price/budget \(1\), \(\pi(p,1)=p\) and permitted discount \(1/2\), every constant \(p\in[0,1]\) has infinite value \(2\). At finite \(T\), underpayment value \(2[1-(p/2)^{T+1}]\) exceeds fair value \(2[1-2^{-(T+1)}]\). Weak optimality survives; strict inevitable inferiority does not.

Even at \(\delta=3/4\), fix any horizon \(T\), set \(\varepsilon=\delta^T/[8(T+1)^2]\), pay \(1-\varepsilon\) before \(T\) and \(1/2\) thereafter. Bernoulli’s inequality gives fair-minus-underpayment cumulative value at most \(2\varepsilon(T+1)^2-\delta^T/2=-\delta^T/4<0\). Choosing a schedule for each horizon is allowed by the claimed supremum over schedules; it does not produce one policy that wins forever under a strict margin.
result: Discount equality permits ties at infinity, and the unrestricted schedule family has no uniform finite crossover. Fixed simulated policies may still cross over.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Separate non-strict optimality, policy-specific crossover and uniform bounds. Fix the policy before the horizon limit; a uniform bound needs restrictions on the policy family. No original-generality replacement is established.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Royalty endpoints miss an internal bundle switch
problems.source_location: Royalty Eqs.(15),(19),(21),(44), Lemma 6
claim: Monotone revenue within one chosen bundle does not prevent a downward revenue jump when the buyer switches between two bundles containing the new dataset.
analysis: Use utilities \((0,1,10,12)\), rate budget \(1/2\), old rate \(\alpha_A=1/2\), shares \(f_A=\mathbf1_{A\in S}\min(\alpha_A/5,1/10)\) and \(f_B=\mathbf1_{B\in S}\alpha_B(1+\mathbf1_{A\in S})/10\). They are nonnegative, coordinatewise monotone and total below \(3/10\). Buyer values for \(B,AB\) are \(10-\alpha\), \(54/5-12\alpha/5\), crossing at \(4/7\), always above outside value \(9/10\). A tie choosing \(AB\) gives seller revenue \(12\alpha/5\) through \(4/7\), then \(\alpha\): unique maximum \(48/35\) at \(4/7\). Both proposed suprema are \(1\), missing it; substituting total share in the printed conditions does not remove the switch. The old share is already revenue-maximized and creation costs \(1/20,1/4\) permit profits.
result: The attained feasible interior optimum defeats the general endpoint characterization, beyond any open-endpoint technicality.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For finite piecewise-affine shares, partition at every buyer-utility tie, budget boundary and coefficient breakpoint; inspect endpoints/one-sided limits with explicit tie/attainment rules. This is a restricted replacement, not a theorem for arbitrary monotone functions.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The final thread reads past packed gap storage
problems.source_location: Section 2.3.2; decode.cu, lines 85–87; encode packing function, lines 164–170
claim: Each of \(512B\) launched threads stores a \(5\)-bit gap. The decoder reads bytes \(q=\lfloor5i/8\rfloor\) and \(q+1\) without a sentinel or conditional.
analysis: The array has \(320B\) bytes. At \(i=512B-1\), \(5i=8(320B-1)+3\), so the second read is index \(320B\), one past storage. A valid example with \(2048\) one-bit and \(2048\) two-bit encoded exponents produces \(768\) compressed bytes and one block, hence reads \(319,320\) from \(320\) gap bytes. Alignment \(3\) shifts by \(8\), discarding the second byte, so its value cannot alter the extracted gap. Allocator padding may make it physically readable; no GPU crash or corrupted-weight result is established.
result: The logical-array contract fails on the final thread of every nonempty launch in this configuration. Accuracy and speed measurements remain unrefuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For alignment \(r=5i\bmod8\le3\), extract from byte \(q\) alone by shifting \(3-r\) and masking \(31\); otherwise retain two-byte extraction. Every requested field is present, and the omitted low byte would have been discarded. CUDA integration/performance remains unverified.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Inactive-tail counting needs an initialization contract
problems.source_location: decode.cu, register_buffer declaration, conditional loads and first counting loop
claim: Threads conditionally load input bytes, but every launched thread copies those registers into its counting buffer.
analysis: For \(768\) bytes at \(8\) bytes per thread, only threads \(0\) through \(95\) receive input; \(416\) tail threads do not. Padded gaps do not initialize those registers. Bounded final writes and suffix counts can nevertheless leave earlier outputs intact. Actual reachable lookup values, loop progress and synchronization need a native GPU check; arbitrary assumed register values do not establish an observed symptom.
result: Missing initialization is a visible source obligation, but its runtime/output consequence and a complete repair remain unresolved.

problems.title: The plotted intervention population is smaller than stated
problems.source_location: Figure 5b/caption, current PDF p.8; Language/analysis/suppress_hall_scores.py, lines 84 and 183–210
claim: The caption assigns mean reduction \(0.19\) to a \(252\)-example top quartile of \(1006\) cases; final plotting applies another within-quartile median filter.
analysis: The first rule selects raw faithfulness below its full-data lower quartile; the second keeps its lower half. Distinct scores yield \(252\), then \(126\). Independently, current-PDF count-axis/vector geometry gives before counts \((11,36,79)\), after \[(11,4,2,8,5,7,5,11,16,57)\], each totaling \(126\). The code uses ordinary unweighted histograms. The mean lines therefore concern the narrower displayed subset rather than a verified full-quartile effect.
result: The plotted population disagrees with its caption. The excluded half’s effect is unknown; its inclusion could coincidentally preserve the rounded mean, but that is not verified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Recompute the full initial cohort or explicitly describe the second selection and smaller population. No corrected full-cohort mean is available.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The maximum-activation statistic is length-scaled
problems.source_location: Section 5; Language/train/hall_score_pls.py, line 41
claim: The paper defines \(\max_ta_{itj}\), but code uses \(\max_ta_{itj}/n_i\).
analysis: Non-BOS rows \((1,2),(3,4)\) have maxima \((3,4)\), versus released \((1.5,2)\). Repeating the rows preserves maxima but changes release output to \((0.75,1)\). A sample-dependent divisor cannot generally be removed by column scaling. This operator example does not assume actual repeated words preserve transformer activations.
result: PLS/VIP preprocessing differs and can encode length. Original activations/logs are needed for changed predictive results.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Remove the divisor to implement the written maximum, or declare the length-scaled statistic and compare maxima/length-only controls on common splits.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The first cross-validation repeat is duplicated
problems.source_location: Language/train/hall_score_pls.py, repeat initialization/append and final plot aggregation
claim: Ten pooled out-of-fold repeat scores are stored as \((r_0,r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_9)\); the point is the first score and the error bar its duplicated-list population deviation.
analysis: For control scores \(r_s=s/10\), deviation becomes approximately \(0.30287875\), versus \(0.28722813\) with each once; first point \(0\) differs from repeat mean \(0.45\). These illustrate aggregation only. PLS fits training folds, so no fitting leakage is alleged. Repeat-level pooled variability is legitimate if identified.
result: Duplicate storage is a release error; point/error-bar conventions require clarification, with no corrected original uncertainty available.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Store each repeat once, declare the point and deviation convention, preserve negative coefficients in records and label the repetition unit.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Categorical purity is not semantic cosine coherence
problems.source_location: Semantic interpretability definition; Vision/analysis/vit-noise-sae-interpretability.py, stats and PURITY_THRESH
claim: The paper describes top-\(16\) label cosine coherence with threshold \(0.75\). Active code uses maximum label fraction with threshold \(0.30\), leaving its cosine helper unused.
analysis: Eight labels each of orthogonal types give majority \(1/2\), passing code, but distinct-pair cosine \(7/15<0.75\). Conversely, \(16\) distinct labels with unit vectors \(e_r=\sqrt{0.9}u_0+\sqrt{0.1}u_r\) have pairwise cosine \(0.9\), passing semantic coherence, but majority \(1/16<0.30\). Including self-pairs preserves both decisions. These are metric-domain witnesses, not claimed pretrained embeddings.
result: The active metric is a different function; original labels/embeddings are required to reconcile interpretability percentages. Qualitative examples remain possible.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Define normalized label embeddings and pair averaging, then apply the stated cosine criterion; alternatively identify the actual categorical statistic under its own definition.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Activation frequency divides batch means twice
problems.source_location: Vision/analysis/vit-noise-sae-interpretability.py and companion maximally-activating-image routine
claim: The code sums batch activation means and divides again by total token count.
analysis: One feature active on all \(4\) tokens yields \(1/4\) in one batch or \(1/2\) in two equal batches, while true frequency is \(1\). For equal batch size \(m\), released frequency is true frequency divided by \(m\); unequal sizes also misweight batches. At \(32\) images times \(49\) patches, the illustrative log shift is \(-\log_{10}1568\approx-3.19535\), potentially moving frequency bins.
result: The quantity depends on irrelevant partitioning and is not empirical activation probability. Actual selected features and percentages remain unrecomputed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Sum integer active counts and token totals, then divide once. Linearity proves partition invariance; regenerate actual bins to assess effects.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Cross-model gains require a common population
problems.source_location: Kinetics-600 Tables 1–2; author README, lines 146–156; official pre-paper MoViNet evaluation configuration
claim: Author documentation explicitly identifies still-accessible labeled test videos, while the cited baseline configuration uses validation data. Baseline values match the official model table.
analysis: For author set \(S_G\), baseline set \(S_B\), the reported difference decomposes as \[A_G(S_G)-A_B(S_B)=[A_G(S_G)-A_B(S_G)]+[A_B(S_G)-A_B(S_B)].\] The second term is unmeasured. A baseline scoring \(72/100\) on one set and \(78/100\) on another can appear \(6\) points behind an identical-prediction modified model tested only on the latter. This establishes non-identification, not actual video-set difficulty. An unseen matched rerun could resolve it.
result: Matched manifests/predictions are required. The internal attention-only versus GRW ablation may remain informative if its protocol is shared; the strongest split evidence concerns MoViNet, not automatically every row or Kinetics-400.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Evaluate all checkpoints on one frozen labeled manifest, with clip/crop and compute conventions explicit. The existing author subset clarification is credited but does not supply matched baseline results.
The authors already published the test-subset clarification. A matched baseline evaluation resolving this comparison is not established.

problems.title: A relative span theorem does not imply unit norm
problems.source_location: Affine-normalization discussion; Appendix A, anchored scalar theorem and Propositions 1–2
claim: The main text attributes near-unit-sphere embeddings to affine-map/GRW optimization; the appendix proves a relative anchored bound.
analysis: Translation by \(c\) leaves all velocities, accelerations and permuted energies unchanged, so \(L_\alpha(Z+c)=L_\alpha(Z)\). Changing affine bias realizes arbitrarily large norms with identical regularizer. This does not refute the theorem’s anchor \(z_1=0\), or analyze classifier/weight-decay interactions. The anchored scalar span proof remains valid.
result: Relative scale does not establish unit radius or shell concentration; empirical norm claims need their own distribution and normalization convention.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
