paragraphs: For any loss sublevel \(L_\alpha(Z)\le\log((T-1)!)\), nonnegative ordering loss and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[\|z_j-z_1\|\le\sqrt{2(T-1)\log((T-1)!)/\alpha}\]. This is relative and conditional, not a unit-sphere theorem.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The counted parity orientation depends on length
problems.source_location: Proposition 3, p.6; Appendix A.3, pp.15–16 and final author remark
claim: The proposition claims arbitrary-length parity from two examples with probability \(1-2^{-H}\), counting either opposite-sign transition orientation.
analysis: A coordinate equals \(h_{0,i}(a_i^{[0]})^{T-k}(a_i^{[1]})^k\). Signs \((+,-)\) encode \((-1)^k\), but \((-,+)\) encode \((-1)^T(-1)^k\). For \(H=1,h_0=1\) and independent symmetric Rademacher entries, only \((+,-)\) succeeds for all lengths. The other outcomes have opposite-label hidden-state collisions: \((+,+)\) and \((-,-)\) collide on inputs zero/one, while \((-,+)\) collide on one/one-one. Thus success is \(1/4\), not claimed \(1/2\). With two coordinates \(A_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1),A_1=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\), training inputs zero-zero/zero-one permit either coordinate readout; only the first extrapolates to odd lengths. Existence therefore does not identify an arbitrary trained readout.
result: The probability and learning interpretation need qualification. The author’s final remark already gives the corrected sufficient-event probability; even-only experimental lengths do not test the unrestricted claim.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Credit the existing author remark: with independent symmetric nonzero entries and nonzero initialization, a selected \((+,-)\) coordinate exists with probability \(1-(3/4)^H\). Known matrices can identify it and two opposite labels orient it. This is a sufficient-event constructive rule, not an exact generic-optimizer probability; fixed length parity separately permits either orientation.
The final Appendix A.3 remark already states the appropriate sufficient-event probability. The proposition and unrestricted two-example learning interpretation remain broader.

problems.title: Even orthogonal dimension does not remove reflection blocks
problems.source_location: Section 2.3 and Appendix A.2, rotation-block explanation
claim: The explanation represents an arbitrary even-dimensional real orthogonal matrix entirely by planar rotation blocks.
analysis: Take \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\). It is orthogonal in dimension \(2\) but determinant \(-1\); every rotation-block-only matrix has determinant \(1\), preserved by similarity. The general real form also includes one-dimensional \(+1,-1\) blocks. The paper’s existence construction explicitly chooses rotations, so it does not need the false universal characterization.
result: The canonical-form explanation is overbroad; the cyclic and finite-product representation construction remains valid.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the real orthogonal form with \(+1,-1\) eigenspaces and conjugate rotation blocks. For a single even-dimensional determinant-one matrix those real signs can be paired; a family additionally needs a compatible common basis.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Positive diagonality still permits absorbing-state tracking
problems.source_location: Section 1 hierarchy and Section 2.1 finite-state simulation definition
claim: A parity obstruction should not be interpreted as absence of every nontrivial finite-state tracking task.
analysis: Let the state report whether any one has appeared. With \(h_0=(1,1)\), \(A_0=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/2)\), \(A_1=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/4)\), all entries are strictly positive contractions. After length \(T\) with \(k\) ones, \(h_T=2^{-T}(1,2^{-k})\). Scores \(2^{-T-k}\) for unseen-one state and \((3/4)2^{-T}\) for seen-one state classify correctly for \(k=0\) versus \(k\ge1\), including empty input. No additive term or length-aware decoder is used.
result: The broad verbal hierarchy needs narrowing to the forbidden cyclic/group tasks. This exact-arithmetic construction proves neither parity nor robust unlimited-length machine arithmetic nor trainability.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Name the specific excluded tasks and distinguish universal finite-state simulation from particular absorbing-state machines. No complete classification of positive-diagonal automata is supplied.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released CDA objective is a different tensor operation
problems.source_location: Eqs.(1)–(4), pp.4–5; src/loss/CDA_loss.py, lines 11–48; src/model/MultiModel_PL.py, lines 199–203
claim: Temporal covariance should be \(HH^{\top}/(T-1)\). The code permutes \((B,d,C,T)\) to \((B,d,T,C)\), reshapes back without undoing the interleaving, zeros the diagonal and uses unsquared Frobenius distance.
analysis: For centered \(H=[(-1,0,1);(-2,0,2)]\), correct covariance is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). The permute/reshape instead forms rows \((-1,-2,0),(0,1,2)\), yielding \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}5/2&-1\\-1&5/2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), then returns diagonal-zero matrix with cross-entry \(-1\), not \(2\), and eigenvalues \(1,-1\). Even otherwise correct diagonal deletion makes \(I_2\) and \(4I_2\) identical despite squared distance \(18\). Separately, a valid covariance difference \(D=[(0,2);(2,0)]\) contributes \(\log(1+\sqrt8)\), not the paper’s \(\log9\). No constant coefficient adjustment equates the two powers generally.
result: The current path does not implement the written covariance/centroid objective. It could define another regularizer, but the interleaving is not a covariance convention; experimental effects remain unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain centered channel/time ordering, compute \(HH^{\top}/(T-1)\) for \(T>1\), preserve diagonals and sum squared centroid differences. The matrix identity proves correspondence; new pretraining and ablations would assess effects.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Checkpoint choice uses final evaluation subjects
problems.source_location: Section 3.3; train_mlp_full.py, lines 39–51 and 92–140
claim: The subjects labeled test determine maximum validation-accuracy checkpoint selection and are reused for final predictions.
analysis: The same loader enters training validation, best-model selection and final scoring. Exclusion from gradient updates does not remove this dependency. For four independent fair test labels and fixed constant-zero/constant-one candidates, selecting the better test accuracy has expectation \(11/16\), while each fixed candidate has expectation \(1/2\). This is a selection illustration, not estimated inflation here. A separate unpublished final-test implementation could change historical attribution.
result: The released score is test-dependent selection accuracy rather than untouched-subject performance. No claim that every published table used this script is made.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use subject-level development data for selection and untouched outer test subjects for final reporting, or fix an epoch before seeing those outcomes.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: DEAP labels require an unavailable ordering contract
problems.source_location: Section 3.1 and Appendix E.8; src/data/io_utils.py, lines 421–465; train_mlp_full.py, lines 68–71
claim: The paper defines participant-rating median splits, but the loader returns \(20\) zeros then \(20\) ones for every subject and evaluation tiles one label vector.
analysis: Two subjects with first/last half ratings \((1,9)\) and \((9,1)\) both have median \(5\), yet complementary correct labels. A single tiled vector cannot match both; this is a valid protocol witness, not actual DEAP data. The code may depend on per-subject label-sorted preprocessing or shared stimulus labels, but the required original trial permutations and affective dimension are unavailable. Subject-specific sorting must also preserve correct stimulus pairing.
result: The released route alone does not specify the rating-based task. Without actual preprocessing/labels, wrong published DEAP accuracy is not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Recover subject/trial/dimension-indexed labels and any permutations, with explicit median/tie rules and stimulus-aligned pairing. No numerical correction is established.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Dimension reduction cannot preserve all source geometry
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Eqs.(6)–(8), pp.6–7
claim: The text invokes rotational invariance after truncating a square orthogonal matrix to align a lower-dimensional teacher, attributing feature-shape preservation to that map.
analysis: In a favorable orientation let \(A=Q_d^{\top}\), \(AA^{\top}=I_d\), \(P=A^{\top}A\). Then \(\|Av\|^2=\|v\|^2-\|(I-P)v\|^2\). With \(D=4,d=2,Q=\exp(0)=I_4\), the projection retains only the first two coordinates: \(e_3,e_4\) collapse to zero despite distance \(\sqrt2\). The data matrix containing the standard basis has full row rank, so a full-rank assumption does not rescue preservation. Multiplication by any fixed projection remains linear regardless of sample count/rank.
result: Norms/distances survive exactly on retained directions, not all source features. Tensor-dimension alignment and possible task-relevant approximate preservation remain intact.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State contraction and retained-subspace isometry. If discarded pairwise components are at most \(\varepsilon\) times original distance, retained distance lies between \(\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2}\) and one times original distance; that data-dependent condition is not established here.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Separate orthogonality does not eliminate shared-gradient conflicts
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, conflict-prevention explanation and Eq.(9)
claim: Per-map identities \(A_iA_i^{\top}=I\) do not control cross-map inner products \(g_i^{\top}g_j=r_i^{\top}A_iA_j^{\top}r_j\).
analysis: Use coordinate projections from \(\mathbb R^4\) retaining first \(2\) and first \(3\) coordinates, both permitted truncations of \(I_4\). At \(z=(1,1,1,0)\), apply softmax to projected features and use teachers \((0.9,0.1)\), \((0.1,0.8,0.1)\). For teacher-to-student KL, shared gradients are \((-2/5,2/5,0,0)\) and \((7/30,-7/15,7/30,0)\), inner product \(-7/25<0\). For the printed reversed KL direction it is \(-\log9\log8/12<0\). Thus improving one term can worsen the other to first order under either convention. Softmax is an explicit favorable domain assumption, not recovered unavailable code.
result: Individual projection orthogonality permits this operational conflict. Conditioning improvements, learned conflict reduction and empirical benefit remain possible; no universal parameter-gradient result follows.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe a per-projection constraint and empirical regularizer; measure defined gradient conflicts. Cross-map orthogonality would suffice at the shared-feature level but is not imposed and may be infeasible; it is not offered as a validated replacement.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The variational expression needs an upper-bound condition
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, Eq.(8), p.5; multi-scale Eq.(9)
claim: The paper claims \(I(X;Z)\le U(q)=\mathbb E_{XZ}\log q(Z|X)-\mathbb E_X\mathbb E_Z\log q(Z|X)\) for a normalized neural conditional without a fitting condition.
analysis: Let independent bits \(A\) be fair and \(N\) have probability \(1/4\) of one; set \(X=(A,N)\), deterministic feature \(Z=A\mathbin{\mathrm{xor}}N\). Then \(I(X;Z)=H(Z)=\log2\), while valid zero-logit conditional \(q(z|x)=1/2\) gives \(U=0\). With \(P=P_{XZ},Q=P_XP_Z,R=P_Xq\), direct cancellation yields \[U(q)-I(X;Z)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|R)-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|R).\] Thus the missing condition is the corresponding nonnegative KL difference. A full-support binary joint with masses \((3/8,1/8;1/8,3/8)\) also has positive MI and zero surrogate under constant conditional, so zero joint probabilities are not essential.
result: The unconditional bound and resulting guaranteed bottleneck relation are invalid. Empirical architecture ranking can still be useful. This caveat is already explicit in original CLUB, Theorem 3.2.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State the inequality only when \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|R)\le D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|R)\), with required finiteness. Fitting the conditional can help but does not by itself guarantee this condition or tightness.
The original CLUB literature already states the needed condition; no author correction to this paper’s unqualified equation is established.

problems.title: Maximizing the bound is not conditional fitting
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, paragraph after Eq.(8); Algorithm 2, p.13, lines 13–15
claim: The conditional estimator parameters ascend the positive-minus-negative log-conditional expression, described as fitting/tightening the bound.
analysis: On the same deterministic distribution, choose \(q_a(Z=A|X)=\sigma(a)\), ignoring \(N\). Joint matching probability is \(3/4\), product matching probability \(1/2\), so \(U(a)=a/4\), with derivative \(1/4\) and no finite maximizer. Actual conditional likelihood is \(L(a)=3\log\sigma(a)/4+\log(1-\sigma(a))/4\), uniquely maximized at \(a=\log3\); it tends to \(-\infty\) as the printed objective increases unboundedly. In the full-support noisy binary control, the same family is well specified and the same failure holds, so misspecification is not the explanation.
result: The printed ascent cannot be interpreted as conditional maximum likelihood or general tightening. The official supplement provides final-model evaluation, not the search/estimator implementation, so historical execution attribution remains unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For fixed encoder/distribution, maximize joint conditional log likelihood \(\mathbb E_P\log q_\phi\), equivalent to minimizing \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|P_Xq_\phi)\), then evaluate the surrogate separately. This restores fitting, not unconditional bound validity or architecture-ranking consistency.
Original CLUB Eq.(16) and Algorithm 1 use conditional likelihood fitting; adoption of that procedure in this paper’s unavailable search code is not established.

problems.title: The stage rule reverses loss improvement and misses plateaus
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, p.7; Algorithm 3, p.14, lines 36 and 40–42
claim: Stage II stores raw loss but transitions when its mean forward difference is below \(\epsilon\operatorname{std}(W)\), using a strict comparison.
analysis: A full \(20\)-point window \((1,0.99,\ldots,0.81)\) has forward difference \(-0.01\) and positive threshold approximately \(2.3065\times10^{-6}\) at \(\epsilon=4\times10^{-5}\); the literal rule transitions during steady improvement. A constant window has both quantities zero, so strict \(0<0\) fails and no transition occurs. Restoring only a nonnegative guard does not fix raw-loss sign. Higher variance also raises the threshold, easing the comparison when improvement is held fixed.
result: The literal pseudocode conflicts with its saturation description. A hidden sign/guard correction may make the actual implementation different; no segmentation failure is asserted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use benefit-oriented values, including negative loss, and a complete stage-specific window. A rule \(0\le\Delta\le\epsilon_{\rm abs}+\epsilon_{\rm rel}\operatorname{std}(W)\), \(\epsilon_{\rm abs}>0\), handles the displayed controls. Reset histories and define deterioration/final-stage policies; no general optimization theorem follows.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The reformulation optimizes a different placement objective
problems.source_location: Section 5.2, Eqs.(2)–(10), p.6; Section 5.3 global-optimality interpretation
claim: The original objective sums weighted maximum row/column spreads; the surrogate counts all pods used plus maximum pods touched by one scheduling group. Homogeneous synchronous communication does not identify them.
analysis: Use equal weights, tensor parallel degree \(8\), a \(2\times3\) node matrix and three pods of capacity \(2\). Placement \(X=[(A,A,B);(C,C,B)]\) has original row/column maxima \((2,2)\), cost \(2\), and surrogate \((3+2)/2=5/2\). Placement \(Y=[(A,B,C);(A,B,C)]\) has original maxima \((3,0)\), cost \(3/2\), but surrogate \(3\). All pods are required and each row exceeds any pod capacity, so every surrogate optimum has row spread \(2\). Such a placement cannot have all columns local, since local columns would force each row to use three pods. Thus every surrogate optimum has original cost \(2\), while true optimum is \(3/2\).

The discrepancy survives counting one local pod as spread \(1\). In a \(6\times6\) matrix with six pods of capacity \(6\), every minimum-surrogate placement puts one full row per pod, giving original cost \(3\) under printed distance or \(7/2\) under occupied-pod count. A placement with pairs of rows sharing two three-column blocks uses row spread \(2\), column spread \(3\), cost \(5/2\) under either convention. No large enumeration is needed.
result: The optimization problems are not generally equivalent. Solver optimality for the supplied surrogate and possible production benefit remain intact; exact original-objective optimality does not follow.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Call the model a surrogate, or retain one-hot assignment variables per logical matrix position with exact group/pod occupancy and epigraph maxima of the original row/column distances. This restores objective equivalence but has untested large-instance scheduling latency.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: GPU requests are converted with the wrong remainder condition
problems.source_location: utils.py, request_gpu_to_nodes, lines 68–75; scheduler.py, schedule call around lines 278–281
claim: The helper increments the integer quotient when the remainder is zero, the opposite of whole-node ceiling conversion.
analysis: With \(8\) GPUs per node, request \(64\) returns \(9\) nodes instead of \(8\), while \(65\) returns \(8\) nodes providing only \(64\) GPUs instead of the required \(9\). Restricting to full-node workloads does not fix the first example. The minimum-one guard only hides some small requests.
result: The current path can change feasibility, utilization and reservation. Which historical simulation/production results used it remains unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For positive integers use \(n=\lfloor(q+g-1)/g\rfloor\). Quotient/remainder decomposition gives \((n-1)g<q\le ng\), proving minimal sufficiency. Invalid/zero requests need a separate explicit API policy.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Graph-mapping scores lose logical rank identities
problems.source_location: graph_mapping.py, build_job_graph, lines 318–329; scheduler.py graph_mapping, lines 1089–1125; utils.py, get_score, lines 97–126
claim: The graph uses row-major logical ranks, but the scorer sorts assigned pod labels before reconstructing communication groups, replacing the evaluated mapping.
analysis: For \(2\times2\) ranks \([(0,1);(2,3)]\), mappings \((A,A,B,B)\) and \((A,B,A,B)\) have respective occupied-pod maxima \((DP,PP)=(2,1)\) and \((1,2)\). Sorting makes both arrays identical and reports the latter pair for both. At communication-role weights \((4/5,1/5)\), the first true score is \(9/5\), not reported \(6/5\). Both mappings satisfy two-node pod capacities. Equal weights can hide the swapped pair but do not restore rank identity.
result: The current graph-mapping baseline scorer can evaluate a different placement. Sorting may be an intentional repacking policy for an unassigned node set, but that would be a distinct baseline requiring its own specification.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Preserve the rank-indexed array and form rows from indices \(i n_{\rm col}+j\), columns from the same expression with \(i\) varying. The graph’s labeling directly proves group correspondence; rescore actual stored allocations before numerical conclusions.
A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Centering at a group mean does not remove spurious variance
problems.source_location: Appendix A.0.6, Case 2, and A.0.7, PDF pp.19–20
claim: The minority-to-majority ID formula omits spurious variance; the matched-group ID formula retains only core and irrelevant variance. The later OOD formula adds core variance and asserts strictly larger expected distance.
analysis: For a random vector \(X\) and deterministic prototype \(p\), \[\mathbb E\|X-p\|^2=\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Cov}(X)+\|\mathbb EX-p\|^2.\] Orthogonal subspaces remove cross terms, not fluctuations within each subspace. Therefore the minority-to-majority identity needs \(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{1-c}^{\rm sp}\), while matched ID distance is \(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_g^{\rm sp}+\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_c^{\rm core}+\operatorname{tr}\Sigma^{\rm irr}\).

A normalized ID witness uses spurious basis \(e_1\), core basis \(e_2\), class-zero core \(3/5\) and class-one core \(-3/5\). Set \(P_0^{\rm sp}\) on \(4/5,-4/5\) with probabilities \(3/4,1/4\), and reverse those probabilities for \(P_1^{\rm sp}\). A majority proportion \(9/10\) is admissible. Every feature has unit norm, and core sign determines class. Class-zero population prototypes are \((2/5,3/5)\) and \((-2/5,3/5)\); both spurious variances equal \(12/25\). Minority-to-majority distance is \(28/25\), whereas the printed formula gives \(16/25\). Minority-to-own distance is \(12/25\), whereas the printed formula gives \(0\). These are means of normalized features, as defined by the appendix; renormalizing the prototypes would change the model.

In the raw-coefficient interpretation, matched OOD has zero core and unchanged nuisance marginals, so its expected distance is \(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_g^{\rm sp}+\|\mu_c^{\rm core}\|^2+\operatorname{tr}\Sigma^{\rm irr}\). Its difference from matched ID is \[\|\mu_c^{\rm core}\|^2-\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_c^{\rm core}.\] Thus positivity requires a signal-to-variance condition. The earlier OOD formula in Case 1 on p.19 has the correct variance structure.
result: The repeated identities and unconditional separation argument are false as written. Group means can remove a spurious mean-mismatch term, but cannot eliminate its variance. The normalized ID witness does not purport to satisfy the incompatible joint OOD assumptions discussed separately; a matched-prototype expectation also does not certify the detector’s minimum-over-prototypes score or AUROC.
assumptions: The prototypes are the deterministic population means defined in Appendix A.0.5.
No independence among orthogonal components is needed for the squared-distance calculation.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain all covariance traces in the population-distance identities and require \(\|\mu_c^{\rm core}\|^2>\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_c^{\rm core}\) for a positive matched expected gap in a coherent raw-feature model. Group recovery, random estimated prototypes and detection-error guarantees need separate arguments.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The joint normalized model excludes a nonzero core
problems.source_location: Appendix A.0.1 and A.0.3–A.0.4, PDF pp.17–18
claim: ID embeddings are normalized. Near-OOD embeddings retain the same spurious and irrelevant coefficient marginals but have neither core nor external components.
analysis: Under the stated orthogonality, unit norms give \[\mathbb E\|\alpha\|^2+\mathbb E\|\beta\|^2+\mathbb E\|\gamma\|^2=1,\qquad \mathbb E\|\alpha\|^2+\mathbb E\|\gamma\|^2=1.\] The common nuisance marginals therefore imply \(\mathbb E\|\beta\|^2=0\), so \(\beta=0\) almost surely. Neither independence nor samplewise ID/OOD coupling is required. A nondegenerate core cannot coexist with these assumptions. In the preceding ID witness, deleting the core leaves norm \(4/5\); renormalization changes spurious mean magnitude from \(2/5\) to \(1/2\), and variance from \(12/25\) to \(3/4\). It therefore does not preserve the assumed marginals.
result: The idealized joint distribution underlying the separation explanation is incompatible with a nonzero core under unit normalization. Allowing an external component could supply the missing norm, but the analyzed near-OOD case expressly sets that component to zero. This does not show that actual normalized SPROD features lack class information.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Explicitly analyze raw features without claiming that this preserves the normalized detector model, or formulate a normalized OOD model with changed nuisance moments and recompute the distance terms. Neither alteration alone proves the detector’s empirical ranking.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The geometric error bound needs a post-correction domain
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.1, Eqs.(15)–(16), PDF p.6; Appendix F, Eqs.(24)–(27), p.24
claim: The main display uses \(K=\lfloor(t-t_0)/\Delta\rfloor\) for time \(t\), while the proof establishes a bound on error just after correction \(K\).
analysis: Write \(e_k^+\) for corrected error. The assumptions imply \[e_{k+1}^+\le\alpha e_k^++B,\quad \alpha=\kappa e^{L_F\Delta}<1,\quad B=\kappa E_{\rm ODE}+\delta_C.\] Hence \(e_K^+\le\alpha^K e_0^++B(1-\alpha^K)/(1-\alpha)\). This is the valid recurrence proved in Appendix F.

An arbitrary-time extension needs an unfinished-flow factor. For ideal trajectory \(0\), exact learned ODE \(\dot y=y\), \(\Delta=1\), initial corrected value \(1\) and correction \(y^+=e^{-2}y^-\), the assumptions hold with \(L_F=1,\kappa=e^{-2},E_{\rm ODE}=\delta_C=0\). Post-correction errors are \(e^{-k}\), but at \(t=1/2\) the error is \(e^{1/2}>1\), exceeding Eq.(16) read literally with \(K=0\).
result: The proof’s explicit post-correction interpretation resolves the principal domain issue. The same floor-indexed bound cannot be used unchanged at arbitrary times between corrections.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Label the bound as applying to \(e_K^+\). If a partial-interval residual \(E_{\rm ODE}(\tau)\) is established, use \(e(t_K+\tau)\le e^{L_F\tau}e_K^++E_{\rm ODE}(\tau)\).
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: A convergent upper envelope does not force error convergence
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.1 after Eq.(16), PDF p.6; final paragraph of Appendix F, p.24
claim: The paper concludes that actual corrected error converges to the nonzero floor \(C_2=B/(1-\alpha)\).
analysis: The inequality establishes only \(\limsup_K e_K^+\le C_2\). For a smooth scalar counterexample take ideal state \(0\), zero learned ODE, \(\Delta=1\), initial state \(0\), and corrected-state map \(G(y)=\cos^2(\pi y/2)\). Its additive corrector is \(G(y)-y\). Since \(|G(y)|\le1\le |y|/2+1\), assumption (b) holds with \(\kappa=1/2,\delta_C=1\); take \(E_{\rm ODE}=0\), so \(\alpha=1/2,C_2=2\). The trajectory alternates \(0,1,0,1,\ldots\), never converging, while satisfying every displayed upper bound. The assumption controls error relative to the ideal state; it does not require pairwise contraction of \(G\).
result: Bounded long-horizon error follows conditionally, but existence of an error limit or equality to the envelope floor does not.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Replace the limit claim by \(\limsup_K e_K^+\le C_2\). If \(B=0\), the existing inequality does imply convergence to zero; otherwise extra dynamical assumptions are needed.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Nonzero additive correction creates a temporal jump
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Eqs.(11)–(12) and final inference paragraph, PDF p.5
claim: The hybrid inference strategy is said to maintain continuity and smoothness although it adds a discrete correction after each ODE interval.
analysis: Equation (12) uses the previous corrected state in a lagged residual. Let the ODE be zero and initial state \(1\); choose \(\lambda=1/2\) and an admissible constant residual \(r_\psi(1)=-1/2\). The state immediately before reset is \(1\), while immediately after it is \(3/4\). The jump is \(-1/4\). In general continuity requires the added residual to vanish at the reset. The theorem explicitly permits pre/post states, so this finding does not contradict its hybrid formulation.
result: Arbitrary-time queries and piecewise smooth ODE segments remain possible; globally continuous trajectories are not guaranteed by the printed reset construction.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe a piecewise smooth hybrid trajectory and state which side of a reset defines a query. A continuously forced replacement would be a different method requiring its own analysis.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: A changing four-vertex neighborhood can break spatial continuity
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, Eq.(4), PDF p.4; Section 3.3, pp.5–6; Algorithm 1, p.22; Appendix C.1, p.23
claim: Relative-position message passing over the four vertices of the query’s cell is used to support spatial continuity.
analysis: Consider adjacent cells \([0,1]\times[0,1]\) and \([1,2]\times[0,1]\). Set all vertex features at \(x=0,1\) to zero and both at \(x=2\) to one; these values can sample the smooth field \(x(x-1)/2\). Choose zero query Gabor initialization, zero positional term and bias, and first message weight \(1\). As a query crosses \(x=1\), Eq.(4) sums features of four vertices: its one-sided outputs are \(0\) and \(2\). A second residual layer with zero weight/bias is the identity, and a continuous ReLU readout preserves this nonnegative jump. Within each fixed cell the map can be continuous; neighbor-set switching is the obstruction.
result: The printed decoder does not guarantee continuity across cell boundaries. Extra interpolation in an unavailable implementation could change this conclusion, and no trained spatial discontinuity is asserted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A shared-vertex bilinear interpolation construction would enforce continuity across cell boundaries, but not necessarily differentiability. This proposed decoder change has not been validated as preserving trained performance.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Zero printed gap can conceal a profitable unilateral deviation
problems.source_location: Section 2, Eqs.(6),(8)–(9), PDF pp.4–5; Algorithm 2, p.8; Theorem 4.2, pp.8–9
claim:
Let \(L(\mu,
u)=\inf_P V^{\mu,
u,P}\) and \(U(\mu,
u)=\sup_P V^{\mu,
u,P}\), using the two players’ prescribed uncertainty sets. Their utilities are \((L,-U)\). Equation (9) substitutes reference equilibrium values for current joint-policy values, and Algorithm 2 combines the maximizing strategy of one zero-sum game with the minimizing strategy of another.
analysis:
True unilateral regret is \[\max\{\max_{\mu'}L(\mu',
u)-L(\mu,
u),\ U(\mu,
u)-\min_{
u'}U(\mu,
u')\}.\] Separate robust envelopes need not form a common zero-sum payoff, even with equal radii.

Take horizon \(2\), states \(s_0,s_1\), two actions per player, and both radii \(1/4\). At time \(1\), at either state set \[R=\begin{pmatrix}3/20&7/20\\1/2&7/10\end{pmatrix},\qquad P(s_1)=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&1/2\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.\] At time \(2\), reward is \(0\) at \(s_0\) and \(1\) at \(s_1\), independent of actions. Direct binary TV optimization gives \[L=\begin{pmatrix}2/5&3/5\\1/2&7/10\end{pmatrix},\qquad U=\begin{pmatrix}9/10&11/10\\3/4&19/20\end{pmatrix}.\] Row \(2\) strictly dominates for \(L\); column \(1\) strictly dominates for minimizing \(U\). The actual equilibrium is \((2,1)\), with reference values \(L^*=1/2,U^*=3/4\).

The separate zero-sum saddles are \((2,1)\) for \(L\) and \((1,1)\) for \(U\). The crossed output is \((1,1)\). Its maximizing-player regret is \(1/2-2/5=1/10\), while minimizing-player regret is zero. Yet the paper’s gap is \(\max\{1/2-1/2,\ 3/4-9/10\}=0\). Interpreting \(U^*\) instead as the separate minimax value \(9/10\) also gives zero.

Uniform initial states and uniform behavior policies give time-one joint occupancies \(1/8\), and time-two joint occupancies \(3/16\) and \(1/16\). Thus \(d_m^n=1/16>0\); the clipped numerator is at most \(1/8\), yielding \(C_r^*\le2\). Sample thresholds can be met by increasing the number of trajectories. The calculation grants correct zero terminal values, exact transitions and vanishing bonuses; strict best-response inequalities persist under sufficiently small estimation errors.
result: The printed certificate does not characterize absence of profitable unilateral deviations, and the exact-model crossed strategy output need not be a robust Nash equilibrium. This rejects the usual equilibrium interpretation of the rate, rather than a numerical bound on the paper’s weaker printed gap. Uncertainty-free common-payoff games remain a valid special case.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use actual robust current-policy values in both unilateral regrets. A known-model backward construction can solve the corresponding bimatrix game with utilities given by each player’s own robust continuation payoff. Its offline statistical rate and computation require a new analysis; replacing a solver does not preserve the stated theorem automatically.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The printed supremum TV dual clips in the wrong direction
problems.source_location: Appendix B.1, Lemma B.1, Eq.(27b), PDF p.23; Eq.(17), p.7
claim: Equation (27b) minimizes \(p^\top[V]_\alpha-\sigma(\alpha-\max_s[V]_\alpha(s))\), with upper clipping \([V]_\alpha=\min(V,\alpha)\) and \(\alpha\in[\min V,\max V]\).
analysis: The maximum clipped entry equals \(\alpha\), so the penalty vanishes; minimizing gives \(\min V\), regardless of \(p,\sigma\). For \(p=(1/2,1/2),V=(0,1),\sigma=1/4\), the printed result is \(0\). Feasible distributions are \(q=(1-t,t)\), with \(t\in[1/4,3/4]\), so the actual supremum is \(3/4\).
result: The general displayed dual is false. The current author source provides important counterevidence: alpha_min_backup uses lower clipping, and the policy routines obtain a supremum by negating an infimum of the negative value vector. Those structural implementations are consistent with the correct operation and were not executed here.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The correct full-simplex dual, with \(m=\min V,M=\max V\), is \[\sup_{\operatorname{TV}(q,p)\le\sigma}q^\top V=\min_{\alpha\in[m,M]}\{p^\top\max(V,\alpha)+\sigma(M-\alpha)\}.\] It follows by applying the valid infimum formula to \(M\mathbf1-V\) and substituting \(\alpha=M-t\). On the binary example its minimum is \(3/4\).
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Nominal joint value does not measure unilateral robust regret
problems.source_location: Section 5, PDF p.10; main.py, generate_VI, figure_wrt_samples and evaluate_policies
claim: The experiments support equilibrium learning, but the available script compares nominal joint-policy values to a nominal baseline, without computing robust current values or unilateral best responses.
analysis: For the one-step game \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), let \(\mu=(1,0)\), \(\nu=(1/2,1/2)\). The joint value and equilibrium value are both \(1/2\), so the released absolute-value score is zero. The minimizing player can switch to column \(2\), reducing its cost to \(0\); regret is \(1/2\). Positive uncertainty radii do not affect a one-step payoff. Statically, generate_VI never uses its sigma argument; evaluate_policies performs expected nominal backups; figure_wrt_samples compares those joint values. The snapshot also differs from the paper in action count, seed count and numerical framework.
result: The available metric cannot certify robust Nash regret. It can legitimately describe joint-value error. The exact producing code and run histories for the published curves are not established by this snapshot, so the paper’s numerical curves are not declared fabricated or reproduced.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Evaluate each player’s robust current value and its robust best response to the fixed opponent, then report both regrets. Existing joint-value error can remain a separate descriptive metric.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The concentration rate cannot cover every bounded adaptive vector
problems.source_location: Lemma D.1, Eq.(46), PDF p.27; dependence discussion, p.28; Appendix G.1, p.51
claim: The lemma permits any \(V\) with \(\|V\|_\infty\le H\), explicitly without independence from the empirical transition row, but gives an empirical-Bernstein rate without a state-dimension term.
analysis: For uniform \(p_i=1/S\), take empirical frequencies \(\hat p\) from \(N\) independent categorical draws and choose \(I=\{i:\hat p_i>1/S\}\), \(V_i=H\mathbf1_{\{i\in I\}}\), \(\sigma=1/(2S)\). If \(\hat p\ne p\), both masses of the nonempty excess set exceed \(\sigma\). Binary TV minimization gives \[\inf_{q\in U_\sigma(\hat p)}q^\top V-\inf_{q\in U_\sigma(p)}q^\top V=H\operatorname{TV}(\hat p,p),\] while \(\operatorname{Var}_{\hat p}V\le H^2/4\).

For completeness set \(Z=\operatorname{TV}(\hat p,p)\) and let \(Y=X-N/S\), \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,1/S)\), with variance \(v=N(S-1)/S^2\ge1\). The fourth moment is at most \(4v^2\); Hölder gives \(\mathbb E|Y|\ge\sqrt v/2\). Hence \(\mathbb EZ\ge\frac14\sqrt{(S-1)/N}\). Changing one observation changes \(Z\) by at most \(1/N\); Efron–Stein gives variance at most \(1/(2N)\). Chebyshev therefore gives \[\Pr\{Z\ge\tfrac18\sqrt{(S-1)/N}\}\ge1-\frac{32}{S-1}.\]

For polynomially large \(N,K\) satisfying burn-in conditions, the proposed right side is at most \[C_4H\sqrt{\log(KH/\delta)/(4N)}+C_4H\log(KH/\delta)/N\]. Any universal \(C_4\) is eventually defeated by the state-dimension factor above. The row example embeds in a full-coverage model with uniform states and transition rows; conditioning on its row count preserves uniform independent next states. It is not asserted that Algorithm 2 produces this particular adaptive vector. Appendix G.1 instead begins with a fixed independent vector and does not supply the claimed independence-removal step.
result: The unrestricted adaptive-vector lemma is false at the stated rate. An algorithm-specific leave-one-out or stability proof could still establish a suitably restricted rate, but is not supplied by the displayed fixed-vector argument.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restrict the lemma to an independent vector and separately establish the independence or dependence control needed for the actual algorithmic iterates. No replacement algorithm-specific rate is claimed here.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The hard-family recursion overlooks other zero-valued absorbing states
problems.source_location: Appendix E.1, Eqs.(86)–(100), PDF pp.37–38; Lemma E.2, Eq.(94); Appendix H.1, pp.59–60
claim: Equation (86) makes every \(m_j\), \(j\ne f\), an absorbing zero-reward state. The full-simplex TV set in Eq.(89) can move mass to those states, while Eq.(94b) assumes its adverse mass moves to \(m_f\).
analysis: Take states \((m_f,n_f,m_j,n_j)\), horizon \(H=16\), two actions, \(c_0=1/4,c_1=1/8,c_2=1/4,\sigma=1/2\), \[p=129/256,\quad \Delta=1/1024,\quad q=515/1024.\] These satisfy \(p>q\ge1/2\), \(H>16\log2\), \(\sigma\le1-c_0\), \(\sigma>c_2/(2H)\), \(\Delta\le c_1\sigma/H\) and \(p+\Delta\le1\). Choose any admissible packing vector and its good action at \(m_f\).

At time \(H\), values are \((0,1,0,1)\). At time \(H-1\), robust values are \((1/256,3/2,0,3/2)\). At \(H-2\), nature can shift mass \(1/2\) from the absorbing \(n_f\) to \(m_j\), at TV distance exactly \(1/2\). Since \(m_j\) has value zero, this is optimal and gives \(V_{H-2}(n_f)=7/4\). Equation (94b) instead adds \(\sigma V_{H-1}(m_f)=1/512\), yielding \(897/512\). The same omitted destination affects Eq.(94a).
result: The literal hard-family recursion and its claimed minimum-state ordering are false. Equation (98) describes a different nonabsorbing background family and is relevant evidence of possible intended wording; adopting it would require coordinated reconstruction of the construction and proof. This finding does not rule out a similar lower-bound rate from another family.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For the displayed family and \(q\ge\sigma\), write \(u_h=p\mu_h(\phi_h\mid m_f)+q\mu_h(1-\phi_h\mid m_f)\). The corrected recursions are \[V_h(m_j)=0,\quad V_h(n_i)=1+(1-\sigma)V_{h+1}(n_i),\] \[V_h(m_f)=(u_h-\sigma)V_{h+1}(n_f)+(1-u_h)V_{h+1}(m_f).\] Induction keeps the \(n_i\) tied and highest-valued, while \(m_j\) remains a minimum; moving adverse mass there verifies the formulas. The information-theoretic separation, coverage and rate must then be reanalyzed.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: A state Kalman gain is not the fresh process-noise posterior
problems.source_location: Appendix B.4, Eqs.(57)–(64), PDF p.21
claim: The appendix claims a filtered posterior for new process noise \(\epsilon_t\), but uses inherited state covariance plus new noise in its gain numerator.
analysis: In a linear Gaussian step, let inherited uncertainty be \(P\), process covariance \(Q\), transition Jacobian \(J\), readout \(W\) and observation covariance \(R\). State prior covariance is \(P^-=JPJ^\top+Q\), but \(\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon_t,y_t)=QW^\top\), not \(P^-W^\top\). For independent scalar inherited state \(N(0,3)\), fresh noise \(N(0,1)\), identity transition/readout and observation noise \(N(0,2)\), observe \(y=1\). The printed state gain gives mean \(2/3\) and covariance \(4/3\). Direct Gaussian conditioning gives the process-noise posterior mean \(1/6\) and variance \(5/6\). The example is exactly linear, so EKF linearization cannot explain the difference.
result: The formulas can describe a state correction, but not the stated posterior of fresh generative process noise when inherited uncertainty is nonzero. If inherited uncertainty vanishes, the gain reduces to the valid greedy formula in Eq.(49). The main deterministic EF mechanism does not require this extension.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For the process-noise interpretation, write \(S=WP^-W^\top+R\) and use posterior mean \(QW^\top S^{-1}(y-W\bar r)\), covariance \(Q-QW^\top S^{-1}WQ\). Alternatively rename the inferred quantity as a state correction; that does not derive a posterior for fresh process noise. Reconstructing the full state posterior requires additional covariance information.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The displayed M-step and experimental loss use different current outputs
problems.source_location: Section 2.3, PDF pp.4–5; Appendix B.3, Eqs.(51),(55)–(56), p.20; RNN_cells.py, lines 85–109; train.py, line 159
claim: The likelihood in Eq.(56) decodes the state after its inferred current correction. The printed deterministic EF mechanism and current source evaluate the present output before correcting the state.
analysis: Hold an inferred correction \(\epsilon^*\) fixed during the parameter step. The two current losses are \[L_{\rm pre}(\theta)=\tfrac12\|Wr_\theta-y^*\|^2,\qquad L_{\rm post}(\theta;\epsilon^*)=\tfrac12\|W(r_\theta+\epsilon^*)-y^*\|^2.\] Stopping gradients through \(\epsilon^*\) does not equate these residuals.

Take a one-step model \(r_\theta=\theta\in\mathbb R^2\), \(W=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\), \(y^*=(1,1)^\top\), \(\theta_{\rm old}=0\), and \(Q=R=I\). Equation (49) gives \(\epsilon^*=(1/2,2/5)^\top\). At the old parameter, \[\nabla_\theta L_{\rm pre}=(-1,-2)^\top,\qquad \nabla_\theta L_{\rm post}=(-1/2,-2/5)^\top.\] The vectors are not collinear, so a scalar learning rate or MSE normalization cannot identify the updates. The implementation returns the unchanged pre-correction output, which train.py uses in the loss.

In the full-row-rank deterministic projection limit with forcing strength \(1\), the corrected output equals its target; its current post-correction residual vanishes, while the pre-correction residual need not. This limiting diagnostic does not claim a finite Gaussian likelihood at zero observation variance.
result: The displayed surrogate does not directly derive the particular experimental pre-correction output loss. The authors acknowledge greedy and approximate inference and describe related stochastic/deterministic mechanisms; the finding is an objective-level gap, rather than a disproof of every Bayesian interpretation or of EF’s observed learning behavior.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the experimental algorithm while explicitly distinguishing its pre-correction loss from the related corrected-output Bayesian surrogate. Optimizing the latter defines a different algorithm whose performance and full-forcing behavior require separate assessment.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Parameter descent does not generally follow the direct activity gradient
problems.source_location: Appendix A.1, after Eq.(35), PDF p.17; Eq.(36), p.18
claim: The text infers that activity changes induced by synaptic parameter updates follow the direction of the direct activity-space loss gradient.
analysis: For \(r=f(\theta)\), Jacobian \(J_\theta\) and \(g_r=\nabla_rL\), the chain rule yields \(\nabla_\theta L=J_\theta^\top g_r\). A parameter step therefore gives \[\Delta r=-\eta J_\theta J_\theta^\top g_r+O(\eta^2),\] which need not be parallel to \(-g_r\). For the exact linear example \(r(\theta)=(\theta,\theta)^\top\), \(W=(1,0)\), target \(1\), and \(L=(Wr-1)^2/2\), at \(\theta=0\) the activity gradient is \((-1,0)^\top\). Parameter descent produces \((\eta,\eta)^\top\), while direct activity descent produces \((\eta,0)^\top\). These vectors are not parallel. Sequence losses can introduce additional cross-time Jacobian terms.
result: The asserted directional identification is false. The formula \(W^\top(Wr-y^*)\) remains the correct direct activity gradient, and the transpose-feedback intervention can still be compared empirically with pseudoinverse feedback.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the Jacobian-mediated displacement above and describe Eq.(36) as a direct activity intervention. Collinearity requires additional structure, such as \(g_r\) being an eigenvector of \(J_\theta J_\theta^\top\).
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The XOR convergence threshold is overwritten
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, PDF p.6; Appendix D, p.23; train.py, lines 134–135,267–270
claim: The paper counts delayed-XOR convergence after MSE below \(0.1\) for ten consecutive epochs. The source first assigns that threshold for MDXOR, then immediately overwrites it with \(0.01\) unless the task is Cue.
analysis: For task MDXOR, the second conditional assignment has a false Cue test and sets \(0.01\). Ten consecutive validation losses \(0.05\) satisfy the paper’s criterion but fail the release’s criterion. This follows by direct case analysis of the two assignments and stopping branch; no training execution is needed.
result: The current released outcome definition is ten times stricter than the stated XOR threshold. Effects on published percentages cannot be quantified without the original histories and producing revision.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use one task-to-threshold assignment with \(0.1\) for both MDXOR and Cue, and \(0.01\) for the remaining task, then assess affected convergence histories under the intended definition.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The sine-task configuration has one output for two target channels
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, PDF pp.6–7; Appendix D, p.23; train_single.py, line 60; tasks/all.py, lines 146–152; RNN_cells.py, lines 89–107
claim: The task uses two phase-shifted waveforms and the task source constructs two channels, while the common configuration sets \(n_{\rm out}=1\), including for Cos.
analysis: For batch size \(2\) and recurrent dimension \(50\), predicted output has shape \(2\times1\), while the target slice is \(2\times2\). Subtraction broadcasts to a \(2\times2\) error. The one-output pseudoinverse has shape \(1\times50\), so feedback attempts \((2\times2)(1\times50)\), with incompatible inner dimensions. Teacher forcing has the same target-product mismatch. Even if feedback were skipped, a broadcast scalar output would be a different task from two independently decoded phase-shifted targets.
result: This configuration cannot implement the declared two-output sine task. The finding concerns the matched current release, rather than proof that the published experiments used this configuration.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Set the sine task’s output dimension to \(2\), while retaining \(1\) for the scalar tasks. Error then has shape \(B\times2\) and feedback matrix \(2\times N\). This checks the local dimensions, not successful end-to-end training.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: A trainable output bias is omitted from the teacher-forcing target
problems.source_location: Eq.(2), PDF p.2; train_single.py, line 75; RNN_cells.py, lines 41,46–47,89,104; train.py, line 107
claim: The configuration requests a frozen output bias, but b_out is created as a trainable parameter and omitted from the flag-setting loop. Decoding adds that bias, while the teacher state still uses \(W^+y^*\).
analysis: Under a linear effective readout \(y=Wr+b\), choose scalar \(W=1,b=1/2,y^*=1\) and full forcing. The released teacher target is \(r=1\), decoding to \(3/2\); the correct state for that affine readout is \(r=1/2\), decoding to \(1\). The error-forcing branch uses the actual output residual and retains the correct bias dependence. Zero-initialized bias is a countercontrol, but its requested training flag is not applied and the optimizer receives it. A ridge of \(10^{-7}\) in the inverse cannot explain the order-one mismatch.
result: The release does not enforce its requested frozen bias, and a nonzero bias changes the correct teacher-forcing target. No claim is made about how far the bias moved in historical runs; effective output scaling must also be handled consistently.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Honor the frozen zero-bias flag, or subtract the output bias in the teacher target and use the same effective linear readout and scaling as decoding.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Dropping the TV conjugate domain changes the SFT equivalence
problems.source_location: Section 3.1–3.2, Eqs.(1)–(5), PDF pp.4–5; Appendix A.1–A.2, Eqs.(12)–(27), pp.15–16
claim: The paper claims TV distribution matching plus KL regularization becomes ordinary SFT because the TV conjugate is the identity, and the KL contribution disappears from the final optimization.
analysis: For \(f(u)=|u-1|/2\) on \(u\ge0\), the conjugate is \[f^*(t)=\begin{cases}-1/2&t<-1/2,\\t&-1/2\le t\le1/2,\\+\infty&t>1/2.\end{cases}\] Extending the absolute-value generator to all real inputs gives identity only on the bounded interval and infinity outside. Either interpretation requires a restriction that Appendix A.1 initially recognizes but A.2 drops. A valid TV dual uses a bounded critic: \[\max_{\|r\|_\infty\le1/2}\{q^\top r-\beta\log\sum_i\rho_i e^{r_i/\beta}\}.\]

Use a one-step terminal model, full-support expert \(q=(0.9,0.1)\), reference \(\rho=(0.5,0.5)\) and \(\beta=1\). For policy \((p,1-p)\), Eq.(1) is \[J(p)=|p-0.9|+p\log(2p)+(1-p)\log(2(1-p)).\] Its minimizer is \(p=e/(1+e)\approx0.731059\), with \(J\approx0.279886\); ordinary SFT selects \(p=0.9\), with \(J\approx0.368064\). Differentiating on either side of \(0.9\) and checking the boundary establishes the global minimum. The bounded critic \((1/2,-1/2)\) gives the matching dual optimum.

An SFT-optimal policy here would require implicit reward span \(\log9>1\); no common reward shift makes that span fit the bounded TV critic. For sufficiently small regularization, specifically \(\beta\le1/\log9\) in this example, the two optimizers can agree. That restricted countercontrol does not imply unrestricted equivalence.
result: The disappearance of the optimization constraint changes the problem. The general policy/implicit-reward representation can remain useful, but it does not establish the claimed exact equivalence to ordinary SFT or elimination of KL’s influence.
assumptions: The example is an allowed one-step instance, with all probabilities strictly positive and no unsupported states or approximation error.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the TV conjugate’s domain and the corresponding bounded reward or reward-span restrictions. The resulting constrained objective is not ordinary unconstrained SFT; a full sequential occupancy-measure formulation needs its own conditions.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The Q/logit identification omits a reference-policy action term
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Theorem 2, Eq.(6), PDF p.6; Appendix A.3, Eqs.(28)–(34), p.16; Assumption 2 and Section 4.4
claim: The theorem identifies raw logits with the Q-function of the implicit reward up to a state-only offset, but its proof uses a reference-free maximum-entropy fixed point for a KL-relative objective.
analysis: For KL regularization relative to \(\rho(a\mid s)\), the relevant optimality relation is \[\pi(a\mid s)=\rho(a\mid s)\exp((Q_r(s,a)-V_r(s))/\beta).\] If policy logits \(\ell\) use temperature \(\tau\), then \[Q_r(s,a)=\frac{\beta}{\tau}\ell_a-\beta\log\rho(a\mid s)+V_r(s)-\beta\log\sum_b e^{\ell_b/\tau}.\] The reference term depends on the action and cannot generally be absorbed in a state-only offset.

For a one-step model with \(\pi=\rho=(0.8,0.2)\), zero reward, and \(\beta=\tau=1\), relative-KL optimization is maximized at \(\pi=\rho\) with \(V=0\). The implicit reward from Eq.(4) is zero and \(Q=(0,0)\). Valid logits are \((\log0.8,\log0.2)\), whose difference is \(\log4\). They cannot equal that Q-vector plus one common constant. A uniform reference removes this specific obstruction; an augmented Q that includes the log reference is a different quantity.

In addition, shifting all logits at a state by arbitrary \(c(s)\) leaves its policy unchanged but shifts its log-sum-exp by \(c(s)\). Therefore policy identities do not establish cross-state value rankings. Assumption 2 is an extra gauge-sensitive empirical assumption. Reported rank correlations for a fixed implementation need not be false, but cannot remove this freedom or prove the theorem.
result: The raw-logit theorem fails for an allowed nonuniform reference even before addressing gauge-sensitive state comparisons. The current theorem does not follow from the valid implicit-reward ratio identity.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Include the action-dependent \(-\beta\log\rho(a\mid s)\) term, the \(\beta/\tau\) scale and a declared state gauge. Distinguish the original reward’s Q-function from any reference-augmented quantity. Cross-state value estimation requires additional gauge control.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The alternative losses do not consistently instantiate the stated dual
problems.source_location: Table 3, PDF p.8; Appendix B, Table 5, p.17; Appendix A.1, Eqs.(18)–(22), pp.15–16
claim: Several rows pair incompatible divergence generators, conjugates or training targets, and drop a value term or conjugate domain required by the dual.
analysis: Use a one-step model with \(\beta=1\), expert \(q\), reference \(\rho\), policy \(\pi\), and \(c=V(s_0)\). Implicit reward is \(r_i=\log(\pi_i/\rho_i)+c\). The complete reward objective is \[F=-\sum_i q_i f^*(-\log(\pi_i/\rho_i)-c)-c.\] For KL, \(f^*(t)=e^{t-1}\), so \[F=-e^{-c-1}\sum_i q_i\rho_i/\pi_i-c.\] It is not a probability difference times an exponential.

For \(q=(0.9,0.1)\), \(\rho=(0.5,0.5)\), \(c=0\), and \(\pi=(p,1-p)\), the correct KL target maximizes \(-e^{-1}(0.45/p+0.05/(1-p))\) at \(p=0.75\). The printed row instead gives \(e^{-1}(0.8p-0.4)\), increasing toward \(p=1\). Moving \(p\) from \(0.75\) to \(0.99\) decreases the correct objective from approximately \(-0.294304\) to \(-2.006615\), while increasing the printed one from \(0.073576\) to \(0.144209\).

The displayed Pearson divergence has denominator \(p\): \(\sum_i(q_i-p_i)^2/p_i\). Its generator is \((u-1)^2/u\), with conjugate \(2-2\sqrt{1-t}\) for \(t\le1\), infinite otherwise. The listed quadratic conjugate \(t+t^2/4\) instead belongs to generator \((u-1)^2\), whose divergence has denominator \(q\); on \(u\ge0\) it also has a constant branch \(-1\) for \(t<-2\). For \(P=(3/4,1/4)\), \(Q=(1/2,1/2)\), the two divergences are \(1/3\) and \(1/4\), respectively.

The missing \(-c\) term is not generally constant under the stated reward optimization. Take \(\pi=q=\rho=(1/2,1/2)\), constant reward \(2\) and hence \(c=2\). For the quadratic generator, the full dual gives \(-f^*(-2)-2=-1\); the printed Pearson target gives \(2-2^2/4=1\), exceeding primal minimum \(0\). Fixing \(c=0\) removes this witness but is an additional gauge restriction.

The squared-Hellinger conjugate is \(t/(1-t)\) only for \(t<1\), and infinite otherwise. Choose \(\pi_1=0.1,\rho_1=0.5,c=0\). Then \(r_1=\log0.2<-1\), so the proper dual is infeasible, while its printed rational expression is finite, approximately \(2.640856\). The half-weighted Jensen–Shannon definition also requires \(-\frac12\log(2-e^{2t})\), with \(t<\frac12\log2\), rather than the listed unhalved conjugate. This scaling changes the objective at fixed regularization strength. The Pearson, Hellinger, JS and GAN targets must all retain the full value term and applicable domains.
result: These are substantive derivation mismatches in the stated alternatives, including optimizer reversal and a weak-duality violation. They do not independently determine which expression an unavailable training implementation actually optimized, or whether the reported empirical improvements persist.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Derive each row from a consistently oriented generator, its full piecewise conjugate and domain, and the complete objective including the initial value term. Keep reference-policy and gauge conventions consistent across all rows; empirical consequences require the actual producing implementation.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Equal token counts do not preserve video coordinates
problems.source_location: Proceedings Appendix B, PDF p.19; current author rose/models/diff_mask_predictor.py; VAE and transformer patch-grid definitions
claim: The predictor reshapes \(28350\) patch scalars to \((10,15,189)\) before trilinear interpolation to \((81,480,720)\). It describes this as spatiotemporal patch supervision.
analysis: The stated causal VAE compression gives latent shape \((21,60,90)\), and the checkpoint/backbone stride \((1,2,2)\) yields actual patch grid \((21,30,45)\). Both products equal \(28350\), so the source’s token-count assertion passes despite different coordinates. Actual row-major index \(j=(30t+h)45+w\) maps \((1,0,0)\) to \(1350\); the documented reshape places it at \((0,7,27)\).

A bounded token field \(z_{t,h,w}=t/20\) is spatially constant on each correct time plane. The documented first plane mixes values \(0,0.05,0.10\) from three actual time planes, creating spatial variation. Trilinear interpolation cannot generally undo this coordinate permutation. The released default matches the displayed reshape; an unpublished training override or compensating learned features could change practical effects.
result: The documented/default supervision grid does not invert the backbone’s flattening. This does not establish failed inference, because the predictor is discarded there, or quantify the trained generator’s quality.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Carry the actual per-sample patch grid and flattening order into the predictor; here reshape to \((21,30,45)\). Use valid unpadded token lengths before interpolation. This restores the coordinate inverse without guaranteeing that changing a trained head preserves performance.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Brightness heuristics do not define image units
problems.source_location: Proceedings Section 5.1, PDF pp.8–9; current author utils/evaluate_video.py, preprocessing lines 20–38 and LPIPS lines 76–104
claim: The evaluator divides by the byte scale only if observed brightness exceeds the unit interval. Its LPIPS branch uses the first frame’s maximum to decide conversion for both frames.
analysis: For byte-valued constant RGB frames \(0\) and \(1\), correct unit-range MSE is \(1/255^2\), giving PSNR \(20\log_{10}255\approx48.1308\) dB. Both maxima are at most \(1\), so the source leaves them unchanged and computes unit-range PSNR \(0\) dB. Encoding the identical images as floating \(0,1/255\) changes this behavior.

For LPIPS, equivalent byte values \((64,192)\) are mapped to approximately \[(-0.4980392,0.5058824)\], but unit-range floating equivalents remain \((0.2509804,0.7529412)\). The latter omits the required symmetric-range conversion. A byte black/white pair also changes conventions when reversed because only the first frame’s maximum controls both. These are input-contract differences, without loading or evaluating a perceptual network.
result: The current metric utility is representation dependent on valid inputs. The exact data format and evaluator used for historical tables are not established, so corrected table values or rankings are not inferred.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Declare input range and RGB layout explicitly: map byte images to \(U=x/255\), accept declared unit-range floats unchanged, then use \(U\) for PSNR/SSIM and \(2U-1\) for LPIPS. Reject unsupported units rather than inferring them from brightness.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: A log-utility calculation does not prove the advertised success optimum
problems.source_location: Proceedings Eq.(7), PDF p.4; Proposition 2, p.6; Theorem 1, p.7; Appendix B.2, p.17
claim: The paper’s independent Beta model minimizes failure \(F(B)=\prod_i\prod_{r=0}^{B_i-1}[\kappa(1-w_i)+r]/(\kappa+r)\), but its proportional-allocation justification switches to weighted logarithmic utility.
analysis: For \(k=2,N=3,\kappa=10,w=(2/3,1/3)\), proportional allocation \((2,1)\) has success \(271/297\), while \((3,0)\) has \(839/891\), an improvement of \(26/891\). This disproves unrestricted finite-concentration optimality, separately from the stated low-confidence regime.

In that regime, take \(k=N=2,w=(9/10,1/10),\kappa=1/100\). Nearest-rounded proportional counts \((2,0)\) give success \(9099/10100\); coverage \((1,1)\) gives \(91/100\), greater by \(92/10100\). As \(\kappa\downarrow0\), these tend to \(0.90\) and \(0.91\). Proper Beta laws and allowed quality scores realize both examples.

The limit rewards covering distinct candidates; if \(N\geq k\), any integer allocation covering all candidates can be optimal. By contrast, \(\sum_jQ_j\log B_j\) genuinely has proportional optimizer, and its KL gap is correct for that utility. No identity turns that gap into a success-probability comparison.
result: The central Bayesian-optimality bridge and success interpretation are unsupported; the log-utility result and empirical DORA comparisons remain distinct.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The existing exact integer optimizer repeatedly chooses a coordinate maximizing \(w_i/(\kappa+B_i)\). Each next rollout reduces log failure by \(-\log[1-\kappa w_i/(\kappa+B_i)]\); these marginal gains decrease along each coordinate, so greedy selection of the largest remaining prefix gain is optimal. This is a result for the independent Beta model, not evidence that actual LLM rollouts obey it.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Finite-temperature affinity does not exactly cancel direction multiplicity
problems.source_location: Proceedings Theorem 1, PDF p.7; Eqs.(10)–(12), pp.6–7; Appendix B.3, pp.17–18
claim: Theorem 1 claims exact recovery of direction-level allocation from the affinity diagonal when scores are equal within each direction, without a separation assumption.
analysis: Use unit embeddings \(e_1=e_2=(1,0)\), \(e_3=(0.99,\sqrt{1-0.99^2})\), zero quality scores and \(T_s=0.01\). Write \(a=e\). Row-softmax diagonals are \(a/(2a+1),a/(2a+1),a/(a+2)\). The normalized total masses are \[W_A=\frac{2(a+2)}{4a+5},\qquad W_B=\frac{2a+1}{4a+5}.\] Equal direction scores require \((1/2,1/2)\), but \(W_A-1/2=3/[2(4a+5)]>0\). The contradiction occurs before rounding.

Actual inverse cluster sizes arise only under extra conditions, such as identical within-cluster embeddings and a zero-temperature limit with strict cross-cluster separation. Finite positive cross-affinities prevent exact inverse-size cancellation in general.
result: The exact recovery theorem fails under its written assumptions; the heuristic may still improve real search.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The supplied restricted result assumes uniqueness weights \(\gamma_i=c/k_j\) within direction \(j\), with a common \(c>0\). Summing quality–uniqueness products then cancels \(k_j\) exactly. A soft approximation requires a quantitative separation/error bound.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Independent rounding and quality pre-pruning change the finite allocation
problems.source_location: Proceedings Eq.(13), PDF p.7; current author scripts/sal/search/dora.py, allocation lines 290–310 and next-iteration beam construction
claim: The fixed rollout constraint is \(\sum_iB_i=N\), but the displayed rule rounds each normalized allocation independently. The release also removes zero quality-rounded candidates before diversity weighting.
analysis: Weights \((0.4,0.4,0.2)\) and \(N=4\) give rounded counts \((2,2,1)\), totaling \(5\). They are realized by orthogonal embeddings and quality scores \((\log2,\log2,0)\). Later truncating a repeated beam list restores its length but makes the allocation depend on order.

With three identical direction-A embeddings and one orthogonal direction-B embedding, quality weights \((0.3,0.3,0.3,0.1)\) round at budget \(4\) to \((1,1,1,0)\), discarding B before uniqueness. Applying quality and inverse-size diversity together instead yields roughly equal final weights and \((1,1,1,1)\). The current source has the quality-only pruning stage; no full author search was run.
result: The displayed/released finite allocation differs from the constrained rule; effects on published model-search accuracy are unmeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For a proportional heuristic, compute all intended weights first and use floor counts plus largest fractional remainders under a declared tie rule to preserve the budget. That restores feasibility, not optimal success; the Beta optimizer is a separate correction.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: A fixed marginal channel does not invert score-conditional noise
problems.source_location: Definition 3.4, PDF p.4; Theorem 4.1 Eq.(1), p.5; Appendix A.4 Eq.(10), p.19
claim: The proof uses \(\widetilde\pi(s)=T^\top\pi(s)\), with \(T=\sum_gP(G=g)T^g\), after removing group conditioning.
analysis: Let groups be uniform; two binary scores \(s_a=(1/3,2/3),s_b=(2/3,1/3)\) have \(P(s_a\mid G=0)=3/4\), \(P(s_a\mid G=1)=1/4\). Let \(Y\) be uniform independent of score/group, \(T^0=I\), \(T^1=\begin{pmatrix}3/4&1/4\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Noise is generated conditional on \((Y,G)\), all channels are invertible, and even \(Y\perp G\), so the unconditional channel really is the paper’s mixture. True group/marginal posteriors are all \((1/2,1/2)\), gap zero. Noisy marginal posteriors are \((15/32,17/32)\), \((13/32,19/32)\). Applying the fixed marginal inverse gives \((15/28,13/28)\), \((13/28,15/28)\), producing claimed normalized gap \(1/28\), not zero. Actual marginalized channel weights are \(P(G\mid Y,S)\), which need not be constant.
result: The central decomposition is false even in binary classification with every inverse and positive group-score cell. Uniform common channels remain a valid special case; no claim is made that every regularized model becomes less fair.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(\pi(s)=\sum_hP(G=h\mid S=s)((T^h)^\top)^{-1}\widetilde\pi_h(s)\). This follows by total probability and the valid groupwise inverse. If retaining the coordinate metric, condition every posterior vector on the same scalar coordinate before inversion.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Coordinate-conditioned and full-score sufficiency are different
problems.source_location: Definitions 3.1–3.2, PDF p.4; Proposition 5.1, p.5; Appendix A.4 Eq.(9), p.19; A.7, p.21
claim: The metric conditions class \(k\) on scalar \(S_k\), while the theorem controls conditional independence and information given the full vector \(S\).
analysis: Use uniform groups and score weights \(3/4,1/4\) as above, \(s_a=(1/3,1/6,1/2),s_b=(1/3,1/2,1/6)\). Let label posteriors given these scores be \((3/4,1/8,1/8)\), \((1/4,3/8,3/8)\), independent of group given score, with identity noise. Thus \(I(Y;G\mid S)=0\) and full-vector gap zero. But \(S_1=1/3\) is constant: class-one group probabilities are \(5/8,3/8\), marginal \(1/2\), discrepancy \(1/8\). Other coordinates distinguish the scores, giving coordinate \(p=1\) gap \(1/24>0\), while the stated information upper bound is zero. Binary coordinates determine the full vector, so the explicit binary lemma is not refuted.
result: The literal multiclass metric/guarantee identification fails, including its uniform-noise interpretation. No calibration assumption in the statement excludes this interior-simplex example.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either use full-vector gap \(D_{g,1}=K^{-1}E[\|\pi_g(S)-\pi(S)\|_1\mid G=g]\), for which Pinsker gives \(\sqrt2\,K^{-1}\sqrt{I/P(G=g)}\), or retain coordinate information \(I_k=I(1_{\{Y=k\}};G\mid S_k)\) and bound the coordinate gap by \[K^{-1}\sum_k\sqrt{I_k/(2P(G=g))}\]. These control different targets.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The information-bound constant does not extend unchanged above one
problems.source_location: Proposition 5.1, PDF p.5; Appendix A.7 extension claim, p.21
claim: The \(p=1\) constant \(\sqrt2/K\) and square-root exponent are extended without restriction to the \(p\)-gap.
analysis: At constant score, equal groups, identity noise, take \(K=3\) posteriors \((0.9,0.05,0.05)\), \((0.05,0.9,0.05)\), marginal \((0.475,0.475,0.05)\). Scalar/full conditioning agree. The \(p=2\) normalized gap is \(\sqrt{2(0.425)^2/3}=0.3470110469\); information is \(0.9\log(0.9/0.475)+0.05\log(0.05/0.475)=0.4626073734\). The printed overall bound is \(0.3206269461\), too small.
result: The unrestricted extension is false; the corrected full-vector \(p=1\) proposition survives. Experiments explicitly using \(p=1\) are not refuted by this extension issue.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For full-vector gaps, \(1\le p\le2\) admits factor \[2^{1/p-1/2}K^{-1/p}\sqrt{I/P(G=g)}\]; \(p\ge2\) admits \(K^{-1/p}(I/P(G=g))^{1/p}\). Positive/negative probability-difference masses both equal TV, so \(\|P-Q\|_p^p\le2\,TV^p\); Pinsker and Jensen prove the stated bounds. Coordinate conditioning still needs its separate repair.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Inverse-noise concentration cannot be uniform over conditioning
problems.source_location: Lemma A.6, PDF p.23; Eq.(8), p.6
claim: The oracle estimator is noise-inverted, but its radius \[3\sqrt2\log(1/\epsilon)\sqrt{\log(6/\delta)/n}\] has no inverse-channel factor.
analysis: At constant score and uniform groups, let true class-one probabilities be \(3/4,1/4\), so all relevant probabilities exceed \(\epsilon=0.1\). Use symmetric invertible channel \(T_\eta=\begin{pmatrix}1/2+\eta&1/2-\eta\\1/2-\eta&1/2+\eta\end{pmatrix}\), \(\eta=10^{-4}\). The exact oracle summand is \(m\pm d\), \(m=\tfrac12\log(3/4)\), \(d=\log3/(4\eta)\), with plus probability \(q=1/2+\eta/2\). Hence \(\widehat I_n=m+d(2B/n-1)\), \(B\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,q)\). At \(n=100,\delta=0.05\), claimed radius \(2.1374991968\) passes only \(B=50\); failure is \(1-\binom{100}{50}q^{50}(1-q)^{50}=0.9204108024\), not at most \(0.05\). Distinct channels \(T_\eta,T_{2\eta}\) also give probability-one failure at \(n=1\).
result: The finite-sample guarantee is false. The proof concentrates a different clean-label plug-in variable. Oracle backward correction can remain unbiased; clipping changes bias and does not prove the unclipped theorem.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Let \(M=\max_g\|(T^g)^{-1}\|_\infty\), \(L=\log(1/\epsilon)\). The actual summand has magnitude at most \(ML\), so Hoeffding gives radius \(ML\sqrt{2\log(2/\delta)/n}\). Preserve the group-probability factor when translating it to a sufficiency bound; nearly singular channels can make it uninformative.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The shared forward-corrected head need not learn the marginal
problems.source_location: Section 5, Eqs.(6)–(8), PDF p.6; oracle premise in Lemma A.5
claim: The group-agnostic head uses group-specific forward correction, then is treated as the clean marginal posterior.
analysis: At constant score, equal groups and class-one probabilities \(0.8,0.2\), take \(T^0=I\), \(T^1=\begin{pmatrix}.75&.25\\.25&.75\end{pmatrix}\). Required marginal is \(h=0.5\), but population risk is \(R(h)=\tfrac12 CE(.8,h)+\tfrac12 CE(.35,.25+.5h)\). Its derivative at \(0.5\) is exactly \(-0.45\), and its unique strictly convex optimum is approximately \(0.6911801733\). An intercept head represents either constant, so this is neither capacity nor optimization failure. Equal clean group posteriors or identical channels are valid exceptions.
result: The proposed population objective does not generally justify the oracle marginal premise. Conditional unbiasedness with genuine oracle heads remains valid; usefulness of heuristic gradients is not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Backward-corrected cross entropy satisfies \[E[[(T^G)^{-1}(-\log h(S))]_{\widetilde Y}]=E[-\log h_Y(S)]\], giving the desired representable population minimizer. Its finite-sample variance/negative losses need separate care. Alternatively mix estimated clean group posteriors with score-conditional group weights.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Uncentered logits condition on extra information
problems.source_location: Last paragraph, PDF pp.6–7; Algorithm 1, p.7; probability-score target in Definition 3.1
claim: The implemented/stated heads use raw logits, although sufficiency is defined for their softmax probability score.
analysis: Let uniform \(G\) determine logits \(Z=(0,0)\) or \((1,1)\), and label probabilities \(0.8,0.2\). Identity noise meets the assumptions. Score \(S=(0.5,0.5)\) is constant, with probability-score CMI \(0.1927447570\) and normalized gap \(0.3\). Yet \(G\) is determined by \(Z\), so \(I(Y;G\mid Z)=0\). Linear affine log-odds heads represent the two true posteriors, so the ideal logit regularizer can vanish without a capacity defect.
result: Zero logit-conditioned CMI does not certify sufficiency of the reported probability score. A logit target can be intentional, but is a different guarantee.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use probability scores or centered logits \(Z^\circ=Z-K^{-1}(\mathbf1^\top Z)\mathbf1\). For finite logits, \(Z^\circ_k=\log S_k-K^{-1}\sum_j\log S_j\), so the two representations determine one another and condition on the same information. Other objective/metric issues remain.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The default CMI path softmaxes auxiliary outputs twice
problems.source_location: algorithms.py, MI_Forward.calc_loss lines 223–252 and _backward_ce lines 170–185; Eq.(8), PDF p.6
claim: calc_loss first converts head logits to probabilities, then the entropy helper softmaxes those probabilities again.
analysis: With exact marginal head \((0.5,0.5)\), exact group heads \((0.8,0.2)\), \((0.2,0.8)\), equal groups, identity noise and batch counts \(8:2,2:8\), true information is \(0.1927447570\). A second softmax maps \(0.8\) to \(r=e^{.8}/(e^{.8}+e^{.2})=0.6456563062\). The resulting entropy difference is \(\log2+.8\log r+.2\log(1-r)=0.1356592301\).
