Both values lie within the optional clipping range. Existing MI_Forward2 passes raw logits and avoids this extra transform, but the inspected default/registry chooses MI_Forward.
result: The post-publication default release differs from the displayed entropy estimator. Historical experiment code, learned-head accuracy and model-ranking effect remain unestablished.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the existing raw-logit convention consistently for both heads, or a helper explicitly accepting probabilities without another softmax. This local correction does not solve population-head or representation issues.
The author repository already contains the corrective raw-logit MI_Forward2 variant; adoption in the inspected default/registry is not established.

problems.title: Inverse-column softmax corrupts identity-channel pseudo-labels
problems.source_location: MC baseline, PDF p.8; algorithms.py, MC._sample_clean_labels lines 833–846; calibration-label path in train.py
claim: The MC baseline softmaxes a column of the inverse channel and samples it as a pseudo-clean label distribution.
analysis: For \(T^g=I_K\), the inverse column is \(e_j\), so the correct observed label is retained only with probability \(e/(e+K-1)\). Expected flips are \(1/(e+1)=0.2689414214\) for binary labels and \(13/(e+13)=0.8270624068\) at \(K=14\), despite zero noise. General inverses need not be stochastic: symmetric \(0.75/0.25\) noise has inverse entries \(1.5,-0.5\). Row normalization does not remove negatives, and softmax supplies no inverse-noise justification.
result: The released baseline uses an altered label process even for noiseless groups. No comparison-ranking change or failure of multicalibration itself is established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Identity channels must preserve labels. General resampling needs a Bayes posterior proportional to \(\pi_i(x,g)T^g_{ij}\), with an explicitly estimated clean prior/posterior; signed inverse weights can instead correct expectations without pretending to be sampling probabilities. No universal pseudo-label repair is certified.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Nonzero noise can preserve a balanced calibrated posterior
problems.source_location: Text immediately following Theorem A.2, PDF p.18
claim: The text infers strictly positive true-label calibration error of the noisy Bayes score whenever noise is nonzero.
analysis: Let \(Y\) be independent of input with probability \(1/2\), and use symmetric channel \(\begin{pmatrix}.8&.2\\.2&.8\end{pmatrix}\), determinant \(0.6\). The noisy Bayes score remains \((.5,.5)\), exactly calibrated to true labels. More generally binary flip rates \(a,b\) give \(q=b+(1-a-b)p\), discrepancy \(|b-(a+b)p|\), zero at the fixed posterior \(p=b/(a+b)\). A reverse-triangle lower bound that may be negative cannot imply strict positivity.
result: The local inevitability statement requires qualification. It does not refute the consistently conditioned reverse-triangle inequality or the possibility that label bias harms calibration.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State positivity only when the score law gives positive mass away from the channel’s fixed posterior; preserve the balanced symmetric-noise exception.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Normalized smooth spectra do not imply a common PAN factor
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v2, Appendix A.3, Proposition A.1 and Eqs.(31)–(39), PDF p.20; proceedings corresponding pp.19–20
claim: The PAN/intensity argument obtains \(I_{{\rm PAN},p}=I_p\int q(\lambda)C_p(\lambda)d\lambda\), then treats the integral as approximately spatially constant from normalized smooth chromaticity and a qualitative broadband response.
analysis: On \([0,1]\), take \(L=1,s=1-(1-a)\lambda\), spectra \(X_+=a\lambda^n,X_-=a(1-\lambda)^n\), and reflectances \(R_\pm=X_\pm/s\). For \(0<a<1\), these reflectances are smooth and in \([0,1]\), and both intensities are \(a/(n+1)\). Their factors are \[k_+=a+\frac{1-a}{n+2},\qquad k_-=1-\frac{1-a}{n+2}.\] With \(a=1/10,n=8\), they are \(19/100\) and \(91/100\); equal intensities produce PAN ratio \(91/19\). The best common positive calibration has worst relative intensity error \((k_--k_+)/(k_-+k_+)=36/55\).

The approximation has no stated tolerance, so a nonzero difference alone is not a refutation of a calibrated apparatus. The family demonstrates that no uniformly small error follows from the written qualitative premises. Flat response or common chromaticity rescues the factor; global image normalization cannot remove material-dependent differences. The valid scalar-illumination cancellation and known-intensity reconstruction algebra survive.
result: The physical-approximation justification needs quantitative calibration assumptions. This does not refute useful empirical PAN guidance or the known-intensity reconstruction method.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The supplied bound is valid if \(\|q-k_0\|_\infty\leq\delta\) for known \(k_0>0\): \(|I_{\rm PAN}-k_0I|\leq\delta I\), hence relative calibrated error at most \(\delta/k_0\). A small actual ratio must be measured, not inferred from smoothness.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Dense top-k masking retains quadratic channel cost
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v2, Section 2.3 and Eq.(23); current author architecture/CIDNet.py, TopkOperation and Topk_WindowSpectralAttn
claim: The spectral-attention discussion attributes a reduction from \(O(C^2)\) to \(O(KC)\) to top-k masking, with fixed retained channel fractions.
analysis: The actual source first forms all \(d^2\) scores, then creates dense masks, dense softmax outputs and a dense value product for each of four fractions. With \(P\) window positions, this retains \(\Theta(Pd^2)\) work. Even ideal sparse aggregation with \(K=\lfloor\rho d\rfloor\), fixed \(\rho>0\), is \(\Theta(Pd^2)\). A valid \(O(KC)\) upper expression therefore does not establish a smaller asymptotic order here.
result: The mechanism sparsifies support; the inspected implementation does not establish the claimed resource reduction. No hardware timing or reconstruction score is contradicted by these analytic counts alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain dense quadratic cost for this implementation and distinguish it from any measured constant-factor benefit. No new sparse kernel is proposed.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Test reconstruction error controls checkpoint saving
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v2 experimental protocol; current author train.py, test-data loading and epoch loop, lines 132–143
claim: The training driver evaluates the named test scenes each epoch, updates the maximum test PSNR, and saves improving checkpoints above its threshold.
analysis: The selected epoch depends on \(\arg\max_e\operatorname{PSNR}_{\rm test}(\theta_e)\). Thus test targets affect model selection even without entering gradient updates. This is separate from the explicitly declared intensity input. A score on the same selected test set is consequently not a wholly untouched holdout estimate under this driver.

The current release matches the implicated supplemental routine. The source alone does not establish which saved checkpoint generated each historical table, whether another final holdout existed, or the size of selection optimism.
result: The current selection protocol uses test error; empirical correction requires the actual checkpoint and evaluation history.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the supplied protocol correction: choose epochs using independent validation or a prespecified schedule, then evaluate on an untouched final test. No post hoc PSNR adjustment is justified.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The printed accounting interface returns zero after positive call paths
problems.source_location: Current proceedings Appendix E, PDF pp.21–22, generated-method listing lines 95–148; comparison arXiv v1 corresponding author listing
claim: The provided case-generation example returns fields for LLM calls, input/output tokens and token cost, but initializes all of them to zero after its generation activity.
analysis: A positive-call helper invokes the client, while the unconditional return block still reports \((N_{\rm calls},N_{\rm in},N_{\rm out})=(0,0,0)\). For any execution making at least one counted call, the reported call count is therefore false. This follows statically without creating an attack or contacting a model.

An external wrapper could maintain an independent ledger and ignore these fields. Current author-repository metadata is inaccessible, so this check concerns the author’s printed example, not an obtained full orchestration implementation. No trace establishes that the reported query-reduction tables used this dictionary.
result: The example’s accounting interface cannot substantiate cost on positive-call paths; no corrected historical query count is inferred.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The supplied correction records counted events at the client boundary and returns before/after ledger differences, with explicit retry/cache and billing conventions. No attack-generation modification or execution is needed.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The table’s comparison and cost claim needs an explicit scope
problems.source_location: Current proceedings Table 2, PDF p.7; Appendix D Table 5, p.18
claim: The table caption describes uniformly higher success at lower cost; the actual comparisons depend on target, comparator, resource unit and amortized setup.
analysis: On GPT-4o the displayed ASRs are \(0.69\) versus AutoDAN-Turbo’s \(0.76\); on Mixtral both are \(0.96\). AutoRedTeamer exceeds PAIR and TAP across the four targets. Lower evaluation-call counts, amortized setup, token expenditure and latency are different comparisons. For example, fixed setup and per-case Llama counts against Rainbow give \(82+14N\) versus \(6000+4N\), crossing at \(N=591.8\). This is a conditional accounting illustration, not a recovered billing trace.
result: Retain the favorable comparisons actually supported by the table and qualify universal caption language. No separate empirical score defect is established.

problems.title: The no-VT baseline explicitly suppresses visual reasoning
problems.source_location: Proceedings Section 4.1, PDF p.5; Table 1, p.6; Appendix C.1, pp.23–24; Appendix B.3 and Figure 11, p.22
claim: The main text describes the no-VT comparator as without extra instructions, while the appendix explicitly instructs it to avoid visual descriptions. The treatment also adds a separate visual-thought generation stage.
analysis: Let \(a\) denote success under a two-stage VT protocol, \(b\) under the suppressed baseline and \(c\) under unrestricted ordinary CoT. Then \[a-b=(a-c)+(c-b).\] The reported positive difference does not identify \(a-c\). Probabilities \((a,b,c)=(0.70,0.40,0.80)\) demonstrate the inference failure without pretending to be measured data.

The authors’ auxiliary direct/suppressed comparison reports \[(13,12),(42,32),(84,31)\], with differences \(1,10,53\) percentage points. This is counterevidence to treating suppression as innocuous. These auxiliary numbers cannot be subtracted from Table 1 without matched protocols/items. Extra calls and tools are legitimate system components, but the comparison does not isolate their individual effects.
result: The comparison is valid for its documented restricted protocol; the broad ordinary-CoT improvement interpretation and main-text baseline description need qualification. No benchmark number is recomputed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the supplied relabeling: report the suppression instruction in the main protocol and describe the measured effect under that restriction. An unrestricted matched comparison would be additional evidence, not a numerical correction obtainable from the existing table.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Local attention and intervention evidence does not measure all information routes
problems.source_location: Proceedings Section 5.2, PDF p.9; Figure 10; Appendix D, p.28
claim: The paper interprets attention, saliency and blocking examples as showing that nearly all image-derived signals pass through visual thoughts.
analysis: The statistic is local sensitivity, not a normalized conserved information quantity. For example, \(z(a)=1/2-4(a-1/2)^2\) and cross-entropy \(L(a)=\log(1+e^{-z(a)})\) have \(aL^{\prime}(a)=0\) at \(a=1/2\), although removing the coefficient to \(0\) changes the correct-class logit from \(1/2\) to \(-1/2\). This limits what zero first-order saliency proves. The paper’s actual blocking experiment remains meaningful local causal evidence; the example is not its model output.
result: Retain evidence for the analyzed inputs and interventions. No exhaustive fraction of information flow or global failure of mediation is established by this focused check.

problems.title: The positivity safeguard fails for the exponential branch
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v4, Section 4.1, Eq.(27), PDF pp.6–7; Appendix E.2.2 exponential specialization
claim: The Dirichlet construction uses \(A=\sum_ca_c,S=\max(A,1)\), \(L=[\prod_c(a_cS-b_c)/(b_c-a_c^2)]^{1/C}\), and \(\gamma=La/A\), asserting that the safeguard ensures positivity.
analysis: For independent Gaussian coordinates with variances \((\log3,\log(3/2))\) and means equal to minus half those variances, exact exponential moments give \(a=(1,1),b=(3,3/2),A=S=2\). Both variances are positive and all moments finite. The ratios are \(-1/2\) and \(1\), so \(L=\sqrt{-1/2}\) is not real. No singularity, underflow or approximate sigmoid integral is involved.

For exact bounded activations \(0<Q_c<1\) with positive variance, \(b_c<a_c\), so the same safeguard does give positive numerators. The current implementation also clips moment ratios before taking logarithms, preventing a non-real result but adding a separate regularization. That is not a proof of the unrestricted exponential formula.
result: Restrict the exponential Dirichlet domain or specify the additional regularization. The main bounded-activation predictive construction and empirical comparisons are not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The supplied sufficient domain is \(a_c>0,b_c>a_c^2,S>\max_cb_c/a_c\). Every factor is then positive, making \(La/A\) well-defined. This establishes existence on that domain, not approximation accuracy.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The current concentration uses the floored normalization twice
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v4 Eq.(27) and Appendix E.2.4; current author probit/utils/predictive.py, get_mom_dirichlet_approximation, lines 446–471
claim: The formula returns \(La/A\); the current source returns \(La/S\), so when \(A<1\) the total concentration is scaled by \(A\).
analysis: For two independent Gaussian coordinates with \(\mu=-2\log3,v=24/\pi\), the stated sigmoid-moment approximations give \(a_c=1/4,b_c=5/32\). Thus \(A=1/2,S=L=1\), with positive unclipped moment ratios. The manuscript gives \(\gamma=(1/2,1/2)\), while the source gives \((1/4,1/4)\). Both means are \((1/2,1/2)\), but component variances are \(1/8\) versus \(1/6\), and expected entropies are \(2\log2-1\) versus \(\pi/2+\log2-2\). The discrepancy affects concentration-dependent uncertainty, not the unchanged mean predictive.
result: The current public function differs from the formula on valid inputs. The source predates the final paper; its attribution to the original uncertainty rankings is unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep \(S\) inside scalar moment ratios but divide the final vector by \(A\), the already-computed sum of first moments. This restores formula correspondence on its valid domain, subject to separately declared clipping.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Negative lognormal covariances defeat an unrestricted variance bound
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v4, Appendix K.1, Eq.(111), PDF p.34
claim: The explanatory bound uses \(\operatorname{Var}(\sum_ie^{X_i})\geq\operatorname{Var}(e^{X_j})\) for general multivariate Gaussian logits.
analysis: Let \(\mu=(0,0)\) and covariance have diagonal \(\log(4/3)\) and off-diagonal \(\log(4/5)\). Its eigenvalues are \(\log(16/15),\log(5/3)>0\). Individual lognormal variances are \(4/9\), covariance is \(-4/15\), and sum variance is \(2(4/9)+2(-4/15)=16/45<4/9\). Positive-definite Gaussian covariance therefore does not supply the displayed lower bound.
result: The appendix needs a covariance restriction. Diagonal and nonnegatively correlated cases retain the bound, and the exact individual exponential moments remain valid.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the full variance sum including cross-covariances, or require nonnegative off-diagonal Gaussian covariances so that all lognormal cross terms are nonnegative.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Segmental F1 counts nonoverlap and repeated matches
problems.source_location: Section 5.1, PDF p.7; utils.py, f_score lines 119–148
claim: The source takes an absolute signed intersection and omits the one-use ground-truth hit guard.
analysis: For four one-hot frames, truth \((A,B,B,B)\), prediction \((B,B,B,A)\), true A interval \([0,1)\) and predicted \([3,4)\) are disjoint. Source absolute intersection is \(2\), union \(4\), artificial IoU \(1/2\); B genuinely has IoU \(1/2\). At threshold \(0.5\), source counts \((TP,FP,FN)=(2,0,0)\), F1 \(100\%\), versus correct \((1,1,1)\), \(50\%\). Independently, truth \((A,A,A,A,A)\), prediction \((A,A,B,A,A)\) has two A predictions each IoU \(2/5\) with one true segment; at threshold \(0.25\), omitted uniqueness gives \((2,1,0)\), \(80\%\), versus \((1,2,0)\), \(50\%\). Repeating frames \(750\) or \(600\) times gives legal \(3000\)-frame cases with identical ratios. For disjoint equal-length intervals, false ratio \(g/(g+2\ell)\) even approaches \(1\) as the gap grows.
result: The evaluator fails ordinary temporal-overlap/cardinality semantics on the one-hot subdomain. Perfect-sequence controls still pass; multi-label annotations cannot justify disjoint matches. Historical table impact remains unestablished.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(I=\max(0,\min(b,d)-\max(a,c))\), \(U=(b-a)+(d-c)-I\), and require an unused compatible ground-truth match. Declare multi-label compatibility and segment conventions separately; no corrected benchmark ranking is supplied.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: EDIT divides by a two-element container
problems.source_location: inference.py, paired ground-truth/prediction lists; utils.py, func_eval lines 159–181
claim: The source sums per-video normalized edit scores but divides by the outer container length \(2\), rather than video count.
analysis: For \(N\) perfect videos with labels \((A,A,B,B)\), every per-video score is \(100\). The true mean is always \(100\), while source returns \(50N\): \(50,100,150\) for one, two, three videos. In general the released statistic is \(N/2\) times the equal-video mean, so dataset duplication changes its scale. Within a fixed equal-cardinality comparison the common factor alone preserves ranking, but not normalization.
result: The aggregation is incorrect for the actual paired-list signature. Published values cannot simply be rescaled without authenticating their driver and the separate label-interface behavior.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Validate equal nonempty paired video lists and divide by their count. If a different weighted edit metric is intended, define its weights explicitly.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Score vectors and class-axis filtering are passed as temporal labels
problems.source_location: inference.py, lines 109–122; utils.py, segmentation and nonzero comparisons lines 64–99,131–136,166–169
claim: The driver passes raw \((T,C)\) scores to discrete segment routines, while its median filter operates across classes in the preceding \((C,T)\) layout.
analysis: Constant argmax A with scores \[(.6,.4),(.7,.3),(.8,.2),(.9,.1)\] should give one segment, but exact-vector change detection gives four and per-video edit \(25\), versus discrete edit \(100\). Separately, nonzero on a class vector returns a one-element tuple, so using its length selects only the top one class; truth \(\{0,2\}\) and scores \((.6,.3,.1,0,\ldots)\) pass Hit@1 membership despite not recovering simultaneous labels. Finally, at each of five frames give class \(68\) probability \(0.9\), all other \(136\) classes \(0.1/136\). Proper temporal median filtering preserves this constant signal; source size-\(30\) filtering across class neighborhoods erases its peak and normalization gives \(1/137\) everywhere. This strictly positive example needs no zero-probability limit.
result: The source conflates confidence changes, labels, set membership and temporal smoothing. Multi-label ACC has no single forced convention, so Hit@1 interpretation is a qualification as well as a tuple-cardinality issue; no actual dataset ranking is inferred.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Filter each class over time. Convert scores with a declared prediction-only label/set rule before run-length segmentation; define per-class versus joint-set segments and name ACC accordingly. Using true-label cardinality to choose predictions is a different truth-dependent rule, not a silent repair.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Training and denoising do not follow the stated branch conditions
claim: The paper uses feature-conditioned branch decoders, but source fixes zero conditioning, shares one decoder call path, substitutes the holistic clean estimate into the partial update and overwrites the second boundary loss.
analysis: With fixed time/noisy labels/parameters, the training decoder receives zeros_like(features), so its output and decoder-loss gradient cannot depend on the feature conditioning tensor. Occasional dropout is not a permanently fixed zero branch; inference instead passes real features. decoder_original is instantiated but unused. For partial DDIM, substituting \(\widehat x_0^h\) for \(\widehat x_0^p\) changes the next value by \(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{\rm next}}(\widehat x_0^h-\widehat x_0^p)\): at \(0.81,0.2,-0.4\), it is \(0.18\) rather than \(-0.36\), difference \(0.54\). Finally second boundary loss is assigned the first reduced loss, giving \(4L_h\) rather than \(2(L_h+L_p)\) and no direct second-branch boundary gradient. Equal clean branch predictions hide the DDIM discrepancy.
result: The current file materially differs from the described branch dataflow/objective. It may be an ablation or incomplete release; no authenticated experiment manifest resolves historical use, and no corrected model quality is claimed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the declared feature conditions, explicitly choose shared or separate decoder parameters, use the partial clean estimate in its own update and reduce its own boundary loss. These restore local dependencies/algebra; architecture/training changes require independent evaluation.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Vector pooled memory is not the matrix recurrence
problems.source_location: Eq.(5), PDF p.6; xLSTM2/xLSTM.py, lines 421–426,477–512
claim: The paper uses matrix cell memory with outer product, per-time update and a bounded inner-product normalizer; source uses pooled vector states, elementwise products and one global maximum.
analysis: From zero state, choose \(i=1,o=1/2,v=(1,0),k=q=(0,1)\). The paper obtains \(C=vk^\top=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\), normalizer \(1\), output \((1/2,0)\). Source elementwise \(v\odot k=0\), and zero-cell layer normalization cannot recover the missing off-diagonal contribution. The source also divides by max of \(n\odot q\) without a lower bound, so \(q=0\) yields zero over zero rather than protected zero. It stores detached batch/time-averaged states across forward calls, and the independent-video driver does not reset them. Consequently order dependence is structurally possible; the earlier bounded component test reported repeated-input differences removed by resetting, which is historical execution evidence, not a new run.
result: The current memory is a different operator with an unprotected domain and unspecified cross-video state. The displayed matrix recurrence itself is not refuted; trained-checkpoint incidence and benchmark impact are unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Reset state at independent sequence boundaries to remove that persistence. Implementing Eq.(5) additionally needs a matrix state, outer product, explicit temporal recurrence/scan and specified bounded inner-product normalizer. A vector-memory alternative needs its own definition; reset alone is not a matrix-memory repair.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The release uses pre-fusion DCT-II instead of post-fusion DFT
problems.source_location: Eq.(6), PDF p.7; model.py dct lines 22–50, training lines 302–305 and sampling lines 424–426
claim: The source adds an unnormalized DCT-II residual before HP-xLSTM, while the paper specifies DFT of the fused features.
analysis: For \(x=(1,0,0,0)\), ordinary DFT is \((1,1,1,1)\), but the implemented DCT-II is \[(2,2\cos(\pi/8),2\cos(\pi/4),2\cos(3\pi/8))\], approximately \[(2,1.847759,1.414214,0.765367)\]. No single global scale makes them equal. A Fourier representation of an extended signal is not the same length transform. For nonlinear fusion \(G\), \(G(z+\mathrm{DCT}_{II}z)\) also need not equal \(G(z)+\mathrm{DFT}(G(z))\); the release constructs no separate post-fusion DFT conditions.
result: The current transform/order differs from the specified operator, without showing cosine features are ineffective or identifying the exact frequency variant behind each table.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Accurately describe the existing pre-fusion DCT-II residual and corresponding configurations, or separately implement/validate the stated post-fusion DFT with an explicit complex-to-real representation. No complete trained replacement is supplied.
A proposed correction is retained where stated; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: An oracle sufficient-representation theorem does not prove the fitted encoder reaches it
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v2, Section 4.3, Definition 4.1 and Theorem 4.1, PDF p.6; Appendix A.1; contribution statement p.2
claim: The formal theorem compares sufficient representations of \((X,T)\) and \(X\), but is used to motivate an algorithmic information-preservation guarantee for an encoder that observes past \(X\) at prediction time.
analysis: Under the stated Markov and sufficiency conditions, the chain rule correctly gives \[I(Z_1;Y)-I(Z_2;Y)=I(T;Y\mid X)\geq0.\] This theorem is not refuted. For a fitted encoder \(Z=f_D(X)\) at fixed independent training state \(D\), however, \(I(Z;Y\mid X,D)=0\). Joint sufficiency additionally requires \(I(T;Y\mid X,D)=0\). Learning to predict a future target does not by itself supply that condition.

Let \(X,Y\) be independent fair bits and \(T=Y\). An oracle \(Z_1=T\) has one bit about \(Y\), while \(Z_2=X\) has zero; the theorem holds. Every deployed encoder of only \(X\), with independent fixed fitted state, still has zero information about the current \(Y\). The witness exposes the missing application bridge, rather than violating the theorem’s assumptions.
result: Retain the theorem as an information-availability motivation; the proposed training loss does not establish its sufficiency premise. Better empirical inductive bias or sample efficiency remains possible.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For two actual encoders of the same prediction input, define \(\delta_j=I(X;Y\mid Z_j,D)\). Then \(I(Z_1;Y\mid D)-I(Z_2;Y\mid D)=\delta_2-\delta_1\). A desired ordering requires a real comparison of those residual information terms, rather than the training protocol alone.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Cosine fitting identifies direction rather than target magnitude
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v2 Eq.(4), PDF p.5; current author src/helpers/loss_helper.py, ScaledCosineLoss
claim: The objective is scaled cosine error; a separate theorem that zero cosine error implies complete task-vector recovery is not stated.
analysis: A concrete scope obstruction uses three valid scaled SQL-aggregate vectors \(T_A=(1,1,1,1,0,0,0)\), \(T_B=(0,0,0,0,1/2,0,0)\), \(T_C=(0,0,0,0,1,0,0)\). They arise from numerical future-row multisets \[\{1,1\},\{0,0,0\},\{0,0,0,0\}\], applying mean/min/max/sum/count/sample-SD, per-column min-max scaling and a zero nonempty flag. A representation merging B and C can predict \(T_C\) for both and achieve zero cosine loss while losing their distinct row counts. With equiprobable types, the lost downstream count information is \(2/3\) bit. This does not prove actual training chooses that representation.
result: This is an objective-identifiability limitation supporting the missing bridge above, not a separate refuted zero-loss theorem. The current source explicitly normalizes both vectors.

problems.title: A drop with a restricted decoder does not identify information loss
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v2 Section 5.3, PDF p.9
claim: The text interprets a performance drop as a signal of lost input information.
analysis: Let \(X\) be uniform on \(\{0,1,2,3\}\), \(Y=\mathbf1\{X\geq2\}\), \(Z_2=X\), and let \(Z_1\) permute those values to \((0,2,1,3)\). Both encoders are invertible and retain one bit about \(Y\). An affine-threshold decoder is perfect on \(Z_2\), but can achieve only \(3/4\) accuracy on the alternating labels ordered by \(Z_1\). Representation geometry and decoder restrictions can reduce accuracy without losing any information.
result: The diagnostic inference is false in general. No particular RelBench score or cause of its observed drop is established by this analytic example.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain information loss, geometry, decoder expressiveness, optimization and finite-sample effects as distinct candidate explanations. No new numerical information estimate is invented.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Target construction and actual augmentation are different claims
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v2 Sections5.4 and Appendix C.2, PDF pp.9,25
claim: The mechanism discussion says TVE does not rely on augmentations; the appendix explicitly includes masking regularization.
analysis: The stated masking probability is \(0.15\). A future-statistic predictive target need not rely on paired augmented views, while the actual training can still use feature masking. The latter does not isolate an augmentation-removal mechanism for stable embeddings.
result: Retain the narrower target-construction interpretation and the documented masking protocol. This is a mechanism clarification, not a separate theorem or numerical error.

problems.title: Per-task smoothness does not give the same constant for the sum
problems.source_location: Current proceedings Eq.(1), PDF p.2; Assumption 3.3 and Theorem 3.4 Eq.(8), p.5; Theorem G.3 and descent-lemma Eq.(17), pp.35–36
claim: The aggregate is the sum \(\mathcal L=\sum_k\mathcal L_k\), but the descent proof applies a coefficient \(L\) supplied only for individual task gradients. The resulting one-step bound drives the conceptual allocation surrogate.
analysis: Use deterministic nonnegative losses \(\mathcal L_1(\theta)=\tfrac12\|\theta+e_1\|^2\), \(\mathcal L_2(\theta)=\tfrac12\|\theta+e_2\|^2\) in two dimensions. At \(\theta=0\), take one sample per task, step \(\eta=1\), individual smoothness \(L=1\), zero noise and local interaction constants \(c=\bar c=0\). The gradients are orthogonal unit vectors, so all stated local interaction assumptions hold and \(\beta=\gamma=1\). The actual update is \((-1/2,-1/2)\), with aggregate loss \(1/2\). The published bound instead gives \[1-(1/2+1/2)+\tfrac12(1/4+1/4)=1/4.\] Thus it requires \(1/2\leq1/4\).

The summed Hessian is \(2I\), despite each individual Hessian being \(I\). More generally, for any positive step and weights \((w,1-w)\), true next loss exceeds the bound by \(\eta^2[w^2+(1-w)^2]/2>0\). Small steps do not restore the upper-bound assertion. The source explicitly imposes the interaction conditions at the current iterate; a global-trajectory counterexample is not claimed.

Changing the objective to an average would also change its linear term and cannot silently repair only the smoothness coefficient. Coordinate-separable examples with aggregate smoothness equal to individual smoothness remain valid controls. The subsequent convergence argument depends on the failed universal bound, but is not declared false under every strengthened sequential hypothesis.
result: The central one-step theorem is false under its printed assumptions, leaving its allocation/convergence use unsupported without a corrected constant or stronger premise. Practical language-model results are not remeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The supplied correction uses aggregate smoothness \(L_\Sigma\), safely \(KL\) when only individual bounds are known. Under independent unbiased samples, apply the descent lemma with \(L_\Sigma\) in both quadratic variance/mean terms. The example is then exact at \(L_\Sigma=2\). A supplied restricted convergence proof additionally requires nonnegative interactions, true statistics and exact feasible integer surrogate minimization; it does not validate arbitrary conflict, estimated statistics or rounding.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Odd-period shifts fail to invert
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Eq.(7), PDF p.6; Table 7, p.28; SGN.py, TemporalSwinTransformerBlock.forward, lines 164–191
claim: The right cyclic shift is said to restore the original coordinates after shifting by \(P/2\). The release uses floor-divided shifts \((-P)//2\) and \(P//2\); the PTB-XL configuration has \(P=25\).
analysis: For \(P=2k+1\), the shifts sum to \(-(k+1)+k=-1\), rather than zero. With an identity feature map, \(P=3\) and input \((0,1,2,3,4,5)\), the two rolls give \((1,2,3,4,5,0)\); the prefix overwrite yields \((0,2,3,4,5,0)\). Even periods give cancelling shifts.
result: The released odd-period coordinate mapping does not implement the stated restoration. This does not establish any change in benchmark accuracy.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Compute \(h=\lfloor P/2\rfloor\) once and use shifts \(-h,+h\); their cyclic maps are inverse for every integer period.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Initialization always loads TDBRAIN assignments
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, PDF p.4; Appendix A, p.24; SGN.py, GumbelGroupEmbedding.__init__, line 237; exp_classification.py, _build_model, lines 44–67
claim: The model initializes grouping from the selected dataset, but the embedding always reads groups_matrix_T.npy.
analysis: The builder writes distinct files for TDBRAIN, PTB-XL, FLAAP and UCI-HAR, with shapes \[(33,4),(12,4),(6,5),(9,6)\]. A clean PTB-XL build writes only its own file, so the fixed TDBRAIN filename is absent. If the TDBRAIN file exists instead, its \(33\) channel rows cannot contract with the \(12\) PTB-XL input channels.
result: The published construction path has a concrete filename/shape mismatch. An unpublished renaming workflow and the experimental snapshot remain unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Pass the selected assignment matrix directly to the embedding and require its shape to equal \((C,G)\).
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Cosine regularization changes assignment preferences
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, Eq.(3), PDF p.5; SGN.py, similarity_regularization, lines 276–280
claim: The paper uses \(L=\sum_{ij}S_{ij}\|M_i-M_j\|^2\), with signed cosine similarities. The release uses weights \((1+S_{ij})/2\) and divides by \(C^2\).
analysis: For \(C=G=2\), assignment rows \((1,0),(0,1)\), and off-diagonal cosine \(s\), the paper gives \(4s\) while the release gives \((1+s)/2\). At \(s=-1\), these are \(-4\) and \(0\); at \(s=0\), they are \(0\) and \(1/2\). The difference includes an unweighted pair-distance penalty and cannot be absorbed into a positive loss rescaling.
result: The documented and released objectives are inequivalent, including interior soft assignments by continuity. Which objective generated the tables is not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify whether signed cosine weights or shifted nonnegative weights are intended, and align the displayed objective and implementation.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Initializer computes squared distance correlation
problems.source_location: Appendix A, Eqs.(9)–(12), PDF p.24; exp_classification.py, distance covariance and similarity functions
claim: The paper clusters rows of distance correlation \(R_n\); the routine returns squared distance covariance and therefore normalizes to \(R_n^2\).
analysis: For \(X=(0,1,2,3)^\top\) and \(Y=(0,1,0,1)^\top\), double-centering gives cross-value \(1/8\) and self-values \(13/16,1/4\). Thus the routine returns \(R_n^2=1/\sqrt{13}\), whereas Eq.(9) gives \(R_n=13^{-1/4}\). Entrywise squaring is nonlinear, so it need not preserve Euclidean row distances used by K-means.
result: The formula/routine discrepancy is established for nonconstant samples. The builder loads precomputed matrices, so this does not determine their provenance or show that the benchmark groupings change.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Take the nonnegative square root of the normalized squared quantity to match Eq.(9), with an explicit zero-variance convention; alternatively document the squared initializer.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: FLAAP loader does not enforce subject separation
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, PDF pp.7–8; Appendix B.3, p.25; data_loader.py, FLAAPLoader.load_flaap_dependent, lines 622–648
claim: The experiment description restricts each subject to one data subset. The released FLAAP loader splits sample arrays twice without receiving subject identifiers.
analysis: The function calls sample-level train_test_split with test fractions \(0.2\) and \(0.25\), producing \(60/20/20\) sample proportions. Subject labels do not enter either call. Therefore windows from the same subject are eligible for different subsets; sample partitioning alone cannot establish the stated subject-disjoint guarantee. TDBRAIN instead uses explicit identifier lists.
result: The release lacks the claimed safeguard. Actual FLAAP subject overlap and score inflation require the unavailable benchmark split manifest; neither is established by this source check.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Partition by subject identifiers and publish the disjoint subject lists, allowing approximate sample proportions when subject sizes differ.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Dimension assumption does not imply the strong-noise bound
problems.source_location: Condition 3.1(C1), PDF p.5; Appendix A.2.3, Eq.(6), p.23; Theorem 3.4 proof
claim: The dimension condition has terms \(n_{\rm wk}^2\log(Cn_{\rm wk}^2/\delta)\) and \(n_{\rm st}\log(Cn_{\rm st}/\delta)\), multiplied by \(C(\log T^*)^2\). The proof defines \[\beta_{\rm st}=4C_{\rm st}n_{\rm st}\sqrt{d^{-1}\log(C_{\rm st}n_{\rm st}/\delta)}\] and asserts \(\beta_{\rm st}\log T^*\leq1/100\).
analysis: Fix sufficiently large constants \(C\geq4,C_{\rm st}>0\), and take \(\delta=1/4,\sigma_p=1,p_e=1/2,p_h=1/(4C),p_b=1/2-1/(4C)\). Let orthogonal signal norms satisfy \(\|\mu\|^2=d^{1/3},\|\nu\|^2=d^{1/4}\), and let \(n_{\rm wk}=\lfloor d^{2/5}\rfloor,n_{\rm st}=\lfloor d^{3/5}\rfloor,m=\lceil C(\log d)^2\rceil,\sigma_0=d^{-10},\eta=d^{-2},\varepsilon=d^{-1}\). A fixed-degree polynomial horizon has \(\log T^*=\Theta(\log d)\). C1 requires only \(O(d^{4/5}(\log d)^3)+O(d^{3/5}(\log d)^3)=o(d)\); C2 holds by diverging samples and width. C3 permits initialization of order \(d^{-13/20}/\sqrt{\log d}\), above the chosen value; C4 holds because \(d^{-2}=o(d^{-3/2})\). For C5 the signal ratio grows as \(d^{1/12}\), and both samples exceed the \(d^{1/3}\) lower scale. In C6, \(Cp_h=1/4<p_b\) and the other required term is \(O(d^{-1/12}\sqrt{\log d})\). Condition 3.2 permits samples of order \(d^{2/3}/\log d\), above both selected sample sizes. Yet the asserted small quantity is \(\Theta(d^{1/10}(\log d)^{3/2})\), which diverges.
result: The deterministic implication used repeatedly in the strong-model proofs is false under the stated assumptions, including the data-scarce regime. This invalidates the current proof route; it is not a constructed training trajectory refuting the final test-error conclusions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Add explicitly the sufficient condition \[d\geq160000C_{\rm st}^2n_{\rm st}^2\log(C_{\rm st}n_{\rm st}/\delta)(\log T^*)^2.\] This restores exactly the small-noise step while shrinking the theorem domain; other proof obligations remain.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Logistic-ratio inequality is reversed
problems.source_location: Lemma B.1, property W3, PDF p.28
claim: For \(a>b\), the proof upper-bounds \((1+e^b)/(1+e^a)\) by \(e^{b-a}\).
analysis: The exact difference is \((1-e^{b-a})/(1+e^a)>0\). For \(a=\log(17/8),b=\log2\), the margin gap \(\log(17/16)\) lies between \(1/32\) and \(1/4\), but the ratio is \(24/25>16/17\). This refutes the scalar inequality, without claiming reachability of that pair by gradient descent.
result: The printed inequality is false. Its intended nonexpansion can nevertheless be recovered under the existing weak-regime margin lower bound, so this local defect does not independently refute the weak-training result.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(\log[g(a)/g(b)]=-\int_b^a e^u/(1+e^u)\,du\). For \(b\geq-1\), this gives \(g(a)/g(b)\leq e^{-(a-b)/(1+e)}\). The induction bounds give \(b\geq-8(1+2/C)/C^2-\kappa_{\rm wk}/64>-1\); with the stated noise-norm ratio the resulting exponent remains negative.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Pseudo-opposite response uses true-opposite coefficients
problems.source_location: Lemma C.2, PDF p.34; signal decomposition in Appendix A.2
claim: The lemma bounds \(F_{-\hat y_i}\) using underlined coefficients associated with the class opposite the true signal.
analysis: If a hard example has true label \(+1\) but pseudo-label \(-1\), then \(-\hat y_i=+1\). Its response to \(\nu_+\) contains the own-class coefficient \(\overline N_{+,r}\), whereas the displayed bound controls \(\underline N_{+,r}\). Bounds on the latter do not algebraically bound the former. Taking the underlined coefficients zero and the overlined response arbitrarily large demonstrates the missing premise, but is not a reachable-iterate counterexample.
result: The cited proof step needs additional time-indexed own-class signal controls. Surrounding simultaneous-induction properties may provide them; a full dynamical counterexample has not been established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Include the stated signal signs and own-class averages bounded by \(Q=\kappa_{\rm st}/64\). Under \(\alpha_{\rm st}\leq0.01\) and \(\beta_{\rm st}\log T^*\leq0.01\), the resulting response bound is \(0.69123<\kappa_{\rm st}/16\approx1.24245\). Each use must establish those premises at the required induction time.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Averaging a maximum is bounded in the wrong direction
problems.source_location: Lemma D.3 proof, PDF p.55
claim: The proof replaces the average of filterwise maxima by the maximum of filter averages as an upper bound.
analysis: For the two nonnegative arrays \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\), the average of pointwise maxima is \(1\), while the maximum average is \(1/2\). The valid general inequality points in the opposite direction. This is an algebraic counterexample rather than a claimed training iterate.
result: The manipulation is invalid, but a fixed signal patch has one type across all filters; the desired local conclusion can be proved without the maximum interchange.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Split by the fixed signal type and whether the pseudo-label agrees with the true label. Apply the relevant signed mean coefficient bound directly; the stated smallness and horizon conditions then recover a signal response at most \(\alpha_{\rm st}+1/2\).
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Universal strict-error formula omits zero margins
problems.source_location: Proposition 2.1, PDF p.3
claim: For every weak-model parameter \(w\), the paper asserts strict hard-example error probability \(\Pr(yf_{\rm wk}<0\mid\mathcal S_h)=1/2\).
analysis: In \(d=6\), use orthogonal signals \(\mu_+=2e_1,\mu_-=2e_2,\nu_+=e_3,\nu_-=e_4\), noise covariance \(\operatorname{diag}(0,0,0,0,1,1)\), positive mixture probabilities and \(w=2e_1-2e_2\). Every hard signal and every noise realization is orthogonal to \(w\), so the hard margin is identically zero and the strict-error probability is \(0\). Easy and both-signal margins are respectively \(8\) and \(4\); this is not the zero classifier.
result: The universal quantifier fails because of ties. Sign symmetry instead gives \(\Pr(M<0)=[1-\Pr(M=0)]/2\). Positive finite trained weak-model iterates can have nondegenerate noise projections, preserving the intended random-guess conclusion in that narrower setting.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State the identity including zero-margin mass, use randomized tie error, or add the nondegeneracy premise \(\sigma_p\|\Lambda w\|>0\).
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Value-based padding deletes a real zero neighbor
problems.source_location: Eq.(4), PDF p.4; methods/lava.py, LAVA.forward, lines 13–21; dataset_augmented.py, slack projection
claim: LAVA sums truncated adjacent-vertex objective gaps. The release treats an all-zero projected vertex as padding.
analysis: Consider minimization on \(0\leq x\leq1\), represented by \(x+s=1\), with true cost \(-x\). The true optimum is \((1,0)\), whose genuine neighbor \((0,1)\) projects to \(x=0\) after slack removal. Predicted cost \(\hat c=1\) selects \(x=0\) with true regret \(1\). The real neighbor gap is \(1\), but the value-based padding test deletes it, yielding zero loss and zero gradient. Separately, mapping gaps below \(-\varepsilon\) to zero differs from the printed clamp: for \(\varepsilon=1/10\), gaps \(-1/5,-1/20\) violate scalar convexity since the midpoint maps to \(0>-1/40\). Their ordinary derivatives nevertheless agree away from the threshold.
result: The zero-neighbor mask changes the defined surrogate and its gradients on an allowed projected LP. The threshold-to-zero scalar difference alone does not establish different updates away from the kink. Proposition 4.1 remains intact.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Carry an explicit neighbor-validity mask or count independent of coordinates, and clamp real gaps at \(-\varepsilon\) to match Eq.(4).
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Integer-solution cache and filtering corrupt relaxed neighborhoods
problems.source_location: Section 5.3, PDF p.8; data/dataset_augmented.py, lines 72–90
claim: The knapsack workflow trains against relaxed optima, but caches neighbors by the integer optimum and removes neighbors equal to that integer solution.
analysis: For \(3x+2y\leq4\), \(x,y\in\{0,1\}\), use costs \((4,3)\) then \((5,3)\). Both integer optima are \(I=(1,0)\); relaxed optima are respectively \(A=(2/3,1)\) and \(B=(1,1/2)\). Their neighbor sets are \(N(A)=\{B,(0,1)\}\) and \(N(B)=\{I,A\}\). Reusing the cache under key \(I\) supplies stale neighbors at \(B\). With predicted maximization cost \(q=(-1,-3)\), stale gaps are \(0,-1/2\), so the release returns no update, while the omitted actual neighbor \(I\) has gap \(3/2\). Even without a cache collision, filtering by the integer solution deletes \(I\). The selected integer decision is the origin, with true regret \(5\) under the second cost.
result: Both data-flow defects are concrete for the supported knapsack/relaxation interface. Their occurrence and effect in the original benchmark arrays are not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Key by the actual relaxed vertex and constraint identity, or disable caching. Remove a self-neighbor only against that same relaxed label; retain all genuine adjacent vertices.

problems.title: Training-time accumulator excludes most training work
problems.source_location: Section 5.1, PDF pp.7–8; utils/train_model.py, lines 43–44 and 66–103
claim: The paper describes training time including adjacent-vertex precomputation and actual training, excluding validation, and uses a \(600\)-second budget. The release times only the loss evaluation.
analysis: The prediction the regressor forward call precedes the timer; elapsed time is added before zero_grad, backward and optimizer.step. Hence an iteration records approximately \(t_{\rm loss}\), rather than \(t_{\rm pred}+t_{\rm loss}+t_{\rm back}+t_{\rm opt}\). These omitted operations are training, not validation. Precomputation is separately included.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Time the complete prediction, loss, backward and optimizer step with a monotonic clock; add precomputation and consistently exclude validation. Remeasure the affected runtime comparisons if this path generated them.

problems.title: Zero-margin optimality leaves solver ties unresolved
problems.source_location: Proposition 4.1 and sentence preceding Eq.(4), PDF p.4
claim: Making a labeled vertex predicted-cost optimal is described as giving zero regret, whereas the regret evaluates one selected optimizer.
analysis: For the unit square with true cost \((1,1)\), true optimum \((0,0)\), and nonzero predicted cost \((1,0)\), both \((0,0)\) and \((0,1)\) are predicted optima. The adjacent-vertex zero-margin loss is zero, but a solver may choose \((0,1)\), with true regret \(1\). Positive strict adjacent margins instead give a unique optimum, and the experiments use \(\varepsilon=0.1\).
result: This is a tie-handling qualification of a zero-margin interpretation, not a refutation of Proposition 4.1 or the positive-margin method. Tie-independent zero regret requires every predicted optimizer to be a true optimizer.

problems.title: Accuracy and F1 pairs exceed a necessary feasibility bound
problems.source_location: Table 2 and Section 5.2, PDF p.7
claim: The AIDE rows report accuracy/F1 percentages \((85.9,94.5)\) on FakeClue and \((65.6,80.2)\) on LOKI.

Allowing every displayed number a rounding error of \(0.05\) percentage points still gives maximum compatible F1 values \(92.4443\%\) and \(79.2636\%\), below \(94.45\%\) and \(80.15\%\). The same bound holds for macro/support-weighted F1 and identical-weight run averages by concavity.

problems.title: Class and overall accuracies imply incompatible prevalences
problems.source_location: Table 3, PDF p.8

Independent rounding intervals of \(0.05\) percentage points give disjoint prevalence ranges \([0.203704,0.207071]\) and \([0.70625,0.71875]\). Each row can be feasible individually, but both cannot use the same pooled set and interpretation.

problems.title: Substring parsing can reverse an explicit synthetic-image label
problems.source_location: scripts/eval.py, lines 152–167; scripts/eval_vllm.py, lines 153–168; Appendix H, PDF pp.27–34
claim: The release searches the first sentence for real before fake and randomly labels unrecognized responses. Prompts request a canonical label sentence.

Canonical “This is a fake image. The shadows are unrealistic.” avoids the collision because the first sentence lacks real. An unrecognized answer takes random.choice rather than an abstention path.

problems.title: AUC averaging and experiment identity remain ambiguous
problems.source_location: Tables 5–6, PDF p.9; Table 2, p.7

However, pooled AUC need not equal an arithmetic mean. Likewise matching accuracy and CSS across two tables do not prove identical checkpoints, runs or protocols.

problems.title: One auxiliary CDF cannot represent every randomized tradeoff
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.1, proceedings PDF p.6; Lemma A.3, full arXiv PDF pp.16–18
claim: The theorem asserts a single CDF \(F_{\rm conv}\) that gives two-way reward/payment dominance between every randomized original strategy and a deterministic auxiliary strategy, for any competing-bid distribution.
analysis: Take one round, value \(1\), and competing bid exactly \(a=1/2\), with ties won. Randomizing between bids \(a\) and zero with probability \(q\) yields reward/payment \((q,aq)\), and every original strategy obeys \(P\geq aR\). Reverse dominance implies any auxiliary bid with positive allocation \(s\) must have \(b\geq a\). Forward dominance of the mixture requires \(s\geq q\) and \(bs\leq aq\). Thus \(aq\geq bs\geq as\geq aq\), forcing \(b=a,s=q\). The same CDF would need \(F_{\rm conv}(a)=1/4\) and \(F_{\rm conv}(a)=1/2\), impossible. Atomic distributions and favorable tie-breaking are explicitly admitted.
result: The all-strategy equivalence theorem fails on its stated domain. This undermines the stated deterministic-reduction justification, while leaving open weaker optimization-specific alternatives.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep the convex set of payment/allocation pairs. On a finite bid menu, randomized bids give exactly its convex hull and each upper boundary edge can be implemented by mixing its two endpoints. A per-round Lagrangian can instead optimize directly under the original CDF.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Fixed-sequence regret and stage comparator claims fail
problems.source_location: Lemma B.2, full arXiv PDF pp.23–24; Lemma B.5, p.27; Proposition 3.2, proceedings p.7
claim: The appendix upgrades an i.i.d. expected-regret bound to every fixed value sequence, and substitutes a global offline comparator for separately ROI-feasible stage optima.
analysis: Let even \(T\), \(F^\dagger=F=\delta_{1/2}\), and \(\varepsilon=0\). Values are \(6/25\) for the first half and \(19/25\) for the second. Starting at \(\lambda=1\), winning a low round has Lagrangian value \(-1/50\), so the algorithm loses with zero update. Every high round has positive value \(19/25+13\lambda/50\), so all are won. Algorithm reward is \(19T/50\); the globally ROI-feasible all-win policy has reward/payment \(T/2\), giving regret \(3T/25\). Stage-feasible low-round reward is zero, so summing stage optima gives only \(19T/50\), below the global optimum. This is the reverse of the needed comparator replacement.
result: The fixed-sequence lemma is false and the stage pooling argument does not prove the global benchmark. This ordered event can be rare under i.i.d. values and therefore does not by itself refute the main expected-regret result.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Preserve expectation over i.i.d. values and compare all stages to one common stationary dual benchmark. The proposed direct-CDF argument recovers expected orders under its stated feedback assumptions, rather than a pathwise claim.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: One-step dual inequality fails for an admissible auction
problems.source_location: Appendix A.2, full arXiv PDF p.22, after Eq.(11)
claim: The proof asserts \(\alpha\lambda_tg_t\leq2(\lambda_t-\lambda_{t+1})+2\alpha^2\), with \(\lambda_{t+1}=\lambda_te^{-\alpha g_t}\).
analysis: Use \(T=100,\alpha=1/10,\lambda_1=1,F=\delta_1,v_1=51/100\). Bidding \(1\) is the strict best response since its Lagrangian value is \(1/50>0\); thus \(g_1=-49/100\) and \(\lambda_2=e^{49/1000}\). The left side is \(-0.049\), but the right side is at most \(-0.078\) by \(e^x\geq1+x\). Multiplying a negative difference by \(2\) cannot supply the claimed larger upper bound.
result: The printed intermediate inequality is false. Its intended dual-sum order has a local replacement, so this defect alone does not refute the final expected-regret rate.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Under \(0<\alpha\leq1,|g|\leq1,\lambda g\geq-1\), use \(\alpha\lambda g\leq(1+\alpha)(\lambda-\lambda e^{-\alpha g})+3\alpha^2\). Splitting by the sign of \(g\) proves the bound; telescoping gives \(\sum_t\lambda_tg_t\leq5\sqrt T\).
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Temporal transition is undefined and permits past edges
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Eqs.(8)–(12), PDF p.5
claim: The sampler uses softmax logits \(w(u,v)/[t(u,v)-t_{\rm last}]\) over the full neighborhood and claims the resulting paths maintain temporal consistency.
analysis: Use one item connected to users at timestamps \(2,1,3\), each with weight \(1\). Follow a valid center prefix whose last timestamp is \(2\). Candidate gaps are \((0,-1,1)\), giving logits \((1/0,-1,1)\), so the printed real-valued transition is undefined. The reverse edge alone produces the zero gap on an undirected graph. Even excluding it leaves positive probability \(1/(1+e^2)\) of selecting timestamp \(1\), violating nondecreasing time.
result: The printed path sampler is neither well-defined on all allowed edges nor sufficient for its temporal-order guarantee. An unstated implementation filter could change the operational behavior, but is not part of the stated formula.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Mask to edges with \(t(u,v)\geq t_{\rm last}\), use a positive offset \(\delta\) in the time-gap denominator, and specify termination or restart when no admissible edge exists. Every retained transition then preserves nondecreasing timestamps.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Contrastive derivatives use the wrong normalizers
problems.source_location: Section 3.5, Eqs.(15)–(18), PDF pp.6–7; objectives (7) and (14)
claim: The displayed gradients give attraction and repulsion the same partition function, summing both positive and denominator exponentials.
analysis: For \(\ell(x)=-\log[A(x)/B(x)]\), direct differentiation gives \(-A^{\prime}(x)/A(x)+B^{\prime}(x)/B(x)\), not a common \(A+B\) denominator. With a self-positive anchor, positive candidate \(1\), negative candidate \(0\) and temperature \(1\), take \(A=e^{x^2}+e^x,B=A+1\). At \(x=0\), the true derivative is \(-1/2+1/3=-1/6\); the printed shared normalizer gives zero. A negative-only denominator does not rescue the formula.
result: The displayed derivative identities and their quantitative weighting interpretation fail. The scalar objectives remain well-defined, and unavailable training code might differentiate those objectives correctly.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Differentiate each log-sum with its own partition function, including candidate/self dependencies and every occurrence in the full loss.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Rotation interpretation depends on normalization
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, Eq.(13), PDF p.6; Appendix A.5, p.23
claim: The paper calls normalized complex-coordinate multiplication a rotation without specifying global or coordinatewise normalization.
analysis: Writing the update as \(T_e(w)=w\odot\overline e\), one has \(\|T_e(w)\|^2=\sum_k|w_k|^2|e_k|^2\). This preserves every distance exactly when every \(|e_k|=1\). Global normalization fixes their squared sum at \(1\), incompatible with that condition in multiple complex coordinates. For real/imaginary halves \(w=(1,0,0,0),e=(1/2,1/2,1/2,1/2)\), the norm contracts from \(1\) to \(1/\sqrt2\).
result: Coordinatewise unit phases validate the multiplicative rotation interpretation. The unspecified normalization leaves a conditional scope qualification; no author-code error or recommendation-performance failure is established.

problems.title: Affine composition does not preserve gradient paths
problems.source_location: Theorem 4.1(2), PDF p.4; Proposition 4.2 and discussion, p.5; Appendix A.2, Eqs.(10)–(12), p.24
claim: The paper claims equivalence in parameter space and gradient-update paths between factorized prompt/classifier optimization and direct affine optimization.
analysis: Use scalar \(z=w(ah+b)\), squared loss \(z^2/2\), and \(h=1,a=w=1,b=0\). All three factor gradients equal \(1\), so a step \(\eta=1/10\) gives \(a_+=w_+=0.9,b_+=-0.1\) and prediction \(0.72\). The direct affine model \(vh+c\), initialized at the identical function \((v,c)=(1,0)\), instead gives \((0.9,-0.1)\) and prediction \(0.8\). Initial effective directions \((-2,-1)\) and \((-1,-1)\) are not proportional. Generally, for \(B=AS\) and \(G=\nabla_B L\), the exact factor update is \[B_+=B-\eta(GS^\top S+AA^\top G)+\eta^2GS^\top A^\top G.\]
result: The central gradient-path equivalence is false, even at the favorable scalar orthogonality initialization in the appendix. Forward functional composition remains correct.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the forward affine identity and state the induced factor-optimization dynamics, rather than Euclidean gradient equivalence.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Reverse affine correspondence requires sufficient rank
problems.source_location: Definition 4.1, PDF p.4; Appendix A.2, Eq.(9), p.24
claim: The proof maps arbitrary affine classifier parameters back to factorized parameters without a stated width restriction, and describes a unique mapping.
analysis: Every augmented coefficient matrix \(B=AS\) has rank at most the prompt width \(d_{\rm p}\). For \(d=k=2,d_{\rm p}=1\), the identity classifier has augmented matrix \([I_2\ 0]\) of rank \(2\), impossible for those factors. Even at sufficient width, \(AS=(AQ^{-1})(QS)\) for every invertible \(Q\), so the factorization is generally nonunique.
result: The unrestricted reverse parameter-space equivalence fails. The one-way functional proposition is valid, and a chosen inverse after fixing additional factors is a narrower notion than a unique reparameterization.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The representable affine maps are exactly those with augmented rank at most \(d_{\rm p}\); all maps are covered when \(d_{\rm p}\geq\min(k,d+1)\). State the nonuniqueness explicitly.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Detached embeddings prevent supervised prompt gradients
problems.source_location: Section 5, PDF pp.5–6; main.py, lines 130–168; model/DGI.py, lines 121–125; model/GRACE.py, lines 42–45
claim: The method jointly trains prompt and classifier through a frozen encoder. DGI and GRACE return detached embeddings on that training path.
analysis: The supervised prompt derivative should contain \((D_\Psi H)^\top D_H L\). Detachment removes that route while classifier gradients still exist. Including prompt parameters in Adam cannot supply the missing task derivative. Freezing encoder parameter weights does not require severing derivatives with respect to its input graph. Recursive graph fusion can still change forward values without supervised prompt updates.
result: These two released branches do not implement the described label-driven adaptation. GraphMAE returns nondetached embeddings, so the defect is not universal across backbones. Published score effects and exact historical code remain unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Return differentiable embeddings during adaptation while freezing encoder weights through parameter settings or optimizer exclusion.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Early stopping does not restore the monitored graph and model
problems.source_location: Appendix B.1, PDF p.24; main.py, lines 172–200
claim: The driver assigns state dictionaries as best states and restores them while retaining the current recursively fused graph.
analysis: A state dictionary holds tensors sharing live parameter storage: a value saved at \(1\) and later updated to \(2\) remains \(2\) in the un-cloned snapshot. Separately, with \(A_0=0,\tau=1/2,P_1=1,P_2=2\), fused graph states are \(A_1=1/2,A_2=5/4\). Restoring first-epoch parameters while keeping \(A_2\) cannot recreate the monitored first-epoch input.

paragraphs: Clone prompt/classifier states and fused edge indices/weights at the monitored forward state, and restore that complete tuple for evaluation.

problems.title: The KL threshold does not imply single-draw accuracy
problems.source_location: Proposition 2, PDF p.7; proof p.26; total-variation convention p.28
claim: The proposition asserts probability at least \(3/4\) of relative partition-estimator error at most \(\varepsilon\) when either path KL is at most \(\varepsilon^2/2\).
analysis: Use one masked coordinate with three clean states and common unmasking rate \(1/(1-t)\). Set proposal \(q=(1/4,1/4,1/2)\), target \(p=(2/5,1/10,1/2)\), and \(U_i=-\log p_i\), so \(Z=1\). The jump-time laws agree and path likelihood ratios are \(p_i/q_i=(8/5,2/5,1)\). For \(\varepsilon=1/2\), success occurs only in the third state, with probability \(1/2\). Yet \(D_{\rm KL}(p\Vert q)\approx0.0963724\) and \(D_{\rm KL}(q\Vert p)\approx0.111572\), both below \(1/8\). The full-support importance estimator is still unbiased.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Under target absolute continuity, Markov and Pinsker give failure probability at most \[\sqrt{2\min(D_{\rm KL}(P\Vert Q),D_{\rm KL}(Q\Vert P))}/\varepsilon\]. The sufficient threshold \(\varepsilon^2/32\) recovers success probability \(3/4\).

problems.title: Potts baseline collapses match counts into Boolean presence
problems.source_location: Eq.(18), PDF p.9; utils_potts.py, Metropolis energy calculation, lines 240–249, and Glauber update
claim: The Potts energy counts every matching neighboring spin. The release adds Boolean NumPy arrays without converting them to integer counts.
analysis: On a periodic \(3\times3\) lattice with three states, \(J=1,h=0,\beta=1.2\), change one spin in the all-zero configuration to state \(1\). Four matching edges disappear, so the correct Metropolis acceptance is \(e^{-4\beta J}\approx0.00822975\). Boolean addition retains one true entry instead of count four, giving \(e^{-\beta J}\approx0.301194\). All reverse one-site moves are accepted, so target-weighted incoming and outgoing fluxes at the all-zero state are respectively \(\pi(s_0)e^{-4\beta J}\) and \(\pi(s_0)e^{-\beta J}\); the target is not stationary for this kernel.
result: The released local sampler is wrong for the stated Potts target. Its exact contribution to published baseline tables requires code-to-run provenance; longer burn-in alone cannot fix the target mismatch.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Cast each comparison to integers before adding, or stack and sum with an integer reduction. Use the resulting integer neighbor count in the Metropolis difference and Glauber conditional.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: UDNS discretization and zero-time boundary lack valid domain conditions
problems.source_location: Appendix F.1, PDF pp.38–40; Algorithm 4 and Appendix F.3, pp.41–42
claim: The UDNS Euler kernel uses nonnegative learned scores and an early start near zero with \(\gamma(t)=1/t\), without an exit-rate step bound.
analysis: For the stated \(D=16,N=2,K=50\), choose \(\epsilon=1/1000\) and the reference score identically one. The first step has \(\Delta t=999/50000\); each flip probability is \(9.99\), and the stay probability is \(1-16(9.99)=-158.84\). Even the reference kernel needs \(\epsilon\geq4/29\). Separately, integrating \(1/t\) from zero gives immediate endpoint independence: \(\Pr(X_t\ne X_0)=1-N^{-D}\) at every positive time, incompatible with right continuity at zero. At finite \(\epsilon\), exact independence is lost; for a two-state target \((3/4,1/4)\), the uniformly initialized exact transformed process instead ends with first-state probability \(3/4-3\epsilon^2/[4(4-\epsilon^2)]\).
result: The literal extension is not a stochastic Euler algorithm throughout its declared score/start domain, and its singular initial path law needs separate formulation. This does not invalidate the distinct one-jump masked process.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Enforce \(\Delta t\max_x[-Q_t(x,x)]\leq1\), with appropriate support restrictions for weights. Formulate the process from a positive initial time or an entrance law and rederive its boundary/weight statements; clipping probabilities alone does not restore them.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: A nonmemoryless reference can have a fixed-initial control optimum
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, PDF p.4; Lemma 8 and Remark 1, p.24
claim: The paper infers nonexistence of an SOC solution when the globally tilted path law fails the prescribed initial boundary.
analysis: For bounded finite-state rates and finite reward, define \(h_t(x)=E_0[e^{r(X_T)}\mid X_t=x]\). The conditional tilt \(dP^\dagger/dP^0=e^{r(X_T)}/h_0(X_0)\) preserves the prescribed initial law \(\mu\). For every admissible \(P\) with that law, \[J(P)=D_{\rm KL}(P\Vert P^\dagger)-E_\mu\log h_0.\] Thus it is the unique minimizing path law, regardless of endpoint independence. For the two-state rate-one switching chain, \(\mu=(1/2,1/2),T=1,e^r=(1,2)\), endpoints remain dependent and \(h_0=((3-e^{-2})/2,(3+e^{-2})/2)\) is nonconstant, yet this admissible optimum exists.
result: Incompatibility of a global tilt does not imply nonexistence of the constrained optimum. The deterministic masked initial state makes global and conditional normalization agree there, preserving that special construction.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the conditional tilt and Doob rates \(Q^\dagger_t(x,y)=Q^0_t(x,y)h_t(y)/h_t(x)\), or explicitly assume \(h_0\) is constant on the initial support before using global-tilt marginals.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Released loss and reward normalizations differ from the estimators
problems.source_location: Eq.(16), PDF p.7; utils_train.py, loss_wdce, lines 72–94; rnd reward accumulation
claim: The release repeats softmax-normalized importance weights and then averages over the full batch; reward callbacks omit the displayed \(D\log N\) offset.
analysis: With normalized weights \(\omega_i\) and \(R\) remasking replicates, the stated self-normalized loss is \(\sum_i\omega_i R^{-1}\sum_r\ell_{ir}\). A mean over \(BR\) weighted entries instead returns this divided by \(B\). For the reward, subtracting \(\log N\) at every unmasking step while supplying only \(-U\) gives \(W_{\rm code}=W_{\rm paper}-D\log N\), so the expectation estimates \(Z/N^D\). At \(D=4,N=2,U=0\) with a uniform model, it returns weight \(1\) although the physical partition sum is \(16\).
result: These are normalization discrepancies. A fixed positive loss scale preserves ideal minimizers, and a common log-weight offset preserves normalized weights and ESS; neither proves wrong normalized samples or a published ranking reversal.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Remove the extra batch averaging factor and state whether the estimated normalizer is a counting-measure partition sum or a uniform-reference expectation. Add \(D\log N\) when reporting physical \(\log Z\).

problems.title: Real phase-retrieval derivative is missing a factor of two

problems.title: Isotropic wrapper is undefined at zero gradients
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1, PDF p.5; Eq.(14), p.7; matrix_factorization/preconditioners.py, lines 18–20; algorithms.py, line 18
claim: The numerical radial wrapper evaluates the scalar preconditioner times \(g/\|g\|\), without a zero branch.

The update calls the wrapper before any zero-gradient termination.

repair.heading: Proposed correction

problems.title: Curvature formula fails in nonorthogonal coordinates
problems.source_location: Section S8.4, arXiv v2 PDF p.23; working-memory notebook wm.ipynb, cell 65
claim: The paper and supplied curvature routine compute Gaussian curvature from the metric entries \(E,F,G\), without requiring orthogonal coordinates.
analysis: Use the regular plane chart \(r(u,v)=(u,e^uv,0)\). Its metric is \(E=1+e^{2u}v^2,F=e^{2u}v,G=e^{2u}\), with positive determinant \(e^{2u}\). The printed expression yields \(K=-1/2\), while the release’s different placement of factors yields continuum value \(K=1\). The surface is exactly a plane, so its independent geometric curvature is \(0\): every normal second-derivative component vanishes. A denominator regularizer changes the wrong nonzero value slightly and cannot restore zero.
result: The curvature computation is invalid on an admissible regular chart, so curvature-based patch selection and interpretations require reanalysis. This does not show the actual trained surface is flat or invalidate independent first-derivative metric analyses.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For \(J=[r_u\ r_v]\), use \(g=J^\top J\), normal projection \(P_\perp=I-Jg^{-1}J^\top\), and \[K=\frac{\langle P_\perp r_{uu},P_\perp r_{vv}\rangle-\|P_\perp r_{uv}\|^2}{\det g}.\] This Gauss formula applies in arbitrary ambient dimension at rank-two points.

problems.title: Energy is treated as geometric length
problems.source_location: Definition S7.2, arXiv v2 PDF p.15; Sections S8.3–S8.4, pp.21–23; wm.ipynb, cell 62
claim: The paper defines curve length by \(\int g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)dt\), and some plotting blocks integrate diagonal metric entries directly.
analysis: On the Euclidean line, \(\gamma_1(t)=t\) and \(\gamma_2(t)=(t+t^2)/2\), \(0\leq t\leq1\), trace the same segment with positive velocities. The printed functional gives \(1\) and \(13/12\), while both geometric lengths are \(1\). With variable duration, \(\gamma_T=t/T\) has energy \(1/T\), so the endpoint infimum degenerates to zero. Even normalized grid positions differ: for embedding \(r(\theta)=\theta+\theta^2\), the half-interval cumulative energy fraction is \(7/26\), versus arclength fraction \(3/8\).
result: The central distance definition and affected grid interpretations use parameter-dependent energy rather than invariant length. Some other source cells use square roots correctly; the finding does not apply to every figure.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(\int\sqrt{g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)}dt\) for length and distinguish fixed-curve arclength from a minimizing geodesic distance. Fixed-duration minimum energy gives squared distance divided by duration, under suitable geodesic existence.

problems.title: Orthogonal-vector subtraction has a different pullback
problems.source_location: Section S8.5, arXiv v2 PDF p.25
claim: The map \(\phi(u_1,u_2)=u_2v_2-u_1v_1\), with orthogonal input vectors, is assigned pullback \(\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]\).

Generally it is \(\operatorname{diag}(\|v_1\|^2,\|v_2\|^2)\). The asserted matrix instead corresponds to \((u_2-u_1)v\) along one unit output direction.

problems.title: Ambient full rank does not ensure tangent immersion
problems.source_location: Proposition S7.2, arXiv v2 PDF p.14
claim: A full matrix-rank ambient Jacobian and an embedded input manifold are asserted to give an immersed manifold after composition.
analysis: Take \(\psi(t)=(0,t)\) and \(\phi(x_1,x_2)=x_1\). The input map is an embedding and the ambient Jacobian \([1\ 0]\) has maximal matrix rank, but \(\phi\circ\psi=0\), with zero tangent derivative. The tangent lies entirely in the ambient kernel.

problems.title: Released scan uses an approximate input coefficient
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, Eqs.(9)–(10), PDF p.7; modem_arch.py, selective scan call; Mamba v2.0.4, selective_scan_ref
claim: The paper specifies exact zero-order hold \(\bar A=e^{\Delta A}\), \(\bar B=(e^{\Delta A}-I)A^{-1}B\). The current author release calls its pinned Mamba selective scan, whose input coefficient is \(\Delta B\).

The exact continuous equation \(\dot h=-h+1\) gives \(h(1)=1-e^{-1}\approx0.632121\), whereas the backend recurrence gives \(h_1=1\). Its transition coefficient is exponential, but its input increment uses no exponential correction.
