problems.title: Morton ordering has block locality rather than a uniform neighbor guarantee
problems.source_location: Appendix A.6, PDF p.19
claim: The locality motivation says nearby image pixels remain nearby in the scan.
analysis: Adjacent pixels \((2^m-1,0)\) and \((2^m,0)\) have interleaved indices \((4^m-1)/3\) and \(4^m\), so their scan gap is \((2\cdot4^m+1)/3\) despite unit spatial distance. Conversely an aligned dyadic square fixes the high interleaved bits and occupies a contiguous interval.
result: The motivation is valid as hierarchical block locality and does not require a universal adjacent-pixel bound. No permutation or inverse-scan defect is established; the empirical scan comparison is not refuted.

problems.title: Orthogonal output actions do not preserve a fixed margin
problems.source_location: Lemmas 2–3 and Theorem 1, PDF p.5; Appendix A.1, p.19
claim: The paper infers fixed-class margin-gradient norm invariance from norm-preserving input and output representations, even using diagonal output signs in its proof.
analysis: Let \(f(t)=(t,t^2-1)\), input action \(t\mapsto-t\), and output action \(\rho=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\). Exact equivariance and orthogonality hold. Class one is uniquely predicted at both \(t=1/4\) and \(-1/4\), but margin \(m=1+t-t^2\) has derivative norms \(1/2\) and \(3/2\). Independent logit sign changes alter cancellation. General output mixing also invalidates the diagonal-only margin identity: with \(f(x)=x\) and a coordinate swap, the transformed margin at \((2,1)\) is \(-1\), whereas the diagonal expression is zero.
result: The central fixed-margin theorem is false under its explicit hypotheses. Full-Jacobian Euclidean norm invariance under orthogonal multiplication remains correct, but does not supply fixed-class margin invariance.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Require the margin covector \(a=e_c-e_j\) to obey \(a^\top\rho=a^\top\), and the inverse input action to preserve the chosen dual norm. Then \(\nabla m(A_gx)=A_g^{-\top}\nabla m(x)\). Relabel transformed classes consistently when using permutations.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Local certificate needs a radius cap and a neighborhood supremum
problems.source_location: Definitions 4–5, PDF p.4; Appendix A.1 final equality, p.19
claim: The certificate uses margin divided by a gradient supremum on a local radius-\(r\) ball, without capping the result at \(r\), and replaces an orbit-neighborhood supremum by a center value.
analysis: For \(m(t)=1-t^2,x=0,r=1/10\), the exact local constant is \(1/5\), giving the uncapped ratio \(5\). But \(t=11/10\) has negative margin despite distance below \(5\). Separately, invariant logits \((1+\|x\|^2,0)\) at radius \(1\) have gradient norm \(2\) on their orbit, while the radius-\(1/4\) orbit neighborhood has supremum \(5/2\). Orbit invariance cannot remove the transverse neighborhood.
result: The stated local certificate can exceed the domain where its bound is valid, and the proof’s final supremum equality is false even with invariant logits.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use strict perturbation radius \[\min\{r,\min_j m_j(x)/L_j(r)\}\]. Under the appropriate scalar-margin/input-isometry hypotheses, local-ball suprema are equal along an orbit, but are not equal to one gradient value.

problems.title: Equivariance does not impose directional gradient dominance
problems.source_location: Lemma 5 and Theorem 2, PDF p.6; Appendix A.2, p.20
claim: Theorem 2 asserts that off-orbit perturbations change gradients much more than equal tangent perturbations under compact-group equivariance.
analysis: For rotation-invariant \(F(x)=s-s^2/6,s=\|x\|^2\), use \(x=(1,0)\), tangent perturbation \((0,t)\) and radial perturbation \((t,0)\). The radial gradient change is \((-2t^2-2t^3/3,0)\), while the tangent change is \((-2t^2/3,4t/3-2t^3/3)\). Their norm ratio tends to zero, reversing the asserted ordering. A tangent straight-line displacement need not remain on the orbit, and constant gradient norm does not make gradient vectors equal. For Lemma 5 separately, averaging untransported gradients of \(\|x\|^2\) over \(\{I,-I\}\) gives zero: the difference from the gradient at \((1,0)\) is \(2\), versus only \(2t\) for a small radial perturbation.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain only \(\nabla F(x)^\top v=0\) for orbit-tangent \(v\), and pull gradients back by \(A_g^\top\) when differentiating group-averaged values. A directional comparison needs additional Hessian/curvature bounds not provided here.

problems.title: Attack clipping and evaluation mode alter the intended comparison
problems.source_location: Section 6.2, PDF pp.8–9; CIFAR-100 baseline attack functions; fullyeqv/test.py, evaluate_attack
claim: The baseline normalizes pixels to \([-1,1]\) but clips attacks to \([0,1]\); another comparator uses \([-1,1]\). The fully equivariant evaluator switches to training mode while attacking.
analysis: A legal raw pixel \(0.25\) normalizes to \(-0.5\). A zero-budget baseline attack then clamps it to \(0\), moving it by \(0.5\) in normalized units. The fully equivariant preprocessing can map legal pixels to \(-2\), but its clip moves them to \(-1\) even at zero budget. model.train activates training-mode layers and can update batch-normalization buffers; enabling gradients does not require that mode.

problems.title: Finite scales and a generic head do not establish global equivariance
problems.source_location: Section 4.5, PDF p.7; Appendix C.1.2, pp.21–22; fullyeqv/model.py, lines 35–36 and 51–53
claim: The theory is applied to a finite positive scaling collection and a model with regular-representation features followed by spatial pooling and an unconstrained linear classifier.
analysis: A finite multiplicative subgroup of positive reals must be \(\{1\}\), since finite order implies \(s^n=1\) and hence \(s=1\). The set \(\{0.5,1,2\}\) is not closed because it lacks \(4\). Bilinear down/up-sampling is also noninvertible. Separately, invariant class logits after regular-channel permutation \(P_g\) require \(WP_g=W\). Spatial pooling followed by an ordinary linear head imposes no such condition: \(v=e_1,w^\top=e_1^\top\) gives output \(1\), but a channel shift to \(e_2\) gives zero.
result: The cited implementations do not establish the whole-logit group premises. Symmetry-inspired multiscale and hybrid architectures may still be empirically useful; approximate symmetry is a separate claim.

paragraphs: Describe finite multiscale aggregation as such, or specify an actual group action. Use group pooling or a constrained invariant/intertwining head before invoking the global theorem.

problems.title: Printed AR conditions do not ensure causal stationarity
problems.source_location: Section 3.1.2, Eq.(1), Sampling Strategy, PDF p.4
claim: The paper says coefficients in \((-1,1)\), \(\sum_i\phi_i<1\) and \(|\phi_p|<1\) enforce stationarity of its ARMA generator.
analysis: Take \(\phi_1=-9/10,\phi_2=9/10,\theta_1=1/5\). Both printed tests hold, but the companion polynomial factors as \((\lambda-3/5)(\lambda+3/2)\), with unstable eigenvalue \(-3/2\). For the stated MA sign, the causal innovation response is \(\psi_k=(4/21)(3/5)^k+(17/21)(-3/2)^k\), whose squared sum diverges. The MA factor does not cancel the unstable root.
result: The manuscript’s sufficient conditions are false for a causal finite-variance recursion. Current S2Generator’s default stationary mode constructs stable roots instead, so this does not show that its current generated inputs are unstable or identify the published corpus’s generator revision.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Require all uncancelled AR lag roots outside the closed unit disk, or conservatively require \(\sum_i|\phi_i|<1\). Exact stationarity also needs the appropriate initial law.

problems.title: Mean ADF p-value does not identify nonstationary prevalence
problems.source_location: Appendix B.3, Table 10, current arXiv v3 physical PDF p.44, printed p.26
claim: The paper interprets an average ADF p-value above \(0.05\), including \(0.0538\), as suggesting most samples are nonstationary.
analysis: A set of \(1000\) p-values with \(940\) equal to \(0.001\) and \(60\) equal to \(0.881\) has mean exactly \(0.0538\), although \(94\%\) are below the rejection threshold. Moreover, failure to reject a unit-root null is not proof of nonstationarity. The table may correctly report its averages; those averages do not determine either the rejection fraction or the underlying prevalence.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Report individual test specifications and rejection indicators, then summarize the nonrejection fraction with sampling uncertainty, without interpreting nonrejection as proof of the null.

problems.title: Spectral concentration is not a certificate of nonchaotic dynamics
problems.source_location: Appendix B.3 and B.5, forecastability interpretation
claim: Forecastability above \(0.3\) is used to conclude that generated outputs are not chaotic and are predictable.
analysis: Consider \(F(x,\theta)=(2x\bmod1,\theta+\pi/4\bmod2\pi)\) and observation \(y_t=\cos\theta_t+\varepsilon(x_t-1/2)\). The expanding coordinate retains Lyapunov exponent \(\log2>0\). For a length-\(256\) sample, the cosine occupies one Fourier bin; as positive \(\varepsilon\) tends to zero, normalized spectral-entropy forecastability tends to \(1\). A dominant periodic observed component therefore does not remove chaos in the generating system.
result: The claimed universal diagnostic implication fails. This example does not establish that the actual synthetic corpus is chaotic, nor deny usefulness of the spectral feature as a descriptive statistic.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Limit the conclusion to spectral concentration under the declared estimator. Claims about chaos or forecast accuracy need separately justified dynamics or out-of-sample forecasting tests.

problems.title: Classification and M4 checkpoint selection uses test targets
problems.source_location: Table 15; SymTime exp/exp_classification.py, train; exp/exp_short_term_forecasting.py; data_provider/data_loader.py, Dataset_M4

problems.title: Masked-time loss includes already invalid padding
problems.source_location: Eq.(2), PDF p.5; models/pretrain_model.py, lines 158–180 and 250–270
claim: The stated loss reconstructs randomly masked real patches, but the release averages every position false in the postmask attention mask.

problems.title: Released upper bound can certify a genuine one-edit flip
problems.source_location: Lemma 6, Appendix A, PDF p.17; var_del_certs.py and var_del_len_certs.py, compute_upperbound
claim: The printed upper relaxation rounds its partial partition upward and includes target outside-event mass. The current repository rounds downward and omits that mass; the conference supplement also rounds downward and uses the wrong residual rate.

The current author release and conference supplement route the supplied edit/lecuyer certification configuration through these bound comparisons; the guarantee is preservation of the smoothed class throughout the returned edit ball.
analysis: For the official supplement, let \(x=\texttt{cdefghija}\), neighbor \(\bar x=\texttt{cdefghijb}\), and deletion rate \(p=q=0.9\). Define class A if a occurs, or the output is one of \(\emptyset,\texttt{c},\texttt{d},\texttt{cd},\texttt{ce},\texttt{cf},\texttt{cg}\). Conditional common-token mass is \(s_0=0.9^8+2(0.1)0.9^7+4(0.1)^2 0.9^6=0.54738423\). Thus A probability changes from \(0.592645807\) to \(0.492645807\), flipping the majority after one substitution. Valid conservative inputs \((0.59,0.41)\) nevertheless give released bounds \(L=0.47829690>U=0.47821403\), falsely passing. The error persists at equal rates, independently of the supplement’s additional wrong-rate term. For identical input ab at rate \(0.8\), event “output a” has probability \(0.16\), while the current upper routine returns approximately \(0.04\).
result: The released certifier is not generally sound, including a conference-supplement path. This does not refute the printed final bounds or establish which original benchmark certificates change; those require their original counts and run provenance.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use an upper ceiling and the target residual mass \(1-q^{n-N}\), or the normalized fractional common-subsequence envelope. Re-certify affected outputs after integration.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Edit search excludes pure-deletion boundaries
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, PDF p.6; var_del_certs.py, search_worst_case_bound, lines 211–218
claim: The implementation enumerates substitutions and insertions, computes deletions as the remaining radius, and skips deletion count at least the radius.
analysis: Pure deletion \((n_{\rm sub},n_{\rm ins},n_{\rm del})=(0,0,r)\) is always skipped. For deletion-only attacks it is the only candidate, leaving the initialized margin at infinity. Take input ab, deletion rate \(0.1\), and class A iff b occurs. Its smoothed A probability is \(0.9\), but deleting b gives nonempty neighbor a with A probability zero. Conservative inputs \((0.89,0.11)\) are valid; the search can return radius \(2\) without evaluating the one-deletion flip.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Admit the pure-deletion endpoint, enforce feasible operation counts, distinguish an empty search from a verified margin, and explicitly handle radius zero.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Common-subsequence normalization is lost in the proof
problems.source_location: Appendix A, Eqs.(9) and (15), PDF pp.15 and 17; Theorem 4 proof p.19
claim: The proof treats normalized common-subsequence mass as though it were unconditional full-input probability, omitting the outside-deletion factor.
analysis: Write \(a=p^{m-N},b=q^{n-N}\). Actual class masses satisfy \(\mu=aT_p+r_x\), with \(0\leq r_x\leq1-a\), and target mass \(bT_q+r_{\bar x}\). Thus normalized common mass lies between \(\ell=\max(0,(\mu-1+a)/a)\) and \(u=\min(1,\mu/a)\). For input ab, neighbor ac and rate \(0.8\), event “no b” has source probability \(0.8\) but normalized common mass \(1\), refuting the printed superset claim. Nevertheless, fractional likelihood-ratio envelopes give valid bounds \(bG_-(\ell)\) and \(1-b+bG_+(u)\). Convexity of \(G_-\), concavity of \(G_+\), and the paper’s extra floor/ceiling slack show that its final printed bounds are conservative relative to these valid bounds.
result: The intermediate derivation needs repair, but this does not establish false final Lemmas 3 or 6. The general normalized probability argument preserves their final bounds on nondegenerate rates.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep the outside-event factors, optimize normalized common masks with fractional final groups, and finish certification by comparing target-class lower and competitor upper bounds at the target input.

problems.title: Stable sets and low query dispersion do not imply zero information
problems.source_location: Remark 1, current arXiv v2 PDF p.6; Appendix G.10, p.38
claim: The paper calls IP and set-size-stability stopping criteria equivalent and uses low dispersion of candidate postquery entropies as a practical stopping diagnostic.
analysis: Let \(Y=X\) be a bit with \(P(Y=0)=0.9\), and let an uninformative predictor always return \((0.95,0.05)\), producing singleton set \(\{0\}\). At \(\alpha=0.1,N=100\), coverage \(0.9\) lies within the stated two-sided range. A query revealing Y leaves that predictor’s set size unchanged but gains \(h_b(0.1)\approx0.468996\) bits. Separately, for a fair bit, candidate queries Y and its complement both have zero postquery entropy and zero dispersion, while each gains one bit.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe the stopping tests as heuristics. An exact no-information condition compares current entropy with the answer-weighted expected postquery entropy; a finite-sample stopping guarantee needs additional estimation control.

problems.title: Released query score differs from log mean set size

problems.title: Prior answer weights do not estimate the history-conditional objective
problems.source_location: Eq.(2), PDF p.3; C-IP rule p.6; src/20q/20q_entropy_closed_binary.py, sample_data and estimate_entropy
claim: The desired next-answer expectation is conditional on the observed history, but the release samples unconditional labels and then appends their answers to that history.
analysis: Let Y be uniform on \(20\) labels and history restrict it to \(H=\{0,1,2,3,4,5\}\). Query A is true for label zero or labels at least six; query B is true for \[\{0,1,2,6,7,8,9,10,11,12\}\]. Both answers remain possible after history. Exact posterior entropies give conditional scores \(H_A=(5/6)\log_2 5\approx1.93494\), \(H_B=\log_2 3\approx1.58496\), so B is preferred. Prior weights instead give \(\widetilde H_A=(5/20)\log_2 5\approx0.580482\) and the same B score, selecting A. Correct inner posteriors cannot fix incorrect outer answer probabilities.
result: The released IP expectation can rank the less informative query first even with an oracle posterior. The first query and history-independent answers are valid special cases; the exact numeric example is not claimed to characterize the full C-IP inclusion/exclusion score.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Sample from the history-conditional law or apply justified likelihood importance weights. General free-text histories require an explicitly validated conditional sampler.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Calibration quantile lacks the general finite-sample adjustment
problems.source_location: Eq.(4), Section 3.1; src/20q/20q_conformal_thresholds_closed_binary.py, lines 162–175
claim: The release uses the higher empirical quantile at \(1-\alpha\), whose calibration rank differs from the split-conformal finite-sample rank.
analysis: For \(N=21,\alpha=0.1\), the code rank is \(\lceil20(0.9)\rceil+1=19\), while the required rank is \(\lceil22(0.9)\rceil=20\). Permute \(22\) distinct valid scores \(s_j=-j/23\), represented by two-label probabilities \((-s_j,1+s_j)\) with true label zero. Exchangeability makes the held-out rank uniform, so the release covers \(19/22<0.9\), while the corrected rank covers \(20/22\). For \(N=50,\alpha=0.01\), the required unavailable rank needs an infinite threshold rather than the largest observed score. The reported \(N=100,200\) settings on the inspected level grid happen to satisfy the rank inequality.
result: The quantile is not generally valid under the advertised exchangeable-score domain. This arithmetic defect does not explain every reported undercoverage curve or resolve adaptive-history exchangeability.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use rank \(\lceil(N+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil\), returning an infinite threshold if it exceeds N, and include scores non-strictly at the threshold.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Representation conditions omit consistency of indifference
problems.source_location: Section 3, PDF p.4; Appendix A.1, p.16; cycle diagnostic in generate_figures.ipynb
claim: The paper says complete pairwise strict preference/indifference classifications and transitivity of strict preference suffice for a real utility representation.
analysis: Take \(A\sim B,B\sim C,A\succ C\), with symmetric indifference and the reverse strict edge. Every pair is classified, and no two-edge strict chain exists, so the printed strict-transitivity condition holds. A scalar representation would require \(U(A)=U(B)=U(C)\), contradicting \(U(A)>U(C)\). Counting only strict cycles and one-tie patterns does not detect this two-tie inconsistency.
result: The stated finite representation criterion omits a substantive tie-consistency condition. A deliberately narrower cycle statistic remains well-defined, and its empirical values are not shown to be miscomputed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use complete transitive weak preference. On a finite set, its indifference classes form a total order and can be assigned real ranks.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: History rewards differ from shared terminal-state rewards
problems.source_location: Appendix D.1, PDF p.20; evaluate_instrumental_values.py, extract_partial_sequences
claim: The description uses two starts and two shared terminal states, but the implementation represents trajectory prefixes and assigns a reward to each terminal history.
analysis: Rollouts \[(s_1,t_1),(s_1,t_2),(s_2,t_1),(s_2,t_2)\] become six options: two start prefixes and four start-terminal histories. Let both starts transition equally to both terminals, and utilities be \(+1\) for every history starting at \(s_1\), \(-1\) for those starting at \(s_2\). At discount one, independent history-terminal rewards fit all six utilities with zero loss. Shared terminal-state rewards instead force both start values to equal \((r_1+r_2)/2\), which cannot equal both \(+1\) and \(-1\).
result: A perfect history-space fit does not establish the stated shared-terminal-state instrumentality interpretation. The observed model-level correlations are not recalculated or shown spurious.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either describe a prefix-tree/history-reward target or use one reward per original terminal state with appropriately elicited state utilities.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Soft Bellman fitting does not yield an exact value function
problems.source_location: Appendix D.1, PDF p.20; evaluate_instrumental_values.py, optimize_reward_function
claim: The optimizer independently fits reward R and value V, forms \(W=R+\gamma PV\), penalizes \(\|W-V\|^2+0.1\|W-U\|^2\), and reports mismatch to W as a best-fit value-function loss.
analysis: For two identical start/two-terminal blocks, set normalized utilities \(U=(a,b,b)\), \(a=\sqrt2,b=-1/\sqrt2\), and \(\gamma=0.99\). Symmetry reduces the objective to \(2(r-v)^2+0.1[(\gamma v-a)^2+2(r-b)^2]\). Its exact minimizer is \(v=[2b+1.1\gamma a]/[2+1.1\gamma^2]\approx0.04089035\), \(r=(v+0.1b)/1.1\approx-0.02710939\). Reported start surrogate \(\gamma v\approx0.04048145\) differs from the actual value of its returned terminal reward, \(\gamma r\approx-0.02683829\). This persists at the exact optimum, independently of numerical convergence.
result: The statistic is an approximate Bellman surrogate rather than an exact value-function fit. Correcting it changes the statistic’s definition; the direction of correlation changes is unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Parameterize two-step values directly as \(Br\), or in a suitable discounted finite model as \((I-\gamma P)^{-1}Er\), and optimize the declared fitting loss on those exact values.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Order averaging does not identify an indifference mechanism
problems.source_location: Appendix K, PDF pp.35–36; Figure 39
claim: Improved utility fit after averaging response orders is interpreted as strong evidence of a learned strategy for expressing indifference.
analysis: Let latent utility difference be d and a first-position response bias be c. Choose the first option when \(d+c>0\) in one order and \(-d+c>0\) in the reverse order. With \(c=2\), both indifference \(d=0\) and strict preference \(d=1\) produce first-option responses in both orders. Outcome-normalized averaging gives probability \(1/2\) in either case, so those observations cannot distinguish the mechanisms.
result: Order normalization can improve predictive fit without identifying why the conflicting responses occur. This does not refute the fitted probabilities or separate probing/intervention experiments.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe operational order-normalized ties and require a discriminating model or intervention before attributing the internal indifference mechanism.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Reciprocal exchange rates are quantity-dependent summaries
problems.source_location: Appendix E.1, PDF p.22; two_way_geometric_exchange_rate
claim: Country/entity comparisons summarize log-utility indifference rates using a reciprocal geometric aggregate.
analysis: For \(U_i(N)=a_i\log N+b_i\), equality \(U_i(M)=U_j(N)\) gives \(M/N=e^{(b_j-b_i)/a_i}N^{a_j/a_i-1}\). It is constant only for equal slopes. With slopes \(1,2\), zero intercepts and quantity grid \(\{1,4\}\), forward ratios are \(1,4\), while the two-way geometric aggregate is \(2^{3/4}\). Reciprocity of a summary does not make it a universal per-unit indifference ratio.
result: This qualifies the interpretation of a valid quantity-dependent index. It does not establish incorrect numerical evaluation of that index; related prompt-framing concerns were previously discussed publicly.

problems.title: Gate-only regularization does not identify modulation strength
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Eq.(5), PDF p.5; Section 3.4, Eq.(7), and threshold setting, p.6
claim: The written relaxed objective jointly learns sigmoid gate \(\beta\in(0,1)\) and unrestricted affine parameters, using \(L(h)=h+\beta[(\alpha-1)h+\gamma]\) and a penalty \(\lambda\sum\beta\), then thresholds the gates.
analysis: For any \(0<t<1\), replace \(\beta\) by \(t\beta\), \(\alpha\) by \(1+(\alpha-1)/t\), and \(\gamma\) by \(\gamma/t\). Every block output is unchanged for every input, while a positive gate penalty strictly decreases. For cached scalar \(h=1\) and target \(2\), choose \(\beta_k=1/k,\alpha_k=1+k,\gamma=0\); the fit is exact and objective \(\lambda/k\to0\), but no finite admissible parameters attain zero. Thresholding at any fixed positive \(c\) eventually drops every such gate and returns output \(1\), not \(2\).
result: The written objective has a nonidentifiable rescaling direction and admits a nonattainment example. The paper states no universal optimizer-attainment theorem; AdamW dynamics or unreported parameter constraints could alter finite runs. No measured speedup or generation-quality claim is refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Explicit bounded affine parameters on a closed gate domain make a continuous finite-sample objective attain a minimum. For retained gates, fold soft coefficients exactly using \(\alpha_{\rm deploy}=1+\beta(\alpha-1),\gamma_{\rm deploy}=\beta\gamma\); dropping gates still needs effect-based validation.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Actual-menu normalization creates higher-order effects in one layer
problems.source_location: Sections 2.2 and 3.2, current arXiv v1 PDF pp.3 and 5–6, Eqs.(4)–(5)
claim: The feature-based architecture averages over actual menu size and asserts that layer l has interaction effects only through order l under its subset decomposition.
analysis: Use scalar features \(x=(1,2,3,4)\), one layer/head, unit weights, and ReLU encoders/modulators acting identically on these positive features. The specified utility is \(u_j(S)=x_j[1+\sum_{k\in S}x_k/|S|]\). For the always-present pair \(1,2\), log odds on menus \(12,123,124,1234\) are \(-5/2,-3,-10/3,-7/2\). The mixed difference for optional items 3 and 4 equals \(-7/2+3+10/3-5/2=1/3\). First-order relative utilities must have zero such difference. The observable odds eliminate any common utility-shift ambiguity.
result: The one-layer interaction-order upper bound is false over the stated variable-menu domain. Permutation equivariance survives; a fixed-cardinality empirical slice does not establish the required subset identities.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Replace actual-size normalization by a fixed positive constant and mask all invalid contributions. With base-only modulators and linear aggregation/readout, Boolean menu-membership degree increases by at most one per layer, proving the repaired order upper bound.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Padded alternatives enter the context summary
problems.source_location: Appendix B.2, current arXiv v1 PDF p.18; Model/FeatureBased.py, DeepHalo.forward, lines 63–76
claim: The appendix says dummy states are reset to zero after residual layers and do not affect aggregation. The release sums all affine projected states before applying a valid-item mask only to the modulator.
analysis: A zero raw feature need not have zero embedding after biased layers and normalization. Even if its state were zero, an affine aggregate projection contributes its bias. With projection weight zero and bias one, five slots containing two real items produce unmasked summary \(5/2\), versus the correct masked summary \(1\). Item-specific modulators can turn that difference into unequal valid-logit changes; final dummy softmax masking cannot remove prior context contamination.
result: The released class violates the specified dummy noninterference. Actual real-data training paths/checkpoints are not available to quantify the published effect.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Mask embeddings and residual states, and mask after each affine aggregate projection before summing. This gives padding invariance by induction for deterministic evaluation.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Named baseline descriptions differ from the cited models
problems.source_location: Appendix C.2.2, current arXiv v1 PDF p.20; RUMnet Section 2.3; TasteNet-MNL Section 3.1
claim: The appendix describes RUMnet as an alternative-order GRU and TasteNet as deriving user representations from mean offered-item features, while interpreting the comparison as involving context-independent approaches.
analysis: The cited RUMnet uses shared feed-forward component utilities, per-component softmax and probability averaging, not an item-order GRU. A scalar GRU recurrence \(h_t=h_{t-1}/2+\tanh(x_t)/2\) can change matched item utility differences when order reverses. Original TasteNet maps fixed consumer characteristics to taste coefficients; replacing those with menu mean changes the object. For the described scalar dot product \(u_j=x_j\bar x_S\), log odds of features 1 and 2 change from \(-3/2\) to \(-2\) when feature 3 is added.
result: The published baseline specifications are different from the cited architectures. Missing baseline training implementations leave open whether the code or the descriptions need correction; no table ranking is recalculated.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Identify and release the actual baseline architectures/inputs and distinguish adapted models from the named originals; rerun faithful versions if the intended comparison is to those originals.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Consistency loss is undefined on allowed real query features
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, Eqs.(7)–(9), PDF p.6; xmuda/train_dg_clip_XDiff3D.py, line 241
claim: Low-rank real query matrices are inserted directly into a KL-like logarithmic ratio against an MLP containing a linear layer and layer normalization. The release also passes raw queries to kl_div and reduces a scalar along dimension one.
analysis: Take rank-one queries \(Q=(1,-1),Q^{\prime}=(1,1)\), with rank-one reconstruction, identity linear map and default unit/zero layer-normalization affine parameters. The transformed denominator is \((a,-a)\), \(a=(1+\varepsilon)^{-1/2}>0\), so the second log ratio is \(\log(-1/a)\), not a real number. SVD truncation and layer normalization do not enforce positivity or probability normalization. Independently, even valid log-probability/probability arguments to default kl_div produce a scalar, so the subsequent sum over dimension one is invalid.
result: The central consistency objective is not mathematically defined throughout its stated feature domain, and the enabled release loss has an additional reduction failure. This does not independently disprove reported mIoU values or identify the historical working implementation.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Define a probability axis and temperature, apply softmax/log_softmax to the query logits, then sum an unreduced KL along that probability axis and average the intended remaining dimensions. This changes and clarifies the mathematical objective.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Extraction and evaluation contracts do not match the described paths
problems.source_location: Experimental inference description, PDF p.7; xmuda/XDiff3D/UniDSeg/xmuda_arch.py; xmuda/data/utils/validate.py
claim: The release’s default diffusion extractor returns no query pair, and its three-dimensional wrapper requires a two-dimensional query argument that validation omits, despite the paper’s three-dimensional-only inference description.
analysis: The extractor returns queries only under its nondefault hook branch, while the default wrapper unpacks its return. Separately, Net3DSeg.forward requires data_batch and object_query_2D and uses the latter unconditionally; validation calls model_3d(data_batch). The missing argument fails at Python binding before input data, hardware or learned weights can affect it. eval mode does not change the required function signature.
result: The current release does not implement a working path with these declared interfaces. It remains possible that another implementation generated the reported results; no complete substitute architecture is invented.

problems.title: Scorer can replace the labeled question with a system instruction
problems.source_location: Appendix D.3–D.4; eval/eval_results.py, get_response, lines 190–201
claim: The evaluator scores against messages[0] instead of selecting the user question by role. Released predictions include a system message before the question.
analysis: Consider two items with identical system instruction, reference letter A and model response happy. In one user question A means happy; in the other A means sad. Correct judgments differ, but selecting only the system message makes both judge prompts identical and omits both option lists. No deterministic or stochastic judge can recover the missing distinction from identical inputs. A directly inspected released VidEmo emotion record uses this system-first schema.
result: The supplied scorer and raw records have an information-losing interface mismatch. A private user-first cleaning stage might have been used historically; the published score impact is not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Select and validate the actual user message, preserve task instructions/options and required dialogue context, and remove only known video placeholders.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Scoring failures change denominators inconsistently
problems.source_location: Appendix D.3; eval/eval_results.py, eval_single and result_evaluate, lines 215–269
claim: Exhausted judge requests can be absent from the stored results. Numeric scores average stored responses, while yes/no accuracy divides by all submitted records.
analysis: For two submitted items with only one successful score of \(100\), the numeric branch reports \(100\), while one successful yes gives accuracy \(50\). The missing numeric value could be anywhere in \([0,100]\), so the full mean is only identified within \([50,100]\). In general, if N are expected, m are scored and observed sum is A, the full mean lies in \([A/N,(A+100(N-m))/N]\).
result: The current metrics use different failure semantics and may summarize different populations. No actual original judge-failure rate or direction of benchmark bias is established; complete successful scoring avoids this problem.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep one indexed status for every expected record, validate accepted scores, and report complete means or an explicit failure policy. Conditional means and worst-case missing-score bounds should be labeled separately.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: The described cosine objective differs from released squared reconstruction loss
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Eq. (1); Appendix C.1; models_tobo.py, forward_loss and decoder projection; engine_tobo.py training loss
claim: The method describes cosine distance between predicted and target patches, while forward_loss computes coordinate-mean squared error after optional target-only normalization.
analysis: Let a nonzero target after optional normalization be \(u\), with predictions \(z=u\) and \(z=2u\). Both have cosine distance \(0\); their squared losses are \(0\) and \(\|u\|^2/d>0\). More generally the cosine radial derivative is \(0\), whereas the squared-loss derivative at scale \(\alpha\) is \(2(\alpha-1)\|u\|^2/d\). LayerNorm precedes the unconstrained final affine projection, so it does not impose unit norm on predicted pixels. The documented training path gives the ToBo branch nonzero weight. Appendix C.1 explicitly discloses the auxiliary Siamese loss, so that branch is not an additional undisclosed change.
result: The current author paper and release optimize different reconstruction objectives. Which objective generated each published checkpoint remains unresolved; downstream performance and the token-bottleneck mechanism are not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: If released squared loss generated the experiments, describe the masked coordinate-mean squared error and target normalization; otherwise identify the cosine-training source and checkpoint configurations. This is a provenance-dependent proposal, not a validated retraining result.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Distinct steering configurations append to an indistinguishable output file
problems.source_location: Official RICE intervention.py, run, lines 35–43, 50–54 and 106–114
claim: For nonempty selected-expert settings, the evaluation function overwrites its configuration-specific filename component with normal, although it still passes the actual steering multiplier and expert set to the model.
analysis: Fix dataset, sampling arguments and output directory, and choose expert string 29:126;39:182 with \(\beta=4\) and then \(\beta=64\). Both valid settings enter the same nonempty branch, assign the identical filename component normal, and open that path in append mode. Each record stores only data identifier, problem and response, so the two interventions cannot be distinguished from those records. Separate output directories or external manifests can avoid the pooling; a single isolated invocation does not mix settings.
result: The official release loses intervention provenance when those settings share an output directory. The source trace establishes the collision without model execution; it does not establish that any published accuracy was computed from mixed outputs.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep the steering/expert component for nonempty configurations and use normal only for the baseline; store intervention metadata with each output. The proposed filename change addresses this collision but not complete run identity.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: The bounded-loss transfer coefficient is too small
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, Eq. (3); Appendix A.2, Eq. (17)
claim: For \(0\le f\le C\), the paper bounds transferred loss by distilled loss plus \(C\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)}/(2\sqrt2)\).
analysis: Let the input be a singleton, \(Q(Y)=P_{\rm tr}(Y)=(4/5,1/5)\), balanced \(P_{\rm te}(Y)=(1/2,1/2)\), and classifier \(\widehat p=(4/5,1/5)\). Label shift holds and \(C=\log5\). Direct evaluation gives \(\ell_Q=0.50040242\), \(\ell_{\rm te}=0.91629073\) and \(\mathrm{KL}(P_{\rm te}\|Q)=\log(5/4)\). The printed right side is \(0.76919756\), strictly below the actual loss. The general bounded-loss argument is \(E_Pf-E_Qf\le C\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)\le C\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)/2}\); its coefficient is twice the printed one.
result: The displayed transfer guarantee is false on a strictly positive admissible two-class model. The corrected coefficient retains a population transfer bound but does not reproduce the ADSA accuracy gains.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Replace the coefficient by \(C/\sqrt2\) and use the bounded-loss/total-variation argument. This corrects the numerical guarantee without proving the calibration algorithm optimal.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Training and test joint KL are identified despite label shift
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.1, Eqs. (4)–(6); Appendix A.2
claim: The discrepancy defined from the training law is called equivalent to decompositions based on the balanced test law.
analysis: On the singleton-input example \(P_{\rm tr}=Q=(4/5,1/5)\) and \(P_{\rm te}=(1/2,1/2)\), the original joint KL is \(0\), while the proposed prior-plus-conditional decomposition is \(\log(5/4)>0\). With \(Q=(1/2,1/2)\), the original KL becomes \(0.19274476\) and the test-law KL becomes \(0\). The difference changes with \(Q\), so a constant independent of the distilled law cannot repair equality.
result: The theorem changes which distributional discrepancy is being optimized. Both ordinary KL chain rules remain valid when consistently applied to the test joint.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Define \(R_{\rm te}=\mathrm{KL}(P_{\rm te}(X,Y)\|Q(X,Y))\) explicitly; its feature/posterior and prior/conditional chain-rule decompositions are exact. Use this new quantity in the corrected population bound.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: A balanced prior does not imply matched conditional features
problems.source_location: Appendix A.2, Eqs. (38)–(40)
claim: The appendix infers zero conditional and feature-marginal KL from a uniform test class prior.
analysis: Use \(P_{\rm tr}(Y)=(4/5,1/5)\), \(P_{\rm te}(Y)=Q(Y)=(1/2,1/2)\), and for both classes \(P_{\rm tr}(X\mid y)=P_{\rm te}(X\mid y)=(4/5,1/5)\), \(Q(X\mid y)=(1/5,4/5)\). All masses are positive and label shift holds. Each conditional KL and the feature-marginal KL equal \((3/5)\log4>0\), while the class-prior KL is \(0\).
result: The zero-discrepancy simplification requires successful conditional distribution matching in addition to equal class counts. The example does not show equal IPC or calibration is practically ineffective.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State equality of every class-conditional distribution as an additional premise. Positive uniform prior weights then make the conditional KL sum zero exactly when each conditional matches.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Unscaled exponential-weights rate violates the stated regret bound
problems.source_location: Official supplement, Algorithm 2, Lemma A.14 and Lemma B.6
claim: Algorithm 2 uses raw-loss exponent \(-\eta\ell\) and \(\eta=\sqrt{8\log N/T}\), while Lemma A.14 claims regret proportional to an arbitrary loss range.
analysis: Take \(N=2,T=100,\tau=2^{-20}\), experts \((1-\tau,\tau)\) and \((\tau,1-\tau)\), and alternating outcomes. Put \(a=-\log(1-\tau),b=-\log\tau\). The exact expected regret is \[\frac{T}{2}(b-a)\left(\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta(b-a)}}-\frac12\right)=321.05863.\] The printed bound is \(b\sqrt{T\log2/2}=81.61184\). All expert masses are positive and losses lie in \([0,b]\). The lemma permits any sequence; the example does not address the final iid learner directly. B.6 additionally conditions an iid online-to-batch argument on a sample-dependent regret event, which need not preserve independence.
result: The operative regret lemma and its proof route to proper learning are invalid as written. This does not falsify the final iid PAC order for a corrected learner.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For loss width \(R\), the potential bound is \(\log N/\eta+\eta TR^2/8\). Scale the rate by the actual width. Apply the corrected expected regret against a fixed population expert, then Markov to the nonnegative excess KL; this avoids event-conditioned independence.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Parallel-bundle deletion gives the wrong exact tree law
problems.source_location: Official supplement, Definition D.11, Algorithm 8 and Claims D.16–D.17
claim: The sampler claims product-weight arborescences, but deletion removes every parallel edge while the acceptance branch records one selected original edge.
analysis: Use the unit-weight complete bidirected graph on \(\{1,2,3\}\), root \(1\), edge order \(12,13,21,23,31,32\). The three rooted trees are \[\{12,13\},\{12,23\},\{13,32\}\], each target probability \(1/3\). Accepting \(12\) has probability \(2/3\); contraction makes \(13\) and \(23\) parallel. Bundle deletion of the next \(13\) leaves zero partition function, so that branch necessarily records \(13\). The resulting law is \((2/3,0,1/3)\), not uniform. Parallel arcs arise internally even from a simple initial graph.
result: The stated deletion convention invalidates the exact sampling guarantee, including the complete-graph application. The matrix-tree identity survives.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Delete one persistently labelled arc. The partition identity \(Z(G)=Z(G\setminus e)+w(e)Z(G/e)\), with preserved parallel labels and positive partition function, proves correct conditional recursion by induction.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: The displayed hardness family admits a zero-sample estimator
problems.source_location: Official supplement, Lemma E.5, Claim E.6 and proof of Theorem E.1
claim: The specified three-bit family is claimed to require \(\Omega(1/\varepsilon)\) samples for KL error \(\varepsilon\), allowing an arbitrary pmf output.
analysis: Each \(P_i\) gives its two common states mass \((1-\varepsilon/2)/2\), and two private exceptional states mass \(\varepsilon/4\). The known mixture \(Q=(P_1+P_2+P_3)/3\) gives each exceptional state mass \(\varepsilon/12\); therefore \(\mathrm{KL}(P_i\|Q)=(\varepsilon/2)\log3<\varepsilon\) for all targets without samples. Pairwise squared Hellinger distance is \(\varepsilon/2\), not the claimed much larger separation. A proper-output restriction would exclude this mixture, but E.5 states none. Independence of target blocks also does not force an arbitrary learner to output only within-block edges or independent errors.
result: This construction and block proof do not establish the stated lower bound. The overall minimax order is not refuted; different product-distribution packings can establish it.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The proposed replacement uses a Hamming-separated family of product Bernoulli laws with coordinate perturbation squared \(32\varepsilon/n\), Hellinger separation and Fano’s information argument, yielding \(\Omega(n/\varepsilon)\) for sufficiently large \(n\) and small \(\varepsilon\). It does not restore every structural claim of E.6.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Adaptive refill can exit with too few effective prompts
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1 and Appendix F; verl/trainer/ppo/ray_trainer.py, lines 1141–1182
claim: The algorithm promises a full effective batch, but last_sampling bypasses the actual accumulated-count condition after a predicted final refill.
analysis: Use the documented \(256\)-prompt target, raw cap \(384\), and \(8\) responses per prompt. A first raw batch yields \(192\) effective groups; the estimated refill is \(1.25(256-192)/(1/2)=160\), setting last_sampling. If that refill yields \(48\), the source exits with \(240<256\) groups. Mixed \(0.1/1\) rewards and constant \(0.1\) rewards realize the effective/ineffective groups. No premise forces identical realized yields across batches. With no effective groups, the code first divides by \(1-\alpha=0\), before its cap can apply.
result: The active release can violate the effective-batch invariant or fail on an admissible zero-yield batch. Historical occurrence and resulting speed/accuracy changes remain unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Permit successful exit only when the accumulated count meets the target; explicitly branch on zero yield and use a retry/abort policy. This proves successful-exit correctness, not termination when effective prompts never occur.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Mean-threshold runs differ from zero-variance streaks
problems.source_location: Equations (3)–(5); presampling_selector.py, easy_probabilistic_skip and hard_probabilistic_skip; ray_trainer.py, lines 1121–1132
claim: The written retention rule uses the most recent consecutive zero-variance groups. The release stores means, counts separate easy/hard threshold runs and applies a retention floor.
analysis: An all-\(1\) group followed by an all-\(0.1\) group has equality streak \(z=2\), hence retention \(0.5^2=0.25\); the hard mean-threshold run counts only the latest group and retains with \(0.5\). A group with four \(0\) and four \(0.1\) rewards has mean \(0.05\), variance \(0.0025>0\), so the written rule retains with \(1\), but the hard branch can retain with only \(0.5\). The rewards are allowed by the released formatting/correctness scheme. Constant same-type streaks agree, and a strictly binary reward domain would avoid the second example; the actual multivalued domain does not.
result: The released pre-filter is a different history statistic, not an implementation of the equality indicator. No claim is made that every skipped prompt would improve future training.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Record the equality indicator before reducing groups to means and update the trailing streak by increment/reset; alternatively describe the released threshold runs. Disclose the \(0.01\) retention floor separately from the minimum exploration base.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: The NDCG helper rewards worse positions within the cutoff
problems.source_location: Section 5.1; calculate_hit metric helper and descending top-k call
claim: The release transforms zero-based relevant-item position into cutoff minus position before logarithmic discounting.
analysis: At cutoff \(K=5\), the best-ranked relevant item receives \(1/\log_2 6\), while the fifth-ranked receives \(1\). Standard single-relevant-item NDCG gives the reverse. The source requests descending sorted scores, so ascending order cannot explain the transformation. Repeating these positions across a trajectory preserves the reversal under the geometric mean.
result: The release does not compute conventional NDCG. HR is unaffected by this rank transformation; effects on published relative rankings require actual predictions and table lineage.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use one-based rank \(r\) and discount \(1/\log_2(r+1)\), with zero for misses; recompute saved predictions and any affected validation selection.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Multiplicative logit masking does not implement Soft-ListMLE
problems.source_location: Equation (9); model/LPDO.py, list_preference_loss, lines 264–272
claim: The formula weights exponentiated scores of previously selected items by \(\gamma\); the active release multiplies their logits by \(\gamma\).
analysis: Use candidates \(A,B\), non-repeating target \((A,B)\), and identical score rows \((\log4,0)\). The first loss is \(\log(5/4)\) for both rules. At the second position the printed loss is \(\log(1+4\gamma)\), versus released \(\log(1+4^\gamma)\). At \(\gamma=0\) these are \(0\) and \(\log2\); at \(\gamma=1\) they agree. Score-shift invariance also holds for weighted probabilities but fails for multiplicatively masked logits.
result: The active surrogate differs even in the original tied-score, non-repeating domain. This does not establish poorer empirical predictions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For non-repeating targets, add \(\log m_i\) to logits, with \(\log0=-\infty\), instead of multiplying by \(m_i\). Repeated targets require an explicit normalized sequential rule.

problems.title: The softened expression needs an explicit sample-space convention
problems.source_location: Equation (9) and Section 4.3 likelihood interpretation
claim: The softened ListMLE factors are used as a likelihood, without fully specifying how repeated trajectories receive mass.
analysis: For two candidates with scores \((\log4,0)\) and \(\gamma=0.3\), the two permutation weights are \(4/11\) and \(8/43\), totaling \(260/473<1\). However a repeat-capable sequential model with numerator weight \(\gamma\) on already selected items is normalized and retains both non-repeating path values. A permutation-mass deficit alone therefore does not refute every likelihood interpretation.
result: The repeated-outcome numerator and sample space need specification. A coherent extension exists, so this is a scoped clarification rather than an established impossibility.

problems.title: The central ELBO derivation interchanges marginal and shared-chain likelihoods
problems.source_location: Sections 4.3–4.4, Eqs. (12)–(15); Appendix B.2 and Appendix C
claim: The derivation replaces a sum of item-chain joint log densities with only one chain log density, then identifies a shared-chain joint bound with a sum of marginal log-likelihoods.
analysis: For a normalized chain density \(P(x)\) and normalized emissions \(r_j\), the product rule gives \[\sum_{j=1}^k\log[P(x)r_j(i_j\mid x)]=k\log P(x)+\sum_j\log r_j(i_j\mid x).\] A shared-chain joint has coefficient one, but its marginal is \(\int P\prod_jr_j\), not the product of separate marginal integrals. With \(X\sim N(0,1)\), \(r(A\mid x)=e^{-x^2/2}\), trajectory \((A,A)\) has joint negative log-likelihood \((\log3)/2\), versus summed marginal negative log-likelihood \(\log2\). The exact joint posterior \(N(0,1/3)\) makes the one-chain variational bound equal \((\log3)/2<\log2\), so it cannot bound both objectives as asserted. Appendix B.2 also uses a point-mass embedding against a continuous kernel, yielding infinite endpoint KL, and labels conditionals over different variables a KL without a common measure.
result: The claimed tight variational derivation does not establish the stated objective. The heuristic loss can remain useful; no accuracy result is inferred false.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify a normalized sequence emission and choose either a shared-chain joint ELBO or separate marginal ELBOs with the appropriate repeated chain terms. Treat deterministic embedding endpoints with a compatible reconstruction likelihood or nondegenerate variational model.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Unequal evaluation batches receive equal weight
problems.source_location: Equation (20); main.py, evaluate aggregation
claim: The evaluator averages batch means rather than all user-level values.
analysis: Three complete-match indicators \((0,0,1)\), partitioned into batches of sizes \((2,1)\), produce \((0+1)/2=1/2\), although the dataset fraction is \(1/3\). The same predictions in one batch give \(1/3\). Equal-size batches are a valid special case. Sequence negative log-likelihood is also averaged this way; per-item log perplexity would additionally divide sequence NLL by fixed trajectory length.
result: The released metrics can depend on evaluation partition. Corrected tables cannot be reconstructed from aggregate means alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Accumulate sample numerators and counts, or weight each batch mean by its actual size before sequence aggregation.

problems.title: Released loss weights and sampling settings differ from the description
problems.source_location: Equation (16), experimental setup; model/LPDO.py, p_losses and sample; main.py sampler construction
claim: The code swaps ranking/reconstruction coefficients, scales linear noise endpoints by \(1000/T\), and iterates all configured diffusion steps.

They differ unless \(\lambda=1/2\) or component values coincide. With \(T=50\) and requested endpoints \(0.0001,0.02\), the source uses \(0.002,0.4\). Its sample loop calls the denoiser at every step, with no distinct one-step inference setting on the documented path.

problems.title: Original-loss smoothness does not give the composite rate
problems.source_location: Section 3.1; Appendix A, Lemma 1
claim: The lemma uses original-loss smoothness for \(\Phi(B,U)=F(BUU^T)\) and simultaneous product-manifold updates.
analysis: Use \(F(W)=W_{12}^2/2\), \(U(a)=(\cos a,\sin a)^T\), \(B_0=\operatorname{diag}(2,0)\), \(a_0=0.05\), and step \(1/2\). The original loss is globally \(1\)-smooth. For \(q=b\cos a\sin a+c\sin^2a\), in \(|b-2|<0.1,|c|<0.1,|a|<0.1\), \(\partial_aq>1.9\cos0.2-0.1\sin0.2>1\), yielding PL constant \(\mu=1\). Exact simultaneous updates give \(a_1=0.05-\sin(0.2)/2\), \(B_{1,11}=1.99750832\), \(B_{1,12}=-0.00012469\). Both endpoints remain there, yet \(\Phi_1=0.00483999>\Phi_0/2=0.00249168\).
result: The claimed rate fails despite the stated smoothness, local PL and exact manifold step; the actual step still decreases loss.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a composite pullback descent constant on an invariant neighborhood. Its reciprocal step condition plus PL gives a geometric value bound; the composite constant need not equal the original one.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Global coverage does not preserve local minima at folds
problems.source_location: Section 3.2; Appendix Theorem 1
claim: Global surjectivity or density of rotations is claimed to preserve local minima.
analysis: Let \(C=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), \(F(W)=\|W-C\|_F^2/2\), \(\bar U=e_1\), and \(a(s)=\pi/4+s^2+s^3\). On \(\theta\ne0\), put \(s=\log|\theta|\), \(R(\theta)=\operatorname{Rot}(a(s))\operatorname{diag}(1,\operatorname{sgn}\theta)\). This smooth map covers \(O(2)\). Minimizing over \(B\) gives \(f(a)=1/2+(3/2)\sin^2a\). Near \(\theta=1\), \(a\ge\pi/4\), so \((C,1)\) is a joint local minimum of value \(5/4\). A smaller ambient angle lowers loss, so its image is not an ambient minimum.
result: A globally covering map can fold locally; density need not even provide an exact preimage.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Require local openness, such as a submersion, for the reverse local-minimum implication and differential surjectivity for stationarity transfer.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Rotation Jacobian stabilizers defeat near-isometry
problems.source_location: Appendix A.1, Jacobian expansion and Corollary 1
claim: The full rotation Jacobian is claimed near-isometric at zero, preserving Hessian conditioning.
analysis: For \(d=3,r=1,\bar U=e_1\) and Frobenius-orthonormal skew generators, \[J(0)=[e_2/\sqrt2,e_3/\sqrt2,0],\qquad J(0)^TJ(0)=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/2,0).\] The last generator fixes the frame. At quadratic optimum \(B=C=e_1e_1^T,U=e_1\), \(H_U=\operatorname{diag}(4,1,1)\) but \(J^TH_UJ=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/2,0)\), violating the claimed positive lower comparison. The skew-exponential integral derivative also gives \(\|J(\theta)\|_2\le1\), excluding the asserted forward singular-value blow-up.
result: Near-isometry fails at the clipped center. Empirical optimizer instability is not inferred.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Remove stabilizer coordinates and use a full-rank chart. For a positive definite Hessian, \(\kappa(J^THJ)\le\kappa(H)\kappa(J)^2\) is a valid conditional comparison.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Reduced orbits can contain an optimum and create traps
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, reduced rotation family
claim: The no-spurious-minimum conclusion is retained if an optimum is reachable or close to the reduced orbit.
analysis: For \(d=4,r=2,\bar U=[e_1,e_3]\), \(C=\operatorname{diag}(1,0,1,0)\), rotate the two planes at speeds \(1\) and \(2\). Minimizing \(\|BUU^T-C\|_F^2/2\) over \(B\) gives \(f(\theta)=[\sin^2\theta+\sin^2(2\theta)]/2\). The orbit has zero loss at \(0\), but at \(\pi/2\), \(f=1/2,f'=0,f''=3>0\), giving a joint restricted local minimum. Rotating only the first column toward its original axis lowers ambient loss.
result: Optimum containment does not prevent restricted-orbit traps. This witness lies outside practical clipping radius \(0.5\), so it does not establish a trapped clipped run.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restrict the landscape statement to the orbit or require all relevant ambient descent directions to be represented.

problems.title: Stochastic decay is an expected bound, not pathwise pruning
problems.source_location: Main projection-removal box; Appendix Theorem 3
claim: The proof reverses the norm/expectation comparison, while the main discussion suggests a pathwise limit.
analysis: Let \(P\) be either coordinate projector equally likely, \(Q=\operatorname{diag}(1,0),\lambda=1,\eta=1/2\), and bounded smooth \(F_x(Z)=3-h(Z_{11})\), where \(h(t)=t\) on \([-2,2]\), \(|h'|\le1,|h|\le5/2\). From zero, \(W_t=w_tQ\) obeys \(w_{t+1}=w_t/2+\xi_t/2\), with independent Bernoulli halves. Thus \(Ew_t=(1-2^{-t})/2\), but arbitrarily long all-one/all-zero blocks give almost surely \(\limsup w_t=1,\liminf w_t=0\).
result: The stronger pathwise reading fails; the formal expected bound survives a corrected proof. Derivatives through trainable projectors remain a separate condition.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Take triangle inequality before expectation to obtain \(y_{t+1}\le(1-\eta\lambda)y_t+\eta Lp_Q\), sum the geometric series, and state an expected limsup.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Average overlap alone does not justify projection removal
problems.source_location: Section 3.5, projection removal
claim: Weight decay is used to infer redundancy of sample-dependent projections.
analysis: Let coordinate projectors \(P_1,P_2\) be equally likely, \(F_i(Z)=1-e^{-\|Z-P_i\|_F^2}\), and \(\lambda=e^{-1/4}\). Gradients are globally bounded by \(\sqrt{2/e}<1\). The regularized objective has Hessian lower bound \((e^{-1/4}-2e^{-3/2})I\succ0\) and zero gradient at \(W_*=I/2\), hence this is its unique optimum. For each sample, removal changes loss from \(1-e^{-1/4}\) to \(1-e^{-1/2}\), an increase \(0.17227012\). No globally idle direction exists.
result: The overlap theorem lacks samplewise residual control even at an optimum. The reported removal/fine-tuning experiment remains separate empirical evidence.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Expected residual \(E\|XW(I-P(x))\|_F\le\varepsilon\) and downstream Lipschitz constant \(K\) suffice for expected loss change at most \(K\varepsilon\); the overlap bound does not establish this premise.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Reported metric triples need their aggregation reconciled
problems.source_location: Tables 1, 5 and 6; Appendix D.2 and D.7
claim: The paper describes ordinary information-extraction F1, precision and recall, but does not fully specify column populations, weights or undefined-case treatment.
analysis: For ordinary per-unit F1 \(h(p,r)=2pr/(p+r)\), the Hessian quadratic form is \(-4(ra-pb)^2/(p+r)^3\le0\). Thus common nonnegative weights imply \(\bar F\le h(\bar P,\bar R)\), including hierarchical common-weight macro averages. Table 1 reports AutoAgent–Stock \((F,P,R)=(73.54,94.37,52.71)\) percent. Even two-decimal rounding requires \(73.535\le h(94.375,52.715)=67.64536\), impossible. However different column weights or populations can violate that necessary bound without an arithmetic error. Mere inequality between macro F1 and the harmonic mean is not itself a defect.
result: The row is inconsistent under a common-weight interpretation, but the actual aggregation remains unresolved. No replacement F1 or changed method ranking follows without scoring code and per-unit data.

problems.title: Whole-block commitment can violate target stopping semantics
problems.source_location: Sections 3.1 and 5.1; vispec/model/spec_model_ours.py, specgenerate; vispec/model/utils.py, update_inference_inputs
claim: The method relies on distribution-preserving speculative decoding, but the release appends a complete verified block before checking EOS and generation budget.
analysis: Choose unique greedy target outputs \(a\), then EOS \(e\), then \(b\) after that EOS prefix, and a matching draft path \((a,e,b)\). All positions satisfy argmax verification, but whole-block commitment returns \((a,e,b)\); ordinary stopped generation returns \((a,e)\). The GQA caller removes EOS strings without truncating the ordinary suffix. Independently, a budget \(M=2\) permits lengths \(2\) then \(3\) because the check is strictly greater after appending; a long block can overshoot even with a non-strict comparison. A separate Vicuna caller does truncate final text, limiting a repository-wide claim.
result: The released general routine does not guarantee the same stopped sequence under admissible EOS/cap boundaries. This does not measure the frequency or quality impact in pretrained benchmark outputs.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Before commitment, truncate the verified block to the remaining budget and earliest stopping token. Advance counters and caches by the committed prefix length and stop immediately when exhausted. The prefix invariant proves stopping correctness conditional on valid target verification.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: The baseline counter stays zero and speed accounting uses different units
problems.source_location: Section 5.1 and Table 1; gen_baseline_answer_gqa.py baseline generation; speed.py
claim: The baseline returns a generated-token field used for logging, while timing analysis is intended to compare cost per generated token.
analysis: The baseline initializes new_token to \(0\) and never updates it, despite appending tokens; the counter-based limit therefore stays inactive. A valid generated suffix \((7,8,2)\), with EOS \(2\), has length \(3\) but the returned count remains \(0\). Evaluation callers also omit a common explicit cap, leaving baseline/speculative defaults \(2048\) and \(512\). Contrary evidence matters: speed.py retokenizes cleaned baseline text instead of using the zero field, so zero recorded counts do not imply its denominator is zero. That script uses a fixed LLaVA tokenizer even for Qwen, while speculative counts use target token IDs; equality of those units is not guaranteed.
result: The release’s baseline field and budget plumbing are defective. Existing timing compensation prevents a direct zero-denominator allegation, and the effect on published speedups is unquantified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Set count from sequence length minus prompt length, pass the same explicit cap and stopping convention, and use comparable validated token units for both sides. Reanalysis requires the actual saved responses and timing records.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Unavailable physics is encoded as zero violations
problems.source_location: Sections 3.2/4.1; Pipeline/app/evaluation.py, eval_scene, lines 68–97
claim: Physical feedback is intended to measure collision and boundary violations, but the missing-file branch fills those fields with numeric zeros.
analysis: When the expected per-iteration physics file is absent, eval_scene assigns zero to OOB Objects and BBL objects and Unknown only to object count. No geometry has been examined, so neither zero is a measured empty violation set. The native present-file schema contains lists, so the fallback also changes type. The valid present-file branch preserves actual measurements; the defect is restricted to missing data.
result: The current release can feed unmeasured zeros into agent feedback. Whether any published scene used this fallback is unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Fail explicitly on the missing record, or use null plus an unavailable status handled by every consumer. This establishes that successful measurements came from actual records, without proving recovery or retry behavior.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Historical exports reuse terminal physics for every iteration
problems.source_location: Pipeline/app/evaluation.py and standalone evaluation.py, statistic_traj
claim: Each exported iteration combines its action and perceptual score with physics loaded using the terminal index.
analysis: For iterations \(0,1,2\), suppose native physics records have object counts \((3,5,7)\) and collision counts \((2,1,0)\). The loop reads the terminal file each time, exporting \((7,7,7)\) and \((0,0,0)\) under distinct iteration labels. This is not a terminal-only schema because action/perception remain iteration-specific. Crucially, the terminal-only final aggregator reads the correct final entry, and direct current feedback uses its own index.

problems.title: Zero counted collisions has a bounded geometric meaning
problems.source_location: Section 4.2 and Table 3; Pipeline/evaluation geometry predicates; author public issue replies
claim: The physical metric excludes selected objects and uses positive penetration/volume thresholds rather than testing every mesh component for any overlap.
analysis: A positive overlap depth \(0.0005\,\mathrm m\) fails a strict \(d>0.001\,\mathrm m\) predicate. A watertight intersection volume \(10^{-5}\,\mathrm m^3\) fails the \(10^{-4}\,\mathrm m^3\) threshold even if depth passes. Rugs and internal components of composite assets can be excluded; prior author replies explain that choice. The boundary predicate uses a buffered floor footprint rather than full three-dimensional enclosure.
result: These are legitimate metric conventions requiring a scoped interpretation, not a newly established benchmark error or a proof of dynamic stability.

problems.title: The inverse-Gram dominant subspace is annihilated by labels
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Theorem 1; Appendix A.2
claim: For balanced classes with within-class similarity \(1-\epsilon\) and between-class similarity \(\epsilon\), the paper approximates least-squares weights by \(\epsilon^{-1}Z^TY_t\).
analysis: The exact block Gram is \(M=\epsilon I+(1-2\epsilon)(I_c\otimes J_k)+\epsilon J_{kc}\). Its within-class contrast projector \(Q_1=I-(I_c\otimes J_k)/k\) has eigenvalue \(\epsilon\), but \(Q_1Y_t=0\). Therefore the supposed dominant inverse term vanishes. The surviving eigenvalues are \(\lambda_2=k(1-2\epsilon)+\epsilon\), \(\lambda_3=\lambda_2+kc\epsilon\), giving \(W_*=Z^T(\lambda_2^{-1}Q_2+\lambda_3^{-1}Q_3)Y_t\), of leading scale \(1/k\), not \(1/\epsilon\). Unit-norm features \(x_{a,j}=\sqrt\epsilon e_{a,j}+\sqrt{1-2\epsilon}f_a+\sqrt\epsilon g\) realize this exact positive-definite model, including disjoint held-out rows. Under this exact symmetry, query scores differ from prototype scores only by positive scale and a class-independent shift, so their argmax still agrees.
result: The weight-matrix approximation and its derivation fail; the practical classifier can nevertheless retain exact decisions under class symmetry. Approximate-data accuracy requires separate conditioning and margin assumptions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the exact block-projector formula and prove decision equivalence directly. Do not extend that equivalence to unspecified approximate similarity without quantitative perturbation and margin control.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Overlapping hyperedges leave unremoved second-order self-information
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Lemma 3, Eq. (11); Appendix Lemma 9; zen.py, RSIs
claim: The claimed two-hop correction squares individual edge contributions, omitting cross terms when a node pair shares multiple hyperedges.
analysis: Define \(C_{ij}=\sum_{e\ni i,j}(d_e-1)^{-1}\) for distinct nodes. Matrix multiplication gives true diagonal \(r_i=d_i^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}C_{ij}^2/(d_j-1)\), which squares the entire common-edge sum. For incidence \(H=J_4-I_4\), every node/edge degree is \(3\), every pair shares two edges, \(A_1^*=(J_4-I_4)/3\), and the true second-hop diagonal is \(1/2\). The printed and released correction subtracts \(1/4\), leaving diagonal \(1/4\), so propagation self-weight is \(\alpha_0+\alpha_2/4\). All inverses exist and no duplicate edges occur. Linear hypergraphs, where distinct edges share at most one node, avoid the omitted terms.
result: Both formula and release violate the central claim of exact independent self-information control for allowed overlapping hypergraphs. The measured classifier may still be useful.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Subtract the actual squared-sum diagonal, or state a linear-hypergraph restriction. The dense correction proves algebraic validity but does not preserve the claimed sparse runtime without further analysis.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Initial residual layers do not collapse into a fixed propagation and one weight
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, Table 1; Appendix B, Table 7
claim: The unified linearization absorbs all learned matrices into one right factor despite repeated initial-feature injections.
analysis: Take \(A=J_2/2\), \(X=(1,0)^T\), injection \(a=1/2\), scalar weights \(W_1=2,W_2=1\). The linear residual recurrence \(H_\ell=((1-a)AH_{\ell-1}+aX)W_\ell\) gives \(H_2=(1,1/2)^T\). The stated fixed propagation yields \(PX=(3/4,1/4)^T\). A common scalar would need to be both \(4/3\) and \(2\), impossible. Different injection depths carry different suffix products of learned matrices; non-residual chains or identity pre-final weights are valid special cases.
result: The unrestricted residual equivalence fails, but ZEN remains independently definable and baseline ranking changes are not inferred.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the path-dependent matrix products, restrict the equivalence to architectures with a common factor, or label the selected propagation as a new surrogate.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Count and share summaries violate necessary covariance identities
problems.source_location: Authors’ arXiv v3, Appendix E.2.6, Tables 5–6, pp. 53–54
claim: Per-seed counts satisfy \(A_r=T_rS_r\), with reported means and standard deviations of counts and shares.
analysis: Cauchy–Schwarz requires \(|\bar A/\bar T-\bar S|\le\sigma_T\sigma_S/\bar T\). Table 5 at FPR \(10^{-3}\) gives \(\bar T=15826,\sigma_T=1239,\bar A=3048,\bar S=0.133,\sigma_S=0.004\). The left side is \(0.05959446\), versus allowed \(0.00031317\); conservative rounding leaves \(0.05905679>0.00035245\). The bound \(T_r\ge\bar T-\sqrt{125}\sigma_T>0\) excludes zero-denominator suppression as an explanation. Table 6 also violates disjoint-bin mean additivity: \(10295+5883=16178\), while the stated union is \(16231\), beyond rounding.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Regenerate all counts, shares, unions and standard deviations from the same per-seed records with an explicit zero-denominator policy. Do not replace mean shares by ratios of means.
