problems.title: An infimum plus inclusive threshold is not the conservative rank rule
problems.source_location: Authors’ arXiv v3, Appendix A, p. 17; Appendix E.2.8, p. 57
claim: The paper defines \(\tau=\inf\{t:\widehat F(t^-)\ge1-\eta\}\), uses \(s\ge\tau\), and claims equivalence to a next-distinct order statistic with empirical FPR at most \(\eta\).
analysis: For OUT scores \((1,2,3,4)\) and \(\eta=1/4\), the qualifying set is \((3,\infty)\), whose infimum is \(3\). Inclusive thresholding accepts two scores, giving FPR \(1/2\). The separately supplied next-distinct rule selects \(4\), giving \(1/4\). An infimum need not itself satisfy the left-limit CDF condition. The correct rank instruction is important counterevidence against assuming the experiments used a broken implementation.
result: The formal threshold and claimed equivalence fail, while the intended rank algorithm can preserve empirical calibration. Population FPR is not guaranteed by either finite-set count alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Take a minimum over observed scores plus \(+\infty\), or use the empirical quantile with a strict comparison. State the endpoint convention and distinguish new-score decisions between observed levels.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Score spacing does not imply inverse-FPR comparison-population size
problems.source_location: Authors’ arXiv v3, Appendix A, Eq. (5), p. 17; Appendix B.2, pp. 19–20
claim: RMIA score spacing \(1/|Z|\) is used to infer a necessary comparison size of inverse minimum FPR.
analysis: Let \(|Z|=2\), both reference ratios be \(1\), comparison constant \(\gamma=1.1\). Of \(1000\) OUT records, give \(999\) ratio \(1\) and one ratio \(2\); give every IN record ratio \(2\). RMIA scores are \(0\) and \(1\). Threshold \(1\) yields FPR \(0.001\), TPR \(1\), despite \(|Z|=2\). An OUT law with masses \(0.999,0.001\) makes both reference draws equal to \(1\) with probability \(0.998001\). Score values and probability mass at those values are different quantities.
result: No distribution-free inverse-FPR requirement follows from quantization alone. Larger comparison sets can still improve the actual measured operating points.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe ties and distribution-dependent tail masses; empirical deterministic FPR resolution depends on the OUT calibration sample size and ties.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Retraining flip rate alone does not determine positive evidence
problems.source_location: Authors’ arXiv v3, Section 5; Appendix E.2.7, pp. 55–56
claim: The paper distinguishes retraining instability but additionally interprets unstable positive calls as approximately coin-toss evidence.
analysis: Take \(s\mid\mathrm{IN}\sim N(0,1)\), \(s\mid\mathrm{OUT}\sim N(\delta,1)\), \(\delta=\Phi^{-1}(0.99)\), and a likelihood-ratio threshold equivalent to \(s\le0\). Positive probabilities are \(1/2\) under IN and \(0.01\) under OUT. IN retrainings have maximal flip rate \(2(1/2)(1/2)=1/2\), yet a positive event has Bayes factor \(50\). Under prior \(1/2\), posterior membership is \(0.5/(0.5+0.01)=0.980392\). It is unstable repeatability but strong IN-versus-OUT evidence. The paper’s binomial non-rejection label does not itself assert the null is proved.
result: Flip rate measures repeatability, not evidential strength without the competing OUT law and prior. No measured histogram or particular real-record posterior is changed by this countermodel.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Report instability alongside conditional error probabilities or likelihood ratios, and define any stronger reliability claim explicitly.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: The real multivector layer takes a square root of an indefinite form
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, Eqs. (7)–(11); Appendix B.1, Eqs. (19)–(22)
claim: The architecture includes real bivector/trivector features but takes the square root of \(q(v)=s^2+\|a\|^2-\|b\|^2-t^2\).
analysis: A valid bivector \(v=e_{12}\) in \(\mathrm{Cl}_{3,0}\) has \(e_{12}^2=-1\), hence \(q(v)=-1\). Grade projection is equivariant and a legal linear layer can retain such a plane component. The nondegenerate points \[(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,2,0),(0,0,2)\] generate plane \(2e_{12}\) and volume \(4e_{123}\), so higher grades are geometrically attainable. Unit-area rescaling leaves the negative sign. Restricting every square-root input to grade one would avoid this but requires an unstated conversion inconsistent with the unrestricted displayed domain.
result: The printed real-valued layer is undefined on permitted plane features. No implementation was available to establish whether trained models encountered non-real values.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the reversion norm \(q_+(v)=\langle vv^\dagger\rangle_0=\sum_Av_A^2\ge0\), which is orthogonally invariant, or state and enforce a genuinely restricted input domain.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Displayed training targets define different conditional optima
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Eqs. (12)–(17); Appendix B.2, Eqs. (38)–(39)
claim: The decoder predicts the clean nucleotide, but one loss targets forward-corruption probabilities and another mixes transformed channel means with categorical probabilities.
analysis: If the clean label is deterministically A and \(t=1/2\), every noisy observation has clean posterior \((1,0,0,0)\), while Eq. (14) is uniquely minimized at corruption law \((5/8,1/8,1/8,1/8)\). This interior-time witness avoids endpoint weights. In the Gaussian categorical channel, \(E(Ke_x-\mathbf1)=Kr-\mathbf1\), not the output probability \(r\). For \(r=(0.30,0.27,0.23,0.20)\), the literal probability-constrained loss in Eq. (38) instead selects \((0.45,0.33,0.17,0.05)\). The clean one-hot squared error selects \(r\).
result: The formulas do not describe one coherent probability target. Which training objective generated the experiments remains unknown; intentional time-density reweighting is not itself an error.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Choose either a consistent categorical BFN channel with loss \((K/2)E[\beta'(t)\|e_x-p_\theta\|^2]\), or a discrete-corruption clean-label model. Do not combine their different targets without a derivation.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: The stated categorical message update is not Bayes’ rule
problems.source_location: Appendix C.2 and Algorithm 1, lines 10–18
claim: The Gaussian class-message channel is followed by a precision-weighted mean update, identified as a categorical Bayesian update.
analysis: With positive prior \(\theta\), message \(y\mid k\sim N(\alpha(Ke_k-\mathbf1),\alpha K I)\) has class-dependent log likelihood \(y_k\) plus a common constant. Exact Bayes therefore gives \(\theta'_k=\theta_ke^{y_k}/\sum_j\theta_je^{y_j}\), or logit addition. For uniform prior, \(\rho=1,\alpha=1,y=(1,0,0,0)\), exact first probability is \(e/(e+3)=0.47536689\); Algorithm 1 uses \(\operatorname{softmax}(y/2)\), giving \(0.35466124\). A neighborhood of this message has positive Gaussian density. The algorithm’s exponential accuracy increments also differ from the quadratic schedule underlying Eq. (17).
result: The printed sampler is not the exact Bayesian process claimed for its stated channel. A heuristic sampler could remain useful; no actual generated-data performance is inferred.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Add messages to log probabilities, and reconcile cumulative accuracy: quadratic training uses increments \(\beta(1)(2i-1)/n^2\); retaining exponential increments requires their matching training derivative.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Wet-experiment success claims conflict with stated pending validation
problems.source_location: Appendix C.3; Section 5; Appendix E
claim: The sampling-budget discussion cites wet-experiment success \(53\%\) and \(44\%\), while the conclusion and limitations say wet-laboratory validation remains unavailable/pending.
analysis: These describe incompatible evidential states if they refer to the same study. No assay protocol, tested sequence count, success criterion or laboratory records reconcile them. Another experiment, external study or stale passage could explain the text, but the inspected paper does not identify it. Computational structure-prediction scores cannot themselves establish wet-experiment success.

problems.title: Recovery gains do not imply uniformly improved structural consistency
problems.source_location: Section 4.3 and Table 3
claim: The discussion extends selected recovery and one-state advantages to broad structural superiority across state counts.
analysis: For matched three-state gRNAde AR-DSS, RBFN’s mean recovery is higher by \(0.008\), but scMCC is lower by \(0.113\), scRMSD worse by \(0.38\), scTM lower by \(0.01\), and scGDT lower by \(0.02\). Within RBFN, one-to-three-state recovery rises \(0.497\to0.548\), while all listed structural means worsen. The selected one-state scTM/scGDT advantages remain valid. These are reported mean directions, not significance tests.

problems.title: The incoherence parameter necessarily scales with tube length
problems.source_location: Assumption 2, Eq. (10); Theorem 2, Eq. (12); sample-complexity discussion
claim: The stated spectral row bound uses \(\sqrt{\mu r/(nL)}\), while the complexity narrative suppresses \(\mu\) and discusses linear tube-length dependence.
analysis: At each Fourier frequency, t-orthogonality gives \(\sum_i\|\widehat U_k(i,:)\|^2=r\). Summing the assumed bounds forces \(r\le\mu r/L\), hence \(\mu\ge L\). A flat rank-one factor \(U(i,1,:)=e_0/\sqrt n\) attains equality. Writing \(\nu=\mu/L\) exposes sufficient per-tube scaling \(\nu^5r^5\kappa^9L^6\log^2N/n\), with the floor \(m\ge1\). This is a theorem-parameter restatement, not a lower bound on algorithmic necessity. Table 1 explicitly measures sensing-operator storage rather than scalar observations.
result: The normalization and resource convention require explicit scope, but this does not refute the theorem for admissible parameters or the storage comparison.

problems.title: Pointwise concentration does not justify adaptive sensing errors
problems.source_location: Lemma 2, Eq. (100); Appendix A.2, Eqs. (41) and (54)
claim: The proof treats input tensors as fixed while applying the bound to errors selected from the same sensing matrices.
analysis: An unrestricted simultaneous reading cannot repair this: choose \(n=4,m=r=1\), one Gaussian sensing row \(z\in\mathbb R^L\), error tube \(\Delta_{11:}=z/\|z\|\), and identity tube in the first row of the right factor. Inputs have unit required norms. The left side is at least \(\|z\|^2-1\), while the proposed right side is only \(2C\sqrt{nL}\log L\). With probability at least \(1-8/L\), the former is at least \(L/2-1\), eventually larger for every fixed \(C\). This input is not claimed to be an actual recovery iterate; it rules out unrestricted uniform reinterpretation. The existence of leave-one-out sequences shows dependence was considered, but does not replace the particular direct application by a proved restricted event.
result: The adaptive invocation lacks the needed concentration justification. The fixed-input lemma and final recovery algorithm are not disproved by this adaptive witness.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State fixed-independent-input quantifiers and supply restricted-uniform or independence-restoring control for actual iterates. Fresh measurements would change the algorithm and budget; no complete repair is established.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Literal auxiliary initialization contradicts its claimed row bound
problems.source_location: Leave-one-out Eqs. (19), (24), (59), (62); Theorem 4, Eq. (28); Appendix Eq. (169)
claim: The literal auxiliary initializer divides the restored ground-truth row by \(m\), while its proof restores that row without division. The auxiliary loss similarly uses coefficient one where later recurrences use \(m\).
analysis: For fixed \(n=16,L=8,r=1\), flat \(u_i=1/4\), ground truth \(\mathcal X^*=uu^Te_0\), admissible \(\mu=L\), condition number \(1\), and independent Gaussian sensing, let \(m\to\infty\). All stated lower sample requirements are eventually met; no upper restriction is imposed. The strong law makes the literal initializer converge to the ground truth with the omitted row zeroed. Its isolated leading singular value stays positive, so its balanced left factor’s omitted row converges to zero under every orthogonal alignment. The true row has norm \(1/4\), while Theorem 4’s right side decays as \(m^{-1/2}\). Its asserted high-probability row bound therefore fails. Separately the literal loss population operator is \(mI-(m-1)P_l\), whereas the proof uses \(mI\); this mismatch already occurs with \(m<L\).
result: The displayed auxiliary process and the analyzed one differ, and the literal initializer’s theorem is false. These proof devices are not computed by the actual recovery algorithm, so its empirical failure does not follow.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restore the omitted slice after, rather than inside, division by \(m\), and weight its auxiliary loss by \(m\). This centers the operator and aligns the displayed recurrences, but all dependent proof bounds and the adaptive concentration step still need checking.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Persistent finite iterators exhaust during hybrid multi-epoch training
problems.source_location: Section 3.2/3.4; train.py, lines 435–443; train.sh
claim: The release constructs both finite loader iterators once before a requested multi-epoch alternating loop.
analysis: For two four-batch loaders, epoch zero consumes two batches from each and epoch one consumes the remaining two. Epoch two’s first video request raises StopIteration; only \(8\) updates occur despite the \(1000\)-epoch request. In general completion needs \(E\lceil L/2\rceil\le L_v\) and \(E\lfloor L/2\rfloor\le L_i\). Re-entering the outer loop does not renew exhausted iterator objects. This reasoning depends only on ordinary finite iterator semantics, not model or accelerator execution.
result: The released loop cannot generally perform its requested training schedule. Historical private training and published scores are not thereby proved wrong.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Renew iterators at each epoch for the equal-length schedule; explicitly choose stopping/cycling/resampling for unequal lengths and define whether an epoch is a full pass through either dataset.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Mask filling changes when unrelated frames are duplicated
problems.source_location: Section 3.3; train.py, lines 504–507; infer.py, line 408
claim: The conditioning expression uses per-frame/channel spatial numerators divided by total mask area across every flattened frame.
analysis: For \(N\) identical constant frames of value \(c\) with common nonempty mask area \(a\), each numerator is \(ca\) and the denominator is \(Na\); masked fill becomes \(c/N\). With \(c=1\), duplication changes fill from \(1\) to \(1/2\), even though the original pixels and mask are unchanged. Unmasked pixels are preserved. The paper does not require a per-frame-mean filling rule, so unintended semantics cannot be concluded from this dependency alone.
result: Cross-frame and frame-count dependence is exact, but whether it violates intended conditioning remains unresolved. No poorer temporal or identity score is inferred.

problems.title: Video-level retrieval percentages require a denominator clarification
problems.source_location: Section 5.1 and Tables 1/3
claim: The protocol states \(200\) generated videos and temporal average cosine comparisons, while reporting Top-1 \(78.3\%\) and Top-5 \(90.2\%\).
analysis: If each video produces one binary ranked result, accuracy lies on multiples of \(100/200=0.5\) percentage points; neither printed value is attainable, including one-decimal rounding. But framewise ranking over \(200\times128=25600\) frames has spacing \(0.00390625\) points, and \(20045\) successes gives \(78.30078125\%\). Repeats, exclusions or different pairing counts could likewise explain finer increments.
result: The direct one-rank-per-video reading is incompatible with the table, but the actual hidden metric convention is unresolved. No replacement accuracy is justified.

problems.title: The sample demo is not the full benchmark protocol
problems.source_location: Appendix A; infer.py, lines 666–667 and 760
claim: The paper evaluates \(128\)-frame videos with \(32\) DDIM steps; the README sample demo caps frame length at \(80\) and requests \(40\) steps.
analysis: A \(128\)-frame input remains divisible by \(8\), then the source cap yields \(80\) frames. The pipeline explicitly receives \(40\) inference steps. The README calls this a sample test, so a separate benchmark implementation could use the published settings.
result: This limits reproduction through the demo rather than disproving a paper result. A matching evaluator needs explicit frame cap, steps, checkpoint and metric configuration.

problems.title: Adding identity transitions can accelerate mixing
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, identity-addition interpretation
claim: The paper states that \((I+A)/2\) preserves stationary state and slows convergence because of increased self-transition.
analysis: Take positive stochastic attention \(A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}.1&.9\\.9&.1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), realizable by finite logits \(Q=I,K=\sqrt2(\log A)^T\). Its nontrivial eigenvalue is \(-.8\); the lazy chain has \(.1\). From a single-state start, total variation to \((1/2,1/2)\) is \((.8)^k/2\) versus \((.1)^k/2\). Thus identity addition accelerates this already aperiodic chain. Stationary-distribution preservation remains valid.
result: The unrestricted mixing-direction explanation is false. TokenRank and reported empirical improvements are not thereby refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State the eigenvalue map \(\lambda\mapsto(1+\lambda)/2\); mixing direction depends on the spectrum. A reversible nonnegative-spectrum restriction supports the narrower spectral-slowdown statement.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Eigenvalue modulus does not certify metastable regions
problems.source_location: Sections 3.1/4.4; Supplement E.1; dino.py eigenvalue weighting
claim: The magnitude of the second eigenvalue is associated with stable metastable regions and used for head weighting.
analysis: Positive stochastic matrices with diagonal entries \(.99\) or \(.01\), respectively, have nontrivial eigenvalues \(.98\) and \(-.98\), hence identical modulus. In a two-state chain, expected singleton residence time is \(1/(1-A_{ii})\): \(100\) for the first, only \(1/.99\) for the second. Large negative modulus describes persistent alternation rather than prolonged residence; the scalar also loses multiplicity information.
result: Modulus alone neither certifies nor counts metastable regions. The measured weighting correlation can still hold for observed attention heads; their negative-mode frequency is unmeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Present modulus as an empirical spectral feature; stronger semantic-metastability claims require structural assumptions and retention/exit measurements.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Nonuniform personalization breaks row stochasticity
problems.source_location: helpers.py, prep_for_power_method, lines 63–83
claim: The helper promises a stochastic personalized transition but uses \(E=ee^T/n\).
analysis: For \(A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}.8&.2\\.3&.7\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(\alpha=.8\) and probability vector \(e=(.75,.25)^T\), the returned row sums are \(.875\) and \(.825\). Generally they equal \(\alpha+(1-\alpha)e_i\sum_je_j/n\), not one. Normalizing later power iterates produces a different Perron iteration, not a stochastic matrix. The default all-ones branch is valid.
result: The optional personalized release branch violates its contract. No evidence shows published demos used that branch.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For normalized positive \(p\), use \(T=\alpha A+(1-\alpha)\mathbf1p^T\). Rows sum to one; positivity gives ergodicity. Zero entries in \(p\) need additional assumptions for that stronger guarantee.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Marginal transport improvement does not establish semantic gain
problems.source_location: Theorem 1, Eq. (4); Appendix A.1
claim: The theorem chains input information bounds into a claimed semantic-information improvement from marginal Wasserstein alignment.
analysis: Let independent fair bits \(C,U\) form \(X=Y=(C,U)\), and \(Z=U\oplus E\) with independent crossover \(E\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/4)\). A decoder reading only the nuisance bit has positive probabilities and globally Lipschitz negative log probabilities after clipped linear extension. Equal marginals give optimal transport reduction \(\Delta=0\). Yet \(I(Z;C)=0\), \(I(Z;X,Y)=r=\log2-h(1/4)>0\), and admissible residual bound \(\varepsilon=r\) makes the printed chain \(0\ge0\ge r\), false. Independently, let \(X=C\) be a fair bit, \(Y=0\), and decoder probability \(q(Z=1\mid x)=1/4+x/2\). Optimal transport maps \(X\) to zero, reducing Wasserstein distance \(1/\sqrt2\to0\), but the rerun encoder’s task information drops \(r\to0\). Regularity holds and no task-sufficiency premise excludes this.
result: The chain omits a necessary residual term, and even restoring it does not prove that marginal alignment preserves or improves semantics. Transport can remain an empirically useful heuristic.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For \(W=(T(X),Y)\) and \(C\to W\to Z_T\), the valid identity is \(I(Z_T;C)=I(Z_T;W)-I(Z_T;W\mid C)\). An upper residual bound gives its corresponding lower bound only; a transport-gain theorem needs task-sufficiency and joint-law control.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: The Gaussian information bound lacks its real-valued domain
problems.source_location: Theorem 2, Eq. (10); Appendix A.2
claim: The bound contains \(-\log(1-\operatorname{Var}(\mu_i)/\sigma_i^2)\) without requiring the ratio below one.
analysis: Choose independent \(\mu\sim N(0,2)\), \(R=\epsilon\sim N(0,1)\), \(\sigma=1\). The joint covariance is positive definite, its normalized cross-covariance matrix is zero and satisfies the stated diagonal domination, but the ratio is \(2\). Actual information is zero, while the printed real logarithm is \(\log(-1)\). Also \(M\preceq\operatorname{diag}(M_{ii})\) forces exact diagonality, since their positive-semidefinite difference has zero trace. Independent encoder noise plus joint Gaussianity makes zero covariance imply independence; heteroscedastic non-Gaussian encoders need not satisfy that idealization.
result: A missing positivity restriction makes the formula undefined on its claimed domain. No real-valued too-small bound or actual learned-encoder violation is asserted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Require \(0\preceq M\preceq D\prec I\) and ratios \(r_i<1\). Gaussian information \(-\log\det(I-M)/2\) and determinant monotonicity then give the restricted logarithmic bound; ratios at least one require an explicit vacuous convention.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Training and evaluation feed different modality order to one encoder
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1/2; datasets/dataset.py; models/ddm.py, Net.forward; models/decom.py
claim: The dataset returns visible then infrared; training aligns infrared and passes aligned-infrared then visible, while evaluation forwards the original order without alignment.
analysis: For constant visible \(1\) and infrared \(0\), balanced transport helper \(.8(PY)+.2X\) yields aligned infrared \(.8\). Encoder inputs become \((.8,1)\) in training and \((1,0)\) at evaluation. An allowed first convolution selecting its second channel gives outputs \(1\) and \(0\), proving no architectural equivalence. The later decoder cannot retroactively change encoded skip features. Omitting alignment appears in inference pseudocode and may be deliberate; the channel reversal is an additional discrepancy.

problems.title: Averaging does not establish statistical significance
problems.source_location: Checklist question 7
claim: The checklist infers statistical significance from averaging many dataset tests.

Mean gain is \(.001\), but exactly half the differences are positive, giving two-sided sign-test \(p=1\); the paired t statistic is about \(.316\). Thus many averaged observations do not by themselves prove significance. This example is a logical diagnostic, not the paper’s scores.

problems.title: The odds theorem is conditional on generator-kernel calibration
problems.source_location: Theorem 4.1, Eq. (8); Appendix D.1–D.5
claim: Equal distances imply equal Gaussian neighbor probabilities; the proof identifies that kernel with actual diffusion attribute probabilities.
analysis: Take \(z_1=(1,0),z_2=(-1,0),u=(0,1),\rho=1\). Equal squared distances \(2\) give kernel probabilities \((1/2,1/2)\). A separate generator can obey every attribute-specific prompt perfectly but generate attributes \((.9,.1)\) from the neutral prompt. A constant concept gives attribute–concept independence. This does not contradict a theorem that explicitly assumes the actual generator is the calibrated Gaussian kernel; it shows that neighbor selection and prompt compliance do not derive that premise.
result: Under the intended calibrated idealization the exponential-distance algebra is valid. Its application to learned diffusion remains a modeling assumption requiring qualification.

problems.title: Normalized centroid cosine changes the intended mean score
problems.source_location: Section 4.2.1, Eqs. (9)–(10); Algorithm 1
claim: The losses replace mean image cosine scores by cosine to an average image embedding, dropping the centroid norm.
analysis: For unit text \(u=(1,0)\), let attribute embeddings be \((.8,\pm.6)\) and \((.2,\pm\sqrt{.96})\), each equiprobable. Centroids \((.8,0)\) and \((.2,0)\) both have cosine \(1\), but squared distances to \(u\) are \(.04\) and \(.64\), giving calibrated odds \((.5744425,.4255575)\) at unit bandwidth. Generally \(E\cos(t,X)=t^T\mu\), whereas \(\cos(t,\mu)=t^T\mu/\|\mu\|\). Attribute-specific rotations preserve the example and give mean-score spread \(.3\) while centroid-cosine spread is zero. Algorithm 1’s raw dot product is valid counterevidence: actual implementation convention is unavailable.
result: The displayed cosine loss differs from the intended mean-score/unnormalized-distance target. This does not show the unreleased experiments used the wrong convention.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use raw centroid dot products for mean cosine. For distance-based odds, retain actual squared distances or explicitly redefine normalized representatives and calibrated model.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: The embedding attention formula does not specify a foreground image
problems.source_location: Section 4.2.2, Eq. (13); Algorithm 1
claim: Attention over image/text embeddings is described as a highlighted image fed back to the image encoder.
analysis: With one pooled image query and one pooled text key/value, the score has one entry, so softmax is \([1]\) and the output is the text value regardless of the image. Its shape is an embedding, not RGB pixels or a spatial mask. With token matrices, the output is a mixture of text values per image token; patch-grid selection, mask aggregation, normalization and upsampling are still needed. A hidden routine could supply them; visual examples do not uniquely define it.
result: The published operator is insufficient to reproduce the foreground module. Actual generated foreground images are not proved independent of input.

problems.title: Spectral ordering needs a decreasing-power premise
problems.source_location: Proposition 4.2; Appendix E
claim: The proposition states a universal low-frequency recovery advantage and assigns attributes to late high-frequency recovery.
analysis: The derived SNR increment is \(\Delta_i(f)=K_iS(f)\), with \(K_i>0\). It decreases in frequency only if signal power does. A positive \(16\)-pixel signal \(x_j=3+\cos(2\pi j/16)/2+2\cos(8\pi j/16)\) has unitary powers \(S(1)=1,S(4)=16\). With cumulative noise values \(.1,.4,.2\) and unit expected noise power, increments are \(1/24\) and \(2/3\), reversing the unrestricted ordering. Dividing pixels by \(6\) fits \([0,1]\) without changing the ratio. A decreasing power-law model gives the claimed conditional ordering, but neither SNR nor frequency alone identifies semantic attribute timing.
result: The universal spectral/semantic explanation fails; the measured two-stage sampler can still work in its tested prompts.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State the decreasing expected signal-power premise and restrict the result to the SNR surrogate; retain semantic timing as an empirical observation.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: The released visual reward computes tag recall rather than predicted-entity precision
problems.source_location: Equation (2); examples/train/grpo/globe/plugin.py, GeoVisalEntityMatching2ORM
claim: The paper averages matching scores over entities extracted from predicted reasoning; the release divides by grounded image-tag count.
analysis: Let grounded tags be road and tree. An explanation containing those alone gets reward \(1\) under both rules. Add three unmatched entities dragon, spaceship and ocean. The paper’s predicted-entity mean becomes \(2/5=.4\), while the source still finds both grounded tags and returns \(2/2=1\). This difference does not rely on substring behavior; partial lexical matching is expressly allowed. Recall can legitimately encourage coverage but does not penalize additional ungrounded entities as the precision-like formula does.
result: The release changes the stated visual-hallucination training signal. Actual hallucination frequency and published model effects remain unmeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify the predicted-entity extractor and matching rule, then average over those extracted entities with an explicit empty-set convention; alternatively identify the release as tag recall and qualify its interpretation.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Country substrings can reward a wrong geographic answer
problems.source_location: Equation (3); plugin.py, GeoLocAccuracyV2ORM; eval.py matcher
claim: The geographic reward must be zero for a wrong country, but the approximate matcher accepts sufficiently long substrings.
analysis: For true Niger/Niamey and predicted Nigeria/Kaduna, niger is contained in nigeria and length ratio \(5/7\ge.7\); the country gate passes and the city gate fails, returning \(.2\) instead of \(0\). Exact aliases are useful, but Niger and Nigeria are different countries. This source predicate need not be the geocoding/distance pipeline behind published threshold metrics.
result: The current reward and string evaluator can conflate distinct countries. No distance-threshold accuracy change is established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Compare canonical geographic identifiers after a versioned alias map, retaining genuine aliases while separating distinct countries.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Truncated first-token probabilities do not identify localizability probability
problems.source_location: Equation (1); plugin.py, GeoLocatablityORM
claim: The release renormalizes hard-coded yes/no spellings found only among the top \(5\) first-token log probabilities.
analysis: A valid distribution on yes, maybe, perhaps, unknown, uncertain, other, no with probabilities \[(.30,.15,.14,.13,.12,.10,.06)\] includes yes but omits no from the top five. The source returns essentially \(1\); unconditional positive mass is \(.30\), while even the complete binary-renormalized value is \(.30/(.30+.06)=5/6\). Missing mass cannot be treated as zero. If both full class masses and all accepted spellings are included, binary renormalization is a valid special case.
result: The probability extraction is not generally the stated positive-class probability. Server-specific incidence and reward calibration remain unresolved; no API request was made.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Define the target probability and score complete fixed-label sequences, then use stable normalization of their full log likelihoods. Explicitly handle alternative tokenization and avoid top-k omissions as true zeros.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Released reward weights reverse preferences relative to the paper
problems.source_location: Equation (4); Appendix Table 11; train_all_rewards.sh
claim: The paper uses localizability/visual/geographic weights \((.2,.5,1)\); the launcher assigns \((.5,.2,1)\) by name and adds format reward.
analysis: With equal format/geographic contributions, response reward triples \(A=(.9,0,0)\) and \(B=(.1,1,0)\) have paper totals \(.18,.52\), but released totals \(.45,.25\). Ordering reverses; subtracting group means and dividing by positive standard deviation preserves that reversal, so GRPO normalization cannot absorb the mismatch as a common scale. A later release configuration could differ from the historical experiment, but those configurations are not equivalent.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use an explicit named weight map matching the intended objective and disclose any fourth format term; reconcile actual training provenance before evaluating changes.
The described correction remains a proposal; author adoption or a corresponding erratum is not established.

problems.title: Overall and scene-specific tables need run/denominator reconciliation
problems.source_location: Tables 1, 2 and 7; public author reply in repository issue 3
claim: The declared test set partitions \(12000\) images into \(2096\) indoor, \(1092\) nature and \(8812\) urban examples; matching scene and overall metrics should share a weighted counting identity.
analysis: At \(200\,\mathrm{km}\), GLOBE’s scene percentages \(64.71,81.40,74.76\) yield weighted overall \(73.60884\%\), while Table 2 gives \(73.83\%\). The \(.22116\)-point difference exceeds the conservative \(.010\)-point two-decimal rounding allowance. Different runs, separately selected best results, valid-geocode subsets or denominators can break the common-evaluation premise. The author’s prior issue reply discusses best-run selection and geocoding service changes for an external reproduction, but does not map these particular cells to runs. A common average across the same runs and fixed denominators would still obey linearity.
