problems.title: The output-length explanation needs a common aggregation convention
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v 2, Appendix C, Table 11 and following paragraph, PDF p.24
claim: The paragraph attributes shorter generations primarily to a larger proportion of correct responses, which tend to be shorter.
analysis: Under response-level pooling, let \(p\) be the correct fraction and \(c,w\) the conditional mean lengths. Then \(m=pc+(1-p)w\). The exact symmetric composition contribution between settings is \[C=\tfrac12(p_1-p_0)[(c_0-w_0)+(c_1-w_1)].\] For short supervision, the table gives \(p_0=1267/2500\), \(p_1=1360/2500\), \((c_0,w_0)=(3189,23145)\) and \((c_1,w_1)=(3906,14921)\). The reconstructed change is \(-4102.4592\) tokens, of which composition contributes \(-576.0606\), about \(14.04\%\). For long supervision the corresponding amounts are \(-2059.2932\) and \(-709.3710\), about \(34.45\%\). Changes within outcome groups account for more under this convention.

The reconstructed row means are \[13031.2992,8928.84,12119.1668,10059.8736\], while the printed overall means are \(12991,8782,11187,9335\). Ordinary rounding cannot explain these differences. However, conditional means averaged equally over questions need not have the same weights as pooled correct/incorrect counts. That alternative can break the displayed pooling identity without making the measurements erroneous. The aggregate table does not identify the convention or the causal mechanism.
result: The principal-composition explanation is unsupported by the pooled interpretation, but the actual weighting/cohort remains unresolved. Response-level records or an explicit aggregation definition are needed before declaring an erroneous empirical table. The reported reasoning accuracies are not refuted.
assumptions: The decomposition requires the same response cohort and compatible conditional/unconditional weights.

problems.title: The forward Brownian identity omits a Laplacian drift
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v 3, Appendix A.2, Eq.(17), PDF p.17; Appendix B, Eq.(35), p.20
claim: For forward Brownian motion \(dX_t=dW_t\), Eq.(17) writes \[U(X_0,0)=U(X_T,T)-\int_0^T\nabla U\cdot dW_t+\tfrac12\int_0^T\|\nabla U\|^2dt.\]
analysis:
For the true heat-flow energy \(U=-\log p_t\), \(\partial_tU=	frac12\Delta U-	frac12\|
abla U\|^2\). Forward Itô calculus therefore gives \[dU=
abla U\cdot dW_t+(\Delta U-	frac12\|
abla U\|^2)dt.\] Take the normalized heat flow \(p_t=\mathcal N(0,1+t)\). Then \(U(y,t)=	frac12\log[2\pi(1+t)]+y^2/[2(1+t)]\) and \(\Delta U=1/(1+t)\). The printed right-hand side exceeds the true initial energy by \(\log(1+T)\) on every Brownian path, almost surely. At \(T=1\), the gap is \(\log2>0\).

A right-endpoint stochastic integral adds the quadratic-covariation term \(\int\Delta U\,dt\), so that convention can rescue the displayed formula. It is not the ordinary forward Itô reading of the stated forward SDE. This is a background estimator identity; the spatial/time-score training objectives do not use this formula.
result: The stated forward interpretation needs a drift correction or an explicit backward-integral convention. This does not establish an error in the reported learned-energy likelihood measurements.
assumptions: The density is positive and smooth; the stochastic integral uses the forward Itô convention.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For a smooth true heat-flow energy, subtract \(\int_0^T\Delta U(X_t,t)dt\) from the printed right-hand side. Alternatively, explicitly define and consistently discretize a right-endpoint integral.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Bayes optimality does not give a pointwise dimensionality upper bound
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v 3, Eq.(11), PDF p.9; Appendix C.3, p.22
claim: Appendix C.3 claims the denoiser-MSE dimensionality estimate upper-bounds the true dimensionality. Equation (11) conditions on an individual clean image \(X=x\).
analysis: Let the true clean law be \(P=\mathcal N(0,1)\), noise variance \(t=1\), and model law \(Q=\mathcal N(0,1/3)\). Both give smooth, normalized heat flows. The true denoiser is \(m(y)=y/2\), while the model-energy denoiser is \(g(y)=y/4\). With \(Y=x+Z\) and \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), \[D(x,1)=(x^2+1)/4,\qquad D_g(x,1)=(9x^2+1)/16.\] Thus \(D_g-D=(5x^2-3)/16<0\) throughout \(|x|<\sqrt{3/5}\), a set of positive probability. At \(x=0\), the estimate is \(1/16\) versus the true \(1/4\).

Bayes orthogonality instead gives the population identity \[\mathbb E\|X-g(Y)\|^2=\mathbb E\|X-m(Y)\|^2+\mathbb E\|m(Y)-g(Y)\|^2.\] Its cross term vanishes after conditioning on \(Y\), not after fixing \(X=x\). In this same example, population dimensionalities are \(1/2\) and \(5/8\), so population Bayes optimality survives.
result: The one-sided interpretation of individual-image dimensionalities is invalid. Their actual observed curves, nonnegativity and the population MSE bound are not disproved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State the upper bound only after averaging over the true clean-data law: \(\mathbb E_XD_g=\mathbb E_XD+t^{-1}\mathbb E\|m_t(Y)-g_t(Y)\|^2\). Individual-image estimates remain nonnegative but have no general one-sided error guarantee.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The homogeneity discussion depends on regularity at the origin
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v 3, Appendix B.2, PDF p.19
claim: The discussion relates a conservative degree-one homogeneous score to Gaussian conditionals along affine lines.
analysis: Degree-one homogeneity with differentiability at the origin implies \(s(y)=Ds(0)y\), by evaluating \([s(hy)-s(0)]/h\) as \(h\downarrow0\). Conservativity then gives a symmetric quadratic potential; normalizability requires a positive-definite precision. Gaussian conditionals follow. A counterexample based on \(V(a,b)=\tfrac12\sqrt{a^4+b^4}\) lacks score differentiability at the origin and therefore does not refute this globally differentiable reading.
result: Retain this as a regularity clarification. No separate error is established under the stronger smoothness interpretation, and no exact Gaussian claim is inferred for the approximately homogeneous trained architecture.

problems.title: The unknown-graph preprocessing claim omits interaction strength
problems.source_location: Proceedings Remark 1.4 and Theorem 1.3, PDF p.3; Definition 1.2, p.2; current arXiv v 1 corresponding passages
claim: Remark 1.4 proposes exact recovery of an unknown MRF dependency graph with complexity \(\operatorname{poly}(n^t,2^\lambda)\), then applies the known-graph junta algorithm. No lower bound on nonzero interactions is included.
analysis: Let \(n=2,\lambda=1,\sigma=1/4\), draw \(\alpha_i\) independently uniformly on \([-1/4,1/4]\), and set \[P_{\eta,\alpha}(x)\propto e^{\eta x_1x_2}(1+\alpha_1)^{x_1}(1+\alpha_2)^{x_2},\qquad0\leq\eta\leq1.\] This is positive, order at most two, degree at most one, and has unperturbed derivative coefficient norms at most \(1\). Its minimal graph is empty at \(\eta=0\), but has an edge for every \(\eta>0\), since its odds ratio is \(e^\eta\). The prescribed external-field smoothing does not change that ratio.

Writing \(F(\eta)=\log Z_\alpha(\eta)\), the sufficient statistic \(x_1x_2\) is binary, so \(F^{\prime\prime}\leq1/4\) and \(D_{\rm KL}(P_{0,\alpha}\Vert P_{\eta,\alpha})\leq\eta^2/8\). For any sample budget \(N\geq1\), choose \(\eta=N^{-1/2}\). Product-law Pinsker gives total variation at most \(1/4\), even if the smoothing coordinates are revealed. Any exact-graph test then has equal-prior average error at least \(3/8\), preventing success \(2/3\) on both alternatives with a budget independent of interaction strength.

This concerns exact minimal-graph recovery. A valid supergraph is a different target; the complete graph is always valid but can destroy the degree-dependent runtime. The formal junta theorem explicitly receives a graph, and the calculation does not refute that known-graph guarantee or rule out a different robust preprocessing method.
result: The stated strength-independent exact-recovery preprocessing is unsupported. Keep the supplied-graph theorem separate from this extension.
assumptions: The disputed target is exact minimal-graph recovery, rather than an arbitrary valid supergraph.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the known-graph theorem, and restrict the cited exact-structure-learning pipeline to the identifiability/nondegeneracy assumptions of the chosen structure learner, including its interaction-strength-dependent sample cost.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The auxiliary fairness domain need not contain its required averages
problems.source_location: Proceedings Section 5.1.1, Eq.(3), PDF pp.6–7; Algorithm 1, p.7; Theorems 5.1–5.2, p.8; current arXiv v 1 corresponding statements
claim: The reformulation restricts \(z_t\in\mathcal Z=\{Ax:A\in\mathcal A,x\in\mathcal X\}\) and claims equal optimum to the original horizon-fairness objective, by choosing each \(z_t\) to be the average fairness vector. The assumptions do not make \(\mathcal Z\) convex.
analysis: Take \(T=2\), \(\mathcal X=\{1\}\), \(\mathcal A=\{-1,1\}\), \((A_1,A_2)=(-1,1)\), zero hitting/switching costs and \(g(z)=|z|\). Then \(\mathcal Z=\{-1,1\}\), and the original optimum is \(0\). The auxiliary equality requires \(z_1+z_2=0\), but each feasible pair has average fairness cost \(1\). The proposed constant choice \(z_t=0\) is infeasible.

The central performance bound also fails on a convex action domain. Set \(T=10^6\), \(\eta=1/100=T^{-1/3}\), \(R=2,\delta=0\), \(\mathcal X=[1,2]\), alternating \(A_t=1,-1\), losses \(f_{2j-1}(x)=(x-2)^2\), \(f_{2j}(x)=(x-1)^2\), \(g=|\cdot|\), \(\beta_1=\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0\), quadratic mirror reference and \(\kappa_1=0\). Then \(\mathcal Z=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]\), diameter \(Z=4\), and \(L=l=\beta_2=1\). The constant comparator \(x_t^*=3/2\) has cost \(1/4\) and satisfies the exact frame restriction. Convexity shows no comparator is better.

Let \(a=1-\eta/2\) and \(k=\kappa_{2j-1}\). The printed exact minimizers and unrestricted mirror update give pair maps \[k\mapsto ak+\eta-3\eta^2/2\quad(k<0),\qquad k\mapsto a^2k-\eta-\eta^2/2\quad(k\geq0).\] They preserve \([-\eta-\eta^2/2,\eta]\), starting from zero. The auxiliary minimizer has the sign of \(\kappa_t\); at zero choose \(z_t=1\), an allowed minimizer. Consequently odd actions are at least \(2-\eta/2\) and even actions at most \(1+3\eta/2\). Average fairness cost is at least \(1/2-\eta=0.49\), so total cost is at least \(0.49\). Yet Theorem 5.1 gives \[J\leq1/4+0.16+\sqrt{0.000816}<0.439.\] Theorem 5.2 has the same failed specialization at its allowed zero-switching boundary with \(\lambda_1=1,\lambda_2=0,m=2\).

This witness follows Algorithm 1’s stated minimization over \(\kappa\in\mathbb R^M\). Nearby prose calls the update projected mirror descent; an additionally projected update would be a different algorithm and is not refuted by the displayed recurrence.
result: The auxiliary equivalence and central stated bounds fail on allowed instances. The independent lower-bound results, positive-switching regimes and data-center empirical tables are not refuted by this construction.
assumptions: Matrices may have real signed entries; the theorem explicitly permits zero switching cost and the stated hyperparameter specialization.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Replace the auxiliary domain by \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\mathcal Z)\) and require the fairness function to be convex and Lipschitz there. Constant average vectors become feasible, and Jensen proves equivalence. The supplied correction proves the Euclidean zero-switching performance case; it does not establish the full general-reference, positive-switching theorem.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The central routing-to-gradient guarantee uses false selection and expectation steps
problems.source_location: Proceedings Theorem 1, Eq.(10), PDF pp.6–7; Appendix D, Eqs.(15)–(21), pp.23–24
claim: Theorem 1 asserts that hierarchical sentence–token routing cannot decrease expected gradient cosine similarity. The appendix models a tracked expert’s gradients as binary gates times iid unit gradients.
analysis: Positive coordinate multiplication does not preserve top-\(k\) selection: with \(k=1\), token scores \(r=(2,1)\) select the first expert, whereas sentence scores \(s=(1,3)\) give \(s\odot r=(2,3)\) and select the second. Softmax preserves these rankings. Thus the proof’s implication \(B=1\Rightarrow A=1\) is false.

Equation (17) also factors \(\mathbb E[Ag]\) into \(\mathbb EA\,\mathbb Eg\) although both quantities depend on a token. Iid tokens do not imply this within-token independence. Further, for a Bernoulli gate, \(\mathbb E[A^2]=p\) but \((\mathbb EA)^2=p^2\); the printed replacement confuses these expressions.

For a complete two-type witness within the proof’s abstraction, draw each type independently with probability \(1/2\). Type \(a\) has \(g=+1,r=(2,1),s=(1,1)\); type \(b\) has \(g=-1,r=(1,2),s=(3,1)\). For the first expert, \((A,B)=(1,1)\) and \((1,0)\). One-hot token features and one-token sentences realize the linear score maps; \(L_t(\theta)=\tfrac12(\theta+g_t)^2\) realizes the unit derivatives at \(\theta=0\). Hence \[\mathbb Eg=\mathbb E[Ag]=0,\quad\mathbb E[Bg]=\tfrac12,\quad\|\mathbb E[Ag]\|^2-\|\mathbb E[Bg]\|^2=-\tfrac14.\] The variances are \(1\) and \(1/4\), reversing the claimed ordering despite actual gate containment.

Cosine at a zero gated gradient is undefined. With zero-embedded dot products the preceding difference is \(-1/4\); with independent active-token cosine the token router has similarity \(1\), while the hierarchical router has \(0\). These are explicit interpretations, rather than assigning cosine to zero. This construction checks the appendix’s binary-gradient model, not all nonlinear LoRA training dynamics.

Theorem 2 explicitly assumes a variance ordering. Monotonicity of its generalization upper bound under that assumption remains valid; the architecture-to-premise argument is what fails. An ordering of upper bounds alone also does not order realized generalization errors.
result: The unrestricted routing guarantee loses its supplied mathematical support through independent false steps and an opposing witness within its own abstraction. Published benchmark accuracies are not remeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The existing restricted statement is valid for a dot-product statistic when the gate is independent of a unit gradient: \(\mathbb E[(Ag)^\top(A^{\prime}g^{\prime})]=p_A^2\|\mathbb Eg\|^2\). It does not establish independence for the actual feature-dependent gates, define zero-gradient cosine, or recover the unrestricted guarantee.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The current stage-two forward path discards the domain-router output
problems.source_location: Proceedings Eqs.(2)–(5), p.5 and Section 3.3, p.6; official supplement HiMoLE/src/finetune_stage2.py, lines 45–64; src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py, LlamaMLP.forward, lines 307–363
claim: The method fuses sentence/domain scores with token scores and jointly trains the hierarchical routers.
analysis: The stage-two installer creates per-domain token routers and a domain router. In the installed gates branch, lines 315–323 concatenate token-router outputs into expert_weight. Lines 334–337 compute the pooled sentence output and assign the domain router’s result to extra_weight. That local tensor is never subsequently used.

The diversity path uses token weights with one-hot group masks, the main projections use unchanged expert_weight at line 358, and the function returns only projected outputs, token weights and optionally diversity loss at lines 360–363. Therefore, absent an external side-effect loss or separately injected parameter use, changing the domain-router parameters has no computational path to these returned quantities. A separate sentence-only branch does not change this hierarchical branch.
result: The current official release does not implement the claimed sentence-conditioned fusion through this path. The source alone does not establish which historical code produced the paper’s benchmark tables.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The existing correction must feed the sentence–token product through the stated softmax/top-k order into the actual expert weights and returned routing statistics. It remains an unadopted implementation proposal without a restored benchmark result.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Signed and absolute cosine losses optimize different objectives
problems.source_location: Proceedings Eqs.(7)–(8), PDF p.6; official supplement src/transformers/models/llama/modeling_llama.py, line 356
claim: Equation (7) averages signed pairwise cosine similarities and adds this diversity loss with a positive coefficient. The release applies an absolute value before averaging.
analysis: For \(e_1=(1,0),e_2=(-1,0)\), the paper’s signed average is \(-1\); the implemented absolute average is \(1\), up to the normalization epsilon. Orthogonal unit outputs give \(0\) in both. Minimizing signed cosine favors antiparallel vectors, whereas minimizing its absolute value favors orthogonality. No general nonnegative-cosine restriction is stated.
result: The two specifications differ in optimization geometry, rather than only scaling or floating-point precision. No conclusion about which choice improves OOD performance follows.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the supplied alternatives: include the absolute value in the mathematical objective if it expresses the intended method, or remove it from the implementation if signed similarity was intended. Author intent and any necessary training rerun remain unresolved.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: A Bellman conditional expectation is treated as a realized return on eventual ruin
problems.source_location: Proceedings Eq.(1), p.3; Eq.(2), p.4; Theorem 2 and preceding definitions, p.7; notation table, p.20; Appendix C, Eq.(17), p.24
claim: The paper defines \(G=\widetilde R+v^*_{t+1}(b+\widetilde R)\) and \(\nu=\mathbb E[G\mid S]\), with \(S\) eventual survival. Theorem 2’s proof uses \[q=-b\Pr(S^c)+\mathbb E[G\mathbf1_S].\]
analysis: Take initial budget \(b=1\), two remaining decisions, one action, and independent raw rewards \(-2,0,3\), each with probability \(1/3\). Apply the paper’s clipping \(\widetilde R=\max(-b,R)\) and absorption at zero. The one-decision continuation values are \(v(0)=0,v(1)=2/3,v(4)=1/3\). Consequently \(G\) equals \(-1,2/3,10/3\), respectively, and \(q=\mathbb EG=1\).

The nine equally likely raw pairs have realized total clipped returns \[(-1,-1,-1,-1,0,3,1,3,6)\]. Exactly the final five survive. Therefore \[\Pr(S)=5/9,\qquad\mathbb E[G\mathbf1_S]=34/27,\qquad\nu=34/15.\] The proof’s expression is \(-4/9+34/27=22/27\), differing from \(q=1\) by \(5/27\). The failure term is actually \(\mathbb E[G\mathbf1_{S^c}]=-7/27\), rather than \(-12/27\).

The path with first reward \(0\) and second reward \(-2\) explains the distinction: realized return is \(-1\), but the first-step Bellman variable remains \(2/3\). Conditioning on later ruin changes the future distribution; the unconditioned tower property does not justify the substitution. The notation table confirms the expected-continuation definition, so treating \(G\) as a realized trajectory return changes the object.

The example meets the finite, bounded reward and optimal-continuation model. With one action, however, it does not satisfy the nontrivial positive competing-action survival-gap premises of the full theorem. The theorem is not declared false by this identity counterexample. One-decision, certain-survival and immediate-ruin controls preserve the decomposition.
result: The supplied proof of the long-term-survival result needs a corrected return definition or an additional conditioning argument. The unchanged sufficient-condition theorem is not established by this proof. The other behavior results, Bellman recursion and empirical dynamic-programming plots are not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The supplied replacement uses realized total clipped return \(H\), which telescopes to \(-b\) on ruin. Writing \(S_a\) for survival probability and \(M_a=\mathbb E[H\mathbf1_{S_a}]\), the exact identity is \(q_a=-b(1-S_a)+M_a\). Hence \[b(S_{\hat a}-S_a)\geq M_a-M_{\hat a}\ \Longrightarrow\ q_{\hat a}\geq q_a.\] This proves a comparison with a different return-gap definition, rather than the original theorem unchanged.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Full-batch centering removes the prescribed outer gradient at unit likelihood ratios
problems.source_location: Proceedings Algorithm 1, PDF p.7, steps 5–6; current author wrapper/RA_C_RL.py, opt_var_update, lines 49–117; utils/storage.py, full_batch_generator, lines 148–170
claim: Algorithm 1 updates risk variables by sample-Lagrangian derivatives. The release instead differentiates a full-batch normalized PPO surrogate with respect to those reward parameters.
analysis: Let the unnormalized advantages be \(A_j(\lambda,t)\) and \(\widehat A_j=(A_j-\overline A)/(s(A)+10^{-5})\). Their sum is identically zero. The full-batch generator shuffles without splitting. With the unchanged policy and matching stored actions/log probabilities, all likelihood ratios are \(1\), and clipping leaves them unchanged. Thus \[\mathcal L_{\rm action}=-N^{-1}\sum_j\widehat A_j\equiv0,\qquad\nabla_{\lambda,t}\mathcal L_{\rm action}=0.\] Returns and value predictions are detached before the value loss, so it cannot restore the outer derivative.

The source stage reward is \(\widetilde r=r+\lambda[c+t-\beta^{-1}(t+v)_+]\). Take rewards \((1,2,3,4)\), velocities \((2,3,4,5)\), \(\gamma=0.9,\beta=0.5,c=1,(\lambda,t)=(0.4,-1)\). Every hinge is strictly active. The fixed-data discounted Lagrangian has derivatives \(\partial_\lambda\widehat L=-16.292\) and \(\partial_t\widehat L=-1.3756\), in contrast to the surrogate’s exact zero. Any positive sum/mean rescaling retains the discrepancy.

The collector permits zero additional action noise, making the unit-ratio case admissible. The paper’s noisy default also has the separate bookkeeping defect below; therefore this argument does not claim that every published noisy run freezes its outer parameters. Nonunit ratios can produce a derivative, but do not derive the prescribed sample-Lagrangian gradient.
result: The inspected current implementation fails to implement the outer update in this valid setting. No published learning curve is declared numerically false from that source discrepancy alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The existing prescription differentiates the fixed-policy sampled Lagrangian directly, then applies \(\lambda^+=\Pi_\Lambda(\lambda-\eta_\lambda\partial_\lambda\widehat L)\) and \(t^+=\Pi_{\mathcal T}(t+\eta_t\partial_t\widehat L)\). Its local derivatives and signs agree with the exact example; full training integration is not established.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Execution noise changes the action but not its stored old likelihood
problems.source_location: Proceedings Section 4.1, PDF p.8; current author wrapper/RA_C_RL.py, collect_data, lines 25–39; wrapper/PPO.py analogous collector
claim: The paper adds Gaussian execution noise of standard deviation \(0.05\). The source samples an action and its log probability, adds noise to that action in place, executes it, and stores the changed action with the earlier log probability.
analysis: With \(a\sim\pi_{\rm old}\) and execution noise \(\epsilon\), reevaluation constructs \(\rho=\pi_{\rm new}(a+\epsilon\mid s)/\pi_{\rm old}(a\mid s)\). The likelihood terms refer to different random variables. Even for an unchanged standard-normal policy, \[\rho=\exp\{-[(a+\epsilon)^2-a^2]/2\},\] which is generally not \(1\). For example, \(a=1,\epsilon=0.05\) yields \(e^{-0.05125}\ne1\).
result: The action-likelihood pairing is inconsistent in the inspected noisy collection paths. This does not measure its effect on returns, costs or published curves.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep the latent sampled action with its original policy likelihood, and send a separate noise-perturbed action to the environment. The independent noise then belongs to the transition kernel. Alternatively, both densities must describe the actual convolved executed-action law. Recomputing only one unconvolved Gaussian density is insufficient.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Unique inner optimizers do not imply a Lipschitz gradient
problems.source_location: Proceedings Appendix A.7, scenario 1, PDF p.19; Assumption 3.8, p.7; Theorem 3.12, p.8; current arXiv v 2 corresponding Appendix A.7
claim: Scenario1 asserts that a smooth base Lagrangian and unique inner maximizers give twice continuous differentiability and hence Lipschitz smoothness of the maximized value.
analysis: An OCE instance realizes \(F(\theta,t,\lambda)=2+(\lambda-1)\theta-\theta^4/4\). Use one recurrent state, actions and policy parameter in \([-1,1]\), \(\gamma=1/2\), linear utility \(g(u)=u\), rewards \(r_0=(1-\gamma)(2-a-a^4/4)\) and \(r_1=(1-\gamma)a\), threshold \(0\), \(\mathcal T=[0,2]\times[-1,1]\), and \(\Lambda=[7/8,9/8]\). Rewards are bounded; the action \(1/2\) is strictly feasible.

The smooth polynomial objective has a unique interior maximizer \(\theta^*=\sqrt[3]{\lambda-1}\). Direct substitution gives \[V(t,\lambda)=2+\tfrac34|\lambda-1|^{4/3},\qquad\partial_\lambda V=\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda-1)|\lambda-1|^{1/3}.\] The derivative quotient at \(\lambda=1\) is \(|h|^{-2/3}\to\infty\). Thus compactness, uniqueness and an infinitely differentiable base objective do not imply the stated smoothness. The inner family contains the exact maximizer; this does not test a separate universal-policy-parametrization premise.

Theorem 3.12 explicitly assumes smoothness, which this example violates. It remains a conditional theorem. The stronger second-order scenarios and the distinct smoothing alternative are not refuted by this example.
result: Restrict the claimed sufficient-condition route; the example refutes that implication rather than the conditional convergence theorem.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The supplied sufficient replacement uses uniform strong concavity \(\mu>0\), a cross-gradient Lipschitz bound \(B\), and joint outer-gradient bounds \(L_{zz},L_{z\theta}\). Variational inequalities give \(\operatorname{Lip}(\theta^*)\leq B/\mu\), then the envelope formula gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla V)\leq L_{zz}+L_{z\theta}B/\mu\). These stronger conditions are not asserted for arbitrary neural RL objectives.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The gradient detector indexes an unretained non-leaf gradient
problems.source_location: Proceedings Section 2.2.1, Eq.(2), PDF p.4; current author src/Confounding_token_detection/run_gradients_{llama,qwen}_{instruct,response}_level.py, compute_token_gradients
claim: The detector needs teacher/student loss derivatives with respect to token embeddings. Each released kernel constructs embedding outputs, calls requires_grad_(True), backpropagates, then indexes inputs_embeds.grad. The inspected loader leaves embedding weights trainable.
analysis: If the embedding matrix \(W\) is trainable, \(E=\operatorname{Embedding}(W,I)\) is a non-leaf operation result. Enabling requires_grad does not detach it or retain its intermediate gradient. Backward can populate \(W\) while leaving \(E.\mathrm{grad}=\mathrm{None}\), which the subsequent indexing cannot use. No detach, retain_grad or explicit returned input-gradient operation appears in the four kernels.

For a concrete derivative oracle, \(L(E)=\sum_{j,d}a_jE_{jd}\) with three-dimensional tokens and \(a=(1,2,4)\) has gradient norms \((\sqrt3,2\sqrt3,4\sqrt3)\), hence normalized sensitivities \((0,1/3,1)\). The failure is retention of that existing derivative, independently of whether the downstream differentiable loss is linear or language-model cross-entropy. Freezing embedding weights before constructing an explicit input leaf is a valid countercontrol.
result: Under the inspected loader configuration, the released detector cannot obtain its gradients through this access. Historical use of frozen parameters, another internal kernel or precomputed outputs remains unresolved; benchmark scores are not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The supplied local correction detaches embedding values, enables their input gradient and explicitly requests the loss derivative with respect to that input. This preserves the requested downstream partial derivative. Retaining the intermediate gradient is another option; full detection and benchmark recovery remain unverified.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The response mask selects shifted target positions incorrectly
problems.source_location: Proceedings Section 2.2.2, PDF p.5; current author src/Causal_attention_distillation/LeaF_instruct_level/distill_instruct_level.py, lines 201,225–229,423–460; LeaF_response_level analogous reduction
claim: The release copies token IDs into labels, ignores prompt labels with \(-100\), and applies the unshifted label mask to raw causal-LM output logits in the separate distillation reduction.
analysis: Raw logit row \(i\) predicts token \(i+1\). Therefore response prediction rows require \(m_i=\mathbf1\{\ell_{i+1}\ne-100\}\) for \(0\leq i<L-1\). Passing labels to the causal model shifts its internal supervised loss, not the returned raw logits. The source instead uses \(\mathbf1\{\ell_i>-100\}\).

Take four positions: two prompt tokens, one response token and EOS, with labels \((-100,-100,0,1)\). At row \(1\), use teacher probabilities \((0.8,0.2)\) and student probabilities \((0.2,0.8)\); set both distributions to \((0.5,0.5)\) at the other rows. The source selects rows \(2,3\) and gives zero KL. The intended response prediction rows \(1,2\) give \[L=\tfrac12[0.8\log4+0.2\log(1/4)]=0.3\log4\approx0.4158883083.\] Thus it omits the first-response prediction and includes the row after the final supervised token.
result: The current response-only distillation reduction represents a different target-position objective. The model’s ordinary supervised cross-entropy is separate and is not alleged to share this defect. Empirical accuracy effects are unmeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: With aligned tokenization, prefixes and vocabulary, compare teacher/student logits at rows \(0,\ldots,L-2\) using labels at rows \(1,\ldots,L-1\). State an empty-target convention. This repairs the one-position relation, but not arbitrary cross-tokenizer or differently pruned sequence alignment.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Countable pointwise convergence is insufficient for the claimed consistency
problems.source_location: Current author copy Theorem 3, PDF p.6; Appendix F, Assumptions 2–4 and Properties 7–8, Eqs.(29)–(30), pp.19–22; final proceedings corresponding locations
claim: Theorem 3 claims that an accepted safe policy is returned with probability tending to \(1\). The stated hypotheses allow a countable class, piecewise Lipschitz costs, a strictly feasible policy, and pointwise sample-loss convergence. The proof upgrades pointwise convergence to eventual uniform accuracy on a countable cover.
analysis: Countable simultaneous convergence still permits parameter-dependent indices: \(\forall\theta\,\exists N_\theta\) is not \(\exists N\,\forall\theta\). For instance, \(f_n(k)=\mathbf1\{k\geq n\}\) converges pointwise to zero while its supremum remains \(1\). A full algorithmic counterexample follows, including the theorem’s assumptions.

Let \(X\) be uniform on \([0,1]\), \(Y=0\), logging prediction \(A^\beta\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) independent of \(X\), and repercussion \(R^\psi=A^\psi\). Use threshold \(\tau=1/2\), confidence parameter \(\delta=1/10\), margin \(\xi=1/10\), and cross-entropy for label zero. Include the safe policy \(q_\star(x)=1/4\). For each finite union \(U\) of rational intervals of total measure at most \(1/4\), include \(q_U=1/8\) on \(U\) and \(7/8\) outside. This class is countable and can be integer-encoded.

The importance estimate is \(2q_\theta(X)A^\beta-1/2\in[-1/2,5/4]\). Predictions depend only on observed \(X\), logging has full support, and the deterministic repercussion mechanism is invariant. Singleton partitions meet the printed Lipschitz and cover conditions. Fixed-policy losses are bounded, so the strong law supplies pointwise convergence. The safe policy has \(g(\star)=-1/4\), permitting \(\epsilon=1/5>\xi\). Every other policy is unsafe: \[g(U)=7/8-(3/4)|U|-1/2\geq3/16.\]

For every finite candidate sample, choose a rational-interval union covering all its feature values with total measure at most \(1/4\). Its empirical loss is \(\log(8/7)\), and every constraint estimate is at most \(-1/4\). The inflated bound obeys \[U^+(U)\leq-1/4+\tfrac72\sqrt{\log10/(2n_f)}\leq-1/40\quad(n_f\geq279).\] Thus it enters the feasible branch of Algorithm 2. The sample maximum loss is \(\log8\), attained by the empty union; every infeasible-branch cost is greater than \(\log8-1/40>\log(8/7)\). Every feasible-branch loss is at least \(\log(8/7)\), while the safe policy has \(\log(4/3)\). A global minimum is attained and every minimizer is unsafe, irrespective of tie breaking.

The independent test can return that unsafe candidate or abstain; it cannot restore the safe policy discarded by selection. Consequently the probability of returning an accepted safe policy is zero for all sufficiently large split sizes. The independent-holdout safety guarantee is compatible with this counterexample because it may reject.
result: The central consistency theorem is false under its printed hypotheses, in both the final proceedings and current author copy. The unbiased importance estimate and independent-test safety result are not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The supplied correction requires genuine uniform convergence and attained minimizers, or a restricted finite class, together with vanishing confidence radii and a strict feasible margin. Countable covers alone cannot provide the missing uniform law.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The multi-constraint penalty rewards cancellation by satisfied constraints
problems.source_location: Current author copy and final proceedings Algorithm 4, PDF p.24, line 16; Appendix F multi-constraint consistency extension, p.19
claim: The infeasible branch returns \(\ell_{\max}+\sum_jU_j^{\rm inflated}\), using signed inflated upper bounds rather than positive violations.
analysis: Use the same valid logging/repercussion model but just two constant policies \(q_s=1/4,q_b=3/4\), thresholds \(\tau_1=1/2,\tau_2=10\), and confidence parameters \(1/10\). Importance estimates have common width \(3/2\). A finite class gives uniform convergence; the safe policy has both constraints strictly negative. Population values are \[(g_1(s),g_2(s),\ell_s)=(-1/4,-39/4,\log(4/3)),\quad(g_1(b),g_2(b),\ell_b)=(1/4,-37/4,\log4).\] The safe branch cost tends to \(\log(4/3)\), while the unsafe penalty tends to \(\log4-9\), which is much smaller. Hence selection chooses the unsafe policy with probability tending to \(1\), despite an available strictly feasible member.

The strongly satisfied second constraint offsets the first violation. Its generous threshold is permitted; the superscript denotes inflation rather than positive truncation. The independent test correctly rejects with probability tending to one, so eventual safe return still fails without compromising test independence.
result: The displayed multi-constraint selector has a separate finite-class consistency obstruction, even when uniform convergence holds. No implementation or experimental rerun is inferred.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The supplied separated cost retains feasible losses and otherwise uses \(\ell_{\max}+C+\sum_j\max\{0,U_j^++\xi/4\}\), with \(C>0\). Every infeasible cost then exceeds every feasible loss. For finite classes, uniform convergence and vanishing radii make a strictly feasible branch available; selection has margin and the independent test accepts with probability tending to one. The same argument needs explicit uniform laws for infinite classes.
The existing correction is retained as a bounded proposal; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The current author copy already states symmetric group equality
problems.source_location: Author-hosted current PDF, Appendix D.2, p.16; final proceedings corresponding formula
claim: The proceedings displays a one-sided group difference, while the current author-hosted presentation includes the absolute value for two-sided approximate equality.
analysis: The current formula is \(|\mu_A-\mu_B|-\epsilon\), equivalently two directed inequalities. It excludes the old one-sided counterexample.
result: Use the author-corrected symmetric definition; this historical notation difference is excluded from current errors.

problems.title: finite squared-hinge penalties and exact feasibility
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 1-2, 6, Eqs. (8)-(9); its cited penalty-theory source arXiv:2410.03955v4, pp. 8-10, Assumptions 1-4 and Theorem 1.
claim: The discussion following Eq. (\(9\)) relates a finite squared-hinge KL penalty to the constrained KKT system, while the abstract/introduction describe trust-region enforcement.
analysis: At a feasible point, the gradient of \(\beta[D(\theta)-\delta]_+^2\) is zero. An active constrained optimum with a positive KKT multiplier can nevertheless have a nonzero objective gradient, so it need not be stationary for this finite penalty. For \(\pi_{\rm old}=(1/2,1/2)\), \(\pi_\theta=(\operatorname{sigmoid}\theta,1-\operatorname{sigmoid}\theta)\), \(J(\theta)=\theta\), and \(D(\theta)=\log\cosh(\theta/2)\), the constrained maximum is \(\theta_*=2\operatorname{arcosh}(e^\delta)\). At \(\delta=10^{-4}\) and \(\beta=1000\), \(\theta_*\simeq0.02828474\), whereas the penalized stationary maximum has \(\theta\simeq0.25371689\) and \(D\simeq0.00802504>\delta\). The bounded objective \(J(\theta)=2\tanh(\theta/2)\) similarly permits \(D\simeq0.00794101\).
result: Finite penalization alone does not imply exact hard feasibility. The cited penalty theorem concerns approximate KKT conditions with tolerance-dependent assumptions and schedules; that theorem is not refuted. Special instances can have exactly feasible penalized optima, so a literal existential claim that this can happen is also not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State approximate stationarity/feasibility and the required assumptions. If exact feasibility is intended, provide an appropriate constrained-update argument. For the scalar example, \(\theta_*=2\operatorname{arcosh}(e^\delta)\) and \(\lambda_*=2/\tanh(\theta_*/2)\).
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: finite groups retain difficulty-dependent selection
problems.source_location: paper pages: 1 7 8 19; paper equations: 7 10; code: verl/verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py:289-314,377-400,470-503,571-602 verl/verl/trainer/config/ppo_trainer.yaml:159-166 scripts/train/run_disco_logL_1.5b_8k.sh
claim: The abstract and Table 1 describe complete removal of difficulty bias. The released loss excludes groups containing only one reward class and divides by the original question count.
analysis: Let a question have success probability \(p\), and let \(K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\) be its number of correct responses. A mixed group is included with probability \(h_n(p)=1-p^n-(1-p)^n\). Since excluded groups contribute zero but the denominator remains the original question count, the expected finite-group contribution retains this difficulty-dependent factor. A question with one correct and one incorrect possible outcome already yields this construction for the full DRO objective. For \(n=8\), \(h_8(0.01)\simeq0.0772553\) and \(h_8(1/2)=0.9921875\); the relative inclusion weight is about \(0.0778636\). The cited configuration disables dynamic filtering, and the rejection-sampling flag defaults to false.
result: The finite fixed-group implementation does not completely remove difficulty-dependent question selection. The population decomposition correctly removes its explicit \(\sqrt{p(1-p)}\) factor, and the method can still provide useful practical reweighting.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restrict the claim to the population normalization and available mixed groups, or specify a justified question-level sampling/inclusion correction. Dividing by the number of valid groups alone does not equalize original-question inclusion.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: a lower bound does not ensure monotonic improvement
problems.source_location: Current arXiv v5, Eqs.(7),(10), PDF pp.5,7, and paragraph following Eq.(10)
claim: The paragraph following Eq. (\(10\)) infers that increasing the lower bound \(J_2\le J_1\) automatically increases \(J_1\).
analysis: The witness has one question and three one-token outputs with rewards \(r(o_1)=1\), \(r(o_2)=r(o_3)=0\). Under the fixed old policy \((0.4,0.3,0.3)\), the conditional positive law is a point mass on \(o_1\), and the conditional negative law assigns \(1/2\) to each of \(o_2,o_3\). With the paper’s log-likelihood score \(s_\theta(o_i)=\log\pi_i\), Eqs.(7) and (10) reduce exactly to \[J_1(\pi)=\log\pi_1-\tfrac12(\log\pi_2+\log\pi_3),\] \[J_2(\pi)=\log\pi_1-\tau\log\{(\pi_2^{1/\tau}+\pi_3^{1/\tau})/2\}.\] The trust-region quantity is \(D_{\rm KL}(\pi_{\rm old}\|\pi)=\sum_i\pi_{{\rm old},i}\log(\pi_{{\rm old},i}/\pi_i)\).

Write \(J_1=J_2+G\), where \(G\ge0\). An increase in \(J_2\) can be outweighed by a decrease in \(G\). A policy-level example uses reference probabilities \((0.4,0.3,0.3)\), temperature \(\tau=10\), and candidate policies \(A=(0.4,0.305,0.295)\) and \[B=(0.4000318,0.2999841,0.2999841)\]. Substitution in the paper's objectives gives \(J_2(B)-J_2(A)\simeq7.481517\times10^{-6}>0\), but \(J_1(B)-J_1(A)\simeq-6.409938\times10^{-6}<0\). Their KL values are approximately \(8.334491\times10^{-5}\) and \(2.106713\times10^{-9}\), both below \(\delta=10^{-4}\).
result: The asserted monotonic implication is false even within the stated KL region. The lower bound and the entropic DRO variational identity can remain correct; practical superiority is a separate empirical question.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Remove automatic monotonicity, or supply a touching-minorizer, gap-control or acceptance condition that actually controls \(J_1\).
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Relative objective/penalty signs in Algorithm 1
problems.source_location: paper pages: 19; algorithm lines: 9 10 11; code: verl/verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py
claim: Algorithm 1 defines \(G_1\) as the objective gradient and \(G_2\) as the positive penalty gradient, then supplies \(G_1+G_2\) to the optimizer.
analysis: Descent on \(-J_2+P\) requires \(-G_1+G_2\); ascent requires \(G_1-G_2\). Adding both gradients gives the wrong relative sign under either convention. The author-released loss minimizes the negative objective plus the positive penalty, so its relative sign is correct.
result: Following pseudocode can give wrong direction; this does not establish wrong public loss or wrong reported training. Actual public objective/penalty relative sign is correct.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For a descent optimizer, write \(-G_1+G_2\) and state the convention.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The historical L-ratio dispatcher defect is fixed
problems.source_location: Author repository Optimization-AI/DisCO, commit 8bdd94eb49a58cd09e68af5392302ba83acf63b2; verl/verl/workers/actor/dp_actor.py, lines 286–296; verl/verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py, compute_policy_loss_disco_Lratio
claim: The original supplemental release routed the full L-ratio branch to a basic loss function that did not accept its tau argument.
analysis: In current author commit 8bdd94eb49a58cd09e68af5392302ba83acf63b2, dp_actor.py, lines 286–296, calls compute_policy_loss_disco_Lratio, whose signature accepts tau. Reading the current call and signature clears the particular dispatch failure. The older supplemental call remains a historical version fact, and no author program was executed in this check.
result: This specific failure is absent from the current author release. Historical experiment provenance and adoption of any external audit remain unestablished.

problems.title: Printed and implemented penalty gradients differ by a factor of two
problems.source_location: paper pages: 6 19; paper equations: 9; code: verl/verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py:318-321,406-409,506-509,604-607
claim: Eq. (\(9\)) uses \(\beta[D-\delta]_+^2\), whose gradient is \(2\beta[D-\delta]_+\nabla D\).
analysis: In each cited implementation branch, the detached coefficient gives only \(\beta[D-\delta]_+\nabla D\). Detachment removes the coefficient derivative, making this the gradient of \((\beta/2)[D-\delta]_+^2\).
result: Numerical beta setting is not an exact Eq \(9\) reproduction; retuning can absorb factor, so less severe than sign error. Penalty direction is correct; beta is tunable.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a consistent \(\beta/2\) convention or double the detached coefficient. Differentiating \(\beta\max(D-\delta,0)^2\) directly gives the printed gradient.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: AMC benchmark year differs from the released evaluation manifest
problems.source_location: paper pages: 7 8 9 18; paper tables: 2 3 4 5; data: deepscaler/deepscaler/data/test/amc.json datasets/deepscaler/data/amc.parquet; code: deepscaler/deepscaler/data/utils.py scripts/data/deepscaler_dataset.py scripts/eval/eval_model_8k.sh

problems.title: MATH500 overlaps and duplicate training pairs
problems.source_location: paper pages: 7; data: deepscaler/deepscaler/data/train/deepscaler.json deepscaler/deepscaler/data/test/math.json datasets/deepscaler/data/train.parquet datasets/deepscaler/data/math.parquet
claim: Paper describes about \(40.3\) thousand unique pairs; delivered train/test files should identify benchmark separation.
analysis: The author-released MATH test indices \(80,285,412\) match training indices \(7202,7141,6976\) after Unicode NFKC normalization, whitespace normalization and case folding; the corresponding answers \(501,440,406\) agree. The first pair is also identical before normalization. JSON and Parquet problem orders agree. There are \(40\,315\) training rows but only \(39\,616\) raw unique problem-answer pairs, \(39\,387\) raw unique problems and \(39\,097\) normalized unique problems. The other five released test sets have no exact normalized match under this narrow comparison.

problems.title: Checkpoint selection and uncertainty: unresolved empirical scope
problems.source_location: paper pages: 7 8 9 10 24 25; code: scripts/train/run_disco_logL_1.5b_8k.sh scripts/eval/eval_model_8k.sh
claim: Paper reports best performance and significant superiority without a complete selection manifest or uncertainty intervals.
analysis: The paper evaluates every \(200\) steps and reports best performance, without a fully specified independent checkpoint-selection rule. Its checklist openly reports no error bars. Averaging \(16\) correctness samples estimates pass@\(1\), rather than pass@\(16\), and does not measure training-seed variability. Dynamic sampling is disabled for all compared methods, which is disclosed. The fixed \(0.001\) KL ablation does not establish failure of every tuned regularizer.
