problems.title: Proposition 1's sign-dependent monotonicity
problems.source_location: paper pages: 4 18 19; paper equations: 3 4 5
claim: Proposition 1 assumes f nondecreasing in x and remark says assumptions hold for GRPO.
analysis: For a negative reward \(y=-1\), the clipped branch is \(f(x,-1)=-\max(x,1-\varepsilon)\), which is nonincreasing. At \(\varepsilon=0.2\), \(f(1,-1)=-1\) and \(f(1.1,-1)=-1.1\), contradicting the claimed nondecreasing condition. The population decomposition itself does not require that extra condition.
result: Correct the sign-dependent assumption; the decomposition identity is not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Remove extra monotonicity of f for all y; retain branchwise assumptions or state sign-dependent monotonicity.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Dr. GRPO's relative question weighting
problems.source_location: paper pages: 4 5 20 21; paper figures: 1; paper equations: 19
claim: The text interprets \(p(1-p)\) as mitigating question imbalance relative to \(\sqrt{p(1-p)}\).
analysis: After normalizing both weights to one at \(p=1/2\), \(r_{\rm GRPO}(p)=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\) and \(r_{\rm Dr}(p)=4p(1-p)=r_{\rm GRPO}(p)^2\). At \(p=0.01\), these are approximately \(0.1989975\) and \(0.0396\). Under the displayed relative-weight criterion, the latter attenuates extreme questions more strongly.
result: The interpretation of the relative weights is reversed. This does not determine empirical performance, and an overall gradient-scale change can be absorbed into the learning rate.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Distinguish absolute scale from relative weighting and other definitions of bias; correct mitigation sentence under displayed criterion.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: PAZO-M step size allows an exact nonstationary two-cycle
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Theorem 4.1, p. 6; Theorem B.3, p. 16; proof condition before Eq. (11), p. 18.
claim: Theorem 4.1/Theorem B.3 assert a finite-time stationarity bound for the prescribed PAZO-M step size without the restriction later used in the proof.
analysis: Choose \(d=q=b=b'=1\), identical public/private per-record losses \(f(x)=1-\cos x\), \(L=M=1\), \(\alpha=0.9\), \(\lambda=10^{-6}\), and zero gradient-variance, similarity and injected-noise parameters. The objective is smooth, Lipschitz, bounded below and bounded in \([0,2]\). Clipping is inactive because the threshold is \(1+\sqrt2\) while the scalar directional derivative has magnitude at most one.

The prescribed step is \(\eta=2.75\). For \(u\in\{-1,1\}\), using \(\operatorname{sinc}(\lambda)=\sin\lambda/\lambda\), the two-point estimator is \(\operatorname{sinc}(\lambda)\sin x\), so the exact recurrence is \(x_{t+1}=x_t-a\sin x_t\), with \(a=\eta[\alpha+(1-\alpha)\operatorname{sinc}(\lambda)]\in(2.7,2.75)\). A nonzero root \(a\sin x_0=2x_0\) lies in \((\pi/3,\pi/2)\); hence \(x_t=(-1)^t x_0\) and \(|\nabla f(x_t)|^2>3/4\).

At \(T=1000\), the complete surviving right side of Theorem B.3 is \(\frac{16(1-\cos x_0)(1-\alpha)}{T(2-\alpha)^2}+\frac{2\lambda(1-\alpha)}{2-\alpha}+\frac{\lambda^2(1-\alpha)}4+\frac{\alpha\lambda}2<0.001324\). It cannot bound a left side greater than \(3/4\). In particular, the proof condition \(\alpha L\eta<1\) fails: its value is \(2.475\).
result: The finite-time theorem is false on its stated domain. This is an analytic cycle, not an empirical training failure. The distinct bounded-loss Theorem B.6 already restricts \(\alpha<2/3\) and is not refuted by this example.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State and enforce \(\alpha L\eta<1\), or cap the step and rederive the bound. With \(s=\sqrt d\), the prescribed step satisfies this condition when \(\alpha<(4s-1-\sqrt{4s^2+1})/(3s-2)\); \(0<\alpha<2/3\) suffices uniformly in dimension. This repairs the exhibited obstruction without recertifying every intermediate line.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: PAZO-S selection invalidates unconditional moment substitutions
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Theorem B.5 proof, pp. 23-24 (selected batch moments and accepted Gaussian perturbation).
claim: Theorem B.5's proof treats a privately selected public-gradient candidate as if its pre-selection moments and zero-mean perturbation were unchanged.
analysis: Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}\) and public per-example loss \(f(x)+\zeta x\), with \(\Pr(\zeta=0.2)=0.01\) and \(\Pr(\zeta=-0.2/99)=0.99\). At \(x=1\), step \(1/4\), three public candidates and exact private comparisons, both candidate positions are positive; minimizing private loss selects the largest \(\zeta\). Thus \(\mathbb E\zeta=0\), but \(\mathbb E\zeta_I=0.00398\), and the selected second moment is about \(2.9502\) times the unselected \(0.0004040404\).

Zero-mean Gaussian perturbations also become biased under acceptance. For one exact public gradient, put \(y=1-1/(4\sqrt2)>0\), \(Z\sim N(0,\epsilon_p^2)\), and \(\eta=1/4\). Acceptance occurs exactly when \(0<Z<2y/\eta\), so \(\mathbb E[Z\mathbf1_A]=\epsilon_p[\phi(0)-\phi(2y/(\eta\epsilon_p))]>0\), where \(\phi\) is the standard-normal density.
result: These are counterexamples to the proof's moment substitutions. They do not by themselves refute the complete finite-time inequality, because a different descent argument could exploit selection.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A selection-safe bound uses \(\mathbb E\|\zeta_I\|^2\le\sum_{j=1}^k\mathbb E\|\zeta_j\|^2\le k\sigma_2^2/b'\). With \(\eta=1/(4L)\), smoothness then yields \(\frac1T\sum_t\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_t)\|^2\le8L\Delta_f/T+(\gamma+\sqrt{k\sigma_2^2/b'}+\sqrt d\,\epsilon_p)^2\). This conservative replacement does not certify the paper's sharper dependence.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Fixed PAZO-S perturbations do not give a vanishing asymptotic error
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Eq. (6) and asymptotic paragraph, p. 7; Theorem B.5 and its asymptotic sentence, p. 23.
claim: The asymptotic paragraph after Eq. (\(6\))/Theorem B.5 claims an \(O(\gamma^2+\sigma_2^2/b')\) error from \(T\to\infty\) and \(\epsilon_p\le d^{-1/2}\), dropping terms retained in the finite-time display.
analysis: A fixed positive perturbation does not vanish. Take \(d=k=b=b'=1\), identical losses \(f=f'=1-\cos x\), \(\eta=1/4\), \(\epsilon_p=1\), clipping threshold \(C=2\) and private-noise multiplier \(\sigma\ge1\). Here \(\gamma=\sigma_2=0\). The baseline candidate is \(y=x-\eta\sin x\), and its perturbed competitor is \(y+W\), with \(W\sim N(0,1/16)\).

Since each true loss is in \([0,2]\), the perturbed candidate is accepted with conditional probability at least \(\Phi(-1/(2\sigma))\ge\Phi(-1/2)>0\). On every interval of length \(\pi\), the set where \(\sin^2(y+w)\ge1/2\) has measure \(\pi/2\). The Gaussian density is uniformly positive on \([-\pi/2,\pi/2]\). Therefore \(\mathbb E[|\nabla f(x_{t+1})|^2\mid x_t]\ge\frac12\Phi(-1/2)\frac\pi2\,\frac{\phi(2\pi)}{1/4}\simeq1.0345190\times10^{-9}>0\), uniformly in \(x_t\).
result: The asymptotic zero-error conclusion is false when its right side is zero. The finite-time theorem retaining \(+1/2\) is not disproved by this example.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the \(d\epsilon_p^2\) contribution and selection-safe variance terms. A vanishing perturbation floor requires, for example, \(\epsilon_p=O((dT)^{-1/2})\), or no perturbation.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Conditioning on no clipping destroys the isotropy identity
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Theorem B.7, pp. 30-33; terms T1, p. 31, and T4, p. 32.
claim: Theorem B.7's proof uses an unconditional isotropy/projection identity after conditioning on the directional queries not clipping.
analysis: The no-clipping event depends on the sampled direction. For \(G=I_2\), \(g=e_1\), \(u\) uniform on the radius-\(\sqrt2\) circle and \(Q=\{|u_1|\le1\}\), direct angular integration gives \(\Pr(Q)=1/2\) and \(\mathbb E[uu^\top\mid Q]=\operatorname{diag}(1-2/\pi,1+2/\pi)\). Consequently \(\mathbb E[GG^\top g-(g^\top Gu)Gu\mid Q]=(2/\pi)e_1\ne0\). The threshold illustrates the conditioning error; it is not asserted to be the optimized threshold in Theorem B.7.
result: Conditional isotropy needs a separate proof or a clipping-bias remainder. The full optimized convergence rate has not been disproved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Work unconditionally. If \(Y^c\) is the clipped estimator, \(Y\) the unclipped estimator and \(p_t=\Pr(Q_t^c\mid\text{past})\), use \(\|\mathbb E(Y^c-Y)\|\le Mk p_t\) and \(\mathbb E\|Y^c\|^2\le2\mathbb E\|Y\|^2+2M^2k^2p_t\), then retain and bound the tail terms. The available replacement restricts to one direction and orthonormal \(G\).
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The smoothing variable in Lemma B.2 must be a ball draw
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Lemma B.2(3), p. 15; ball-smoothing definition, p. 3.
claim: Lemma B.2 uses sphere smoothing in a formula requiring ball smoothing.
analysis: In dimension one, sphere smoothing of \(f(x)=\sin x\) gives gradient \(\cos(\lambda)\cos x\). The mean symmetric two-point estimator is \(\operatorname{sinc}(\lambda)\cos x\). These differ for general \(\lambda\), whereas uniform ball smoothing gives the required estimator identity.
result: Local correctable error, not evidence that every smoothing argument fails.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the uniform ball expectation, consistent with the main-text definition.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Serial PAZO-S stores aliased candidate dictionaries
problems.source_location: Official supplement and pinned pinned author GitHub source: experiments/pazo-s.py, lines 159-179; GitHub mnli/pazo-s.py, lines 199-218, and experiments/pazo-s.py, line 77.
claim: Serial PAZO-S is intended to compare \(k\) public-gradient candidates and retain the privately selected one.
analysis: tmp_g is allocated outside the candidate loop and appended repeatedly; all candidate entries are the same dictionary. The serial file also references pre_trained whereas shared configuration uses pretrain.
result: The exercised serial helper collapses \(k\)-way public selection to the last candidate. Which published runs used these files remains unresolved; no table accuracy is invented or assumed to have been reproduced.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Allocate a fresh dictionary in each iteration and store detached cloned gradients, handling None consistently. Correct the pre_trained attribute reference. Add a real k-distinct-gradient regression fixture.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: MNLI vectorized PAZO-S uses candidate parameters as gradients
problems.source_location: Official supplement and pinned pinned author GitHub source: mnli/pazo-s_vec.py, lines 150-164.
claim: The vectorized candidate-selection branch should update the parameters corresponding to the candidate it evaluates.
analysis: The winning candidate variable best_g_noise contains parameters \(\theta-\eta(g+z)\), but the source assigns that value to p.grad before optimizer.step(). It therefore uses a candidate position as a gradient; that update does not generally equal the candidate evaluated by the private comparison.
result: The parameter actually updated differs from the candidate whose private loss won the selection. Defect is file-specific and present in both audited versions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Represent candidate gradient and candidate parameters separately. Assign g+z to p.grad and evaluate the candidate consistent with the actual optimizer; if assigning parameters directly, reconcile momentum and weight-decay state.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The implemented sampler is not the accountant's mechanism
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Section 3.4, pp. 5-6. pinned author GitHub source: trainers/model_base.py, lines 149-251; privacy_analysis/compute_privacy_sgm.py, lines 8-51; privacy_analysis/rdp_accountant.py, lines 355-399.
claim: The reported differential-privacy accounting is used with the author-released training sampler.
analysis: The author's fixed-size DataLoader uses shuffled epochs and drops the last incomplete batch. Its compute_rdp helper instead accounts for a sampled Gaussian mixture at \(q=b/n\). Epoch reshuffling is not that sampling mechanism; even independent fresh fixed-size batches would be a different rule. The code contains a separate without-replacement helper but does not use it on this path.
result: The displayed accounting does not establish the released loop's stated budgets. This is a certification-scope gap, not a proved numerical privacy violation. Counting all nominal epoch steps is conservative relative to dropping incomplete batches.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use independent Poisson inclusion with fixed public expected-batch normalization and explicit empty-batch behavior, or supply a matching reshuffling accountant and adjacency analysis. Recompute budgets and handle PAZO-S's adaptive final query/shared batch explicitly.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Private-derived preprocessing and diagnostics expand the privacy boundary
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Appendix C.1, p. 34. pinned author GitHub source: data/generate_imdb_vocab10k.py, lines 36-56 and 85-124; experiments/pazo-s.py, lines 148-153.
claim: The privacy interpretation must specify which preprocessing-dependent models and diagnostic outputs are released.
analysis: Deterministic top-token vocabulary is built from private training text, saved, and used for all datasets. Training code writes raw private accuracy and candidate diagnostics; data preparation prints decoded private examples.
result: The stated scalar mechanism does not protect the whole raw-record preprocessing/output pipeline. Conditional DP for fixed preprocessed examples is a narrower possible claim.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Fix a public tokenizer independently of protected records, or privately construct it with composed budget. Define the released object; privatize or exclude raw private diagnostics and data artifacts. Address private model selection and multiple released runs where applicable.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The historical PAZO-M public-norm scaling has been corrected
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Algorithm 1, p. 4; Appendix A, p. 14; implementation disclosure, p. 34. Supplement and pinned author GitHub source: experiments/pazo-m.py, lines 85-90; mnli/pazo-m.py, lines 126-131.
claim: The older conference supplement scaled Gaussian search directions by the public-gradient norm. The latest author repository uses a different dimension-dependent scale.
analysis: The older public-norm rule has conditional mean \((\|g_{\rm pub}\|^2/d)\nabla f\), whereas the checked current author release uses \(Z/d^{1/4}\) in experiments/pazo-m.py and the corresponding MNLI implementation. Freshly retrieved current files confirm that the historical norm-dependent scaling is absent. This comparison identifies a code revision; it does not identify the revision used by the published runs.
result: The particular historical scaling defect is cleared as a current-source allegation. The current implementation and the original experimental provenance must remain separate.

problems.title: Fixed seeds and test-based stopping do not establish significance
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Appendix C.2, p. 34, and statistical-significance checklist, p. 43. pinned author GitHub source: experiments/pazo-s_vec.py, lines 62-92; mnli/pazo-s.py, lines 86-116.
claim: The paper uses fixed-seed and hyperparameter stability observations to discuss significance.
analysis: Paper acknowledges seed \(0\) and no error bars but claims significance from fixed seed and hyperparameter stability. Several code paths use test_accu for patience-based stopping.
result: Small reported advantages, especially \(0.2\) percentage points on Tiny-ImageNet at \(\varepsilon=0.1\), have no established statistical significance. Magnitude of selection bias is not quantified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use multiple independent seeds, paired per-seed comparisons and uncertainty; choose configurations/stopping on a validation split and evaluate once on a separate final holdout. Label existing results single-seed measurements.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Data construction and model initialization are not reconciled
problems.source_location: Official PDF: experimental setup, pp. 7-8; Appendix C.1 and Table 3, pp. 34-35. pinned author GitHub source: data/generate_imdb_vocab10k.py, lines 72-75; data/generate_mnli_snli.py, lines 57-108 and 271-273; trainers/model_base.py, lines 84-89.
claim: The stated public-data sizes and model initialization describe the settings behind the reported tables.
analysis: Paper says \(2000\) public IMDB examples; generator selects \(1000\) with unspecified shuffle seed. Few-shot MNLI/SNLI script chooses first qualifying records and uses first \(1000\) dev_matched examples as test. Tiny model descriptions include pretrained ViT-small, random initialization, and code vit_tiny plus warmup weights.
result: An exact independent reproduction cannot identify the original setup solely from these artifacts. Public-only baseline and public warm-start disclosure are present and are not flagged as missing.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Publish exact split/index hashes, preprocessing seeds, model architecture identifier and initialization/checkpoint hashes per result. Reconcile paper text with the actual run recipe.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The IMDB speedup ratio and timing interpretation
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Section 5.3, pp. 9-10; Tables 8-9, pp. 36-37. pinned author GitHub source: experiments/pazo-s.py, lines 138-145.
claim: The paper reports an IMDB speedup of up to fifteen times the comparison baseline.
analysis: IMDB largest baseline \(0.252\) seconds divided by fastest PAZO \(0.019\) is \(13.263\), not \(15\). Rounding cannot bridge the difference. Timing covers \(20\) iterations and does not specify explicit accelerator synchronization/warmup in the measurement code.
result: CIFAR up-to-\(16\times\) relative to GEP is supported by the table; not all runtime claims fail. No GPU performance reproduction was conducted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Correct the IMDB ratio or publish the missing underlying timing that justifies it. Name the baseline for each speedup. Report synchronized repeated timings, warmup/compile treatment and end-to-end time to matched utility. Measure actual peak memory for memory claims.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The noisy interpolation derivative is wrong in the paper and incomplete in the released target
problems.source_location: Paper p. 5, Eqs. (8)–(10), preceding definition of epsilon_t rectified/rectified_flow.py:53–98, especially 78–91 rectified/rectified_train.py:314–317
claim: Eq. (\(9\)) identifies the velocity target with the derivative of the noisy interpolation path.
analysis: The bridge adds \(\epsilon_t=(1-t)\sigma z\), with \(\sigma=0.05\). Differentiating its plus sign gives \(+d\epsilon_t/dt=-\sigma z\). Equation (\(9\)) instead subtracts \(d\epsilon_t/dt\), giving \(+\sigma z\). The released sample_path omits the entire derivative of the auxiliary noise, returning only the derivative of the sinusoidal interpolation. These are three different targets. The code comment describes its incomplete target as the path derivative. Its sigma_t return value, derived from \(\sigma_{\min}=0.002\) and \(\sigma_{\max}=80\), is not consumed by the training loss; the actual extra noise amplitude is \(0.05(1-t)\). Thus the p. 5 claim that the separate \(0.002\)–\(80\) schedule controls trajectory noise is also unsupported by this implementation.
result: The exact flow-matching justification does not apply to the written/released target. This is a definite mathematical issue even if the numerical effect of \(\sigma=0.05\) turns out small in a corrected experiment. A sinusoidal scalar interpolation without the additional z term can trace a geometrically straight line; changing linear time to sinusoidal time is not itself an error. No assertion is made that this defect alone explains the reported image-quality differences.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(v_*=s'(t)(x_1-\eta)-\sigma z\), where \(s(t)=\sin(\pi t/2)\), and retain the sampled z explicitly. Match the sampler's initial marginal \(N(0,(1+\sigma^2)I)\), or remove the auxiliary perturbation and use a consistently defined bridge/prior. Remove the unused sigma schedule from the description or incorporate a mathematically derived schedule into both bridge and target. Retrain before making empirical claims about the corrected objective.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The advertised spatial regularizer contributes no gradient in the released training branch
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 7–8, spatial regularization claim; pp. 23–27, Appendix E, Eq. (11) rectified/rectified_train.py:335–364 src/spatial_graph_loss.py:220–282 and 284–362
claim: The spatial regularizer is intended to constrain the trained generator through the loss.
analysis: The training routine detaches approx_generated before evaluating either spatial loss, disconnecting the spatial term from model parameters. The segmentation branch separately converts to NumPy and constructs a new tensor without autograd, so removing only the caller detach would not make that branch differentiable. This identifies the source graph; the historical paper-training version remains unknown.
result: The current branch cannot enforce the claimed spatial training constraint through gradients. Improvements attributed specifically to this regularizer require fresh evidence with a functioning loss. The optional spatial stage can still change training duration, early stopping, or checkpoint selection. Therefore it is incorrect to claim two complete runs must have identical weights or outputs. The paper-run configuration and whether its historical code had the same detach remain unverified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep the generated-image branch attached for the differentiable Sobel/texture surrogate. Use a path-consistent differentiable endpoint estimate or explicitly justify an alternative training surrogate. A bridge-consistent correction derives \(\widehat x_1\) from the sinusoidal bridge without an unstable division near \(t=1\). For segmentation, use a differentiable soft-mask/feature network if this is intended as a training loss; otherwise describe it as evaluation or model selection. Demonstrate a nonzero gradient norm and an actual ablation after retraining.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The active DOPRI5 solver has an incorrect embedded stage and does not enforce tolerance or endpoint completion
problems.source_location: Paper p. 5, fifth-order adaptive integration claim rectified/rectified_flow.py:198–270, 272–297, 331–368 rectified/utils.py:35–68
claim: The paper describes an adaptive fifth-order integration procedure for generation.
analysis: The first six Dormand–Prince stages and fifth-order weighted update are correct. Stage seven is not: lines 249–251 rebuild the sixth-stage state using a[\(5\)], rather than evaluate the derivative at the fifth-order endpoint. The embedded fourth-order estimate is therefore wrong. Independently, every proposal is accepted even when normalized error exceeds one. The loop stops after num_steps and returns a clamped sample even when \(t<1\); the final log labels this completed generation. Both single- and multi-cell generation helpers use this solver, so it is an active path.
result: The released generator does not provide the adaptive accuracy/completion guarantee invoked in the paper. Sampling-step budgets are also not equivalent to network evaluations: each attempt here costs seven calls. The fifth-order proposal itself is preserved correctly; this audit does not call the entire tableau wrong. Actual terminal times of the released checkpoints were not measured. A corrected implementation must be tested on those fields before assigning an empirical effect size.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the correct seventh stage \(f(x_5,t+h)\), reject proposals whose scaled error exceeds tolerance, cap the accepted endpoint at \(t=1\), and raise or report incomplete generation if the attempt budget is exhausted. Prefer a maintained solver or a separately verified reference; report accepted/rejected steps and function evaluations.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Unsorted cell IDs invalidate reproducible splits across training and evaluation processes
problems.source_location: src/dataset.py:40–43, CellImageGeneDataset.__init__ rectified/rectified_main.py:279–285 rectified/rectified_evaluate.py:395–400 src/utils.py:249; train.sh and eval.sh
claim: The released training and evaluation workflow should recreate the same biological-cell split.
analysis: CellImageGeneDataset computes a set intersection and converts it directly to a list. Python process hash randomization changes the order of string IDs. Training and standalone evaluation then independently recreate an \(80/20\) split of integer indices with Torch seed 42. Identical integer-index partitions do not imply identical biological-cell partitions when the underlying order changes. No PYTHONHASHSEED setting or persisted split-ID manifest was found in the released workflow.
result: The released standalone workflow can evaluate on cells already used for training. This is a much stronger concern than ordinary spatial correlation because it can involve the identical named cell and its image. The measured \(77.5\%\) belongs to the synthetic reproduction, not to the paper's actual data. Actual contamination requires the original process settings and cell-ID manifests. This specific set-order mechanism is in the single-cell class; the patch class preserves mapping iteration order and should not automatically be assigned the same bug.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Sort the common cell IDs deterministically, then save training, validation, and test cell IDs in versioned manifests and load those IDs during evaluation. Include dataset/source hashes and reject missing or changed IDs. Recompute results on untouched test IDs. Sorting alone fixes ordering but does not solve overlapping crops or validation reuse, addressed separately in F 05.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The released evaluation protocol does not implement the stated folds or establish independent biological generalization
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 5–7, Sections 4.1–4.2; Table 4; Appendix B.3 p. 17 rectified/rectified_main.py:279–285 rectified/rectified_evaluate.py:395–414 rectified/rectified_train.py:649–738 utils/prepare_xenium_data.py:1071–1086; src/dataset.py:397–998
claim: The manuscript describes three-fold evaluation and uses the results to discuss biological generalization.
analysis: The paper states three-fold cross-validation within each dataset. Public training/evaluation uses a single random \(80/20\) item split, and checkpoint selection minimizes the validation loss on that \(20\)%. Standalone evaluation recreates that same \(20\%\) rather than an independent test set. The split is at cell/patch level, including after combining HEST samples, without a patient, slide, or spatial-block grouping rule. The paper explicitly creates \(256\times256\) patches with \(100\)-pixel overlap and uses unmasked cell-centered crops. Those are correlated observations, not independent donors.
result: Current released results cannot be interpreted as clean patient-level generalization or a faithful reproduction of the stated three-fold experiment. Validation reuse can bias selected-model estimates, and overlapping crops can further inflate apparent generalization. The paper does contain a genuine cross-dataset experiment (Table 4) and explicitly says those models use \(126\) common genes in Appendix B.3. It would be incorrect to say no transfer experiment exists, or to allege that differing gene dimensions alone invalidate it. Original fold leakage and the donor relationship of C1/C2 remain unknown; absence of a manifest is not proof that the historical experiment used the current script.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Publish immutable grouped fold manifests and a separate model-selection set, or use nested cross-validation. Split source patients/slides before cropping. If the scientific goal is within-slide interpolation, state that goal and use spatial blocks separated by a buffer at least as wide as the crop footprint. For HEST, report sample/organ-level held-out evaluation. Quantify exact shared pixels/cell IDs across partitions and report donor-level rather than crop-level uncertainty for population claims.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Table 1 does not reconcile its C2 cell-type counts with its total
problems.source_location: Paper p. 5, Table 1; p. 15, cell-type annotation description
claim: Table 1's cell-type subtotals and total describe one reconciled C2 population.
analysis: The C2 column lists endothelial \(4\,182\), epithelial \(4\,203\), fibroblast \(9\,694\), macrophage \(12\,088\), melanoma \(33\,309\), and T cells \(15\,272\), summing to \(78\,748\), while the displayed total is \(70\,178\). The text describes clustering and cell-type annotation without explaining overlapping categories or different filtering stages in this table. The fresh current publisher PDF retains these values.
result: The population underlying the reported experiments is not reconstructable from Table 1. Downstream class balance and subgroup comparisons should not be inferred from the unreconciled counts. This does not establish fabricated data. The current 10x Genomics pages also have version-specific raw counts, so differences between those pages and a processed release are not automatically errors. The confirmed issue is internal consistency of the paper's displayed C2 population definitions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Provide a flow diagram or tabulation of raw, quality-controlled, image-matched, classified, and split counts for each dataset. If categories overlap or totals refer to different stages, label that explicitly. Otherwise correct the affected total or category counts from a versioned cell-ID manifest.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Universal performance claims contradict Table 2 SSIM values
problems.source_location: Paper abstract p. 1; p. 6 narrative and Table 2; Appendix B.2 p. 16
claim: The main text describes rectified flow as outperforming the diffusion baseline across all metrics.
analysis: The main text describes rectified flow as outperforming the diffusion baseline across all metrics. In Table 2, diffusion has higher SSIM for P1 single (\(0.20\) versus \(0.17\)), C1 multi (\(0.30\) versus \(0.28\)), and C2 single (\(0.36\) versus \(0.35\)). Rectified flow has better FID and Inception feature distance in all six rows. The p. 6 description of a \(3\)–\(6\)-fold FID improvement is also not the full displayed range.
result: The all-metrics statement should be corrected. The FID and feature-distance advantage remains a real reported result and should not be erased by the SSIM correction. Appendix B.2 already acknowledges that diffusion can match or exceed SSIM. That is evidence of appropriate nuance in the paper, but it does not repair the inconsistent main-text wording. Overlapping standard deviations do not, by themselves, prove no difference.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State that rectified flow improves the displayed FID/feature-distance measures while SSIM is mixed. Report the actual range if a ratio summary is retained. Use paired confidence intervals on independently held-out units before making inferential superiority claims.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The component ablation table favors removing gene attention on most reported metrics
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 7–8, ablation discussion and Table 6; Appendix B.2/Figure 8 p. 16
claim: The component-removal discussion attributes performance declines to removing the encoder components.
analysis: The prose argues that removing components causes performance declines. In Table 6, removing gene attention lowers UNI2-h FID from \(39.27\) to \(26.46\) and improves UNI2-h similarity, circularity, solidity, and all three spatial similarities. Full rectified wins only Inception feature distance (\(14.50\) versus \(14.89\)) and eccentricity similarity (\(0.964\) versus \(0.959\)). Other component-removal columns also show favorable changes on multiple metrics. The separate simple-encoder experiment is a different comparison.
result: The table does not justify the asserted empirical necessity of all encoder components. A simpler ablated model may be preferable under several of the paper's own quality criteria. The data do support that the more elaborate encoder can improve FID relative to the fully simplified encoder. No significance level can be assigned to Table 6 differences from the reported summaries alone, and improved attention ablations do not imply gene conditioning is useless.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Rewrite the conclusion as a performance/interpretability tradeoff rather than a universal advantage. Re-evaluate matched seeds, training budgets, and independent folds for full, attention-ablated, and simple encoders. Report parameter count, speed, and uncertainty, and select the architecture according to a predeclared objective. If interpretability is the reason to retain attention, validate that property directly.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: A conditional noise-to-image flow does not establish a bijection between expression and images
problems.source_location: Paper abstract p. 1; Methods p. 3; Figure 2 and Sections 3.1–3.2
claim: A conditional noise-to-image flow does not establish a bijection between expression and images.
analysis: The abstract describes an expression/image bijection, but Methods constructs \(I=\Phi_X(\eta)\): a noise-to-image map for fixed expression condition \(X\). ODE uniqueness can establish invertibility between \(\eta\) and \(I\) under its regularity assumptions; it does not establish an inverse between \(X\) and \(I\). Multiple expression profiles may give the same conditional image law, and one expression profile may generate many images.
result: The method can remain a useful conditional generator. The abstract's bijection argument does not resolve the biological many-to-one inverse problem. Methods p. 3 itself largely states the correct conditional-noise interpretation. This finding is about the stronger abstract/conceptual claim, not a proof that conditional generation is mathematically impossible. A dimension argument alone is insufficient because the intrinsic biological manifold dimensions are not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe the model as a conditional generative distribution p_theta(I|X). Restrict invertibility statements to a sufficiently regular continuous ODE at fixed X and distinguish numerical integration/postprocessing. Use posterior uncertainty, cycle tests where justified, or independent expression recovery experiments for any stronger cross-modal claim; do not infer them from the sampler type.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The conditioning representation cannot identify a particular cell arrangement or absolute replicated cell count
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 3–4, Eqs. (1)–(7); Appendix A p. 15; Appendix D pp. 20–22 src/multi_model.py:169–253 and 342–360
claim: The gene-set condition is used to support reconstruction of multicell histological structure.
analysis: The multi-cell encoder transforms each gene vector and forms normalized attention-weighted means across cells. It receives no cell coordinates. num_cells masks padding; it is not passed as a separate count embedding to the UNet. Permuting cells leaves the embedding unchanged. Replicating every cell the same number of times also leaves normalized weighted means unchanged. The single-cell model is conditioned on one cell's expression while the unmasked image contains its neighborhood.
result: This bounds the biological meaning of spatial reconstruction and perturbation claims. Image realism does not imply recovery of the actual cell arrangement or neighbor relationships. Permutation invariance is desirable for a set encoder and is not a bug. The limitation applies to identifying a particular arrangement from insufficient inputs, not to learning plausible conditional image distributions. Real expression values can correlate with density, but that does not remove the constructed ambiguity.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: If exact spatial reconstruction is the objective, include aligned coordinates, a spatial graph or layout condition, and explicit density/count information, and evaluate consistency under permutations of storage order. If expression-only synthesis is the objective, define a distribution over plausible arrangements, quantify diversity/uncertainty, and avoid treating a single generated arrangement as an observed biological interaction.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Velocity-energy gradients do not measure endpoint morphology influence
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 8–9, Section 4.3; Appendix C pp. 19–20 src/utils.py:449–561, especially 506–535
claim: Velocity-energy sensitivity is interpreted as gene importance for the generated morphology.
analysis: The statistic differentiates \(\|v_\theta(x,t;X)\|^2\) with respect to genes, rather than an endpoint morphology \(m(x(1))\). For constant velocity \(v=X\), initial point zero and identity endpoint readout, \(x(1)=X\): the energy derivative is \(2X\), zero at \(X=0\), while the endpoint derivative is one. Full endpoint sensitivity generally requires the trajectory sensitivity equation. The released routine also queries standard Gaussian states at every time rather than the time-dependent bridge/trajectory. This supports a narrower exploratory interpretation, not a claim that every identified gene is irrelevant.
result: The ranking can serve as an exploratory model-internal heuristic, but its stability/enrichment does not establish which genes causally or even endpoint-wise control morphology. The paper itself frames some downstream uses as hypotheses and candidates for experimental validation; that is appropriate. The counterexample does not show every identified gene is biologically irrelevant, only that the proposed statistic lacks the claimed general interpretation.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For model sensitivity, differentiate a specified image feature m(Phi_X(eta)) through a differentiable ODE solve or use controlled finite differences with common noise and an appropriate gene-expression perturbation scale. Sample relevant trajectory states if reporting velocity sensitivity and name that statistic precisely. Compare with input scaling, expression abundance, cell-type-only baselines, and gene shuffling. Reserve causal or regulatory claims for intervention data or explicitly justified causal assumptions.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Pathway enrichment and overlap statistics need assay-aware null models and complete reporting
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 8-9, Figure 4; Appendix C, pp. 19-20, Figure 13 and Table 10; author-described Xenium panel selection.
claim: The overlap/enrichment results are used as biological evidence for the identified gene sets.
analysis: The paper enriches \(34\) genes shared among the top \(50\) in its two panels. Assay-specific eligible genes, complete rankings, library versions and the family of overlap tests are not fully specified. The 10x Genomics panel already targets skin cell types and cancers, so panel selection matters to the null. Table 10 calls pathways significant but includes adjusted \(P=0.0918\), and describes ten pathways while showing six. Adjusted values are reported, and several meet \(0.05\); a missing correction is not established merely because a complete analysis record is absent.
result: The current enrichment is hypothesis-generating evidence whose statistical calibration and independence from panel selection are unresolved. The significant genes/pathways should not be treated as independent proof of causal morphological mechanisms. No incorrect background or missing correction is asserted as a confirmed historical failure merely because it is unreported. The paper does report adjusted P values for enrichment, and several displayed pathways meet 0.05. The narrower confirmed errors are the ambiguous significance description and the six-versus-ten caption.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Publish ranked genes and all contingency tables. Use the measured, quality-controlled eligible panel genes as the enrichment universe, or state and justify a different sampling model. For unequal panels, use a common eligible universe with consistent ranking or a panel-specific permutation null. State the multiple-testing procedure and threshold, distinguish raw from adjusted P, and label coagulation accordingly. Compare enrichment against rankings driven by expression and cell-type composition.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The released cell-type accuracy is degenerate for the documented eight-image evaluation batch
problems.source_location: rectified/utils_uni2h.py:195–234 and 295–303 README.md, custom evaluation batch_size 8
claim: The released cell-type accuracy routine is used as a biological agreement diagnostic.
analysis: classify_cell_types_uni2h assigns every sample label zero whenever a batch has fewer than ten items. Real and generated embeddings are classified separately and their integer labels are compared as if they were biological cell classes. Thus eight unrelated generated embeddings receive perfect agreement with eight real embeddings by construction. For larger batches, independent PCA/scaling/KMeans fits still have arbitrary cluster-label identities and are not trained cell-type classifiers.
result: The released evaluation summary can report perfect biological classification for unrelated inputs. This affects the software's advertised biological-validation output. Cell-type accuracy is not a reported column in Tables 2–6, so this audit does not use the defect to invalidate those particular numbers. The README's eight-image example is the relevant configuration; the CLI's numerical default need not be eight for the counterexample to matter.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use an externally validated, frozen cell-type classifier with a shared label vocabulary; fit any preprocessing only on training data. If measuring unsupervised clustering similarity, use a permutation-invariant statistic and accurately name it. Small batches should return unavailable metrics rather than perfect biological accuracy. Remove this statistic from composite biological plausibility until repaired.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Several biological similarity statistics discard the structure they are used to support
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 7–8, Tables 5–6; rectified/utils_uni2h.py:123–193, 237–280, 306–340
claim: The named embedding/spatial statistics are used to support cellular organization and biological similarity.
analysis: UNI2-h embedding similarity is one minus a scalar KS statistic after flattening all feature coordinates across images. It loses coordinate identity and multivariate structure. The reported spatial complexity and feature magnitude reduce each embedding to its standard deviation and mean absolute value, without direct cell coordinates or a spatial correspondence test. Nuclear features are extracted from Otsu-thresholded grayscale connected components in this evaluator, not validated nucleus instances. Those are legitimate image statistics when named accurately, but do not by themselves demonstrate cellular organization or diagnostic fidelity.
result: The high scalar similarity values in Tables 5–6 have a narrower interpretation than the prose implies. They cannot on their own clear the identifiability and spatial-reconstruction limitations. The paper also reports UNI2-h FID, which retains means and covariances; the flattened-metric objection does not apply to that separate statistic. A simple Otsu method is not automatically invalid, but its accuracy for these stained nuclei is unestablished without annotations.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain pooled multivariate feature distances and add paired feature/morphology measures with a declared target. Validate the nucleus segmentation against independently annotated nuclei or an appropriate pretrained model on these images. Evaluate cell count, position, type, shape, adjacency and uncertainty at image and sample level. Report embedding scalar summaries as descriptive diagnostics unless their relationship to spatial organization is empirically validated.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: GLCM angles are supplied in degrees to an API that expects radians
problems.source_location: rectified/utils_uni2h.py:258; paper Tables 5–6 spatial energy Official scikit-image graycomatrix documentation, angles parameter
claim: The texture evaluator intends to compare four conventional GLCM directions.
analysis: The texture evaluator passes angles \([0,45,90,135]\) to graycomatrix, whose documented unit is radians. At unit distance, these induce offsets \[(0,1),(1,1),(1,0),(0,-1)\], repeating a horizontal direction under symmetric counting and omitting the intended opposite diagonal. Both real and generated images use the same convention, so the sign of its effect on comparative rankings is not known.
result: Spatial energy and related texture comparisons are based on a different directional weighting than intended. Both real and generated images pass through the same metric, and a common unit bug does not predetermine which method it favors. Its effect on the reported table rankings has not been measured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Pass \([0,\pi/4,\pi/2,3\pi/4]\), state the angular convention, and recompute affected GLCM metrics. Include a small asymmetric image check so that repeating a horizontal direction cannot silently pass.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The optional DDIM baseline uses the wrong previous time when timesteps are skipped
problems.source_location: baseline/diffusion.py:318–352, 373–384, 523–540 baseline/diffusion_evaluate.py:149–152; diffusion_evaluate_ddp.py:613–616
claim: The accelerated DDIM path should transition between the selected diffusion times.
analysis: For a selected sequence of diffusion times, DDIM must transition to the preceding selected time. The implementation uses \(\bar\alpha_{\rm prev}(t)=\bar\alpha_{t-1}\), even when its next model evaluation is at a much earlier selected index. The state therefore carries the wrong noise level into the next denoising prediction.
result: Results obtained with the accelerated baseline path cannot support a fair DDIM comparison until this is corrected. Both standalone evaluation parsers default to DDPM; the DDPM path is not affected by this particular bug. Training-time preview helpers default to DDIM. The paper does not identify the historical sampling flag clearly enough to attribute its baseline disadvantage to this defect.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(\bar\alpha_{t_{i-1}}\) or one for the final clean endpoint, and test respacing against a maintained DDIM implementation. Match sampling method, noise schedule, training checkpoint, and network-evaluation budget in comparative experiments.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Optional stain matching uses the paired held-out target image
problems.source_location: rectified/rectified_evaluate.py:732–761 src/stain_normalization.py:8–76; src/utils.py:326–332
claim: The optional stain-normalized evaluation is presented alongside expression-conditioned synthesis.
analysis: When enable_stain_normalization is set, each generated RGB image is histogram-matched to its own corresponding real evaluation image before image and feature metrics are computed. The evaluated pipeline then has access to target-image information that would not be available when synthesizing an unknown histology image from expression alone.
result: Enabled results would estimate a different, easier pipeline than gene-only generation and should not be presented as the same task. The flag is store_true and therefore off by default; the reviewed example evaluation scripts do not establish that it was enabled for the paper tables. This is not a confirmed allegation of historical target leakage through stain matching.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Disable per-target matching for the primary expression-only benchmark. If stain standardization is scientifically needed, choose a fixed reference from training data and apply the same predeclared transformation consistently to real/generated images and all models. Clearly label a per-target matching experiment as an oracle-assisted analysis.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The implemented spatial losses do not reproduce the appendix objectives
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 23–27, Appendix E, Eqs. (19)–(33) src/spatial_graph_loss.py:131–174, 220–282, 284–362, 436–468
claim: Appendix E's morphology, arrangement, density and texture objectives specify the intended spatial losses.
analysis: Appendix E specifies nuclear morphology, matched-neighbor arrangement and density losses, and a separate kNN gradient/texture objective including higher texture moments. The released segmentation loss instead combines centroid assignment and edge-length-distribution distances. The simple loss uses multiscale Sobel magnitudes and local means/variances, with no kNN graph, skewness or kurtosis. The custom centroid function labeled approximate Wasserstein does not enforce uniform transport marginals and can ignore a distant unmatched cell. The segmentation routine recomputes segmentation rather than implementing the stated periodic cache.
result: A reader cannot reproduce Appendix E simply by running the public spatial-loss module. Even after the detach bug is repaired, a faithful experiment requires choosing a consistent mathematical objective. The corrected kernel prefactor would be a scale change at a fixed bandwidth and could be absorbed into a loss weight; it is not evidence of a large empirical failure. The centroid defect is confined to the optional segmentation branch and is not identified as the evaluator used for Table 5 nuclear statistics.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Choose and document the actual differentiable objective, align equations and code, and report which loss produced each result. Use a valid balanced or unbalanced transport formulation if Wasserstein terminology is retained. If Eq. (\(22\)) is intended as normalized planar density, use \(1/(2\pi h^2)\); otherwise call it an unnormalized kernel and state its scale. Remove redundant neighbor notation or introduce the intended neighboring feature difference.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Reported uncertainty and FID aggregation are insufficiently tied to independent experimental units
problems.source_location: Paper Tables 2–4, 6–9; Figure 8 p. 16; checklist p. 30 rectified/rectified_evaluate.py:801–840, 946–1044
claim: The means and standard deviations summarize the stated image-quality and biological evaluations.
analysis: The paper reports means and standard deviations, so absence of error bars is not the issue. It does not consistently identify whether variability comes from folds, model seeds, images, or batches. Figure 8 explicitly labels Batch FID Mean. The released evaluator exports both pooled overall FID and a mean of batch FIDs; it computes SSIM/feature-distance standard deviations over images and biological-statistic standard deviations over batches. Those are not interchangeable with variation over independently trained models or donors.
result: The reported summaries cannot support precise statistical superiority claims or a faithful fold-level reproduction without additional metadata. Batch FID can still be reported as an explicitly named diagnostic, but should not silently replace standard pooled FID. No particular table is asserted to use the wrong estimator without the result file that generated it. Standard deviations overlapping does not prove equality, and non-overlap would not repair correlated sampling. The checklist's claim that all metrics have standard deviations is broader than Tables 5–6, whose overall FID rows show point estimates.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Declare the estimator, feature extractor, image count, batch size, independent training-run count and meaning of each uncertainty interval. Keep per-image spread distinct from donor/run-level inference.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The perturbation and minimally invasive diagnostic claims exceed the demonstrated evidence
problems.source_location: Paper abstract p. 1; pp. 9–10, Section 4.4 and Discussion; Figures 3, 6, 9 Primary 10 x sample descriptions; Appendix F p. 27
claim: The broader discussion links conditional generation to perturbation analysis and diagnostic applications.
analysis: The experiments use observational paired FFPE Xenium/histology samples. No genetic or chemical intervention dataset, prospective diagnostic trial, or minimally invasive specimen acquisition workflow is demonstrated. The human study uses three ACVP-certified pathologists and two residents, \(20\) similarity pairs and \(20\) preference pairs. Its \(86\%\) preference for rectified outputs describes image preference, not disease sensitivity/specificity. Diagnostic examples are representative qualitative cases without a reported complete case denominator or accuracy/confidence analysis.
result: Neither conditional association nor reader preference establishes causal intercellular effects, reliable diagnosis, or replacement of a tissue-based diagnostic process. The Discussion already calls the tile system a proof of concept and acknowledges several practical limits. The human evaluation is real evidence of perceived image quality; it is not dismissed because the certification is veterinary, and no claim is made about misconduct, lack of required approvals, or diagnostic harm.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep the claim at conditional image synthesis and hypothesis generation. Release the complete blinded reader-study protocol and per-image/per-reader results, analyze crossed reader/image variation, and evaluate disease classification on an independent patient cohort before diagnostic claims. Test perturbations against held-out experimental interventions with explicit uncertainty and out-of-distribution checks. Define the proposed specimen acquisition workflow before claiming reduced invasiveness.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Small mathematical/architectural notation defects should be corrected without being mistaken for implementation failures
problems.source_location: Paper p. 3 input matrix orientation; p. 4 feature-gating formula; Appendix D pp. 21–23 src/single_model.py:179–203; src/multi_model.py:239–252
claim: The matrix orientation, feature gate and block descriptions specify the encoder architecture.
analysis: The input matrix is defined as \(C\times G\) but described once as genes in rows/cells in columns. The p. 4 gating expression uses Zfinal on both sides, whereas Appendix D and code implement a feedforward gate from the pre-gated embedding. Appendix D's residual-block descriptions also vary from the main text and the released normalization/activation choices. These are avoidable obstacles to implementation from the paper alone.
result: These corrections improve clarity/reproducibility but do not themselves invalidate reported performance. The encoder code clears the possible concern that the gate is actually circular. Likewise, padding uses masked_fill rather than literal floating-point \(0\times\infty\), so the symbolic Eq. (\(4\)) notation is not evidence of a runtime NaN bug.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use one \(C\times G\) orientation consistently; write \(Z_{\rm final}=Z_{\rm gate}\odot\sigma(W_gZ_{\rm gate}+b)\); provide a versioned architecture/configuration table matching the released model. Clarify which appendix equations are schematic and which are exact implementation definitions.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Correct stationary limit and a graph-level counterexample
problems.source_location: Main PDF p.4, Section 2.2, Theorem 1, Eqs 1-2 Main PDF p.5, Section 3.2
claim: Theorem 1 identifies the deep symmetric-normalized propagation limit with an arithmetic-mean projector and uses it to infer graph-level collapse.
analysis: For a connected aperiodic graph with augmented degrees \(\widetilde d_i\), the normalized adjacency power converges to \(uu^\top\), where \(u_i=\sqrt{\widetilde d_i}/\sqrt{\sum_j\widetilde d_j}\). For the self-looped three-node path, \(u=(\sqrt2,\sqrt3,\sqrt2)/\sqrt7\), which is not the uniform vector. Thus \(uu^\top\ne\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top/3\). In the paper's linear identity-weight setting, equal initial features on this path and a regular triangle need not have equal limiting mean readouts: degree factors remain. The arithmetic-mean limit and the resulting universal graph-level conclusion therefore fail.

With constant scalar initial node feature \(1\), the self-looped path has limiting mean readout \((11+4\sqrt6)/21\), while the self-looped regular triangle has limiting mean \(1\). Their equal initial feature means therefore do not imply equal limiting graph readouts under the theorem’s own linear identity-weight simplification.
result: The counterexample refutes the stated stationary identity and graph-level implication. It does not deny empirical oversmoothing in graph networks.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the degree-dependent projector and specify conditions on limiting graph readouts. Distinguish mean/sum pooling, regular/disconnected graphs, weights and nonlinearities.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Smaller spectral radius does not establish anti-collapse
problems.source_location: Main PDF p.7, Section 4, Eqs 11-12 and following paragraph
claim: Section 4 treats a reduced spectral radius as sufficient evidence against collapse.
analysis: Admissible equal two-view gates produce \(M=S/2\), with spectral radius \(1/2\). If \(S^L\to uu^\top\), then \(M^L=2^{-L}S^L\to0\): features collapse to zero. Relative eigenvalue ratios are unchanged by this scalar rescaling, so normalized oversmoothing is not removed either.
result: Reducing the absolute spectral radius does not establish the claimed anti-collapse property. Learned gates and nonlinearities need their own analysis; classifier accuracy is not determined by this linear example.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Analyze relative spectral decay under the actual recurrence. A qualified linear remedy is persistent initial-feature injection with convergent resolvent; its assumptions and effect on accuracy would still require verification.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Evaluation-time BatchNorm and node-order dependence
claim: The graph classifier's evaluation should respect node relabeling and its stated normalization convention.
analysis: Fresh BatchNorm1d uses node index as channel and remains training-mode even after parent.eval(); it is unregistered and called unconditionally once. Helper batch-change error \(2.15487\); five full-model seeds produce relabeling differences \(0.000326\)–\(0.007388\).
result: Symmetric full-model input yielded only \(1.19\times10^{-7}\) relabeling difference; that negative result is retained. Synthetic differences are not benchmark accuracy changes.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use registered, appropriately masked feature normalization or per-node LayerNorm; preserve evaluation mode and node equivariance.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Parameter registration can be lost on device transfer
problems.source_location: code/model.py:20-22,71-73
claim: The learned convolution parameters must remain registered after device placement.
analysis: nn.Parameter(cpu_tensor).to(device) returns an ordinary non-leaf Tensor when a device copy occurs, losing module parameter registration. Actual GraphConv has weight/bias on CPU but no named parameters on meta device.
result: CUDA execution was not performed. A no-op CPU conversion can conceal the issue; no inference about undisclosed historical training is made.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Create tensors on the target device before wrapping, or move the completed module. Check named_parameters, state_dict and optimizer membership; retrain after repair.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Padding is treated as graph content
problems.source_location: code/main.py:104-126 code/model.py:134-135,173-177
claim: Zero padding should not become extra graph content in normalization or readout.
analysis: Real-node counts are not used as a mask; affine/normalization/readout operations include padded positions. Adding two zero-padded nodes to an unchanged graph changes full-model logits by 0.137769.
result: Synthetic counterexample establishes release sensitivity, not its effect under the authors fixed dataset padding. Corrected model accuracy is untested.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Pass real-node masks; zero padded features after transformations and exclude padding from assignments, pooling and normalization.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The implemented recurrence differs from the analyzed recurrence
problems.source_location: Main PDF pp.5-6, Eqs 4-7 code/model.py:122-136,166-172
claim: The released recurrence is intended to implement the multiview propagation analyzed in the manuscript.
analysis: Paper specifies fixed initial assignments and separate view states propagated before final fusion. Release recomputes assignments and fuses every layer. Literal Eqs \(5\)-\(6\) also gate the first state twice, while release gates once; release adds normalization operations.
result: Alternative implemented architecture can be legitimate; discrepancy does not identify which private code generated tables.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Choose a canonical recurrence: preserve view states/fixed assignments as written, or revise equations and analyze layer-indexed assignments/fusion. Publish actual run configuration.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Cross-validation and coverage are not reproduced by the entrypoint
problems.source_location: Main PDF p.8, Section 5.1 code/main.py:146-166,223-240
claim: The manuscript describes repeated ten-fold cross-validation for its graph-classification results.
analysis: Entrypoint uses fold \(0\) once rather than looping over ten repetitions of ten-fold CV. With \(188\) graphs, floor-width folds test only \(180\) indices; \(180\)-\(187\) are never tested and excluded from final-fold training.
result: Public reproduction path is incomplete; this does not prove the authors omitted their stated protocol in private scripts.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use stratified complete outer folds and inner selection; preserve splits/seeds and publish \(100\) outer-fold scores plus repetition summaries.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Additional concrete reproduction faults
problems.source_location: code/main.py:76,108-109,114-115,195-200,235-238 CLI and evaluation paths in code/main.py
claim: The released command-line and evaluation interfaces are intended to support the listed dataset settings.
analysis: Two-class head cannot accept six-class targets; two dimension arguments become strings when explicitly supplied. Final returned model is epoch \(99\) but accuracy is epoch \(90\); graph truncation uses first node indices and squeeze can scalarize singleton batches.
result: No benchmark rerun or corrected accuracy. Truncation is a defined release behavior requiring an explicit dataset protocol.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Derive class count, type integer arguments, return matching checkpoint/score, support dataset capacity or sparse batching, and use reshape(\(-1\)) for labels.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Error bars have incompatible definitions
problems.source_location: Main PDF p.8, Section 5.1 and Table 1 Main PDF p.10, Table 3 Main PDF p.16, checklist item 7
claim: The uncertainty annotations describe the same statistic and independent evaluation unit.
analysis: Text describes standard deviation while captions/comparison/checklist describe standard error. Imported baseline rows may use incompatible uncertainty conventions; fold scores are not independent repetition-level measurements.
result: No independent significance claim is verified; the actual historical uncertainty calculation is unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Publish fold/repetition scores, identify independent unit and each plus/minus quantity, and recompute consistent paired summaries.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Average-rank audit
problems.source_location: Main PDF p.8, Table 1
claim: Table 1's average ranks summarize the stated within-dataset ranking convention.
analysis: Standard descending within-dataset ranks with average ties give DGK \(12.5714\) vs \(10.57\), RWGK \(14\) vs \(13.14\), WLSK \(8.1429\) vs 7.14. MultiNet mean rank \(16/7\simeq2.285714\) is reproduced and remains strongest under this convention.
result: An unstated alternative ranking convention could explain differences; classified unresolved rather than a proved historical calculation error.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Publish ranking universe, code and handling of missing entries; avoid mixing imported ranks from different tables.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The directional-diversity proxy is explicitly distinguished from the formal definition
problems.source_location: Main PDF pp.3-4, Definition 1 Main PDF p.9, Eq 13 and Section 5.3
claim: Directional diversity is compared with the formal diversity definition.
analysis: Authors acknowledge cosine-distance measure does not satisfy Definition 1. Vectors \((1,0)\) and \((2,0)\) have zero cosine distance but unequal magnitude; zero vectors need a convention.
result: The authors acknowledge this proxy limitation. It is a scoped clarification, not a current author error or a newly established anti-collapse guarantee.

problems.title: Claim calibration and checklist consistency
problems.source_location: Main conclusion Main PDF p.8, Table 1 Limitations and existing-assets checklist items Section 5.4
claim: The conclusion and checklist should reflect the displayed dataset wins, assumptions and assets.
analysis: Table 1 has MultiNet losses on ENZYMES and DD, so universal superiority exceeds five wins out of seven. Checklist NA answers conflict with disclosed assumptions/space limitations and use of public datasets; three variants are said but four listed.
result: Reporting corrections do not allege license violations or independently invalidate experiments.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State five dataset wins and strong average rank; disclose limitations/assets and correct variant count.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Cross-space raw distances do not demonstrate robustness
problems.source_location: Main PDF p.9, Fig 8 and discussion
claim: Figure 8 interprets smaller raw distances in different feature spaces as greater robustness.
analysis: The image-space distance \(47.70\) and feature-space distances \(27.01,12.16,7.71\) have different dimensions and scales. Multiplying any representation by \(0.001\) reduces its raw perturbation distance by a factor of \(1000\), without improving relative error or semantic discrimination. Therefore these raw cross-space distances alone cannot establish robustness.
result: This limits the robustness diagnostic; it does not refute the usefulness of the learned features or the measured interpolation results.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Define perturbations and compare dimensionless sensitivity with semantic discrimination/downstream reconstruction on matched examples.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Signal-to-noise ratio is interpreted in the wrong direction
problems.source_location: Supplement PDF p.4, Table 4 and discussion
claim: The supplement treats its lower SNR values as evidence of greater robustness.
analysis: Supplement treats lower SNR as greater robustness but provides no formula or units. Standard \(\mathrm{SNR}=10\log_{10}(P_{\rm signal}/P_{\rm noise})\): noise amplitude \(0.1\) gives \(20\) dB; amplitude \(0.5\) gives \(6.0206\) dB; higher is cleaner.
result: Unknown definition prevents determining which repair matches original calculations; do not speculatively invert table values.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Publish exact statistic; rename noise-to-signal/error quantities or correct standard-SNR direction and use comparable representations.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The implemented loss differs from Eq. 3
problems.source_location: Main PDF p.5, Eq 3 code/model/ourModel.py:116-118
claim: The released second-stage training objective should match the coefficients in Eq. (3).
analysis: Paper stage-two weights: Laplacian weight \(0.2\) and branch weights \(0.1\). Release uses \(1.0,0.5,0.1\) respectively. Feature alignment uses MSE; generic manuscript \(L^2\) wording does not specify reduction across scales.
result: Historical table-generating objective unknown. Repair requires retraining to assess empirical consequences.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(L_{\rm LPIPS}+0.2L_{\rm Lap}+\sum_s(L_{{\rm MSE},s}^{\rm main}+0.1L_{{\rm MSE},s}^{(0)}+0.1L_{{\rm MSE},s}^{(1)})\), or amend paper/configs to actual asymmetric objective.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Frozen parameters still allow the pretrained state to change
problems.source_location: code/model/ourNet.py:11-14 code/model/ourModel.py:53-54,109 code/util/utils_func.py:346-369
claim: The pretrained feature extractor is intended to remain fixed during subsequent training.
analysis: Freezing parameters and initial eval do not survive recursive parent.train() for BatchNorm buffers. Actual ResNet feature wrapper with frozen parameters changes running mean by \(0.0679887\) after synthetic forward.
result: No pretrained weights used for this test; no measured effect on published output or accuracy.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restore fixed generator/backbone eval after parent.train(), or override train. Preserve gradients through decoder inputs rather than applying blanket no_grad.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Evaluation has incompatible return values and signatures
problems.source_location: code/predict/pred_utils.py:110-124,164 code/predict/vimeo90k.py:67 code/predict/hsergb.py:88 code/predict/gopro.py:52,73-74
claim: Dataset evaluation callers and prediction helpers must agree on returned values and metric arguments.

problems.source_location: supplement p. 3, Algorithm 1
claim: Supplement Algorithm 1 reverses the latent and guidance sequence but reuses the same frame-dependent weights without an explicit backward-coordinate redefinition.
analysis: Supplement Algorithm 1 reverses the latent and guidance sequences before the backward pass, but retains the same frame-indexed \(\gamma_t\). The weights must follow their frames: \(\widetilde x'_0=(\widehat x'_0+R(\gamma_t)\odot R(g))/(1+R(\gamma_t))\), with elementwise division.

For \(\gamma=[9,0,0]\), \(g=[10,20,30]\) and zero denoised predictions, forward fusion gives \([9,0,0]\). The printed backward rule, realigned to forward order, gives \([0,0,27]\); the reversed-weight rule gives \([9,0,0]\). Blending with \(\beta=[1,0.5,0]\) therefore introduces a spurious final-frame value \(27\) under the literal pseudocode. Zero weights are permitted by Eq. (\(5\)).

The author release already reverses the weights: SVD_2pass_prob_uncertain.py, lines 681-687, flips guidance, masks, latent order and lambda_ts; its Post variant does likewise at lines 693-698. This is a printed-algorithm discrepancy, not evidence that the released generator uses misaligned weights.

problems.title: Diffusion time units and nonnegative spatial weights need a common definition
problems.source_location: Main PDF: diffusion notation, p. 4; Eqs. (2) and (5), pp. 5-6. Supplement: p. 2 and schedule/Algorithm 1, pp. 5-6.
claim: The main schedule is normalized to the unit interval, the supplement uses a reverse-step scale near \(100\), and a nominally positive scalar weight later becomes spatial and may be zero.
analysis: The main schedule uses a threshold on \([0,1]\), while the supplement uses \(\tau=70\overline U+30\) on a reverse-step scale near \(100\). At \(\overline U=0.5\), these conventions give \(0.65\) and \(65\). State whether the comparison is \(t/T\le0.7\overline U+0.3\) or \(t\le T(0.7\overline U+0.3)\), and distinguish reverse indices from scheduler noise timestamps.

The preliminaries write \(g^2(x)\) although the diffusion coefficient is \(g(t)\), and call \(\sigma_t\) a variance while using \(dx=(x-\widehat x_0)\,d\sigma/\sigma\). With variance \(v=\sigma^2\), the equivalent expression is \(dx=(x-\widehat x_0)\,dv/(2v)\).

Eq. (\(2\)) calls \(\gamma_{t,i}\) a positive scalar, but Eq. (\(5\)) allows zero and spatial variation. Nonnegative diagonal/broadcast weights resolve the type issue. The unweighted quadratic term keeps the Hessian positive definite, so Algorithm 1's elementwise minimizer is correct, including zero-weight entries.

problems.title: The pose-selection heuristic has a chosen translation scale
problems.source_location: supplement p. 4, Eq. (S-8)
claim: Supplement Eq. (S-8) combines translation distance and angular distance with coefficients set to one.
analysis: The pose score combines translation distance with angle using unit coefficients. Candidate \(A\) with distance \(0.1\), angle \(0.8\) radians scores about \(0.40657\); candidate \(B\) with distance \(0.5\), angle zero scores \(0.60653\). Multiplying translation coordinates by ten gives \(0.16530\) and \(0.00674\), reversing their ranking under a unit change. Normalize scene scale or specify reciprocal-unit coefficients. The author function correctly converts camera centers, so that separate error is not alleged. A pose heuristic need not measure actual occlusion/field-of-view overlap.

Equation (S-8) explicitly introduces two balancing parameters and fixes them for the reported implementation. Its dependence on translation units does not alone refute a stated scale-invariance theorem, because no such theorem is given. A reproducible implementation should keep the same scene scaling and parameter convention; changing units without transforming the coefficient changes the heuristic itself.
