problems.title: The acoustic code treats a coherent fraction as a coherent-to-diffuse ratio
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Section 4.3, p. 6; Appendix F.3, pp. 34-35. SAVVY/utils/doa_aria.py, lines 24-54 and 436; SAVVY/utils/avmap_utils.py, lines 331 and 356.
claim: Under the equal-power, uncorrelated coherent/diffuse model in main §\(4.3\) and Appendix F.3, range calibration is intended to use a coherent-to-diffuse power ratio.
analysis:
Let \(\rho\) denote coherent/direct power divided by diffuse power. Under the standard equal-power, uncorrelated-component coherence model, \[
\Gamma_x=\frac{\rho\Gamma_s+\Gamma_n}{1+\rho}.
\] This model and its inversion are given by Schwarz and Kellermann, Eqs. (\(8\)), (\(9\)), and (\(15\)). The same algebra applies to real parts under the corresponding assumptions. The published SAVVY implementation instead computes \[
\frac{\gamma_x-\gamma_n}{\gamma_s-\gamma_n}
=\frac{\rho}{1+\rho}=\alpha.
\] The result is the coherent fraction of total power, not \(\rho\). Yet the downstream code fits \(K=r^2\alpha\) and predicts \(r=\sqrt{K/\alpha}\), as though \(\alpha\) obeyed the inverse-square relation intended for the coherent-to-diffuse ratio. For a physical inverse-square constant of \(4\,\mathrm{m}^2\), a source at \(1\) m has \(\rho=4\), while one at \(4\) m has \(\rho=0.25\). Calibrating the implemented rule at \(1\) m gives \(K_{\mathrm{fit}}=0.8\). Its prediction for the \(4\) m source is then \[
\widehat r=\sqrt{0.8/0.2}=2\ \mathrm{m}.
\] Correctly converting these ideal fractions to \(\rho=\alpha/(1-\alpha)\) returns \(4\) m. More generally, the implemented rule compresses distances toward the calibration range when direct sound dominates. This directly undermines the claimed physical interpretation of the audio distance component, although the size of its effect on the fused benchmark score remains unmeasured.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Invert the coherence model to obtain the coherent-to-diffuse ratio; a coherent fraction is a different quantity.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The calibration constant depends on observation order
problems.source_location: SAVVY/utils/avmap_utils.py: get_audio_track, lines 319-345.
claim: The released calibration uses DBSCAN to obtain a stable distance constant, selecting cluster label zero.
analysis: In get_audio_track, candidate calibration constants are clustered with min_samples set to one, then the mean of clusters[\(0\)] is used. Cluster zero is the first discovered cluster, not necessarily the dominant one. For the ordered constants \([100,1,1,1]\), the chosen mean is \(100\); for the same observations ordered as \([1,1,1,100]\), it is \(1\). Since range scales as \(\sqrt K\), this creates a factor-\(10\) range difference. This is a deterministic consequence of the cited source's cluster selection, not an estimate of the paper's benchmark error.
result: The released calibration rule is order-sensitive. Its frequency and influence in the original scene-mapping runs remain unknown.

problems.title: Depth serialization loses metric precision and the bearing map ignores rectified intrinsics
problems.source_location: SAVVY/scripts/get_seg.py: lines 61-67, 257, 267-284 and 290. Official PDF: Appendix E.1, p. 31.
claim: The Seg branch converts estimated metric depth and image position into spatial tracks, using the rectified-image setting stated in Appendix E.1.
analysis: The depth routine writes \(\lfloor256d\rfloor\) to a \(16\)-bit PNG, but the later default cv2.imread call decodes it as \(8\)-bit color. That drops the lower eight bits, giving an effective integer-meter value \(\lfloor d\rfloor\) rather than restoring \(d\). Positive submeter depths can therefore become zero and be removed by the positive-depth filter, leaving an undefined mean for an all-submeter mask. This is material to submeter thresholds, but averaging and zero exclusion prevent inferring one universal direction of aggregate error.

The bearing routine maps normalized horizontal offset linearly to \(\pm90^\circ\). A rectilinear camera instead uses \(\theta=\arctan((u-c_x)/f_x)\). With an illustrative \(90^\circ\) field of view, a point halfway from center to edge has bearing \(\arctan(1/2)\simeq26.565^\circ\), whereas the linear rule gives \(45^\circ\). Actual rectified intrinsics and the distinction between optical-axis depth and ray range are needed for the paper's recordings.
result: The released depth/bearing conversion has local defects. The segmentation/depth models were not rerun, so their total effect on the published localization results is unmeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Decode depth without losing \(16\)-bit precision, restore physical units and use calibrated rectilinear intrinsics.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Table 6 uses Cartesian accuracy rather than the stated angular/radial accuracy
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Section 5.1, p. 7, and Tables 4-6. SAVVY/main.py: lines 344-360.
claim: Section 5.1 defines localization accuracy for Tables 4--6 by an angle threshold and a radial-distance threshold.
analysis: Section 5.1 defines success by angular error below \(45^\circ\) and radial error below \(1\,\mathrm m\). SAVVY/main.py instead tests Cartesian position error below \(1\,\mathrm m\). At equal ranges \(1\,\mathrm m\) and angle error \(50^\circ\), Cartesian error is \(2\sin25^\circ\simeq0.845\,\mathrm m\): the code passes and the stated angular gate fails. At equal ranges \(4\,\mathrm m\) and angle error \(30^\circ\), Cartesian error is \(8\sin15^\circ\simeq2.071\,\mathrm m\): the code fails while the written gates pass.

The released benchmark positions yield \(1196/1522\simeq78.5808\%\) within one Cartesian meter, matching Table 6's \(78.6\%\). Thus Tables 5 and \(6\) cannot be interpreted as a gain under one unchanged localization definition. This does not invalidate the separate QA-task scores.

problems.title: The printed coordinate maps omit yaw and use the wrong microphone plane
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Stage 2 equation, p. 5; steering vector, p. 6; Appendix E.2 microphone coordinates, p. 31; Algorithm 1, line 2, p. 36.
claim: The world mapping at p. 5 and the steering definition at p. 6 should agree with camera-relative bearings and the Appendix E.2 microphone geometry.
analysis: The printed world map adds \([r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta]\) to camera position without camera heading. A camera at the origin observing a fixed object at \((2,0)\) and then turning \(90^\circ\) can therefore place that object at \((0,2)\), a false displacement \(2\sqrt2\). For the stated right-positive convention, the heading-aware expression is \(\mathbf p=\mathbf L+r[\cos(\psi-\theta),\sin(\psi-\theta)]^\top\). The author's get_possible_locs function includes heading and avoids this printed error.

The printed steering vector lies in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane although microphones \(3\) and \(5\) differ only along \(z\), by \(0.1\,\mathrm m\). It consequently predicts zero delay for that front/rear baseline at every azimuth. The author steering implementation uses the \(x\)-\(z\) plane and preserves that directional information.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.

problems.title: The disclosed input differences define a complete-system comparison
problems.source_location: Official PDF: experimental inputs, p. 7; Appendices D-F, especially pp. 31-34; Table 6. SAVVY/main.py: baseline/system input paths.
claim: Main pp. 7 and \(31\)-\(-34\) compare the complete SAVVY system with baselines using different frame, microphone and pose inputs.
analysis: SAVVY has \(7\)-channel recordings available and uses a selected four-microphone array, \(128\) sampled frames for Seg, and calibrated closed-loop 6DoF Project Aria trajectories. The open AV-LLM baselines receive \(32\) frames and compressed mono audio. These conditions are disclosed, particularly in Appendices D-F, but mean the main comparison evaluates a richer complete system. It does not isolate an improvement in an otherwise identical AV-LLM's intrinsic spatial reasoning. The camera poses are additional sensor-derived inputs; they should appear explicitly in the task/interface formulation. Table 6 and the mapping ablation provide useful partial controls. A more decisive study would compare methods with matched frame budgets and pose availability, include a pose/depth-based visual geometric baseline, and separate gains from spatial channels from gains due to the fusion rule. No allegation of an impermissible comparison is intended: the present comparison is informative for system performance, while a causal architectural attribution requires these controls.
result: The richer-input comparison is disclosed and is informative about complete-system performance. It does not isolate architecture-only causation, but this limitation alone does not establish a current paper error.

problems.title: Question-level counts do not equal independent scene replication
problems.source_location: Official PDF: benchmark description, p. 4; Table 2; Appendix F.2; statistical-significance checklist, p. 18. Released benchmark/cache: question IDs, sequence prefixes and answer labels.
claim: The cache has \(1522\) questions, while Appendix F.2 and the checklist discuss operating points and negligible repeated-inference variation.
analysis: The released metadata has \(59\) video IDs, \(30\) paired recording-sequence prefixes and three location prefixes, rather than \(1522\) independent scenes. The main text's \(58\) scenarios need a definition mapping, not an automatic contradiction.

An always-A response scores \(194/463\simeq41.9\%\) on egocentric direction, and a difficulty-conditioned majority response scores \(34.4\%\) on allocentric direction. These describe the released label distribution, not independently selected competitors. Resemblance to a named model's rounded score does not identify its answers.

Conditional resampling of the \(30\) sequence groups gives a macro-score interval \(53.91\%\)–\(61.26\%\) between the \(2.5\) and \(97.5\) percentiles over \(5000\) resamples. This is a sensitivity calculation, not a population confidence guarantee for three convenience locations or a paired Gemini test. Low repeated-inference variation does not remove sampling uncertainty.
result: The released counts and conditional resampling describe the finite convenience benchmark. Independent scene-level population uncertainty and paired superiority remain unestablished; the valid question-level sample count is not itself an error.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Report sequence/location units and appropriate grouped uncertainty without calling all questions independent scenes.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Human and LLM judging require distinct reliability evidence
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Section 5.1; Appendices C.2-C.4, D.2-D.3 and K (annotations, object referral, human evaluation and reasoning examples).
claim: Appendices C--D describe annotation correction, human responses and a partly LLM-based object-referral metric.
analysis: The annotation procedure is detailed and includes manual correction, but the paper does not quantify independent agreement or positional/timing uncertainty at the \(0.1\) m scale used by the finest distance thresholds. A doubly reviewed subset would allow sensitivity analyses around annotation uncertainty and category boundaries. The object-referral metric also relies partly on LLM judging; its judge version, prompt, alias rules, and audited disagreement cases should accompany results. These are validation requests, not evidence that the ground truth or judge is wrong. The human score aggregates six evaluators who received disjoint shuffled portions of the questions, rather than six ratings per question. It is a useful task baseline but does not establish inter-rater reliability. Qualitative reasoning displays are illustrative explanations; because the standard proprietary-model prompt asks for constrained answers, any separate explanation-generation procedure should be stated before interpreting those narratives as faithful traces of the originally scored inference.
result: The available material identifies a scope or evidence gap; it does not prove that the reported empirical effect is false.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Document independent annotation agreement and LLM-judge version, prompt and disagreement audit.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The demonstrated planar task and component timing bound deployment claims
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Appendices C.3 and D.3 (planar task); Appendix G, pp. 36-37 (component timing); conclusion and Appendix I.
claim: The task templates use horizontal-plane distances, while broader spatial and efficiency interpretations appear in the conclusion and Appendix G.
analysis: The benchmark's distance templates and human guidelines explicitly use points projected onto the horizontal plane. Thus the 2D map and horizontal distance evaluation are deliberate, not a hidden mathematical error. However, success on these tasks establishes scene-grounded planar relations, not arbitrary vertical or full 3D reasoning. Generalization to outdoor/driving acoustics, multiple overlapping sources, new microphone geometries, and other camera trajectories remains untested in the reported experiments. Efficiency is likewise a partial-stage analysis. Appendix G reports approximately \(0.52\) s/frame/object for Seg and \(0.44\) s/frame for depth. The Seg number alone corresponds to about \(66.6\) seconds of serial processing for \(128\) frames and one object; the paper should clarify whether the separately quoted depth time is included before adding them. End-to-end latency depends on reuse, parallelism, object count, clip duration, and AV-LLM latency. A streaming latency/throughput experiment is needed to substantiate a deployment claim, even though the system can clearly trade frame count for accuracy.

problems.title: The released stacked RNN passes future information between layers
problems.source_location: Author supplement/repository: language_modeling/rnn_models.py, RNNLM.forward, lines 30-42; paper pp. 6-7, Table 2, and Appendix C.1.3, p. 18. Next-token shifting occurs in language_modeling/language_model.py, function shift_logits_labels and eval_ppl_runner
claim: The language-model experiment and Appendix C describe a conventional stacked RNN evaluated by next-token perplexity.
analysis: In RNNLM.forward, the state returned after processing the entire sequence in one recurrent layer initializes the next layer: \(h_0^{(2)}=h_T^{(1)}\). Then \(h_t^{(2)}=\tanh(W_2h_t^{(1)}+U_2h_{t-1}^{(2)})\), so even \(h_1^{(2)}\) depends on \(x_2,\ldots,x_T\). Shifting logits afterwards cannot remove this dependency.

This violates prefix causality in the released autoregressive model. Each layer requires its own initial state, carried only from a preceding chunk when stateful operation is intended. Both guided and unguided baselines use this class, so the direction of the effect on their difference is unknown. For copying, whose outputs follow the source sequence, the same state flow changes the stated architecture without automatically establishing target-label leakage.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Maintain an independent initial recurrent state per stacked layer so prefix outputs cannot depend on future tokens.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: CKA orientation and minibatch layer indexing are inconsistent in the manuscript
problems.source_location: paper p. 3; Algorithm 1, p. 16; Eqs. (2)-(6), p. 17. original printed equations
claim: The prose and Algorithm 1 define how CKA-derived guidance is computed and applied.
analysis: For nondegenerate centered representations, normalized linear CKA is \(1\) for identical representations, and the loss \(1-\operatorname{CKA}\) is zero. The prose reverses those endpoints and elsewhere says to minimize CKA; the author helper uses the standard orientation.

With \(H=I_b-\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top/b\), \(K_c=HXX^\top H\) and \(L_c=HYY^\top H\), the standard ratio is \[\langle K_c,L_c\rangle_F/(\|K_c\|_F\|L_c\|_F)\]. A singleton batch gives \(H=0\), so a degeneracy rule is needed. The printed tr(K,L) also needs a matrix-product or Frobenius-product definition; a common HSIC scale cancels from the ratio.

Algorithm 1 mixes single-example and minibatch operations, one-based and zero-based indexing, target and guide indices, and similarity versus dissimilarity, and omits an explicit parameter update. With \(50\) target and \(18\) guide layers, reusing the target index can request guide layer \(49\), outside its range. These are manuscript-specification defects, not evidence that the correctly oriented author helper optimized the opposite loss.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use standard centered minibatch CKA orientation and minimize its complement; specify degenerate-batch handling and layer indices.

problems.title: The random-guide result does not isolate architectural causation
problems.source_location: paper pp. 2, 4, 8-10; Appendix D, p. 20; Appendix E, p. 21; Appendix I.1, p. 25
claim: The discussion interprets gains, high alignment and earlier stitching theory as evidence of a purely architectural transfer mechanism.
analysis: A random guide has not learned task labels through weight optimization, but its representations still depend on initialization distribution, normalization, the input distribution, and the particular alignment metric. Improvement with that guide establishes that pretrained task weights are not necessary in those configurations. It does not uniquely identify which architectural property causes the improvement. The noise-guide experiment is compatible with a generic geometric regularizer. In particular, biased finite-batch CKA can be close to one for independent high-dimensional random features. For fixed batch size \(b\), independent Gaussian matrices \(X\in\mathbb R^{b\times d}\) and \(Y\in\mathbb R^{b\times d'}\) satisfy \(XX^\top/d\to I_b\) and \(YY^\top/d'\to I_b\) as widths grow. Centering gives matrices proportional to \(H\), so their CKA approaches one even though the feature sets are independent. This is a counterexample to reading high alignment as sufficient evidence of shared task information, not a demonstration that the paper's ImageNet gains are artefacts. It motivates a small set of discriminating controls: random features with matched Gram spectra, permuted sample correspondence, guide architectures with matched width and normalization, and a matched extra-forward/BatchNorm control. The last is relevant because guidance performs another target forward pass, updating BatchNorm statistics again during image training. The stronger claim that residual connections must be trained before influencing representation space is also unsupported. A residual block \(x+F_W(x)\) differs from \(F_W(x)\) before any weight update, and its input Jacobian contains an identity contribution. The failure of one random ResNet-50 guide to improve one target supports a statement about that experiment, not a necessity theorem about residual connections.
result: The available material identifies a scope or evidence gap; it does not prove that the reported empirical effect is false.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use matched random-feature, normalization, width and sample-correspondence controls before assigning architectural causation.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Correctness consistency is distinct from class-label agreement
problems.source_location: Fig. 3 and accompanying discussion, pp. 8-9; Appendix F, Eq. (7), p. 22; Fig. 13, p. 24
claim: Equation (\(7\)) uses an accuracy-derived expected-agreement null while parts of the prose describe agreement of predicted labels.
analysis: The null \(a_1a_2+(1-a_1)(1-a_2)\) describes agreement of correctness indicators, not multiclass labels. If two classifiers are correct on the same one of ten cases and choose different wrong labels on the other nine, correctness agreement is perfect but class-label agreement is \(0.1\). Combining \(0.1\) with the correctness null gives \(\kappa=-4\), showing the incompatible definitions.

The paper's guided-model pair has consistency \(0.49\), its guide pair \(0.53\), while matched target-guide values are \(0.047\) and \(0.020\). Similar within-pair scalars alone do not establish strategy inheritance: independent pairs can each have within-pair \(\kappa=0.5\) and zero cross-pair association. Original evaluation code is needed to identify the statistic actually plotted.

problems.title: The printed distillation loss reverses the cited KL direction
problems.source_location: Eq. (8), Appendix H, p. 23; Fig. 5, p. 10; model-distillation discussion, pp. 3-4
claim: Appendix H Eq. (\(8\)) labels student and teacher distributions and invokes the standard soft-target distillation baseline.
analysis:
The paper defines \(Q\) as student logits and \(P\) as teacher logits, then writes \[
\mathrm{KL}(\sigma(Q/T)\|\sigma(P/T)).
\] Standard soft-target distillation in the cited Hinton formulation minimizes cross-entropy from teacher probabilities to student probabilities, equivalent up to a teacher-only constant to the opposite direction, \(\mathrm{KL}(p_T\|q_T)\). This is not a notationally interchangeable choice. For teacher probabilities \((0.8,0.15,0.05)\) and student probabilities \((0.25,0.25,0.5)\), the two divergences are \(0.73876755\) and \(0.98821125\), respectively. The gradients and behavior under finite student capacity differ. A correctly stated baseline is \[
L_{KD}=\alpha T^2\mathrm{KL}(p_T\|q_T)
+(1-\alpha)L_{CE}(q_1,y).
\] If reverse KL was intentionally used, label it as a separate baseline and include the referenced forward-KL method. The released materials inspected here do not contain the original distillation experiment code, so the direction used to produce Fig. \(5\) remains unresolved. The related-work section itself acknowledges representation-based distillation and prior use of CKA. Consequently, beating one logit-distillation setting at \(\alpha=0.5,T=2\) does not establish superiority over representation distillation generally. A matched intermediate-feature or CKA-distillation comparator would identify what the random guide, cross-architecture design, and mapping add. That is a targeted comparison, not a demand for every existing distillation method.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State the intended KL direction; the cited teacher-to-student distillation baseline uses teacher probabilities as the reference distribution.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Uncentered activation SVD is not PCA explained variance
claim: Appendix I defines an ID regularizer through the explained-variance spectrum of activation matrices.
analysis: Eq. (\(9\)) needs the smallest integer crossing the variance threshold; otherwise many dimensions satisfy it. More substantially, Eqs. (\(10\))-(\(12\)) take the SVD of raw activations and call the squared singular values explained variances. PCA variance requires centering over samples. Without centering, a common feature offset changes the quantity although the covariance geometry is unchanged. The PCA threshold dimension is an operational linear effective dimension. Calling it the true complexity of the data manifold is stronger than this estimator warrants. The useful result would be that this specified spectral regularizer improves the chosen FCN, rather than a general causal conclusion that low intrinsic dimension causes overfitting. The linear-decoding argument on p. 28 also exceeds its evidence. A probe trained on \(4000\) images for \(1000\) classes is a limited-data test. Accuracy above the \(0.1\%\) chance level, even if below \(0.8\%\), does not demonstrate absence of linearly decodable information. The same paragraph cites a larger-data result with higher accuracy. A more accurate conclusion is that this small probe did not extract strong classification performance. Learning curves or a stronger probe would be optional ways to assess the mechanism further. Let \(X\) have rows \[(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)\] and let \(X'=X+\mathbf1(100,0)\). Both matrices have four samples and two finite real features. Centering gives \(HX'=HX=X\) and \(X^{\mathsf T}X=\operatorname{diag}(2,2)\), so the \(90\%\) variance threshold requires two dimensions. Without centering, \((X')^{\mathsf T}X'=\operatorname{diag}(40002,2)\), whose leading ratio is \(40002/40004=0.999950005\ldots\); the raw-SVD rule instead returns one. The constant offset is permitted by the stated activation-matrix domain, so translation invariance cannot be assumed unless centering is part of the definition.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Center activations across samples before PCA variance accounting, and state whether the regularizer targets an exact dimension or a lower bound.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The nearest-neighbor query must be the predicted dense vector
problems.source_location: §3.4, p. 6, Eq. (6), immediately after the dense query is defined in Eq. (5).
claim: Equation (\(6\)) supplies the discrete identifier to ANN after Eq. (\(5\)) defines the continuous query vector.
analysis:
The first argument of ANN is the generated discrete ID, although the surrounding procedure predicts a dense vector precisely to perform similarity retrieval. An ID can select an index partition, but it is not the continuous query vector whose cosine similarity to candidate embeddings is required. Figure 3 and Algorithm 1's similarity operation support a vector-query interpretation . A consistent replacement is \[
A_k = \operatorname{ANN}\bigl(\widehat v_k,
\{v_j:j\in C(c_k)\},N\bigr),
\] where \(c_k\) is the generated sparse ID and \(C(c_k)\) is the corresponding item bucket. If ANN also needs an index selector, write that as a separate argument with a declared signature. The returned object should contain item identities and their scores, rather than losing the item-embedding mapping. This is a confirmed error in the written equation, not evidence that the unavailable production code makes the same mistake.

problems.title: BeamFusion needs explicit normalization domains
problems.source_location: Eq. (7), p. 6; Algorithm 1, p. 24.
claim: Equation (\(7\)) multiplies two normalized scores but does not state the index sets of the softmax operations.
analysis: Eq. (\(7\)) does not identify the two softmax normalization domains. One is presumably over generated IDs; the other could range over a full bucket, its retrieved subset or a pooled candidate set. These choices change cross-bucket rankings.

Let bucket masses be \(0.6,0.4\), similarities \(A:(0.90,0.89)\), \(B:(0.90,-1.00)\), and multiplier one. With separate retrieved-list normalization at \(N=1\), leading scores are \(0.6,0.4\), so \(A\) wins. At \(N=2\), they are approximately \(0.3015,0.3480\), so \(B\) wins without any changed model output. problems.title: The disclosed fusion ablation changes support as part of the system
problems.source_location: §4.1 ablation paragraph, p. 8, with Tables 2 and 3, pp. 8-9.
claim: The no-BeamFusion condition replaces multiple sparse IDs with the single top ID before nearest-neighbor retrieval.
analysis: The no-BeamFusion variant uses one sparse ID; the full method uses several, changing both candidate support and scoring. If \(C_{\rm top1}(S)\) is the selected bucket, every restricted ranker satisfies \(\operatorname{Recall@K}\le\Pr\{Y\in C_{\rm top1}(S)\}\). For example, a first bucket covering \(60\%\) of true targets and a second covering the remainder permit a coverage gain without any benefit from the fusion formula.

The industrial no-dense variant additionally changes the semantic ID from two levels of \(32\) entries to three of \(256\). This is a legitimate alternative-system comparison, but it does not isolate removal of the dense branch.

problems.title: The entropy theorem needs a shared law and does not prove better fitted learning
problems.source_location: §3.5, Theorem 1 and the paragraph following it, p. 7; Appendix F, pp. 24-25.
claim: Theorem 1 and Appendix F compare independent and cascaded representations and interpret smaller entropy as a learning advantage.
analysis: For one fixed joint law \(P\) with the required finite entropies, \(H_P(ID\mid S)+h_P(V\mid S)-H_P(ID,V\mid S)=I_P(ID;V\mid S)\ge0\). This validates the same-law identity in Appendix F; independently fitted neural distributions need not share the marginals used in that comparison.

Lower fitted entropy does not imply better prediction. Fix a sequence \(S\). Let truth give probability \(1/2\) to \(ID=0\) with \(V\) uniform on \([0,1]\), and probability \(1/2\) to \(ID=1\) with \(V\) uniform on \([2,3]\). A cascaded fit with the same conditional unit-width uniform densities but ID probabilities \(0.999,0.001\) has joint mixed entropy about \(0.0079\) nats and expected negative log-density about \(3.4544\). An independent fit with uniform ID and equal mixture density on both intervals has entropy and expected negative log-density \(\log4\simeq1.3863\). Thus the lower-entropy fit is worse under the true law. This continuous-density construction respects the appendix’s differential-entropy setting and does not estimate COBRA’s performance.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.

problems.title: Baseline provenance and the nearest hybrid comparison remain unresolved
problems.source_location: §2, p. 3; baseline list and results, pp. 7-8; Appendix B, p. 22.
claim: The comparison section reports public baselines and discusses hybrid methods including LIGER.
analysis: All \(108\) baseline cells in COBRA Table 1 match the earlier TIGER paper's Table 1 exactly after aligning dataset order: nine methods, three datasets, four metrics. This comparison was performed against the official TIGER proceedings PDF, p. 7, not a third-party leaderboard . Reusing published baselines is legitimate; exact matching is not evidence of fabrication, plagiarism, or whether an author also reran a model. The necessary reporting correction is to distinguish copied published values from new reruns and identify the common evaluation protocol. Without that information, readers cannot evaluate feature parity, tuning budgets, or a paired significance comparison. LIGER is already cited in the paper as a hybrid generative/dense approach, but it is absent from both the public performance table and the industrial comparison. Its original paper and author repository confirm direct relevance . The currently available comparison does not establish superiority over the nearest hybrid alternative. This is an empirical gap, not proof that COBRA lacks novelty.
result: The available material identifies a scope or evidence gap; it does not prove that the reported empirical effect is false.

problems.title: Missing configuration details prevent a unique reproduction
problems.source_location: §4.1 implementation details, p. 7; §4.2 implementation details, p. 9; Appendices C and E-G, pp. 23-25; checklist items 4-6, pp. 15-16.
claim: Implementation sections and the reproducibility checklist describe a repeatable method without releasing company code.
analysis: The paper identifies the public leave-one-out split and the industrial \(60\)-day/next-day split, along with some layer and codebook counts. Those are useful. The exact dates and availability rules for advertisements matter to a prospective deployment interpretation, although their absence is not proof of future-data leakage. problems.title: Transformer orders do not account for the full retrieval cost
problems.source_location: Appendix G, p. 25, Tables 5 and 6.
claim: Appendix G Tables 5--6 give encoder/sequence-model complexity in support of scalable retrieval.
analysis: For \(H\) sparse tokens per item and history length \(L\), interleaving yields approximately \((H+1)L\) tokens. Standard dense prefill costs \(O(((H+1)L)^2D+(H+1)LD^2)\), reducing to the paper's \(O(L^2D+LD^2)\) when \(H\) is fixed. The displayed order is therefore not false for suppressing that fixed factor. A complete retrieval cost also includes beam/ID decoding, dense queries, index search, bucket scoring and selection. Exact bucket scoring costs \(O(D\sum_k|C(c_k)|)\); global scoring has a different catalogue term, and ANN cost depends on its index and recall target.

problems.title: The finite random-frequency bound fails at an admissible modulus
problems.source_location: Theorem 4.7, p. 6; Theorem C.1 and proof, Appendix C, pp. 22-24.
claim: Theorem 4.7/Theorem C.1 claim minimum incorrect-answer margin exceeding \(\delta m'\) with probability at least \(\rho\) when \(m\) distinct uniformly sampled half-spectrum frequencies exceed \([2\log n-2\log(2-2\rho)]/[\log(\pi/\delta)-1]\). No prime/coprime or large-modulus restriction appears in the operative statement.
analysis: Take \(n=6\), \(m=m'=1\), \(\delta=0.001\), \(\rho=0.9\), and inputs \(i=j=0\). The stated frequency-count threshold is approximately \(0.964539<1\), so its premise holds. Frequencies \(1,2,3\) are equally likely. Frequency \(1\) has minimum incorrect margin \(1/2\); frequency \(2\) ties the correct answer at displacement \(3\), and frequency \(3\) ties it at displacement \(2\). Success probability is exactly \(1/3<0.9\), contradicting the claimed guarantee.

The main text samples uniformly from \(\{1,\ldots,n/2\}\), while Appendix C uses \(\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\). The witness also defeats the latter convention: at \(n=6\), only frequencies \(1,5\) avoid a tied incorrect answer, giving success probability \(2/5<0.9\). Thus the sampling-domain discrepancy does not rescue either stated finite guarantee. The appendix explicitly calls its Taylor/volume/Stirling argument a heuristic and says a rigorous proof needs more precise bounds; that is important counterevidence against treating it as a rigorous finite-grid argument, but does not make the main theorem’s unconditional probability statement true.
result: The theorem is false on its stated finite-spectrum domain. This does not deny successful prime-modulus networks or prove any claim about training universality.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A replacement concentration statement must account for the finite frequency population, coprimality and confidence conditions. No claim of corrected training convergence is made.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The frequency-normalizing function map is reversed
problems.source_location: Definition 4.2, p. 4; supplementary plots_multilayer.py, lines 628-635.
claim: Definition 4.2 (p. 4) uses the inverse frequency to normalize the sinusoid, but prints the map in the direction \(g(dx)=h(x)\).
analysis:
For a coprime frequency, write \(d=f^{-1}\pmod n\) and \(h(x)=\cos(2\pi fx/n)\). The printed definition is \[
g(dx)=h(x),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad g(x)=h(d^{-1}x).
\] This multiplies the frequency by \(f\), producing \(f^2\bmod n\); it does not generally normalize the frequency to one. The correct reparameterization is \[
g(x)=h(dx)=\cos(2\pi x/n).
\] Equivalently, when moving an old sample at index a to a new plotting location, set the new index to f a mod n. Function composition and moving array entries use opposite-looking maps, which likely explains the printed reversal. For the concrete case \(n=7,f=2,d=4\), the printed definition produces frequency four, whose real-FFT representative is three, rather than frequency one. The maximum discrepancy from the frequency-one sequence is approximately 1.52446. The corrected definition agrees to numerical precision. The author-supplied plotting code assigns new indices \(a_{\rm new}=fa\bmod n\) and \(b_{\rm new}=fb\bmod n\). That is consistent with the corrected reindexing when the frequency is coprime to the modulus. This is evidence that a written inverse error need not have corrupted the displayed prime-modulus plots. For composite moduli and a noncoprime frequency, multiplication by f on all n indices is not a permutation: it repeats destinations and leaves others unused. A general implementation must operate on the quotient or explicitly aggregate equivalent indices. A bijective prime-modulus check is insufficient to certify the composite-modulus plotting path.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(g(x)=h(dx)\) for the function reparameterization and distinguish it from moving array indices.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: An approximate coset needs the full quotient preimage
problems.source_location: Definitions 4.1-4.3, p. 4; Appendix A.2.1; Appendix B, p. 22.
claim: Definitions \(4.1\)-\(-4.3\) and Appendix B move between a quotient cycle and supports in the original cyclic group.
analysis: Definition 4.3 writes a progression in quotient vertices without the full preimage that lifts it to the original cyclic group. At \(n=66,f=11\), the exact phase-zero fiber is \[\{0,6,12,18,24,30,36,42,48,54,60\}\], whereas the literal minimal progression contains \(-1,0,1\pmod{66}\). Positive minimum radii also exclude the radius-zero case needed for exact fibers.

Set \(g=\gcd(n,f)\), \(q=n/g\), quotient map \(\pi:C_n\to C_q\) and \(d=(f/g)^{-1}\pmod q\). A consistent object is \(\pi^{-1}\{\pi(c)+jd\pmod q:-r_-\le j\le r_+\}\), with nonnegative radii. Appendix B's inverse must similarly be taken modulo \(q\), not \(n\): at \(n=12,f=8\), \(f/g=2\) has an inverse modulo three but not twelve.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Define approximate cosets as full preimages of quotient arcs with nonnegative radii, allowing radius zero.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Positive hidden activation does not guarantee positive evidence for the answer
problems.source_location: simple-neuron model, pp. 3-4; Theorem 4.4, p. 4; Appendix B, pp. 21-22.
claim: Theorem 4.4 and its surrounding interpretation relate a simple neuron's approximate-coset activation to a correct-output support.
analysis:
A hidden neuron's activation is a function of the input pair \((a,b)\). Its outgoing weights form a different function of the candidate answer \(c\). The theorem describes activation on an approximate coset containing the correct answer, but its proof does not fully specify the relation between these two domains or show that positive ReLU activation guarantees positive output evidence at the correct answer. Consider the paper's own simple-neuron parameterization with \(n=12\), frequency one, phases \(s_A=s_B=0\), and positive amplitude one. Take \(a=b=2\). The input preactivation is \[
\cos(\pi/3)+\cos(\pi/3)=1,
\] so ReLU is positive. The correct answer is \(c=4\), but its outgoing weight is \[
\cos(2\pi\cdot4/12)=\cos(2\pi/3)=-\tfrac12.
\] The neuron's contribution to the correct logit is therefore \(-1/2\). The correct answer is outside the positive support of that outgoing sinusoid despite positive hidden activation. Positive activation alone does not prove the strong answer-support interpretation used in parts of the discussion. This construction does not refute successful addition by a complete phase-balanced cluster. Other neurons can compensate, and the aggregate cosine construction in Appendix C is a different object. Nor does it rule out calling a sufficiently large quotient arc an approximate coset containing the answer. It shows why the theorem needs an explicit, nonvacuous statement: which support is a set over inputs, which is over outputs, what radius is allowed, and what quantitative relationship is guaranteed? The last step of Appendix B says that later ReLU layers preserve linear combinations of approximate cosets because ReLU removes negative elements. For a signed sum of overlapping components, thresholding may create a different union of intervals or supports. It is not automatically the same linear combination. Conversely, if arbitrary linear combinations of all singleton indicators are allowed, every function on a finite domain has such an expansion, and the claim provides no mechanism-specific restriction. A useful theorem must define the basis, coefficients, closure property, and sparsity or geometry that make the statement informative.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Separate input activation support from output-logit support and state a quantitative cluster-level relationship if required.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The projection sign is wrong and coordinate bounds do not exclude a representation
problems.source_location: Appendix D, pp. 24-25.
claim: Appendix D projects a standard rotation with a negative sine component, then identifies the result with a phase difference; it also discusses weights beyond \([-1,1]\).
analysis:
The appendix uses the usual planar rotation acting on (\(1\), \(0\)) but writes a projection vector with components \((\alpha\cos\phi,-\alpha\sin\phi)\). Their dot product equals \[
\alpha\{\cos\phi\cos\theta-\sin\phi\sin\theta\}
=\alpha\cos(\theta+\phi).
\] The following expression instead uses the plus sign appropriate for \(\alpha\cos(\theta-\phi)\). At \(\theta=\pi/3,\phi=\pi/6\), the written vector gives zero whereas the claimed phase-difference expression gives approximately 0.8660254. Change the second projection component to \(+\alpha\sin\phi\), or explicitly reverse the rotation convention. State the convention once and use it consistently. The separate observation that learned scalar weights can exceed the interval \([-1,1]\) cannot by itself exclude a group representation. That interval describes entries of a normalized planar rotation matrix in an orthonormal basis. A representation in \(\operatorname{GL}(V)\), as defined in Appendix A, may be written in another basis. For example, conjugate the \(90\)-degree rotation by \(S=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\). The resulting generator is \[
S\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}S^{-1}
=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\1/2&0\end{pmatrix}.
\] Its fourth power is the identity, so it gives a valid representation of the cyclic group of order four, although one entry has magnitude two. Embeddings and readouts derived from a representation may also include scaling and projection; the resulting readout arrays need not themselves be group homomorphisms. A raw coordinate-range observation only rules out a particular normalized parameterization. Appendix D already introduces scaled projections and acknowledges compatibility with the representation hypothesis. That acknowledgment should also constrain any broader exclusion suggested by the section's heading or discussion. This criticism does not establish that the prior group-composition interpretation is universal. It concerns the specific argument used to exclude it here. A stronger comparison would test whether a common change of basis and readout makes the learned operators approximately satisfy the relevant group law, then quantify the residual. The paper can still argue that the coset description is more explanatory in particular networks, but coordinate magnitudes alone do not settle that comparison.
result: The stated limitation or local discrepancy is supported within this source version. Stronger causal, historical-run or population conclusions remain unverified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Correct the projection sign and use basis-invariant criteria when discussing group representations.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The reported logarithmic fits are valid finite empirical evidence
problems.source_location: Paper Figure 3, p. 6; Appendix E experiment settings; author-released make_figure_logn_scaling_plot.py.
claim: Figure 3 fits frequency counts against log modulus from author-supplied aggregate data while experiment settings also change.
analysis: The author-supplied finite aggregate values yield slopes on log modulus of \(1.174595\) (Clock), \(1.189408\) (Pizza), and \(0.726435\) (MLP), with \(R^2\) approximately \(0.989\)–0.990. problems.title: The mechanism evidence is conditioned on successful models and a detector
problems.source_location: introduction, pp. 1-2; results and discussion, pp. 7-10; Appendix E.5, p. 28; Appendices G.4-G.5 and G.9.
claim: The introduction and conclusion discuss universality while Appendix E.5 selects successful models and Appendix G describes approximation and manual circuit-classifier adjustments.
analysis: Appendix E.5 selects models that achieve at least \(99.9999\%\) final accuracy and drops neurons below the stated activation threshold. Appendix G also presents unsuccessful or atypical cases and describes approximations in the circuit detector, including manual adjustment for some runs. These are useful disclosures. They mean the analyzed population is conditioned on successful training and on the operational definition of a usable neuron or circuit. The evidence should therefore be described as common structure observed across the evaluated successful models. It does not establish the same structure in all optimization outcomes, all hyperparameter regimes, all architectures, or all functions performed by all neurons. Calling limitations open questions does not remove this selection boundary. The circuit detector is part of the measurement process. To use its outputs as evidence for a universal mechanism, report its criteria before classifying models, the amount of manual tuning, the rate of ambiguous/unclassified neurons, and sensitivity to thresholds. A blinded validation set of hand-inspected neurons or small circuits would help separate a robust phenomenon from flexibility in the classifier. The appendix's acknowledgment that its approximation is not fully accurate should remain visible in the main claim. Theorem 4.7 assumes sinusoidal components and analyzes their combined logits. It does not prove that training converges to this family. Theorem 4.4 likewise starts from the simple-neuron assumption. Empirical support for that assumption and a conditional theorem are complementary, but together they do not turn a restricted model family into an unconditional theorem about all neural networks. The extension from cyclic groups to a universal abstract mechanism covering other groups also needs its own statement and evidence. Existing coset observations in another task motivate that extension; they do not by themselves prove an exhaustive classification of mechanisms across group families. A useful next paper could specify the proposed abstraction as an explicit algorithm with inputs, intermediate state, decoder, approximation error, and falsifiable exclusions.
result: The available material identifies a scope or evidence gap; it does not prove that the reported empirical effect is false.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State the successful-model selection and detector criteria, including manual adjustments and unclassified cases.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Redundancy and margin formation do not yet define an error-correcting code
problems.source_location: Appendix G.9.3 and related discussion.
claim: Appendix G.9.3 interprets redundant components in error-correction terms.
analysis: Redundant components can improve margins or reduce loss without constituting an established error-correcting code. A coding claim requires the encoded object, codeword map, error channel, distance notion, and decoder to be specified. The relevant statement is then whether the decoder recovers the answer under a defined number or distribution of perturbations. For this paper, one concrete route would encode an answer by its vector of selected phase or cosine features, define corruption at the feature or cluster level, and test a stated decoder under random and adversarial feature changes. Measure minimum separation over answers and compare it with the corruption radius. Ablating redundant neurons and observing performance changes is useful but does not alone establish such a code or its correction capability. The current evidence supports redundancy and aggregate margin formation. Present the coding interpretation as a hypothesis unless the additional operational definitions and tests are supplied.
result: The available material identifies a scope or evidence gap; it does not prove that the reported empirical effect is false.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Treat error-correction as a hypothesis unless a code, channel, distance and decoder are defined and tested.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Figure variables, toy readout and factor-count conventions need explicit definitions
problems.source_location: Official PDF: Figure 12, p. 22; Appendix A.2.2; coset-type/factor-count and half-frequency discussions.
claim: Figure 12, Appendix A.2.2 and related discussion use margin, frequency-count, toy-logit and factor-count descriptions that require distinct definitions.
analysis: Figure 12, p. 22, fixes modulus \(59\) and varies the number of frequency components over a small range, while its caption invokes growth with \(\log n\). Those variables are different. The plotted average margin also differs from the minimum margin over all incorrect outputs used in Theorem 4.7. An average can be positive while an incorrect output still ties the correct one. Relabel the independent variable and identify whether the plotted statistic is an average, a minimum, or a success probability. Appendix A.2.2 has a repeated component label in its toy discussion and does not fully specify the readout needed to reconstruct the listed toy logits. Under a direct literal cosine readout, the displayed values do not follow without additional scaling or indicator choices. This is a request for an executable toy specification, not a claim that the intended toy mechanism is impossible. The discussion of a number of coset types growing logarithmically uses a large-modulus example without defining exactly what counts as a type. Classical CRT decomposes into pairwise coprime prime-power factors, whose count differs from counting prime factors with multiplicity or a chosen hierarchy of subproblems. State the counting convention before using the example as complexity evidence. References to a half-frequency response should distinguish a continuous interpolation used to visualize a finite sequence from a character frequency of the finite cyclic group. Every function on a finite cycle has an expansion in its integer-indexed discrete Fourier basis. Observing a shape that resembles a half-frequency sinusoid under one plotting convention does not contradict that fact. Any claimed failure of an earlier mechanism must use that mechanism's actual assumptions and quantitative predictions.

paragraphs: Define figure variables, readout normalization, minimum-versus-average margins and factor-count conventions.

problems.title: Global dynamic slots require quadratic routing
problems.source_location: Current paper, Section 2.4, p. 6; author release src/models/soft_moe/soft_moe_with_dynamic_slots.py, lines 99–129 and 235–244.
claim: The dynamic hierarchy has linear routing complexity.
analysis: Let \(N\) be the input length, \(K\) the fixed group size, and \(E_1,S,E_2\) fixed expert/slot counts. The author implementation concatenates first-level slots into length \(L=\lceil N/K\rceil E_1S\). The next dynamic-slot layer pads to \(L'=E_2\lceil L/E_2\rceil\) and explicitly creates logits of shape \(B\times L'\times E_2\times(L'/E_2)\).

That tensor has \(B(L')^2\) entries, and its dot products cost \(\Theta(B(L')^2d)\). Thus global routing is quadratic in \(N\) at fixed grouping/width constants, despite constant-factor compression. For the stated first-stage settings, doubling \(N\) from \(110592\) to \(221184\) doubles global length from \(864\) to \(1728\), and multiplies logits entries from \(746496\) to \(2985984\). These are shape counts, not total GPU-memory measurements.
result: The strict linear-scaling explanation does not describe the author-released global routing. Small-input speed or memory benefits can still be real.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Report the full grouped/global complexity. Fixed global slot count \(Q\) would give \(O(BLQd)\) routing, but that changes the architecture and would need new training.

problems.title: The two-stage algorithm differs from the execution graph
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 4–5, 3
claim: The published two-stage equations describe the released execution graph.
analysis: The current paper uses learned slot embeddings and a group softmax router, whereas HierarchicalDynamicSlotsSoftMoE.forward generates embeddings from group means, uses learned scalar expert gates and a sigmoid group gate, and applies DynamicSlotsSoftMoE to all concatenated group slots. The actual source performs global dispatch and has the quadratic routing counted above; the Mamba branch also supplies long-range dependence.

problems.title: Translation variance is scale-dependent
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 6, 14
claim: The temporal translation variance is a heuristic for anchor refinement.
analysis: Equation (6) averages squared translation deviations over \(16\) sampled times. This correctly exposes length-squared units. The paper calls the quantity normalized variance but does not assert coordinate-scale invariance; normalization can mean division by the number of time samples. problems.title: The binary term is not Shannon entropy
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 7
claim: The binary confidence penalty encourages endpoints and is combined with a sparsity penalty.
analysis: The penalty \(\alpha(1-\alpha)\) is Bernoulli variance, or a binary Gini/Tsallis-type impurity, rather than Shannon entropy. The combined regularizer \(0.5\alpha+0.2\alpha(1-\alpha)\) has derivative \(0.7-0.4\alpha>0\) on \([0,1]\); its preference for zero is consistent with its declared sparsity purpose, while reconstruction supplies the competing incentive. The paper does not identify this function specifically as Shannon entropy.

problems.title: Teacher-forced PCR does not establish small distributional changes
problems.source_location: PDF pp.2–3 Eq 1–2; Appendix C.1 p.26
claim: The preliminary PCR study motivates the hypothesis that RL changes probabilities mainly at a small set of reasoning-related tokens.
analysis: Take a vocabulary of \(100\) tokens. Let two next-token laws be \[p=(0.02,0.98/99,\ldots,0.98/99)\] and \[q=(0.99,0.01/99,\ldots,0.01/99)\]. Both have the same unique argmax, but \(\|p-q\|_{\rm TV}=0.97\). Repeating this construction on every teacher-forced prefix gives perfect argmax preservation while distributional change remains large. Teacher-forced prefixes also differ from prefixes generated by a model's own earlier tokens.
result: Identical teacher-forced argmax decisions do not establish small probability changes or free-running path agreement. The paper presents a motivating hypothesis, not a formal total-variation or knowledge-preservation theorem; the counterexample limits that interpretation without refuting measured reasoning gains.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.

problems.title: The general Bellman recurrence needs monotonicity
problems.source_location: Paper pp. 4
claim: The general path-cost recursion can be evaluated using minimum prefixes.
analysis: The current general framework allows transition cost to depend on accumulated prefix cost, then moves the minimum inside that transition. analysis: Use one calibration sample and target coverage \(1/2\). Let \(X\in\{A,B\}\) be equiprobable, \(Y\sim U(0,1)\), and \(f=0\). problems.title: Weighted erase/retain composition does not preserve shared directions as claimed
problems.source_location: PDF p.5 Eq 4–5; Fig 2 p.4; AppendixC pp.23–24
claim: The finite-weight operator in Eq. (5) removes only discriminative forget directions while preserving components shared with a nonempty retain set.
analysis: Use \(E_f=E_r=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{0.8},\sqrt{0.2})\) and \(\alpha=2\). Eqs. (\(1\))-(\(5\)) give \(P_f=P_r=\operatorname{diag}(8/9,1/3)\). The purported distinct-forget operator is \(P_f(I-P_r)=\operatorname{diag}(8/81,2/9)\), so the edit is \(A=\operatorname{diag}(73/81,7/9)\). Both directions are completely shared, yet both are attenuated. Zero-padding embeds the example in the paper's higher-dimensional space. Choosing \(W=I\), or a rectangular cross-attention row that reads either affected direction, makes the corresponding output change explicit. The current Appendix C disclaims global optimality and worst-case behavioral guarantees, but the finite linear shared-component assertion after Eq. (5) is still contradicted. Main Tables 1–4 use \(P_r=0\), so this witness is not a reconstruction of those measured outcomes.

Even hard projectors do not generally have intersection projector \(P_fP_r\): for \(P_f=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) and \(P_r=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), their subspaces intersect only at zero but \(P_fP_r\ne0\). However, a truly hard retain projector still preserves every \(v\) with \(P_rv=v\), because \([I-P_f(I-P_r)]v=v\). The soft-retain counterexample must not be generalized to that hard-retain property.
result: The unconditional shared-direction preservation interpretation is false for the paper's finite soft weights. Main tables using \(P_r=0\) are not thereby shown numerically wrong.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe the edit as soft spectral attenuation, or residualize forget directions against an orthonormal retain basis \(Q_r\). A residual basis \(Q_d\subset R^\perp\) gives \(A_{\rm corr}=I-Q_dQ_d^\top\), with \(A_{\rm corr}Q_r=Q_r\) and \(A_{\rm corr}Q_d=0\). This linear guarantee does not certify all semantic behavior.

problems.title: L2 concentration guarantee omits dimension
problems.source_location: PDF pp.38–40, Lemma A.22, Theorem A.23, equations 31–33
claim: The coordinatewise concentration argument supplies the stated vector-L \(2\) guarantee.
analysis: The proof reverses event inclusion: \(\|e\|_\infty\ge\epsilon\) implies \(\|e\|_2\ge\epsilon\), but not conversely. For instance \((0.8,0.8)\) has both coordinates below one and Euclidean norm above one.

A legal one-qubit instance uses \(\rho=I/2\), \(M=Z\), label \(y=1\), and \(1000\) fixed unitary layers, each with one inverse-noise coordinate, all true and inverse noise parameters zero at the evaluated point. Every true gradient is zero because the maximally mixed state is invariant. Select every coordinate, \(p=\Gamma=\epsilon=1\), \(\delta=0.05\), and \(N=5426\) shots per coordinate, split into independent batches of \(n=2713\). Algorithm 3 gives \(g_j=-4(1-A_j)B_j\), with independent Rademacher sample means \(A_j,B_j\); Algorithm 5 independently calls these coordinate estimates. This is the paper’s ideal independent-sampling algorithm, separate from the released reseeding defect.

Put \(\mu_2=1/n\), \(\mu_4=3/n^2-2/n^3\). Then \(\mathbb Eg_j^2=16(1+\mu_2)\mu_2\) and \(\mathbb Eg_j^4=256(1+6\mu_2+\mu_4)\mu_4\). For \(Z=\sum_{j=1}^{1000}g_j^2\), these give \(\mathbb EZ\simeq5.8997042\) and \(\mathbb EZ^2\simeq34.8762510\). Paley-Zygmund yields \(\Pr(Z>1)\ge(\mathbb EZ-1)^2/\mathbb EZ^2\simeq0.688351\), whereas the printed tail bound is \(2d\exp(-2N/32^2)\simeq0.049949\).

The printed Theorem A.23 says “at least,” which is a necessary-budget claim. The witness directly refutes Lemma A.22 and Eqs. (31)–(32), and shows that solving that tail bound does not provide a sufficient Euclidean-error budget. It does not by itself refute the same smaller number as a possible necessary lower bound; a sufficient concentration argument also cannot establish information-theoretic necessity.
result: Lemma A.22's Euclidean tail guarantee is false, and the derived sufficient shot budget is not established. Theorem A.23's literal necessary-budget wording is not separately refuted by this counterexample; sufficiency does not establish necessity.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Applying the coordinate tail bound at \(\epsilon/\sqrt m\) gives the sufficient budget \(N\ge512\Gamma^4m\epsilon^{-2}\log(2m/\delta)\) per selected coordinate, rounded to an allowed even value. This is not an optimality lower bound. Alternatively restrict the guarantee to the infinity norm.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Summable steps do not guarantee stationarity
problems.source_location: PDF p.7 Theorem 3.2; pp.43–45 TheoremA 31
claim: Summable steps imply the claimed stationary convergence.
analysis: For the allowed quantum loss \(F(\theta,\sigma)=(1-e^{2\sigma}\cos2\theta)^2\), use \(\theta\in[0,\pi/2]\), \(\sigma\in[0,1/1024]\), initial \((\pi/8,0)\), and \(\eta_t=2^{-t-12}\). The total step is \(1/2048\).

Every sampled \(\theta\)-gradient estimate has magnitude at most \(4\Gamma_{\max}(1+\Gamma_{\max})\simeq8.0234757\), with \(\Gamma_{\max}=e^{2/1024}\). Nonexpansive projection therefore keeps every path in \[[0.388781369,0.396616794]\]. Throughout this interval and the full \(\sigma\) box, \(\partial_\theta F\ge4(1-\Gamma_{\max}\cos2\ell)\sin2\ell\simeq0.80251458>0\), where \(\ell=\pi/8-4\Gamma_{\max}(1+\Gamma_{\max})/2048\). Thus no path approaches a constrained stationary point.

The current Theorem A.31 actually states a finite weighted objective-gap upper bound with a nonvanishing constant. The all-path witness refutes the further stationarity interpretation under its permitted summable steps, rather than supplying a numerical violation of that nonzero upper bound. The proof of that upper bound separately contains the smoothness and second-moment errors below.
result: The summable-step conditions do not justify the stationary-convergence interpretation. This does not numerically refute the theorem's distinct finite-time objective-gap bound, which contains a nonvanishing constant.
assumptions: Only the author-released source version and stated claim are assessed.

problems.title: The clipping contribution is confounded
problems.source_location: Current paper, Appendix C.3 and Table 13, p. 24; clipping interpretation, p. 6 and Appendix D.1, p. 25.
claim: The comparison interprets Table 13 as clipping contributing more than training noise.
analysis: Table 13 gives printed noisy-evaluation averages \(62.92\), \(65.44\) and \(65.96\). The first change adds a complete adaptation/training and quantization pipeline including clipping; the second adds training noise within that already adapted pipeline. If \(A(B,C,N)\) denotes the score with non-clipping adaptation \(B\), clipping \(C\), and noise \(N\), the table supplies \(A(0,0,0)\), \(A(1,1,0)\) and \(A(1,1,1)\), but omits \(A(1,0,0)\). Consequently the isolated clipping effect \(A(1,1,0)-A(1,0,0)\) may be larger, smaller or negative while retaining all three observations. The \(2.52\)-point composite gain and \(0.52\)-point conditional-noise gain do not identify that comparison. The SNR/quantization mechanisms remain compatible with clipping helping in practice.
result: This remains a bounded scope or unresolved-source concern; broader experimental invalidity is not established.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Narrow attribution to the compared composite settings or provide matched component ablations.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.
