problems.title: Mirror-symmetrization notation needs implementation evidence
problems.source_location: Final proceedings, Appendix A.1, p. 21, connection-group definition and both weight-symmetrization equations; Figure A1.
claim: Appendix A.1 divides each connection group by \(2n_{st}\), while the group key retains both source and target lateralizations. It says the resulting matrix gives identical weights to mirror-related connections while preserving overall strength.
analysis: Take four neurons \(a_L,a_R,b_L,b_R\), with lateralization-free labels \(a,a,b,b\), and only the two mirror-related directed connections \(a_L\to b_L\) and \(a_R\to b_R\), of weights \(2\) and \(6\). They belong to different displayed keys, \((a,b,L,L)\) and \((a,b,R,R)\), each with \(n_{ab}=1\). The printed rule therefore returns weights \(1\) and \(3\): they remain unequal and their total changes from \(8\) to \(4\). Removing only the factor \(2\) would still leave the groups separate.

This demonstrates that the literal grouping does not establish the stated invariants. It does not determine the actual preprocessing: the implementation could additionally merge mirror groups or count their multiplicities differently. The current official supplement repeats the same equations; the final paper also supplies Figure A2, a control without symmetrization using separately tuned left and right populations.
result: The displayed definition requires clarification. Without the actual grouping function and matrices, this remains an unresolved implementation-versus-notation concern rather than a finding that the published dynamics fail.
assumptions: The connection key and \(n_{st}\) are interpreted literally as defined in Appendix A.1, with no additional unreported mirror-group merger.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Clarify the actual pairing and group-count convention and provide the preprocessed matrix. No experiment-restoring correction is established.
No correction of the printed definition was found in the current final paper or official supplement; the intended implementation convention remains unresolved.

problems.title: The signed-speed loss may omit a direction convention
problems.source_location: Final proceedings, Section 4.2, pp. 5–6, signed velocity inputs and linear-consistency loss; Figure 2 and Appendix A.7, Figures A9–A10, pp. 26–27.
claim: The paper trains an integrator with inputs \(u\in[-U,U]\) and signed decoded angular velocity \(v=\delta\theta(t)\). Its linear-consistency loss takes the variance of \(v/|u|\) around a common mean across nonzero inputs.
analysis: For equally weighted nonzero inputs \(u=1,-1\), let the correct bidirectional response be \(v=u\). The two ratios \(v/|u|\) are \(1,-1\), their mean is \(0\), and the displayed mean squared deviation is \(1\). The direction-insensitive response \(v=|u|\) gives ratios \(1,1\) and loss \(0\). This is a contradiction between the literal signed-ratio definition and the stated linear-response objective.

The current paper nevertheless shows bidirectional integration and reversal of heading motion in Figure 2 and Figures A9–A10. Section 4.2 and Appendix A.7 explicitly inject velocity through opposite GLNO populations. Those observations make an omitted magnitude or direction-group convention plausible; they do not supply the actual decoder, unwrapping and loss computation.
result: The notation does not settle whether the implemented loss is incorrect. Bidirectional trajectories and possible separate directional averaging are retained as counterevidence; no failed experiment or invalid dynamical result is established.
assumptions: The displayed mean pools both signs of nonzero \(u\), and \(\delta\theta(t)\) retains its signed meaning rather than a magnitude or a direction-normalized value.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify whether the ratio uses signed velocity, speed magnitude or separate directional groups. No new network repair or rerun is asserted.
The current final paper retains the absolute-input denominator; its implemented directional convention remains undocumented in the inspected materials.

problems.title: Deterministic conditional mutual information is zero
problems.source_location: Final proceedings, Theorem 4.1 and Eqs. (4)–(6), p. 5; Appendix A, Eqs. (28)–(29), pp. 21–22.
claim: Theorem 4.1 takes the deterministic representation \(U=F(H)\), assumes \(F\) is a measure-preserving bijection, and equates maximization of \(I(U;Y\mid H)\) with an interventional mutual-information objective. Eqs. (4)–(6) use that equivalence to justify the supervised InfoNCE term as backdoor adjustment and noise removal.
analysis: For every measurable deterministic \(F\), the conditional joint law given \(H=h\) is exactly the product of its conditional marginals: \[P_{U,Y\mid H=h}=\delta_{F(h)}\otimes P_{Y\mid H=h}=P_{U\mid H=h}\otimes P_{Y\mid H=h}.\] Therefore every conditional KL divergence is zero and \(I(F(H);Y\mid H)=0\). This proof applies to discrete and continuous representations without subtracting potentially infinite differential entropies. Bijectivity or volume preservation cannot restore a representation-selection signal.

Appendix A additionally treats a fixed label marginal as implying \(P(Y\mid H)=P(Y)\). That implication is false: fixed marginal prevalence is compatible with completely predictive features. An algebraic manipulation of the observational distribution also cannot define a changed interventional probability law without specifying the intervention distribution and its label marginal.

A complete witness to different maximizers can be given under the volume-preserving reading used by Appendix B. Let \(I_j=[j,j+1)\), for \(j=0,1,2\), and let \(H\) have densities \(1/2,1/4,1/4\) on those intervals. Let \(F_0\) be the identity and \(F_1\) swap \(I_0,I_1\) by translation while fixing the remainder of the real line. Both are Lebesgue-measure-preserving measurable bijections. Define \(U_j=F_j(H)\), \(R_j=H-F_j(H)\), and the same label mechanism \(Y=\mathbf1_{\{U_j+R_j\in I_1\}}\). Both schemes have the identical observational label \(Y=\mathbf1_{\{H\in I_1\}}\), and both conditional-information objectives are zero.

Define randomized intervention by sampling \(U_j\) from its own observational marginal independently of \(H\), retaining \(R_j(H)\) and the stated label mechanism. The input interval probabilities are \(q_0=(1/2,1/4,1/4)\) and \(q_1=(1/4,1/2,1/4)\). For \(F_0\), the three conditional label probabilities are \((0,1,0)\); for \(F_1\), they are \((1/4,1/4,1/2)\). With binary entropy \(H_b\) in bits, the corresponding mutual informations are \[I_{q_0}(U;Y)=H_b(1/4)=0.8112781245,\qquad I_{q_1}(U;Y)=H_b(5/16)-\tfrac34H_b(1/4)-\tfrac14=0.0375796392.\] Thus both maps maximize the constant CMI over this two-map family, whereas only \(F_0\) maximizes this defined interventional objective. If preservation instead means preservation of a specified nonuniform probability law, this particular interval swap need not qualify; the general CMI identity remains unchanged.
result: The current deterministic conditional-information objective is degenerate, and the published proof does not establish its replacement by the stated causal objective. The explicit randomized-intervention witness also separates maximizer sets under the declared volume-preserving interpretation. The supervised loss can remain a useful predictive regularizer; its empirical usefulness does not repair this causal derivation.
assumptions: The representation \(U=F(H)\) is deterministic, as specified in Theorem 4.1.
The additional maximizer witness uses Lebesgue-volume preservation and replaces only the structural equation for \(U\) during randomization, leaving \(R(H)\) and the label mechanism fixed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A valid replacement identity is \(I(F(H);Y\mid H)=0\). If \(F\) has a measurable inverse, data processing in both directions also gives \(I(F(H);Y)=I(H;Y)\). Treat InfoNCE as predictive supervision unless a nondegenerate, identifiable intervention model and its estimator are separately established. This does not restore the original causal theorem.
The current final paper and freshly obtained official appendix retain the implicated construction; no adopted correction is established.

problems.title: Layerwise constraints do not certify the aggregate map
problems.source_location: Final proceedings, Eqs. (7)–(8), pp. 5–6; Appendix B, Algorithms 1–3, p. 23.
claim: The paper asserts that its URD construction is a measure-preserving bijection. It constrains linear-layer singular values and constructs orthogonal affine layers, while the complete map aggregates three weighted residual decompositions with real-valued, linearly projected gates \(w_k\in\mathbb R\).
analysis: The actual aggregate is \[U=F_f\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{3}w_kU_k\right),\quad U_k=F_d(H_k),\quad H_1=H,\quad H_k=H-\sum_{i<k}w_iU_i.\] Choose one-dimensional identity component maps, zero biases and zero coefficients in each gate projection, so \(w_1=w_2=w_3=0\). Identity component matrices have singular value \(1\), satisfy the \(10^{-5}\) lower bound, and can be obtained from Algorithm 3 by \(W=[1]\), since \(\exp(W-W^\top)=1\).

Every residual input then equals \(H\), but the weighted sum and output are identically zero. In particular, inputs \(H=0\) and \(H=1\) both map to \(U=0\). The full map is not injective and sends an interval of length \(1\) to a point. More generally, any deterministic outer component would return the constant \(F_f(0)\), regardless of unspecified activation details. The printed real linear gates do not exclude this allowed zero choice.

The positive control is important: Algorithm 3 itself is correct for a square affine layer. For \(A=W-W^\top\), \(Q=e^A\) satisfies \(Q^\top Q=I\) and \(\det Q=e^{\operatorname{tr}A}=1\); translation does not change volume. Pure compositions preserve this property. Weighted sums and residual feedback are not pure composition. Even an additional hypothetical equal softmax gate would yield \(U=[1-(1-1/3)^3]H=(19/27)H\) with identity components, which is invertible but not volume preserving. That control is not a claim that the paper uses softmax.
result: The constraints do not guarantee the complete URD map is a measure-preserving bijection, although the isolated affine-layer construction is valid. The counterexample refutes a universal architectural guarantee; it does not show that the trained representation actually collapsed.
assumptions: The real-valued linear gate projection in Eq. (7) allows zero coefficients, with no additional nonzero or whole-Jacobian constraint.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the valid affine-layer statement and remove the unsupported whole-map guarantee unless a full-network invertibility and Jacobian argument is supplied. No architecture-preserving causal repair is established.
The current final paper and freshly obtained official appendix retain the implicated construction; no adopted correction is established.

problems.title: Unequal clusters invalidate the risk bound
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v1, Section 3.1, p. 4; Theorem 3.1/Eq. (1), p. 5; Appendix C, pp. 14 and 16, especially Eq. (3).
claim: Theorem 3.1 promises a simultaneous high-probability bound for the empirical risk averaged over all samples from \(m\) independent centers and their local redundant samples. It permits unequal cluster sizes \(k_i\), but its redundancy term depends only on \(\eta=m^{-1}\sum_i k_i^{-1}\), without controlling the largest sample weight \(k_i/n\).
analysis: Take a singleton hypothesis class containing \(f_0(x)=0\), with \(L^1\) loss, and independent centers with deterministic labels \(Y=Z\), where \(Z\) is Bernoulli with probability \(1/2\). Set \(m=1000\), \(k_1=10^9\), \(k_i=1\) otherwise, and \(\delta=0.05\). The local distribution for each center is its own point mass, so redundant samples are exact copies and conditionally independent given that center. Their supports lie in the true support, labels are noise-free and losses lie in \([0,1]\). An additional independent continuous input coordinate makes center coordinates almost surely distinct if desired.

The true risk is \(R(f_0)=1/2\); the singleton constant-predictor Rademacher complexity is zero. With \(S=\sum_{i=2}^{1000}Z_i\), the actual sample-weighted risk and its uniform lower deviation satisfy \[R_{\rm emp}(f_0)=\frac{10^9 Z_1+S}{10^9+999},\qquad |R-R_{\rm emp}|\ge\frac12-\frac{999}{10^9+999}=0.499999001000998.\] This holds for every possible \(Z_1\) and \(0\le S\le999\).

Yet \(\eta=0.999000000001\), and the claimed upper bound is \[\sqrt{\frac{2\log40}{1000}}+\sqrt{\frac{0.999000000001\log40}{8000}}+\frac{2\log40}{3000}=0.10981586563536902.\] Its success probability is therefore \(0\), rather than at least \(0.95\). Even an alternative absolute-loss-class complexity of at most \(1/\sqrt{1000}\) would not close this gap.

The current Appendix C replaces the actual weighting \(\sum_i(k_i/n)\bar\ell_i\) with an approximately equal-center average. It also bounds cluster-mean variance by \(1/(4k_i)\); unconditional exact copies still have variance \(1/4\). Conditioning on the center can reduce that variance, but does not remove unequal center weights. Equal cluster sizes eliminate this particular weighting mismatch; they do not by themselves supply the missing local-distribution and uniform-control argument.
result: The latest Theorem 3.1 is false in its stated unequal-cluster generality, and its current proof cannot establish the claimed algorithmic guarantee. This finding does not show that distribution reshaping harms real IQA accuracy.
assumptions: The empirical risk is the all-sample mean defined in Section 3.1, and the theorem has no equal-size or maximum-cluster-weight restriction.
Local distributions may be point masses at their centers; these satisfy the stated support and noise-free conditions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A narrower finite-class replacement explicitly records both missing terms. For \(|\mathcal F|=M\), bounded losses, independent centers, \(w_i=k_i/n\), center losses \(\ell_i(f)\), and cluster means \(\bar\ell_i(f)\), define \[T(w)=\tfrac12\sum_i|w_i-1/m|,\qquad B_f=\sum_iw_i|\bar\ell_i(f)-\ell_i(f)|.\] Then with probability at least \(1-\delta\), simultaneously over the finite class, \[|R(f)-R_{\rm emp}(f)|\le\sqrt{\frac{\log(2M/\delta)}{2m}}+T(w)+B_f.\]

Triangle inequality separates the independent-center mean error, the reweighting error and the within-cluster deviation. Since losses lie in \([0,1]\) and the signed weight differences sum to zero, reweighting is bounded by \(T(w)\). Two-sided Hoeffding and a union bound give the first term. This allows arbitrary within-cluster dependence; it adds a finite-class assumption and does not restore the unrestricted original theorem or prove either algorithm improves risk.
The current preprint and inspected author-release paths retain the implicated statements or behavior. The bounded proposed corrections are not established as adopted or empirically validated.

problems.title: Fixed-cluster downsampling increases eta
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v1, discussion after Theorem 3.1, p. 5; Section 3.3.2, p. 6; Algorithm 3 and the following explanation, p. 7.
claim: DRCDown is explicitly motivated as decreasing \(\eta=m^{-1}\sum_i1/k_i\), thereby lowering the third term of Theorem 3.1.
analysis: Within one fixed collection of nonempty clusters, deletion gives \(1\le k_i^{\prime}\le k_i\), so \[\eta^{\prime}-\eta=\frac1m\sum_i\left(\frac1{k_i^{\prime}}-\frac1{k_i}\right)\ge0,\] strictly if any cluster loses samples. For example, two clusters of size \(100\) with \(T_u=20\) are both reduced by Algorithm 3 to size \(50\); \(\eta\) rises from \(0.01\) to \(0.02\), increasing the displayed square-root term at fixed \(m,\delta\).

Reallocating a fixed total number of samples to balance cluster sizes is a different operation: Jensen gives \(\eta\ge m/n\) at fixed \(m,n\). Actual deletion decreases \(n\). Re-extracting features can also redefine the cluster set, but needs a separate analysis and does not reverse the fixed-cluster calculation.
result: The current monotonicity explanation has the wrong direction for the stated quantity and deletion rule. This corrects the theoretical motivation without demonstrating that downsampling lowers real accuracy or overturning the reported empirical improvements.
assumptions: The comparison holds the nonempty cluster collection and \(m\) fixed while deleting members within clusters, as in one application of Algorithm 3.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Remove the claim that this fixed-cluster deletion lowers the defined \(\eta\). Any theory for reweighting or changing clusters must state the changed quantity and assumptions; empirical benefit alone does not prove the printed monotonicity.
The current preprint and inspected author-release paths retain the implicated statements or behavior. The bounded proposed corrections are not established as adopted or empirically validated.

problems.title: Released epoch selection uses target-test labels
problems.source_location: Li-aobo/SynDR-IQA, current commit b8e53fe2c937265a00cefb15abb1b3fae7c47fdd: train_test_IQA_cross.py, main(), lines 30–67; BaseIQASolver.py, test(), lines 75–100; latest paper Section 4.1, p. 7.
claim: The paper describes source-database training and target-database testing. The actual released cross-database script computes target-test correlation at every epoch and retains the best target-test epoch.
analysis: In main(), test_data is built from config.test_db at line 33. Each epoch calls solver.test(test_data) at line 43; lines 44–46 update best_srcc and the corresponding best_plcc when target-test SRCC improves. Lines 52–62 optionally save the selected checkpoint, and lines 66–67 print the best cross-database metrics. In test(), lines 95–98 average patch predictions and ground-truth scores and compute Spearman and Pearson correlations. Thus target labels participate in the selection \[\widehat k=\arg\max_k\widehat\rho_{\rm test}(f_k).\]

A concrete dependence check needs no training: candidate score vectors \((0,1,2,3)\), \((0,2,1,3)\), and \((3,2,1,0)\) have SRCCs \((1,0.8,-1)\) against labels \((0,1,2,3)\), but \((0.8,1,-0.8)\) against labels \((0,2,1,3)\). The positive-best selection therefore switches from the first candidate to the second when only target labels change. These are transparent score comparisons, not new executions of the author function or actual benchmark outputs.

The current head is the same December 2025 commit, and the freshly fetched operative files are byte-identical to the earlier author release. This confirms the released behavior persists, but does not establish that the paper tables were generated with that path. The README names a different entry point that is absent at this pinned URL; no behavior is inferred for that unavailable file.
result: The inspected released path uses the target set for model selection, so its maximum cannot be interpreted as performance on an untouched target-test set. The historical table attribution and the magnitude of any score bias remain unresolved; no corrected SRCC or PLCC is asserted.
assumptions: The finding concerns the actual released main() path and optional best-checkpoint rule, not an assumed historical or unavailable entry point.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Select epochs on source or independent validation data, or predeclare the epoch, then evaluate the frozen model on held-out target data. An allowed labeled-target validation design requires a separate target test set and an explicit task description. No corrected benchmark evaluation was run.
The current preprint and inspected author-release paths retain the implicated statements or behavior. The bounded proposed corrections are not established as adopted or empirically validated.

problems.title: Generated paraphrases do not identify the observational marginal
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, p.4, Eq.4; Appendix C, p.24, Figure 7.
claim: Section 4.1 substitutes equal weights on jointly generated question variants for the observational marginal \(P(Q)\) in the front-door formula.
analysis: Generated variants follow a proposal \(g(q^{\prime}\mid q,T)\), which need not be the observational marginal \(P(Q)\). Consider independent-noise binary structural equations: \(C\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(4/5)\); \(Q=C\) with probability \(9/10\); \(E=Q\) with probability \(4/5\); and \(A=E\mathbin{\mathrm{XOR}}C\). This has exactly the front-door paths \(C\to Q,C\to A,Q\to E\to A\), and all conditioning cells are positive. The marginal of \(Q\) is \((13/50,37/50)\). For \(E=0\), the conditional answer probabilities across the two question values are \((4/13,36/37)\); for \(E=1\), they are \((9/13,1/37)\). Direct intervention at \(Q=1\), and the correctly weighted front-door formula, both give \(8/25=0.32\). Replacing only the question weights by \((1/2,1/2)\) gives \[\frac15\frac12\left(\frac4{13}+\frac{36}{37}\right)+\frac45\frac12\left(\frac9{13}+\frac1{37}\right)=\frac{200}{481}\approx0.4158004158.\] Equal-probability generation, even if exact, does not identify the different observational law.
result: The current Section 4.1 substitution is not generally an estimator of the stated front-door marginal. The classical front-door formula remains valid in this same counterexample. Multiple paraphrases may still improve empirical answers, but that observation does not establish causal identification.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use an identified observational marginal or justified importance weights \(P(Q)/g\) on common support. This does not identify the unknown proposal of an actual LLM.

The current proceedings Section 4.1 retains the simultaneous-generation uniformity justification; the current author repository is empty. The conditional importance-weighting identity remains an applicable analytic correction, not evidence of an adopted implementation.

problems.title: Evidence union changes the expectation target
problems.source_location: Section 4.2 and front-door Eq.3; evidence aggregation and voting steps.
claim: Section 4.2 substitutes a union of retrieved evidence for the outer front-door evidence average.
analysis: Let the evidence values be \(E_0=\{r_0\}\), \(E_1=\{r_1\}\), and \(E_2=\{r_0,r_1\}\), with probabilities \((9/20,9/20,1/10)\) conditional on the fixed question. Let the answer mechanism return the cardinality of its evidence, independently of the question wording. The original outer mixture therefore gives answer \(2\) with probability \(1/10\). Even granting two independent samples from exactly the correct evidence law, their union has cardinality \(2\) with probability \[1-2(9/20)^2=119/200=0.595.\] With \(n\) samples that probability is \(1-2(9/20)^n\to1\), while the target remains \(0.1\). The union remains within the original evidence support, so the discrepancy does not rely on evaluating an undefined evidence state. The inner question average is immaterial here, isolating the outer-operator substitution.
result: The current union step changes the evidence random variable and can reverse the modal answer. It does not generally implement the original front-door expectation, even with correct sampling and increasing sample size. This does not quantify any actual TableQA benchmark effect.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Average conditional answer probabilities over the intended evidence mixture and its weights, rather than treating evidence union as that expectation.

The current proceedings Section 4.2 and its evidence-aggregation prompt retain the union operation. Preserving a probability mixture is an analytic alternative; redefining the union as a new mediator would require its own identification assumptions.

problems.title: The operational model does not establish full mediation
problems.source_location: Eq.1, Section 3.2 and the front-door graph.
claim: The depicted front-door graph has no direct Q-to-A path.
analysis: The answer prompt receives both \(Q\) and \(E\). This signature does not prove a direct causal effect, but it does not establish the full-mediation assumption \(Q\to E\to A\) either. That assumption needs a causal model or suitable evidence; the classical identification formula is conditional on it.
result: Full mediation is an additional unverified causal assumption for this operational prompt interface. The presence of both inputs alone proves neither a direct effect nor its absence; this concern is not a counterexample to the classical front-door theorem.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State and justify mediation/support assumptions explicitly; the classical identification formula remains conditional on them.
The current Eq. (1) still supplies both question and evidence to the answer prompt. No additional causal-model verification was available from the empty author repository.

problems.title: The printed iteration does not compute spectral norm
problems.source_location: Appendix A.5, p.28, Algorithm 1; p.29, Eqs.60,64.
claim: Algorithm 1 uses normalized \(Aq\) iteration and final \(q^\top Aq\) as a spectral-norm estimate.
analysis: For \(R=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(A=2R\), \(\|A\|_2=2\), but \(q^\top Aq=0\) for every real \(q\). Since \(A\) is invertible, every normalization step is defined. The printed procedure returns zero regardless of iteration count. Its implementation in the paper's training was unavailable.
result: Algorithm 1 is mathematically false as a general spectral-norm estimator, including for the skew operator it is explicitly asked to measure. The actual training estimator and the provenance of published finite norm values remain unresolved; this is not a claim that every experimental value is wrong.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a singular-value iteration through \(A^\top A\), with nullspace and stopping conditions; a finite iteration count alone does not certify an arbitrary operator norm.

Both the current proceedings and latest arXiv v2 retain the Rayleigh-quotient iteration. The current release README and file tree provide test scripts, without identifying an operative spectral-training routine that could resolve the implementation question.

problems.title: The allowed ADMM range admits an exact two-cycle
problems.source_location: Theorem 4.1, p.7; Appendix A.6, pp.29–31, Eqs.67–76.
claim: Theorem 4.1 claims full-sequence convergence for the printed gamma/t interval.
analysis: Take \(\beta=1,\gamma=0.1,t=0.2\), and let \(b_*\in(0,0.5)\) be the positive root of \(1.4b_*=0.8\tanh(2b_*)\), approximately \(0.33204524\). Define \[F_0(x)=0.1x^2-0.8\log\cosh x,\qquad F(x)=F_0(x)-b_*x,\qquad P=\operatorname{prox}_F,\qquad D=(P-0.8I)/0.2.\] Here \(F''\in[-0.6,0.2]\); thus \(F\) is smooth, coercive and real analytic, hence KL. Its proximal subproblem is strongly convex and \(P'\in[5/6,5/2]\), giving \(D'\in[1/6,8.5]\subset[0,10]\). The denoiser is conservative in one dimension and \(0.1\)-cocoercive, with \(D^t=P\). The paper’s constants \(r=L=9/14\) are valid bounds. Its characteristic polynomial at \(t=0.2\) is \(-0.0416<0\), so the parameter is allowed.

Use zero-count Poisson fidelity \(G(x)=2x+\iota_{[0,\infty)}(x)\), with \(\operatorname{prox}_G(z)=\max(z-2,0)\), and the stated zero initialization. If \(P_0=\operatorname{prox}_{F_0}\), the root identity and oddness give \(P_0(b_*)=2b_*\), \(P_0(-b_*)=-2b_*\), and \(P(z)=P_0(z+b_*)\). Therefore the printed ADMM equations produce \[u_k=0,\qquad(v_k,b_k)=\begin{cases}(2b_*,-2b_*),&k\text{ odd},\\(-2b_*,0),&k\text{ even}.\end{cases}\] The largest input to the fidelity prox is \(4b_*<2\), which verifies the asserted zero values inductively. The sequence does not converge and its consensus residual remains \(2b_*>0\). The claimed positive descent coefficient instead equals \(1/2-9/28-(9/14)^2=-23/98\).
result: The allowed universal parameter range in current Theorem 4.1 is disproved by an exact, well-defined Poisson instance satisfying its assumptions. This does not imply failure of the principal experiments at their different parameter choice. Restoring the descent coefficient alone does not supply the separate boundedness and joint-KL requirements.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A positive descent coefficient requires the additional restriction \(t<\min(t_0,\gamma/(1-\gamma))\). Boundedness and joint-KL conditions remain separate; experiments at another \(\gamma\) are not shown to cycle.

Current Theorem 4.1 and Appendix A.6 retain the same range and reversed comparison in the second Lipschitz branch; latest arXiv v2 has the same steps. The existing stricter sufficient range addresses the coefficient only, with full convergence requiring additional conditions.

problems.title: General convex fidelity does not ensure bounded iterates
problems.source_location: Theorems 4.1,4.4 and their convergence proofs.
claim: Theorems \(4.1\) and \(4.4\) allow general lower-semicontinuous convex G with the listed F assumptions.
analysis: Let \(F(x)=0.1\sqrt{1+x^2}\), \(G(x)=-x\), \(\gamma=0.25,t=0.2\). The former is smooth, convex, coercive and analytic; the latter is proper closed convex as the general theorems allow. For each stated \(\beta\), put \(P=\operatorname{prox}_{F/\beta}\) and \(D=(P-0.8I)/0.2\), so \(D^t=P\). At \(\beta=1\), \(D'\in[6/11,1]\subset[0,4]\); at \(\beta=2\), \(D'\in[16/21,1]\subset[0,4]\). These maps are conservative and \(0.25\)-cocoercive. The ADMM parameter is within \(t<1/3\), and the PEGD parameter satisfies the printed step-size bound.

Since \(\operatorname{prox}_G(z)=z+1\), ADMM reduces to \(v_{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_F(v_k+1)\). Proximal optimality and \(|F'|<0.1\) imply \(v_{k+1}-v_k>0.9\). For PEGD, the unit-parameter Moreau envelope is \({}^1G(x)=-x-1/2\); at \(\beta=2\), the increment similarly exceeds \(0.45\). Thus both sequences diverge. The respective objective derivatives are below \(-0.9\), so there is no finite stationary point to converge to. The affine fidelity is not the paper’s experimental Poisson fidelity: the contradiction concerns the literal general convex-fidelity quantifier.
result: The current general convergence statements do not follow from their listed assumptions. Coercivity of the denoiser potential alone cannot control a jointly unbounded-below objective. The result does not refute convergence for a separately justified Poisson objective or establish divergence of a learned network.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Require boundedness/coercivity of the relevant complete objective and valid joint-KL/step conditions. Safe numerical steps alone do not supply them.

The latest paper versions retain the general convex-fidelity wording and omitted boundedness/joint-KL conditions. Existing conditional sufficient revisions add assumptions; they are not a proof of the original unrestricted statement.

problems.title: Pointwise Jacobian splitting is not a Helmholtz decomposition
problems.source_location: Section 2.2, p.5, Eq.13; interpretation on p.6.
claim: Section 2.2 identifies symmetric/skew Jacobian parts with Jacobians of conservative/divergence-free components.
analysis: For \(D(x,y)=(0,x^2)\), the symmetric Jacobian part is \(\begin{pmatrix}0&x\\x&0\end{pmatrix}\). If this were a field Jacobian, its first component would satisfy \(\partial_x d_1=0\) and \(\partial_y d_1=x\); their mixed derivatives would be \(0\) and \(1\), a contradiction. A smooth compact cutoff can preserve this local contradiction. Pointwise matrix splitting is therefore not a general integrable field decomposition.
result: The current pointwise matrix-to-field identification is false, even locally for a smooth field. The symmetric-Jacobian criterion for a conservative field on a suitable domain remains valid, and the independent proximal characterization is not refuted by this example.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the antisymmetric Jacobian as a local curl penalty. A genuine Helmholtz/Hodge field decomposition needs a domain, boundary conditions and a separate construction.

Current Section 2.2 and latest arXiv v2 retain the claimed Jacobian correspondence. Interpreting the skew penalty as a local nonconservativity measure avoids this false decomposition; it does not establish the stronger field or denoising interpretation.

problems.title: The transformed Pareto variable need not have skewness two
problems.source_location: Proposition 1, p.4; Appendix A, p.21, Eq.7 and densities.
claim: Proposition 1 assigns skewness \(2\) to \(\log(1+T)\) for a standard Pareto time difference.
analysis: For standard Type-I Pareto \(T\) with shape \(\alpha\) and minimum \(c>0\), the density of \(Y=\log(1+T)\) is \[f_Y(y)=\frac{\alpha c^\alpha e^y}{(e^y-1)^{\alpha+1}},\qquad y\ge\log(1+c),\] rather than a shifted exponential density. With \(\alpha=4,c=1\), its first three moments are approximately \[(0.833333333333,0.718517562805,0.648490931824)\], giving skewness \(2.571420899\), rather than \(2\). More generally, write \(T=cV\) for \(V\sim\operatorname{Pareto}(1,\alpha)\), \(\alpha>3\). As \(c\downarrow0\), \(\log(1+cV)/c\to V\) and is bounded by \(V\). Dominated convergence of the first three moments implies its skewness approaches that of \(V\), which exceeds \(2\); it therefore cannot equal \(2\) for every scale. If the intended assumption is instead that \(1+T\) is Type-I Pareto, the shifted-exponential conclusion does hold.
result: The exact constant in current Proposition 1 is not valid for an arbitrary standard Type-I Pareto time difference. This is a distribution/shift condition issue; it does not refute empirical benefits of logarithmic compression or the paper’s acknowledged non-Pareto data behavior.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State the appropriate shifted-Pareto/Lomax model or use the log-ratio transform.

Current Proposition 1, Appendix A and latest arXiv v1 retain the same shift and density. Specifying a Pareto law for the shifted variable is the existing conditional correction; the author’s intended convention remains unconfirmed.

problems.title: Equal-time memory can include non-past events
problems.source_location: Sections 3.1/3.3, PDF pp. 3–6; current models/modules.py, decoder forward/TRCMemory; evaluate_models_utils.py, positive-batch update
claim: The task definition predicts at \(\tau\) from the graph strictly before \(\tau\).
analysis: The current decoder retrieves memory by node pair without a query-time filter; positive-batch prediction then updates that memory. Consider two events for pair \((1,2)\), both at timestamp \(1\), in successive batches with initially empty memory. Set the current one-dimensional edge embedding to \(1\), the historical aggregation weight to \(1/2\), and the final logit to the stored historical coordinate. The first prediction has logit \(0\), then stores \(1/2\); the next same-time prediction reads logit \(1/2\), yielding probability \(\sigma(1/2)\approx0.6224593312\) rather than \(0.5\). Under the paper’s strict \(G_{<1}\) semantics, neither event is available to the other, so both should read empty historical memory. A strictly later query may legitimately read the first event, and events kept in one batch read the same pre-batch state. These controls isolate the equal-time batch boundary.
result: The current author release still permits this strict-time information mismatch. No current AP change, prediction change count or historical experiment contamination rate was measured. A protocol ordered by timestamp and event index could permit such reads, but would require a different declared information clock.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Score an entire timestamp group before insertion, or filter stored events strictly before each query time.

The latest author decoder removed an unused timestamp argument but still has no timestamped memory lookup. Current evaluation updates positive memories after each batch. The existing strict-time-group alternative remains an analytic proposal, not an adopted or benchmark-verified correction.

problems.title: Silent outputs do not imply all surrogate gradients vanish
problems.source_location: Theorem 1, p.5; supplementary S1.1; AT-LIF discussion pp.6–8.
claim: Theorem 1 argues that a silent layer causes all-weight zero gradients and a saddle point.
analysis: Use one neuron, one time step, zero initial state, external input \(1\), weight \(w=1/2\), threshold \(1\), zero bias and loss \(L(s)=(s-1)^2+0.1s^2\). Its membrane value is \(1/2\) and hard output is \(s=0\), while the stated triangular surrogate derivative is \(1/2\). Surrogate backpropagation therefore gives \[\frac{\widetilde\partial L}{\partial w}=(-2)\cdot\frac12\cdot1=-1.\] All computational-layer outputs are silent, yet an external input connection has nonzero surrogate gradient. In contrast, a connection whose every presynaptic input is zero has zero gradient by the input factor in supplementary Eq. (S5), assuming no separate direct weight loss. If the theorem’s layer quantifier includes an all-zero external input layer, the nonzero-input example is outside that stronger domain and the claim must be restricted accordingly.

The saddle inference fails independently of that input-layer convention. The same neuron’s ordinary hard-forward loss is \(1\) throughout \(w<1\) and \(0.1\) for \(w>1\). Near \(w=1/2\) it is a constant nonoptimal plateau, with no local higher and lower values. Zero ordinary derivative and nonglobal optimality do not prove a saddle; moreover the actual surrogate update at this point is nonzero. The proof cannot interchange ordinary hard-forward geometry and surrogate training gradients.
result: The current theorem’s broad all-weight/saddle argument is not supported. Its zero-presynaptic-input connection identity survives with explicit conditions. No universal claim about AT-LIF avoiding saddles, training failure, or benchmark accuracy follows from this example.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restrict the claim to connections with zero presynaptic inputs and remove the unsupported whole-network saddle classification.

The current proceedings theorem and freshly retrieved official supplementary S1.1 retain the argument. The existing restricted connection-gradient statement is analytically valid; no author clarification of the input-layer quantifier or adopted theorem revision was found in these sources.

problems.title: The later threshold backward multiplies the surrogate twice
problems.source_location: Current Eq. (13), PDF p. 6; models/submodules/layers.py, Surrogate.backward, lines 68–74; official cpp_neuron.cpp, lines 87–100
claim: Eq. (\(13\)) gives threshold derivative \(-g\), where \(g\) is the triangular surrogate.
analysis: The current Python backward first sets grad_input to the upstream derivative \(q\) times the triangular surrogate \(g\), then multiplies it by \(g\) again in the threshold gradient. For the scalar input \(m=1/2\), threshold \(\theta=1\), no activity regularization and probe loss equal to the returned output, \(q=1\) and \(g=1/2\). The chosen Eq. (13) rule requires threshold gradient \(-qg=-1/2\), but the function returns \(-qg^2=-1/4\). Single-element input excludes mean/sum conventions as an explanation. The two expressions agree at \(g=0,1\) or \(q=0\); those controls do not establish general equality. The freshly retrieved official C++ single-step path contains one factor, which is counterevidence against attributing this later Python defect to the original tables.
result: The current later Python implementation still changes the selected threshold-update rule. This is a Minor release-specific mismatch, with no established effect on the paper’s historical C++ experiments or reported performance.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Remove the duplicate factor in the affected Python threshold backward; no full benchmark repair is asserted.

The current GitHub head retains the repeated factor. The freshly retrieved official supplementary ZIP is byte-identical to the earlier official artifact and its C++ path does not have this particular duplication; no historical-table correction is inferred.

problems.title: Lemma16 uses a false intermediate exponential bound
problems.source_location: Official Lemma 16, Appendix B, p.23; arXiv v1 Lemma 15, pp.11–12.
claim: For \(\varepsilon>0,\alpha>1,a,b\in(0,1)\) with \(a^{1-\alpha}b^\alpha\le e^{\varepsilon(\alpha-1)}\), Lemma 16 bounds \[(1-a)^\alpha(1-e^{-\varepsilon(1+\ell)}b)^{1-\alpha}\le\exp(e^{-\varepsilon(1+\alpha\ell)}).\] Its proof first claims the stronger intermediate upper bound \(\exp((\alpha-1)e^{-\varepsilon(1+\ell)}b-\alpha a)\).
analysis: Take \(\alpha=2\), \(\varepsilon=\log2\), \(\ell=1\), \(a=1/200\) and \(b=1/10\); the coupling hypothesis holds at equality. The displayed product is \(39601/39000\), exceeding the claimed intermediate bound \(e^{3/200}\). Indeed \(e^{3/200}<200/197<39601/39000\), with the last comparison reducing to positive integer difference \(1397\). The lemma's final bound \(e^{1/8}\) remains valid; only the intermediate step is refuted.
result: The first inequality of the current proof is false under the lemma’s own hypotheses. The counterexample does not falsify the lemma’s final statement or establish a larger privacy budget. Replacing that proof step suffices at the level established by the existing conditional derivation.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep the lemma’s domain and constants. Set \(p=\alpha/(\alpha-1)\), \(\lambda=e^{-\varepsilon(1+\alpha\ell)}\), and \(z=be^{\varepsilon\ell(\alpha-1)}\); the hypothesis gives \(a\ge\lambda z^p\). If \(z\ge1\), the original product is at most \(1\). If \(0<z<1\), its logarithm is at most \(L(\lambda)\), where \(L(s)=\alpha\log(1-sz^p)-(\alpha-1)\log(1-sz)\). To show \(L'(s)\le1\), multiply by the positive denominator: its numerator is \[H(s)=1-(\alpha-1+s)z+(\alpha-s)z^p+(s^2-s)z^{p+1}.\] On \([0,\lambda]\), \(H'(s)\le0\), so \(H(s)\ge H(1)=1-\alpha z+(\alpha-1)z^p\ge0\) by convexity. Integrating from \(L(0)=0\) gives \(L(\lambda)\le\lambda\), the original bound. This restores the lemma with unchanged constants; it is not an author-adopted erratum or an independent audit of every privacy proof.

The current proceedings Lemma 16 and latest target arXiv v1 Lemma 15 retain the false intermediate step. The supplied general alternative proof is preserved as an analytic proposed correction. The separately titled later accuracy-first RDP paper is background work, not a newer version of this paper.

problems.title: MRR lacks the requested cutoff and empty predictions count as correct
problems.source_location: Section 5.1, PDF p. 8; current src/blockrank/utils.py, evaluation metrics lines 352–358 and 412–443; scripts/eval_attn.py, incremental evaluator
claim: The paper reports MRR@\(10\) and P@1.
analysis: The current evaluation requests untruncated recip_rank and copies that one result into every reported MRR cutoff. For one query with \(11\) candidates, only the last relevant, predicting only the first \(10\) causes unpredicted candidates to be filled with zero scores. The relevant item then contributes \(1/11\) to the release’s MRR@\(10\), although no relevant item was returned within the cutoff and the correct truncated value is zero. Separately, an empty prediction becomes an empty top-one set; the code’s subset test accepts it against any ground-truth set. Precision@\(1\) requires an actual relevant first item, so this empty-output success is false. These are current source behaviors, not reconstructed historical table measurements.
result: The current released metric helpers still violate their cutoff and empty-output contracts. Correcting affected scores requires predictions and relevance labels; no numerical change to the paper’s original tables has been established.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Apply the rank cutoff before reciprocal-rank scoring; return zero for empty predictions; preserve IDs/scores explicitly.

The latest author default head retains both the copied untruncated reciprocal-rank result and empty-set subset check. The original paper explicitly used JAX/TPU, so the later PyTorch evaluator is not assumed to be its historical evaluator.

problems.title: The later scoring denominator changes document rankings
problems.source_location: Sections 4.2/4.3, PDF pp. 7–8; current src/blockrank/losses.py, document score normalization lines 65–80; December 2025 normalization change
claim: The paper normalizes query-to-document attention over document tokens.
analysis: The paper normalizes each head over document tokens. The current release instead includes instruction/query token mass in each denominator, reweighting heads before aggregation. For two one-token documents and two heads, let document exponential masses be \((0.9,0.1)\) and \((0.2,0.8)\), with other-token masses \(9\) and \(1/9\), respectively. All values are positive and hence realizable by finite logits. Document-only means are \((0.55,0.45)\), ranking A first; the current all-token means are \((0.135,0.365)\), ranking B first. A single head or equal document-mass fractions across heads preserves ranking, which bounds the counterexample. The change is attributed to the author’s later public normalization commit and may be intentional; it is not established to be an accidental defect.
result: The current release is a mathematically distinct scoring variant and cannot be assumed equivalent to the written document-only normalization. The finding is a Minor version/replication mismatch, not proof of an invalid original ranking method or worse performance of the variant.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the documented document-token denominator or explicitly describe the alternate scoring variant. Historical table attribution remains unresolved.

The current default head retains the later all-token denominator. The change is historically attributed to the December 2025 author commit. Restoring document-only normalization is conditional on seeking the paper’s scoring definition; no claim of author intent or adoption is made.

problems.title: SDPA ranking logits omit attention scaling
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, PDF p. 7; current blockrank_std_attention.py, SDPA return-score construction lines 640–645
claim: The SDPA and eager attention backends should return equivalent ranking logits for the same query/key tensors.
analysis: The hidden-output SDPA call receives the correct scaling, but its separately returned ranking logits are \(QK^\top\) plus mask, omitting \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\). Set \(d_k=4\), query \(q=(1,0,0,0)\), and key first coordinates \[(-20,-20,4,-4,3,3,-20,-20),\] with other coordinates zero; the middle two pairs are documents A and B. Correct scaled document exponential sums satisfy \(e^2+e^{-2}<2e^{1.5}\), ranking B first. Unscaled returned sums satisfy \(e^4+e^{-4}>2e^3\), ranking A first. A common positive scaling of individual logits does not preserve a ranking obtained after exponentiation and token aggregation. The hidden-output operation remains correctly scaled; the discrepancy is specifically in the returned score path.
result: The current SDPA ranking-score path still differs from the specified scaled attention and can reverse document rankings. This particular omission does not apply to the separately scaled eager path; no original JAX benchmark effect is established.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Apply \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to returned logits under the same convention, then check backend parity.

Current SDPA code retains the missing scale in the independent returned-logit construction. The existing local correction scales that product before adding its mask; it changes no already-correct hidden-output computation and has no demonstrated benchmark result.

problems.title: The O-set need not minimize asymptotic variance
problems.source_location: Current arXiv v4 Theorem 4.3 and Definitions 4.1–4.2, PDF pp.6–7; Appendix C.5 proof
claim: Theorem 4.3 says all non-treatment parents of Y form a universally variance-optimal allowed adjustment set.
analysis: Use the DAG \(A\to B\to W\to Y\), \(A\to Y\), \(E\to W\). Let \(A,E\) be independent Bernoulli-\(1/2\), \(\Pr(B=1\mid A)=1/4+A/2\), and \(\Pr(W=1\mid B,E)=1/20\) when \(B=E\), \(19/20\) otherwise. Let \(Y=AW+\epsilon\), with independent noise variance \(1/100\). All sixteen discrete cells have positive probability, the stated adjustment conditions hold, and WCDE is \(1/2\).

The mediator set is \(M=\{B,W\}\); choose \(Z_1=\{B\}\), \(Z_2=\{E\}\). The only mediated path is blocked by \(B\), and fixing \(A,B\) gives \(\mathbb E[Y\mid do(A=a,B=b)]=a/2\). Condition C3 requires only \(W\perp A\mid B\), which holds; it does not require \(W\perp E\mid B\). For \(O=\{W\}\), the contrast influence function is \(2(2A-1)\epsilon+W-1/2\). For \(Z\), it is \[\frac{A}{\pi(B)}(W-q(B,E)+\epsilon)-\frac{1-A}{1-\pi(B)}\epsilon,\qquad\pi(0)=1/4,\quad\pi(1)=3/4.\] These give the variances below directly.

Substituting these probabilities and regressions into the paper's unrestricted-observation influence function gives asymptotic variance \(29/100\) for \(O=\{W\}\) and \(9/50\) for \(Z=\{B,E\}\). Since \(9/50<29/100\), the asserted universally optimal O-set is not optimal. These are the paper-defined variances, not a comparison to a graph-model efficient bound.
result: The universal optimal-adjustment theorem is false under its own admissibility and positivity conditions; the influence-function identity itself is not refuted.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restrict or re-establish the optimality theorem. No general replacement optimal set is proved; the reported influence function itself remains a valid retained component.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The estimator halves the residual correction
problems.source_location: Paper Eq. (5.1), p. 9; author asia.py, lines 205-212, and parallel released estimator implementations.
claim: Eq.5.1 is presented as an influence-function-based AIPW construction.
analysis:
Eq. (\(5.1\))'s outer \(1/2\) multiplies one inverse-probability residual term and two marginal regression terms. It therefore equals a plug-in estimate plus half the required residual correction. With correct weights and limiting regression \(
u\), its limit is \((T_{m true}+T_
u)/2\), not generally \(T_{m true}\). In the explicit positive-support case with \(T_{m true}=1/2\) and \(T_
u=0\), this is \(1/4\). Correct nuisance regression can hide the bias.
result: The printed AIPW formula does not retain the full residual correction, so its stated nuisance-robustness interpretation fails. Published finite-sample scores were not recalculated.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Double the residual correction inside the overall one-half factor. This algebra restores that cancellation identity; flexible-nuisance regularity/normality needs additional conditions.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Four ASIA comparisons lack structural positivity
problems.source_location: Paper Table 3, pp. 9-10; author-released asia.bif, either and lung conditional probability tables.
claim: Table 3 uses seven adjustment sets to compare nonparametric regular-estimator efficiency.
analysis: The author's ASIA CPT forces either \(=1\) whenever lung \(=1\). Thus \(\Pr(\mathrm{either}=0,\mathrm{lung}=1)=0\), although \(\Pr(\mathrm{lung}=1)=11/200>0\). Four compared adjustment sets containing lung require unsupported outcome cells. Extrapolation does not supply nonparametric overlap; the three sets without lung retain support, and the supported O-set effect remains \(3/8\).
result: Four ASIA adjustment comparisons lack the required outcome-cell support. The supported comparisons and the O-set effect remain valid controls.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Exclude unsupported sets from the nonparametric efficiency comparison or label the extra outcome-extrapolation model; full table reruns remain undone.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: C3 necessity must distinguish means from contrasts
problems.source_location: Lemma 2.6, p.4; Appendix B.1, pp.27–28; CDE counterevidence pp.24–25.
claim: Lemma 2.6 calls the adjustment conditions both sufficient and necessary for WCDE.
analysis: In the graph \(A\to B\to W\to Y\), \(C\to W\), \(C\to Y\), with no direct \(A\to Y\), condition C3 fails for \(Z_1=\{B\},Z_2=\{C\}\). Yet \(Y\perp A\mid B,C\), so the standardized treatment contrast is zero, matching the controlled direct effect for every Markov law on that graph. Two treatment-specific means can be misidentified while their difference cancels. The authors already discuss this distinction for CDE.
result: The claimed necessity condition is too strong for a contrast whose two mean-identification errors cancel. Its sufficiency and nonzero-effect applications are not refuted.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Narrow the necessity claim to its correctly established target/domain. No new complete necessary-and-sufficient adjustment criterion is provided.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The strong-convexity bound omits infeasible initial error
problems.source_location: Theorem 6, Appendix C.1, p.22.
claim: Theorem 6 gives objective-gap decay proportional to \(e^{-2\mu t}\) without requiring feasible initialization.
analysis: Let \(f(s,r)=((s-1)^2+r^2)/2\), \(h(s,r)=s\), \(T=I,K=1,\mu=1\), with initial point \((-1,0)\). The constraints have full row rank and the Hessian is \(I\). The exact flow is \(s=-e^{-t},r=0\). Its constrained-optimum objective gap is \(e^{-t}+e^{-2t}/2\), whereas the claimed envelope is \(3e^{-2t}/2\). At \(t=\log2\), these are \(5/8\) and \(3/8\). Convergence still occurs; the claimed envelope does not.
result: The quantitative strong-convexity envelope fails at an allowed infeasible initialization; convergence itself survives this example.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Require feasible initialization for the projected-gradient proof, or add an explicit normal-infeasibility term.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Finite squared-residual integral does not imply terminal convergence
problems.source_location: Theorems 1,4, pp.4–7; terminal-limit proofs, p.21 and Appendix E, p.25.
claim: Theorems \(1\) and \(4\) conclude that last-time KKT gaps vanish from a finite integral bound.
analysis: Let \(\phi\) be a smooth compactly supported unit-height bump and \(g(s)=1/(1+s^2)+\frac12\sum_{k\ge1}\phi((s+k)/2^{-k-3})\). Define \(F(s)=\int_{-\infty}^s g(u)\,du\), \(f(s,r)=F(s)\), \(h=r\), \(T=I,K=1\). The sum is locally finite; \(f\) is smooth, lower bounded and has bounded gradient.

The exact flow is \(\dot s=-g(s),\dot r=-r\). It crosses every \(s=-k\) at times tending to infinity, where the KKT residual is at least \(1/2\). Nonetheless \(\int g(s(t))^2dt=\int g(s)\,ds\) along the descending trajectory is finite. Narrowing peaks preserve finite integral without a vanishing terminal residual. The source's Jacobian/multiplier assumptions do not supply the missing uniform continuity.
result: A finite residual integral does not ensure the claimed last-time KKT convergence without an additional regularity condition.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Add and verify a condition implying uniform continuity of the residual, then use an appropriate integral-to-limit theorem. The integral and best-iterate guarantees are not refuted.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The specified momentum merit can initially increase
problems.source_location: Theorem 5, p.9; Appendix F, pp.26–28.
claim: Theorem 5 gives numerical thresholds intended to make its particular merit function nonincreasing.
analysis: Use \(f(x)=0.01\log\cosh x\), \(h(x)=10^{-4}x\), \(T=K=1\), \(a_1=1,a_2=100000,\alpha=200000\), \(x_0=0.1,z_0=0\). Bounds \(M=1,D=20000,L_f=0.01,L_1=100,L_2=1.04\) satisfy the printed thresholds \(a_2\ge93200\) and \(\alpha\ge108003.05\). Direct differentiation of the full stated merit gives \(0.01[0.01\operatorname{sech}^2(0.1)-0.001]\simeq8.9006629\times10^{-5}>0\). This refutes its nonincrease claim, not stability under every alternative energy.
result: The theorem’s own sufficient constants permit a positive derivative of its stated merit function, disproving its nonincrease claim.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Rework the specific merit/threshold proof; no complete general replacement theorem is asserted.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The OPF code omits the complementarity absolute value
problems.source_location: Paper KKT-gap definition, p.6; two OPF MATLAB metric paths.
claim: The paper defines KKT gap using the absolute value of lambda-transpose h.
analysis: The paper's gap uses \(|\lambda^\top h|\), while both author MATLAB metric paths insert the signed \(\lambda^\top h\) into a maximum with nonnegative residuals. A large negative value is then hidden. This is a local metric-definition mismatch; corrected OPF curves require the original per-step values.
result: The public OPF metric omits the absolute value in the declared complementarity term. Historical curves cannot be corrected without their per-step values.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(|\lambda^\top h|\) consistently in that metric.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Reward scaling alone does not bound the true soft Q
problems.source_location: Appendix B, p.25; Appendix C.2, pp.26–27, Eqs.2–3.
claim: Appendix C.2 motivates reward normalization as keeping modeled returns within fixed categorical support.
analysis: Consider a self-transition model with continuous state, uniform actions on \([-1,1]\), reward \(1\), \(\gamma=0.99\), \(V_{\max}=10\) and \(\alpha=1/(10\log2)\). Then \(\alpha H=0.1\), the ordinary discounted reward-return bound is \(100\), and the entropy return is \(10\). The printed scale is \(c=1/11\). problems.title: A known-label bridge is substituted for a marginal reverse law
claim: Eq. (\(6\)) treats the known-\(y_0\) reverse bridge as the marginal reverse law conditioned only on \(y_t,x\).
analysis: The marginal is a mixture over \(q(y_0\mid y_t,x)\). If bridge means are \(a_ty_0+b_ty_t\) and common bridge covariance is \(\widetilde\beta_tI\), total covariance gives \(\operatorname{Cov}(y_{t-1}\mid y_t,x)=\widetilde\beta_tI+a_t^2\operatorname{Cov}(y_0\mid y_t,x)\). A two-point label posterior with nonzero weights has positive extra covariance whenever the bridge coefficient is nonzero. Deleting \(y_0\) from conditioning cannot delete that term, even with arbitrarily small positive forward noise. The proposed universal decoder-gradient necessity does not follow.

Thus arbitrary label numbering can alter the training objective. A symmetric unordered-pair rule can restore numbering invariance, but neither its optimality nor corrected benchmark performance is established.

For a realizable co-occurrence count matrix with pair counts \(c_{01}=1,c_{02}=3,c_{12}=1\), row normalization gives upper-pair scores \((1/4,3/4,1/2)\). A batch containing those three label pairs receives approximately \((1/2,1,3/4)\) after the released min–max scaling. Simultaneously swapping class IDs \(0,1\) and the matrix axes changes the pair scores to \((1/2,3/4,1/2)\), and scaled weights to approximately \((1/2,1,1/2)\). The lower-ID directional lookup changes a sample weight despite unchanged label relations.
result: The released weighting rule is not invariant under arbitrary relabeling of class IDs. No corrected benchmark performance is inferred.

problems.title: Bayesian linear-regression information loss omits observation noise
problems.source_location: Appendix D.6, Example 4, p.28; common proof p.29.
claim: Example \(4\) substitutes X Sigma X-transpose into a future-observation Gaussian determinant ratio.
analysis: Use prior variance \(2\), observation-noise variance \(2\), and repeated scalar input \(1\). After one observation, latent posterior variance is \(1\). Two future latent values therefore have singular covariance \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), so the printed noise-free determinant ratio diverges. Future observations instead have covariance \(K=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\), giving finite divergence \(\frac12\log(9/8)\simeq0.0588915178\). The covariance does not depend on the observed response.
result: Example4 omits observation-noise covariance and can return a divergent expression for a finite Gaussian information loss.
assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.

repair.heading: Proposed correction

problems.title: The GP formula mixes KL directions
problems.source_location: Example 5, p.28; Appendix D.6.1, p.29.

Forward KL is \(\frac12\log(4/3)\simeq0.1438410362\), while reverse KL is \(0.1894922971\). Thus swapping the labels does not fix the formula. Positive observation noise makes both Gaussian laws nonsingular.

assumptions: The exact source version and operative conditions stated in this analysis.
