problems.title: Expected patch variance drops a mean-covariance term
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Eq. (2), PDF p. 4; supplement A, Eqs. (2) and (5)–(10), PDF pp. 21–22.
claim: The paper uses population-pixel covariance in the expected within-patch variance formula and substitutes the square of the expected patch mean for its expected square.
analysis: Take paired patches \(c_0=(B+S_0,B-S_0)\), \(c_1=(B+S_1,B-S_1)\), with equiprobable \(B\in\{2,4\}\) and independent signs. Pixel marginals are stationary and nonnegative, endpoint spatial variances are one, and population pixel covariance is one. At \(t=1/4\), the printed equation gives one, but directly centered variance is \((3/4)^2+(1/4)^2=5/8\). The missing cross contribution is \(2t(1-t)[\operatorname{Cov}(p_0,p_1)-\operatorname{Cov}(\mu_0,\mu_1)]\); subtracting \((\mathbb E\mu_t)^2\) instead of \(\mathbb E\mu_t^2\) loses patch-mean variation.
result: The stated stationarity conditions do not remove patch-mean variation. The missing term is a genuine local formula error; the code directly estimates sample statistics, so no dataset-level performance change follows from this witness.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use expected within-patch covariance or explicitly change the target to pooled pixel variance. The algebra alone does not repair an experiment.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Mean-standard-deviation scaling does not give unit expected variance
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF p. 4; supplements A–B, PDF pp. 22–23; author model/normalizer.py, lines 35–48.
claim: SCIN is said to ensure zero expected mean and unit expected variance, while the documented procedure and code average per-patch standard deviations.
analysis: With exact scale \(s=\mathbb E\sigma>0\), expected normalized within-patch variance is \(\mathbb E\sigma^2/(\mathbb E\sigma)^2=1+\operatorname{Var}(\sigma)/(\mathbb E\sigma)^2\). For equiprobable contrasts \(1,3\), the mean scale is \(2\), and expected variance is \((1/4+9/4)/2=5/4\), rather than one. The nonnegative patches \(4+AS(1,-1,-1,1)\), with \(A\in\{1,3\}\) and independent sign \(S\), realize this witness. Under the release's sample-standard-deviation convention, average sample variance is \(1.25\) and population variance \(0.9375\); conventions must not be mixed.
result: Unit expected variance is not guaranteed, while the weaker unit mean standard deviation in the supplement is valid. No segmentation or unmixing score change is established.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the algorithm and state unit mean standard deviation, or use \(\sqrt{\mathbb E\,v}\) if expected within-patch variance is the intended normalization. Changed scaling requires empirical evaluation.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Index-dependent shortest-path ties break edge-bias equivariance
problems.source_location: Section 2.2.2, Eq. (4) and complete-attention invariance statement, PDF pp. 4–5; author modeling/ft_datasets/algos.pyx, floyd_warshall, lines 9–55.
claim: The full graph attention is described as permutation invariant, with edge scores averaged over a selected shortest path.
analysis: Use a diamond graph with paths \(0\to1\to3\) and \(0\to2\to3\), both of length two. Give the first path edge bias zero and the second bias two. The author's Floyd-Warshall implementation updates only on strict distance improvements and processes intermediate indices in order, so it selects the first path. Swapping nodes \(1,2\) and all their attributes while fixing endpoints \(0,3\) switches the chosen bias: \(B_{03}=0\), \(B'_{03}=2\), although equivariance requires \(B'=PBP^\top\) and equality at those fixed endpoints. Distance bias itself remains equivariant; the selected heterogeneous edge bias does not.
result: The unconditional edge-bias equivariance guarantee needs a path-tie condition or invariant aggregation. Unique paths/equal path scores remain unaffected; no checkpoint-specific failure rate or reachability claim is established.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Aggregate shortest-path edge information equivariantly, or state the unique-path/equal-score restriction. This changes the definition and is not a verified trained-model repair.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Control feature sizes match only a restricted resolution class
problems.source_location: Eqs. (5)–(6), PDF pp. 5–6; author cunet_arch.py, lines 96–165; inference entry, line 123.
claim: The inference tool accepts RAW images and relies on model padding/cropping, but its control branch adds a fixed two rows before alignment.
analysis: The backbone addition uses size \((4\lceil H/16\rceil,4\lceil W/16\rceil)\), while the control branch uses \((\lfloor H/4\rfloor+2,\lfloor W/4\rfloor)\). At \(H=W=32\), these are \(8\times8\) and \(10\times8\). Compatibility requires \(H\bmod16\in\{8,9,10,11\}\) and \(W\bmod16=0\). The paper's packed camera shape \(2344\times3520\) satisfies the condition, so the witness does not refute that default geometry.
result: The code arithmetic proves an input-domain defect without running a model. It does not show failure at the original camera geometry.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Align control size to the padded backbone feature shape, or state the restricted input domain. No end-to-end corrected model result is asserted.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: The released training path omits zero residual initialization
problems.source_location: Text following Eq. (6), PDF p. 6; author cunet_arch.py, lines 8–11 and 28–40; stage-two training configuration.
claim: The method describes zero-initialized convolutional residual blocks.
analysis: The zero_module helper is defined but the four ResidualBlock instances construct default Conv2d layers without invoking it. A fresh stage-two network has no pretrained network_g in the traced configuration, so loading the ratio estimator cannot initialize these residual branches to zero.
result: A specific release/training-recipe discrepancy is supported. Nonzero trained weights alone would not be evidence, and the original historical training version remains unknown.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Initialize the residual branch as specified, or identify the historical initialization actually used. Zeroing its final convolution gives zero initial residual algebraically.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Requested \(16\)-bit pixel values wrap during final \(8\)-bit export
problems.source_location: Author UltraLED inference documentation; image_process_ultraled.py, lines 87–88 and 126–131.
claim: The script exposes output bit depth but always casts the returned array to uint8 before saving.
analysis: On the requested 16-bit path, valid values \[[0,255,256,32768,65535]\] cast to uint8 become \([0,255,0,0,255]\). This is modular truncation, not monotonic 16-to-8-bit rescaling. The cast occurs after selected-bit-depth postprocessing and before imwrite.
result: The nondefault 16-bit export path has a concrete encoding defect. Default 8-bit behavior and original evaluation scores are outside this counterexample.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Preserve uint16 for the 16-bit output path; explicitly rescale and label an 8-bit preview if desired.
Proposed correction; independent verification and author adoption remain unestablished.

problems.title: Decoder topology and input mutation differ from the intended reusable DAG representation
problems.source_location: Section 3 graph representation; current MoCo model_collaboration/method/text_heterogeneous_swarms.py, graph_decode
claim: The paper presents general DAG collaboration; the release attaches each newly selected node to one existing node and reuses adjacency rows.
analysis: A successful \(n\)-node decode adds \(n-1\) edges with one successor per nonterminal node. It cannot represent every DAG, for example \(0\to1,0\to2,1\to2\). The current author port still assigns adjacency_matrix[selected_node] to a working row without copying it. NumPy row indexing returns a view, so zeroing entries for the unselected nodes changes the caller’s matrix. This is a restricted graph family and a side effect; the output remains acyclic, and corruption of every optimizer state is not established.
result: The same two local properties remain in the latest author-directed MoCo port. Their effect on saved optimization trajectories or published scores has not been established.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Copy the row before mutation. That repairs the side effect but does not enlarge the graph family; intended edge-sampling semantics remain to be specified.

The author’s original repository directs readers to MoCo. The current MoCo dev branch retains the row view and single-successor construction; no correction of those properties was found in the inspected function.

problems.title: The latest evaluator corrects the historical numeric substring mismatch
problems.source_location: Current MoCo model_collaboration/data/eval.py, extract_answer_text, calculate_exact_match and get_scores
claim: The original evaluator treated inclusion of the reference string as an exact match and had a separate judge branch with different score units. The latest author port extracts the final answer and uses type-appropriate equality or numeric comparison.
analysis: For the GSM8K example, the correct answer is \(14(6+2)=112\), whereas the wrong answer \(1120\) contains its decimal substring. That distinguishes the old substring rule from exact final-answer comparison. In the current calculate_exact_match, normalized numeric strings are parsed and checked by _numbers_match; these two numbers fail its relative tolerance of \(10^{-2}\). Text falls back to normalized equality after final-answer extraction. The earlier integer-judge branch is not used by the current swarm method’s get_scores path.
result: The precise historical false-positive witness is corrected in the latest author implementation and is not counted as a current problem. This does not establish that historical predictions or tables were recomputed.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

problems.title: Finite random assignments can leave JFK-score undefined
problems.source_location: Current paper Algorithm 2, PDF p. 5; current MoCo text_heterogeneous_swarms.py, run_method
claim: Algorithm 2 divides a model’s summed sampled utility by the number of appearances in a finite set of IID assignments, without requiring positive coverage of every model.
analysis: With \(10\) models, \(10\) assignments and \(10\) positions per assignment, there are \(100\) IID model draws. A specified model is absent with probability \(0.9^{100}>0\). For example, appearance counts \[(12,16,15,0,7,9,9,9,8,15)\] sum to \(100\) but give the absent model utility and frequency both zero. Its prescribed ratio is therefore \(0/0\), even for constant positive assignment utility. The latest MoCo port instead fixes model_names and optimizes adjacency; it omits this frequency-based role-selection stage. That removal prevents attributing the same division to the current port, but does not define the score in the still-current published Algorithm 2.
result: The current paper’s finite-sampling definition lacks a zero-frequency convention. This is a domain defect with a positive-probability event, not evidence that a reported run encountered it or that the current MoCo port performs the same division.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Define behavior for zero-frequency models. Conditioning samples on complete coverage makes denominators positive but changes the sampling law; no unbiasedness equivalence is asserted.
The current paper retains the unguarded finite-sampling score. The later MoCo port omits that role-selection stage rather than providing a corrected implementation of its stated ratio.

problems.title: The latest stable softmax corrects the historical overflow witness
problems.source_location: Current MoCo text_heterogeneous_swarms.py, softmax and graph_decode
claim: The original decoder exponentiated reciprocal row sums directly. The latest author port subtracts their finite maximum and separately handles masked or nonfinite entries.
analysis: Positive row weights can yield reciprocal row sums \((5000,1,1)\). Direct float64 exponentiation of \(e^{5000}\) overflows despite a well-defined real softmax. The current implementation calculates exponentials after subtracting the maximum finite value, so this witness becomes \((e^0,e^{-4999},e^{-4999})\) before normalization. Its code also handles positive infinity and masks explicitly. This is the previously identified issue and later author correction, not a novelty claim.
result: The exact historical overflow defect is corrected in the latest author port. No general claim is made about every possible nonfinite input or downstream numerical operation.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

problems.title: Table 7 supports a mean advantage but not every-task superiority
problems.source_location: Appendix D, Table 7, PDF p. 28.
claim: The text says the mixed \(7\)-billion/\(2\)-billion-parameter system exceeds the best single \(7\)-billion-parameter model, without explicitly claiming superiority on every task.
analysis: The four mixed-minus-single scores are \[(-0.028,0.134,-0.043,0.029)\], with arithmetic means \(0.31875\) and \(0.29575\). Thus the aggregate advantage is consistent with the table, while two task reversals remain. The rounded aggregate arithmetic in Table 1 is also consistent.
result: This is a scope clarification, not an additional demonstrated error. Table 1’s rounded \(18.5\%\) aggregate remains a positive arithmetic control.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

problems.title: The first feasible prefix is skipped
problems.source_location: Corollary 3.1.1, PDF p. 4; Algorithm 1 and Appendix A.2, pp. 22–23; current rdd/algorithms.py, max_sum_partition and rdd_score
claim: Under additive interval scores and allowed lengths, Algorithm 1 is said to find an optimal full partition.
analysis: Take \(N=4\), minimum length \(2\) and maximum length \(4\). All frame features can equal \((1,0)\); a single two-frame prior interval has duration \(1\), so its endpoint feature matches every candidate. With the author scorer’s default mode, \(\alpha=1\) and \(\beta=0\), angular distance is zero and its score is the negative frame count times \(|1-(e-s)|\). Two-frame segments score \(0\), while the four-frame segment scores \(-8\). The loop begins at \(3\), leaving \(D_2=-\infty\), and hence returns \(-8\) rather than the feasible two-segment optimum \(0\). Interpreting the paper’s outside duration as \(e-s\) instead gives the full segment \(-6\), with the same strict contradiction. If the maximum length is \(3\), the valid two-segment solution is still missed. Invalid-edge scores of \(-\infty\) do not restore the omitted feasible state.
result: The listed algorithm and matching author release fail the stated universal optimum guarantee. Standard additive dynamic programming remains valid; no robot success-rate effect is inferred.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Start at the shortest feasible prefix, preserve genuinely infeasible states and backtrack a full partition. The corrected standard recurrence is distinct from a new robot experiment.

The latest target arXiv version and freshly retrieved proceedings Algorithm 1 retain the omitted prefix; the current author repository retains the same loop lower bound. The existing standard-recurrence correction is analytic, with no new robot execution or author adoption established.

problems.title: Linear scorer calls do not bound total implementation cost
problems.source_location: Corollary 3.1.1, PDF p. 4; speed discussion, PDF pp. 8–9; Appendix A.2, PDF p. 23.
claim: With bounded segment length, the paper counts linear scoring calls and later describes linear algorithm runtime.
analysis: With allowed lengths \(2\) through \(4\), the release checks all previous breakpoints before discarding illegal lengths. It makes \(N(N+1)/2+N-5=\Theta(N^2)\) length checks but only \(3N-7\) scorer calls. Full-prefix partition copies add further work. The finite Table 14 budget \(44549/386\simeq115.41\,\mathrm s\) is a valid call-count calculation, not a total asymptotic-runtime proof.
result: The call-count result is preserved; an asymptotic linear total-runtime claim needs restricted candidate loops and path storage assumptions. Finite empirical timings are not refuted.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restrict candidate breakpoints to the valid length band and store predecessor links. With declared interval-access and scoring cost \(C_J\), that gives \(O(NW(1+C_J))\) time for width \(W\).

The current author function still scans every previous breakpoint before checking lengths and copies full partition prefixes. The bounded scoring-call statement remains valid; no new end-to-end timing was measured.

problems.title: Initial-condition replay and stored-action replay are different actor updates
problems.source_location: Sections 2.4 and 3.3, PDF pp. 4–5; Appendix C, Algorithm 2, PDF p. 19.
claim: The body says current-policy rollouts restart from sampled contexts; Algorithm 2 instead loads a saved trajectory and updates its stored actions without behavior correction.
analysis: In a one-step bandit, let rewards be \(1,0\), current good-action probability \(0.2\), replay good-action probability \(0.9\), and action-independent critic baseline \(2\). The true current-policy logit gradient is \(0.2(0.8)=0.16\). Reusing stored actions instead gives \(0.9(0.8)(-1)+0.1(-0.2)(-2)=-0.68\). An action-independent baseline cancels under on-policy sampling; it need not cancel under the replay law. Terminal masking permits this one-step case within a longer maximum imagination horizon.
result: The two written algorithms are not generally equivalent. The witness does not show that the actual experiments used old actions or encountered this state; original implementation/logs are needed for that determination.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Make the pseudocode match initial-context replay with fresh current-policy actions, or specify and justify the off-policy alternative. No performance-preserving drop-in repair is established.

The freshly retrieved proceedings and latest target arXiv v2 retain the conflicting body and Algorithm 2 descriptions. The current author project page still says Code (coming soon); no released implementation was available to decide the historical execution path.

problems.title: Accumulated positive TD residuals and their mean reverse rankings
problems.source_location: Eq. (7), PDF p. 5; Appendix C, Algorithm 2, PDF p. 19; horizon interpretation, PDF pp. 8 and 20.
claim: Eq.(7) sums future discounted positive TD residuals for every starting position; Algorithm 2 takes their plain mean.
analysis: For horizon \(H=5\), \(q=0.985\cdot0.95=0.93575\), and positive TD residual vectors \(A=(0.9,0,0,0,0)\), \(B=(0,0,0.75,0,0)\), plain means are \(0.18,0.15\). The accumulated future-residual score instead gives \(0.18\) and \(0.15(1+q+q^2)=0.421706709375\), reversing their ranking. Binary terminal rewards and value estimates in \([0,1]\) can realize these vectors; the witness does not require illegal reward timing.
result: The priorities are different functions, even at equal horizon; endpoint indexing cannot resolve the reversed ordering. A horizon trend under the accumulated form can partly reflect its position weights, rather than independently demonstrating difficulty.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify which of the two priority functions is intended. Changing horizon normalization also changes the curriculum; no benchmark-equivalent substitution is asserted.

The freshly retrieved proceedings and latest target arXiv v2 retain the conflicting body and Algorithm 2 descriptions. The current author project page still says Code (coming soon); no released implementation was available to decide the historical execution path.

problems.title: The documented six-stack resident-weight configuration lacks capacity
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v1, Sections 4.1/5.1/5.2 and Tables 1–2, PDF pp. 6–8
claim: The setup lists \(30.5\) billion parameters, FP16 weights and six HBM2 stacks of \(8192\) MB, with distributed resident weight storage.
analysis: One FP16 copy needs \(30.5\times10^9\cdot2=61\times10^9\) bytes. Even treating each listed stack as \(8192\) MiB gives only \(48\) GiB \(=51539607552\) bytes, a shortfall of \(9460392448\) bytes. Assigning all \(17\cdot100\) tiles' \(2.265\) MiB SRAM to weights still gives only about \(55.577\) GB. A smaller per-token active parameter count does not store the remaining experts; another memory/offload/compression layer could, but must be identified.
result: The documented resident-weight interpretation is inconsistent by capacity arithmetic. Host/offload/extra-stack traces could resolve it; the source does not establish that no such unreported mechanism exists. Simulator throughput and energy values were not independently recomputed.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Provide the actual memory hierarchy and trace. Added storage, offload or compression changes the capacity/performance model and requires explicit evaluation.

The later arXiv version, posted in March 2026, retains the six-stack FP16 configuration and the listed capacities. The current author repository README provides no additional memory hierarchy or simulator trace resolving this arithmetic.

problems.title: Tightness of a general upper bound depends on the layout quantifier
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v1, token-copy upper bound and expert/attention layout in Section 4
claim: The token-copy quantity bounds remote all-to-all traffic, with equality requiring zero local copies.
analysis: With two devices, one expert each and top-\(k\) routing with \(k=2\), each token makes one local and one remote copy. The universal bound \(2\) is valid; the tight remote count for that fixed layout is \(1\). Under unrestricted per-token expert routing, the fixed-layout maximum is \(\sum_i n_i\min(k,N_e-m_i)/\sum_i n_i\). A source device holding no experts can attain the general bound.
result: This is a quantifier clarification, not a counterexample to the original inequality or the concrete Mozart attention-source layout. It must not be counted as a second disproved theorem.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

problems.title: Bounded cosine energy does not define the stated prior on an unbounded space
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Eqs. (1)–(4), PDF p. 5; Section 3.3, PDF p. 6; Appendix A.2.4, PDF p. 17 (Gaussian variational family).
claim: The bounded cosine energy kernel \(e^{-H}\) is treated as a normalized prior on an unbounded space and used with an untruncated Gaussian variational law.
analysis: For a finite graph, \(z_i\in[0,1]\), finite \(d_i>0\) and cosine similarities \(|c_{ij}|\le1\), the written energy satisfies \[0\le H(S;u)\le\sum_{i\in I_G}z_i|N(i)|e^{d_i}+|I_G|\sum_{i=1}^n(1-z_i)e^{d_i}=:M(u)<\infty.\] This bound is independent of the amplitude of \(S\). Consequently \[\int_{\mathbb R^n}e^{-H(S;u)}\,dS\ge e^{-M(u)}\int_{\mathbb R^n}1\,dS=\infty.\] Excluding zero-window null sets or stabilizing the cosine denominator does not supply confinement. The paper’s untruncated Gaussian variational family has unbounded support; restricting only the prior to a bounded pixel box would instead make the variational KL infinite.
result: This is a general normalization obstruction for the written prior. A bounded-support prior would also require matching the Gaussian variational support; treating the kernel as a regularizer is a different interpretation.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a proper confining/base measure or consistently bounded support, or treat the energy solely as a regularizer. None of these alternatives alone constitutes a repaired full ELBO.

The freshly retrieved official paper retains the cited formula or definition. The current author repository head retains the implicated implementation where available. Existing local algebraic corrections do not establish a complete repaired model, retraining result or author adoption.

problems.title: The d-update reverses energy signs and is only approximate Gamma conjugacy
problems.source_location: Eq. (14), PDF p. 6; Appendix A.2.3, Eqs. (35)–(43), PDF pp. 16–17; author get_gamma_d.
claim: The update combines log p(d) with log p(S|..), but subsequent equations add the energy terms with the opposite sign.
analysis: The negative energy expands as \(-Ae^{-cd}-Be^{cd}=-A-B+(A-B)cd+O(d^2)\), opposite to the displayed linear sign. With prior shape \(2\), rate \(10^{-4}\), mean latent \(1/2\) and cosine \(1/2\), the off-graph example gives printed rate \(10^{-4}\), versus sign-correct first-order rate \(0.2501\). The original exponential dependence on \(d\) is not Gamma-conjugate. Taylor approximation, MGF clipping and the partition-function problem remain separate limitations.
result: The local sign/approximation issue is supported. Neither the first-order fix nor a one-variable integral is asserted to be the correct full posterior, particularly given the prior-normalization problem.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Preserve the negative-energy sign and label the Taylor-Gamma update as approximate; the full consistent prior/posterior still requires analysis.

The freshly retrieved official paper retains the cited formula or definition. The current author repository head retains the implicated implementation where available. Existing local algebraic corrections do not establish a complete repaired model, retraining result or author adoption.

problems.title: The Beta-KL log-Beta sign changes training gradients
problems.source_location: Appendix A.2.4, Eqs. (54)–(57), PDF p. 17; author losses.py, lines 42–49, and graphseg.py, line 599.
claim: Appendix A.2.4, Eq. (56), PDF p. 17, prints a positive \(\log[\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)/\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)]=\log B(\alpha,\beta)\) term for the variational Beta distribution in the KL defined by Eqs. (54)–(55). The correct variable normalization term has the opposite sign. The active author losses.py function, lines 42–49, called by graphseg.py at line 599, repeats the printed sign.
analysis: Exact Beta KL includes \(\log B(\alpha_0,\beta_0)-\log B(\alpha,\beta)\). The active expression uses a positive sign on the latter term. At \(q=p=\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\), both parameter gradients are \(-5/3\), whereas a correct KL is minimized there with zero gradient. No additive constant changes this. For \(\operatorname{Beta}(3,3)\) versus \(\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\), the true KL is \(0.0427712457674\), while the centered source expression is \(-3.17610457910\).
result: The wrong log-Beta sign is present in the paper itself, Eq. (56), and in the called loss function. It changes the core variational objective and its gradients; an unused alternate source function has the correct structure. No performance effect or corrected segmentation score is established.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restore the full Beta-KL sign structure while preserving numerical dtype. This algebraic correction does not establish a repaired model experiment.

The freshly retrieved official paper retains the cited formula or definition. The current author repository head retains the implicated implementation where available. Existing local algebraic corrections do not establish a complete repaired model, retraining result or author adoption.

problems.title: Entropy and reconstruction normalization alter relative loss weights
problems.source_location: Appendix A.2.4, Eqs. (47) and (51)–(53), PDF p. 17; author losses.py, lines 5–10, and graphseg.py, lines 589 and 603–605.
claim: The objective is presented as a variational decomposition with per-element normalization.
analysis: Gaussian negative entropy has variable term \(-\frac12\sum\log\sigma^2\); the paper uses coefficient \(-1\) and the active code \(-2\), while the other terms retain their own weights. Reconstruction is averaged and then divided again by element count \(N\). For unit residuals and \(N=4,8,16\), this yields \(0.25,0.125,0.0625\), whereas the stated half-per-element quadratic is \(0.5\). These are parameter-dependent relative-weight and size effects, not one additive constant.
result: The source objective has parameter-dependent relative-weight and batch-size differences. These cannot all be absorbed into an additive constant or common scalar.
assumptions: The finding concerns the stated source version and mathematical or released-code scope.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the intended one-half entropy coefficient and one declared reconstruction normalization; full probabilistic consistency and retraining outcomes remain open.

The freshly retrieved official paper retains the cited formula or definition. The current author repository head retains the implicated implementation where available. Existing local algebraic corrections do not establish a complete repaired model, retraining result or author adoption.

problems.title: Returned SoftDice is replaced by label-optimized hard Dice
problems.source_location: Appendix B.1, PDF p. 19; author metrics.py, lines 143–205, and find_best_dice_threshold, lines 5–38.
claim: The paper defines SoftDice using continuous probabilities and a squared denominator; the release overwrites its soft_dice variable with the best hard-threshold score on the supplied labels.

Hard F1 at threshold \(0.5\) is zero; searching thresholds \(0,0.01,\ldots,1\) selects \(0.49\) and returns hard Dice \(1\). The source overwrites its soft_dice variable with that label-optimized hard score; its earlier soft value also has a different linear denominator.

problems.title: Integer interfaces do not identify a valid local expert
problems.source_location: Appendix B.2, PDF pp.26–28, Eqs.(13)–(14)
claim: Appendix B.2 infers a valid interval from the maximum of the triangular scores \(\tau_i(t)=(t-i+1)_++(t-i)_+-2(t-i+1/2)_+\). It then invokes the selected expert’s local approximation guarantee for arbitrary inputs.
analysis: At every integer interface all scores are zero. Take three exact affine experts \(g_1(t)=t\), \(g_2(t)=2t-1\), \(g_3(t)=3t-3\), each used on its corresponding unit interval. Their joined target is continuous. At \(t=2\), a lowest-index tie selects \(g_1(2)=2\), although both valid adjacent pieces give \(f(2)=3\). Local errors are zero but the constructed pointwise error is \(1\). A fixed score-only tie cannot select appropriate intervals at every endpoint.
result: The displayed pointwise assignment fails at interfaces. This null-set failure does not refute an essential-supremum bound or the existence of another valid router.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use affine nearest-center scores \(a_i(t)=2c_it-c_i^2\), where \(c_i=i-1/2\). They order the centers by distance; adjacent endpoint ties involve only intervals containing that endpoint. A constant feature implements the intercept in a linear gate.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Finite training plateaus do not establish an approximation floor
problems.source_location: Section 6, PDF p.10, finite-width MoE experiment
claim: Section 6 interprets the plateau of a six-expert model over the tested widths as limited expressive power.
analysis: Set every expert equal to the same dense ReLU network \(g\). The top-one output is then \(g\) for every router decision, so this class contains the corresponding dense class. A finite optimization plateau cannot establish a positive asymptotic approximation-error floor for that containing class.
result: The observed table is not contradicted. A fixed-resource depth advantage remains compatible with this containment argument.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

problems.title: Depth-loss inputs are warped RGB tensors
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, PDF p.5, Eqs.(8)–(9); Warp/newCodes/train.py, lines 78–115
claim: Section 3.1, Eqs.(8)–(9), defines an alignment loss on the estimated depth maps. The released transformation trainer instead passes the RGB warp outputs into that discrepancy.
analysis: Equal depth maps under identity geometry should give identical compared depth tensors and zero residual. The traced RGB arguments can differ despite those equal depths; the finite identity-geometry example yields \(7/3\) rather than \(0\). This follows from the input dataflow and does not require a trained model.
result: The released loss call mixes modalities. It does not identify which historical training program produced the paper’s tables.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Warp the depth maps and validity masks with the already predicted transformations, then compare those depth outputs. For equal nonconstant maps under identity geometry, each residual vanishes directly.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Deployment conversion freezes replacement decoder modules during training
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF pp.5–6, Eq.(14); Fusion/newCodes/network.py, build_model and RepConvN.fuse_convs; Fusion/newCodes/train.py, lines 42–48, 77 and 105
claim: Section 3.2 describes optimizing the fusion-mask network. `Fusion/newCodes/train.py` constructs its optimizer before `build_model` invokes deployment conversion inside the training loop.
analysis: The conversion replaces branch parameters with frozen convolution modules. The optimizer retains the old parameter objects, while the replacements are not trainable. Backpropagation therefore cannot perform the intended decoder-branch updates. This concerns the decoder path, rather than a blanket prohibition on branch fusion in the separate transformation estimator.
result: The public fusion trainer does not preserve the intended trainable decoder parameterization. The historical experimental path remains unidentified.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the unconverted decoder during training and convert an evaluation copy after optimization. Training a fused architecture is a different recipe and requires trainable replacement parameters and a matching optimizer.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Constant depth maps make min–max normalization undefined
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, PDF p.5; Warp/newCodes/loss.py, lines 134–165
claim: `Warp/newCodes/loss.py`, lines 134–165, normalizes with pooled minimum \(m\), maximum \(M\), and denominator \(M-m\).
analysis: For equal constant maps, \(M=m\), so both normalized maps contain \(0/0\). This boundary is finite and nonempty; it is the normalizer, rather than the underlying geometric comparison, that is undefined.
result: The public loss requires a constant-map convention. The frequency of this boundary in the reported training data is unknown.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a documented positive floor \(s=\max(M-m,\epsilon)\), \(\epsilon>0\), or explicitly map equal constant inputs to zero residual. The floor must suit the representation and precision.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Promoting the output does not recover rounded Lorentz intermediates
problems.source_location: Appendix A, PDF p.21; Appendix D.2, PDF p.23; openhype/utils/lorentz.py, get_time_comp and pairwise_dist; openhype/openhype_ae/hyperbolic_ae.py, distance call
claim: Appendices A and D.2 use Lorentz maps and distances, with a radial cap for stability. The release promotes only part of the distance calculation.
analysis: Let \(R=2^{14}\), \(x=(\sqrt{R^2+1},R,0)\), and \(y=(\sqrt{R^2+2},R,1)\), with curvature parameter \(1\). Rationalization gives \[-\langle x,y\rangle_L=(3R^2+2)/(\sqrt{(R^2+1)(R^2+2)}+R^2)\], hence distance approximately \(0.962424\). Single-precision squared norms lose the unit increments before the Lorentz subtraction, so a later double-precision output cannot restore them. The points satisfy the configured cap. A distinct finite-loss CPU case had invalid gradients, whereas the corresponding CUDA controls had finite gradients. The CPU/CUDA outcomes are historical measurements from the stated source snapshot, not new runtime executions in this pass; the original recommended dependency environment remains untested.
result: The distance path is precision-sensitive. Neither universal gradient failure nor invalidity of the published CUDA training is established.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Promote operands before the squared norms, reconstructed time coordinates and Lorentz product. Keep the backend-specific passing controls; changing only the final dtype does not address prior cancellation.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The selected margin disables the negative-pair term
problems.source_location: Section 2.5, PDF pp.6–7, Eqs.(24)–(28); Section 3.1 parameter setting
claim: Section 2.5 defines cosine similarities \(S_{ij}\) of normalized nonzero embeddings and negative loss proportional to \(\max(0,S_{ij}-\xi)\). Sections 3.1 and 3.5 select \(\xi=1\).
analysis: Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(S_{ij}\leq1\), so every negative hinge is zero whenever \(\xi\geq1\). Collapsed same-direction embeddings and an orthogonal two-class construction can both attain zero for this pairwise subobjective. Thus the selected setting cannot supply the stated negative-pair repulsion.
result: The negative component is inactive as written. This does not establish collapse of an unknown complete training objective or refute the retrieval measurements.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A margin \(m<1\) restores a nonempty active region \(S_{ij}>m\). At \(m=0\), two collapsed negative pairs contribute \(2\), while orthogonal negatives contribute \(0\). This only repairs the hinge’s active region.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The loss-to-hash-parameter connection is underspecified
problems.source_location: Section 2.4, PDF pp.5–6, Eqs.(13)–(23); Section 2.5 loss inputs
claim: Equations (13)–(23) introduce auxiliary channel weights and hash-probability parameters, whereas Section 2.5 names the earlier mapped features as the loss inputs.
analysis: Under the literal upstream-feature reading, the loss does not depend on the separate downstream parameters, and their partial derivatives are zero. If the feature notation instead denotes downstream outputs, or another loss is used, that conclusion need not hold. The implementation needed to choose between these readings is unavailable.
result: Whether the actual auxiliary and hash parameters receive training gradients requires additional evidence.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify the actual loss inputs, trainable parameter groups and computational graph. No replacement objective or claim that the authors left parameters untrained is established.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Operator norms do not lower-bound every directional gain
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, PDF p.4, paragraph before Remark 1
claim: Section 3.1 uses a restoration Jacobian norm above one to infer amplification of slight input changes, then invokes a larger detector norm.
analysis: Take \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1/10)\) and \(M=\operatorname{diag}(20,1/10)\). Their operator norms are \(2\) and \(20\), but the cascade maps \(\epsilon e_2\) to \((\epsilon/100)e_2\). These smooth linear maps therefore contract that finite perturbation despite large maximum gains.
result: Necessary amplification in every direction does not follow. Existence of amplified directions and the empirical observations remain possible.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The valid upper bound is \(\operatorname{Lip}(D\circ R)\leq\operatorname{Lip}(D)\operatorname{Lip}(R)\). A particular first-order gain is \(\|J_DJ_Rv\|/\|v\|\); a universal local lower bound requires a minimum-singular-value condition.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Training-point alignment does not control the global envelope
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, Remark 3, PDF p.6; Appendix A, PDF p.13
claim: Remark 3 assumes restoration-gradient alignment at a training point \(x^\star\), then bounds the derivative of the global Jacobian maximum \(C(\theta)\).
analysis: For \(B_\theta(x)=x+\theta(x^2-x)\) on \([0,1]\), \(0<\theta<1/2\), use losses \(L_r=2-\theta\), \(L_d=3-2\theta\), and weight \(1\). Then \(g_r=-1\), \(g_d=-2\), and at training point \(x^\star=0\) the required alignment is \(1\). Nevertheless \(C(\theta)=1+\theta\), attained at \(x=1\). Gradient flow has \(\dot\theta=3\), so \(\dot C=3\), while the printed bound is \(1\). Correcting only the detection-term sign does not repair the missing maximizer condition.
result: The stated sufficient condition does not establish this ancillary stability bound. It does not refute improved performance of the joint model.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Under the usual compactness and differentiable-envelope conditions, require alignment at every active maximizer. Use the signed detection contribution \[\max_{x\in\arg\max\phi}[-\langle\nabla_\theta\phi,g_d\rangle]\]. Strict decrease needs this term to be smaller than the restoration contribution.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Public losses differ from the displayed parameter-Jacobian objective
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, Remark 4 and full objective, PDF p.7; Table 4, PDF p.9; released loss path
claim: Section 4.2 uses \(L_d+\lambda L_r+\lambda_p\|\nabla_\theta f_\theta(x)\|\), with a Charbonnier restoration loss and stated weights \(\lambda=10\), \(\lambda_p=0.01\).
analysis: The public recipes assemble weighted absolute-error/perceptual reconstruction terms and clipping or loss-gradient penalties. A loss-gradient norm is not generally the model-output parameter-Jacobian norm in the equation; clipping is an optimizer operation rather than that objective. No configuration-to-table mapping establishes which historical experiment used these recipes.
result: The inspected recipe is insufficient to reproduce the exact displayed objective. No published table entry is numerically contradicted.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Provide the exact loss, norm, reduction and experiment configuration. An operator norm must not silently become a Frobenius estimator; implementing another regularizer requires its own interpretation and evaluation.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Repeated queries mutate cached curvature eigenvalues
problems.source_location: Sections 2–3, PDF pp.3–5; Appendix C, PDF p.31; Appendix E, PDF pp.33–34; official supplement logix/analysis/influence_function_utils.py, precondition_kfac, lines 27–36
claim: For fixed cached eigenvalues \(D\) and explicit damping \(\lambda\), the influence preconditioner should use \((D+\lambda)^{-1}\) without changing the stored curvature.
analysis: In the same-device branch, the temporary tensor aliases the cache and damping is added in place. For a scalar eigenvalue and query gradient both equal to \(1\), with \(\lambda=0.1\), successive identical calls therefore return \(1/1.1\), \(1/1.2\), and \(1/1.3\), rather than the fixed value \(1/1.1\). Positive curvature, matching dimensions and same-device storage suffice; singularity is unnecessary.
result: The routine’s output can depend on prior query count. Whether the published experiments exercised that aliasing path is unresolved.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep \(D\) immutable and form \(D+\lambda\) out of place, or clone before an in-place update. This removes query-count dependence at this interface.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Default damping depends on layer enumeration order
problems.source_location: Appendix C, PDF p.31, damping definition; official supplement logix/analysis/influence_function_utils.py, precondition_kfac module loop
claim: Appendix C describes damping based on \(0.1\) times the mean eigenvalue. The release initializes the shared damping variable inside its module loop only while it is unset.
analysis: For scalar layers with eigenvalues \(1\) and \(100\), per-layer damping is \(0.1\) and \(10\). Processing the small layer first instead uses \(0.1\) for both; reversing the order uses \(10\) for both. The small layer’s output changes from \(1/1.1\) to \(1/11\) under a pure dictionary-order change. This is separate from cache mutation because the factorized branch creates fresh tensors.
result: The default preconditioner is not determined solely by each layer’s statistics and the declared damping policy.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Create a fresh \(\lambda_m=0.1\operatorname{mean}(D_m)\) for each layer, while preserving a user-supplied fixed value when provided. Do not overwrite the shared user option inside the loop.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The fractional-trust threshold lies in the wrong interval
problems.source_location: Lemma A.1(3), PDF pp.20–21; Section 2, PDF p.5
claim: Lemma A.1(3) places the zero-growth forecast error \(\epsilon^*(\lambda)\) in \((0,1/2)\) for its stated fractional-trust range.
analysis: At \(\lambda=1/2\), correct and incorrect predictions give wealth factors \(13/8\) and \(7/8\). Chance-level expected log growth is \(\tfrac12\log(91/64)>0\). Since growth decreases linearly in the prediction-error probability, the root is \(\log(13/8)/[\log(13/8)-\log(7/8)]\approx0.78429\), above \(1/2\). More generally the interior range \(1/3<\lambda<1\) has its root in \((1/2,1)\).
result: The below-chance fragility interpretation of this lemma is incorrect. The RAM guarantee is a separate statement.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the actual logarithmic root and distinguish the endpoints \(\lambda=1/3\) and \(\lambda=1\). Fractional trust can retain positive growth at chance-level forecasts in this two-asset example.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Ranking groups do not match the row order
problems.source_location: Section 3, PDF pp.9–10, Table 4; official notebook cells 34–35
claim: The official notebook’s `prepare_long` and `build_lgb_dataset`, cell 34, are intended to form one cross-sectional ranking query per date.
analysis: The melt operation yields asset-major rows, but the supplied group sizes assume contiguous same-date rows. In a complete panel of three assets and four dates, the first size-three query contains the first asset on dates one through three rather than three assets on one date. Labels, features and weights therefore enter the wrong query grouping.
result: The notebook’s ranking interface is inconsistent. The published wealth values are not recalculated or directly contradicted.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Sort the entire feature/label/weight table by date before splitting arrays and constructing consecutive query groups. This repairs membership without claiming recovered investment performance.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The geometric-mean floor does not imply BCRP universality
problems.source_location: Theorem 2.1, PDF p.6; introduction/discussion protection interpretation
claim: Theorem 2.1 supplies \(S_n^{\mathrm{RAM}}\geq(\prod_{i,j}x_j(i))^{1/m}\).
analysis: With constant two-asset returns \((2,1/2)\) and consistently wrong ranks, the stated RAM behavior cycles to wealth \(1\) at even horizons, whereas the best constant rebalanced portfolio attains \(2^n\). This separates the geometric-mean comparator from a sublinear log-regret guarantee against BCRP.
result: Theorem 2.1 remains valid in this example. It should be interpreted with its proved comparator.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

problems.title: Final sampling prevents the claimed dimension-one rate
problems.source_location: Theorem 4.1, PDF p.6; Algorithm 2, PDF p.5, line 9
claim: Theorem 4.1 covers \(d=1\) and claims \(\widetilde O(dD\sigma^{1/d})\) error. Algorithm 2 ends by drawing \(m\) independent samples, with \(m\) of order \(\sigma^{-1}\) up to logarithmic factors.
analysis: Use target \(\mu=(\delta_0+\delta_1)/2\). For any candidate distribution on \([0,1]\), its independent empirical CDF at an interior threshold is \(K/m\), with \(K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,p)\). For even \(m\), the symmetric convex expected deviation from \(1/2\) is minimized at \(p=1/2\) and equals \(\tfrac12\binom{m}{m/2}2^{-m}\asymp m^{-1/2}\). Integrating the CDF deviations over \((0,1)\) gives the same lower bound for \(\mathbb E W_1\), uniformly over the preceding candidate law and therefore also over its randomness. The prescribed sample count is of order \(\sigma^{-1}\) up to logarithms, giving a \(\sigma^{1/2}\) obstruction incompatible with the asserted dimension-one \(\sigma\) rate.
result: The theorem’s stated dimension-one conclusion fails for its own final sampling step. Dimensions at least two and other output algorithms are not refuted.
assumptions: The output consists of independent equally weighted samples; the theorem includes \(d=1\).

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The established balancing recurrence supports the exponent \(1/\max\{d,2\}\), yielding \(\widetilde O(dD\sigma^{1/\max\{d,2\}})\). Use integer sample counts and an iteration horizon controlling the residual term.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: A fixed-dataset accuracy premise cannot imply the packing bound
problems.source_location: Lemma 3.1, PDF p.5; Definition D.1, PDF p.17; proof, PDF p.28
claim: Lemma 3.1 states accuracy at a fixed dataset \(S\) and concludes \(\varepsilon\geq\log M(\Omega,\rho;2\eta)\). Its packing convention permits distances equal to \(2\eta\).
analysis: A mechanism that always returns that fixed \(S\) is perfectly private and perfectly accurate there, regardless of the larger domain’s packing number. Even uniform closed-ball accuracy permits the constant midpoint on \([0,1]\) when \(\eta=1/2\), since the endpoint accuracy balls touch. Uniform input accuracy and strict separation are therefore necessary for the proposed disjoint-event proof. Diameter and ambient dimension alone also do not lower-bound packing growth.
result: The lemma as quantified admits trivial counterexamples. A dimension-dependent interpretation additionally requires domain geometry.
assumptions: Accuracy is read with the printed fixed-input quantifier and closed accuracy balls.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Require accuracy at every input and centers separated by more than \(2\eta\). The neighboring-dataset disjoint-event argument then gives \(\varepsilon\geq\log((M-1)(1-\tau-\delta)/\tau)\) under the stated error ranges.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The histogram proposition can return a nonprobability measure
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, Proposition 4.1, PDF pp.7–8; Appendix H, PDF pp.26–28
claim: Proposition 4.1 normalizes retained noisy mass when positive and otherwise returns the zero histogram, then states an ordinary probability-measure \(W_1\) bound.
analysis: For one positive bin with \(n=1\), \(\varepsilon=1/2\), and \(\delta=0.1\), all mass is discarded with probability \(0.95\). The returned zero measure has total mass zero, so the asserted ordinary \(W_1\) quantity is undefined. The proof also omits absolute values on negative discarded noise. The simulation caller’s fallback and Algorithm 2’s simplex projection avoid this particular output defect and must remain distinct.
result: The proposition is not well-defined on its stated output branch. This does not show that Algorithm 2 returns a zero measure.
assumptions: \(W_1\) denotes ordinary Wasserstein distance between probability measures, not an independently defined unbalanced transport distance.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: On empty retained mass, return a probability distribution fixed on the public candidate support, then analyze the fallback probability and discarded absolute mass. This is probability-valued post-processing, with privacy conditional on the support’s provenance.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The class-name selector uses position rather than dataset class identity
problems.source_location: Section 6, PDF p.9; Figures 3–4, PDF p.10; PE_cifar10_code.ipynb, cell 8
claim: The CIFAR notebook’s `Cifar10` selector iterates the length of the requested class-name list instead of resolving those names against the dataset class map.
analysis: A one-name dog request therefore selects class index \(0\), which is airplane, rather than dog index \(5\), while retaining dog metadata. The mismatch follows directly from the selector.
result: The release can mislabel the selected subset. Which historical code produced the published dog figures is unverified.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Resolve requested names through the dataset’s actual class map and keep a separate local subset label.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Per-state policy KL does not uniformly control discounted occupancy
problems.source_location: Theorem 1, Eq.(6), PDF p.6; Appendix A.2, PDF pp.15–16
claim: Theorem 1 assumes \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\beta(\cdot\mid s)\Vert\pi(\cdot\mid s))\leq\varepsilon\) at every state and asserts \(J(\beta)-J(\pi)\leq R_{\max}\sqrt{2\varepsilon}/(1-\gamma)\).
analysis: Use states \(u,b\), start at \(u\), and let \(b\) be absorbing. At \(u\), positive actions enter \(b\), nonpositive actions stay; rewards are \(r(u,a)=0\), \(r(b,a)=-1\). Behavior is uniform on \([-1,0]\); the learned policy places mass \(0.99\) there and \(0.01\) uniformly on \((0,1]\). At \(b\) the policies agree. Every conditional KL is at most \(\varepsilon=-\log0.99\). With \(\gamma=0.99\), the behavior return is zero and the learned return is \(-[1/(1-\gamma)-1/(1-0.99\gamma)]\approx-49.74874\). The asserted bound is only \(\sqrt{-2\log0.99}/0.01\approx14.17768\). Conditional action closeness does not supply uniform future occupancy closeness.
result: Theorem 1 is false under its stated conditional-policy premise. The counterexample uses the same start law, kernel and bounded rewards. No Gaussian-policy restriction is stated in this theorem.
assumptions: Policies share an initial law and transition kernel; current-state rewards have absolute value at most \(1\); the theorem has no Gaussian-policy restriction.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The original return bound follows if every joint state-action marginal instead has KL at most \(\varepsilon\). Under only the original per-state premise, the trajectory chain rule gives prefix KL at most \((t+1)\varepsilon\), leading to the weaker sum \(R_{\max}\sum_{t\geq0}\gamma^t\sqrt{2(t+1)\varepsilon}\).
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The Gaussian radius omits necessary dimension dependence
problems.source_location: Lemma 4, Appendix A.1, PDF pp.14–15; Theorem 2 proof, PDF pp.16–17
claim: Lemma 4 asserts \(\Pr(\|a-\mu\|_2\leq\sqrt{2\Lambda\log(1/\delta)})\geq1-\delta\) for \(a\sim\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)\), where \(\Lambda=\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)\).
analysis: Take \(a\sim\mathcal N(0,I_4)\) and \(\delta=1/20\). The squared radius is \(2\log20\). Exact \(\chi^2_4\) coverage is \(1-(1+\log20)/20\approx0.800213\), below the promised \(0.95\). The missing trace and dimension terms cannot be discarded from a norm concentration inequality.
result: The lemma and uses of this radius in Theorem 2’s proof are invalid as stated. This does not measure any empirical policy error.
assumptions: The covariance is positive definite and the stated probability claim applies in every dimension.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A valid Gaussian bound uses squared radius \(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma+2\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^2)x}+2\Lambda x\), with \(x=\log(1/\delta)\). It follows from the centered Gaussian quadratic-form moment bound and Chernoff’s inequality.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Mixture KL cannot be assigned to each component without an information term
problems.source_location: Appendix A.3, PDF p.17, step (2); Eq.(8), PDF p.6
claim: Appendix A.3 uses \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\beta\Vert\pi)\leq\varepsilon\), with \(\beta=\sum_iw_iP_i\), to infer \(\|\mu_i-\mu_\pi\|\leq\sqrt{2\varepsilon\Lambda(\Sigma_\pi)/w_i}\) for every Gaussian component.
analysis: Let \(\beta=\tfrac12\mathcal N(-1/2,1)+\tfrac12\mathcal N(1/2,1)\) and \(\pi=\mathcal N(0,1)\). Its KL is at most \(\log\cosh(1/4)\leq1/32\), yet either mean shift \(1/2\) exceeds the inferred \(\sqrt{1/8}\). For component label \(Z\), the exact identity is \(\sum_iw_iD_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_i\Vert\pi)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\beta\Vert\pi)+I(Z;A)\). The omitted mutual information is nonnegative.
result: The component-mean inference fails. This example alone does not refute every separately capped final radius.
assumptions: Gaussian component weights are positive and the target Gaussian covariance is positive definite.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Using \(I(Z;A)\leq H(w)\) gives component KL at most \((\varepsilon+H(w))/w_i\) for \(w_i>0\); replace the numerator in the mean bound accordingly. Remove zero-weight components before dividing.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The released actor path differs from forward-KL replay alignment
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF pp.4–5, Eqs.(2)–(5); Algorithm 1, PDF p.6; released policy loss
claim: Section 3.2 derives a replay-action expectation of \(-\log\pi_\theta(a_\beta\mid s)\). The applicable author paths are `boom/boom_alg.py`, `update_pi`, lines 235–284, and `boom/common/math.py`, `gaussian_logprob`, lines 26–31.
analysis: `update_pi` ignores the replay action, samples current-policy actions and substitutes the current-policy standard deviation, so it does not evaluate the derived replay-action cross-entropy. This concern was previously raised in repository issue #2; closure alone establishes neither correction nor author acceptance. Separately, the density helper multiplies an already summed residual by the dimension. For \(d=2\), standardized residual \((1,1)\) and log standard deviation \(0\), it gives approximately \(-3.837877\) rather than the correct \(-2.837877\).
result: These are public implementation discrepancies. Their effect on the original experiments is unknown.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For diagonal Gaussian density, sum coordinate residuals once and subtract \(d\log(2\pi)/2\) once. To implement the stated forward-KL target, evaluate policy density and intended weights on the same replay actions; specify any stopped-gradient weights and transformed-policy Jacobian.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Invalid answers change the refusal-rate denominator

problems.source_location: Section 3.1, PDF p.4, Eqs.(5)–(6); network.py, lines 131–178

problems.title: The information expression is not the stated Fisher information
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, PDF p.6, Eq.(9); loss_function.py, lines 6–23; train.py, line 186
claim: For Gaussian measurements with mean \(\mu(d)\) and variance \(V(d)=\mu(d)+\nu\), Eq.(9) requires \(J=\mu^{\prime2}/V+V^{\prime2}/(2V^2)\). `loss_function.py` introduces a second-derivative term and different coefficients.
analysis: Taking the expectation of the squared Gaussian score yields the displayed nonnegative Fisher expression. A second derivative of the mean does not appear in that identity. A finite positive-variance quadratic mean can make the implemented sum negative while Eq.(9)’s finite-difference sum is positive, so the discrepancy is not a common normalization. Such a quadratic is a diagnostic mean, not an asserted learned code curve.

assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction

problems.title: The unsquared error rate is too fast
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.12, PDF p.7, Eq.(20); Appendix E, PDF pp.28–29
claim: Theorem 3.12 claims both loss and unsquared \(L^2\) error are \(O(R_N)\), where \(R_N=N^{-(1-3\alpha)/2}\sqrt{\log N}+N^{-\alpha}\) and stopping time is of order \(N^\alpha\).
analysis: On \((0,1)\), let \(\phi_j=\sqrt2\sin(\pi jx)\), kernel \(K(x,y)=1+xy+\sum_je^{-j^2}\phi_j(x)\phi_j(y)\), and solution \(u^*=\sum_je^{-j^2/2}\phi_j/j\). The kernel and forcing are smooth and \(\|u^*\|_H^2=\sum_jj^{-2}<\infty\). For the Laplacian with zero endpoint data, mode decay is \(e^{-2\mu_jt}\), \(\mu_j=e^{-j^2}(\pi j)^4\). At \(t_j=(2\mu_j)^{-1}\), error is at least \(e^{-1}e^{-j^2/2}/j\), so \(t_j\|v_{t_j}-u^*\|_2\to\infty\). Bounded residual features give empirical mean-square perturbation \(O(t^2/N)\) by the contraction-semigroup identity. Taking \(\alpha=1/10\), \(N_j=\lceil t_j^{10}\rceil\), makes that perturbation negligible relative to the mode lower bound, while \(R_{N_j}=O(t_j^{-1})\). The unsquared empirical rate therefore also fails along this subsequence.
result: The quantitative norm rate is contradicted under smooth, noiseless, uniformly sampled admissible data. The construction remains consistent and does not reject qualitative convergence.
assumptions: The fixed smooth kernel and solution satisfy the RKHS source condition; interior and boundary sampling are uniform and noiseless.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The stated loss-to-error argument yields \(\|\hat u_T-u^*\|_2^2=O(R_N)\), equivalently norm \(O(R_N^{1/2})\). A stronger norm rate requires an additional source condition or argument.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The RKHS embedding is used in the wrong direction
problems.source_location: Lemma E.2, PDF p.28, Eqs.(142)–(144); Corollary A.7, PDF p.19
claim: Corollary A.7 bounds \(\|u\|_{C^2}\) by \(C\|u\|_H\), whereas Eq.(142) needs the converse.
analysis: The functions \(h_j=e^{-j^2/2}\sqrt2\sin(\pi jx)\) have RKHS norm \(1\) and \(C^2\) norm tending to zero. Thus the invoked reverse inequality is unavailable. However, along the intended population flow, \(d\|v-u^*\|_H^2/dt=-4\mathcal L(v)\); integration and monotone loss recover \(\mathcal L(v_t)\leq\|u^*\|_H^2/(4t)\).
result: The written proof step fails, while its loss conclusion has an independent energy proof.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

problems.title: Polynomial Gaussian features need not be sub-exponential
problems.source_location: Assumption 5.2, PDF p.8; Lemma F.8, PDF p.32, Eqs.(175)–(179)
claim: Lemma F.8 invokes generic sub-exponential tails from polynomial growth under Assumption 5.2’s smooth activation bounds.
analysis: The allowed activation \(\sigma(z)=z^3+\sin z\) makes a positive feature product grow as the sixth power of a Gaussian variable. Its positive exponential moments diverge, so the asserted generic sub-exponential premise is false. Polynomial growth alone cannot justify that Bernstein application.
result: The concentration proof needs another argument. This does not independently establish failure of the claimed kernel-value convergence rate.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Truncate Gaussian parameters at a multiple of \(\sqrt{\log m}\), apply concentration to independent bounded truncated features, then control the tail event and bias. Complete highest-derivative control under only \(C^3\) regularity remains unresolved.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The Gaussian linear-map estimate hides width dependence
problems.source_location: Appendix F.3, PDF p.42, Eqs.(263)–(269); Theorem F.15
claim: Equation (267) bounds the norm of the map \(\varphi(x)=\sum_{p\ne q}a_pb_qx_{pq}\) by a universal multiple of \(\log N\), independent of layer width.
analysis: Its derivative operator norm squared is \((\sum_pa_p^2)(\sum_qb_q^2)-\sum_pa_p^2b_p^2\). For independent standard Gaussian coordinates and width \(m\), the norm divided by \(m\) tends to \(1\). A universal width-independent threshold cannot hold over unrestricted widths. Coordinatewise maximum conventions also require a dimension dependence.
result: The cited deep-network proof estimate fails. No counterexample to the full deep-network theorem follows from this item alone.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

problems.title: Point anchoring does not give unrestricted high-dimensional coercivity
problems.source_location: Section 5.1, PDF p.9, Eqs.(25)–(28); Theorem 5.9
claim: Section 5.1 transfers the loss-to-\(L^2\) conclusions to \(\mathcal L_M(u)=|u(p)|^2+\|\Delta u-f\|_2^2\) on tori without a dimension restriction.
analysis: For normalized \(\mathbb T^d\), \(d\geq4\), let \(S_R=\sum_{0<\|k\|_\infty\leq R}|k|^{-4}\) and \(u_R=1-S_R^{-1}\sum|k|^{-4}e^{ik\cdot x}\). These smooth real functions satisfy \(u_R(0)=0\), \(\|\Delta u_R\|_2^2=1/S_R\to0\), yet their constant Fourier coefficient is \(1\), and \(\|u_R\|_2\to1\). Thus vanishing anchored loss need not control solution error. This is not an assertion about the particular zero-initialized trajectory for zero forcing.
result: The unrestricted coercivity transfer is false even for smooth functions. Low-dimensional point anchoring is not contradicted.
assumptions: The torus measure is normalized and Fourier frequencies satisfy the displayed Laplacian convention; every witness is smooth.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restrict this point-evaluation argument to dimensions where \(H^2\) controls point values, such as \(d\leq3\), or replace the point anchor by a specified mean gauge. The latter changes the loss but controls the constant mode in every fixed dimension.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Equal Laplacian frequencies need not share a torus-kernel eigenvalue
problems.source_location: Appendix H, PDF p.49, argument before Eq.(349)
claim: Appendix H treats a torus inner-product NTK as scalar on each full Laplacian eigenspace.
analysis: Translation invariance diagonalizes Fourier modes but does not impose rotational symmetry on a product torus. The admissible sinusoidal NTK gives distinct eigenvalues to \((5,0)\) and \((4,3)\), approximately \(0.000192508\) and \(0.0000418808\), although both have squared frequency \(25\). Positive-series bounds separate these values; simultaneous diagonalization itself survives.
result: The common-eigenvalue identification is too strong. The underlying finite-mode approximation can be indexed more carefully.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(K(x,y)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}\lambda_ke^{ik\cdot(x-y)}\). State positivity for the modes needed by the approximation, rather than equating all \(\lambda_k\) at the same \(|k|^2\).

problems.title: Proportional allocation is not the guaranteed greedy algorithm

problems.title: A local feature can remain invariant and useful under both shifts
problems.source_location: Appendix A, PDF p.21, reverse proposition, Eqs.(18)–(20); Section 1, PDF p.3
claim: Appendix A’s reverse implication rules out effective invariant features without a receptive field spanning both domains.
analysis: Let \(X=(U,A)\), with balanced \(U\), nuisance probabilities \(P_s(A=1)=1/4\), \(P_t(A=1)=3/4\), and \(P_s(Y=U\mid A)=0.95-0.20A\), \(P_t(Y=U\mid A)=0.75+0.20A\). Both raw and conditional laws shift. Yet the local feature \(f(X)=U\) has identical balanced domain laws, zero domain information and zero population MMD; its Bayes classification accuracy is \(0.90\) in each domain.

problems.title: Mixed-input gradients do not follow from the displayed weighted objective
problems.source_location: Appendix A, PDF p.21, forward argument, Eqs.(15)–(17)
claim: Appendix A’s forward argument identifies a mixed-input gradient with a weighted source/alignment gradient and then asserts near-zero domain information.
analysis: For inputs \(x_s=1\), \(x_t=3\), mixture weight \(1/2\) and a logistic linear feature at parameter zero, the mixed supervised gradient is \(-1\), while the displayed weighted gradient is \(-1/4\). If Eq.(16) defines a weighted objective instead, the algebra is valid but concerns another object. Equation (17) additionally assumes the near-equality \(H(D\mid Z)\approx H(D)\) needed for invariance.

problems.title: Quantization error alone does not order full reconstruction error
problems.source_location: Appendix A, Proposition 2, PDF p.15, Eq.(15); Claim 2 SVD setup
claim: Proposition 2 compares \(\|Q(A)+Q(B)-A-B\|_F\) with \(\|Q(A+B)-A-B\|_F\) and infers the same ordering for approximation of the original matrix \(W\).
analysis: Put \(T=W-A-B\), \(d=Q(A)+Q(B)-A-B\), and \(e=Q(A+B)-A-B\). Actual errors are \(\|T-d\|_F\) and \(\|T-e\|_F\), so their squared difference contains \(-2\langle T,d-e\rangle_F\). A complete counterexample uses the same entrywise sign quantizer on each nonzero entry and orthogonal matrices \[U=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}1&-2&-2\\-2&1&-2\\-2&-2&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad V=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}-1&-2&-2\\-2&2&-1\\-2&-1&2\end{pmatrix}.\] Set \(W=U\operatorname{diag}(3,2,1)V^\top\), \(A=3u_1v_1^\top\), \(B=2u_2v_2^\top\). Thus \(A+B\) is genuinely the rank-two truncated SVD with a nonzero third-mode tail. Direct rational arithmetic gives \(\|d\|_F^2=7/3<32/9=\|e\|_F^2\), but total squared errors \(\|W-Q(A)-Q(B)\|_F^2=10/3>3=\|W-Q(A+B)\|_F^2\). No zero-entry convention, numerical SVD or changed quantizer explains the reversal.
result: The stated sufficient condition is incomplete; learned residual quantization-aware training itself is not refuted.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The exact criterion is \(\|d\|_F^2-\|e\|_F^2<2\langle T,d-e\rangle_F\). If the cross terms vanish, the simpler comparison becomes sufficient under that additional condition.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Factorized weights do not themselves imply a latent KV cache
problems.source_location: Current arXiv v5 Section 5, PDF p.10; Figure 5 and Table 4, PDF p.9; quantization/modules/attention.py, PhiQKVSplitAttention.forward

Exact comparison over arbitrary signed input requires accounting for those cross edges. Counting only sampled assignment work omits the pseudocode’s full scoring step. Approximate sampled ranking can support a separately specified randomized procedure.

problems.title: The conjecture has known subsequent author refutation
problems.source_location: The original three-quarter conjecture; authors’ MLG 2026 follow-up, Theorem 3
claim: The original \(3/4\) guarantee is labeled a conjecture; the authors’ MLG 2026 follow-up Theorem 3 refutes it.
analysis: For \(n=256\), random independent edge signs give a finite existence argument: there are at most \((2n)^{2n}\) interval-overlap patterns, while each fixed pattern’s chance of agreement above the target is bounded by \(\exp(-\binom n2/8)\). Their product is below one. This is a probabilistic existence argument, not an enumerated optimum or new discovery.

The elementary universal guarantee is \(|E|/2\): the better of all-overlapping and pairwise-disjoint interval assignments satisfies at least half the signed edges. The author follow-up limits a larger uniform constant in its stated asymptotic setting. This contextualizes known subsequent progress; it is not a repair of a falsely proved theorem.
result: A conjecture can be disproved by later work without constituting a false proof in the original paper. Historical attribution remains with the authors.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

problems.title: The covariance merge underweights between-batch scatter
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, PDF p.5; utils/layerwrapper.py, WrappedGPT.add_batch, lines 44–64; compression/preprocess.py, lines 66–130; compression/model_prune.py, lines 48–68

Two symmetric two-point batches then give \(\operatorname{diag}(3/4,4/3)\) rather than \(\operatorname{diag}(3,4/3)\), reversing the principal axis and changing the rank-one reconstruction error from \(4\) to \(9\). Equal-mean batches are unaffected.
