problems.title: Dot-product softmax is not the quadratic MMSE optimizer
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, p. 5, Eqs. (7)–(8); Appendix E.1, pp. 23–25; E.3.5, p. 27.
claim: Equations (7)–(8) and Appendix E identify scaled dot-product attention with a simplex-constrained quadratic MMSE solution.
analysis: In dimension \(3\), use mean-zero tokens \(v_1=\sqrt{3/2}(1,-1,0)\) and \(v_2=(1,1,-2)/\sqrt2\). Each has squared norm \(3\), so they meet unit-coordinate-variance LayerNorm normalization and have Gram matrix \(G=3I\); they are not unit Euclidean vectors. Set deterministic mediator \(\mu=3v_1/4+v_2/4\). The true simplex MMSE weights \((3/4,1/4)\) give zero risk. Scaled scores have gap \(\sqrt3/2\), so softmax gives approximately \((0.703918,0.296082)\), with risk \(0.0127413\). The quadratic KKT equations contain \(G\alpha\); replacing them by exponentiated linear scores drops this dependence. Sending linear-score temperature to zero selects a vertex of risk \(3/8\), rather than the interior optimum.
result: The claimed MMSE identity and zero-temperature derivation fail, even in the simple orthogonal case.
assumptions: Tokens are mean-zero three-dimensional LayerNorm-compatible vectors of squared norm \(3\), with a simplex attention constraint and squared reconstruction risk.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Solve \(\min_{\alpha\in\Delta}\alpha^\top G\alpha-2b^\top\alpha\). An entropy-regularized version gives an implicit softmax equation retaining \(G\alpha\), not the asserted general explicit linear-score softmax.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Fixed similarity weights converge to a tilted mean
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, p. 6, Eq. (9); Appendix E.3, pp. 26–27, Eq. (E.25).
claim: Equation (9) and Appendix E.3 claim that an expanding softmax-weighted bank converges to the marginal mean under bounded similarity and moment assumptions.
analysis: Let independent \(X\) take values \(\pm1\) equally, query \(q\in\{-1,1\}\), and similarity \(qX\). The ratio law of large numbers gives limit \(\mathbb E[Xe^{qX}]/\mathbb E[e^{qX}]=q\tanh1\), not marginal mean zero. In a balanced bank of \(100\) tokens, the weight distance from uniform is \(\tanh1\approx0.76159\), exceeding the asserted bound \(2(e^2-1)/100\approx0.12778\). Independence is stronger than the stated stationarity.
result: The proposed marginal-mean consistency fails under its assumptions. This does not refute front-door identification as a separate causal formula.
assumptions: The memory samples are independent with bounded support and fixed bounded similarity, stronger than stationarity alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Uniform weights with suitable independent or stationary-ergodic assumptions estimate the marginal mean. Retaining fixed similarity instead requires identifying and analyzing the tilted target; a vanishing-temperature parameter needs its own limit argument.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Microbatch averaging differs from equal-question weighting
problems.source_location: Eq. (6), p. 5; Appendix A.1/Eq. (7), p. 14; core_algos.py lines 302–333 and dp_actor.py line 272.
claim: Equations (6)–(7) define \(L=Q^{-1}\sum_qN_q^{-1}\sum_{i,k}\ell_{qik}\), where \(N_q\) is the total response-token count for question \(q\).

Unequal question lengths make these coefficients depend on partition. Two questions, each with eight responses of lengths \(32\) and \(288\), give loss \(-0.1707128\) in one microbatch versus \(-0.1260209\) in two question microbatches, with identical valid autoregressive observations. This differs from the written equal-question loss \(Q^{-1}\sum_qN_q^{-1}\sum_{i,k}\ell_{qik}\), where \(N_q\) is fixed across the complete response group.

problems.title: The strict stability rate omits a logarithmic factor
problems.source_location: Proceedings Proposition 2, p. 7; separate supplement §A.6, p. 21.
claim: Proposition 2 gives a constant-factor second-order SGD rate under the stated polynomial step, batch and horizon scalings.
analysis: Let the common background records have feature zero, and choose four distinct added records with features \((1,1,0,0)\). The four size-\(N\) datasets contain respectively \(k=2,1,1,0\) unit-feature records. Use scalar loss \(\ell(w;z)=-a(z)w\), start \(w_0=0\), step \(N^{-1/4}/t\), batch size \(N\) and horizon \(N\). A bounded smooth utility can equal \(w^2\) on \([-2,2]\), extend as \(8-(4-|w|)^2\) for \(2<|w|<4\), and equal \(8\) outside; it has bounded derivative and Lipschitz derivative. Every reached iterate is below \(2\). Without replacement, \(w_T(k)=kN^{-5/4}H_N\), where \(H_N=\sum_{t\leq N}1/t\). Thus the four-utility difference is \(2N^{-5/2}H_N^2\). Independent with-replacement batches give \(2N^{-5/2}(H_N^2-H_N^{(2)}/N)\), with \(H_N^{(2)}=\sum_{t\leq N}t^{-2}\). Scaling by \(N^{5/2}\) diverges, contradicting the strict power-only bound under the stated regularity. This does not establish an optimal alternative rate.
result: The exponent-only bound needs qualification. This does not refute conditional faithfulness or prove an optimal alternative rate.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

paragraphs: Retain the supplement’s capped exponent \(\nu_{\rm eff}=\min\{2\tau_1+\tau_2-1/2,1/2\}\) and its two-term bound, or explicitly account for the logarithmic factors under the example’s scaling.

assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

problems.title: Disconnected components do not identify a global ranking
problems.source_location: Sections 3.1–3.2, p. 4, Eq. (2); Section 4.2, p. 6.
claim: The stated pairwise likelihood estimates a global paper ranking without an explicit connected-component completion rule.
analysis: Two balanced-win components \(\{1,2\}\), \(\{3,4\}\) have centered equally maximizing scores \((c,c,-c,-c)\) for every \(c\). Component offsets, and hence cross-component order, are unidentified. With \(7158\) papers and \(1000\) pairwise comparisons, at most \(2000\) papers appear, leaving at least \(5158\) untouched.
result: The likelihood alone does not uniquely determine all global ranks in the allowed sparse regime. A regularizer or completion rule adds information.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State graph connectivity, completion/tie rules and any prior or penalty. Restrict unregularized interpretation to identifiable score differences.

problems.title: Connected comparisons need not have a finite maximum
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, p. 4, Eq. (2) over real-valued coefficients.
claim: Connectivity alone is sometimes read as sufficient for finite unregularized score estimation.
analysis: For two papers with one observed win, the comparison graph is connected and centered log likelihood is \(\log\sigma(t)\), where \(t\) is their score difference. It increases toward zero as \(t\to\infty\), so no finite maximum is attained. The pairwise ordering itself is still supported.
result: A finite estimate requires stronger conditions or a different explicit estimator.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A declared positive ridge penalty makes the logistic objective coercive and strictly convex, supplying a unique finite penalized estimate. This is distinct from the unregularized likelihood.

problems.title: Full-action orientation does not identify the spin image
problems.source_location: Appendix B, Property 3, pp. 27–28.
claim: Property 3 characterizes the spin image using grade preservation and positive determinant on the entire Clifford algebra.
analysis: In \(\mathrm{Cl}(2)\), conjugation by \(g=e_1\) has matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1,-1)\) in the scalar/vector/bivector basis. It preserves grades and has full determinant \(+1\), but its grade-one block has determinant \(-1\), a reflection unavailable to a \(\mathrm{Spin}(2)\) rotor. More generally the full exterior lift has determinant \((\det R)^{2^{n-1}}\), losing the sign for \(n\geq2\).
result: The characterization is too broad. The actual even-rotor forward parameterization is not shown to realize that reflection.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Impose \(\det(N_g|_{\mathrm{Cl}^1})=1\) on the grade-one action, together with the stated orthogonality and grade conditions.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Detached decomposition omits fixed-point dependence
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, PDF pp.5–6; Appendix B, Theorems 2–3; rotor_layer.py, Rotor._update_rotors, lines 164–180
claim: The release solves a decomposition without gradient tracking, then reruns with detached warm-start vectors.
analysis: For bivector \(b=1.2e_{12}+0.6e_{34}+he_{13}\), the selected matrix entry’s recomputed exponential derivative is approximately \(-0.23271515\), whereas the released backward path gives \(-0.22552789\). Recomputed forward finite differences support the former. Detaching spectral/fixed-point state omits its parameter dependence.
result: The backward rule is not the derivative of the recomputed rotor map on this control. Surrogate-gradient training may still be useful.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Track the relevant decomposition iterations or supply a valid implicit derivative under stated nondegeneracy conditions. A local differentiable-iteration control does not prove stability at all spectral collisions.

problems.title: Zero simple components need an exponential limit and stable shape
problems.source_location: Eq.(5), PDF p.5; current author README prescribed torch_ga_fix submission branch at 376a48bfeeba2e76ef42abee6fe516a349d8d3bb, torch_ga/torch_ga.py, exp_simple_batched
claim: The author README prescribes the torch_ga_fix submission branch. Its current exp_simple_batched divides a component by its norm before multiplying by sine and squeezes a singleton dimension.
analysis: A zero component therefore gives \(0/0\) instead of the identity exponential. Even nonzero simple input \(e_{12}\) in \(\mathrm{Cl}(4)\) leaves a zero second component after decomposition, so zero input is not the only boundary. A singleton batch can additionally lose the axis needed by concatenation.

The dependency’s separate default-main branch contains another API with an explicit zero-angle branch. That is opposing evidence against a claim covering every dependency version; it does not remove the defect from the current author-prescribed submission branch.
result: The helper is undefined on legitimate simple-component inputs. Random dense-training incidence is unknown.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use \(\exp(b)=\cos q+\operatorname{sinc}(q/\pi)b\), \(q=\|b\|\), with normalized sinc value \(1\) at zero, and preserve the batch axis.
The currently prescribed submission branch retains the defect. A different default-main implementation has zero-angle handling, but its integration into the paper release was not established.

problems.title: String identity does not establish semantic equivalence
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, PDF p.5; Appendix B.5, PDF p.18, Table 8
claim: Section 3.3 compares generated formula strings with source formulas and then describes the natural-language reasoning as validated.
analysis: The valid symbolic tree is \(P\to Q,P\vdash Q\). Let the English first premise instead mean \(Q\to P\), while attaching the expected string \(P\to Q\). Every formula-string comparison passes. The valuation \(P=\mathrm{true},Q=\mathrm{false}\) satisfies the actual English premises and falsifies the conclusion. This is a constructed failure of certification, not an observed training row. Appendix B.5 separately reports consistency judgments of \(97.6\%\) and \(96.8\%\).
result: The gate does not supply a universal semantic-validity guarantee. The source already presents quality improvement and residual fallibility.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A sound symbolic tree yields a valid English conclusion if every instantiated statement is semantically equivalent to its formula. String matching does not prove that additional premise; no corrected dataset is established.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Additive calibration conflicts with the defining transmission integral
problems.source_location: Current arXiv v2 Section 6, PDF p.7, Eq.(7); Appendix B.1–B.2, PDF pp.21–22
claim: Section 6, Eq.(7), uses \(T_r=T_p-C_p(0)+C_r(0)\) to calibrate reused-ray transmittance. Appendix B defines density from the clipped logarithmic derivative of the logistic CDF \(C\).
analysis: On a monotone entering ray the integral gives \(T(u)=C(u)/C(0)\). Use the true planar SDF \(f=(x+z)/\sqrt2\) and unit logistic scale. Origins \((0,0,\sqrt2\log3)\) and \((-\sqrt2\log2,0,\sqrt2\log3)\) lie in the same aperture plane and have CDFs \(3/4\), \(3/5\); choose their common endpoint at CDF \(1/2\). Then \(T_p=2/3\), but additive calibration gives \(31/60\), while the receiver ray requires \(5/6\). All values are finite and positive, and both straight rays are monotone for this planar SDF.
result: The central calibration formula is not derived from the stated density, even before nonmonotone path complications. No reconstruction benchmark is remeasured.
assumptions: The SDF is exact, unit-gradient and planar; both rays enter monotonically and the logistic scale is one.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For monotone entering rays, the correct origin adjustment is \(T_r=T_pC_p(0)/C_r(0)\). General paths instead depend on accumulated downward variation of \(\log C\), so this endpoint ratio is not a universal ray-reuse repair.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The printed magnitude derivative omits the complex resultant
problems.source_location: Current arXiv v2 Appendix A.5, PDF p.19, Eq.(13); Algorithm 1, PDF p.20
claim: Appendix A.4 differentiates \(P_j=|z_j|\) but omits the resultant needed in its magnitude derivative.
analysis: For one positive real input with coefficient \(1\) and signal \(2\), \(P=2\), true derivative is \(1\), while the printed rule gives \(1/P=1/2\). This real subcase avoids complex-gradient convention ambiguity. The later `rf_rendering.py` instead computes real/imaginary outputs followed by `torch.hypot`, which retains the needed chain rule.
result: The printed formula is wrong; a current released gradient defect and historical benchmark effect are not established.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For \(z\ne0\), use \(d|z|=\operatorname{Re}(\bar z\,dz)/|z|\), with a declared convention for the final real-loss complex gradient and the zero boundary.

problems.title: The supported encoder string bypasses GNN preprocessing
problems.source_location: Appendix A.1 and A.4, PDF pp.14–15; released main.py, lines 57, 91–139 and 149–164

problems.title: Non-rejection does not establish distributional equality
problems.source_location: Appendix B.9.1 and Figure 11, PDF p.20
claim: Appendix B.9.1 and Figure 11 infer the same performance distribution from non-rejecting paired signed-rank tests on nine trials per initialization.
analysis: Nine nonzero differences with absolute ranks one through nine and positive rank sum \(25\) give exact two-sided probability \(0.8203125\). That non-rejecting rank/sign pattern has positive probability under a continuous symmetric difference law centered at a nonzero shift. Thus non-rejection cannot establish equality, even under a valid test model. The raw trials and pairing are not reconstructed.
result: The tests did not detect differences in that sample. No actual difference between the paper’s initialization populations is asserted.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State non-detection at the nominal \(0.05\) level. A practical-equivalence claim requires a prespecified tolerance, effect estimates and an appropriate uncertainty analysis.

problems.title: Target class labels determine adaptation-sample selection
problems.source_location: Introduction and Section 4.3, PDF pp.1 and 7; main.py, lines 61–84 and 129
claim: `main.py` constructs the target training `CoordDataset` with class balancing enabled; the loader obtains labels from filename prefixes before downsampling.
analysis: Changing only those target class annotations can therefore change which image identities enter adaptation, even if minibatch labels are later discarded. In the balanced-subset operation, label information has already affected the training input. An externally predeclared curator subset would be a different protocol.
result: The release is not strictly label-blind target adaptation. Accuracy advantage, patient leakage and historical split preprocessing are not established.

problems.title: Target-test AUC selects saved checkpoints
problems.source_location: Section 5, PDF pp.7–9; main.py, lines 130–135 and 552–559
claim: The release repeatedly evaluates the dataset explicitly opened in testing mode and saves model components when its AUC improves.
analysis: For fixed scores \((0.1,0.9,0.6,0.7)\) and \((0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4)\), labels \((0,0,1,1)\) give AUCs \((0.5,1)\); reversing labels gives \((0.5,0)\). The selected epoch changes with test labels while predictions are fixed. This is model selection rather than logging alone.

problems.title: The classifier branch backpropagates without stepping its optimizer
problems.source_location: Section 4.3, Eq.(9), PDF p.7; main.py, lines 373–388 and 521–543
claim: Section 4.3 specifies classifier optimization. The classifier branch calls backward, but the only optimizer step in the surrounding loop is inside the diffusion branch.
analysis: For \(L(w)=w^2/2\) at \(w=1\), backward creates gradient \(1\) but leaves the parameter unchanged; SGD at rate \(0.1\) would give \(0.9\). The diffusion optimizer owns different parameters and cannot substitute. Batch-normalization buffers may still change.
result: The public classifier branch omits parameter optimization, not every possible change in its function.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

paragraphs: Use a persistent classifier optimizer, matching scheduler and explicit intended trainable parameter set; clear gradients, backpropagate and step in that phase.

problems.title: Guidance is bypassed and its dormant derivative is incomplete
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, Eq.(3), PDF p.5; Algorithm 2, PDF p.15; main.py, lines 278–321
claim: The reverse function sets `guide` false internally; its dormant routine returns a normalized residual without the clean-estimator Jacobian and ignores its locally zeroed cutoff scale.
analysis: With \(A_t=1/4\), denoiser \(\epsilon(x)=2x/\sqrt3\) and reference \(1\), the clean estimate is \(2x-\sqrt3\epsilon(x)=0\). The norm of its difference from the reference is constant, so its derivative is zero. The dormant normalized residual is instead \(-1\). This occurs away from the norm’s nondifferentiable boundary.
result: The release neither applies requested guidance nor computes the stated full derivative if merely enabled.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Honor the guidance flag and cutoff, and differentiate through the declared clean-image estimator, or explicitly specify and evaluate a different approximation.

problems.title: The custom sampler doubles variance and mismatches time indices
problems.source_location: Eq.(2), PDF p.3; Algorithm 2, PDF p.15; main.py, lines 259–274, 318–319 and 596
claim: The custom reverse step combines a deterministic direction with an unreduced additional noise variance; its loop skips ten indices while the step uses the immediate preceding index.
analysis: For a point-mass clean distribution and exact denoiser with \(A_t=0.64\), \(A_s=0.81\), the step gives \(x_s=\sqrt{0.19}\epsilon+\sqrt{0.19}z\) for independent standard normals, hence variance \(0.38\) instead of \(0.19\). A loop at times \((30,20,10,0)\) first transitions using index \(29\), then treats that output as time \(20\). The final \(T=5\) setting never reaches a clean endpoint under that stride.
result: The released kernel and time sequence are inconsistent. No full image-quality effect is measured.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Choose an actual destination \(s<t\) and a consistent DDIM variance, direction and endpoint convention. For example, use \(\sigma^2=\eta^2(1-A_s)(1-A_t/A_s)/(1-A_t)\) and direction variance \(1-A_s-\sigma^2\).
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The target round trip selects the target model twice
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, Eqs.(5),(7), PDF p.6; main.py, lines 499–507
claim: The claimed target-to-source-to-target cycle needs source reverse dynamics followed by target reverse dynamics; the target branch passes `model_T` to both calls.
analysis: Even deterministic inverse maps show the consequence: with \(D_S(x)=2x\), \(D_T(x)=x/2\), the intended composition sends \(1\) to \(1\); the selected double-target composition sends it to \(1/4\). The source arguments establish the selector error independently of this illustration.

assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

paragraphs: Pass the source model to the first target-cycle reverse call and the target model to reconstruction. Reconcile guidance, sampling and optimization separately.

problems.title: Positive regularization does not remove rank-cutoff ties
problems.source_location: Introduction, PDF p.2, first contribution bullet; Proposition 1 and Theorem 1
claim: The introduction claims a unique regularized rank-constrained solution for every calibration matrix \(X\).
analysis: For \(W=X=I_2\), rank budget \(1\) and \(\mu=1/2\), the objective is \(3\|I_2-W^\prime\|_F^2/2\). Both \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) and \(\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\), and every rank-one orthogonal projector, attain global minimum \(3/2\). The discarded singular-value bound proves optimality. Positive definite weighting does not make the rank-constrained feasible set convex.
result: The universal introductory statement is too strong. The gap-conditioned theorem and Proposition 1’s allowance of multiple solutions are explicit countercontrols.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: After the invertible rank-preserving change \(Y=W^\prime(XX^\top+\mu I)^{1/2}\), apply ordinary truncated SVD. At a nontrivial cutoff, uniqueness requires a strict gap in the weighted matrix’s singular values.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The QR helper compares feature count with the wrong factor dimension
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1, PDF p.4; released lib/TSQR.py, qr_one_device, lines 38–77
claim: `lib/TSQR.py`, `qr_one_device`, compares a new block’s feature-row count with the intermediate reduced QR factor’s row count.
analysis: A full-row-rank \(4\)-by-\(5\) matrix may be split into \(4\)-by-\(2\) and \(4\)-by-\(3\) blocks. Reduced QR of the first transpose gives \(R_0\) of size \(2\)-by-\(4\). Comparing the next feature count \(4\) with its row count \(2\) rejects valid common-feature blocks. Stacking \(R_0\) with the next transpose is dimensionally valid.
result: The public helper rejects a valid streamed partition. A square-first-block control and a separate concatenation path can avoid it.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Compare against the factor’s column count or the saved feature count. The update then preserves \(R^\top R=\sum_iX_iX_i^\top\), including short initial blocks.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Cache insertion order does not preserve task identity
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, PDF p.6; Algorithm 1, PDF p.25; modeling_llama_lsh.py, lines 120–171 and 1522–1535
claim: The matching loop is cache-first, while deletion and sequential reinsertion use current-batch indices. Neither sorted current indices nor unique current targets are enforced.
analysis: Matches \((0,1),(1,0)\) delete the first two current rows, leaving value \(12\). Insert cache value \(100\) at row \(1\), then \(101\) at row \(0\): output is \([101,12,100]\), while task-specific assignment requires \([101,100,12]\). Zero attention logits and constant row values transfer the same mismatch to the attention output. Single or correctly ordered matches can pass.
result: The released assembly can associate a task with another task’s values. Historical incidence is unknown.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Choose at most one cache entry per current task under a declared tie rule, then assign each final row by its original task index rather than insertion order.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Already rotated keys receive another rotary transform
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, PDF p.6; modeling_llama_lsh.py, lines 153–171, 753–782 and 2172–2197
claim: The traced producer stores post-RoPE keys; the consumer inserts those keys before applying RoPE to the assembled tensor.
analysis: At position \(p=1\), raw key \((1,0)\) is stored as \((\cos1,\sin1)\). Equal-position reuse should retain it, but the consumer returns \((\cos2,\sin2)\). A correspondingly rotated query changes its dot product from \(1\) to \(\cos1\). Position zero is a passing special case.
result: The producer/consumer representation contracts disagree. An unrotated-cache convention is a different contract.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Insert post-RoPE caches after rotating new keys. To move a cached key from position \(p\) to \(q\), apply \(R_qR_p^\top\) with trustworthy positional metadata.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: A fresh target-layer cache is appended to itself
problems.source_location: forward_predict_prompt, modeling_llama_lsh.py, lines 2172 and 2239–2254
claim: `forward_predict_prompt` overwrites the incoming-cache variable with the current output, then concatenates its target layer with the same output layer.
analysis: With no incoming past and a three-token prompt, both operands are \((K,V)\). The target cache becomes \(([K;K],[V;V])\); a three-layer layout has lengths \((3,6,3)\) instead of \((3,3,3)\). The duplication occurs after initial hidden states are computed.
result: The returned generation cache is wrong for this fresh-prompt case. Nonempty-prefix behavior requires a separate accumulated-cache contract.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep the incoming cache under a distinct name and return the fresh target cache once. Append a prefix only where the documented backend returns new segments rather than already accumulated states.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Reference bits do not implement exact LRU
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, PDF p.6; Appendix B.1, PDF p.23; Algorithm 1, PDF p.25; source lines 1544–1547 and 2214–2234
claim: The branch labeled LRU stores a reference bit and clears leading set bits rather than recording chronological recency.
analysis: For slots \([A,B,C]\), access order \(B,C,A\) leaves bits \((1,1,1)\). The code clears them and replaces slot zero, evicting most-recent \(A\); true LRU evicts \(B\). The same bit vector represents several different recency orders.

assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

paragraphs: Specify the reference-bit approximation, or maintain timestamps/an ordered recency structure and evict the actual oldest access under a deterministic batch convention.

problems.title: Unequal prompt lengths fail the tokenwise matcher
problems.source_location: Public repository issue #1; modeling_llama_lsh.py, lines 1522–1535
claim: The matcher directly compares tokenwise cached and current embeddings without a common-length alignment contract.
analysis: Nonzero shapes \((1,2,2)\) and \((1,3,2)\) cannot broadcast across token dimensions \(2\) and \(3\). Equal padded widths avoid this failure, as in fixed-width settings, but do not solve general K/V alignment. Repository issue #1, opened 30 April 2026, already reported the concern.

assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

problems.title: New generation modules are not initialized as parameter copies
problems.source_location: Figure 2 and Section 3.2, PDF p.4; Appendix A, PDF p.17; submitted constructor and train_fsdp.py
claim: Figure 2, Section 3.2 and Appendix A specify copies of pretrained attention, MLP and normalization parameters. The constructor instead creates new modules after loading the base model.
analysis: `add_vision_attention` creates new linear projections; analogous MLP/norm methods create new state, while copy operations appear only in comments. A loaded four-dimensional query projection with every weight \(2\) and bias \(1\) maps the first basis vector to \((3,3,3,3)\); a newly initialized projection does not read those values. The fresh training path has no intervening copy pass. Inference and resumed training can separately load learned generation weights, which is a critical countercontrol.
result: The fresh recipe does not implement the stated copy initialization. It does not show that inference uses random generation weights or that original checkpoints began incorrectly.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Create independent copies of the intended loaded modules before optimizer creation, preserving equal initial values and distinct storage. Do not overwrite an explicitly loaded trained generation checkpoint with a fresh copy.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Averaging tensors is not sampling a temporal mixture
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF p.6, Eqs.(13)–(16); Appendix B, Algorithm 1, PDF p.21
claim: Equation (16) uses \(\tilde X=\sum_t\alpha_tX^{(t)}\), whereas Algorithm 1 samples/concatenates activation rows before covariance estimation.
analysis: Let \(X^{(1)}=((1,1),(-1,-1))\) and \(X^{(2)}=-X^{(1)}\). Equal scores give weights \(1/2\). The elementwise average is zero, with zero covariance; the row mixture has covariance \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\). Reversing one timestep’s row order changes the average but leaves the mixture unchanged. KLT–Hadamard equalization of a specified covariance remains valid.
result: The two calibration objects are not equivalent without extra assumptions. Either can be an intentional heuristic if its interpretation is stated.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For a mixture, use mean \(\mu=\sum_t\alpha_t\mu_t\) and covariance \(\sum_t\alpha_t[C_t+(\mu_t-\mu)(\mu_t-\mu)^\top]\). Otherwise align the pseudocode and claims with the synthetic tensor average.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: Signed maxima change the score and unshifted exponentials can overflow
problems.source_location: Eq.(13), PDF p.6; current dit/ptq_inference.py, get_incoherence_norm; analogous author PixArt/Open-Sora routines
claim: Equation (13) uses the largest absolute entry. Released `get_incoherence_norm` instead uses the signed maximum and directly exponentiates scores.
analysis: Rows \((-10,1)\) and \((10,-1)\) have equal required scores and weights \((1/2,1/2)\). Signed maxima give approximately \((0.14072,1.40720)\) and weights \((0.21986,0.78014)\). A finite \(505521\)-element tensor with one unit entry has score \(711\), whose direct exponential exceeds finite double range even though a single-timestep normalized weight is exactly \(1\).
result: The release differs from the stated sign-invariant score and has a defined-input numerical boundary. Real activation incidence is unknown.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use maximum absolute entry, require nonzero finite norm, and subtract the maximum finite logit before exponentiation or use a stable softmax.

problems.title: GPTQ calibration uses a different basis from inference

problems.title: A single-draw quantile does not bound a fixed maximum
problems.source_location: Introduction, PDF p.3; Section 2.1, PDF p.4, paragraph after Problem 1

analysis: Use query \((1,0)\), ninety-nine points \((0,j)\), \(1\leq j\leq99\), and one point \((100,0)\). Mean score is \(1\), variance \(99\), and maximum \(100\). At \(\delta=0.8\), threshold \(1\) already covers \(0.99\) of one-draw scores, above the required \(0.9\), yet the fixed maximum is still \(100\). Even \(1+3\sqrt{99}\) is below that maximum without violating the one-draw lemma.

problems.title: Two-sided sketch error does not preserve one-sided coverage
problems.source_location: Section 2.3, PDF pp.5–6; Definition 1, Eq.(8), Lemma 2 and Algorithm 1
claim: The router substitutes a masked covariance sketch into the exact-covariance quantile score. Lemma 2 controls approximation error, not covariance domination.
analysis: Take orthonormal vectors \(u=(1,1,0,0)/\sqrt2\), \(q=(0,0,1,1)/\sqrt2\), \(r=(1,-1,0,0)/\sqrt2\), \(s=(0,0,1,-1)/\sqrt2\). For each group \((n,a)=(7,\sqrt{18/5})\) or \((18,-7/\sqrt{90})\), set \(\theta_j=2\pi j/n\), \(0\leq j<n\), and \[x_{n,j}=a q+\sqrt{18/5}\cos\theta_j\,u+\sqrt{2/5}\sin\theta_j\,r+\sqrt{6/5}\cos(2\theta_j)\,s.\] Finite trigonometric sums give mean zero and covariance with diagonal ones and correlation blocks \(4/5\), \(2/5\). Its eigenvalues along \(u,q,r,s\) are \(9/5,7/5,1/5,3/5\). The rank-one masked sketch is \(I+(4/5)uu^\top\), so query variance is \(1\) instead of \(7/5\). At \(\delta=1/2\), threshold \(\sqrt3\) lies below the seven positive scores \(\sqrt{18/5}\), covering only \(18/25=0.72<0.75\). Exact threshold \(\sqrt{21/5}\) covers all points. The sketch’s spectral error still satisfies Lemma 2; two-sided approximation does not imply covariance domination.
result: The exact quantile guarantee cannot be inherited automatically. No separately stated universal sketch-coverage theorem or benchmark recall is refuted.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Inflate the quadratic form by \(D_{\max}\max(\lambda_{t+1},0)\|q\|^2\), where \(\lambda_{t+1}\) is the largest discarded normalized residual eigenvalue. This upper-bounds omitted positive variance and restores the one-draw guarantee under the original lemma’s assumptions.

analysis: Unit points \((-1/2,\pm\sqrt3/2)\) have centroid \((-1/2,0)\). Query \((1,0)\) gives score \(-1/2\), which becomes \(-1\) after centroid normalization. Division by a norm below one raises a nonnegative score but lowers a negative one.

assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

problems.title: A nonzero Dirac posterior has no finite ordinary ELBO here
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, Eqs.(5)–(7), PDF pp.4–5; Section 4.3, Eqs.(11)–(14), PDF pp.6–7
claim: Section 4.3 explicitly replaces distributional sampling by deterministic point estimation and formalizes \(q_z=\delta_{f_\Phi(x)}\) in Eq.(13). Nevertheless, p.7 still calls the primary objective the ELBO before adding auxiliary regularizers. The preceding prior is a spike at zero plus a continuous Gaussian slab.
analysis: For \(a=f_\Phi(x)\ne0\), posterior probability of \(\{a\}\) is \(1\), but prior probability is \(0\). Absolute continuity fails, hence \(D_{\rm KL}(\delta_a\Vert P)=+\infty\). With finite expected log likelihood, the ordinary ELBO is negative infinity. Adding a gate cannot repair a singular marginal. Separately, a literal variable-dependent mixture weight in Eq.(12) need not normalize: in the centered Gaussian case, \(\Omega(z)>\Omega(0)\) almost surely, giving mass greater than one. A fixed-point-prediction interpretation can resolve that notation, but not the exact Dirac KL.
result: The deterministic stage is not the same finite ordinary ELBO. Earlier positive-variance variational inference and deterministic point estimation remain legitimate distinct formulations.
assumptions: The Gaussian prior slab is nondegenerate, its only atom is zero, and the deterministic coefficient is nonzero.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep a genuine positive-variance spike-and-slab variational law during training, or explicitly formulate the deterministic loss as a different penalized point-estimation surrogate.

problems.title: The exploration loss has an escape direction to negative infinity
problems.source_location: Appendix B, PDF p.24, Eqs.(30)–(32); Eq.(14), PDF p.7

analysis: Hold a finite batch and coefficient network fixed and set \(\psi_1=\psi_2=t\to\infty\). Nonnegative uncertainties give thresholds \(t(1+tU)\geq t\); bounded coefficients are gated to zero, and prediction loss approaches the finite base-model loss. Boundary and uncertainty terms stay bounded, while \(L_e=-2\log t+o(1)\to-\infty\). Positivity of the parameters does not prevent this path. The supplemental module does not implement this logarithmic objective.

problems.source_location: Theorem 3.1, Eq.(5), PDF pp.4–5; Appendix A.1, PDF pp.24–25, Eqs.(19)–(31)
claim: Theorem 3.1 claims \(P(\hat y_2\mid c)>\delta/(D_{\rm seq}+\epsilon)\) under its coherence and semantic-class assumptions.

problems.title: The skip contribution breaks the common-latent lower bound
problems.source_location: Eqs.(2)–(5), PDF p.4; Section 3.3 and footnote 2, PDF p.5; Implication paragraph, PDF p.6; Appendix D, PDF p.38
claim: Section 3.2 introduces Eq.(4) as a variational IB lower bound and Eq.(5) as its empirical estimate. The implemented likelihood receives \(\hat Z=(1-\alpha)c(X)+\alpha\tilde Z\), while the KL regularizes unmixed \(\tilde Z\). Footnote 2 and Appendix D explicitly acknowledge the different laws, yet the p.6 Implication paragraph still says that Vittle maximizes the variational IB lower bound.
analysis: Let \(X=\pm2\) equally, label \(Y\) constant, \(c(X)=X\), and \(\tilde Z\mid X\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) matching its prior independently of \(X\). At \(\alpha=1/2\), the mixed objective is zero for a decoder assigning the sole label probability one. Yet \(\hat Z\mid X=\pm2\sim\mathcal N(\pm1,1/4)\), so \(I(X;\hat Z)>0\), while \(I(Y;\hat Z)=0\). The actual information-bottleneck value is \(-\beta I(X;\hat Z)<0\), so zero is above rather than below it. A finite-softmax likelihood arbitrarily close to zero preserves the strict contradiction.
result: The stated auxiliary-KL objective is not a general lower bound for the representation actually decoded. A useful auxiliary regularizer remains a different interpretation.
assumptions: The posterior Gaussian has positive variance, the prior is input-independent, and the decoder actually receives the interpolated representation.

problems.source_location: Proposition 3.2 and interpretation after Eq.(7), PDF p.6; Appendix E.2, PDF pp.39–41

Let latents be domain-identical and input-independent, and model output a fair independent label. Conditional independence holds; all retained latent-divergence and marginal entropy-gap terms are zero. True mutual information changes from zero to \(\log2\), so EMID is \(\log2\). The residual is \(2\log2\); retaining it leaves the full proposition uncontradicted. Lowering model entropy can also enlarge an absolute gap to a fixed fair-target entropy.

assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

problems.title: Pointed-node WL can separate after the individual-size cutoff
problems.source_location: Current arXiv v2 Section 2, PDF p.3, WL cutoff and following all-depth classifier implication; Krebs and Verbitsky, universal-cover lower-bound family
claim: Section 2 defines indistinguishability after \(\max(|G|,|H|)\) rounds and then asserts indistinguishability by every permitted depth classifier.
analysis: Krebs and Verbitsky’s known family with parameters \(s=7,t=3\) gives two connected simple graphs, each with \((t+1)(s+10)-5=63\) vertices, maximum degree three and degree-one roots. Their rooted views agree through depth \(2[t(s+5)-1]=70\) and separate at \(71\). Joint exact color refinement has the same equality/separation. Thus the printed cutoff \(63\) passes a pair that an allowed depth-\(71\) classifier separates. This is a pointed-node result, not a claim about equal whole-graph color histograms.
result: The short cutoff is inconsistent with the following all-depth implication. The relation defined by the entire classifier family and the main hierarchy are not refuted.
assumptions: Initial labels agree and one injective shared color encoding is used across both graphs; the conclusion concerns pointed nodes.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Define equality at every depth, or refine the disjoint union to partition stability. A safe fixed cutoff is \(|G|+|H|-1\), since a partition can strictly split at most that many times.
An explicit local correction is described; author adoption and a corresponding published erratum are not established.

problems.title: The multiset formula does not exclude absent neighbor types
problems.source_location: Current arXiv v2 Proposition 2.4, PDF p.4; Appendix A, PDF p.16, induction formula for a target neighbor multiset
claim: Appendix A fixes multiplicities only for types appearing in a target multiset \(Z\). For empty \(Z\), its count conjunction is empty.
analysis: Take a single edge with both vertices labeled \(p\), initial scalar embeddings \(1\), degree bound \(1\), and one-layer sum aggregation with combination equal to the aggregate. Output zero is attainable at an isolated \(p\) vertex. The printed zero-output disjunct for \(Z=\varnothing\) reduces to \(p\), so it incorrectly accepts the edge endpoint, whose actual output is \(1\).
result: The translation formula is incomplete. Proposition 2.4’s existence statement is not disproved.
assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Add total degree at most \(|Z|\), or include zero counts for all other finite previous-layer types. Positive count classes already exhaust \(|Z|\) neighbors, so the added condition excludes every extra type.

problems.title: The proposed decomposition misses inter-fibre connections
problems.source_location: Current arXiv v2 Proposition 5.7(1), PDF p.8; proof, PDF pp.25–26
claim: Proposition 5.7’s proof joins each equal-parent edge bag only to its endpoint vertex bags and calls the resulting structure a tree decomposition.
analysis: For triangle \(a,b,c\), let \(\operatorname{dep}(a)=\bot\), \(\operatorname{dep}(b)=\operatorname{dep}(c)=a\). The admissible rank-one map gives bags \[\{a\},\{a,b\},\{a,c\},\{a,b,c\}\]. The listed edges connect the latter three in a path but isolate \(\{a\}\); bags containing \(a\) are disconnected. The triangle still has treewidth \(2\), satisfying the stated inequality.

assumptions: Only the cited paper version and explicitly described mathematical or implementation conditions are assessed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Connect a representative bag from each nonroot parent-fibre component to its parent bag; connect root components in a tree. Well-founded parent levels prevent cycles and no bag enlarges. In the triangle, one link to the isolated parent bag suffices.

problems.title: Soluble-expression measurements do not uniquely identify improved thermodynamic stability
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, PDF p. 9 (training stability); Section 3.1, PDF p. 6 (assay scope).
claim: Paraphrase: Section 4.2, p. 9, first uses ESMFold/PyRosetta analyses to evaluate predicted stability. It then measures the two lowest-perplexity generations from pretrained and stability-aligned ProGen3-46B for each of \(32\) prompts with split-GFP. The paper reports higher expression for \(8\) prompts, lower expression for \(3\), and no significant difference for \(21\), and concludes that alignment’s improvement in the stability of generated sequences is verified computationally and experimentally.

Section 3.1, p. 6, gives the necessary qualification: this assay measures soluble protein abundance and can depend on mRNA abundance/stability, translation, folding equilibrium, kinetic stability, degradation, aggregation, and toxicity. Appendix D, pp. 24–30, describes the expression assay and SDS-PAGE checks.
analysis: An expression readout can increase with translation or total abundance while folding free energy stays fixed. The source itself lists these confounders. Thus the final experimental stability inference is not identified by split-GFP alone; measured expression changes remain interpretable.
result: Supported inference-scope qualification, not a demonstrated error in the fluorescence data.

paragraphs: The proposed clarification recommends describing improved soluble expression and requiring direct thermodynamic measurements for a stronger stability conclusion.

problems.title: The released all-experts MoE branch has both a rank mismatch and an expert-order mismatch
problems.source_location: Appendix B.1, Eq. (2), PDF p. 20; released moe.py eager-routing implementation.
claim: Appendix B.1, Eq. (2), p. 20, defines a routed weighted sum of expert outputs. The paper normally activates two of eight experts and uses Megablocks for training.

The released implementation additionally defines an eager SparseMoeBlock in src/progen3/model/moe.py. Its forward method accepts hidden states of shape \((B,S,D)\). Lines 99–105 implement the branch where the number of experts equals the number selected per token. ProGen3Config explicitly allows this configuration: it clamps the selected count to the expert count and only requires both to be positive. The problematic source occurs identically in the official conference supplement and the pinned public repository.
analysis: For hidden states of shape \((B,S,D)\), stacking \(E\) expert outputs yields shape \((B,S,D,E)\), but the released einsum declares only three axes for that operand. A second independent mismatch remains after flattening: top-k probabilities are in score order, whereas expert outputs are stacked in expert-index order. Those weights cannot be paired by position without restoring the index correspondence.
result: The explicit all-experts eager branch violates its tensor/routing contract; the paper’s standard top-two Megablocks configuration does not enter that branch.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Flatten token dimensions consistently and restore expert-index correspondence before the weighted sum. This proposal concerns the all-experts eager branch; it does not test the paper's usual top-two Megablocks configuration.

problems.title: Reference-sequence perplexity does not determine total cluster generation mass
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, PDF p. 6 (cluster natural perplexity).
claim: Paraphrase: Section 3.1, p. 6, uses the average perplexity of natural proteins in clusters to assess whether additional sampling from a smaller model could recover clusters generated by a larger model. High perplexity of the reference naturals is interpreted as low probability of generating a member of that cluster, motivating an out-of-distribution interpretation.
The directly observed finite-sample cluster coverage is distinct from this inference about possible additional sampling.
analysis: Consider one natural reference in a cluster and one additional cluster member, with all sequences equally long. Model \(A\) assigns probabilities \((0.01,0.40)\), model \(B\) assigns \((0.02,0)\), and each assigns its remaining probability outside the cluster. The reference has lower perplexity under \(B\), but total cluster mass is \(0.02\) under \(B\) versus \(0.41\) under \(A\). Reference likelihood therefore cannot determine cluster sampling mass.
result: Supported qualification of the likelihood-to-coverage implication; observed generated-cluster coverage is not refuted.

problems.title: Reduced claims are recorded but are not supplied to the perturbation generator
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, PDF pp. 5–6; Algorithm 1, PDF p. 47.

The same released pathway also calls save_file_jsonl with a path before its records, whereas the author helper declares data before path. This adjacent persistence mismatch blocks that route when reached; it does not establish which program produced the paper’s training dataset.

problems.title: Batched likelihood scoring uses logits after the target token and can reverse the preference label
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, PDF p. 6; Algorithm 1, lines 19–24, PDF p. 47.
claim: Section 4.2, p. 6, and Algorithm 1 lines 19–24, p. 47, choose preferences using
\[ \Delta=\ell_{\mathrm{orig}}-\ell_{\mathrm{perturb}}, \qquad z=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\Delta), \]
analysis: In a causal language model the logit at position \(t-1\) predicts token \(t\). For prompt \((1,2)\), original response \((3,4,5)\), and perturbed response \((5,5,5)\), take a vocabulary of size \(12\) and logits \(6\) for the successor of the current token and \(0\) elsewhere. Correct alignment gives \(\ell_{\rm orig}=-0.0269011709\), \(\ell_{\rm perturb}=-6.0269011709\), and \(z=\sigma(6)\approx0.997527\). The current batched code includes the final post-target logit and takes its last three positions, giving both averages \(-6.0269011709\) and \(z=0.5\). The strict test \(z>\tau\) therefore selects different preferences at \(\tau=0.5\). Padding introduces an additional endpoint problem; the correctly shifted single-example source is an unaffected control.
result: The one-position causal shift can reverse the selection statistic, but the score pathway used for the published trained models is not established.

paragraphs: The proposed correction aligns each response token with its preceding-position logit and excludes padding.

problems.title: Forward support indices do not establish reverse coverage of the original claims
problems.source_location: Section 2.3, PDF p. 4; Appendix B.2.2, PDF p. 31.
claim: Section 2.3, p. 4, defines precision and recall through semantic equivalence, with recall applying support to an input claim against the generated claim set. Appendix B.2.2, p. 31, similarly counts unique input claims actually present in the response. This is a coverage requirement.

The operational prompt, however, asks whether an output claim is supported by one or more input claims; it does not require equivalence or ask whether the supporting input claim is fully recovered. The released claim_verifier.py, lines 27–34, implements that forward direction. Then metrics.py, lines 21–24, computes recall by counting distinct indices returned as forward support.
analysis: The input statement ‘exactly two votes’ supports the output ‘at least one vote’, but the output does not recover the input. Returning input index \(1\) as forward support and counting distinct such indices gives recall \(1\), even though reverse entailment fails. Forward support and input coverage require separate decisions.
result: Forward entailment indices do not certify full input recovery; the witness exposes a metric capability without measuring its occurrence in benchmark outputs.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The proposed clarification separates output support from reverse input-coverage judgments.

problems.title: Malformed judge responses can be scored as support, and empty outputs acquire invented unsupported counts
problems.source_location: Appendix B.2, PDF pp. 30–31; released claim_verifier.py, lines 61–66, and empty-output/index handling in the metrics.

It does not require the supported label, a valid index list, or an index within the input range. The metric code counts unique indices without range validation.

problems.title: A failure of perfect full-PIC F1 is not necessarily an unsupported-content hallucination
problems.source_location: Abstract and introduction, PDF pp. 1–2; task-evaluation definition, PDF p. 4.
claim: The abstract, p. 1, introduces faithfulness hallucination in terms of generated information not substantiated by the input. The introduction on the same page explicitly includes omissions, distortions, and fabrications in its broader usage of hallucination. The introduction, p. 2, and task evaluation, p. 4, relate a less-than-\(30\%\) perfect full-PIC F1 rate to a greater-than-\(70\%\) hallucination statement. Under the explicitly broader convention, an omission can coherently count as a hallucination. The issue below concerns reading that headline as a measured rate of unsupported generated content under the abstract’s narrower description. It is a terminological and inference-scope clarification, not a newly measured hallucination-rate correction.
analysis: For input \(\{A,B\}\) and output \(\{A\}\), precision is \(1\), recall is \(1/2\), and \(F_1=2/3\), despite no unsupported assertion. This limits a narrow unsupported-content interpretation of the headline. The introduction explicitly includes omissions in its definition, so the example does not contradict the authors' broader convention.
result: Terminology/scope clarification only; no new numerical benchmark error is established.

problems.title: The \(0.75\) lower constant in Lemma 4.5 fails inside the stated initialization set
problems.source_location: Lemma 4.5, PDF p. 7; proof in Appendix E.4, PDF p. 25.
claim: Lemma 4.5, PDF p. 7 and Appendix E.4, PDF p. 25, claims \(0.75L_2\le\widehat L\le3.3L_2\) for every stated initialization before \(T_4=\min\{t\ge0:b_2(t)\ge0.5\sqrt{\lambda_1\eta/2}\}\). Here \(L_2=(\lambda_2/2)(1-ab_2)^2\). To exclude a transcription-scale explanation, use the favorable intended surrogate \(\widehat L_c=(\lambda_2/2)(1-Ab_2)^2\), with \(A=\sqrt{2/(\lambda_1\eta)}\). The lower comparison still fails.
analysis: Set \(\lambda_1=100\), \(\lambda_2=1/100\), \(\eta=1/10\), and \((a,b_1,b_2)=(1/3,3/2000,11/10)\). These values satisfy the stated initialization and pre-stopping conditions. Even using the favorable intended normalization of the surrogate, direct substitution at \(t=0\) gives losses \(0.00129065045\) and \(0.00200555556\), whose ratio is \(0.64353762<0.75\). The lemma's lower bound therefore fails without relying on the omitted scale factor.
result: Lemma 4.5's stated universal lower comparison is false on its claimed domain. This invalidates that quantitative component of the analysis; it does not demonstrate failure of the observed training phenomenon.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For \(r=Ab_2\le1/2\) and \(u=a/A\in[\sqrt{0.55},\sqrt{2.1}]\), the ratio \(((1-r)/(1-ur))^2\) lies between \(0.631504254974859\) and \(3.295443406779994\). Thus replace the lower constant on this pre-threshold domain; the stronger upper bound \(1\) survives when \(a\le A\). The first discrete crossing may overshoot and needs separate treatment.
The specified local mathematical proposal is retained; no current author correction or adoption is established.

problems.title: The symmetric three-feature restriction is not the claimed Euclidean gradient-descent reduction
problems.source_location: Appendix C, PDF pp. 14–15 (symmetric reduction).
claim: Paraphrase: Appendix C, PDF pp. 14–15, adds an independent relevant feature \(x_3\) having the same variance as \(x_2\), sets the target to \(x_2+x_3\), and considers symmetric initialization \(b_2=b_3\). After substituting this equality, it identifies the resulting loss with the original model after replacing \(\lambda_2\) by \(2\lambda_2\), and asserts equivalent gradient-descent dynamics.
The equality of restricted loss values is correct. The equivalence of Euclidean gradient updates in the chosen common coordinate is not.
analysis: For a symmetric loss \(F(b_2,b_3)\), the tied loss \(g(b)=F(b,b)\) has derivative \(g'(b)=\partial_2F+\partial_3F=2\partial_2F\). The original symmetric Euclidean update uses \(b^+=b-\eta\partial_2F\), whereas unadjusted gradient descent on \(g\) uses twice that change. Equal restricted loss values therefore do not imply the claimed equal-learning-rate dynamics.
result: The asserted Euclidean-GD equivalence for the higher-dimensional extension fails; equality of restricted loss values and preservation of symmetry remain valid.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The tied-coordinate embedding induces metric \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1,2)\). Use the reduced update \(\theta^+=\theta-\eta\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1/2)\nabla F\), or an orthonormal sum coordinate with target amplitude \(\sqrt2\), before transferring the theorem.
The specified local mathematical proposal is retained; no current author correction or adoption is established.

problems.title: The sharpness proof substitutes a Gauss–Newton quadratic form for the full Hessian
problems.source_location: Theorem 4.1; proof in Appendix E.2, PDF p. 22.

Write the squared-residual model as \(L= rac12\sum_i\lambda_i r_i^2\). Then \(

abla^2r_i)\). The displayed quadratic form keeps only the first term. For bilinear residuals, \(

For the stated loss, the missing matrix has off-diagonal entries \(R_{12}=\lambda_1ab_1\) and \(R_{13}=\lambda_2(ab_2-1)\), with symmetric counterparts. At \[(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,a,b_1,b_2)=(100,0.01,0.5,0.005,0.6)\], the full-Hessian largest eigenvalue is approximately \(25.00999844\), whereas the printed Gauss–Newton form gives \(25.00250036\). problems.title: Decreasing bounds on gradient-flow-solution sharpness do not imply stepwise monotonicity
problems.source_location: Introduction, PDF p. 2; Section 5.1 and Theorem 5.2, PDF pp. 8–9.
claim: The discussion on PDF p. 2 and Section 5.1, PDF pp. 8–9, presents the result as a decrease of gradient-flow-solution (GFS) sharpness along gradient descent. The precise Theorem 5.2 encloses this sharpness between functions that decrease as \(b_2\) increases. The text also uses a near-monotonic description. This analysis does not assert that Theorem 5.2’s displayed enclosing bounds are false. It checks whether the stronger interpretation, monotonicity of the exact GFS sharpness at every GD step, follows. It does not.
analysis: The gradient-flow invariant is \(\gamma=a^2-b_1^2-b_2^2\). With the model's unit target normalization, zero loss has \(b_1=0\) and \(ab_2=1\), so \(q=a_\infty^2=(\gamma+\sqrt{\gamma^2+4})/2\) determines the limiting state used for GFS sharpness. Decreasing upper and lower envelopes do not imply a decrease of the exact quantity at every discrete gradient-descent step. The near-monotone description and displayed envelopes can remain valid despite a small local increase.

For \(\lambda_1=100\), \(\lambda_2=0.01\), \(\eta=0.1\), and admissible \(\theta_0=(1/3,1/1500,1)\), two projected-GD updates leave projection inactive. The exact invariant difference is \[\gamma_2-\gamma_1=\frac{4884795542280911349753184700897}{12611344042968750000000000000000000000}>0.\] Since \(q\) increases with \(\gamma\) and the \(\lambda_1q\) branch dominates, exact GFS sharpness increases from approximately \(64.98729109\) to \(64.98730259\). This is compatible with decreasing envelopes and near-monotone wording.
result: The stronger stepwise-monotonic interpretation is not implied by the theorem. Its displayed decreasing envelopes and the paper's near-monotone qualification are not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe decreasing envelopes or a near-monotone trend rather than strict all-step monotonicity of exact GFS sharpness.
The specified local mathematical proposal is retained; no current author correction or adoption is established.

problems.title: The unsigned angle score does not by itself identify a convex ear
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Hole Filling, Eq. (8), PDF p. 6.
claim: Section 3.3, Hole filling, PDF p. 6, Eq. (8), specifies the score
\[ A_i=\operatorname{atan2}\!\left( \|d_{i-1\to i}\times d_{i\to i+1}\|_2, -d_{i-1\to i}\cdot d_{i\to i+1}\right). \]
analysis: The counterclockwise polygon with vertices \[(0,0),(10,0),(10,10),(5.5,10),(5,1),(4.5,10),(0,10)\] has a narrow reflex notch. The cross-product norm removes the orientation sign, so a reflex vertex can receive the smallest unsigned angle even though the proposed ear lies outside the polygon. Uniform scaling preserves the counterexample, including for small holes.

At the notch vertex \((5,1)\), incoming and outgoing vectors \((-0.5,-9)\) and \((-0.5,9)\) have signed cross product \(-9\) and negative dot product \(-80.75\). Its unique minimum score is \(\operatorname{atan2}(9,80.75)\approx6.35966^\circ\), while the triangle centroid \((5,7)\) lies in the excluded notch. The written unrestricted selection therefore chooses an exterior triangle. An implicit standard ear-admissibility guard would reject it, so this does not prove a defect in unavailable code.
result: The unrestricted written angle rule fails on a simple planar boundary. Whether the actual hole-filling implementation already applies a valid-ear guard remains unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restrict candidate ears using a planar convexity and interior-admissibility test before ranking their angles. This local proposal does not establish a triangulation guarantee for arbitrary nonplanar boundaries.

problems.title: The stated softmax \(\ell_1\)-Lipschitz constant misses an essential contribution
problems.source_location: Lemma 2, Eq. (12), PDF p. 8; Lemma 4, Eqs. (109)–(110), PDF p. 45.
claim: Paraphrase: Lemma 2, PDF p. 8, Eq. (12), and its expanded Lemma 4, PDF p. 45, Eqs. (109)–(110), state that whenever both vectors have spread at most \(\delta>0\),
\[ \|s(z)\|_\infty\le e^\delta/L, \qquad \|s(z)-s(\bar z)\|_1\le(e^\delta/L)\|z-\bar z\|_1. \]
analysis: Take \(z=(0,0,0)\), \(\bar z=(0.01,0,0)\), and \(\delta=0.01\). Both spreads satisfy the hypothesis. The exact change is \(\|s(z)-s(\bar z)\|_1=4(e^{0.01}-1)/(3(e^{0.01}+2))\approx0.004451827\), but the claimed bound is \((e^{0.01}/3)0.01\approx0.003366834\). The first probability bound remains valid; the Lipschitz inequality does not.

The Jacobian is \(\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top\): column \(j\) contributes \(p_j(1-p_j)\) on the diagonal and the same total off diagonal, so its induced \(\ell_1\) norm is \(\max_j2p_j(1-p_j)\). At uniform probabilities this exceeds \(1/L\) whenever \(L>2\). The earlier cited softmax result contains an analogous problematic constant; no priority claim is made.
result: The stated softmax Lipschitz constant is false, so later stability bounds cannot use that constant without a new derivation. No experimental performance reversal follows from this calculation.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the exact induced Jacobian norm \(\max_j2p_j(1-p_j)\). On a fixed support of size \(n\), \(\min\{1/2,2e^\delta/n\}\) is a safe bound; keep probability and derivative constants distinct and rederive downstream estimates.
The stated local proposal is retained; the current paper or author source still has the identified behavior. No author adoption is established.

problems.title: The heavy-hitter support-change proof drops common-support normalization terms
problems.source_location: Lemma 6, PDF pp. 54–56, especially Eqs. (229)–(230), PDF p. 55.
claim: Lemma 6, PDF pp. 54–56, seeks a Lipschitz comparison of \(s_b(z)\) and \(s_{\bar b}(\bar z)\), with \(b=m(z)\), \(\bar b=m(\bar z)\), \(k\) selected logits, selected spread at most \(\delta\), and gap at least \(\Delta>0\). In Eq. (229), it applies a fixed-mask bound at an intermediate vector. In Eq. (230), PDF p. 55, it bounds the full distance between two differently masked softmaxes by contributions on indices where the masks differ. Both steps need conditions or terms that are absent.
analysis: The endpoint pair \(z=(1,2,0)\) and \(\bar z=(1,0,2)\) has the respective top-two masks in the claim, selected spread \(\delta=1\) and positive gap \(\Delta=1\), so it meets the stated endpoint conditions without a tie.

At \(\bar z=(1,0,2)\), compare masks \((1,1,0)\) and \((1,0,1)\). Their common first coordinate changes because the two normalizers differ. The full \(\ell_1\) distance is \(2e/(e+1)\approx1.462117\), whereas summing only the two changed-support coordinates gives \(1\). Thus Eq. (230) drops a positive contribution even without a support-boundary tie; the separate fixed-mask intermediate step also needs its own domain conditions.

The intermediate fixed-mask step is also unjustified: \(z=(0,0,-10)\) and \(\bar z=(0,-10,0)\) each have own-support spread \(0\) and gap \(10\), but applying the old mask to \(\bar z\) selects logits of spread \(10\). The endpoint assumption \(\delta=0.01\) therefore does not hold at that intermediate vector.
result: The displayed support-change estimate is not a valid proof of the claimed bound. A corrected argument must retain common-support normalization changes.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: On the stated positive-gap domain, the weaker valid constant is \(\max\{C_{k,\delta},1/\Delta\}\), where \(C_{k,\delta}\) is a valid fixed-support constant. Different supports require an input change of at least \(2\Delta\), while probability-vector distance is at most \(2\). This avoids the invalid intermediate steps but does not restore the claimed favorable dependence on \(k\).

problems.title: The multilayer loss bound can be negative because the geometric-series formula lacks its domain condition
problems.source_location: Theorem 2, Eq. (11), PDF p. 8; Corollary 1, Appendix F.3, Eq. (79), PDF p. 42.
claim: Theorem 2, PDF p. 8, Eq. (11), and Corollary 1 in Appendix F.3, PDF p. 42, Eq. (79), give
\[ \lambda_{\mathcal L}=\alpha\left[\Xi+q^\tau\left(1+ \frac{\lambda_\theta}{L(q-1)}\right)\right], \quad q=\lambda_{\mathcal X}. \]
analysis: The hypotheses do not require \(q>1\). On the intended bounded domain, choose dimension and sequence length \(d=L=2\), depth \(\tau=1\), bounds \(B=\Xi=1\), and LayerNorm scale \((0.6,0.6)\), shift zero, and \(\epsilon=1\). Valid conservative attention constants \((\lambda_X,\lambda_W,\lambda_V)=(0.01,0.02,2)\) give the paper's block constants \(q=0.7272\) and \(\lambda_\theta=3.8544\). With \(\alpha=1\), its loss constant is \(1+0.7272[1+3.8544/(2(0.7272-1))]\approx-3.410116\).

For an actual positive difference, take zero attention/feed-forward weights and input tokens \((0.5,-0.5)\). Two LayerNorm applications give \[(0.1554963166,-0.1554963166)\]. Comparing readouts \((1,0)\) and \((0,0)\) with sample loss \(|f|\) yields loss difference \(0.1554963166>0\), despite the negative claimed upper bound. All outputs and readout norms stay within the stated unit bounds.
result: The unrestricted geometric-series simplification is false on an admissible bounded domain. It is undefined at q equal to one and can be negative below one; this does not imply the experiments used that regime.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the nonnegative finite sum \(\alpha[\Xi+q^\tau+(\lambda_\theta/L)\sum_{j=0}^{\tau-1}q^j]\). The sum is \((q^\tau-1)/(q-1)\) for \(q\ne1\) and \(\tau\) at \(q=1\). Alternatively impose \(q>1\) for the looser printed bound. This repairs only the composition step; its attention constants still require justification.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.
The stated local proposal is retained; the current paper or author source still has the identified behavior. No author adoption is established.

problems.title: Released attention applies dropout during evaluation
problems.source_location: Appendix D, PDF p. 29; released multihead_attention.py, scaled_dot_prod.
claim: Appendix D, PDF p. 29, specifies dropout probability \(0.01\). In released multihead_attention.py, scaled_dot_prod calls functional dropout with the supplied dropout_p and the default active training mode. MultiHeadAttention.forward supplies the same positive probability in evaluation mode.

problems.title: ListOps skips one example and divides evaluation totals by the full dataset size
problems.source_location: Appendix D (ListOps implementation); released ListOps training and evaluation denominator calculations.

problems.title: The loss-landscape code does not compute the direction-normalized estimator in Eq. (306)
problems.source_location: Figure 5, PDF p. 10; Appendix G.5, PDF pp. 62–65, especially Eq. (306), PDF p. 63.
claim: Figure 5, PDF p. 10, Appendix G.5, PDF pp. 62–65, and Eq. (306), PDF p. 63, interpret neighboring loss-grid differences as directional estimates of the loss Lipschitz constant. The displayed estimator divides by both the coordinate step \(\epsilon\) and the norm of the perturbation direction:
\[ \frac{|\mathcal L(\Theta+x\vartheta_1+y\vartheta_2) -\mathcal L(\Theta+(x+\epsilon)\vartheta_1+y\vartheta_2)|} {\epsilon\|\vartheta_1\|}, \]
analysis: Let \(\theta=2\), \(L(\theta)=\theta\), direction \(v=2\), and step \(\epsilon=0.005\). The loss change is \(0.01\). Dividing only by \(\epsilon\) gives \(2\), whereas the direction-normalized quotient in Eq. (306) is \(1\). The released quotient changes under direction rescaling, so it is a different estimator.
result: Omitting direction norms changes the measured landscape statistic; the required norms are unavailable for reconstructing corrected published curves, and no performance reversal follows.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For horizontal edges, divide each difference by \(h_x\|\vartheta_1\|\); for vertical edges, divide by \(h_y\|\vartheta_2\|\). Normalize these two sets before pooling their quantiles, because the direction norms can differ. The norms must use the same parameter metric as the theorem being evaluated; with the paper’s tuple norm, this is the maximum spectral norm across matrix parameter blocks, with an explicit convention for vectors and auxiliary learned parameters. Alternatively normalize both complete directions to unit norm in that metric before producing the grid.

problems.title: The feature compensation rescales the target mean instead of restoring it
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, PDF pp. 5–6; released CLIP/inversion/cont_model.py, contrastive_selection.
claim: Section 3.3, PDF pp. 5–6, motivates alignment of synthetic and real features. Released CLIP/inversion/cont_model.py, contrastive_selection, lines 177–188, and the corresponding ResNet compensation around lines 545–556 target a prescribed mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\). For selected mean \(\bar z\) and standard deviation \(s\), they use \(b=\mu-\bar z\), \(a=\sigma/(s+10^{-8})\), and \(z_i^{\rm code}=(z_i+b)a\).
analysis: The mean of that expression is \((\bar z+\mu-\bar z)a=\mu a\), rather than \(\mu\). For selected features \((10,18,26)\), mean \(18\), sample standard deviation \(8\), and targets \(\mu=10\), \(\sigma=4\), the result is approximately \((1,5,9)\), with mean \(5\) and standard deviation \(4\). Centering first and restoring the mean after scaling gives \((6,10,14)\). The stabilizing epsilon changes the approximation slightly but not the mean-restoration defect.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Center the selected sample, rescale its residuals, and add the target mean after scaling. Any reported finite implementation checks are historical; benchmark effects are unmeasured.
