problems.title: The contrastive loss, selection ranking, and temperature explanation use different objectives
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Eq. (6), PDF p. 6; Algorithm 2; Appendix D.3, Eq. (28), PDF p. 21; current CLIP/inversion/cont_model.py, lines 54–79.
claim: Section 3.3, PDF p. 6, Eq. (6), defines the negative contrastive objective as
\[ L_{\rm cont}(x,S)=\log\frac1{|S|}\sum_{y\in S} \exp\{\cos(f(x),f(y))\},\qquad x\notin S. \]

The prose selects by mean cosine similarity, the named equation uses log-mean-exponentiated similarity, and Appendix D.3 argues that temperature does not change rankings. The current selection code uses the former, while its training code includes self-pairs excluded in the equation.
analysis: For selected unit vectors \(e_1,e_2\), choose unit candidates \(A=(0.7,-0.7,\sqrt{0.02})\) and \(B=(0.1,0.1,\sqrt{0.98})\). Their mean cosines are \(0\) and \(0.1\), while their log-mean-exponential scores are \(\log\cosh(0.7/T)\) and \(0.1/T\). The first exceeds the second at \(T=1\), but is smaller for sufficiently large \(T\). Mean cosine, log-mean-exponential and diagonal-inclusive objectives therefore need not induce the same ranking.

At \(T=1\), the log-mean-exponential scores are \(0.2272702294\) for \(A\) and \(0.1\) for \(B\); at \(T=4\), they are \(0.0152349749\) and \(0.025\), reversing the preferred candidate. For two orthogonal unit features, diagonal-excluded loss is \(0\), while the current diagonal-inclusive loss is \(\log((e+1)/2)\approx0.6201145070\). These are distinct objectives, not a universal additive shift.
result: Valid unit-vector examples reverse the stated rankings and expose different self-pair treatment; the method’s empirical benefit is not disproved.

The current contrastive training function additionally constructs Adam, whereas the paper’s contrastive-MLP protocol specifies SGD. This protocol discrepancy is retained without assigning a measured benchmark effect.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either implement log-mean-exp selection with self-exclusion in training and acknowledge temperature-dependent ranking, or explicitly distinguish the existing mean-cosine selection from a self-including training objective. Choosing the intended alternative requires author intent and experimental provenance.
The existing local proposal is retained; no author correction of the cited current formula or release path was identified.

problems.title: A real-data evidence density is not constant under a changing synthetic marginal
problems.source_location: Eq. (3), PDF p. 4; Appendix B, Eq. (19), PDF p. 16; full-model objective Eqs. (5)/(22), PDF pp. 5/17.
claim: Eq. (3), PDF p. 4, and its detailed derivation in Appendix B, Eq. (19), PDF p. 16, use Bayes’ rule to obtain

\[ \begin{aligned} D_{\rm KL}(p_s(o_{l-1}\mid o_l)\Vert p_r(o_{l-1}\mid o_l)) ={}&D_{\rm KL}(p_s(o_{l-1}\mid o_l)\Vert p_r(o_{l-1}))\\ &-\mathbb E_{p_s(o_{l-1}\mid o_l)}\log p_r(o_l\mid o_{l-1}) +\log p_r(o_l). \end{aligned} \]
analysis: An evidence density can be constant with respect to parameters in a frozen-target PMI subproblem yet depend on the synthetic marginal when that distribution changes. Dropping it is justified only for the former optimization. The following two-state construction addresses the latter scope, not every frozen-layer update.

Let one deterministic identity layer act on \(\{0,1\}\), with real marginal \(r=(0.9,0.1)\) and positive synthetic marginal \(q\). The original joint objective is \(D_{\rm KL}(q\Vert r)\), minimized at \(q=r\). The inverse-conditionals are identical point masses, so their prior term \(-\log r_z\) cancels evidence \(+\log r_z\). Dropping the averaged evidence leaves \[\widetilde J(q)=\sum_zq_z\log q_z-2\sum_zq_z\log r_z,\] whose minimizer is \(q_z\propto r_z^2\), namely \[(0.9878048780,0.0121951220)\]. This differs from \(r\) even though the conditional-independence approximation is exact. The later Gaussian surrogate and fixed-target PMI subproblem are not disproved by this discrete diagnostic.
result: Supported derivation-scope qualification; no universal claim that the complete continual-learning method fails is established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For a theoretical joint objective, retain the full averaged evidence term, or explicitly state and enforce a fixed marginal over the targets. Restoring it in this example cancels the spurious cross-entropy contribution and recovers \(D_{\rm KL}(q\Vert r)\), with minimizer \(q=r\). That restoration follows exactly from Bayes’ rule and the displayed calculation.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.
The existing local proposal is retained; no author correction of the cited current formula or release path was identified.

problems.title: Margin change need not order distance to the boundary or susceptibility to the stated attack
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, Eqs. (2)–(5), PDF p. 4; Section 4.2, Eq. (6), PDF p. 5.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 4.1, p. 4, interprets a larger absolute change of margin between a natural input and its adversarial example as indicating that the natural input is harder to attack, hence less vulnerable. This motivates the negative sign in Eq. (2); Eqs. (3)–(5) replace the hard maximum by log-sum-exp. Section 4.2 then favors higher scores through Eq. (6), p. 5.

The paper does not state this interpretation as a theorem with extra restrictions on logit derivatives, local linearity, or identical sensitivity across examples. Its checklist also explicitly says that it does not contain theoretical results. The claim assessed here is therefore the general explanatory interpretation of the score, not a nonexistent formal theorem.
analysis: Use ten logits on \(x\in[0,1]\), with true-class logit \(g(x)=10(x-1/2)-9\operatorname{ReLU}(x-11/20)\) and nine competing logits zero. Both \(x_A=0.51\) and \(x_B=0.90\) are correctly classified. At temperature \(\tau=5\), the soft margin is \(g(x)-\log(9)/5\), so its change equals the change of \(g\). Cross-entropy FGSM with \(\epsilon=8/255\) moves each point left by that budget without clipping. It flips \(A\), whose boundary distance is \(0.01\), while \(B\), at distance \(0.4\), remains robust throughout the allowed interval.

The score gives \(V_A=-16/51\) and \(V_B=-8/255\), and the paper’s two-point sampling formula yields \(P_A=1/4\), \(P_B=3/4\). Thus the robust point is prioritized. This valid counterexample disproves the general explanatory identification; it neither measures its frequency in trained models nor refutes the heuristic’s empirical usefulness. The filtering-specific budget was not separately established, so the witness uses the stated FGSM probe and an explicit valid evaluation budget.
result: A valid FGSM example reverses the explanatory ranking, while the paper presents a heuristic and its measured accuracy gains remain unchallenged.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe negative margin change as an empirical heuristic that need not order true robustness; restrict performance claims to the evaluated settings. No validated efficient replacement algorithm is supplied.
The local qualification or neutral-tie proposal is retained. Current accessible paper text still has the cited rule; author implementation and adoption are unestablished.

problems.title: Equation (6) is undefined when the vulnerability scores are equal
problems.source_location: Section 4.2, Eq. (6), PDF p. 5.
claim: Paraphrase of Eq. (6), Section 4.2, p. 5: for each training example,
\[ P_i=\frac12\left(\frac{V_i-\bar V}{D_i}+1\right),\qquad \bar V=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^nV_j,\qquad D_i=\max_{1\le j\le n}|V_i-V_j|. \]
analysis: With affine true-class logit \(x-1/2\) and zero competing logits, the correctly classified inputs \(0.51\) and \(0.90\) have equal margin-change score \(-8/255\). Their centered scores and dispersion denominator are both zero. Equation (6) therefore contains \(0/0\), although their boundary distances differ.
result: The written probability rule omits a valid tied-score case; unavailable author code may already guard it, and no occurrence in published runs is established.

paragraphs: The proposed clarification defines neutral equal-score probabilities and checks normalization; no released-code claim is made.

problems.title: The small-bandwidth gradient does not imply principal-component learning
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.1, Eqs. (9)–(10), PDF p. 6.
claim: Paraphrase of Theorem 3.1, p. 6, Eqs. (9)–(10): for the covariance \(C=N^{-1}\sum_i h_i h_i^\top\), the APV gradient has the expansion
\[ \nabla_a\mathcal L=-\frac{2}{\sigma^2}Ca+R(\sigma), \qquad \|R(\sigma)\|=O(1),\quad \sigma\to0^+. \]
analysis: Use centered embeddings \(\pm e_1\) and projection \(a=(1,1)/\sqrt2\). The Gaussian cross-weight is \(q=\exp(-4a_1^2/\sigma^2)\). As \(\sigma\to0^+\), smoothing approaches the identity and the projection derivative decays exponentially. In contrast, the asserted term \(-2Ca/\sigma^2\) is nonzero and diverges for this covariance. Even choosing the linear-loss gradient as the identity cannot reconcile those limits.

With loss \(\mathcal L=(\|z_1\|^2+\|z_2\|^2)/2\), the proof’s linear-gradient assumption holds with \(W=I\). Writing \(t=\tanh(2a_1^2/\sigma^2)\), the exact derivative is \[\nabla_a\mathcal L=\left(\frac{8a_1}{\sigma^2}\tanh\frac{2a_1^2}{\sigma^2}\operatorname{sech}^2\frac{2a_1^2}{\sigma^2},0\right)^\top\to0.\] Separately, for covariance \(\operatorname{diag}(1/4,1/2)\) and step \(0.4\), the written normalized iteration multiplies coordinates by \((0.9,0.8)\), so it selects the smaller-eigenvalue direction, rather than the principal one.
result: The claimed leading PCA-gradient expansion is false on the stated finite-embedding domain. This invalidates that theoretical explanation, not the reported classification measurements.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain exact quotient-rule differentiation. For fixed finite embeddings with positive projected separation \(\delta\) and bounded loss gradients, the derivative is \(O(\sigma^{-2}e^{-\delta^2/\sigma^2})\to0\). This valid restricted statement does not repair the original PCA-identification claim.
The existing restricted mathematical or implementation proposal is retained; the current paper/source still has the cited statement. No author adoption is established.

problems.title: The sorting limit needs a tie condition, and its convolution bound is incorrect
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.2, Eq. (11), PDF p. 6.
claim: Paraphrase of Theorem 3.2, p. 6, Eq. (11): for kernel-smoothed embeddings sorted by their scalar scores, and any fixed zero-padded convolution \(\operatorname{Conv}_W\),
\[ \|\operatorname{Conv}_W(\widetilde Z)-\operatorname{Conv}_W(\widetilde H)\|_F\to0 \quad(\sigma\to0^+). \]
analysis: Take embeddings \((0,1)\) and \((0,-1)\) and projection \(a=e_1\). Their projected scores tie, so kernel smoothing averages both to zero for every bandwidth. A one-tap identity convolution of the original embeddings retains them, giving Frobenius difference \(\sqrt2\) rather than a limit of zero. A tie restriction and a valid convolution estimate are needed.

The convolution proof also underestimates overlapping contributions: scalar taps \((1,1,1)\) acting on \((1,1,1)\) with zero padding produce \((2,3,2)\), of norm \(\sqrt{17}>3\), exceeding the claimed product \(\sqrt3\sqrt3\). This is independent of the tie witness.
result: The stated universal limit is false without additional score-separation conditions. Its failure concerns the formal guarantee; the actual frequency of score ties is not measured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The correct fixed-input limit averages embeddings within each equal-score class. Distinct scores, or identical embeddings within each tie class, recover \(Z\to H\). The convolution constant \(\sum_\tau\|W_\tau\|_{\rm op}\) is valid by the triangle inequality for zero-padded shifts; neither correction proves equivalence to an implemented architecture without that convolution.
The existing restricted mathematical or implementation proposal is retained; the current paper/source still has the cited statement. No author adoption is established.

problems.title: The global convergence bound omits the cost of mixing heterogeneous objectives
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.3, Eq. (12), PDF p. 7.
claim: Theorem 3.3, p. 7, Eq. (12), assumes: every local loss is \(L\)-smooth; stochastic gradients are unbiased with variance at most \(\zeta^2\); every loss satisfies a \(\mu\)-Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality; and
\[ \rho=\sup_t\|\Omega^{(t)}-\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top/K\|_2<1. \]
analysis: Let the two client objectives be \(f_1(\theta,a)=\tfrac12(\theta-1)^2+\tfrac12(a-1)^2\) and \(f_2(\theta,a)=\tfrac12(\theta+1)^2+\tfrac12(a-1)^2\). They are smooth and PL, with exact gradients. From common state \((0,1)\), a local step moves \(\theta\) oppositely; perfect averaging returns both clients to \((0,1)\). Their average local-optimum gap remains \(1/2\), even with zero gradient noise and perfect mixing. A bound forcing that gap to zero omits the cost of heterogeneous optima.

Take \(Q=1\), \(\eta=1/4\), \(L=\mu=1\), and equal client weights. Their nonzero APVs stay at \(1\), giving exactly the prescribed uniform mixing and \(\rho=0\); exact gradients give \(\zeta=0\). After the first local step the two task parameters are \(1/4\) and \(-1/4\), so mixing resets both to zero. The actual average gap is \(1/2\), whereas Eq. (12) bounds it by \((1/2)(3/4)=3/8\). Thus every stated assumption is met and the theorem fails already at one round.
result: The stated convergence guarantee cannot hold for every permitted heterogeneous-client problem. The example does not show that the method fails for all datasets or that a global-objective guarantee with a different target is impossible.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A common convex objective with doubly stochastic mixing permits a narrower local-descent argument. The heterogeneous personalized setting instead needs explicit control of losses at other clients’ parameters; no corrected theorem with the original assumptions is established.
The existing restricted mathematical or implementation proposal is retained; the current paper/source still has the cited statement. No author adoption is established.

problems.title: Sign-equivalent local representations receive opposite server similarities
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF p. 5; Appendix C.1.1, PDF p. 24.
claim: Section 3.2, p. 5, interprets APV cosine similarity as similarity of the local subgraphs. Appendix C.1.1, p. 24, explicitly recognizes that the local kernel and classifier are unchanged when \(a\) is replaced by \(-a\). These two facts are incompatible without an orientation convention.
analysis: Replacing \(a\) by \(-a\) leaves every squared projected difference, kernel weight and local prediction unchanged, but changes cosine similarity with \(a\) from \(1\) to \(-1\). At similarity temperature \(10\), a sign-equivalent partner can receive relative weight \(1/(e^{20}+1)\). This is descriptor non-identifiability; shared initialization may nevertheless maintain orientation in practice.
result: Sign reversal preserves the complete local function but changes server similarity; common initialization may preserve orientation, and no incidence of harmful sign flips is measured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A sign-invariant comparison such as \(\cos^2(a,b)\) or projector \(aa^\top/\|a\|^2\) removes this exact descriptor ambiguity. Averaging the vectors also requires a sign-alignment/tie policy to avoid cancellation. These are unvalidated design proposals, not recovered benchmark performance.
The existing restricted mathematical or implementation proposal is retained; the current paper/source still has the cited statement. No author adoption is established.

problems.title: The released kernel uses per-node cosine normalization instead of the paper’s common normalization
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, PDF p. 3; released models/fedpub_aux/nets.py, MaskedGCN._kernel_aggregate, line 59.

problems.title: The claim of winning every setting is contradicted by Table 1

problems.title: Equation (4) is a table probability, not the claimed Fisher p-value
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Eq. (4), PDF p. 5.
claim: Section 3.2, p. 5, states, in paraphrase, that Fisher’s test returns the probability of the observed contingency table or a more extreme table under independence. Equation (4) then defines
\[ \operatorname{Fisher}_{\mathrm{printed}}(T) =\frac{(a+b)!(c+d)!(a+c)!(b+d)!}{a!b!c!d!G!}. \]
analysis: For a \(2\times2\) table with every cell equal to \(2\), the feasible conditional masses are \((1,16,36,16,1)/70\). The observed mass is \(18/35\), but every feasible table is no more probable, so the probability-ordered two-sided Fisher p-value is \(1\). Equation (4) prints one hypergeometric mass, not the stated tail. The released algorithm does include tail summation, which limits the impact of this printed-formula discrepancy.
result: The displayed statistic is not its stated p-value, but the released algorithm already performs the missing tail summation in principle, limiting the finding to the printed specification.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Replace the single mass with the specified probability-ordered tail: sum \(\binom{s}{k}\binom{n-s}{r-k}/\binom nr\) over feasible \(k\) whose numerator weight is no larger than the observed one. The existing code’s tail operation is affirmative counterevidence against assuming it trained on the literal single mass.
The local formula, numerical or scope proposal is retained; current cited passages and author-source paths still contain the relevant behavior. Author adoption is unestablished.

problems.title: Float32 ties and the exact-\(p=1\) gate change the released association score
problems.source_location: Eq. (5), PDF p. 5; released Fisher-tail routine and exact-p-equals-one gate.
claim: Released compute_key_tokens.py, fisher_exact_test, lines 26–51, computes masses using float32 log-gamma expressions and selects terms by literal probability comparison. Lines 157–159 apply the exact \(p\ne1\) gate corresponding to Eq. (5).
analysis: For table \(\begin{pmatrix}0&5\\2&9\end{pmatrix}\), the exact feasible masses are \(11/24,11/24,1/12\), so the two-sided p-value is \(1\). Rounding can separate the equal masses and exclude one tied term. problems.title: CogVideoX inference changes the target image’s pixel range before CAMA
problems.source_location: Section 3.3 and Figure 3, PDF p. 5; Section 3.5, PDF p. 6; released CogVideoX CAMA input path.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 3.3, page 5, describes the target image and the first frame of each reference video as inputs to the same DINO appearance encoder and resampler. Figure 3 depicts that common image-encoding path. Section 3.5, page 6, uses the trained CAMA component during inference. No separate target-only brightness transform is specified.

The current src/data/dataset.py, lines 88–96, scales physical pixels to \([0,1]\) and then normalizes with mean and standard deviation \(0.5\), producing \([-1,1]\). Training target frames and reference first frames follow that convention. The shared inherited DINO preprocessing maps \(x\) to \((x+1)/2\) before channel standardization.

The inference wrapper first restores \(u\), then applies the same preprocessing again, yielding \(P(u)=(u+1)/2\). Thus black becomes \(0.5\) in the target branch but stays \(0\) in training/reference branches. A constant image makes this comparison independent of resizing.

paragraphs: Make the helper’s input range explicit. For the inference caller, convert \([0,1]\) back to \([-1,1]\) only before CAMA; preserve the base generator’s \([0,1]\) image. The direct training helper already receives \([-1,1]\), so an unconditional conversion in the shared helper is an invalid general patch.

problems.title: With equal uniform marginals, the plan cannot identify the minimum-cost goal
problems.source_location: Text after Eq. (3), goal argmax, and Theorem 3.1 proof, PDF p. 6.
claim: Paraphrase: page 6 immediately after Eq. (3), the paper selects a goal by maximizing \(T_{ii}\). The proof of Theorem 3.1 then infers that this goal minimizes \(C_{ii}\) under the semantic constraint. This is the specific implication checked here.
analysis: With both marginals uniform on two nodes, the sole finite-cost coupling is \(T=I/2\), regardless of the diagonal costs. For diagonal costs \((2,1/2)\), both nodes maximize \(T_{ii}\), including the more expensive one. In general the plan is \(I/m\), so maximizing its diagonal cannot imply minimum-cost goal selection.

problems.title: The orthogonality penalty is not a well-defined measure of orthogonality
problems.source_location: Appendix A.9.1, PDF p. 33; separate supplement Section 6.2, p. 13.
claim: Paraphrase: final Appendix A.9.1, page 33, and separate supplement Section 6.2, page 13, define a centroid matrix \(D\in\mathbb R^{K\times d}\) with unit-norm rows, its Gram matrix \(G=DD^\top\), and \(G_{\rm off}=G-I_K\). The displayed penalty is

Exact orthogonal unit rows additionally require \(K\le d\), since \(\operatorname{rank}(DD^\top)\le d\). At dimension \(256\), resolutions above \(256\) cannot satisfy \(DD^\top=I_K\). A soft decorrelation objective remains meaningful. The current default total_loss comments out this regularizer, so no NaN failure of default training or error in its ablation table is inferred.

problems.title: Zero-shift spectral inversion can fail on a valid spatial graph
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF p. 5; released sparse_spectral_clustering zero-shift eigsh call.
claim: Section 3.2, PDF p. 5, forms the graph Laplacian \(L=D_{\rm degree}-W\) and requests its smallest eigenvectors. The released sparse_spectral_clustering path calls eigsh in shift-invert mode at \(\sigma=0\), which requires solving with \(L-\sigma I=L\).
analysis: Every exactly formed unnormalized graph Laplacian satisfies \(L\mathbf1=0\), so \(L\) is singular even for a connected graph. A zero-shift inverse solve can therefore fail on an otherwise valid spatial graph. Floating-point perturbations can allow some factorizations to proceed; this is not evidence that every complete run crashes.

A connected three-voxel path with unit edge weights gives \[L=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix},\] whose eigenvalues are \(0,1,3\). The desired smallest two exist, but the current \(\sigma=0\) shift requests inversion of singular \(L\). This is independent of the negative-edge centering concern.
result: An admissible connected graph makes the released inverse-shift solve singular; this input-dependent solver defect does not establish failure of every complete DCA run.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Request smallest algebraic eigenpairs without a zero inverse shift, or use a separately validated nonzero-shift/preconditioned solver with residual checks. Nearest-to-zero and smallest algebraic eigenvalues differ for signed graphs.

problems.title: The pair-dependent Gaussian expression is not a valid covariance for every permitted graph
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, Eq. (4), PDF p. 4.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 3.1, Equation (4), PDF p. 4 uses
\[K_{ij}=\exp\!\left[-\frac{a_{ij}(x_{i,k}-x_{j,k})^2}{2\Theta^2}\right]\]
analysis: A positive-semidefinite matrix with unit diagonal and \(K_{12}=1\) must satisfy \(K_{13}=K_{23}\): the first two unit feature vectors have inner product one and must coincide. The allowed choice \(x_1=x_2\), with different positive pair weights to a third node having \(x_3\ne x_1\), gives \(K_{12}=1\) but \(K_{13}\ne K_{23}\). The displayed pair-dependent Gaussian therefore fails to be a covariance on its stated graph domain.

Take \(x=(0,0,1)\), \(\Theta=1\), and positive pair weights \(a_{12}=1\), \(a_{13}=2\log2\), \(a_{23}=2\log4\). Then \[K=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1/2\\1&1&1/4\\1/2&1/4&1\end{pmatrix}.\] For \(v=(1,-1,-1/4)^\top\), \(v^\top Kv=-1/16\), an impossible covariance quadratic form. This complete connected weighted graph satisfies the written domain; a single global weight is a valid RBF control.
result: The formula does not define a positive-semidefinite covariance for every permitted graph. This contradicts the central covariance justification; no new prediction-error or benchmark estimate follows.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Define one global filtered feature \(Z=H(L)X\) and apply the RBF kernel to \(Z_{ik}-Z_{jk}\), as in the later architecture. Its Fourier representation gives a nonnegative expected squared modulus, proving PSD. This is a changed covariance construction, not an algebraic identity with pair-dependent rescaling.

problems.title: The robustness theorem imports a bound with the wrong matrix domain and order conditions
problems.source_location: Theorem 4.2, PDF p. 6; Appendix A, PDF p. 21; Lemma A.1, Eq. (11), PDF p. 22.
claim: Paraphrase: Theorem 4.2, PDF p. 6, repeated in Appendix A on p. 21, bounds every node’s prediction change by \(CK\epsilon D\|X\|_2\). Lemma A.1, Equation (11), p. 22, applies the corresponding filter bound to \(H(L)=\sum_{h=0}^{R}\alpha_hL^h\), explicitly taking \(L\) to be the normalized Laplacian. Its constant is
\[K_{\rm printed}=\frac14\|\alpha\|_1(R^2-1) \left(\frac{R-1}{R+1}\right)^R.\]
analysis: The imported higher-order result controls powers of \(L-I\), whose spectrum lies in \([-1,1]\), and treats first order separately. The paper instead uses powers of an unshifted normalized Laplacian. At \(R=1\), the printed factor \(R^2-1\) makes \(K=0\), although choosing the nonconstant filter \(H(L)=L\) allows a nonzero response to graph perturbation. Thus neither the matrix-domain substitution nor the missing order restriction is justified by that imported bound.

For the normalized Laplacians of the three-node path and triangle, choose \(X=e_2\), \(H(L)=L\), and scalar readout \(g(z)=\sqrt2\cos z\). The first-node outputs differ by approximately \(0.1659409412\), while the printed order-one constant is zero. Even repairing the reciprocal ratio leaves a matrix-domain failure: for \(H(L)=L^6\), the filter difference norm is approximately \(53.00267785\), exceeding the source-style bound \(41.84124064\); the shifted \(L-I\) control satisfies that bound.
result: The stated robustness theorem is not established by the cited argument, and its unrestricted first-order specialization cannot hold as written. Reversing a transcription ratio does not resolve these substantive conditions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For unshifted normalized Laplacians of nonnegatively weighted undirected graphs, use \(K=\sum_{h=1}^R h2^{h-1}|\alpha_h|\). The noncommutative telescoping identity for \(\widehat L^h-L^h\) and \(\|L\|,\|\widehat L\|\le2\) prove it. Multiply by the stated RFF/readout constants for output stability; this restores a qualitative finite-degree bound with a different constant.

problems.title: A Laplacian coefficient does not directly measure one hop’s contribution
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF p. 6; Section 6.1, PDF p. 8; Section 6.3, Figure 4(c), PDF p. 9; Appendix C.3, PDF p. 26.
claim: Paraphrase: The interpretation around Figure 4(c), Section 6.3, PDF p. 9, identifies each \(\alpha_h\) with information from the \(h\)-hop neighborhood. Related language occurs in Section 3.2/p. 6 and Appendix C.3/p. 26. Section 6.1/p. 8 describes explanatory curves against raw input feature values.
analysis: Let \(S=I-L\) and \(\alpha=(1,-2,1)\). Then \(H(L)=I-2L+L^2=S^2\). On a three-node path, an endpoint has no immediate-neighbor contribution in \(S^2\), although \(|\alpha_1|=2\) is largest. Laplacian-basis coefficients mix walk lengths and do not directly measure a single hop's contribution.

The same path/filter also defeats an unconditional raw-feature curve: changing \(X=(0,0,0)^\top\) to \((0,0,1)^\top\) leaves the first node’s raw value zero but changes its filtered value from \(0\) to \(1/2\). Its nonlinear contribution therefore depends on neighbor context. Feature-channel additivity and the radius bound remain valid.
result: Laplacian coefficients and filtered-channel outputs do not uniquely identify exact-hop or unconditional raw-feature effects; the architecture remains additive and finite-range.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe the parameters as coefficients in the Laplacian polynomial basis. Any exact-distance interpretation must first combine the relevant polynomial terms for the specified graph and input.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The public implementation’s R=\(1\) ablation uses no graph edges
problems.source_location: Eq. (6) and Algorithm 1, PDF pp. 5–6; Section 6.2, PDF p. 8; released models/gnamrff model implementations.
claim: Paraphrase: Equation (6), Algorithm 1 (pp. 5-6), and the one-hop interpretation of the \(R=1\) row in Section 6.2/p. 8 use degree \(R\), with powers zero through \(R\). The audited public implementation instead allocates torch.randn(R) and loops over range(\(1\), R) in models/gnamrff.py lines 18-31 and models/gnamrff_graph.py lines 23-35.
analysis: The released loop treats \(R\) as the number of coefficients. For \(R=1\), only the identity term survives and no edge information is propagated. That graph-free setting differs from the paper's degree-one convention, which includes both \(I\) and \(L\).
result: The current order convention removes all edge dependence at its first setting; exact historical ablation configuration and resulting accuracy changes remain unknown.

problems.title: The public graph experiment runner performs repeated holdouts rather than the specified \(10\)-fold protocol
problems.source_location: Section 6.4, PDF pp. 9–10; Appendix C.1, PDF p. 25; separate supplement p. 6.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 6.4 and Appendix C.1, pp. 9-10 and \(25\), specify \(10\)-fold graph cross-validation, with three random seeds per fold. The same protocol is stated on supplementary PDF p. 6.
analysis: Repeated random holdouts do not form a \(10\)-fold partition: test sets can overlap and examples need not be tested exactly once. Thus the public runner implements a different evaluation protocol; the source alone does not identify all historical table-producing runs.

The loader also resets the Torch seed to the fold after the caller sets a training seed, so the intended independent seed variation is not realized through that ordering. Within each call the train, validation and test slices are disjoint; this is a protocol mismatch, not demonstrated within-run test leakage.
result: The public reproduction path implements repeated holdouts and resets the training seed, rather than the stated fold/seed hierarchy; no inflation of historical means is established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Generate one immutable partition of graph IDs into ten test folds. For each outer fold, reserve its test IDs and choose validation IDs only from the remaining training pool. Save all IDs. Train three independently seeded models per fold, using a separate split generator and setting the training seed after split selection. Average according to the declared hierarchy and state whether the reported uncertainty is across folds, seeds, or both.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The Gittins reference is not exactly optimal for the finite \(40\)-pull task
problems.source_location: Section 5, Figure 2, PDF p. 6; Appendix A.2, PDF p. 14.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 5, PDF p. 6, identifies the Gittins-index solution as the Bayes-optimal reference for the two-armed Bernoulli experiment, including Figure 2. Appendix A.2, p. 14, specifies the independent \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\) priors, episode length \(40\), and discount \(0.95\), and uses the same optimality characterization.

In the released code, utils/bayes_optimal_agents.py, class BernoulliGittinsAgent, stores one fixed lookahead_window. get_action chooses the larger cached index. update changes the posterior counts and recomputes that arm’s index, but does not reduce the lookahead as the episode approaches its deadline. The performance path supplies lookahead \(40\); a state-machine reference path requests one auxiliary transition and can use lookahead 41.
analysis: With one action remaining, information has no future value, so the optimal action maximizes the current posterior mean. A fixed-window index can still favor an exploratory arm with a smaller mean, unlike a remaining-horizon Bellman policy. The released policy never reduces its lookahead with the remaining episode length. This establishes the optimality qualification without relying on a rerun or treating the small historical value gap as a new experiment.

A positively reachable \(39\)-pull history with first reward one and subsequent rewards zero has counts \((s_1,f_1,s_2,f_2)=(1,25,0,13)\), hence posteriors \(\operatorname{Beta}(2,26)\) and \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,14)\). The historical calculation for this unchanged release gives indices \(0.08984375<0.09765625\), selecting arm two. With one pull left, the means are \(1/14>1/15\), so the conditional loss is exactly \(1/210\). The ordered history has prior probability \(B(2,26)B(1,14)=1/9828>0\). This historical reachability/index calculation was not executed again; the current source still keeps the same fixed lookahead.
result: The exact-reference characterization requires correction; the unchanged source supports retaining the narrower approximate-reference interpretation. The historical prior-averaged discounted gap is approximately 0.001359, rather than evidence of a large behavioral reversal.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a remaining-horizon Bellman reference or describe the fixed-window Gittins baseline as near-optimal for this finite task. The four Beta posterior counts remain sufficient statistics.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.
The existing reference-policy or metric-definition proposal remains relevant to the current author source; no author adoption is established.

problems.title: The released bandit output metric is an undiscounted statistic
problems.source_location: Appendix A.4, PDF p. 18 (separate supplement p. 5); Appendix A.2, PDF p. 14.
claim: Paraphrase: Appendix A.4, PDF p. 18 / supplementary PDF p. 5, describes output dissimilarity \(D_o\) in terms of expected-return differences. The Bernoulli task’s stated performance objective uses \(\gamma=0.95\), Appendix A.2/p. 14.

This finding is a verified implementation/metric-scope mismatch, not a claim that an aggregate return statistic is inherently invalid. In utils/state_machine_analysis.py, get_output_dissimilarity (lines 1250-1361), the stationary-bandit branch obtains each arm’s expected immediate rewards from the sampled task parameters, sums the differences with no discount weights, takes an absolute value per episode, and averages across episodes. It cannot be interpreted as the difference of the discounted task returns without further qualification.
analysis: For arm rewards \(0.9\) and \(0.1\), choosing the better arm for the first \(20\) rather than the last \(20\) actions gives the same undiscounted arm counts. With \(\gamma=0.95\), the discounted-return difference is \(0.8(1-0.95^{20})^2/(1-0.95)\approx6.584645\). A count-only output statistic cannot represent that discounted objective.
result: Supported metric-scope mismatch; no revised trained-agent return is inferred.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either label the statistic as an undiscounted reward-sum comparison or multiply each per-step expected-reward difference by the task discount before summing. This remains a comparison along evaluated reference histories, not necessarily an on-policy return difference.
The existing reference-policy or metric-definition proposal remains relevant to the current author source; no author adoption is established.

problems.title: Separate averaging of rotated queries and keys introduces absolute-position cross terms
problems.source_location: Eqs. (13) and (15), PDF pp. 5–6; Appendix A.2 and Eq. (20), PDF p. 15.
claim: Equation (13), PDF p. 5, uses ordinary RoPE's relative-position rotation. The hierarchical extension in Eq. (15), PDF p. 6, averages the rotated embeddings over frequency bases; Appendix A.2, Eqs. (20)–(21), PDF p. 15, describes the resulting attention as relative-position rotation.
analysis: Averaging rotated queries and keys separately gives terms \(\exp(i(\theta_a p-\theta_b r))\) for every frequency pair. Translating both positions by \(c\) multiplies a cross term by \(\exp(i(\theta_a-\theta_b)c)\), which is generally not one. Ordinary same-frequency cancellation therefore does not remove absolute-position dependence from the averaged construction.

Using the stated four bases, head dimension \(24\), channel \(t=1\), and content \(q=k=1\), frequencies are approximately \[(0.5623413252,0.3162277660,0.1778279410,0.1)\]. At equal positions \(p=r=c\), attention is \[\left|\frac14\sum_{a=1}^4e^{i\theta_ac}\right|^2,\] equal to \(1\) at \(c=0\) but approximately \(0.9694978734\) at \(c=1\). Relative displacement and content are unchanged. This limits a pure-relative reading; the weaker statement that the embedding contains relative information is not disproved.
result: A common translation changes the averaged encoding’s dot product, limiting pure-relative interpretation; mixed absolute/relative information can still be useful empirically.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Average matched-base query/key dot products, or concatenate the base-specific rotated copies with scaling \(1/\sqrt h\). Their dot product is then the average of \(q\bar k e^{i\theta_a(p-r)}\), which preserves relative invariance algebraically. This architecture change has no demonstrated reconstruction gain.
The existing local mathematical or consistency proposal remains applicable to current v2/current-head source; no author adoption is established.

problems.title: The configured 21/21/22 real-coordinate split does not implement three rotary blocks
problems.source_location: Eqs. (12)–(14), PDF p. 5; Appendix A.2; released stage 1–3 configurations with dimension 768 and 12 heads.
claim: Equations (12)-(14), p. 5, use complex rotations for position embedding. Appendix A.2 explicitly pairs real coordinates to form complex query/key entries. The final-supplement configuration files config/stage1.yaml, stage2.yaml, and stage3.yaml all set decoder dimension \(768\) and \(12\) heads, giving \(64\) real coordinates per head.

The corresponding croco/models/pos_embed_con.py defines RoPE3DContinuous. Its forward method splits a nondivisible head into widths \(\lfloor64/3\rfloor,\lfloor64/3\rfloor,64-2\lfloor64/3\rfloor\), namely \(21\), \(21\), and 22. rotate_half calls chunk(\(2\)) and concatenates the negative second chunk with the first. get_angle_emb duplicates the frequency vector and truncates it to the requested width. The same substantive implementation is present in the current repository. croco.py instantiates this class for RoPE3D100; the decoder attention code passes per-head tensors to it.
analysis: The configured \(64\)-real-coordinate head is split into widths \((21,21,22)\). The odd-width blocks have unequal half lengths, so chunking and concatenation no longer align coordinate pairs with duplicated sine/cosine frequencies. They are not collections of orthogonal two-dimensional rotations. Even-width single-base blocks and position zero supply matching controls; this does not imply failure for every width or input.

For the produced width \(21\), input \(e_0\), coordinate \(\pi/2\) and base \(10\), rotate_half moves the active entry to coordinate \(10\), whose sine frequency is \(10^{-20/21}\). The output norm is \(\sin((\pi/2)10^{-20/21})\approx0.174386468\), rather than \(1\). This isolates an individual purported rotation, independently of deliberate cross-base averaging.
result: The actual head configuration produces odd axis widths that violate the advertised rotation property; trained-model compensation and benchmark impact are unmeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Allocate complete real/imaginary pairs on every axis; for a \(64\)-coordinate head, real widths such as \((22,22,20)\) permit pairwise rotations. Verify norm preservation per base, and separately address the average-before-product issue. Changed allocation requires model evaluation before claiming recovered accuracy.
The existing local mathematical or consistency proposal remains applicable to current v2/current-head source; no author adoption is established.

problems.title: The memory-fusion threshold uses different point sets in Eq. (19) and the released code
problems.source_location: Memory-fusion description, PDF p. 5; Appendix A.1, Eq. (19), PDF p. 15.
claim: Equation (19), Appendix A.1, p. 15, defines the threshold as the Euclidean norm of the existing memory’s coordinate ranges divided by axis constants, each set to 20. Its explanatory sentence identifies the coordinates as those of the memory \(\mathcal M_{t-1}\). The fusion description on p. 5 then uses this threshold to decide whether an incoming pointer should replace a nearest memory entry or be appended.

The final supplement dust3r/point3r.py, around lines 590-595, instead takes coordinate ranges over the concatenation of existing memory pointers and current incoming pointers. The current repository does the same in src/dust3r/point3r.py, lines 688-693.
analysis: For existing memory x-coordinates \(\{0,1\}\) and incoming coordinates \(\{2,100\}\), with common positive depth and other coordinates fixed, memory-only range gives threshold \(1/20=0.05\), so both incoming points append. Current code uses the union range, giving \(100/20=5\); distance \(1\) now merges the incoming point at \(2\) into the old point at \(1\), while \(100\) appends. The same nearest distances therefore produce four entries under the written rule and three under the release.
result: Changing the threshold’s point set changes a valid memory update; this is a reproducibility discrepancy without an established accuracy direction.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either compute the range from existing memory to match the equation, or document the union of existing and incoming pointers to match current code. Neither consistency option is established as scientifically superior.
The existing local mathematical or consistency proposal remains applicable to current v2/current-head source; no author adoption is established.

problems.title: The published pooled-span Gaussian KL penalty differs from the released tokenwise MSE objective
problems.source_location: Section 4, Query Projection with KL Constraint, PDF p. 7.
claim: Paraphrase: in Query Projection with KL Constraint, Section 4, p. 7, the last-layer representations are pooled over each contiguous B/I span and compared with the corresponding pooled frozen teacher representation through a Gaussian KL penalty. Footnote 3 identifies mean pooling. The displayed formula is unnumbered. With \(N_+\) spans and \(m_s\) tokens in span \(s\), it is
\[L_{\mathrm{paper}}=\frac1{N_+}\sum_{s=1}^{N_+} \frac{\|\bar h_s-\bar t_s\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2},\qquad \bar h_s=\frac1{m_s}\sum_{k\in s}h_k,\quad \bar t_s=\frac1{m_s}\sum_{k\in s}t_k.\]
analysis: For one two-token span, let student vectors be \((1,0),(-1,0)\) and teacher vectors both zero. The pooled means agree, so the paper's penalty is \(0\), while tokenwise MSE is positive. In general tokenwise MSE adds the within-span variance of the student–teacher deviations. Changing a scalar loss weight cannot remove that extra term.

For dimension \(d=2\) and \(\sigma=1\), the current elementwise-mean loss gives \(1/4\) for that span. Generally it equals the pooled penalty divided by \(d\), plus \((2\sigma^2md)^{-1}\sum_k\|\Delta_k-\bar\Delta\|^2\). This extra nonnegative within-span variance term is structural, while one-token and constant-displacement spans are matching controls up to dimensional scaling.
result: The current release penalizes token-level variation absent from the stated pooled objective; the actually trained objective and resulting benchmark effect remain untraced.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either pool each student and teacher span first and sum squared coordinate differences as stated, or document the actual tokenwise feature-averaged loss and its extra variance term. Any change of loss scale needs separate empirical assessment.
The existing objective or interpretation proposal remains applicable to current v3/current-head source; no author adoption is established.

problems.title: Image-balanced macro-gIoU does not establish improved segmentation of rare part classes
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Segmentation Evaluation, PDF p. 6; Appendix C.2–C.3, PDF p. 18.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 3.3, Segmentation Evaluation, p. 6, defines micro-gIoU by averaging all part-mask IoUs and macro-gIoU by first averaging within each image, then averaging the image means. The text interprets the latter as less affected by common parts. Appendix C.2-C.3, p. 18, attributes reported macro advantages to rare or uncommon part performance.

The released evaluator confirms the averaging unit: src/evaluation/evaluators/masks.py, lines 47-74, appends one mean per update in the macro branch and all paired mask IoUs in the micro branch. No part-class label is used for this reduction.
analysis: Averaging first by image equalizes image weights, not part-class frequencies. With one mask in each of ten images, nine common-class successes can dominate a complete rare-class failure in the tenth image. Therefore a higher image-macro gIoU need not imply better rare-class performance. The metric remains well defined and useful for image balancing.

An explicit ranking reversal uses nine common-class masks and one rare-class mask, one per image. Model A has IoUs \(1\) on common masks and \(0\) on the rare mask; model B has \(7/9\) and \(1\). Image-macro favors A, \(0.9>0.8\), while rare-class performance favors B, \(0<1\), and class-macro favors B, \(1/2<8/9\). Binary masks on a nine-pixel ground truth realize all values.
result: Metric-inference clarification; the metric itself is well defined.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Interpret the current metric as a mean of per-image mask IoUs. Tie stronger rare-part conclusions to explicitly defined class identities, frequencies and class-stratified results.
The existing objective or interpretation proposal remains applicable to current v3/current-head source; no author adoption is established.

problems.title: Several comparative conclusions in Appendix C do not follow from its own printed tables
problems.source_location: Appendix C.1–C.3, PDF p. 18; Tables 9–11, PDF pp. 18–19.
claim: Appendix C.1-C.3, p. 18, makes stronger statements than some entries in Tables 9-11, pp. 18-19, support. The relevant claims, paraphrased, concern uniform superiority over the zero-shot baselines, a maximum two-point micro-gIoU gap after finetuning, and a macro-gIoU advantage used to diagnose another model’s treatment of uncommon parts.

This analysis checks these as substantive claims about comparative performance. It does not count numerical formatting, spelling, or table-caption mistakes as errata. The mismatch matters because it can reverse which method is favored on a task.
analysis: The appendix's uniform-superiority wording has a PartImageNet Intersection-macro exception. Its claimed maximum micro-gIoU deficit of two points is also contradicted by the PACO comparison, whose gap is \(3.8\) points. The macro result alone cannot diagnose another model's rare-class behavior, for the image-versus-class averaging reason in the preceding problem. These are corrections to conclusions drawn from the printed tables, not new performance measurements.

Current Table 10 gives PLUM \(12.2\) versus PixelLM \(12.8\) for zero-shot PartImageNet Intersection macro, and finetuned Difference macro \(60.7\) versus GLaMM \(65.4\), reversing the asserted advantage. Current Table 9 gives finetuned PACO Difference micro \(32.2\) versus PixelLM \(36.0\), a gap of \(3.8\), exceeding the stated two-point limit. Favorable cells remain; no new IoUs or significance test were computed.
result: Narrow the appendix comparisons to their individual printed wins and losses. No new significance test or overall ranking is established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A correction supported by the printed evidence is: PLUM leads most zero-shot segmentation comparisons in these tables, with a PartImageNet Intersection-macro exception; after finetuning it leads the six Identification/Intersection macro cells, while its micro-gIoU gap reaches \(3.8\) points on PACO. Difference-macro results depend on the dataset and comparator. They do not establish uniform dominance or a per-class diagnosis.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.
The existing objective or interpretation proposal remains applicable to current v3/current-head source; no author adoption is established.

problems.title: Zero-shot requires the stated training-stage qualification; it does not mean absence of part-mask supervision
problems.source_location: Section 5, Implementation Details, PDF p. 7; Appendix A.1, PDF pp. 15–16; Appendix C.1, PDF p. 18.
claim: Section 5, Implementation Details, p. 7, explicitly defines the zero-shot baseline as the checkpoint after initial adaptation on a mixture that includes PACO-LVIS, Pascal Parts, and PartImageNet, before further PARTONOMY task finetuning. Appendix A.1, pp. 15-16, also describes this preliminary training stage. In contrast, Appendix C.1, p. 18, includes a statement that PLUM uses no part masks during pretraining.
analysis: The source qualifies zero-shot by training/evaluation stage. Prior part-mask supervision is compatible with that narrower usage; it is only incompatible with an unqualified claim of no part-mask training. Retaining the stated qualification resolves the apparent contradiction.
result: No additional error established beyond terminology scope.

problems.title: The current correctness guard preserves hallucinated labels
problems.source_location: Section 2.2.2, PDF p. 4; Appendix B.1, PDF p. 21; separate supplement PDF p. 8, printed p. 24.
claim: Section 2.2.2 and Appendix B.1 classify a response as typical or creative only after the correctness gate. The original supplementary evaluator overwrote hallucinated labels in its final novelty loop; the current author repository instead guards that loop.
analysis: In current src/labeling.py, any evaluator rejection assigns Hallucinated_Solution. Lines 131–138 run novelty assignment only when that label is absent. A response rejected by both judges therefore retains its hallucinated label. This directly removes the historical overwrite counterexample.
result: The historical supplementary defect is fixed in the current source. Which version produced the published measurements is not established, and no current labeling defect is asserted from this witness.

problems.title: The binary APm column is not the same metric across the released evaluation strategies
problems.source_location: Section 4.3, PDF p. 7; Table 3, PDF p. 9; Appendix Tables 11–15, PDF pp. 28–30.
claim: Section 4.3, PDF p. 7, defines APm as macro Average Precision with equal class weights; Table 3 and Appendix Tables 11–15 use that heading for binary hallucination detection. The released evaluation strategies under src/evaluation_strategy use positive-class-only AP in some paths and the mean of classwise AP values in others.
analysis: For labels \((0,0,0,1)\) with tied class scores \((0.5,0.5)\), positive-class AP is \(0.25\), negative-class AP is \(0.75\), and macro AP is \(0.5\). These distinct quantities cannot share a macro-AP label without qualification. Perfect predictions give one under both conventions, so agreement on that control does not establish equivalence.
result: The current binary evaluation paths compute different AP quantities under a common macro-AP heading. Published table values have not been recomputed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Average the independently computed classwise AP values in every strategy, or explicitly label positive-class AP separately.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Prototype AUROC and AP discard the continuous distance ordering
problems.source_location: Sections 4.2–4.3, PDF p. 7; released prototype.py, lines 324–361.
claim: Section 4.2, p. 7, defines the prototype classifier using Euclidean distance to class center embeddings and the nearest class. Section 4.3 then reports AUROC and AP alongside F1. The later implementation’s prototype.py, lines 324-349 for multiclass and \(351\)-\(361\) for binary classification, passes one-hot predicted class labels to the ranking metrics. The MLP, XGBoost, and TabM strategies pass class probability scores.
analysis: One-hot class predictions discard the continuous prototype-distance ordering. Under standard tie credit their binary AUROC is \((\mathrm{TPR}+\mathrm{TNR})/2\). Two examples assigned the same class can still have different distances, so this evaluates a coarser score than the probability-ranking metrics used by other strategies. Hard-label AUROC itself remains defined.

For one-dimensional prototypes at \(0\) and \(1\), queries \(0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4\) with labels \(0,0,1,1\) all receive hard label \(0\). Hard-label AUROC and positive-class AP are both \(0.5\), whereas the score \(-|z-1|\) ranks both positives above both negatives and gives both values \(1\).
result: Supported metric-comparability clarification, not an assertion that hard-label ROC is undefined.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep nearest-prototype labels for F1 and accuracy. To assess distance ranking, retain a class score such as \(s_c(z)=-\|z-\mu_c\|_2\) and use those scores for the classwise ROC/AP calculations, with the explicit averaging rule from Problem 2. ROC/AP depend on score order, so negative values themselves cause no problem. If normalized scores such as a distance softmax are chosen instead, specify that choice and any temperature fixed using reference/validation data. In multiclass settings, softmax normalization can alter a class’s one-versus-rest ranking; no equivalence between these different score constructions is asserted here.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Released input datasets and generation requests do not identify the described final filtered experiment
problems.source_location: Sections 2.3–2.3.1, PDF p. 4; released final-input filtering and reference-cap path.
claim: Sections 2.3–2.3.1 describe a final extended set of \(4545\) problems, a disjoint \(29\)-problem REF and \(371\)-problem TEST split, and at most two supplied reference solutions for non-REF prompts. The current data files and generation loop are the corresponding author-released inputs.
analysis: The current AMC, AIME and AHSME JSON lists contain \(2228,935,1732\) records, totaling \(4895\), which is \(350\) above the stated final count. Equality of full problem text after whitespace normalization gives \(16\) AMC–TEST matching pairs and zero REF–TEST pairs. This checks released inputs, not an unavailable final experiment manifest.

Current generation_and_feature_extraction.py loops through every supplied reference count. A non-REF record with three solutions therefore permits \(k=3\); with three generations per reference count it requests \(9\) responses, including a third-reference prompt. The stated cap is not enforced in this loop.
result: The release does not identify the described final filtered corpus, and its default generation path permits more than two non-REF references. These findings do not prove overlap or excess references in the actual table-producing runs.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Release the final filtered split manifest and apply the stated two-reference cap to non-REF requests. Preserve REF exceptions explicitly rather than deleting records solely to force a target count.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released mesh encoder violates rotation rules before its equivariant blocks
problems.source_location: Introduction, PDF p. 2; Section 3, PDF p. 4; Section 4, PDF pp. 5–6; Appendix G.1.2, PDF pp. 26–27.
claim: Paraphrase: The introduction, p. 2, describes an end-to-end \(SO(3)\)-equivariant mapping. Section 3, p. 4, bases that property on each component being equivariant. Section 4, pp. 5-6, and Appendix G.1.2, pp. 26-27, use Equiformer v2 to encode meshes into harmonic features before spherical decoding. The public README makes the corresponding architectural claim.

Two concrete operations in the pinned mesh path fail the prerequisites of that composition argument. They are grouped here because they invalidate the same proposed implementation guarantee; repairing either one alone leaves the other unresolved.
analysis: A nonzero edge \((1,-1,0)\) is removed by the released coordinate-sum test, but a rotation can give it nonzero coordinate sum and retain it. Separately, axis-bin lookups populate \(\ell=0\) scalar slots with coordinate-dependent values that change under rotation. Thus the released preprocessing violates the prerequisites of the equivariant-block composition argument. This identifies a release-level failure of the claimed implementation contract, not the historical experiment path.

For the nondegenerate triangle \[(0,0,0),(1,-1,0),(0,0,1)\], a quarter-turn about the last axis changes an edge coordinate sum from \(0\) to \(-2\), with unchanged edge length. Separately, scalar initialization \(E_{q(x)}+E_{q(y)}+E_{q(z)}\), with admissible \(E_j=j^2\), changes from \(14827\) at \((1,0,0)\) to \(9874\) at its half-turn image \((-1,0,0)\), contrary to the degree-zero rotation rule.
result: The inspected release is not justified as end-to-end equivariant by the stated component argument. Its use in the published runs and the effect on benchmark accuracy are unestablished.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a rotation-invariant nonzero-edge norm predicate and initialize scalar channels from invariant quantities such as \(\|p\|_2\). These repairs address the exhibited intermediate rules, without proving full-model equivariance.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Released split procedures do not produce an independent evaluation set
problems.source_location: Section 5.1, Figures 3–4, PDF pp. 7–9; Table 1, PDF p. 6; Appendix J.1, PDF p. 31.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 5.1 and Figures 3-4, pp. 7-9, assess generalization to unseen geometries. Appendix J.1, p. 31, separates radar train/validation material from test material. Table 1, p. 6, reports prediction MSE averaged over three seeds. These uses require a clear separation between examples used for model selection and the final test examples.

The public launcher, scripts/train.py, lines 17-21, seeds the global generators once and then constructs separate train, validation, and test dataset objects. The release contains two distinct split problems: independently regenerated drag partitions and radar validation selected directly from the test file.
analysis: Independent random repartitioning of the same source on train/validation/test construction does not produce complementary partitions and can overlap identities. The radar configurations are stronger counterevidence: validation and test explicitly use the same retained file. Neither observation identifies all historical table-producing splits.
The radar configuration samples validation from test_radar.nc and tests on that entire file. Thus \(V\subseteq T\) and \(V\cap T=V\), independently of seed. Radar train/test overlap is not inferred.
result: The released split construction does not guarantee independent held-out evaluation. The historical table-producing partitions are not identified, so no numerical leakage effect or corrected performance estimate is asserted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Save and reuse one identity manifest; draw radar validation from training material and preserve the test file for final evaluation. Respect shared-geometry groups as well as rows.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The drag MSE logger broadcasts predictions across the batch
problems.source_location: Table 1, PDF p. 6; released g2s/lightning/drag.py, lines 44–46 and 59–94.
claim: Paraphrase: Table 1, p. 6, reports mean squared prediction errors for mesh-to-sphere tasks. The corresponding public drag module logs {stage}/mse_error in g2s/lightning/drag.py, lines 44-46 and \(59\)-94.

The source trace is important because the bug is not in every loss calculation. Mesh2Drag.forward, g2s/models/geometry_2_sphere.py, lines 187-197, returns a spherical harmonic evaluation for one direction per sample. In the linked EquiHarmony implementation, SphericalHarmonics.forward, lines 85-98, that path returns shape \((B,1,1,1)\) for one output channel. The dataset target is reshaped to \((1,)\), so batch collation gives \((B,1)\). The logger subtracts the two tensors without aligning their shapes.
analysis: Prediction shape \((2,1,1,1)\) and target shape \((2,1)\) broadcast into all cross-sample differences. For perfect paired values \((-1,1)\), the resulting differences are \((0,-2,2,0)\), whose mean square is \(2\), while paired MSE is \(0\). This is a logger shape mismatch, separate from the correctly aligned loss paths.
The configured training loss squeezes both tensors and checkpoint selection monitors that loss; this does not establish an all-pairs training objective or identify the metric exported to Table 1.
result: A perfect-prediction witness disproves the logger, while the aligned training loss and unknown table-export path bound its demonstrated impact.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Reshape predictions and targets to the same sample-feature shape and assert equal dimensions before subtraction. For scalar targets, a common shape \((B,1)\) produces the intended mean of corresponding squared errors.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Repeated access overwrites the stored physical flight conditions
problems.source_location: Appendix J.2, PDF p. 31; released DragDataset.__getitem__, lines 114–117.
claim: Appendix J.2, p. 31, defines the drag samples using geometry, flight conditions, and a drag coefficient at the supplied orientation. In the public DragDataset.__getitem__, lines 114-117, the first three floating-point fields are converted with torch.from_numpy(self.float_data[idx][:\(3\)]), then each resulting tensor element is normalized by an in-place assignment.

The issue is functional preprocessing state, not a manuscript spelling error: from_numpy shares the NumPy slice’s storage. Assigning normalized values through that tensor overwrites the dataset’s original physical values. A later access therefore normalizes values that have already been normalized.
analysis: torch.from_numpy shares storage with the source slice. The first in-place normalization maps midpoint physical conditions to stored values \((0,0,0)\); the next access treats those normalized zeros as physical inputs and normalizes them again. The sample therefore depends on how often it has been accessed, rather than being a fixed preprocessing function.

For physical values \((25,250500000,0.25)\), first access stores normalized zeros. A second access then gives \((-1,-1-2/499,-1)\), instead of unchanged zeros. Fresh nonpersistent worker copies can prevent accumulation across epochs.
result: Repeated access mutates one stored sample; actual exposure depends on worker and access lifecycles.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Copy the source slice or clone its tensor before in-place normalization.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: A mesh with no padding is reduced to an empty vertex array
problems.source_location: Released g2s/datasets/mesh_dataset.py, MeshXarrayDataset._unpad_mesh_data, lines 211–224.
claim: The radar mesh path uses MeshXarrayDataset._unpad_mesh_data, g2s/datasets/mesh_dataset.py, lines 211-224. The helper requires a two-dimensional array with three columns and uses a configured sentinel, normally \(-10\), to identify placeholder rows before mesh reconstruction. Its explicit assumption is that a real mesh row does not have the sentinel in all three coordinates.
analysis: With no padding rows, num_placeholders is \(0\), and the released slice input[:-num_placeholders] becomes input[:\(0\)], an empty array. A valid unpadded triangle is erased. Appending one sentinel row gives a positive count and correctly restores the triangle, explaining why ordinary padded examples can pass.
result: The no-padding boundary empties a valid mesh; its incidence in the evaluated dataset is unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain non-sentinel rows directly, preserve unchanged data when padding is disabled, and reject all-padding meshes before downstream geometry.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released discrete state update selects a mode instead of sampling the declared categorical path
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, Eqs. (6)–(8) and Algorithm 2 final discrete step; uniform initialization, PDF p. 5.
claim: Paraphrase of the manuscript: Under the conditional path in Eq. (6), an atom type has categorical probabilities \(q_\alpha\). The vector-field construction in Eq. (7), its update in Eq. (8), and Algorithm 2’s final discrete step provide the sampling procedure for this path. Initialization uses uniformly distributed atom types (Section 4.1, page 5). Algorithm 2, line 13, page 23, explicitly calls for sampling from the updated categorical distribution.

The relevant public implementation is models/molopt_score_model_guide.py, function sample_guided_flow_VP, beginning at line 659. Lines 673–674 initialize the accumulator with the one-hot initial category. Lines 726–729 sample a predicted clean endpoint using torch.multinomial. Lines 732–735 update the accumulator. Lines 737–738 apply a softmax to that accumulator and then call argmax to choose the next atom type. The wrapper scripts/sample_flow_VP_guide.py initializes categories uniformly; the atom-type guidance weight defaults to zero. These locations concern the guided sampler actually being examined, rather than a similarly named function in the unguided model file.
analysis: Let the initial category \(a_0\) be uniform on \(\{e_1,e_2\}\), the endpoint be \(e_1\), and \(\alpha=1/4\). The conditional probabilities are \((1-\alpha)a_0+\alpha e_1\). Selecting their mode gives \(e_1\) with marginal probability \(1/2\), while drawing categorically gives \((1+\alpha)/2=5/8\). Earlier endpoint sampling cannot turn the later argmax into the declared categorical draw.
result: The current guided source still uses the mode. The exact conditional-oracle reduction disproves equivalence to the declared intermediate categorical law, without reproducing a full trained trajectory.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For the fixed-endpoint construction, draw from \((1-\alpha)a_0+\alpha a_1\); averaging over uniform \(a_0\) gives exactly the declared conditional marginal. A complete learned, guided sampler still needs a derivation ensuring valid probabilities; sampling softmax of an already normalized probability vector is not equivalent.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Gaussian-noise improvement does not imply proximity to an affinity minimum
problems.source_location: Appendix A.4, Eqs. (30)–(33), arXiv v2 PDF p. 22.
claim: Appendix A.4, PDF page 22, Eqs. (30)–(33), compares deterministic affinity \(f(n)\) with \(E[f(n+\delta Z)]\). A second-order expansion yields approximately
\[ E[f(n+\delta Z)]\approx f(n)+\frac{\delta^2}{2}f''(n). \]
The following prose infers that the predicted count lies near a local affinity minimum from the observed benefit of Gaussian noise.
analysis: Let \(\Phi\) be the standard normal CDF and \(f(x)=\Phi(x-1)\), a bounded smooth strictly increasing function with no local minimum. For \(n=1/2\) and \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), Gaussian convolution gives \(\mathbb E f(n+\delta Z)=\Phi(-1/(2\sqrt{1+\delta^2}))>\Phi(-1/2)=f(n)\) whenever \(\delta>0\). Noise improvement can therefore arise from curvature without proximity to a minimum.
result: The bounded monotone counterexample removes the minimum interpretation while allowing the reported empirical noise benefit to remain true.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain a conditional curvature statement: if \(f\in C^4(\mathbb R)\) with \(|f^{(4)}|\le M\), then \(\mathbb E f(n+\delta Z)-f(n)=\delta^2 f^{\prime\prime}(n)/2+r\), with \(|r|\le M\delta^4/8\). This does not imply stationarity or a nearby minimum, nor automatically describe the clipped and rounded integer-count pipeline.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The prefix quantity is residual prior entropy mass, not conditional Shannon entropy
problems.source_location: Section 3.1, Eqs. (4)–(5), PDF p. 4; released code/trie.py, lines 39–61 and compute_information_gain from line 126.
claim: Section 3.1, Eqs. (4)–(5), PDF p. 4, interprets a prefix score as Shannon uncertainty and its parent-minus-child difference as information gain. The displayed \(R_s\) sums fixed prior terms \(-p_i\log p_i\) over compatible items without conditional renormalization. Released code/trie.py, lines 39–61 and compute_information_gain from line 126, implements that same prior-mass sum.
analysis: For prior \((0.8,0.1,0.1)\), a prefix retaining the last two items gives posterior \((0.5,0.5)\). Its entropy is \(\log2\approx0.6931\), greater than the original \(0.6390\), but removing the first item's contribution produces a positive declared gain. If the retained mass is \(M\) and its normalized entropy is \(H\), the implemented residual is \(MH-M\log M\), not \(H\). The score remains a definable heuristic, with a different information-theoretic interpretation.
result: The normalized-entropy interpretation fails, but the implemented pruning score has a coherent unchanged interpretation and no recommendation-accuracy refutation follows.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe the unchanged quantity as residual prior entropy mass, or separately define and evaluate a conditionally normalized entropy score. These alternatives are different scoring rules.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Converting item-ID frequencies to title frequencies overwrites collisions
problems.source_location: Released code/compute_item_freq.py, load_item_titles, lines 9–29, and count_item_frequencies, lines 32–56.
claim: This is a released-code correctness finding, not an assertion that the paper contains a theorem about duplicate titles. In code/compute_item_freq.py, load_item_titles, lines 9–29, accepts a tab-separated title followed by an integer item ID. count_item_frequencies, lines 32–56, counts interaction rows by item ID and converts that counter to a dictionary keyed by title.
analysis: Two item IDs have frequencies \(5\) and \(7\) but share a title; a third title has frequency \(11\). Repeated title-key assignment overwrites the first frequency, producing total \(18\) instead of \(23\). Summing colliding frequencies restores title-level mass; keeping distinct item identities requires retaining an identifier.
result: Conditional preprocessing defect; its exposure in the actual benchmarks was not established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For title-level aggregation, add frequencies on title collisions rather than overwriting them. If item identity matters, preserve the separate item ID as well.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Adding a predictive modality need not increase confidence for each sample
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Proposition 1 and Eq. (1), PDF p. 5.
claim: Paraphrase of Proposition 1: For a sample with modality set \(M\), any nested subsets \(B\subseteq C\subseteq M\), and any multimodal classifier, the confidence on \(x_B\) is strictly less than the confidence on \(x_C\), which is no greater than the confidence on \(x_M\) (Section 3.2, PDF page 5). The surrounding discussion assumes that all modalities are predictive and motivates a positive relationship between confidence and additional modalities for a reliable classifier. Equation (1)’s benefit uses a related confidence comparison.

The problem is the pointwise guarantee. Conditional entropy is an expectation over observations, and its monotonicity does not imply monotonic confidence on every observed sample. The counterexample uses a proper inclusion \(B\subset C=M\), so it does not depend on the strict inequality’s trivial failure when two subsets are equal.
analysis: Take a balanced binary label and two conditionally independent predictive signals with accuracies \(0.9\) and \(0.8\). Observing a positive first signal gives posterior \(0.9\) and odds \(9\). On the positive-probability event that the second signal is negative, its likelihood ratio is \(1/4\), so the posterior becomes \(9/(9+4)=9/13<0.9\). This is the exact calibrated Bayes classifier. Expected conditional entropy can improve while confidence decreases on an individual observation.
result: The stated universal pointwise confidence monotonicity is false even for informative modalities and calibrated prediction. This undermines that theoretical justification; it does not by itself measure the training strategy's utility.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Replace the pointwise proposition by the average information inequality \(H(Y\mid X_C)\le H(Y\mid X_B)\), or weak average Bayes-accuracy monotonicity under its posterior assumptions. Neither result implies a per-sample confidence gate.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Released benefit scoring omits the confidence gate and changes the operational contribution scale
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Eq. (1), PDF p. 5; Section 3.3, Eq. (4), PDF p. 6; Eq. (5), PDF p. 7.
claim: Eq. (1), Section 3.2, PDF p. 5, gates benefit on both correct prediction and the specified confidence comparison. Eq. (4), Section 3.3, PDF p. 6, defines contribution \(\Phi_m\), while Eq. (5), PDF p. 7, applies the weak-modality threshold \(\Phi_m\le1\). The released scoring omits that confidence gate and uses a rescaled contribution.
analysis: Omitting the confidence comparison changes eligibility for the benefit. Independently, a contribution rescaling \(c_m=\Phi_m/2\) requires changing the weak-modality threshold \(\Phi_m\le1\) to \(c_m\le1/2\). Retaining threshold one after rescaling changes decisions for \(1<\Phi_m\le2\). Neither operation is an equivalent rewriting of the stated gate and contribution units.

A shared linear-fusion realization has correct-class probabilities \(0.9\) for audio alone, \(0.8\) for visual alone and \(0.7\) for both. With log-odds \(L_A,L_V,L_F\), choose shared bias \(b=L_A+L_V-L_F\) and contributions \(L_A-b,L_V-b\). Both proper confidence comparisons fail, yet the current correctness-only scorer gives full benefit \(2\). When full confidence instead equals \(0.95\), the gate passes and paper contributions are \(2\), versus code scores \(1\); the loader adds a weak-modality copy at \(1\) but none at \(2\).
result: An architecture-realizable probability fixture changes the gate and augmentation branch; the historical table-producing implementation remains unidentified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A manuscript-faithful implementation needs an explicit policy for the comparison subset in Eq. (1), must compute the stated confidence gate, and must use the Eq. (4) contribution in units consistent with all subsequent transformations and thresholds. A normalized contribution \(c_m=\Phi_m/2\) can also be used, but the paper’s weak threshold \(\Phi_m\le1\) then becomes \(c_m\le1/2\). Every dependent branch, masking rule, and transformation must be expressed in the same units; changing a single displayed constant does not prove the whole strategy coherent.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released loop selects saved checkpoints using test-set accuracy
problems.source_location: Released CMoB.py, dataset construction at lines 273–291 and checkpoint selection at lines 356–387.
claim: This finding concerns the released procedure and its ability to supply an independent final evaluation. CMoB.py, lines 273–275, creates a training dataset, a second dataset named train_val_dataset using training mode, and a dataset using test mode. Lines 291 onward wrap the latter in test_dataloader. At line 356, each epoch calls the evaluation function with that test loader. Lines 358–359 compare the returned accuracy with best_acc; lines 361–387 construct and save a checkpoint when it improves.

The data route is not inferred from variable names alone. datasets/dataloader.py, lines 29–40, maps training mode to train.csv, validation mode to val.csv, and the remaining test route to test.csv. A separate validation branch exists. The function name valid does not change the fact that the actual argument is test_dataloader.
analysis: Using test-loader accuracy to decide when to save a checkpoint makes that set part of model selection. The selected score is consequently not an independent final-test assessment for this loop. The public snapshot does not prove that the paper's historical tables used exactly this selection path.

For two independent fixed models with population accuracy \(1/2\), selecting the larger correctness bit on one test example reports expected accuracy \(3/4\). Selection on independent validation instead leaves expected test accuracy \(1/2\). This establishes the mechanism, not its magnitude in CMoB.
result: Current source routes test.csv into checkpoint selection; the amount of selection optimism and historical table provenance are unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Select checkpoints using an independent validation set, then evaluate the selected model once on an untouched test set. No new training or corrected test accuracy is supplied.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.
