problems.title: Absence of a rejection template does not establish semantic harmful compliance
problems.source_location: Appendix A.4.1, Eq. (12), arXiv v3 PDF pp. 16–17; Tables 5–6, p. 18; Section 4.4 and Table 4, p. 8.
claim: Paraphrase: Appendix A.4.1 states that an attack is successful when the response contains none of the predefined rejection templates; the ASR is the proportion of such responses. It describes these as non-rejecting and potentially unsafe responses, and states that automatic exact matching is used without manual labeling for this metric. See Eq. (12), pp. 16–17, and Tables 5–6, p. 18. The black-box figures of \(75.24\%\), \(70.06\%\), and \(56.55\%\) appear in Table 4 and Section 4.4 on p. 8.
The definition itself is explicit. The concern arises only when this operational score is interpreted as the proportion of responses that semantically assist a prohibited task.
analysis: For a prohibited request, the response ‘I decline.’ refuses assistance. The listed template ‘I must decline’ is not its substring, and the other listed templates do not match it. The lexical rule therefore labels success without semantic harmful compliance. This disproves equivalence between the two predicates; it does not recompute a reported success rate.
result: The latest paper retains lexical non-rejection as the operational ASR. It is not identical to substantive harmful compliance. The paper explicitly calls non-rejecting responses potentially unsafe and separately reports human semantic evaluation; no actual response-level error rate or revised ranking is established.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Describe the score as a lexical non-rejection proxy and distinguish it from a separate semantic compliance assessment. No new attack or unsafe-response generation is involved.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: A fixed \(0.2\) expert cap disagrees with Eq. (5) and can make class normalization undefined
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, Eq. (5), PDF pp. 6–7; released expert-weight cap and class-normalization implementation.
claim: Paraphrase preserving the relevant domain: Section 3.4, pp. 6–7, assigns newly introduced experts weight \(\alpha\), increases it by \(\beta\) per subsequent task, and caps each non-base weight at \(1/K\). Equation (5) gives, for active experts,
\[ w_i(t)=\min\{\alpha+\beta(t-i),1/K\}\quad(i>0),\qquad w_0(t)=1-\sum_{i=1}^{\min(t,K-1)}w_i(t). \]
analysis: For \(K=3\), the stated saturated expert weights are \((1/3,1/3,1/3)\), but a fixed \(0.2\) cap gives \((0.6,0.2,0.2)\). For \(K=6\), five non-base weights of \(0.2\) leave base weight zero, so a class eligible only for the base expert encounters normalization \(0/0\). These permitted settings show a local cap mismatch, not failure of every default run.

The explicit legal schedule uses \(K=6\), initial weight \(0.10\), increment \(0.05\), and \(40\) base classes followed by \(20\) tasks of \(3\) classes. At task \(7\), the five non-base weights reach \(0.2\), making the base residual zero. Under the paper cap \(1/6\), the residual is at least \(1/6\). The default \(K=5\) cap agrees with the formula.
result: The general expert-count release can become undefined, but the main five-expert configuration passes this specific cap control.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use cap \(1/K\), with initial weights also in \([0,1/K]\) and nonnegative increments. At most \(K-1\) non-base weights then leave residual at least \(1/K>0\), preserving positive class denominators through the always-eligible base expert.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released shared, frozen ResNet prefix can change during later-expert training
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF p. 5; Section 4.1, PDF p. 8; Appendix C.3 and Table 9, PDF pp. 23–24; released clover.py sharing loop.
claim: Section 3.2, PDF p. 5, states a shared encoder frozen after the first task. Section 4.1 and Appendix C.3, PDF pp. 8 and \(23\)–\(24\), describe sharing its first layers. Released clover.py, lines 74–81 and \(211\)–\(229\), chooses parameter names \(\texttt{conv1\_starting}\) and \(\texttt{bn1\_starting}\), aliases selected parameters and disables their gradients. The actual network stem in resnet_linear_turbo.py is named \(\texttt{conv1}\) and \(\texttt{bn1}\). Each training epoch also calls model.train().
analysis: The requested stem names do not match the actual \(\texttt{conv1}\) and \(\texttt{bn1}\) parameters, leaving those parameters trainable. Even corrected parameter aliases omit BatchNorm running-mean and variance buffers, which model.train() updates. Freezing gradients therefore does not preserve the claimed single shared frozen encoder function.
result: Stem-name mismatch and mutable BatchNorm state defeat the claimed released prefix invariant; corrected benchmark accuracy and historical checkout correspondence remain unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Share the actual prefix modules, freeze their parameters, and restore the frozen BatchNorm modules to evaluation mode after each general training-mode call. Parameter flags alone do not freeze buffers.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released foresight routine does not execute its requested DDIM interval under the checked dependency
problems.source_location: Section 3.2 and Algorithm 1, arXiv v1 PDF p. 5; current foresight_sampling_update and Diffusers DDIM/InverseDDIM step methods.
claim: Section 3.2 and Algorithm 1 define a selected forward-and-return interval. The current author routine assigns a custom timestep array before calling standard DDIM schedulers. Both the historical dependency examined and the latest Diffusers source instead select coefficients by the configured global stride.
analysis: With \(1000\) training steps and \(40\) inference steps, that stride is \(25\). A forward call at \(975\) uses \(950\), even when the custom array requests \(850\); the inverse call at \(850\) uses coefficients for \(825\to850\). Consequently the requested \(975\to850\to975\) interval is not executed, even with deterministic zero noise prediction. This is a scheduler-endpoint mismatch, not a general claim of exact reversibility for learned diffusion.

For a deterministic zero noise field, \(x=1\) and \(\bar\alpha_t=[1+(t/1000)^2]^{-1}\), the intended forward value is \(1.0641608508\), versus \(1.0125688439\) for the actual coefficient pair. The resulting mismatched round trip is \(1.0001850408\), while explicit reversed endpoints cancel to \(1\). This is direct arithmetic, with no image-generation claim.
result: Latest scheduler source still ignores the substituted endpoint array for these coefficient choices; the release/algorithm discrepancy does not refute the abstract fixed-point construction or quantify image quality.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a DDIM operator with both coefficient endpoints passed explicitly. This local reformulation does not establish improved image-benchmark scores.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Feasibility stopping does not certify the CAD projection
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1; Appendix C.1, PDF pp. 24–25 (arXiv v1 pp. 17–18).
claim: Appendix C.1, PDF pp. 24–25 (arXiv v1 pp. 17–18), explains stopping when \(\max_i(Ax^{(k)}-b)_i\le\epsilon\). Paraphrase preserving the qualification: the authors numerically observed that \(\|x-x^{(k)}\|_2\) is strictly increasing; assuming that observation holds generally, feasibility at zero tolerance is treated as equivalent to reaching \(P_C(x)\). The discussion then proposes lower and upper bounds on \(\|x-P_C(x)\|_2\) using the current distance and a Hoffman feasibility bound. This is presented as an empirical observation with an explicitly conditional argument, not as a proved monotonicity theorem. Algorithm 1 implements the feasibility-based stopping rule.

The precise suspect inference is from small constraint residual to small error relative to the projection of the original input. Feasibility measures proximity to any point of \(C\). Projection additionally minimizes distance to that input. A feasible nonoptimal iterate separates the two properties.
analysis: Feasibility bounds distance to the feasible set, whereas projection minimizes distance from the original input. A concrete CAD instance uses \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\-1&2\\-1&-4\\3&-3\end{pmatrix}\), \(b=(1,4,1,2)^\top\), and \(x^{(0)}=(6,-4)^\top\). Its origin is strictly feasible, all coordinate degrees equal four, and its only recession direction is zero. The exact projection is \(z^*=(11/21,-1/7)\), certified by nonnegative multipliers \((34/147,0,0,703/441)^\top\) satisfying stationarity and complementary slackness.

For the paper's equal-degree parallel Dykstra recurrence, the historical exact-rational calculation gives its first feasible iterate at \(k=40\), approximately \[(0.5223756630,-0.1442116690)\], with projection error \(0.001972485\). The squared distance from the input falls from \(44.8715776762\) at iteration \(39\) to \(44.8714720330\) at iteration \(40\), contrary to the monotonicity premise. A fresh independent rational evaluation of the displayed recurrence confirms the iterate and residual; the KKT certificate states the comparison target directly.
result: Feasibility stopping alone does not provide the asserted projection-error certificate, and the conditional monotonicity premise fails on this bounded example. The asymptotic CAD convergence theorem is not refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use feasible primal and nonnegative dual points with \(F(z)=\|z-x\|_2^2/2\) and \(d(\lambda)=\lambda^\top(Ax-b)-\|A^\top\lambda\|_2^2/2\). The gap gives \(\|z-P_C(x)\|_2\le\sqrt{2(F(z)-d(\lambda))}\); a feasibility residual alone does not.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Proposition 1’s exactness criterion needs a dimensionality qualification
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Proposition 1(2), PDF p. 7; proof in Appendix A.2, PDF p. 23.
claim: Proposition 1, part \(2\), Section 3.3, PDF p. 7, and its proof in Appendix A.2, PDF p. 23, assert the following equivalence. Paraphrase: for a polytope represented by nonredundant linear inequalities and a point where projection is differentiable, \(S(x)=J(x)\) if and only if \(x\) lies in the ambient interior of \(C\), or \(P_C(x)\) lies in the interior of all but one defining half-space. The statement does not explicitly require \(C\) to be full-dimensional.

The converse proof identifies a locally \((n-1)\)-dimensional boundary with exactly one active defining inequality. That inference requires additional geometric qualifications and fails for lower-dimensional polytopes represented by inequalities.
analysis: The bounded set \(C=\{(u,v):u\le0,-u\le0,v\le1,-v\le1\}=\{0\}\times[-1,1]\) has four individually nonredundant inequalities. Near \(x=(1,0)\), projection is \((u,v)\mapsto(0,v)\), so \(J(x)=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\). The residual direction is \((1,0)\), giving the same surrogate \(S(x)=I-dd^\top\), despite two active inequalities and empty ambient interior. A dimensionality or representation-independent active-rank qualification is necessary.
result: The universal necessity statement omits a geometric qualification. This lower-dimensional example does not occur in a strictly feasible full-dimensional benchmark construction and does not refute the other surrogate properties.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State full dimensionality and an irredundant facet representation, or outside the set use the representation-independent condition \(S(x)=J(x)\) exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}J(x)=n-1\), at differentiability points.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The stated constraint generator does not guarantee bounded polytopes
problems.source_location: Appendix B.2, PDF p. 24 (random constraint generator).
claim: Appendix B.2, PDF p. 24, describes a sparse matrix with nonzero rows, independently sampled unit-length columns, and \(b=u+As\) with \(u_i\sim U(0.1,1)\) and Gaussian \(s\). Paraphrase: the construction produces nonempty bounded polytopes and guarantees that a radius-\(0.1\) ball fits inside the feasible set. The positive offsets indeed make \(s\) strictly feasible. They do not constrain recession directions.
analysis: Take \(A=\begin{pmatrix}3/5&5/13\\4/5&12/13\end{pmatrix}\), \(u=(1/2,1/2)\), and \(b=u+As\). Both columns have norm one, every row is nonzero, and \(\det A=16/65\). Yet \(v=(-1,-1)\) satisfies \(Av=(-64/65,-112/65)^\top<0\), so \(s+tv\) is feasible for every \(t\ge0\). The set is strictly feasible but unbounded.

Column normalization also does not guarantee a radius-\(0.1\) inscribed ball. In three dimensions, choose rows \(\pm(3/5,3/5,3/5)\) and \(\pm(\sqrt{14}/10)e_j\) for each axis, with offsets \(0.101\). Columns have norm one and the coordinate constraints make the set bounded, but the first row pair confines it to a slab of width \(2(0.101)/(3\sqrt3/5)\approx0.194375<0.2\). No radius-\(0.1\) ball can fit.
result: The generator's algebraic conditions establish strict feasibility, but do not guarantee boundedness or the stated inradius. No claim is made that the authors' stored experimental matrices actually had these defects.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Enforce row margins \(u_i\ge0.1\|a_i\|_2\) and finite box constraints around the feasible center with half-widths at least \(0.1\). These conditions certify the ball and boundedness, but they change the generated instance distribution.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Candidate factor-of-two discrepancy in the printed DCP update
problems.source_location: Appendix D.6, Eq. (D.1), PDF p. 27 (arXiv v1 p. 20).
claim: This item is not counted as a supported substantive error under the requested exclusion of typographical mistakes. Appendix D.6, equation (D.1), PDF p. 27 (arXiv v1 p. 20), decomposes \(Q=D-C\) and prints an update whose linear term contains \(Dx^{(k)}\). For the displayed quadratic objective \(F(z)=z^TDz-z^TCz+c^Tz\), differentiation gives \(2Dx^{(k)}\) when \(D\) is symmetric diagonal. The source code for this baseline was unavailable to this audit, so the executed baseline cannot be inferred from that line alone.
analysis: Differentiating \(z^\top Dz\) for symmetric \(D\) gives \(2Dz\). In the scalar case \(D=3\), \(C=2\), \(c=0\), feasible interval \([-1,1]\), and current point \(1/2\), the printed update maximizes \(3(1/2)z-2z^2\), yielding \(3/8\). The stated objective \(F(z)=z^2\) decreases from \(1/4\) to \(9/64\). The baseline source is unavailable, so this remains a literal-formula concern whose implementation impact is unresolved.
result: Literal-formula discrepancy supported; effect on the executed baseline remains unresolved and is not counted as an established empirical defect.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The tangent update uses \(2Dx^{(k)}\); maximizing its touching global lower surrogate gives a nondecreasing objective. This local ascent property does not imply global nonconvex optimality.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Rotating a closed tour creates an impossible positive label
problems.source_location: Task 2, arXiv v1 PDF p. 4; Appendix B.1.2, pp. 15–16; data_gen.py compare_routes, lines 185–218.
claim: Task \(2\), PDF p. 4 and Appendix B.1.2, PDF pp. 15–16, defines a positive candidate as an optimal next-node connection. Released sample_codes/1_data_gen/data_gen.py, compare_routes, rotates closed tours to align them while retaining their repeated terminal vertex.
analysis: Take the simple closed tour lists \(O=(0,6,1,2,3,4,5,0)\) and \(G=(0,6,3,1,2,4,5,0)\), aligned from vertex \(4\). The source forward rotation makes \(O\) into \((4,5,0,0,6,1,2,3)\), while the greedy sequence begins \((4,5,0,6,\ldots)\). Their first reported divergence is therefore \[(\mathrm{current},\mathrm{negative},\mathrm{positive})=(0,6,0)\]. A self-edge cannot be a next unvisited choice in any Hamiltonian cycle; moreover \(\{0,6\}\) is an edge of the supplied optimal tour.

Rotating only the distinct cycle vertices instead yields the first divergence \((6,3,1)\). The defect is preservation of cycle representation, before any probe fit. The paper describes an additional constrained-optimality filter that is absent from this sample path and could protect a different historical pipeline.
result: The current sample generator can create an impossible supervised target, but its exposure in the original filtered probing datasets is unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Remove the repeated closure endpoint before modular rotation or reversal; validate distinct candidates and source-tour adjacency, then perform the stated forced-negative and forbidden-positive optimization checks.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Held-out rows are not held-out routing instances
problems.source_location: Appendix B.2.1, arXiv v1 PDF p. 17; example_probing_exp.ipynb cells 7 and 15.
claim: Appendix B.2.1, PDF p. 17, describes training/test splits but does not require grouping by routing instance. The released probing notebook creates a positive and a negative Task \(2\) row for each instance, then splits rows rather than instance identifiers.
analysis: Positive and negative probe rows share one underlying routing instance and embeddings. Splitting rows independently can put one member into training and the paired member into testing. The resulting score measures held-out rows, not generalization to independent routing instances; grouping by instance is required for that interpretation.
result: The released split supports generalization to held-out rows, not necessarily new routing instances. The paper does not explicitly state the stronger grouping rule, and the historical score inflation is not quantified.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: If the intended claim concerns unseen routing instances, assign and retain an instance_id before creating rows. Split those IDs, or use GroupShuffleSplit, and place every row and every repeated extraction from an instance in the same partition. For model comparisons, preserve the same grouped split across models and layers. Any hyperparameter selection or feature selection must remain within training groups.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released plotting cell does not identify the stated adjusted-significance analysis
problems.source_location: Adjusted-significance statement, PDF p. 8; released sample notebook, cell 19.
claim: The paper's PDF p. 8 states Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control over \(256\) dimensions; the released sample notebook's cell 19 marks raw p-values.
analysis: Raw thresholds do not implement BH adjustment. However, an unadjusted example cell does not prove the correction was never run elsewhere. The complete p-value family, correction operation and adjusted output are needed to verify the reported adjusted decisions.
result: Evidence gap concerning historical adjusted-significance provenance; no substitute significance verdict is supplied.
assumptions: Bounded to the stated source/component; no published-run provenance inferred.

problems.title: The small-mask byte encoding removes foreground before supervision
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, Eq. (8), PDF p. 6; released scene/dataset_readers.py, lines 162–175.
claim: Section 3.4, Eq. (8), PDF p. 6, includes small-object supervision. Released scene/dataset_readers.py, lines 162–175, thresholds a Pillow mode-L mask by whether each pixel exceeds \(128\). utils/general_utils.py, lines 23–25, divides the resulting bytes by \(255\), and utils/camera_utils.py, lines 46–48, applies threshold \(0.5\). train.py skips small masks that become empty.
analysis: The mode-L threshold stores foreground bytes as \(1\), not \(255\). Dividing by \(255\) therefore gives \(1/255\), below the next threshold \(0.5\). Foreground inputs such as \(129\) and \(255\) are erased before the small-mask supervision loop. This is deterministic for the inspected reader, while its role in historical table-producing runs remains unidentified.
result: The current byte reader deterministically erases small foreground; exposure in historical scene training and the corresponding mIoU change are unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Preserve the byte convention by returning \(255\) for foreground and \(0\) otherwise before division by \(255\), or use a consistently Boolean path.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Initialization does not consistently preserve frame, granularity, and object identity
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, Eq. (4), PDF p. 5; released helpers/object_specific_initialization.py.
claim: Section 3.3, p. 5, assigns an object ID using the visible point’s mask region and merges duplicate object tracks using the means of their Gaussian centers and colors; Equation (4) describes that distance. The following three subcases concern the released helpers/object_specific_initialization.py. They are separate failure mechanisms within one correspondence invariant. The README’s existing To be verified status applies directly to this helper.
analysis: Three distinct identity mechanisms fail: a training-only frame counter indexes masks loaded for all frames; small-object means use middle-object membership; and merged masks are renumbered while Gaussian IDs retain old labels. Each can associate valid geometry with the wrong supervision independently of mask encoding.

With sorted frames \(0,1,2\), only \(0,2\) used for training, the second accepted observation reads frame \(1\) masks because the counter advances only for training frames. A point owned by object \(0\) in both actual training frames can therefore be assigned object \(1\).

For small groups with centers \[0.005,10.005,20.005,-9.795\], nested into middle groups \(\{0,1\}\) and \(\{2,3\}\), the wrong selector compares middle centers \(5.005,5.105\). Colors \[(0,0,0),(2,2,2),(1,1,1),(3,3,3)\] yield implemented distance \(0.1+20\sqrt3/255<0.5\), whereas the intended first two small groups give \(10+40\sqrt3/255>0.5\).
Merging initial IDs \(0,1\) among \(0,1,2\) leaves point IDs \((0,0,2)\), but compacted mask folders are \(0,1\). The surviving last object thus has incompatible identifiers.
result: The inspected correspondence helper violates those source-level identity contracts. Its own README marks it ‘To be verified’; this is affirmative reason not to infer that the published experiments used the same incomplete helper.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Align frame keys, select membership from the matching granularity, and apply one explicit merge/reindex map to both masks and Gaussian IDs.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The Gaussian persistence loop cancels every pruning proposal
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, PDF p. 6; released scene/gaussian_model.py, GaussianModel.densify_and_prune, lines 387–421.
claim: Section 3.4, PDF p. 6, protects an object against complete pruning. Released scene/gaussian_model.py, GaussianModel.densify_and_prune, lines 387–421, clears an object's pruning flags when its original count is below \(1000\). Otherwise it compares that count with a new sum over the same unfiltered object membership and clears the flags when they agree.
analysis: The persistence loop compares each object's original count with a fresh sum over that same unfiltered membership, an identity. It consequently clears every nonempty object's pruning flags, even for \(1001\) points proposing one deletion with \(1000\) survivors. The loop does not implement a test of the number of proposed survivors.
result: The current membership-count identity cancels all valid scalar-ID pruning proposals; its full-scene memory and accuracy effects remain unmeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Count proposed survivors \(r_g=\sum_{j\in S_g}(1-P_j)\) and explicitly enforce the selected minimum. Comparing the original membership count with itself cannot detect extinction.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The query helper changes both the score and eligible object levels
problems.source_location: Granularity definitions, PDF p. 4; Section 3.5, Eqs. (9)–(11), PDF p. 7.
claim: Section 3.5, Equations (9)–(11), p. 7, averages per-view object embeddings, embeds the text query, and selects the object with maximal cosine similarity. The method also introduces large, middle, and small granularities on p. 4.

In helpers/evaluation.py, extract_CLIP_embeddings at line 72 calls model.encode_image and averages the resulting features. calculate_IoU calls model.encode_text at line 143 and forms matrix products at lines 148–149, with no normalization of these mean embeddings. The small-level similarity and selection are commented out at lines 150 and \(156\)–158. The final branch at lines 165–170 compares only large and middle candidates.
analysis: For query \((1,0)\), raw dot products rank object \((2,2)\) above \((1,0)\), with scores \(2\) and \(1\). Cosines reverse that order, giving \(1/\sqrt2\) and \(1\). Unnormalized averaged image embeddings therefore do not implement the stated cosine ranking. Independently, omitting small-level candidates prevents selecting a legitimate small-level winner.
result: Unnormalized means can reverse cosine rankings and small candidates are excluded, without a measured benchmark-query failure rate.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The proposed correction normalizes final nonzero object means and query, and evaluates the explicitly declared candidate granularities with identities attached.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: IoU threshold filtering alone does not guarantee unique pixel ownership
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, PDF p. 5.
claim: The source describes IoU-based mask filtering as ensuring one object per pixel at a granularity.
analysis: Masks \(\{0,1,2,3\}\) and \(\{3,4,5,6\}\) overlap at one pixel but have IoU \(1/7<0.5\), so both survive the stated threshold. Filtering by overlap magnitude does not guarantee disjoint pixel ownership. A later single-valued assignment also does not make the input masks themselves disjoint.
result: Supported scope qualification of the uniqueness guarantee; no arbitrary semantic overlap-resolution rule is invented.
assumptions: Bounded to the stated source/component; no published-run provenance inferred.

problems.title: A common requested generation budget becomes \(140\) tokens only on the non-verification branch
problems.source_location: Tables 2–5; Appendix C experimental settings; released defense_query and nondefense_query max_new_token interfaces.
claim: The released evaluation caller requests \(512\) new tokens through defense_query. It routes verification-enabled requests to meta_defense and other requests to nondefense_query, which replaces the requested budget with \(140\); the verification branch does not make the same replacement. This concerns the protocol behind Tables 2–5 and Appendix C.
analysis: The same caller budget therefore produces branch limits \(512\) and \(140\). EOS can stop either branch earlier, but it does not make these different permitted budgets equal. This is an interface/protocol discrepancy, not a new attack-success measurement.
result: A hard-coded branch budget changes the evaluation contract; no actual ASR or latency effect is measured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Forward the caller response budget unchanged and cap each chunk by its remaining budget; report diagnostic-token accounting separately.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released decision rule and check interval differ from Algorithm 1
problems.source_location: Algorithm 1, lines 4, 9, 13 and 16, PDF p. 6.
claim: Algorithm 1, PDF p. 6, lines 4 and \(13\), rejects when the next-token diagnostic probabilities satisfy \(p_h>p_b\), for harmful and harmless labels. Lines 9 and \(16\) set the next interval to \(k=\gamma p_b\). Released meta_defense instead checks generated diagnostic text for the harmful substring and applies a different clamped interval update.
analysis: A valid first-token distribution can have \(p_h=0.3\), \(p_b=0.2\), and another token with probability \(0.5\). The printed comparator rejects. Unrestricted greedy generation instead selects the third token, whose continuation need not contain the harmful substring, allowing the text rule to accept. A two-label-constrained diagnostic is a matching special case, but the release does not impose that restriction.
For \(\gamma=32\) and harmless probability \(0.2\), the printed interval is \(6.4\), while the current half-scale clamp schedules \(16\). This is not an integer-rounding difference.
result: Valid diagnostic probabilities and low-confidence scheduling differ from Algorithm 1; real-model disagreement frequency remains unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the already-computed two-label probabilities with a stated tie policy, or explicitly specify and evaluate the generated-text decision. State a coherent rounded and capped interval policy.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Early termination does not establish the stronger claim that flagged content is blocked before exposure
problems.source_location: Abstract, PDF p. 1; Algorithm 1, line 14, PDF p. 6; Appendix D.12–D.13, PDF p. 22.
claim: Original claims and locations (paraphrase). The abstract on p.1 describes stopping generation to prevent further harmful content. That is a limited stopping objective. Appendix D.12–D.13, p.22, uses stronger language: the mechanism can block staged harm before emission and prevent unsafe content exposure. Algorithm 1, p.6, line 14, instead returns the accumulated partial response plus a safety reminder after detecting that partial response as harmful.
analysis: Algorithm 1 returns the accumulated flagged response with a reminder; the current mid-generation rejection branch returns that decoded response and a rejection flag, without adding the reminder. The evaluator stores the response as output. Thus a successfully detected neutral marker would still be returned, independent of its content. Stopping later chunks does not withhold the flagged prefix; the abstract's narrower continuation-prevention claim survives.
result: Supported limit on the stronger exposure-prevention statement, without claiming every early-stop defense is ineffective.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Either state the retained-prefix early-stop scope, or buffer unapproved content and withhold it when flagged. A reminder cannot retract already exposed text, and classifier false negatives remain outside a conditional withholding contract.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The claim of lower ASR across every architecture and baseline contradicts Tables 2–4
problems.source_location: LLMClassifier baseline, PDF p. 7; Section 5.1, PDF p. 8; Tables 2–4.
claim: Claim/location (paraphrase). The summary at the end of Section 5.1, p.8, states that MetaDefense consistently has lower ASR across all architectures/templates than alignment, finetuning, inference, and hybrid baselines. LLM-Classifier is expressly identified as an inference-stage baseline on p.7 and included in Tables 2–4.
analysis: Tables 2–4 report higher MetaDefense ASR than LLM-Classifier in \(8\) of \(12\) architecture/template averages, including every LLaMA-2 comparison. For example direct LLaMA-2 ASR is \(1.0\%\) versus \(0.1\%\); Qwen refusal-suppression ASR is \(11.1\%\) versus \(0.4\%\). These displayed means contradict universal lower-ASR wording. They do not establish significance or negate the single-model memory advantage.
result: The universal lower-ASR wording is not supported by every displayed comparator. The individual table entries and other advantages are not rejected.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State the mixed LLM-Classifier comparison and the separate memory/utility tradeoff; retain the displayed numerical tables.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The asymmetric relative-error definition does not imply the square approximation-ratio bound
problems.source_location: arXiv v1 Eq. (5), PDF p. 7; Theorem 3.1, p. 8; Theorem 4.1, p. 12; proof Eq. (9), p. 13.
claim: Eq. (5), PDF p. 7, and the proof supporting Theorem 3.1 use the relative-error definition \(e=\sup_C|f_P(C)-f_S(C)|/f_S(C)\) to claim an approximation-transfer factor \((1+e)^2\). The weighted subset may have nonnegative weights and \(e\in(0,1)\).
analysis: Let \(P\) contain nineteen zeros and one one, and let \(S\) put weight \(10\) at each support point \(0,1\). For center \(c\), costs are \(f_P(c)=20c^2-2c+1\) and \(f_S(c)=20c^2-20c+10\). With \(u=c-1/2\), the ratio \(18|u|/(20u^2+5)\) has supremum \(e=0.9\). The \(S\)-optimal center \(1/2\) has \(P\)-cost \(5\), while \(\operatorname{OPT}_P=19/20\). Its ratio \(100/19\approx5.263\) exceeds \((1+0.9)^2=3.61\), even with no noise.
result: The square-factor transfer claim is false for an admissible weighted subset. The error definition gives factors one minus and one plus the error, rather than reciprocal one-plus-error bounds.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For \(e<1\), retain \((1-e)f_S\le f_P\le(1+e)f_S\). Comparing an approximately optimal coreset solution with the true optimum then gives the valid transfer factor \((1+e)/(1-e)\), multiplied by the coreset solution's approximation factor.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Admissible independent noise makes the current relative-error bound infinite with probability \(16\%\)
problems.source_location: arXiv v1 Lemma 4.2, PDF p. 12; proof pp. 14–15 (conference Lemma C.2).
claim: Lemma 4.2, PDF p. 12, claims a finite relative-error bound with probability greater than \(0.9\) under independent centered unit-variance Bernstein noise, without restricting the noise to a Gaussian law. Its proof supports Theorem 3.1.
analysis: Set \(P=\{-a,a\}\), \(a=\sqrt5/2\), and corrupt both points independently with noise taking \(-a,0,a\) with probabilities \((0.4,0.2,0.4)\). This noise is centered, has variance \(1\), is bounded and satisfies the Bernstein moment condition. The event that the two noises are respectively \(a,-a\) has probability \(0.16\) and collapses the noisy dataset to \(\{0,0\}\).

On that event, for every \(c\ne0\), \(f_{\widehat P}(c)=2c^2\) and \(f_P(c)=2c^2+5/2\). Hence \(|f_{\widehat P}-f_P|/f_{\widehat P}=5/(4c^2)\to\infty\) as \(c\to0\). The finite-bound success probability is at most \(0.84<0.9\), even though the clean optimum \(5/2\) exceeds the total noise variance \(2\).
result: Current Lemma 4.2 is false on its stated noise domain; a convention at a zero denominator cannot repair divergence through positive denominators. Guarantees depending on that lemma need a replacement argument or stronger assumptions.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A sufficient extra condition is \(q=\sqrt{R/\operatorname{OPT}_P}<1\), where \(R=\sum_p\|\xi_p\|_2^2\). The distance-vector triangle inequality gives \((1-q)^2f_P\le f_{\widehat P}\le(1+q)^2f_P\), hence error at most \((1-q)^{-2}-1\). This conditional replacement does not recover the unrestricted theorem.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Gaussian fourth moments and conditional normality are used under a non-Gaussian model
problems.source_location: arXiv v1 Claim 4.4, PDF pp. 13–14, Eq. (11); Claim 5.6 and Lemma 5.7, pp. 17–19.
claim: Claim 4.4's proof, Eq. (11), PDF p. 14, uses Gaussian chi-square variance to bound the sum of squared noises under the broader Bernstein model. Claim 5.6 and Lemma 5.7 also invoke Gaussian conditional distributions.
analysis: A centered unit-variance Laplace variable has \(\mathbb E\xi^4=6\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(\xi^2)=5\), exceeding the Gaussian value \(2\) and the relaxed printed bound \(3\). A one-variable sum remains Laplace, not Gaussian. However, the intermediate Claim 4.4 probability conclusion can instead follow from \(R\ge0\), \(\mathbb ER=\theta nd\), and Markov's inequality, which gives \(\Pr(R\le60\theta nd)\ge59/60>0.95\). The invalid proof step does not by itself falsify that conclusion.
result: The displayed Gaussian moment argument is invalid under the broader noise class, but the cited intermediate probability conclusion has a distribution-free Markov proof; this local proof correction is Minor.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Replace the Gaussian-specific proof of the stated intermediate norm bound by Markov’s inequality using \(\mathbb ER=\theta nd\). Recalculate other bounds for the actual noise class rather than assuming conditional normality.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Two arguments for the new metric use invalid inequalities
problems.source_location: arXiv v1 proof of Lemma 5.4, PDF p. 23; Claim A.2 and proof Eq. (17), p. 41.
claim: The two proofs use a near-optimal-set ratio bound and a union-optimum/containment implication under their stated overlap assumptions.
analysis: For \(S=\widehat P=\{-1,1\}\), \(\alpha=2\), and center \(0\), all approximation ratios equal one. Lemma 5.4's displayed intermediate estimate would require \(0\le1/2-1=-1/2\). Separately, for disjoint sets \(\{-3,-1\}\) and \(\{1,3\}\), the one-center optima sum to \(4\), but their union optimum is \(20\); the stated overlap setup does not justify the proof's \(20\le4\) step. These are two invalid arguments, not complete counterexamples to every final new-metric theorem.

For the union example, set \(\alpha=17\) and \(\alpha^{\prime}=1\). Each component’s optimal mean has ratio \(17\) on the other component, satisfying both stated overlap conditions. At center \(5/2\), the union ratio \(9/4\) lies below the claimed near-optimal threshold \(13/5\), but the first component ratio is \(85/4>17\), also falsifying the asserted containment.
result: The specified intermediate inequalities are false. Their effect on all final new-metric guarantees has not been established, so the finding is kept as a bounded Minor proof defect rather than a blanket theorem rejection.

problems.title: The released proposed construction uses clean data to choose which noisy points to retain
problems.source_location: arXiv v1 Algorithm 1, PDF p. 12; observation-only scope p. 7; implementation p. 27; current algorithms.py our_coreset.
claim: Algorithm 1 constructs from noisy observations, and p. 7 explicitly excludes clean-data access. Current algorithms.py fits KMeans to X_noise but computes the construction distances with clean X before trimming.
analysis: Hold observations \(\widehat X=(0,1,2,3,4)\) fixed, with one fitted center \(2\). Clean inputs \(X_A=(0,1,2,3,4)\) and \(X_B=(0,1,2,3,100)\) give clean distances \((2,1,0,1,2)\) and \((2,1,0,1,98)\). The stated radius rule retains all five noisy points in the first case and discards the last in the second. Thus unobserved clean inputs can change a construction intended to depend only on the identical observations. Its historical benchmark impact remains unidentified.
result: Identical observations can produce different retained sets when only the unavailable clean input changes; the published-run identity and empirical effect remain unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Compute construction radii and retained indices from noisy observations only; reserve clean data for final evaluation and keep it out of the construction interface.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Sampled points receive weights indexed by their new row rather than their source cluster
problems.source_location: arXiv v1 Algorithm 1, PDF p. 12; implementation p. 27; algorithms.py our_coreset weight assignment.
claim: Algorithm 1 and Appendix G.1 require a point sampled from cluster \(i\) to receive weight \(|P_i'|/|S_i|\). Released code/algorithms.py builds S_indices and a new sampled array, but uses labels indexed by the new row number rather than by its selected source index.
analysis: If sampled output row \(j\) came from source row \(s_j\), its weight must use the cluster label of \(s_j\). The label of source row \(j\) may belong to a different cluster, so indexing the old label array by the new row number can assign another cluster's weight. When every point is retained in original order the indices agree, explaining that matching control.
result: The current index mismatch assigns weights from another cluster; a global mass check can miss it and actual benchmark distortion is unmeasured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the cluster label at each sampled source index, consistently for numerator and sample count, when assigning its output weight.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The baseline uses with-replacement importance weights after without-replacement sampling
problems.source_location: arXiv v1 implementation of CN, PDF p. 27; current algorithms.py get_coreset.
claim: The released baseline samples without replacement but assigns weights derived from with-replacement draw probabilities. The concern is the resulting estimator, not an asserted failure of every coreset guarantee.
analysis: Without-replacement inclusion probability \(\pi_i\) generally differs from \(mp_i\), so weighting by \(1/(mp_i)\) does not yield the usual unbiased estimator. At \(m=n\), every point is included with probability one, but unequal \(p_i\) still produce unequal weights and distort the full empirical measure. This proves the sampling/weighting mismatch, while the effect on a particular high-probability coreset guarantee remains unresolved.
result: Supported implementation/statistical distinction; effect on the cited baseline guarantee is unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use with-replacement draws with multiplicity-aware weights, or a specified without-replacement design with inclusion weights \(1/\pi_i\). A full-population shortcut should return unit weights.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Equal covariance does not make every bivariate-distribution edge rule equal
problems.source_location: Theorem 1 and Corollary 1, PDF p. 5; Appendix C, PDF p. 25.
claim: Claim and location (paraphrase). Theorem 1 and Corollary 1, p.5, consider dimension at least three, equality of all second-order lagged moments used by the edge rule, and at least one differing cumulant of order at least three. They conclude that every pairwise generator from the preceding bivariate-distribution definition returns the same adjacency. Appendix C, p.25, supplies the proof.
analysis: At every time independently, process \(A\) is \((U,V,UV)\) for independent fair Rademacher variables \(U,V\). Process \(B\) has independent coordinates each taking \(-\sqrt2,0,\sqrt2\) with probabilities \((1/4,1/2,1/4)\). Both are bounded, stationary, centered, have covariance \(I_3\), and have zero nonzero-lag covariances. Their third joint cumulants are \(1\) and \(0\).

The permitted bivariate edge functional \(\mathbb E[X_1^4X_2^2]\) is \(1\) for \(A\) and \(2\) for \(B\). Thresholding it at \(3/2\) gives different binary edges. Equal second moments therefore do not make every bivariate-distribution edge rule equal. Restricting the rule to covariance, or matching full bivariate laws, restores the corresponding restricted implication.
result: The theorem's universal bivariate-rule conclusion is false. This narrows its impossibility claim while preserving the motivation that some higher-order interactions are invisible to pairwise information.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Restrict the rule to matched second-order inputs, or strengthen the premise to equality of the full bivariate laws used by each rule. Equal-pair-law XOR examples still establish a restricted higher-order non-identifiability result.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Positive conditional variance does not imply different marginal distributions
problems.source_location: Appendix B, Lemma 2, PDF pp. 24–25; Theorem 3.
claim: Claim and location (paraphrase). Appendix B, pp. 24–25, Lemma 2 states that \(\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)>0\) almost surely implies \(X\) and \(Y\) are not equal in distribution. Theorem 3 applies this along project, group, subject, and sample levels and concludes all six pairs of graph distributions differ.
analysis: Independent \(X,Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) have the same marginal law, yet \(\operatorname{Var}(X\mid Y)=1/4>0\) almost surely. Equal distributions do not imply equality on each outcome. Likewise, take four independent Bernoulli edge indicators for two-node graphs at the hierarchy levels. Every parent-conditioned edge variance is \(1/4\), but all four graph laws coincide. Neither the lemma nor all six claimed pairwise distinctions follow.
result: The formal distributional-distinction argument is false. Different semantic hierarchy levels or empirically different fitted graphs do not repair that universal implication.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State conditional nondeterminism as the consequence of positive conditional variance; provide assumptions or statistics distinguishing marginal laws before asserting distributional separation.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The higher-order expressivity proof contains independent invalid steps and does not prove optimization convergence
problems.source_location: Theorem 2, PDF p. 6; Section 7, PDF p. 10; Appendix D, Theorem 4 and Lemmas 3–5, PDF pp. 26–27.
claim: Claim/location (paraphrase). Theorem 2, p.6, and Theorem 4, Appendix D, pp. 26–27, claim arbitrarily small classification risk for measurable higher-order rules and a class-separable measurable label map. The sentence following Theorem 2, and Section 7 on p.10, additionally attribute convergence of GCM to that theorem. Appendix D uses Lemmas 3–5.
analysis: The printed sampler first places its edge parameter \(A\) in \((0,1)\). For standard Gumbel noise \(M\), the desired off-edge event satisfies \(\Pr(\operatorname{sigmoid}((A+M)/\tau)<1/4)=\exp[-\exp(A+\tau\log3)]\le e^{-1}<0.368\). Increasing the earlier raw parameter cannot make that event arbitrarily probable after the intervening sigmoid.

A separate lemma claims any continuous injective node map has an injective tagged sum. The identity map with distinct one-hot tags gives equal sums for feature triples \((0,2,0)\) and \((1,1,0)\), despite different tagged inputs. Finally, a continuous MLP cannot uniformly approximate the measurable step \(\mathbf1\{x_1\ge0\}\) below error \(1/2\) on the whole cube. These invalidate the supplied expressivity argument; representational existence would not establish optimizer convergence in any event.
result: The supplied proof establishes neither its unrestricted expressivity statement nor optimization convergence. Suitable restricted or alternative constructions may still be possible; this is not a claim that higher-order learning is impossible.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: A revised proof must use a sampler capable of the stated graph approximation, an explicitly suitable tagged encoder, and a valid probability/risk approximation argument. Treat optimizer convergence separately from representational existence.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Both released binarizers return all-ones graphs; the released loss also omits the stated sparsity term
problems.source_location: Section 5, Eq. (3), PDF p. 6; BBA ablation, PDF pp. 8–9; Algorithm 2, PDF p. 27; current models.py and official supplementary code/models.py.
claim: Claim/location (paraphrase). Section 5, p.6, Eq. (3), Algorithm 2, p.27, and the BBA ablation discussion, pp.8–\(9\), require selection of a bounded number of high-scoring edges. The method’s loss is \(L=L_1+\alpha L_2+\beta R\) with an \(\ell_1\) sparsity term. The relevant released functions are in the current models.py and in the official supplemental code/models.py.
analysis: Both released binarizers scatter scalar \(1\) into sorted_indices, a permutation of all \(N^2\) matrix positions, while leaving the computed top-k mask unused. Every forward adjacency is therefore the all-ones matrix, including its diagonal. A straight-through estimator can still return a nonzero surrogate gradient, which does not change that constant forward graph. The active loss separately omits the stated sparsity term. The historical table/figure-producing program remains unidentified.
result: The release cannot produce sample-dependent sparse hard graphs through these functions. This is a substantial release defect, but published-figure provenance and central empirical damage are not established, so its impact label is Minor.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For the intended undirected loop-free forward graph, select a rank mask on strict-upper-triangle scores, mirror it and zero the diagonal. Explicitly define the edge budget, backward estimator and actual regularization objective; a one-line scatter edit alone is incomplete.

problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Eq. (4), PDF p. 6; released optimize_image.py extraction, lines 50–55.

analysis: Let \(D\) downsample, \(U\) upsample, \(x\) be the original image and \(z\) the optimized low-resolution image. The specified perturbation is \(U(Dx-z)\), while the helper uses \(x-Uz\); their difference is \(x-UDx\). problems.title: The geometric-series term in Equation (20) exceeds its claimed bound
problems.source_location: Section 3.5, Theorem 1, PDF p. 5; Appendix F.1 restatement p. 16 and Eq. (20), p. 18.
claim: Mathematical transcription, with surrounding assumptions paraphrased: Theorem 1, Section 3.5, PDF p. 5, and Appendix F.1, p. 16, asserts
\[\operatorname{ERR}(\pi;D^\ast) \leq \operatorname{ERR}(\pi;D) +\frac{\alpha-1}{2\alpha} +\frac{\alpha-2}{2\alpha}\mathbf 1_{\{\alpha>2\}},\]
analysis: Set \(H=2\), \(H'=3\), \(\gamma=3/4\), and \(\alpha=3/2\), satisfying the printed scalar restrictions. The geometric term is \((1+3/4)/3=7/12\), whereas the claimed upper bound is \((\alpha-1)/(2\alpha)=1/6\). The proof's \(7/12\le1/6\) step is false. This calculation invalidates that step without purporting to refute every possible proof of the final task-error statement.
result: The cited geometric bound needs replacement or stronger assumptions. No task-performance or learning experiment was rerun.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The scalar term is at most \(H/H^{\prime}\) for \(0\le\gamma<1\), since every summand is at most one. Replacing this one bound does not by itself repair the full task-error theorem.

problems.title: Table 6 uses two-sided p-values where a one-sided Welch test is specified
problems.source_location: Section 4.3, PDF p. 8; Appendix D.2, PDF p. 15; Table 3, PDF p. 16; Appendix H, Table 6, PDF p. 20.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 4.3, PDF p. 8, and Appendix H, p. 20, specify a one-sided Welch comparison to the best-performing method, with significance level 0.05. Table 6 gives language-conditioned t- and p-values; Table 7 gives image-conditioned values. Appendix D.2, p. 15, specifies five baseline trials, while Table 3, p. 16, lists ten task trials.

For cloth folding, Table 1 reports TRA \(1.00\) and LCBC 0.40. Table 6 reports \(t=2.45\), \(p=0.070\). The table formatting treats this comparison as not significantly different from the best method.
analysis: Under the documented binary-success trial interpretation, ten successes versus two successes in five trials give Welch \(t=\sqrt6\) and \(4\) degrees of freedom. The one-sided p-value is \(0.035242\), while the two-sided value is \(0.070484\), matching the printed \(0.070\). Thus this reconstructed comparison crosses the stated unadjusted \(0.05\) threshold under the specified directional test. The conclusion is conditional on that published trial protocol.
result: The reconstructed binary-trial comparison changes a nominal significance annotation, in the direction of strengthening the observed TRA advantage; raw trial logs are still needed for a complete table audit.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: If the stated one-sided Welch comparison is the intended prespecified test, the folding p-value under the published binary-trial reconstruction is approximately \(0.035\), and its ‘not significantly different’ marking changes under the nominal unadjusted \(0.05\) rule. This is conditional on that trial interpretation; no unreported comparisons or multiplicity correction are inferred.

problems.title: The stated online positive and negative conditions have overlapping domains
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, PDF p. 6 (threshold definitions).
claim: Mathematical transcription, with the surrounding procedure paraphrased: Section 3.3, PDF p. 6, defines the thresholds
\[T_q^+=\max_{d\in D_q^-}p(d),\qquad T_q^-=\min_{d\in D_q^+}p(d),\]
The following rule labels a document positive when \(p(d)>T_q^+\), negative when \(p(d)<T_q^-\), and otherwise discards it, without an explicit conflict rule.
analysis: When calibration negatives all lie below positives, \(T^+=\max p_{\rm neg}<T^-=\min p_{\rm pos}\). Any new score \(p\in(T^+,T^-)\) satisfies both \(p>T^+\) and \(p<T^-\), hence both printed label conditions. An explicit overlap rule or branch priority is needed; no observed double-label rate is inferred.

For a two-token gold answer \((a,b)\), let each required conditional probability be \(r\) versus alternative \(1-r\), followed by certain end-of-sequence. Fifty calibration documents with \(r=0.1\) fail greedy exact match and have gold probability \(0.01\); fifty with \(r=0.9\) succeed with probability \(0.81\). Both pools are nonempty. A later document with \(r=0.6\) has gold probability \(0.36\), strictly inside the overlap and satisfies both predicates.
result: A normalized autoregressive example proves ambiguous membership; unavailable training code leaves actual priority and double-insertion incidence unknown.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Explicitly state branch priority, or use the proposed conservative rule: positive above \(\max(T_q^+,T_q^-)\), negative below \(\min(T_q^+,T_q^-)\), and abstain otherwise. The latter is logically disjoint but has untested learning behavior.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The re-indexing comparison changes both retrieval representation and indexing strategy
problems.source_location: Section 5.1, Figure 5, PDF p. 10; Appendix H, PDF pp. 22–23.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 5.1, PDF p. 10, interprets the comparison in Figure 5 as favoring late-parametric retrieval over periodic re-indexing. Appendix H, pp. 22–23, gives the detailed setup and attributes the weaker re-indexed configuration to index staleness.

The Appendix H baseline description uses SIDR for the late-parametric system and DPR for the periodic-re-indexing system. It states that the dimensionalities are \(30522\) and \(768\) respectively and explains the change by available GPU memory. The following training description nevertheless characterizes the models as differing only in their in-training retrieval strategies.

Adding and subtracting \(Y(\mathrm{SIDR},\mathrm{periodic})\) separates a strategy effect from an unmeasured representation effect. The appendix discloses dimensions \(30522\) and \(768\), so this is documented confounding, not concealment. The two-system comparison cannot identify the sign or size of the strategy-only effect.

problems.title: Compactness and continuity do not prove the stated pure-strategy equilibrium
problems.source_location: Section 2.5, Assumptions 1–2 and Theorem 1, Eq. (8), PDF p. 5; Appendix A, PDF pp. 13–14.
claim: Paraphrase: Assumption \(1\) and Assumption \(2\) in Section 2.5, p. 5, require a compact finite-dimensional joint strategy space and continuity in each player’s own strategy. Theorem 1, Eq. (8), concludes that a deterministic strategy tuple exists satisfying all unilateral best-response inequalities. Appendix A, pp. 13–14, strengthens the discussion to joint continuity and invokes Glicksberg as if compactness plus continuity guaranteed a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. The same appendix then presents zero-gradient conditions for teacher and students in Eqs. (27), (\(28\)), and (\(32\)), pp. 14–15.

The student minimizes \(R_S=\lambda_u L_{\rm unsup}+\lambda_{\rm adv}L_{\rm adv}\); the generator maximizes expected entropy; the teacher’s simultaneous-game payoff is validation accuracy of the fixed students. Appendix A uses teacher constraints \(0\leq\tau,\lambda_u,\lambda_{\rm adv}\leq1\), \(\lambda_u+\lambda_{\rm adv}\leq1\), a bounded student parameter ball, and an \(\ell_\infty\) perturbation ball.
analysis: Compactness and continuity alone do not imply a pure-strategy equilibrium. For example, on \(x,y\in[-1,1]\), let player one maximize \((x-y)^2\) and player two minimize it. The second player's best response is \(y=x\), where the first can always improve by changing \(x\); no pure equilibrium exists. This disproves the generic inference, not the paper's full game. Its allowed zero loss weights yield a separate degenerate equilibrium with uniform students, so asserting nonexistence for that complete domain would be wrong.
result: The general compact-continuous-game proof is insufficient, but the paper's full zero-weight domain permits a degenerate equilibrium. This does not establish a false existence conclusion for that full game, so Minor is appropriate.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a mixed-strategy statement for the generic compact continuous game, or supply a proof using the actual payoff structure. Preserve the direct zero-weight equilibrium as bare existence; replace boundary zero-gradient assertions with constrained optimality conditions and treat convergence separately.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The public teacher update scales a training gradient instead of differentiating validation performance
problems.source_location: Section 2.3, Eqs. (5)–(7), PDF p. 4; Algorithm 1, line 16, PDF p. 5; Appendix B, PDF pp. 15–16.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 2.3, p. 4, Eqs. (5)–(7), and Algorithm 1, p. 5, line 16, update teacher parameters according to the validation effect of the student update. Appendix B, pp. 15–16, describes a one-step unroll and validation differentiation through the inner gradient, while also using a first-order/Reptile description. Section 3, p. 6, says the initial threshold and weights are \((0.05,0.5,0.5)\) and are adaptively learned.
analysis: Let the inner loss be \(\lambda(w-1)^2/2\), \(\lambda=\operatorname{sigmoid}(\phi)\), start \(w=0\), and use step \(\eta=0.1\). The one-step student is \(w'=0.1\lambda\). For validation loss \((w'-1)^2/2\), differentiation at \(\phi=0\) gives \(-0.02375\). Scaling a direct training derivative does not compute that mixed derivative, and a Boolean threshold supplies no ordinary gradient. This distinguishes the released heuristic from the stated unrolled validation objective.

The current helper multiplies the direct training derivative \(0.125\) by detached validation loss \(0.45125\), giving \(0.05640625>0\), opposite to the one-step validation derivative \(-0.02375\). The threshold enters only a Boolean comparison and receives no ordinary derivative.
result: The current scalar-rescaled training gradient can oppose the specified validation meta-gradient and cannot adapt the hard threshold by ordinary differentiation; benchmark exposure is unresolved.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use an explicitly differentiable inner update when computing the outer validation derivative, or describe and evaluate the implemented heuristic as a different update. No restored benchmark performance is claimed.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The public cross-view targets differ from the stated ensemble pseudo-labels
problems.source_location: Eqs. (1)–(2), PDF p. 3; Algorithm 1, lines 6–8, PDF p. 5.
claim: Paraphrase: Eq. (1), p. 3, defines MI from the ensemble predictive mean. The text accepts samples when \(I>\tau\), and the definition following Eq. (2) uses \(\hat y^{(i)}=\arg\max_y\bar p^{(i)}(y)\). Each student’s accepted pseudo-label is sent to the other student. Algorithm 1, p. 5, lines 6–8 repeats MI selection and cross-view supervision.
analysis: Dropout predictions \[(0.9,0.1),(0.1,0.9),(0.1,0.9)\] have ensemble argmax class \(1\), while the first draw selects class \(0\). A first-draw target is therefore not the stated ensemble target. Sender-based acceptance and an intersection of both students' acceptance masks are also distinct policies; the source must identify which it implements.
result: Current first-draw targets disagree with the explicitly defined ensemble, and acceptance-mask provenance is a separate policy choice; actual benchmark target errors are not measured.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Compute the mean predictive probability vector before selecting its label, and specify whether acceptance uses the sending student or both students. Reversing an uncertainty inequality alone is not established as an accuracy repair.

problems.title: Detaching MI removes its entire contribution to the generator gradient
problems.source_location: Section 2.2, Eq. (3), PDF p. 4; Algorithm 1, line 9, PDF p. 5.
claim: Section 2.2, Eq. (3), PDF p. 4, and the generator docstring use entropy plus a weighted mutual-information term. Algorithm 1, line 9, instead shows entropy alone, which is retained as counterevidence. Released methods/trico/generator.py, lines 11–17, differentiates its perturbed input, but utils.py, line 15, detaches the MI value, so that path has \(\nabla_x I=0\).
analysis: Detaching the computed mutual information makes its gradient with respect to generator parameters zero. It may remain a reported scalar or selection statistic, but cannot contribute the claimed differentiable MI pressure to that generator objective through the detached path.

With binary dropout logits \((x,0)\) and \((-x,0)\), let \(h(x)\) be their single-draw entropy. Their mean is uniform and \(I=\log2-h\). At \(x=1\), the intended \(h+2I\) derivative is \(+0.1966119332\), but detaching \(I\) leaves derivative \(-0.1966119332\). Sign perturbations of size \(0.1\) therefore go to \(1.1\) and \(0.9\), respectively.
result: The current detach removes the entire MI gradient and can reverse the stated joint-objective perturbation, while preserving the entropy-only variant and perturbation bound.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Provide differentiable MI for the generator while detaching a separate selection statistic, or explicitly adopt and evaluate the entropy-only algorithmic variant.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The public launcher feeds the official test split into teacher updates
problems.source_location: Section 3, PDF p. 6 (validation/testing protocol); released launcher.

This separation matters even if the teacher update is the heuristic identified in Problem 2, because the feedback still changes parameters used in later student learning.

result: The actual launcher routes official test labels into adaptive teacher feedback; unchanged private experiment provenance and numerical score effects remain unknown.

Keep its labels out of inner supervised training, preserve the declared label budget, and pass only this validation loader to teacher updates. Keep the official test loader solely in evaluation. Save split indices and seeds so disjointness and label counts can be checked independently. Runs produced by the defective path need retraining and fresh evaluation; reports from an independently correct private path would instead require provenance showing that separation. No numerical adjustment to existing accuracies can repair an adaptive test-label dependency.

problems.title: The MI inequality needs a reliability-versus-uncertainty interpretation
problems.source_location: Eq. (1) and pseudo-acceptance discussion, PDF p. 3.
claim: The source uses a dropout mutual-information threshold in selecting pseudo-labels.
analysis: High epistemic disagreement does not itself guarantee a reliable label. It can be an intentional uncertainty curriculum, but that is a different rationale from confidence filtering; reversing the inequality alone has not been validated as an accuracy repair.

problems.title: Detaching the ODE state breaks the gradients used for airfoil editing
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, arXiv v4 PDF pp. 5–6; Appendix B, Algorithm 3, p. 17; sample_process_with_log_prob composite_drift.
claim: Section 3.2, PDF pp. 5–6, and Appendix B, Algorithm 3, PDF p. 17, differentiate editing loss through the sampled ODE trajectory. Released airfoil_generation/model/optimal_transport_functional_flow_model.py, OptimalTransportFunctionalFlowForRegression.sample_process_with_log_prob, lines 1202–1371, detaches the state inside composite_drift at lines 1271–1278, while using ordinary Euler differentiation.
analysis: Take \(u_0=1\), \(v_a(u)=au\), \(a=0.4\), and two Euler steps of size \(1/2\). The forward endpoint is \((1+0.5a)^2u_0=1.44\), with derivatives \(\partial u_1/\partial u_0=1.44\) and \(\partial u_1/\partial a=1.2\). Detaching drift inputs preserves the forward value but keeps only the direct state path and local parameter terms, giving derivatives \(1\) and \(0.5+0.6=1.1\). Matching forward output therefore does not validate those editing gradients.
result: Current editing code omits state-chain-rule terms, with explicit scalar derivative discrepancies; forward generation and benchmark editing errors have not been refuted.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Preserve the incoming ODE state graph, enabling local state differentiation only when necessary without replacing the state by a detached leaf. This restores the ordinary Euler sensitivity recurrence; density and solver alternatives still need separate checks.
