problems.title: Jointly changing the density is not equivalent to MAP under a fixed pretrained prior
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Eq. (7), PDF p. 5; joint optimization discussion, PDF p. 6.
claim: Section 3.2, Eq. (7), PDF p. 5, derives an edited-sample posterior under a trained prior and drops evidence constant in the sample. The subsequent procedure on PDF p. 6 and Algorithm 3 optimizes both the sample-generating flow and its initial function, so the density itself changes.
analysis: A fixed-prior MAP objective is reconstruction cost minus \(\log p_{\theta_0}(u')\). Changing \(\theta\) while evaluating \(p_\theta(u')\) changes the reference density. For the smooth scalar contracting flow \(F_c(a)=e^{-c}a\) with standard-normal base and fixed sample \(a=u'=0\), reconstruction stays zero but negative log density is \(\tfrac12\log(2\pi)-c\), decreasing without bound as \(c\to\infty\). A fixed pretrained density assigns that unchanged sample a fixed cost. This proves non-equivalence, not collapse of the actual airfoil model.
result: A smooth invertible contraction changes self-density at a fixed edited sample, disproving fixed-prior MAP equivalence without demonstrating actual model collapse.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: An intended adaptive-density editing heuristic is consistent with the implemented scalar objective. Under that interpretation, the objective is not inherently a programming error; the needed correction is to state its changing reference distribution and avoid presenting the fixed-prior Bayes calculation as an equivalence proof. If the intended posterior is instead \(p_\theta(u'\mid z)\) while also optimizing \(\theta\), its evidence \(p_\theta(z)\) generally depends on \(\theta\) and cannot be dropped merely because it is constant in \(u'\). If a joint posterior over \(u'\) and \(\theta\) is intended, it requires an explicit model/prior for \(\theta\); Eq. (7) does not provide one. These are distinct modeling choices.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Raw smoothness and diversity scores change under resampling of the same airfoils
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, Eq. (9), PDF p. 6; Section 4.2, Table 2, PDF pp. 7–8.
claim: Paraphrase: Section 4.1, p. 6, defines the smoothness score in Eq. (9) as the sum of distances from each point to the line through its two neighbors. It defines diversity through log determinants of similarity matrices based on Euclidean distances between sampled airfoils. Section 4.2 and Table 2, pp. 7–8, compare generated airfoils at \(257\), \(513\), and \(1025\) points using those metrics to assess resolution changes. The question here is whether raw score changes can be attributed to geometric quality or diversity independently of sampling resolution.

The released super-resolution evaluator implements at lines 249–270 and at \(273\)–285. Smoothness is an unnormalized sum. Diversity flattens all coordinates, computes Euclidean pair distances \(d\), forms \(S_{ij}=\exp(-d_{ij}^2/2)\), and reports a log determinant. There is no quadrature or point-count normalization.
analysis: For a fixed radius-\(R\) circle sampled at \(N\) equally spaced points, the raw neighbor-chord distance sum is \(NR(1-\cos(2\pi/N))\sim2\pi^2R/N\), although geometry is unchanged. For two fixed sinusoidal airfoils with amplitudes \(b_1,b_2\), unweighted squared separation is \((b_2-b_1)^2(N-1)/2\), so their kernel log determinant also changes with \(N\) while continuous squared separation remains \((b_2-b_1)^2/2\). Cross-resolution interpretation requires an explicit sampling normalization.
result: Supported metric-scope qualification; within-resolution comparisons remain interpretable.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Compare smoothness on a common reference grid, or define a justified continuous regularity functional. Use a fixed-bandwidth quadrature distance for diversity so point-count changes do not change the underlying geometry measure.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released success path does not enforce preservation of the requested theorem
problems.source_location: Section 3.3, PDF pp. 4–5; Section 5.1, PDF p. 5; released Prove.run and verifier.
claim: Sections 3.3 and \(5.1\), PDF pp. 4–5, describe completing the requested proof and verifying it with Lean 4. Released dsp/prove.py, check_proof, warns when the requested theorem is changed or commented out, but run can still mark an otherwise error-free, sorry-free returned program as finished; run_direct returns the underlying completion result without enforcing target identity.
analysis: An unrelated declaration proving True can be error-free and sorry-free without proving a requested False statement. A target-mismatch warning that does not block the success branch therefore fails to enforce theorem identity. This is a controller-contract argument; no false Lean theorem or actual kernel acceptance of a false proposition is claimed.

Placing the exact requested target text inside a Lean block comment also passes the whitespace-substring check. Thus elevating the existing warning alone would not repair target preservation. These are conditional controller witnesses using a successful compiler-response interface, not claims of a newly compiled proof.
result: The current controller can accept a different completed declaration, but no actual target mismatch was found in the historical released-solution inventory and no benchmark score is revised.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Keep the target declaration immutable and restrict generation/repair to its proof body. Make acceptance depend on compiler-aware declaration name/type/assumption and admitted-axiom checks; a comment-stripping specimen guard is not a complete Lean parser.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The unrestricted-hypothesis fallback is inactive by default and fails when enabled
problems.source_location: Appendix A.1, PDF p. 21; released fallback send_request.
claim: Appendix A.1, PDF p. 21, describes both hinted-hypothesis and unrestricted-context proof search. In the released proving interface, run and run_direct leave the strict retry disabled by default; its enabled branch calls send_request without a required argument.
analysis: Normal calls leave the strict flag false, so the unrestricted retry is not reached. Enabling it exposes a missing required send_request argument and fails before the request. Both mechanisms are version-bounded control-flow/interface defects; their benchmark incidence is unmeasured.
result: The current fallback is unreachable under default calls and raises a missing-argument error when enabled; search coverage changes, without invalidating accepted Lean proofs.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Pass both proof blocks and the current bfs_list to the retry, and explicitly enable the intended fallback policy. This restores the local interface, without establishing an improved theorem-proving success rate.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Reproduction of the authors’ known logarithm-domain issue in miniF2F
problems.source_location: Appendix F, PDF pp. 27–28 (known nested-logarithm contest formalization).
claim: Appendix F, PDF pp. 27–28, already diagnoses and corrects the original miniF2F nested-logarithm formalization. The inspected author dataset contains the strengthened domain condition. No discovery credit is claimed.
analysis: Under Lean's totalized Real.logb convention, \(n=1\) makes both nested logarithms zero and satisfies the original formal equation, while its decimal digit sum is \(1\), not \(13\). The informal contest problem's positive logarithm domains exclude this endpoint. This reproduces the authors' disclosed formalization issue.

The current author dataset explicitly requires \(1<n\), excluding this witness. On that domain, writing \(t=\log_2 n>0\) reduces the equation to \(\log_2t-2=(\log_2t-1)/2\), hence \(n=256\) and digit sum \(13\).
result: The author-disclosed historical domain error is corrected in the current dataset. It is retained as history and supplies no current issue severity.

problems.title: The released LPIPS call omits the conversion from \([0,1]\) to \([-1,1]\)
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, PDF p. 7; metrics_mixgs.py, lines 24–50; train_mixgs.py, lines 263–277; lpipsPyTorch/modules/networks.py, lines 40–54.
claim: Section 4.1 reports LPIPS image quality. In the current author release, metrics_mixgs.py converts RGB images to tensors in \([0,1]\), and the training evaluator clamps images to that same range. Both pass these tensors directly to the bundled LPIPS wrapper. The LPIPS authors specify inputs in \([-1,1]\), or an explicit affine conversion before feature scaling.
analysis: The bundled feature network standardizes its red channel with mean \(-0.030\) and scale \(0.458\), without any preceding range conversion. For a valid input \(x\in[0,1]\), the released and intended feature inputs are therefore \[z_{\rm release}(x)=\frac{x+0.030}{0.458},\qquad z_{\rm intended}(x)=\frac{2x-1+0.030}{0.458}.\] Their difference is \((1-x)/0.458\). A black pixel produces approximately \(0.065502\) instead of \(-2.117904\); at white, both transformations agree. This algebra establishes a preprocessing mismatch independently of the learned network weights.

The local wrapper has no hidden normalization option: it constructs LPIPS and forwards both inputs directly to its feature network. The official reference implementation separately exposes an explicit normalization option for precisely the missing \(2x-1\) operation. Identical-image distances can still vanish under either convention, so that control would not clear this defect.
result: The current released evaluators do not compute the stated LPIPS preprocessing convention. The nonlinear feature network prevents inferring either the direction of score bias or a changed ranking from the input shift alone. PSNR and SSIM do not use this LPIPS transformation. Published values require identification of the actual evaluation path and, if affected, rescoring of the relevant rendered/reference images.
assumptions: RGB image tensors enter the inspected wrapper in \([0,1]\), as produced or clamped by the identified call sites.
No claim is made that the published tables used this exact public path.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Convert both images with \(2x-1\) at the two LPIPS call sites, or provide an explicit wrapper range option that applies that conversion exactly once. The rearranged red-channel expression \((x-0.485)/0.229\) verifies the intended affine map algebraically. This does not supply recomputed perceptual scores.
An affine input-range correction is proposed; adoption in the current author release is not observed in the inspected call sites.

problems.title: The joint-stage implementation stops cross-branch derivatives through coarse attributes
problems.source_location: Eqs. (5) and (11), PDF pp. 5–6; Section 3.4, PDF p. 7; train_mixgs.py, lines 87–92 and 153–160; gaussian_renderer/__init__.py, lines 75–107.
claim: The paper jointly fine-tunes coarse Gaussians \(G_c\) and learned detail parameters \(\Phi\). Its decoded positions satisfy \(\widetilde\mu_i=\mu_i+o_i\). The current implementation detaches coarse attributes before detail encoding and detaches coarse anchors in the decoded branch, while retaining direct coarse-render gradients and stepping both parameter-group optimizers.
analysis: This changes the derivative convention. For the scalar analogue \(F(g,o)=L_c(g)+L_d(g+o)\), ordinary differentiation gives \[\partial_gF=L_c\prime(g)+L_d\prime(g+o),\] whereas detaching the decoded anchor gives only \(L_c\prime(g)\); the offset derivative remains \(L_d\prime(g+o)\). Thus merely making coarse parameters trainable does not recover decoded-branch chain-rule terms.

However, updating both groups through selected derivative paths is still a form of joint training. Neither the cited prose nor a convergence theorem requires every composite-objective derivative to be propagated. The forward anchor equation is unchanged. The observed stop-gradient choice therefore does not establish that the joint-training claim is false or that a full-gradient variant would perform better.
result: This concern is retained as a method-specification qualification, with no current paper error established. Explicitly stating the stop-gradient convention would aid reproduction; it is not evidence of failed scene reconstruction or a validated alternative optimization method.
assumptions: The assessment concerns the cited joint-training wording and the inspected derivative paths, with visibility and the other attributes held fixed in the scalar illustration.

problems.title: The advertised checkpoint resume path omits the learned MixGS representation
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, PDF p. 7; train_mixgs.py, lines 40–57 and 143–164; scene/gaussian_model.py, capture/restore; scene/mixgs_model.py, construction and save_weights/load_weights.
claim: The released training interface advertises checkpoint saving and resumption for a representation containing coarse Gaussians and a learned hash encoder/decoder. The checkpoint save statement serializes only gaussians.capture() and the iteration, while the resume branch constructs a fresh MixGSModel and restores only the Gaussian object.
analysis: GaussianModel.capture includes Gaussian tensors, Gaussian optimizer state and associated metadata; it does not contain the separately constructed encoder, decoder or their optimizer. Consequently the saved payload cannot reconstruct those learned parameters. Restoring a late iteration while retaining newly initialized detail parameters cannot continue the complete prior training state. This follows directly from serialization coverage, without executing the training program.

Separate save_weights/load_weights methods do exist, and normal scene saving writes encoder/decoder weights. This is a positive control against claiming that the representation cannot be saved at all. The checkpoint resume branch does not invoke those methods or restore the detail optimizer. A manually arranged warm start therefore differs from complete continuation through the provided interface.
result: The current checkpoint/resume path is incomplete for interrupted MixGS training. The default checkpoint list is empty, and this omission does not refute uninterrupted runs or independently saved evaluation weights. No resumed scene-quality result is claimed.
assumptions: The user requests the provided checkpoint/resume interface after the detail representation has acquired learned state.
No undocumented external restoration of the separate MixGS state is assumed.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a complete checkpoint containing Gaussian state, encoder and decoder state dictionaries, both optimizer states, iteration, and compatible schedule/configuration metadata. Random and data-loader state is additionally needed if exact continuation is promised. This is a state-coverage proposal; uninterrupted-versus-resumed equivalence has not been tested here.
Complete checkpoint-state coverage is proposed; the current save and resume branches still omit the separate learned detail state.

problems.title: Held-out evaluation success influences retries and candidate selection
problems.source_location: Section 3.4, PDF p. 6; Section 4, Evaluation Benchmarks, PDF p. 7; Appendix C, Algorithm 1, PDF p. 19.
claim: Section 4, PDF p. 7, reserves held-out tests for assessment, while Section 3.4 and Appendix C, Algorithm 1, use task-visible feedback. Released datasets_utils.py, lines 173–260, separates public test_list from held-out eval_test_list. eg_cfg_session_manager.py, solve_problem_with_eg_cfg_wrapper and solve_single_problem, lines 491–731, instead use held-out success to stop retries and guidance search.
analysis: Let the public test require \(f(0)=0\), satisfied by both candidate \(A:f(x)=0\) and candidate \(B:f(x)=x\), generated in that order. A held-out requirement \(f(1)=0\) makes the controller stop at \(A\), while changing only that held-out requirement to \(f(1)=1\) makes it continue and select \(B\). Candidate and attempt count depend on held-out feedback even when the held-out text never enters a prompt. This is a source-level selection argument, not a new model-generation run.
result: The inspected release performs test-dependent selection. This known release-level concern does not by itself establish the historical benchmark's affected fraction or a corrected score.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use only task-visible feedback for selection and retries, reserving the held-out tests for one final assessment of the selected candidate.
Known evaluation-selection issue independently reproduced by the proposed clarification; historical table impact remains unresolved.
Known evaluation-selection issue independently reproduced by the proposed clarification; historical table impact remains unresolved.

problems.title: Top-five zero filling can change the token selected by the stated CFG rule
problems.source_location: Sections 3.2–3.3, Eqs. (13)–(14), PDF p. 6; Algorithm 2, lines 29–31, PDF p. 19; released endpoint top-five path.
claim: The token rule in Sections 3.2–3.3, Eqs. (13)–(14), PDF p. 6, and Algorithm 2, lines 29–31, p. 19, applies guidance and takes the resulting argmax. The endpoint implementation requests only five token log probabilities (consts.py:\(215\), inference_endpoint_utils.py:\(432\)–\(472\)). model_utils.py:\(57\)–\(67\) creates a zero vector for the vocabulary and fills only returned probabilities. probs_utils.py:\(38\)–\(48\) applies guidance to those reconstructed vectors.
analysis: For six tokens, take full positive probability vectors

Both sum to one. At \(\gamma=1/2\), the full rule assigns token \(6\) weight \(\sqrt{0.0094}\approx0.09695\), greater than every competing weight (at most \(\sqrt{0.00225}\approx0.04743\)). At \(\gamma=3\), its weight is \(0.94^3/0.01^2=8305.84\), again uniquely largest. The endpoint zero-fills token \(6\) in the prior because it lies outside that prior’s top five. The outer factor in \(\widetilde P_i[(\widetilde P_{c,i}+\epsilon)/(\widetilde P_i+\epsilon)]^\gamma\) then makes its guided mass zero. Epsilon inside the ratio cannot restore it. The explicitly optimized \(\gamma=1\) path and local full-logit path remain valid countercontrols.
result: This is a supported local finding within the stated source/formulation scope. Its effect on the paper's aggregate experimental results remains unmeasured.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For available full positive distributions, use the stated log score \((1-\gamma)\log P_i+\gamma\log P_{c,i}\). If only truncated probabilities are available, identify the sparse approximation explicitly; the full-distribution guarantee is unavailable.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The result comparator loses semantic distinctions and rejects correct empty results
problems.source_location: Appendices C–D, PDF p. 25; released PostgreSQL utility preprocess_results, lines 10–29, and ex_baselines, lines 92–134.
claim: Appendices C–D, PDF p. 25, describe functional SQL evaluation. The released PostgreSQL utility preprocess_results, lines 10–29, and ex_base, lines 86–132, discard duplicates/time-of-day and reject empty answers. Required ordering is also not enforced by set comparison.
analysis: Set comparison equates the row sequences \(((1),(1))\) and \(((1))\), losing multiplicity and any required order. Rejecting either empty list rejects two identical valid empty answers. Formatting timestamps as dates equates same-day values \(22\) hours apart. These are distinct valid-answer contracts that a general semantic comparator must preserve; their frequency in the final task tests is unknown.
result: This is a supported local finding within the stated source/formulation scope. Its effect on the paper's aggregate experimental results remains unmeasured.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

problems.title: Removing DISTINCT with text operations changes valid SQL values and query structure
problems.source_location: Released PostgreSQL utility remove_distinct, lines 32–61; retained conference and current-source versions.
claim: The conference remove_distinct, lines 32–61 of the PostgreSQL utility, splits each complete SQL string on whitespace, removes tokens equal to distinct, and joins the remainder with single spaces. The current version instead uses a case-insensitive regular expression replacing every whole-word occurrence of DISTINCT with an empty string. The authors’ README explicitly announces an evaluation-code update to this function on \(8\) January 2026.
analysis: The current helper applies a case-insensitive whole-word regular expression to the entire SQL string. Thus the valid statement SELECT 'DISTINCT' AS value is changed into SELECT '' AS value. This changes a string value, rather than a SQL keyword. The former split/join behavior that collapsed double spaces or moved a statement into a line comment has been fixed and is excluded from the current defect. Actual benchmark incidence remains unknown.
result: This is a supported local finding within the stated source/formulation scope. Its effect on the paper's aggregate experimental results remains unmeasured.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

problems.title: The denominator and stopping rule for Table 4’s average tries require clarification
problems.source_location: Section 4, PDF p. 5; Section 6.4, Table 4, PDF p. 9.
claim: Section 4, PDF p. 5, describes SIX-GYM as containing approximately \(3301\) generated training instances. Section 6.4 and Table 4, p. 9, compare trajectory generation on SIX-GYM. The Reject + f-Plan row has at most five tries, \(2560\) successful trajectories, and an average of \(1.7\) tries. The same table values remain in arXiv v4. The table itself does not explicitly specify its average’s denominator.

Suppose average tries means the mean over all \(3301\) tasks; each successfully solved task consumes at least one try; and each final failure exhausts all five allowed tries. These are an explicit interpretation being tested, not assumptions asserted as supported facts about the run.
analysis: Assume the mean covers all \(3301\) tasks, every one of \(2560\) successes takes at least one try, and each of \(741\) failures exhausts five tries. The mean must then be at least \((2560+5\cdot741)/3301\approx1.89791\), inconsistent with \(1.7\). A success-only denominator, early aborts or another averaging unit removes this contradiction. The table does not establish the assumptions, so no incorrect entry or replacement value is asserted.
result: Reporting ambiguity requiring denominator/stopping-rule evidence; no incorrect table entry or replacement number is established.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Specify the averaging unit, total attempts, success count and terminal-failure behavior.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: A stable constant-weight error recursion is monotone, contradicting the claimed inevitable U-shape
problems.source_location: Section 4.1, Theorem 4.1, PDF p. 6; Appendix G.4, Theorem G.1, PDF pp. 25–26; Lemma G.3, Eq. (14), PDF p. 26; Lemma G.5, PDF p. 27.
claim: Theorem 4.1, PDF p. 6, and Appendix G.4, Theorem G.1, PDF pp. 25–26, assert a unique finite optimal reasoning depth with error decreasing and then increasing. Lemma G.3, Eq. (14), and Lemma G.5 make related constant-weight/deterministic-alignment claims. The counterexample uses integration/alignment weights in \((0,1)\), positive initial error, independent finite-variance noise and zero alignment bias.
analysis: Set \(\alpha=\gamma=1/2\), initial squared error \(1\), zero bias \(\Delta=0\), and independent unit Gaussian noise. The resulting stable recursion gives \(E_N=4/7+(3/7)(9/16)^N\). This is strictly decreasing at every finite \(N\) and converges to \(4/7\). The variance contribution contracts to a finite limit, so the stated assumptions do not force a rising tail or an interior optimal depth.
result: The inevitable U-shape and unique finite optimum are false under the stated assumptions. This does not deny that particular empirical tasks exhibit a U-shaped trend.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For deterministic integration weights independent of the stated noises and alignments, retain the exact second-moment recursion \(E_N=q_NE_{N-1}+\sigma^2\gamma_N^2\), where \(q_N=(1-\gamma_N\bar\alpha)^2+\gamma_N^2\tau^2\). For constant \(q<1\), this gives \(E_N=L+(b_0-L)q^N\), with \(L=\sigma^2\gamma^2/(1-q)\); the curve is decreasing, increasing or constant according to \(b_0-L\). This preserves the moment analysis without claiming an inevitable U-shape.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Lemma G.7 does not ensure an interior optimum of the integration weight
problems.source_location: Appendix G.6, Lemma G.7, PDF pp. 27–28.
claim: Lemma G.7, Appendix G.6, PDF pp. 27–28, fixes \(N\geq1\), deterministic \(\alpha,\gamma\in(0,1)\), and \(\tau^2=0\). Part \(2\) claims that error as a function of \(\gamma\) always has a unique critical point in \((0,1)\), decreasing before it and increasing after it. Its proof asserts that the derivative becomes positive as \(\gamma\uparrow1\). Section 4.2, p. 7, uses the optimal-weight interpretation to motivate intervention. These are paraphrases.
analysis: At one step, with \(\alpha=1/2\), initial squared error \(1\), and noise variance \(0.01\), the stated recurrence yields \(E(\gamma)=1-\gamma+(13/50)\gamma^2\). Its derivative \(-1+(13/25)\gamma\) is negative throughout \((0,1)\); its unconstrained minimizer \(25/13\) lies outside. The permitted interval has an upper-boundary infimum, not the claimed interior optimum.
result: This is a supported local finding within the stated source/formulation scope. Its effect on the paper's aggregate experimental results remains unmeasured.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: For one step, the unconstrained minimizer is \(\gamma_0=\alpha b_0/(\alpha^2b_0+\sigma^2)\). An interior minimizer exists exactly when \(\sigma^2>\alpha(1-\alpha)b_0\); on the closed interval use \(\min\{1,\gamma_0\}\). General-depth uniqueness requires its own argument.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released Blackjack rule predicates omit legal prime hands and accept more than one pair
problems.source_location: Appendix B.4, PDF p. 21 (SR1/SR3); released BJ/create_blackjack/rules.py, lines 16–17 and 32–39.
claim: Appendix B.4, PDF p. 21, specifies five-card hands. In paraphrase, SR1 makes any prime total win even when it exceeds \(21\), and SR3 makes a hand with exactly one pair of different suits a special loss. The corresponding public functions are BJ/create_blackjack/rules.py:\(16\)–\(17\) and:\(32\)–\(39\); card ranks, values, and the prime set are in cards.py. generate_data.py:\(7\)–\(24\) uses these predicates when assigning sampled observations to active rules.
analysis: The legal hand ten-hearts, ten-diamonds, nine-spades, six-clubs, two-hearts totals prime \(37\) without aces, but the released prime list stops at \(31\), despite the stated inclusion of busts. Separately, two-hearts, two-diamonds, three-hearts, three-spades, four-clubs has two pairs and passes an any-pair predicate although the rule requires exactly one pair. Their incidence in the final benchmark remains unmeasured.
result: This is a supported local finding within the stated source/formulation scope. Its effect on the paper's aggregate experimental results remains unmeasured.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use a primality test covering every attainable hand total and count pairs according to the stated rule. An extension involving aces requires an explicit convention for which total the prime condition uses; it is not chosen silently here.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The released repair routine ignores the requested order
problems.source_location: Section 3.6 and Figure 3, PDF p. 5; Table 1, PDF p. 7; Appendix G, Table 10, PDF p. 24.
claim: Paraphrase. Section 3.6 distinguishes sequential, high-to-low, low-to-high, and random repair orders. Figure 3 illustrates their different trajectories; the lower panel of Table 1 and Appendix G, Table 10 report different detection results for the order variants pp. 5, 7, 24. Their meaning requires the repaired token sequence to depend on the chosen order.

The matching implementation is auc_perplexity in dna_detectllm/metrics.py, lines 53–210. Its active order-selection block is at lines 79–87 and the repair loop begins at line 89. The conference supplement and the pinned GitHub copy have identical bytes for this file. compute_anomaly_level calls this routine with repair_order="h2l"; the default compute_score instead calls sum_perplexity.
analysis: The function computes/shuffles sorted_indices according to the requested order, but the active update loop iterates unchanged change_indices. Its returned trajectory is therefore independent of every accepted order string for fixed inputs. Distinct order-ablation results cannot be reproduced by changing this parameter alone in the supplied routine.
result: This is a supported local finding within the stated source/formulation scope. Its effect on the paper's aggregate experimental results remains unmeasured.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

problems.title: The paper and code assign opposite directions to cross entropy
problems.source_location: Eq. (1), PDF pp. 3–4; Section 4.1, PDF p. 6 (model roles).
claim: Eq. (1), PDF pp. 3–4, places reference-model probabilities from \(M_1\) outside the logarithm and observer-model probabilities from \(M_2\) inside it. Section 4.1, PDF p. 6, assigns those roles to Falcon-7B-Instruct and Falcon-7B. Interpreting the omitted vocabulary sum charitably gives cross entropy \(H(P,Q)=-\sum_iP_i\log Q_i\); the finding does not count the omitted sum as an error.
analysis: The released helper receives observer then reference distributions and computes \(H(Q,P)\), while the numerator retains reference probabilities. Cross entropy is asymmetric: for \(P\ne Q\), those expressions need not agree and can rank detector scores differently. Reversing model names only inside the denominator does not restore the full stated role contract.

For example, \(P=(0.9,0.1)\), \(Q=(0.5,0.5)\) give \(H(P,Q)=\log 2\approx0.69315\), while \(H(Q,P)=-\tfrac12\log(0.09)\approx1.20397\). With the same reference numerator these are different scores. This is an arithmetic witness to the direction mismatch, not a benchmark rerun.
result: This is a supported local finding within the stated source/formulation scope. Its effect on the paper's aggregate experimental results remains unmeasured.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

problems.title: Probability order does not universally determine repair-score order
problems.source_location: Section 3.6, PDF p. 5 (probability-order intuition).
claim: Paraphrase. Section 3.6 associates high observed-token probability with smaller repair changes and describes high-probability repairs first as producing a higher trajectory score p. 5. The preceding discussion uses typically, so this analysis distinguishes an empirical tendency from a universal implication. The latter is not valid under the stated definitions. The result below is a scope clarification, not a refutation of the empirical curves.
analysis: Take valid four-token distributions \((0.40,0.50,0.05,0.05)\) and \((0.30,0.31,0.20,0.19)\), observing the first token in each. Their repair log changes are \(\log(0.50/0.40)\approx0.22314\) and \(\log(0.31/0.30)\approx0.03279\), so the higher observed probability gives the larger change. A uniform observer holds the denominator fixed. This excludes a universal ordering but is compatible with the source’s explicit typical-behavior qualification and empirical curves; it is not counted as a current error.
result: No current error is established by the universal interpretation. The source explicitly qualifies the probability-order explanation as typical and presents repair-order behavior empirically. The counterexample limits a stronger universal claim that is not required by that qualified wording.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

problems.title: Orthogonal projection does not preserve an objective after a positive finite step
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.1, PDF p. 5; Theorem B.2, PDF p. 14.
claim: Paraphrase: Theorem 3.1, p. 5, and its restatement as Theorem B.2, p. 14, assert that differentiable \(L\)-smooth individual and collective objectives both do not decrease under the FCGrad update for sufficiently small \(\eta>0\). The conflict-case proof uses \(b^\top g=0\) to infer preservation of the collective objective.
analysis: At \((0,0)\), take bounded \(1\)-smooth objectives \(I(x,y)=\sin x+\sin y\) and \(C(x,y)=1-\sin x+\cos y\). Their gradients are \((1,1)\) and \((-1,0)\); conflict projection leaves direction \((0,1)\), orthogonal to \(\nabla C\). Nevertheless \(C(0,\eta)=1+\cos\eta<2=C(0,0)\) for every sufficiently small \(\eta>0\). A zero directional derivative does not ensure a nonnegative finite-step change.
result: The theorem's finite-step protection is false under its smoothness assumptions. The example leaves observed empirical gains unadjudicated.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: The existing direction supports first-order protection only: smoothness gives \(C(\theta+\eta g)-C(\theta)\geq-L\eta^2\|g\|^2/2\). A separate proposed common-ascent modification applies only to noncollinear conflicting gradients: for \(q=a^\top b<0\), let \(h=a-qb/\|b\|^2\), \(m=\|h\|^2>0\), and \(d=h+mb/[2(-q)]\). Then \(a^\top d=m/2>0\), \(b^\top d>0\); a sufficiently small step improves both fixed-agent objectives. This changes the algorithm and does not establish fairness convergence or simultaneous-agent improvement.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Recurrent conflicts can leave a nonzero value gap forever
problems.source_location: Theorem 3.2, PDF p. 5; Theorem B.5, PDF p. 16.
claim: Paraphrase: Theorem 3.2, p. 5, and Theorem B.5, p. 16, assume \(L\)-smooth values, \(\delta_t=V_{\rm ind}(\theta_t)-V_{\rm col}(\theta_t)\), positive steps satisfying
\[\eta_t\leq|\delta_t|/L,\qquad \sum_t\eta_t=\infty,\qquad \sum_t\eta_t^2<\infty,\]
analysis: Let \(I(\theta)=\sin\theta\), \(C(\theta)=1-\sin\theta\), and \(\theta_0=0\). Their opposing gradients \(1,-1\) project to zero, so every iterate remains zero and the value gap stays \(-1\). Steps \(\eta_t=1/(t+1)\) satisfy the upper bound, divergent sum and square-summable condition with \(L=1\). Conflict recurs forever without progress toward equal values.
result: The universal fairness-convergence conclusion requires a nondegeneracy or progress assumption absent from the stated theorem.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

problems.title: Local guarantees do not imply individual improvement under simultaneous multi-agent updates
problems.source_location: Paragraph following Theorem 3.1 and Section 3.1 single-agent parameters, PDF p. 5.
claim: The paragraph immediately after Theorem 3.1, p. 5, extends the single-agent result to all agents when all use FCGrad. The mathematical objects in Section 3.1 are gradients with respect to the parameters of one agent.
analysis: Take returns \(R_1=\sin\theta_1-3\sin\theta_2\) and \(R_2=3\sin\theta_1+4\sin\theta_2\), with collective return \((R_1+R_2)/2\). At zero, with the allowed mixing weight \(\beta=1/2\), the nonconflict FCGrad directions are \(1.5\) and \(2.25\). Each own-coordinate update improves its local objectives, but their simultaneous effect on \(R_1\) has derivative \(1.5-3(2.25)=-5.25\). The single-agent argument leaves these cross-agent terms uncontrolled.
result: The stated simultaneous-update extension does not follow and fails on this bounded smooth game. A separate multi-agent guarantee would need additional assumptions.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

problems.title: Enlarging the intervention set can reduce MACE, invalidating the unrestricted nonnegativity theorem
problems.source_location: Section 3.2, Lemma 1 and Theorem 2, PDF p. 5; proof, PDF p. 6; Appendix A.1, Lemma 2, PDF p. 13.
claim: Paraphrase of the complete relevant claims: Appendix A.1, Lemma 2 (p. 13), asserts that \(A\subseteq B\) implies \(m(A)\leq m(B)\). Section 3.2, Lemma 1 (p. 5), asserts monotonicity of \(r\) on the redundancy order. Theorem 2 (p. 5; proof on p. 6) then asserts \(C(\alpha;Y)\geq0\) for all antichains. No assumption of independent source variables or monotonicity of the actual interventional response ranges is attached to these claims. The paper explicitly discusses correlated dynamical contexts in Section 4.2.
analysis: Let \(A,H\) be independent fair bits, \(E\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/4)\) independent, \(B=H\oplus E\), \(C=H\), and \(Y=A\oplus B\oplus C\). All observable source assignments have positive probability and no source causes another. Under \(\operatorname{do}(A)\), \(Y=A\oplus E\), giving \(\operatorname{MACE}(A)=1/2\). Under \(\operatorname{do}(A,B)\), \(C\) remains fair and \(Y\) is fair for every imposed assignment, giving \(\operatorname{MACE}(AB)=0\).

Adding interventions replaces mechanisms; the resulting response distributions need not contain those of the smaller intervention family. The decrease contradicts unrestricted intervention monotonicity, and the stated inversion produces a negative partial contribution \(-1/2\). Correlated contexts are permitted by the source, so independence cannot be silently added to remove the example.

For an explicit two-source decomposition, choose analyzed sources \(\{A,B\}\) while \(C\) remains background. Then \(m(A)=1/2\), \(m(B)=0\), \(m(AB)=0\) and the minimum redundancy is \(0\). Möbius reconstruction gives the joint-only atom \(m(AB)-\max\{m(A),m(B)\}=-1/2\). Every source assignment is supported, so this does not rely on unspecified off-support responses.
result: The unrestricted monotonicity and universal nonnegativity claims are false. The decomposition can still be studied with an explicit monotonicity assumption or a separately defined envelope; those changes alter its scope or meaning.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: State and justify a monotonicity assumption for the intervention-effect set function, or define a monotone-envelope variant and disclose its changed scientific meaning. Neither is a replacement proof of the unrestricted original claim.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: The reported finite two-dimensional congestion problem is regularized in code but singular in the mathematical definition
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v3, Appendix F.4, PDF p. 23; current author parametric_pushforward/obstacles.py, congestion_cost.
claim: Appendix F.4, PDF p. 30, defines
\[\mathcal C(\rho)= \int_{\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d} \frac{2}{|x-y|^2}\rho(x)\rho(y)\,dx\,dy. \]
analysis: In two dimensions, a smooth density positive near a point makes the near-diagonal contribution of \(|x-y|^{-2}\) proportional to \(\int_0^\epsilon r^{-1}\,dr=+\infty\). Removing exact empirical self-pairs does not remove this population singularity. The implementation uses denominator \(|x-y|^2+1\), a bounded regularized functional, so its finite numerics do not evaluate the literal displayed objective.

problems.title: Absolute continuity alone does not justify the diffeomorphic static formulation
problems.source_location: Section 2.1, PDF p. 3; Section 3.1 and Theorem 1, PDF p. 5 (diffeomorphic endpoint maps).
claim: Section 2.1, PDF p. 3, restricts the distributions to Lebesgue-dominated densities. The introduction, p. 1, describes a continuous velocity field. Section 3.1, p. 5, defines the static endpoint maps to be orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms and infers that this set is nonempty from the existence of endpoint densities. Theorem 1 then equates the dynamic problem (6) with the diffeomorphic static problem (11).

Appendix B, latest arXiv v3 PDF pp. 14–15, starts the forward direction by treating a dynamic local minimizer as a \(C^1\) diffeomorphic flow. Absolute continuity of the endpoint measures and continuity of the velocity do not establish this flow regularity.
analysis: Starting from uniform density on \([-1,1]\), continuous velocity \(v(x)=2\operatorname{sign}(x)\sqrt{|x|}\) sends nonzero particles to \(\operatorname{sign}(x)(\sqrt{|x|}+t)^2\). At positive time the endpoint density has two separated support components and finite action. A global diffeomorphism maps the initial connected support to a connected set, so no such diffeomorphism matches that endpoint. The example belongs to the broad weak continuity-equation class, while stronger continuously differentiable flow assumptions exclude it.
result: Endpoint absolute continuity and continuous velocity do not establish the claimed unrestricted diffeomorphic admissibility/equivalence. Matching stronger flow regularity changes the problem scope and must be explicit.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

problems.title: Appendix A’s optimality equations need correction, while fixed-endpoint minimizer equivalence can be retained
problems.source_location: Latest arXiv v3, Section 2.2, PDF p. 4; Appendix A, optimization problems (17)–(18) and displayed KKT equations, PDF p. 14.
claim: Section 2.2, PDF p. 4, and Appendix A, Eqs. (17)–(18), latest arXiv v3 PDF p. 14, relate a deterministic continuity-equation action with Fisher information to stochastic control with diffusion coefficient \(\sigma^2/2\), using \(\Phi=S+(\sigma^2/2)\log\rho\).
analysis: With \(v=\nabla S\) and positive potential action, the variational Hamilton–Jacobi equation has the opposite displayed signs for the potential/Fisher terms; the stochastic multiplier equation also requires its diffusion Laplacian. However, setting \(a=\sigma^2/2\) and \(u=v+a\nabla\log\rho\) changes the integrated action only by a fixed endpoint-entropy term under the stated regularity and boundary conditions. Thus the appendix equations need correction while the fixed-endpoint minimizer correspondence can survive.
result: The local optimality-equation derivation needs correction. The entropy-boundary argument preserves fixed-endpoint minimizers under its regularity and boundary restrictions.

problems.title: AwA2 and FishNet evaluate the classifier with training-mode dropout active

claim: Section 5.1, PDF p. 6, and Appendix H, pp. 28–29, evaluate frozen visual features with task classifiers. The AwA2 and FishNet scripts construct a head with a hidden width of \(512\), a dropout probability of \(0.5\), and an output layer for the task labels.

problems.title: The theoretical quadratic proxy needs an additional confidence assumption and a controlled approximation
problems.source_location: Theorem 5.1, PDF p. 8; Appendix C, PDF pp. 22–23.
claim: Theorem 5.1, PDF p. 8, assumes nearly orthogonal species prototypes and presents a quadratic expression governing the residual \(\delta=z-\mu_s\). Appendix C, pp. 22–23, expands (R2), then additionally supposes that the true-species softmax weight is close to one, replaces the weighted prototype mean by \(\mu_s\), and discards the linear term.

The manuscript explicitly describes this latter step as an approximation. The issue is therefore not that an approximate expression was asserted to be an exact equality. The concerns are the mismatch between the main theorem’s hypotheses and the extra confidence assumption, and the lack of an error regime supporting the approximation.
analysis: Let \(m=\sum_k w_k\mu_k\) be the softmax-weighted prototype mean at the expansion point. The Taylor linear term is \((m-\mu_s)^\top\delta/\tau\), and the quadratic covariance is \(\sum_k w_k\mu_k\mu_k^\top-mm^\top\). Nearly orthogonal prototypes alone do not make the true-species weight close to one. Replacing \(mm^\top\) by \(\mu_s\mu_s^\top\) can lose positive semidefiniteness. Since the appendix explicitly calls this an approximation, the finding is missing confidence/error control, not an assertion that the authors claimed an exact identity.
result: This is a supported local finding within the stated source/formulation scope. Its effect on the paper's aggregate experimental results remains unmeasured.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Retain the complete Taylor terms or state an explicit high-confidence approximation regime and its error bound. This does not revalidate full-model performance.

problems.title: Even-width pooling can duplicate a token instead of deleting only
problems.source_location: Sections 3.1–3.2, Eq. (1), PDF p. 4; Appendix D, PDF p. 23 (pooling defaults).
claim: Paraphrase. Section 3.1 defines compression by dropping tokens, and Section 3.2 constructs the compressed prompt from retained tokens in their original order p. 4, Equation 1. The output is therefore intended to be a subsequence of original positions. Appendix D sets average pooling with kernel width \(32\), using observation windows \(16\) for Llama and \(4\) for Phi p. 23.

The active implementation is standard_dis_index in my_baseline/GemFilter/gem_filter_utils.py, lines 92–131. It is called by find_context, which passes the returned indices to the model layer. get_layer_context in my_utils/my_generation.py, lines 9–20, sorts and gathers those indices, then appends the last observation window.
analysis: Stride-one symmetric pooling of \(M\) prefix scores with width \(r\) produces \(M+2\lfloor r/2\rfloor-r+1\) outputs. For even \(r=32\), this is \(M+1\). The extra index \(M\) already belongs to the original suffix. If selected by top-k and then followed by the appended suffix, it occurs twice, so the result is not a deletion-only subsequence.

An explicit valid indexing fixture has \(N=80\), suffix window \(W=16\), prefix length \(M=64\), target budget \(k=48\) and pool width \(r=32\). Use one-dimensional unit queries, with prefix keys zero except key \(63\) equal to \(20\). Its dominant positive attention score contributes to every pooled position from \(48\) through \(64\). All these \(17\) positions belong to the top \(32\), so the out-of-prefix index \(64\) is selected and then appended again with suffix \(64,\ldots,79\). No author routine was executed in this reassessment.
result: This is a supported local finding within the stated source/formulation scope. Its effect on the paper's aggregate experimental results remains unmeasured.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Before top-k selection, restrict the pooled scores to the original prefix length \(M=N-W\). The selected prefix indices then lie in \(\{0,\ldots,M-1\}\), disjoint from the appended suffix \(\{M,\ldots,N-1\}\); sorting gives exactly \(k\) distinct original positions for the valid budget \(W\leq k\leq N\). This repairs the indexing invariant, not benchmark accuracy.
A local correction or qualification is proposed where specified; author adoption is not established.

problems.title: Released NMI timing double-counts prefill and mislabels per-token time
problems.source_location: Section 5.1, PDF pp. 8–9 (EMI); Appendix F, PDF p. 24 (NMI); released my_utils/my_generation.py, lines 147–185 and 226–247.
claim: Appendix F reports separate prefill and decode-per-token speed ratios for NMI, while Section 5.1 has a distinct EMI compression-time comparison pp. 8–9, 24. The following defect is in the released NMI implementation, not a direct reconstruction of the published timing table.

eval/LongBench/pred.py calls my_greedy_generate_config for the compressed-prompt path and stores its returned times fields alongside predictions. Other native-model paths call my_greedy_generate_standard_time. The relevant functions are in my_utils/my_generation.py, lines 147–185 and \(226\)–247.
analysis: Write selection, compressed-prefill and decode intervals as \(C,P,D\). The released latency sums \(C+2P+D\), although the main elapsed interval is \(C+P+D\). Its per-token field is \((P+D)/G\), including prefill, and its time-to-first-token adds a separate post-response generation probe. Those labels do not partition the declared operation. The published timing-table incidence is unestablished.
result: This is a supported local finding within the stated source/formulation scope. Its effect on the paper's aggregate experimental results remains unmeasured.
assumptions: The finding is restricted to the identified paper version and identified released component; published experiment provenance is not inferred from public code alone.

repair.heading: Proposed correction
paragraphs: Use the main elapsed interval for latency and measure the actual first and last generated-token events. With start \(t_0\), first token \(t_F\), last token \(t_L\) and \(G>1\), define TTFT as \(t_F-t_0\) and TPOT as \((t_L-t_F)/(G-1)\), stating synchronization and overhead conventions. The post-first-token mean is undefined for \(G=1\). This does not reconstruct the published speed table.
